units.la: NCI[?] sunt ferè q. [illegible, ~5 letters] or & viginti, Ge[illegible, ~3 letters] ner[illegible, ~3 letters]e Comes Philippe, ex quo tātum in arte Dialectica praesidium ad juris civilis cognitionem esse animadverti, ut ex eo tempore nunquam ferè desistiterim, quae ad illius artis usum pertinere arbitrabar, privato mihi studio notare atque seponere. Quinetiam omnes ferè Aristotelis de arte illa libros in Latinum fermonem exercendi excolendíque ingenii mei causa converti: quoniam incredibile quoddam illius Philosophi acumen in tradendis artis illius praeceptis mihi perspicere videbar. Cum autem quatuor abhinc annis latron[illegible, ~6 letters]ficio[?] in eruditissimi viri [illegible, ~12 letters] taurei Senatoris [illegible, ~8 letters] bibliothecarii Regii co[illegible, ~3 letters]tudinem incidif[?]fem, otiúmque ex infelicitate publica felicissimum nactus essem, cœpi observationes illas meas cū illo præstanti & singulari viro cōmunicare: quo certè neminē magis vel in Aristotelis libris exercitatu, vel bonis omnibus instructū disciplinis, nostra Gallia, nostra, stra, inquam, cùm in alios cŏplures, tum in illum ingrata Gallia, jampridem vidit. Sic autem ille observationibus istis nostris delectabatur, quinetiā ita libēter quæ nō placebant meo rogatu emēdabat, vt iā tum illarum à me promulgationē[?] exposceret: præsertim propter nouas hominum quorūdam opiniones, q juventute ab Aristotelis præcepit: revocabāt: quorū ille se rationibus atque institutis infestissimū semper præbuit. Post vero intermissis ciuilibus latrociniis cùm illas easdem obseruationes meas Lutetiam ad exercitatissimos Dialecticos emēdandi, siquid vellet, caussa misissem, eásque ipsis mirificè probari intellexissem : tandem consilium cepi, quicquid istud erat, in vulgus edere : partim ut si iuuentuti prodesse posset, utilitate hanc illi ætati nō inuiderem: cuius me studiorum adiutore atque administrum Deus constituit: partim etiam quòd multas meas lucubrationes in illis latrociniis ac turbulentis tempestatibus, crebrisq; fortunarum mearū[?] naufragiis, & binis bibliothecæ meæ direptionibus, magno cum animi mei luctu ac mœrore perdidi. verebarq; ne posthac idem fortasse (ut sunt humana) in his Dialecticis nostris lucubrationibus, ceterisque aduersariis & scriptionibus nostris accideret. quod tamen Deus omen omẽ in latronum caput ac perniciem cōuertat. Eò accedebat nostra huius Academia noua ratio: in qua (etsi ex illis nostris Dialecticis partim Montaurei consilio, partim aliorum permultorum suasu exempla è Iure nostro depromta, ne alios studiosos deterreret, magna ex parte sustuli) cupiebam legum nostrarum candidatis gustum huius suavissima disciplina prabere, & Seruium illis Sulpitium ad imitandū proponere: quem M.Tullius testatur Iurisprudentia principatum huius unius artis prasidio adeptum fuisse: & cùm aliis Iurisconsultis iuris usum tribuat, illi uni artem concedit. qua laude haud
units.tr: It is now nearly twenty-five years, most noble Count Philip, since I first perceived that dialectic offers no small help to the study of civil law. From that time onward I have almost never ceased to note down privately, and to set apart, whatever I judged pertinent to the use of that art. Moreover, I have translated almost all of Aristotle's books on that art into Latin, to exercise and sharpen my own talent, since I seemed to myself to discern in that philosopher an incredible acuteness in setting out the precepts of the art. Then, four years ago, when I had fallen into the acquaintance of a most learned man, the Senator of Montaurus [...] and royal librarian [...], and had gained a most fortunate leisure from the public misfortune, I began to share those observations of mine with that outstanding and singular man. No one in our France, nor in ungrateful France itself, had long seen him more practised in Aristotle's books or better furnished with all sound learning, both among many others and in particular. He took such delight in these observations of ours, and so willingly corrected at my request what did not please him, that even then he asked me to publish them. This was especially because of the new opinions of certain men, which recalled the young to the precepts of Aristotle, and against which he had always shown himself most hostile, both in his arguments and in his methods. Afterwards, when the civil brigandage had ceased, I sent those same observations of mine to Paris, to the most practised dialecticians, so that they might correct whatever needed it. When I learned that they were greatly approved by them, I finally resolved to put out to the public whatever this was. Partly I wished that, if it could be of use to the young, I should not begrudge them this advantage, since God has made me a helper and servant of their studies. Partly too it was because in those brigandages and turbulent storms, through the repeated shipwrecks of my fortunes and the two plunderings of my library, I lost many of my writings to my great grief and sorrow. I feared that the same might perhaps happen again, as human affairs go, to these dialectical labours of ours and to my other writings. May God, however, turn this omen against the head and ruin of the brigands. To this was added the new plan of our Academy, in which (although I had removed from those dialectical works of ours, for the most part, the examples taken from our law, partly on the advice of Montaurus and partly at the urging of very many others, so as not to deter other students) I wished to offer the candidates of our laws a taste of this most pleasant discipline, and to set before them Servius Sulpicius for imitation. Of him Marcus Tullius bears witness that he attained the leading place in jurisprudence by the aid of this one art alone; and while he grants the practice of law to other jurists, he grants the art to him alone. With this praise [...]

units.la: scio an alia tribui Iurisconsulto maior possit. nam ceteri, quid de quaque re iuris sit, & (vt Aristoteles loquitur) τὸ ὅτι vsu tàtùm & tractatione cognoscunt: hic etiam qua de caussa quidꝙ iuris sit : hoc est (vt idem loquitur) τὸ διότι animaduertit: siquidem Ars est, (vt idem luculenter definit) rei cuiusque per suas caussas cognitio, quæ aliter se habere nō possunt. Etenim (vt ex doctissimi viri Matthæi Delii præceptis atque sermonibus eruditissimis iampridem cognouisti) à Dialecticis certa quadã veri falsiq; in omnibus disputationibus cognoscendi ratio animaduersa est. Idem rem vniuersam in partes distribuunt[?], latentes explicat definiedo, obscuras explanant interpretando, ambiguas primum vident, deinde distinguunt, tum quod cuique consentaneum sit, quid repugnans animadvertunt. Qua tibi omnia, Generosissime Comes, nota (ut dixi) & perspecta esse confido: neque ullam esse artem arbitror dignam adolescentis liberaliter educati studio, quam non a pueritia degustaris: cui laudi tantum tribuo, ut ei ne nobilitatem quidem generis vestri, aut vetustatem, aut potentiam, anteponam. Sed cum omnes animi, atque ingenii tui dotes sunt eximia, tum vero mores illi aurei (ut illud Poeta verbum vsurpem) tum illa comitas, facilitas, humanitas ad quā te lectissimus vir Paulus à Velsperg suo exemplo à pueritia informauit: cuiufque nuper nobis specimē cùm hīc apud nos esses, edidisti, vehementer me ad dignitatem tuā amandam atque obseruandam incitauit: vt etiam cùm huic libro Patronus, scriptorum omnium consue etudine, quærendus esset, primus mihi cuius illum auctoritati ac patrocinio commendarem, in mentem venires: partim vt splen didissimi nominis tui præsidio tutior atque ornatior in manus hominum veniret: partim etiam vt aliquod iudicii mei de tuarum virtutum indole testimonii extaret:quam indolem Deum Opt. Maximum oro, ut ad frugem & maturitatem perducat: teq;, Generosissime Comes, ita benevolentia sua complectatur, ut te quā primum inter summos Germania proceres florentem, beatum, atque illustrem videamus.
units.tr: I know not whether any greater praise can be given to a jurist than this. For the others know what is right in each matter of law, and (as Aristotle puts it) the "that" [τὸ ὅτι] only, through practice and handling; but he also notices the reason why a thing is law, that is (as the same author puts it) the "why" [τὸ διότι]. For art is, as the same author clearly defines it, knowledge of each thing through its causes, which cannot be otherwise. Indeed, as you have long since learned from the precepts and most learned discourses of the very learned man Matthaeus Delius, the Dialecticians have observed a certain method of knowing truth and falsehood in all disputations. They divide the whole matter into its parts, explain what is hidden by defining, clarify what is obscure by interpreting, first see what is ambiguous and then distinguish it, and then note what is consistent with each thing and what is contradictory. I am confident that you, most noble Count, know all these things (as I have said) and understand them well, and I think there is no art worthy of the study of a liberally educated young man that you have not tasted from boyhood. I give such praise to this art that I would not put before it even the nobility of your family, its antiquity, or its power. But although all the gifts of your mind and talent are outstanding, still more so are those golden manners (to use the poet's phrase), and that courtesy, affability and humanity, to which the most distinguished man Paul of Welsperg has trained you from boyhood by his own example; and when you were here with us, you gave a sample of these qualities, which greatly moved me to love and respect your dignity. So when, according to the custom of all writers, a patron had to be sought for this book, you came to my mind first, and I resolved to commend it to your authority and protection, partly so that it might come into people's hands safer and more adorned under the shelter of your most splendid name, and partly so that there might be some testimony of my judgment on the character of your virtues. I pray to God, the Best and Greatest, to bring that character to fruition and maturity, and to embrace you, most noble Count, with such goodwill that we may soon see you flourishing, happy and illustrious among the foremost nobles of Germany.

Galliarum Regis priuilegio sancitum est, nequis Typographus imprimere, neu quis bibliopola diuendere hos Franc.Hotomani Iurisc. quatuor de Institutione Dialectica libros audeat ante decennium, absque eiusdem Franc.Hotomani consensu. Qui secus faxit, multa illi esto confiscationis librorum. Datum Ambosiæ VI. Ianuarij, Anno à Christo nato MDLXXII.
units.tr: By the privilege of Charles IX, King of the French, it has been decreed that no printer shall dare to print, and no bookseller to sell, these four books of Franc. Hotoman, jurisconsult, on the Institution of Dialectic, for ten years without the consent of Franc. Hotoman himself. Whoever acts otherwise shall be liable to a heavy penalty of confiscation of the books. Given at Amboise, 6 January, in the year of Christ's birth 1572.

units.la: Coignet.
units.tr: Coignet.

units.la: FRANC. HOTOMANI IVRISC. INSTITVTIO- NIS DIALECTICÆ LIBER PRIMVS.
units.tr: Franciscus Hotomanus, Jurisconsult: The First Book of the Institution of Dialectic

units.la: Dialectica & Logica definitio. CAP. I.
units.tr: Definition of Dialectic and Logic. Chapter I.

units.la: QVID est Dialectica? Est ars, quæ ex cuiusq; rei & verbi afsectione diuidédi, definiendi, & argumentandi ratione commõstrat: quæ eadem & Logica vulgò nominatur.
units.tr: What is Dialectic? It is the art that teaches, from the relation (affectio) of each thing and word, the method of dividing, defining and arguing. This same art is commonly called Logic.

units.la: Quid est Rei & verbi affectio? Est ratio, quam quæque res & dictio habet ad alteram. Vt Homo est species animalis: Membrum est pars corporis. Græci λόγον appellant. Itaque commodius Rationem appellare possemus. Sed vitandæ ambiguitatis caussa nomen Assectionis delegimus: quo eodé Cicero & in Topicis & in Partitionibus hac eadem in re est usus. Rationis autem verbum à Mathematicis sumptum est, qui λόγον definiunt duarum eiusdem generis quantitatum comparationem. Interpretes Proportione Latinè nominárunt: quidam Habitudinem: nonnulli Habitū: qui commodius, Respectū. Barbari fortasse Correspondentiam appellarent.
units.tr: What is the affectio of a thing and a word? It is the relation (ratio) that each thing and expression has to another. Man is a species of animal; a limb is a part of the body. The Greeks call this logos, so we might more conveniently call it "ratio." But to avoid ambiguity we have chosen the word affectio, which Cicero also used in the same sense in both the Topics and the Partitions. The word ratio, however, is taken from the mathematicians, who define logos as the comparison of two quantities of the same kind. Translators have rendered it in Latin as proportio; some as habitudo; some as habitus, though respectus would be more suitable. Barbarians might perhaps call it correspondentia.

units.la: Quænā illius λόγου, sive respectus vis ac facultas est? Declarat videlicet, quænam rei cuiusque, aut dictionis cum altera ratio fit: quemadmodum inuicem affectæ sint: quomodo se inter se habeant, qualis inter ipsas comparatio atque affectio fit. veluti, sintne pares, vt in quantitatibus duo cubiti, & duo binaririj: an impares, vt cubitus cum pede, & quaternarius cum binario collatus. Nam res omnis & dictio quæ in Dialecticam disputationem cadit, iccirco cum altera comparatur, vt quemadmodum inter se affectæ sint, id est, sintne verbi gratia, pars an totum, genus an species, consentaneæ an dissentaneæ, eædem an diuersæ, congruentes an contrariæ: intelligatur.
units.tr: What is the power and function of that logos, or respectus? It shows, namely, what relation each thing or expression bears to another: how they are affected towards one another, how they stand in relation to each other, and what kind of comparison and affection exists between them. For example, whether they are equal, as two cubits and two twos in quantities, or unequal, as a cubit compared with a foot, or four compared with two. For every thing and expression that falls under dialectical discussion is compared with another so that it may be understood how they are affected towards each other: whether, for instance, they are part or whole, genus or species, consistent or inconsistent, the same or different, agreeing or opposed.

units.la: Cur in definitione addidisti Et verbi: cùm verborum ars vel Grammaticæ, vel Rhetoricæ propria esse videatur? Quia nihil ambigi potest (ait Cicero) in quo non aut res controversiam faciat, aut verbum. Et alio loco: Cùm omnis controversia aut de re soleat, aut de nomine esse, vtraque earum nascitur, si aut res ignoratur, aut erratur in nomine. In dictionibus igitur æquè atque in rebus, Dialectica versatur, τυγχάνει γάρ [?] (vt Chrysippus, auctore Laertio, dicebat) περὶ σημαινόμενα [?]. Idque eo magis, quia etiam si de-rebus nudis instituta esset disputatio, tamen verbis, quasi notis, vti cogeremur, quemadmodum ratiocinatores calculis. Hac enim similitudine Ariftoteles vtitur.
units.tr: Why did you add "and of the word" to the definition, since the art of words seems to belong to grammar or rhetoric? Because, as Cicero says, nothing can be in doubt in which either the thing or the word causes the controversy. And in another place: since every controversy usually concerns either a thing or a name, both kinds arise if either the thing is unknown or there is an error about the name. Dialectic therefore deals with words as well as with things, for (as Chrysippus, according to Laertius, used to say) it is concerned with things signified [τυγχάνει γάρ ... περὶ σημαινόμενα]. And this all the more so because, even if the discussion were conducted about bare things, we would still be obliged to use words, as signs, just as reckoners use counters. Aristotle uses this very comparison.

units.la: Vnde Dialectica & Logica dictæ sunt? Vtranque à sermone, siue oratione dictam apparet. sed illa proprie ab eo genere sermonis, qui cum altero interrogando & respondendo commiscetur. Fictum enim verbum est ἀπὸ τὸ διαλέγεσθαι [?] : quod est, verba cum altero commutare, colloqui, disputare, sermocinari, fermones cædere. Nam cùm Philofophorū confuetudo hæc effet, vt de rebus ad artes suas pertinentibus sæpe inter se commentarentur, eruditas illas collocutiones διαλόγους [?] (vt idē Laertius in Platone scribit) appellarunt: earúmque habendarum artem, Dialecticam. Qua de caussa eandem Laertius eodem loco definit artem sermonis, per quam ex eorum quibuscum sermo est interrogatione & refpofione, aliquid vel confirmatur, vel refellitur. Quod cùm ita fit, difficile dictu est, Dialectice nomen non eius sermonis esse proprium, qui in Dialogis habetur: cùm perpetua non continuatur oratio, sed in rebus singulis insistitur, & intelligitur quid quisque concedat, aut abnuat: vt ex concessis disputatio concludatur.
units.tr: Whence are Dialectic and Logic named? Both are clearly named from speech or discourse, but Dialectic properly from that kind of speech which is mixed with another by questioning and answering. For the word is a coinage from "to converse" [διαλέγεσθαι], which means to exchange words with another: to talk, dispute, discourse, hold conversation. Since it was the custom of philosophers to debate often among themselves about matters belonging to their arts, they called those learned conversations dialogues (as Laertius writes of Plato too), and the art of conducting them, Dialectic. For this reason Laertius, in the same place, defines it as the art of discourse by which, through the questioning and answering of those with whom one converses, something is either confirmed or refuted. Given this, it is hard to say that the name Dialectic belongs only to that discourse found in dialogues, since no continuous speech is maintained there; rather one keeps to single points and sees what each person concedes or denies, so that the argument is concluded from what has been granted.

units.la: Et quinam istorum inuenterees laudantur? Laertius eodem loco Platonis inuentum esse scribit, vocabulum Dialecticæ: Logicæ autem nomen Ariftoteli tribuitur. Vtrāque autem Cicero differendi rationem multis locis Latinè interpretatur: id est, (vt Graeci dicunt) [illegible, ~24 letters]. Sic enim, eodem auctore Laertio, Stoici definiebãt. Ex quo intelligi potest, cùm & Græcorum & Latinorũ consuetudine nihil quicquam inter Dialecticæ & Logicæ verbum præter vocis sonum interest, videri tamen Logicæ vocabulum ad eã differendi rationem quæ perpetua oratione constat, & qua hodie plurimum utimur, ac multo magis ad eas disputationes quæ literis mandantur, accommodatum esse. Verùm utcunque sit, nos eam Dialecticæ definitionem, quæ ad nostri temporis usum & consuetudinem accommodata videbatur, delegimus.
units.tr: And which of these inventors are praised? Laertius, in the same place, writes that the word Dialectic was invented by Plato, while the name Logic is attributed to Aristotle. Cicero renders both in many places into Latin as the method of disputing, which the Greeks call [illegible, ~24 letters]. For so, on the same authority of Laertius, did the Stoics define it. From this it can be understood that, although in the usage of both Greeks and Latins there is no difference between the words Dialectic and Logic beyond the sound, the word Logic seems better suited to that method of reasoning which consists in continuous discourse, and which we use most today, and much more to those disputations that are committed to writing. However that may be, we have chosen the definition of Dialectic that seemed adapted to the use and custom of our own time.

units.la: De materia Dialectica, & quatuor quaestio- num generibus.
units.tr: On the matter of Dialectic, and the four kinds of questions.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: VAE est materia Dialecticae? Dialectica nullum habet certum ac proprium materiae genus, in quo solo versetur: eoque a ceteris artibus fere omnibus discrepat, quibus sua certa & definita materia subiecta est: ut Arithmeticae, numeri: Geometriae, magnitudines: Musicae, soni: Iurisprudentiae, lites: Medicinae, morbi. At Dialectica per omnes artes ac disciplinas fusa est. Omnibus enim usus sui praestandi munerisque fungendi facultatem praestat: ac plane tanquam instrumentum quoddam est,quo reliquæ artes usum sui hominū generi præstant. Itaque sine illa ceteræ artes omnes non minus mancæ essent, quàm aut Pictura sine penicillo, aut Geometria sine radio, aut Architectura sine securibus atq; asciis, ceterisque cuiusque generis instrumentis. Quod igitur opificibus omnibus instrumentum est, id eruditis disputationibus est Dialectica.
units.tr: What is the matter of Dialectic? Dialectic has no certain and proper kind of matter in which alone it is occupied; and in this it differs from almost all the other arts, each of which has its own fixed and defined subject matter: arithmetic has numbers, geometry magnitudes, music sounds, jurisprudence lawsuits, medicine diseases. But Dialectic is spread through all the arts and disciplines. For it offers its service and its function to all of them, and it is quite like an instrument by which the other arts render their use to the human race. Thus without it all the other arts would be no less maimed than painting without the brush, geometry without the ruler, or architecture without axes, adzes and the other tools of every kind. Therefore what is an instrument to all craftsmen, that Dialectic is to learned disputations.

units.la: Quænam in singulis artibus materia est, in qua instrumentum istud Dialecticæ adhibetur, atque, ut ita dicam, operatur? Genus omne quæstionis: hoc est, quæcunque in disputationem & humani ingenij disquisitionem cadere possunt. Est autem Quæstio (ut Cicero definit) cognitionis appetitio.
units.tr: What, in each of the arts, is the matter in which this instrument of Dialectic is applied and, so to speak, goes to work? The whole genus of question: that is, whatever can fall into disputation and the inquiry of the human mind. Now a question (as Cicero defines it) is the desire for knowledge.

units.la: Quotuplex est quæstio? Quadruplex: An sit, quid sit, quale sit, & quæ causa sit. Aristoteles enim quatuor illas posuit: εἰ ἔςι, τί ἔςι, τὸ ὅτι, & τὸ διότι: hoc est, An sit, quid sit, an ita sit, & cur ita sit. Quamuis autem multis verbis idem ostendat, quæstionem quid sit, vi ipsa eandem esse cum quæstione quæ causa sit: quia nosse quid sit, & quæ causa sit, vi ipsa idem est: tamen perspicuitatis causa, nequid confundatur, satius visum est, utranque distinguere. Idque eo magis, quia reliquæ omnes à prima vim inter se quodammodo implicatam atque permistam obtinent.
units.tr: How many kinds of question are there? Four: whether it is, what it is, of what sort it is, and what its cause is. For Aristotle laid down these four: whether it is [εἰ ἔςι], what it is [τί ἔςι], the that [τὸ ὅτι], and the why [τὸ διότι]; that is, whether it is, what it is, whether it is so, and why it is so. Although he shows in many words that the question what it is is by its very force the same as the question what its cause is, since to know what a thing is and to know its cause are by their very nature the same, nonetheless, for the sake of clarity, lest anything be confused, it seemed better to distinguish each. And this all the more because all the others have, from the first, a force somehow entangled and mixed together with one another.

units.la: Qualis illa implicatio est? Primùm quia neque quid res sit (ut modò dicebamus) scixi[?] potest, ut non simul, quænam eius causa fit, noscatur. qua de causa definitio (ut scribit Aristoteles) quae docet quid res sit, & causam cur res sit, eadem est. veluti, Quid est defectio Lunae? Est obscuratio Lunae, quae interpositu terrae efficitur. Quamobre deficit Luna? quia lumen eius terrae interpositu obscuratur. denique cui responsum est ad quaestionem quid sit, superuacanea est quaestio, quae illius causa sit.
units.tr: What is that entanglement? First, because what a thing is (as we were just saying) cannot be known without at the same time knowing what its cause is. For this reason the definition (as Aristotle writes) which teaches what a thing is and the cause why the thing is are the same. For example: What is an eclipse of the Moon? It is the obscuring of the Moon, which is brought about by the interposition of the earth. Why does the Moon fail? Because its light is obscured by the interposition of the earth. Finally, once an answer has been given to the question what a thing is, the question of what its cause is becomes superfluous.

units.la: Quaenam altera quaestionum implicatio est? Quia iciri[?] quid res sit, plane & commode non potest, nisi simul an ita sit, hoc est, qualis sit, intelligatur. nam cui respondetur ad quaestionem quid sit, ut ipsa responderi videtur ad quaestionem, an ita sit. ut iam prope superuacanea haec posterior videatur: veluti, Quid est Rhetorica? est ars copiose loquendi. qua responsione illi alteri satisfactum est: Qualis est Rhetorica? vel, An Rhetorica est ars copiose loquendi? qua formula quaestio An ita sit, continetur.
units.tr: What is the other entanglement of the questions? Because what a thing is cannot be plainly and properly understood unless at the same time whether it is so, that is, what sort it is, is understood. For the one to whom an answer is given to the question what it is, has, as it were, been given an answer to the question whether it is so. So that this latter question seems almost superfluous: for example, What is rhetoric? It is the art of speaking copiously. By this answer that other question has been satisfied: What sort of thing is rhetoric? or, Is rhetoric the art of speaking copiously? In which formula the question whether it is so is contained.

units.la: Quid? quaestionis An sit, quaenam natura est? Haec sola vim habet propriam, & praecipuam, neque cum aliis implicata est. nam cui interroganti, verbi gratia, Sūntne Pygmaei, an non? respondetur, Sunt Pygmaei: certe non est superuacanea quaestio, quid sunt, aut an ita sunt, aut cur ita sunt? hoc est, suntne homines, an non: an ita sunt statura bipedali, ut ferunt: & cur ita sunt breues, cur gruibus infesti, cum quibus belligeratur. Quanquam harumduarum postremarum quaestionum formula veteribus proprie dialectica non erat.
units.tr: Again, the question whether a thing is, what sort of nature is it? This alone has its own and principal force, and is not entangled with the others. For to one who asks, for example, Are there Pygmies or not? the answer is, There are Pygmies. Surely it is not superfluous to ask what they are, or whether they are so, or why they are so: that is, whether they are human beings or not; whether they are so of two-foot stature, as they report; and why they are so short, and why hostile to cranes, with which they wage war. Yet the formula of these last two questions was not, strictly speaking, dialectical for the ancients.

units.la: Quid? Ecquamná Dialecticarum quæstionum formulam appellas? Intelligendum est, in illis Philosophorum dialogis, de quibus paulò ante diximus, institutum eorum hoc fuisse, ut quavis quæstione proposita paratos se profiterétur, utram adversarius vellet partem vel defendere, vel evertere. Itaque quæstionis formulam ad illud institutum accommodabant. δεῖ γὰρ δεδόσθαι [?] (inquit Aristoteles) ἐν τῆς ἐρωτήσεως, ἑλέσθαι ὁπότερον βούλεται τῆς ἀντιφάσεως μόνον ἀποφάσθαι [?]. Oportebat (inquit) per interrogationem dari optionem adversario, utram vellet contradictionis partem explicari. veluti, Súntne Cétauri an non? Estne voluptas summum bonum, an non? Súntne expetédi honores, an non? ut quæstionis formula & conceptio anceps esset, atque apta & parata vel Etiam vel Non recipere. quæ solæ (ut Aristoteles & Gellius scribunt) Dialecticarum responsionum erant legitimæ formulæ. Qua de causa quæstionem Dialecticam Aristoteles definit petitionem responsionis, ut alterutra contradictionis pars accipiatur. Simplicem autem interrogationis formulam, veluti, Estne in hominum genere sapientia? cui additum non esset, An non: Propositionem Aristoteles multis locis appellat: eámque inter Quæstionem & Propositionem differentiam constituit.
units.tr: What then? Do you call any formula a dialectical question? It must be understood that in those dialogues of the philosophers, of which we spoke a little earlier, their practice was this: that, whatever question was proposed, they professed themselves ready either to defend or to overturn whichever side the opponent wished. Therefore they framed the form of the question to suit that practice. "For it is necessary," says Aristotle, "that in the question the choice be given, [ἑλέσθαι], which side of the contradiction one wishes to be explained alone." He says that by the question an option must be given to the opponent, which part of the contradiction he wishes to be set forth. For example: Are there Centaurs or not? Is pleasure the highest good or not? Are honours to be sought or not? So that the form and conception of the question is double-edged, and ready to receive either Yes or No. These alone (as Aristotle and Gellius write) were the lawful formulas of dialectical answers. For this reason Aristotle defines the dialectical question as a request for an answer, so that one or other part of the contradiction is taken. A simple form of interrogation, for example, Is there wisdom in the human race? to which nothing has been added, Or not, Aristotle often calls a proposition; and he set up a difference between the question and the proposition.

units.la: Quótnam igitur quæstionum genera constituemus? Quoniam vis artis Dialecticæ per omnia (ut modò diximus) cognitionum genera susa est, neque hoc tempore veteres illas disputandi formulas observamus: quamuis quæstionis concipiendæ formula veterum instituto Dialectica non fit: tamen vim & materiam potius, quàm verborum conceptionem ponderabimus: & quatuor illa siue quæstionum, siue propositionum genera retinebimus; An fit,quid fit,quale fit,& quæ causa fit.
units.tr: What kinds of question, then, shall we establish? Since the force of the art of Dialectic extends (as we have just said) through all kinds of knowledge, and since in our time we do not observe those old formulas of disputing; although the form of conceiving a question is not Dialectic in the practice of the ancients, nevertheless we shall weigh the force and matter rather than the conception of the words; and we shall retain those four kinds, whether of questions or of propositions: whether it is, what it is, of what sort it is, and what its cause is.

units.la: Quoniam superius dixisti Dialecticam versari in rebus & dictionibus, quæro nunquid illæ ad Physicos potius, hæ verò ad Grammaticos pertinent: aut quid inter horum trium studia interest? Physicus res per se, ac seorsim considerat. Dialecticus & Grammaticus rerum & dictionum aptam vel ineptam confecutionem: Id est,earum inter se conuenientiam in oratione, vel discrepantiam. verùm illud inter hos interest, quòd ille insitam earum inter se rationem, habitum, respectum, affectionem: hic verò tantùm accidentia,& popularis sermonis in iis iungendis consuetudinem exquirit.
units.tr: Since you said earlier that Dialectic is concerned with things and words, I ask whether these belong rather to the natural philosophers, and those to the grammarians; or what is the difference between the pursuits of these three? The natural philosopher considers things by themselves and apart. The dialectician and the grammarian consider the fitting or unfitting combination of things and words; that is, their agreement or disagreement with one another in speech. But the difference between these is this: the former seeks out their inherent relation to one another, their habit, respect and affection; while the latter seeks only their accidents and the custom of popular speech in joining them.

units.la: Cedo harum rerum familiare aliquod exemplum. Sumatur illud pene puerile: Physici notio est, qua ex materie confici commodè nauis malus possit. Dialectici, conueniántne hæc inter se ex affectuū[?] ratione, an non: Malus est arbor: Arbor est malus: Malus non est arbor: Arbor non est malus. Affectus autem in eo est,quòd malus frugifera eundem habet respectum ad arborē, quem speciesad genus: malus nauis eundem habet respectum ad nauem, quem pars ad totum: & quod superiora de inferioribus dici possunt, inferiora de superioribus non possunt. Grammatici verò iudicium est, conveniántne hæc inter se ex accidétibus,id est genere, numero,casu: Malus naualis est infructuosus. Malus hortensis est fructuosa. Hic ex sermonis consuetudine iudicandi regulam exquirit: ille ex affectuum ratione: &, ut barbari loquuntur, ex correspondentia.
units.tr: Give me some familiar example of these matters. Let us take that almost childish one: the notion of a physicist is, what a ship's mast can conveniently be made of. For the dialectician: do these agree with one another in respect of their affection, or not? A mast is a tree; a tree is a mast; a mast is not a tree; a tree is not a mast. The affection lies in this: that the fruit-bearing mast has the same relation to the tree as the species to the genus; the ship's mast has the same relation to the ship as the part to the whole; and what can be said of the superior things about the inferior, the inferior cannot be said of the superior. But the judgement of the grammarian is whether these agree with one another in respect of their accidents, that is, gender, number and case: A naval mast is unfruitful. A garden mast is fruitful. Here he seeks the rule of judging from the custom of speech; the other from the reason of affections: and, as the barbarians say, from correspondence.

units.la: De partibus, causis, & fine Dialectica.
units.tr: On the parts, causes, and end of Dialectic.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: UT sunt partes Dialecticæ? Quatuor. Notio affectionum, diuisio, definitio, & argumentatio. Sicenim Cicero Tusc. 5: Differendi ratio & scientia (inquit) quæ per omnes partes sapientiæ manat & funditur, rem definit, genera dispartit, sequentia adiungit, perfecta concludit, vera & falsa diiudicat. Harum autem partium quatuor argumentatio principatum obtinet. superiores enim omnes non modo ei uni seruiunt, eiusque sunt quodammodo ministræ: verumetiam ab ea sola probantur, ac iudicantur.
units.tr: What are the parts of Dialectic? Four: the notion of affections, division, definition, and argument. For thus Cicero says in the Tusculan Disputations, book 5: "The method and science of disputation (he says), which flows and spreads through all parts of wisdom, defines a thing, divides genera, adds consequences, concludes what is complete, and judges true and false." Of these four parts, argument holds the chief place. For the other three not only serve it alone and are in a sense its handmaids, but are also approved and judged by it alone.

units.la: Quibus rebus Dialectica comparatur? Natura,arte & exercitatione. Nam in artifice suturo primü acumen exquiritur ingenij: quod naturæ bonum est: tum artis & doctrinæ perceptio: postremò usus, qui cùm rerum omniū Magister est fummus, tum etiam Magiftrorū omnium præcepta superat.
units.tr: By what means is Dialectic acquired? By nature, art and practice. For in the future artist, first, a keenness of mind is sought, which is a gift of nature; then the grasp of art and doctrine; and finally use, which, while it is the supreme master of all things, also surpasses the precepts of all teachers.

units.la: Estne igitur Dialectica quædam naturalis, quædam artificiosa? Nequaquam: sed eius initia & femina quædam in hominum mentibus natura ingenerauit, quæ cùm præceptis ac disciplina, tum vsu & assiduitate excoluntur: eadémque cùm aliarum artium omniū, tum præcipuè Musicæ ratio est. nam omnibus ànatura rudis quædam canendi facultas data est: ab arte verò, quam naturæ notatio atque animaduersio peperit, certa ratio traditur. non enim ars naturam imitatur tantummodo: verumetiam (vt veteres docuerunt) emendat, confirmat & amplificat, causámque cur quidque vel hoc, vel illo modo fieri debeat, reddit. quod præstare natura non poteft, eáque sola re artifex ab inscio difcernitur.
units.tr: Is there then a kind of natural Dialectic and a kind of artificial Dialectic? By no means. But nature has implanted in human minds certain beginnings and seeds of it, which are cultivated both by precepts and training, and by practice and constant application. And this is also the principle of all the other arts, but especially of Music. For to all people nature has given a certain rough faculty of singing; but from art, which the observation and attention to nature has produced, a fixed method is handed down. For art does not merely imitate nature; it also (as the ancients taught) corrects, strengthens and enlarges it, and gives the reason why each thing ought to be done in this or that way. This nature cannot achieve, and by this alone the artist is distinguished from the unskilled.

units.la: Quis est finis Dialecticæ? Satis constat, nullam in sese artem versari: sed esse aliud artem ipsam, aliud quod propositum fit arti. Itaque cuiusque artis finis extra ipsam artem quærendus est. Vt igitur medicinæ finis propofitus est, valetudo: arti militari, victoria: architecturæ, opus: sic Dialecticæ finis propositus est Demonstratio: id est, veri & falsi diiudica-tio: tio: siue facultas iudicandi, quemadmodum verum à falso internoscatur: quidnam in oratione consentaneum sit, aut dissentaneum; quæ sit apta aut inepta verborum consecutio: & quamobrem ea vel apta vel inepta esse pronuntianda sit.
units.tr: What is the aim of Dialectic? It is well established that no art is concerned with itself; rather, the art itself is one thing, and what is proposed to the art is another. Therefore the end of each art must be sought outside the art itself. Thus, as the proposed end of medicine is health, of the military art victory, and of architecture a building, so the proposed end of Dialectic is demonstration: that is, the judging of true and false, or the faculty of discerning how the true is distinguished from the false, what in a discourse is consistent or inconsistent, which sequence of words is apt or inept, and why it ought to be pronounced apt or inept.

units.la: De Notionibus, quibus rerum & verborum inter se comparationes fiunt.
units.tr: On Notions, by which comparisons of things and words are made among themselves.

units.la: CAP. IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: [?]GESIS, deinceps singulas Dialectice partes eo quo propositum ordine persequamur. Et quoniam superius quid esset affectio, siue λόγος cuiusque rei & dictionis, exposuisti: quæro primùm unde illa affectionum ac respectu scientia nascatur? Non ex sensibus certè, sed ex notionibus. Notionem autē appellamus, insitam à natura animis nostris & antè perceptam cuiusque formæ nō satis explicatam, ideoque enodationis indigentem cognitionem. Sic enim eam variis locis Cicer. definit: atque à Græcis tum ἔννοιαν, tum προλῆψιν appellari scribit. Notitiam quoque idem appellat, in hominis mente informatam & anteceptam, sine qua nec intelligi quicquam, nec quæri, nec disputari potest.
units.tr: Let us now take up the individual parts of Dialectic in the order we have proposed. Since you have already explained above what an affection is, that is, the λόγος of each thing and of each word, I first ask: from what source does our knowledge of these affections and of relations arise? Certainly not from the senses, but from notions. We call a notion a cognition implanted in our minds by nature and grasped beforehand, of the form of each thing, not fully explained, and therefore in need of unfolding. Cicero defines it in this way in various places, and he writes that the Greeks call it both ἔννοια and πρόληψις. He also calls it a notion or conception formed and anticipated in the mind of man, without which nothing can be understood, sought, or disputed.

units.la: Unde notiones illæ nascuntur? Ex iis quas Plato Ideas, hoc est formas & species appellauit: quas tanquam cœlestis animæ particulas, in animis hominum, (quos ex Diuinitate delibatos credidit) insitas putabat: ac proinde ab iis quæ sensibus subiecta sunt avulsas, per fe ac seorsim constare. Alij verò nasci eas putarunt ex imaginibus & simulacris corporum: cùm impulsione oblata extrinsecus, species rerum sic in animis imprimuntur, tanquam imagines in speculis: aut potius quasi annulorum signa in cera. veluti cùm ex Oloris aut Pauonis aspectu imago quædam omnium illiusmodi auium in animo imprimitur, quæ post in memoria ita perpetuò circunfertur, ut ubiuis ea species agnosci possit. Verùm hæc eadem planiusex rei definitione & diuisione intelligentur.
units.tr: Where do these notions come from? From those things which Plato called Ideas, that is, forms and species. He thought they were implanted in the minds of men (whom he believed to be drawn from the divine nature) as particles of a heavenly soul, and therefore that they are separated from the things subject to the senses and stand on their own and apart. Others, however, thought that they arise from the images and likenesses of bodies: when an impression is made from outside, the appearances of things are imprinted on the mind just as images are in mirrors, or rather as the marks of rings are in wax. For example, from the sight of a swan or a peacock an image of all birds of that kind is impressed on the mind, and afterwards is carried about in the memory so constantly that this kind can be recognised anywhere. But these matters will be understood more plainly from the definition and division of the thing.

units.la: - Quid est Res? Quod vel animo & ratione intelligi, vel sensu, qui rationis expers est, percipi potest. Nos illam Intellectam, hanc verò Corporatam appellabimus. Intellectã Plato vere ac proprie esse dicebat, Ideámque appellabat, quæ neque gigneretur, & semper esset uniusmodi, ac ratione & intelligentia contineretur. veluti apud Philosophos, Virtus, sapientia, iustitia: apud Iurisconsultos, Seruitus, usus, usufructus. Corporatam alij οὐσία[?] proprie dici disputarunt, quam Latini modò Natura, ut Varr. & Cic. modò Essentiã, modò Substantiam appellarunt: quæ per se tangi ac videri potest: ut Fundus, Stichus. Atque ut hæc minui controuersia posset, duplicem substantiam induxerunt, primam & secundam.
units.tr: What is a Thing? That which can be grasped either by the mind and reason, or perceived by the sense, which has no share in reason. We shall call the former intellectual and the latter corporeal. Plato said that the intellectual alone is truly and properly being, and he called it Idea: it is that which is neither generated, always remains of one kind, and is contained by reason and understanding. Examples among philosophers are virtue, wisdom, justice; among jurists, servitude, use, usufruct. Others have argued that the corporeal is properly called οὐσία [substance], which the Latins have called now Nature, as Varro and Cicero did, now Essence, now Substance; it is that which can be touched and seen in itself, such as a farm or a slave. And so that this controversy might be lessened, they introduced a twofold substance, the first and the second.

units.la: Quæ est prima Substantia? τὸ ὑφεστηκὸς [?], corpus, quod sensibus subiectum, cerni ac tangi potest: vel quod neque in aliquo inest, neque de aliquo dicitur: sed cùm alia omnia in ipso insunt, tum de ipso dicuntur. Hoc idem Individuum Dialectici appellant: Græci ἄτομον vel καθ᾽ ἕκαςον: vt Plato,Socrates, Stichus, aut Pamphilus: hic homo, hæc nauis, hic fundus, hoc prædium.
units.tr: What is the first Substance? τὸ ὑφεστηκός [that which stands under], a body which is subject to the senses and can be seen and touched; or that which is neither in anything else nor is said of anything else, but while all other things are in it, it itself is said of them. The dialecticians call this the Individual; the Greeks call it ἄτομον or καθ᾽ ἕκαστον: for example Plato, Socrates, Stichus, or Pamphilus; this man, this ship, this farm, this estate.

units.la: Quare dicitur indiuiduum? Quia diuidi in partes corporatas sine interitu non potest. Nam si Totū in partes distrahatur, nulla pars erit Totum, neque Totius nomine appellari poterit. Itaque neque truncus, neque ramus, neque radix arbor dici poterit. Nauem duorum communem si diuidas (inquibat iocans Cascelius Iurisconsultus) neque tu, neq; socius habebitis. Sic Stichus debitus solui ac præstari per partes corporatas sine certissimo interitu nō potest. Et quanuis fundi diuisi partes omnes quantumuis multæ, fundus dicantur, tamen nulla illarum dici poterit fundus ille qui antea fuerat.
units.tr: Why is it called individual? Because it cannot be divided into bodily parts without destruction. For if a whole is pulled apart into parts, no part will be the whole, nor can it be called by the name of the whole. Thus neither a trunk, nor a branch, nor a root can be called a tree. If you divide a ship owned by two, said the jesting jurist Cascellius, neither you nor your partner will have a ship. So too Stichus cannot be paid over and delivered in bodily parts without certain destruction. And although all the parts of a divided farm, however many, are called a farm, yet none of them can be called that farm which was there before.

units.la: Quæ est secunda Substantia? Quæ non sensu illa quidem, sed tamē sensuum opera & ministerio, ac tanquam instrumento, à ratione & intelligentia percipitur: qua de caussa illam Secundæ nomine appellarūt. vt cùm Leone conspecto, imago quædam omnium illius formæ belluarum in mente & memoria ita imprimitur, vt postea Leones vbique omnes agnosci possint. Notiones igitur indiuiduis cohærere putarunt, sicuti rerum obiectarum imagines, oculis, aut speculis inhærent.
units.tr: What is the second Substance? That which is perceived by reason and understanding, not indeed by sense, but by the work and service of the senses, as by an instrument; for this reason they called it the second. For example, when a lion is seen, an image of all beasts of that form is impressed on the mind and memory, so that afterwards all lions can be recognised anywhere. They therefore thought that notions cohere in individuals, just as images of objects cling to eyes or mirrors.

units.la: Expone istud, fi potes, planius. Plato ea demum esse vere ac proprie dicebat, quæ a fensibus remota tantum ratione & animo perciperentur: propterea quod semper vniusmodi effent, neque ortum, neque interitum habe rent: cùm indiuidua infinita, fluxa & caduca effent, orirenturque & occiderent, nec diutius vno & eodem statu essent. Ariftoteles vero nullas putabat esse extrinsecus fubftantias: sed intellectam plurimorum inter fe differentium similitudinem, vel genus, vel speciem appellabat. Primus Ariftoteles (ait Cicero) species labefactauit, quas mirifice[?] Plato fuerat amplexatus, vt in iis diuinum quiddam esse diceret. Ac de vtrisque istiusmodi substantiis, idem Cicero in lib. de Vniuersitate ex Platonis Timæo ita scribit: Quid est quod semper fit (hæc idea est) neque vllum habet ortum: & quod gignatur (hoc indiuiduū est) nec vnquam fit. quorum alterum intelligentia & ratione comprehenditur, quod vnū semper atque idem est: alterum quod affert opinionem per sensus, rationis expers, quod totum opinabile est, id gignitur & interit, nec vnquam esse vere potest?
units.tr: Explain this more plainly, if you can. Plato said that those things are truly and properly what is perceived by reason and mind alone, apart from the senses, because they are always of one kind and have neither origin nor destruction; whereas individuals are infinite, fluid and perishable, and come into being and pass away, and do not remain for long in one and the same state. Aristotle, however, thought there are no substances outside, but called the understood likeness of many things differing among themselves either genus or species. Aristotle first (says Cicero) weakened the species which Plato had wonderfully embraced, so that he said there was something divine in them. And concerning both kinds of substance, Cicero in his book On the Universe, taken from Plato's Timaeus, writes thus: "What is it that always comes to be (this is the idea), has no origin, and what is generated (this is the individual) never truly is? Of these two, the one is grasped by understanding and reason, being always one and the same; the other, which brings opinion through the senses, lacking reason, is wholly a matter of opinion, is generated and perishes, and can never truly be?"

units.la: Vtrius igitur illorum probabilior sententia videtur? Non est humilitatis nostræ tantam inter fummos omnium Philosophos controuersiam disceptare. Magis tamen aliquanto ad notionum nostrarum rationem accommodata Platonis sententia videtur: quippe, cùm satis constet, non omnes notiones ex oblata extrinsecus indiuiduorum corporũ impulsione existere: sed quasdam per se cōstare, neque vel aliunde originem habere, vel alio quàm suo ac proprio fundamento niti. quo in genere sunt intelleãæ resomnes: vt quátitates, & qualitates. veluti, Lógitudo, Latitudo, & Altitudo. Item, Iustitia, Temperantia, Eloquentia. Item, Morbus, Valetudo, Imbecillitas. Quæ si in subiecto aliquo insunt, per se tamen, & tanquam auulsæ & abstractæ considerantur.
units.tr: Which of these two opinions, then, seems more probable? It is not for our lowliness to settle so great a controversy among the highest of all philosophers. Yet Plato's opinion seems somewhat better suited to the account of our notions: since it is quite certain that not all notions arise from the impression made from outside by individual bodies, but that some stand on their own, and derive their origin neither from elsewhere nor rest on any foundation other than their own. In this class are all intellectual things, such as quantities and qualities: length, breadth, and height. Likewise justice, temperance, eloquence. Likewise disease, health, weakness. Although these are in some subject, yet they are considered in themselves, as if drawn away and abstracted.

units.la: Cedo familiare aliquod exemplum. Nos vero etiam è pinguiore Minerua perspicuitatis caussa sumemus. Videsne quam sutores & calceolarij formam calceorum appellent? nimirum lignum oblongum, calcei instar proportione aptum, atque incisum. At iidem formam calcei aliam in mente atque intelligentia impressam atque insignitam habent: quæ una vere proprieque tum Idea, tum Forma & est, & dici debet: ad quam, tanquam pictores ad exemplar suam picturam, ita illi opus suū dirigunt. Forma igitur calcei lignea subiectū est: species in mente insita, auulsa atque abstracta est.
units.tr: Let me give a familiar example. I shall take one from the fuller stores of Minerva, for the sake of clarity. Do you see what the shoemakers and cobblers call the form of a shoe? Surely an oblong piece of wood, fitted and cut to the proportion of a shoe. Yet the same men have another form of the shoe impressed and stamped on their mind and understanding, which alone is truly and properly both Idea and Form, and ought to be called so; and to it, as painters to a model, they direct their work. So the wooden shape of the shoe is the subject; the species implanted in the mind is drawn away and abstracted.

units.la: Quæ est altera rerum diuisio? Secunda rei diuisio, quæ quidem ad Dialecticæ artis rationem atque vsum accommodata fit, similiter bipertita est. Nam aliæ dicūtur, Eædem, quarum scilicet vna eáque angustissima notio est, quamuis nomine fortasse discrepent: vt vestis, & vestimentum: ensis, & gladius: dialectica; & logica: homo & animal rationis particeps. Aliæ diuersæ, quæ non eadem notione continentur, sed alia atque alia intelligentia comprehenduntur. vt Animal, Elementum, Arbor, Sydus. Item, Leo, Aquila, Muræna, Platanus. Sed hæc diuisionem posterius vbi rerum affectiones cognoueris, paulo subtilius explicabimus. Tantùm illud hoc loco intelligendum est, earum rerum quæ sunt eædem, nullam in Dialectica nasci quæstionem posse: propterea quod omnis quæstio Dialectica in rerum affectionibus, comparationibus, & proportionibus versatur, quæ nisi in diuersas & differentes res cadere non possunt.
units.tr: What is the second division of things? The second division of things, which is adapted to the method and use of the art of Dialectic, is likewise twofold. For some are called the same (Eadem), namely those of which there is one and that a very narrow notion, although perhaps they differ in name: such as garment and clothing; sword and blade; dialectic and logic; man and rational animal. Others are different, which are not contained under the same notion, but are comprehended by one understanding after another: such as animal, element, tree, star; likewise lion, eagle, moray, plane-tree. But we shall explain this division more subtly later, when you have learned the affections of things. For the present it must be understood that no question can arise in Dialectic about things which are the same, because every dialectical question is concerned with the affections, comparisons and proportions of things, which can only fall upon things that are diverse and different.

units.la: Quæ est tertia rerum diuisio? Hæc tripartita est. nam aliæ dicuntur esse prius, aliæ posterius, aliæ simul. Prius autem aliquid est, aut tempore, aut ordine, aut non reciprocante cõsecutione essentiæ. His enim tribus modis ad huius institutionis vsum contenti esse possumus. Prius autem ex non reciprocante essentiæ consecutione, ἀφ’ ἧ μὴ ἀντιστρέφει ἢ τῷ ἕπ[?] ἀκολούθησις[?] sic æstimatur: veluti cùm dicimus vnum esse prius duobus, quia si duo sunt, etiã est vnum: at non, si vnùm est, continuò sunt duo. Itéque animal prius equo: quia si equus est, etiam animal sit necesse est. at non ex contrario. Quid sit autem Esse posterius, hoc ipso intelligitur: nam contrariorum eadem scientia est.
units.tr: What is the third division of things? This division is threefold. For some things are said to be prior, others posterior, others simultaneous. Now something is prior either in time, or in order, or by a non-reciprocating consequence of essence. For we can be content with these three ways for the purposes of this introduction. Something is prior by non-reciprocating consequence of essence (ἀφ᾽ ἧς μὴ ἀντιστρέφει ἡ τοῦ ἑπομένου ἀκολούθησις) and is judged in this way: for example, when we say that one is prior to two, because if there are two, then there is also one; but not conversely, if there is one, there are not necessarily two. Likewise animal is prior to horse, because if there is a horse, there must also be an animal; but not the reverse. What it is to be posterior is understood from this itself: for the knowledge of contraries is the same.

units.la: Quot modis simul res esse dicitur? Duobus: tempore, & natura. Tempore, cùm singulorum ortus eodem tempore est: veluti cùm in diuidendo res eodem ex genere & capite diducuntur. vt Belluarum aliæ sunt volatiles, aliæ terrenæ, aliæ aquatiles. Natura autem, cùm in essentiæ consecutione reciprocatio est, quanuis neutrum alteri ortus & essentiæ causam attulerit. vt si duplum sit, etiam est simplum: & si simplum sit, certè est duplum. Si sol lucet, dies est. Si dies est, sol lucet. Atque hæc ἀντιστροφὴ [?], siue reciprocatio, diligenter notanda est: quoniam eius vsus in hac arte longè est maximus.
units.tr: In how many ways are things said to be together? In two: in time and in nature. In time, when the coming into being of each occurs at the same time, as when things are divided within the same genus and category, for example, of beasts, some are flying, some land-dwelling, and some aquatic. In nature, when there is reciprocity in the consequence of being, although neither has supplied the cause of the other's origin or essence, as when, if there is a double, there is also a single, and if there is a single, there is certainly a double. If the sun shines, it is day; if it is day, the sun shines. This conversion (ἀντιστροφή), or reciprocity, must be carefully noted, since its use in this art is by far the greatest.

units.la: Altè verò Dialecticę principia repetis. Sed difficillimū est (vt Plato scribit) in omni conquisitione rationis exordium. Deinceps de dictione differemus. Quid est dictio? Nota qua quæque res significatur. Nam quod Aristoteles σύμβολον [?] dicit, notá Cic. cóuertit: & verba rerum notas definiuit. vt enim forma publica nota est numorum: sic dictiones, nomina, vocabula, & appellationes, rerū notæ sunt. iisque notis similiter in rebus enūtiādis vtimur, quomodo in ratiocinationibus vtimur calculis.
units.tr: You trace the principles of dialectic from far back. But, as Plato writes, the beginning of every inquiry into reason is most difficult. Next we shall discuss the word (dictio). What is a word? A mark by which each thing is signified. For what Aristotle calls a symbol (σύμβολον), Cicero translated as a mark (nota), and he defined words as marks of things. For just as the public stamp is the mark of coins, so words, names, terms and appellations are marks of things. And we use these marks in expressing things in the same way as we use counters in calculations.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: Q[?]VONIAM prius est (vt ait Quintilianus) concipere animo res, quàm enuntiare, prius de rei affectionibus differamus. Sed primùm omnium quotuplex huius doctrinæ de ratione est vsus? Quadruplex. nam primùm mutuam (vt sæpe iam dixi) rerum ac dictionum omnium affectionem ostendit: id est, vel conuenientiam, vel repugnantiam. Deinde materiam diuidendi, definiendi, & argumentandi suppeditat. Qua de causa Peripatetici, cùm ad argumentorum tractationem peruenerunt, quoniam ex iis argumenta depromunt, τόπος[?] illos appellant: Cicero Latinè locos, sedes, fontes nominat. Nos eorum in diuidendo, definiendo, & argumentando vsum atque opportunitatem ostendemus.
units.tr: Since (as Quintilian says) it is first necessary to conceive things in the mind before we state them, let us first discuss the affections of things. But first of all, how many kinds of use does this doctrine have? Four. For first, it shows the mutual affection of things and of all words, that is, either agreement or disagreement (as I have often said already). Second, it supplies the matter for dividing, defining and arguing. For this reason the Peripatetics, when they came to the treatment of arguments, called them topoi, since they draw their arguments from them; Cicero calls them in Latin loci, sedes, or fontes. We shall show the use and usefulness of these in dividing, defining and arguing.

units.la: Quæ est affectionum diuisio? Rerum (vt modò dictum est) aliæ sunt eædem, quæ in dialecticam quæstionem non cadunt: aliæ diuersæ, quarum ab arte dialectica comparatio fit. Earum igitur aliæ consentaneæ sunt, quarum inter se rationes consentiunt: vt in musica numeri, & voces, & modi: itaque ex iis argumenta de éòucnientia[?] sumuntur: aliæ dissentaneæ, quæ inter se discrepant.
units.tr: What is the division of affections? Of things (as has just been said), some are the same, which do not fall into dialectical question; others are different, and the art of dialectic makes a comparison between them. Of these, then, some are consonant, whose relations agree with one another, as in music numbers, voices and modes; and so arguments about agreement are drawn from them. Others are dissonant, which disagree with one another.

units.la: Quot sunt rationes consentaneæ? Quindecim, Genus, Species, Totum, Partes, Cauf-fa, fa, Affectus, Proprium, Relatio, Antecedens, Consequens, Adiunctum, Accidens, Comparatio parium, Comparatio minorum, & Similitudo.
units.tr: How many are the consonant relations? Fifteen: Genus, Species, Whole, Parts, Cause, Effect, Affection, Proper, Relation, Antecedent, Consequent, Adjunct, Accident, Comparison of equals, Comparison of lesser things, and Similarity.

units.la: Quot sunt Rationes diffentanæ? Septem, Adversa, Privantia, Negantia, Repugnantia, Disparia, Comparata ex maioribus; & Dissimilia.
units.tr: How many are the dissonant relations? Seven: Opposites, Privation, Negation, Contrariety, Disparates, Things compared by greater things, and Dissimilars.

units.la: Ecquemnam igitur in iis exponendis ordinem sequemur? Eum nimirum, qui naturæ accómodatus est maximè: ut quo quisque rei propositæ adiunctior est, eum potissimum explicemus: quo remotior est, postremum. Primum igitur de iis dicemus, qui in re ipsa insiti sunt, hoc est de Genere, Specie, Toto & Partibus. Tum deinde de externis: è quibus eos primùm qui consentanei sunt, tum eos qui dissentanei, persequemur. & quoniâ contrarij inter dissentaneos summum locum obtinent, ab iis exordiemur.
units.tr: In what order, then, shall we proceed in setting these out? Surely that order which best fits nature: so that whichever is more closely attached to the thing proposed, we explain first; whichever is more remote, last. First, then, we shall speak of those that are implanted in the thing itself, that is, of Genus, Species, Whole and Parts. Then next we shall pursue the external ones: of these, first those that are consonant, then those that are dissonant. And since contraries hold the highest place among the dissonant, we shall begin with them.

units.la: De Genere, Specie, & Differentia.
units.tr: Of Genus, Species, and Difference.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: QVID est Genus? Notio, quæ sui similes communione quadam, species autem differentes, duas aut plures amplectitur partes: quæ definitio Ciceronis est. Illa autem Aristotelis: γένος ἐςὶ τὸ κοινὸν ἀλε-[?] ἀλλήλων ἢ διαφερόντων τῷ εἴδει ἐν τῷ τι ἔχει κατηγορού-[?] μενον, id est, Genus est, quod de pluribus, specie differentibus, in quæstione quid sint, dicitur. Sic enim conuertendum arbitror,non qv ıD[?] sıT[?]. nisi forte hoc potius interpretemur modo in quæstione quid eorum quidque fit. Ut plura dici ab Aristotele intelligantur ea, quorum aliqua communio, & quasi cognatio est. veluti cum quæritur aceruatim, quid fit homo, quid auis, quid piscis, quid quadrupes: apte de universis semel respondebitur, animal.
units.tr: What is a genus? It is a notion that embraces two or more parts that are like one another through some common bond, while the species are different from one another. That is Cicero's definition. Aristotle's definition is: "Genus is what is common to several things differing in species, being predicated of them in the question 'what is it?'" [γένος ἐστὶ τὸ κοινὸν ἀλλήλων ἢ διαφερόντων τῷ εἴδει ἐν τῷ τί ἐστι κατηγορούμενον]. That is, a genus is what is said of several things that differ in species, when the question is what they are. I think this is the right rendering, unless we prefer to interpret it as: when the question is what each of them is. Then "several things" are understood as those which share some common bond or kinship, as when we ask in a heap what a man is, what a bird is, what a fish is, what a quadruped is, and can rightly answer all of them at once with one word: animal.

units.la: Quæ sunt igitur quæ generis eiusdem dicuntur? Quæ superioris alicuius communione inter se continentur: ac de quibus omnibus vnum respondetur. Nam (ut Zeno apud Laertium definit) γένος ἐστί, πλειόνων συνομοιάτων συλλογισμός[?]. Itaque plures cognati qui sanguinis eiusdem communione inter se cohærent, quam ab vno eodemque capite duxerunt, circo a Græcis appellantur ὁμογενεῖς vel συγγενεῖς: cum alij qui gentis ac stirpis alterius sunt, ἑτερογενεῖς vel ἀλλογενεῖς[?], id est alieni, & extranei nominentur. quocirca plures res de quarum singulis non vnum idemque respondetur, diuersi generis sunt: appellanturque Diuersæ, Disparatæ, Variæ, Differentes, Dissimiles: nullo tamen certo & proprio vocabulo. veluti, Homo, Ignis, Arbor, Lapis, Linea, Candor: de quibus si quæratur, quid eorum quidque fit, responderi vnum atque idem nomen non potest.
units.tr: Which things, then, are said to belong to the same genus? Those which are contained among themselves under some higher common bond, and of which one and the same answer is given. For, as Zeno defines it in Laertius, "genus is a collection of several things alike" [γένος ἐστί, πλειόνων συνομοιάτων συλλογισμός]. Hence those relatives who are bound together by the common bond of one blood, and who descend from one and the same head, are called by the Greeks homogeneis or syngeneis [ὁμογενεῖς, συγγενεῖς]; those who belong to another family and stock are called heterogeneis or allogeneis [ἑτερογενεῖς, ἀλλογενεῖς], that is, strangers and outsiders. Therefore several things of which one and the same name is not given in answer to the question about each individually are of different genera. They are called diverse, disparate, various, different, dissimilar, yet there is no fixed and proper word for them. For example: man, fire, tree, stone, line, whiteness. If one asks what each of these is, one and the same name cannot be given in reply.

units.la: Quid est Species? Notio angustior quæ cum altera pluribus siue aliis generis eiusdem comcōmunione cōtinetur. veluti, Platanus, notio estq; cum Lauro, Piro, Pomo, Quercu, & Ceraso arboris communione comprehenditur. Nonnulli tamen Species etiam appellant notiones angustissimas quarum proprietates in nullum aliud conueniunt: quæ vulgò ἄτομοι, siue indiuidua nominantur. Nam Iurisconsulti ex Stoicorum (vt opinor) sententia Stichum & Pamphilum & certum quoduis aliud corpus Speciem appellât. l.talis,30, l.cùm res, 4.§.1, D.de legat.j.l. in stipulationibus,45, D. de verb. obligat. Genus contrà plerunque appellant, quàm Speciem nominauimus: veluti Fundū, aut Seruum, siue Hominem, cuius notione serui omnes comprehenduntur. Quinetiam Speciem interdum pro parte, Genus pro toto vsurpant. vt cùm in §. lex est, de iur. nat. Plebs à populo eo differre dicitur, quod species à genere. Item Speciem pro re singulari: & Genus, pro Vniuersitate. vt in Regula iuris, Generi per speciem derogatur. veluti si Peculium legatum sit, & vicarius liber esse iussus sit. l.si peculium,10, D.de manu.testam.
units.tr: What is a species? It is a narrower notion, contained under a genus together with other notions of the same genus. For example, the plane tree is a notion which is comprehended under the common genus of tree together with the laurel, the pear, the apple, the oak and the cherry. Some, however, also call the very narrowest notions species, notions whose properties apply to no other thing; these are commonly called atoma, or individuals. For the jurists, following (I think) the opinion of the Stoics, call Stichus, Pamphilus, or any other particular body a species (Dig. 30, l. talis; Dig. 4 §1, l. cum res; Dig. 45, l. in stipulationibus). On the other hand they usually call a genus what we have named a species, as for example "farm", "slave", or "man", under whose notion all slaves are comprehended. Indeed they sometimes use species for part and genus for whole, as when in §lex est, on natural law, the plebs is said to differ from the people as a species differs from a genus. Likewise they use species for a single thing and genus for the universal whole, as in the rule of law: "the general is derogated from by the specific", as when a peculium is bequeathed and a slave is ordered to be freed (Dig., l. si peculium).

units.la: Quid si plures sint eiusmodi notionū gradus? Tū verò ancipiti vti nomine cogemur, & respectu superiorum, Speciem: inferiorum, Genus appellare. hoc Græci solent ὑπαλλήλον nominare, nos interiectum, vel intermedium, vel (vt vulgò) subalternum dicere possumus: cuius rei exemplum vsitatum ex summis & infimis substantiis apponemus.
units.tr: But what if there are several such grades of notion? Then we shall be forced to use the term ambiguously, calling a notion a species with respect to those above it and a genus with respect to those below it. The Greeks are accustomed to call this hyperallelon; we may call it intermediate, or middle, or (as is common) subaltern. We shall set out a customary example of this, drawn from the highest and lowest substances.

units.la: I. Genus summū ab Indivi-duis remotissimum.
units.tr: 1. The highest genus, most remote from individuals.

units.la: 2. Genus intermedium;
units.tr: 2. An intermediate genus.

units.la: 3· Genus & species intermedia.
units.tr: 3. A genus and an intermediate species.

units.la: 4. Genus & species intermedia.
units.tr: 4. A genus and an intermediate species.

units.la: 5. Species infima & proxima.
units.tr: 5. The lowest species, nearest to the individual.

units.la: 6. Indiuiduum. I. Substantia Corporea Incorporea 2. Corpus Animatum Inanimatū 3. Corpusanimatū Sentiens Non sentiens 4. Animal Rationis particeps Rationis expers 5. Homo. 6. Socrates, Aristides.
units.tr: 6. The individual. 1. Substance: corporeal, incorporeal. 2. Body: animate, inanimate. 3. Animate body: sentient, non-sentient. 4. Animal: partaking of reason, lacking reason. 5. Man. 6. Socrates, Aristides.

units.la: Sed profer exemplum aliquod ad Iuris ci-vilis, & vitæ communis usum pertinens. Ex-emplum ex libris nostris hoc esto. RES quarum commercium est:aliæ Corporales Incorporales. Corporalium Animatæ Inanimatæ. Animatarum Rationales Irrationales Rationalium Seruus Ancilla Seruorum Stichus, Dauus, Pamphilus.
units.tr: But let us offer an example that pertains to civil law and to the common use of life. Let this be an example from our books: Things which can be the subject of commerce are either corporeal or incorporeal. Of corporeal things, some are animate and some inanimate. Of animate things, some are rational and some irrational. Of rational things, a slave; a maidservant; of slaves, Stichus, Davus, Pamphilus.

units.la: Quotuplex est Genus? Disciplinae caussa triplex fingitur: Summum, quod Græci γενικόν[?], id est latissimum ac fusissimum nominant. medium quod (vt diximus) ὑπαλλάλον[?], & subalternum appellant: ac postremò infimum, quod idem εἰδικώτατον[?] vocant.
units.tr: How many kinds of genus are there? For the sake of teaching, three are distinguished: the highest, which the Greeks call genikon, that is, the broadest and most extensive; the middle, which (as we said) they call hyperallelon, and we call subaltern; and finally the lowest, which they also call eidikotaton.

units.la: Quod est Summum Genus? Quo nullum neque antiquitate, neque amplitudine maius est, longissimeque omnium à sensibus abest. Itaque cùm species esse non possit, de omnibus sub se subiectis enuntiatur. veluti apud Philosophos Substantia: apud Iurisconsultos, Res quae in superioribus figuris supremum locum obtinent.
units.tr: What is the highest genus? That than which there is none greater either in antiquity or in breadth, and which is furthest removed from the senses of all things. Since it cannot be a species, it is predicated of all the things subordinate to it. For example, among philosophers, substance; among jurists, the thing, which holds the highest place in the preceding divisions.

units.la: Quod est Medium? Quod inter superius atque inferius interiectù, huic genus, illi species est. veluti, Corpus. itaque cum Re collatum, species est: cum animatis, genus. Sic Pater inter auum & filium ita interiectus est, vt illi sit filius, huic pater.
units.tr: What is the middle? That which, interposed between the higher and the lower, is a genus to the one and a species to the other. For example, body: compared with thing it is a species; compared with animate things, a genus. So a father, interposed between grandfather and son, is a son to the one and a father to the other.

units.la: Quod est infimum? Quod angustissimum est, neque ullum in se aliud complectitur. vt Animal respectu Hominis est infimum: at respectu Auis est medium: Nam Auis genus est inferius, cui diuersæ species subsunt: ut Aquila, Columba, Coruus.
units.tr: What is the lowest? That which is most narrow and embraces no other thing within itself. For example, animal is the lowest with respect to man, but with respect to bird it is intermediate, for bird is a lower genus under which various species lie, such as eagle, dove, raven.

units.la: Quoniam quid esset species suprà demonstratū est, quæro quotuplex est Species? Vulgò in scholis ex Porphyrij sententia duplex numeratur: quarum prior infima dicitur, quæ de multis numero tantùm differentibus, id est indiuiduis ac singularibus rebus enuntiatur; quæque verè ac proprie Species est: ut pote nulla sub se species habés, sed indiuiduis proxima, ut apud Philosophos Homo. Altera dicitur Media, quæ cum superioribus collata, species est: cum inferioribus, generis gradum obtinet: quod modò Genus subalternum appellauimus. Nam sæpenumero id accidit, ut una res alteri fit genus, alteri species, veluti, Animal respectu corporis (ut modò diximus) species est: respectu piscis, genus. Homo respectu animalis species est: respectu liberorū & seruorum est genus. Piscis respectu animalis, species est: respectu Murænarum, genus. Item Homo respectu animalis, species est: respectu Gallorum, Germanorum, Italorum, genus. Item ut respectu Pygmæorum, aut Gigantum. Itaque quoniam species duas hasce partes in animi notione sustinet, iccirco notionem ipsius, non unam, sed duplicem esse oportet. Nam cùm genus est, latior ac fusior notio est; cùm species, artior atq; angustior. Sed Stoicorum sententia triplex Species constituitur. nam (ut Diogenes Laertius in Zenonis vita testatur) ἴδιον ἰδιώτατον[?] Zeno appellabat, quę cùm fit species, speciem non habet: hoc est, quod Aristoteles individuum appellat: veluti Socratem, aut Pamphilum. quam rationem Iurisconsulti (ut dixi) secuti sunt.
units.tr: Since it has been shown above what a species is, I ask how many kinds of species there are. Commonly in the schools, following Porphyry's opinion, two are counted. The first is called the lowest, which is predicated of many things differing only in number, that is, of individual and singular things, and which is truly and properly a species, since it has no species under it but is nearest to the individuals, as man is among philosophers. The second is called intermediate, which, compared with the higher things, is a species, but compared with the lower things holds the rank of a genus; this we have just called subaltern genus. For it very often happens that one and the same thing is a genus to one thing and a species to another. Thus animal is a species with respect to body (as we just said), but a genus with respect to fish. Fish is a species with respect to animal, but a genus with respect to murenas. Likewise man is a species with respect to animal, but a genus with respect to Gauls, Germans, Italians; likewise with respect to pygmies or giants. Therefore, since a species sustains these two parts in the mind's notion, the notion of it must be not one but double. For when it is a genus it is a broader and more extensive notion; when a species, a narrower and more confined one. But according to the Stoics' opinion a threefold species is set up. For (as Diogenes Laertius testifies in the life of Zeno) Zeno called the individual the most individual [ἴδιον ἰδιώτατον], which, when it is a species, has no species under it; this is what Aristotle calls the individual, such as Socrates or Pamphilus. The jurists (as I said) followed this view.

units.la: Utrorum igitur verior sententia est? Non nostrum inter vos (dicebat ille) tantas componere lites. Sed inter Speciem & Individuum notari hoc discrimen potest: quòd illa, notione & intelligentia comprehenditur: hoc, percipitur sensu, qui rationis expers est. Denique Speciei proprietates pluribus conveniunt; Individui proprietates in nullum aliud conveniunt. nam Rationis particeps dicitur de pluribus. Hic fundus, vel Socrates de uno tantùm.ac nullam quidem individuorum notionem ac scientiam in animis nostris à natura impressam, Plato censebat. Itaque disputationem quæ à Generibus ad imas species perducta erat, sisti atque inhiberi iubebat: neque ad individua progredi: quoniam & erant infinita, & scientia nulla comprehendi poterat. quam ob rem ne definiri quidem possunt, ut posterius intelliges. Sed cùm Iurisconsulti corpora omnia in partes non modò corporatas, quibus totum interit, verùm etiam in intellectas, per quastotum[?] non interit, diuiderent, propterea Individua hæc non nominarunt, sed Species, quæ plures notiones habere posfent. nam cū Dauus aut Bucephalus plurium dominorum esse possint, necesse est plurium dominiorum plures notiones in vna eademque renotari. veluti si seruus duorum communis aliquid acquirat,singulis,pro qua parte domini sunt,acquirit.l.5,D.de stip.ser.qua de caussa duorum seruorum personam sustinere dicitur.L.1,§.communis,eod.
units.tr: Which of these opinions, then, is the truer? "It is not for me to settle such great disputes between you," as that man used to say. But the difference between species and individual may be noted thus: the species is grasped by notion and understanding, the individual is perceived by the senses, which lack reason. Again, the properties of a species apply to many things, whereas the properties of an individual apply to no other thing. For "partaking of reason" is said of many, but "this estate" or "Socrates" of one only. Plato held that no notion or knowledge of individuals is impressed on our minds by nature. Therefore he ordered that the disputation, which had been led from the genera down to the lowest species, be halted and checked, and not advanced to individuals, since they are both infinite and cannot be comprehended by any knowledge; for this reason they cannot even be defined, as you will understand later. But since the jurists divided all bodies not only into parts that are embodied, by whose loss the whole perishes, but also into intellectual parts, which do not perish with the whole, they therefore did not call these individuals but species, since they can have several notions. For although Davus or Bucephalus can belong to several masters, it is necessary that several notions of several ownerships be marked in one and the same thing. For example, if a slave acquires something for two co-owners, he acquires it for each in proportion to his share as master (Dig. 5, l. de stipulationibus servorum); for which reason he is said to sustain the person of two slaves (Dig. 1 §communis, eod.).

units.la: Quomodo ex genere constituitur species? Per differētiā,quæ est forma rei,& caussa propter quam quæque res est id quod est. Verùm id perpetuum non est,tanta enim differentiarum ignoratio est, vt sæpe species sui generis nomine appellentur.veluti apud Cæsarem ,initiolib.1. Gallorum alij sunt Belgæ , alij Aquitani, alij Galli. Interdum per particulam NON alteri speciei contradicente designentur : veluti, Animalium aliud est rationale, aliud non rationale. Ius aliud est Scriptum, aliud non scriptum. Furtum aliud est manifestum,aliud nec manifestum.
units.tr: How is a species constituted from a genus? By the difference, which is the form of the thing and the cause on account of which each thing is what it is. Yet this is not always so, for there is such great ignorance of differences that species are often named by the name of their genus, as in Caesar at the beginning of book 1: some of the Gauls are Belgians, others Aquitanians, others Gauls. Sometimes they are designated by the particle NOT, the one species being opposed to the other: for example, of animals, one is rational, another not rational; of law, one is written, another not written; of theft, one is manifest, another not manifest.

units.la: Quid? differentia qualis notio est? Quæ sui adiūctione rem vniuersalé in species contrarias notata cuiúsque qualitate distinguit.
