units.tr: What then? Is a difference a kind of notion? It is that which, by being added to a universal, marks it off into contrary species and distinguishes each by its quality.

units.la: Itaque in quæstione Quale quídque fit, vsurpatur. veluti, Rationis particeps. nam & , si quæratur, Homo quale fit animal , respondebitur, Rationis compos: & rursus , si quæratur,quid à brutis differat , idem respondebitur. Denique differentia est forma rei, & causa propter quam res est id quod est. Sed de differentiis postea cùm ad diuisionem ventum erit, vberius exponemus.
units.tr: Therefore it is used in the question "What sort of thing is it?" For example, "partaking of reason". For if one asks what sort of animal man is, the answer will be "endowed with reason"; and again, if one asks what differs him from the brutes, the same answer will be given. In short, the difference is the form of the thing and the cause on account of which the thing is what it is. But we shall set out differences more fully later, when we come to division.

units.la: Potésne hunc notionum & intelligentiarū ordinem aliquanto dilucidius exponere? Ex Platonis certè & Ariftotelis doctrina, planissimè id possumus. Jubent enim poni Calliam procul ad nos longo interuallo venientem. Ea species extrinsecus oblata sensibus continuò generis universi notitiam in animo informat. primùm enim corpus esse intelligimus. mox, ubi propius accessit, animal. tum hominem: ad extremum Calliam. Sic, qui in statione sunt, & procul aliquem venientem intuentur, primùm corpus esse animadvertunt. secundò ex cursu animal esse iudicant. Tertiò, equitem. quartò ex colore, amicum vel hostem. postremò, Titium, vel Sempronium. Atque hi sunt nimirum, de quibus superius diximus, notionum & intelligentiarum gradus.
units.tr: Can you explain this order of notions and understandings somewhat more clearly? From the teaching of Plato and Aristotle we can do so most plainly. For they bid us imagine Callias coming towards us from a long distance. The species, presented to the senses from outside, at once forms in the mind a notion of the whole genus. First we perceive that it is a body; then, as he comes nearer, an animal; then a man; and at last Callias. So too, those who stand on watch, and see someone approaching from afar, first notice that it is a body; secondly, from his running, they judge that it is an animal; thirdly, a horseman; fourthly, from his colour, a friend or an enemy; lastly, Titius or Sempronius. These, surely, are the degrees of notions and understandings of which we spoke above.

units.la: Superest una quaestio. Genus & Species vtrum prius ac posterius sunt, annè simul? Genus propterea specie prius est, quoniam (vt superius diximus) consecutio essentiæ reciprocationem non admittit. nam si est equus, est animal: at non cōtinuò si est animal, etiam est equus. Sic qui magnificus, idem continuò liberalis: qui autem liberalis, idem non continuò magnificus.
units.tr: One question remains: are genus and species prior and posterior to one another, or are they simultaneous? The genus is therefore prior to the species, since (as we said above) consequence does not admit of reciprocity. For if it is a horse, it is an animal; but it does not follow at once that if it is an animal, it is also a horse. So too, he who is magnificent is at once liberal; but he who is liberal is not at once magnificent.

units.la: De Toto & partibus.
units.tr: On the Whole and its parts.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: vt est Totum? Notio, quæ rei cuiusque partes inter fecópactas & compositas completitur. Non enim separatæ partes quamuis omnes totum efficiunt, sed compactæ & sua forma constantes. Physicorum auté ratione Totum est,cui nulla pars deest.
units.tr: What is the Whole? It is the notion by which the parts of each thing are completed, joined and compacted together. For separate parts, however many, do not make up a whole; the parts must be compacted and held together by their form. According to the natural philosophers, the Whole is that to which no part is lacking.

units.la: Quotuplex est Totum? Philofophorü diʃputatione multiplex. sed ad huius institutionis vsum quintuplici eius partitione contenti esse possumus: quarum hæc prima est, vt aliud fit integrum, ὅλον, quod corporatum est, sesque percipitur, & cerni tangíque potest: veluti corpus hominis,aut domus,aut nauis : aliud Vniuersale, τὸ καθόλου, quod quasi genus animo & intelligentia cóprehenditur : vt Respublica,familia,hereditas,dos,peculiü,mundus muliebris. Itémque artes omnes, vt Medicina, Arithmetica, Rhetorica: quam ipsam propterea Cicero partitione, non diuisione explicauit.
units.tr: How many kinds of Whole are there? Philosophers dispute this at length, but for the purpose of this introduction a fivefold division will suffice. The first division is this: one whole is ὅλον [holon], which is embodied, perceived by the senses, and can be seen and touched, such as the body of a man, a house, or a ship. Another is the universal, τὸ καθόλου [to katholou], which is grasped by the mind and understanding as a genus, such as the commonwealth, a family, an inheritance, a dowry, a peculium, a woman's adornments. So too are all the arts, such as medicine, arithmetic and rhetoric, which Cicero for this reason explained by partition rather than division.

units.la: Quæ est altera? Totum,aliud est continuü, quod vel vnius naturæ est, vt homo , fundus,equus, statua : vel ex pluribus compactum : vt domus,nauis,sphæra:aliud deiunctum,veluti, Populus, grex, armentum,exercitus, familia, l.rerum mixtura,30,D.de vsurpat.
units.tr: What is the second division? A whole is either continuous, which is of one nature, such as a man, a farm, a horse or a statue, or compacted of several things, such as a house, a ship or a sphere; or else it is disjoined, such as a people, a flock, a herd, an army or a family. See l. rerum mixtura, 30, D. de usurpat.

units.la: Quæ est tertia? Totum aliud est perfectũ, quod per se constat, neque alterius pars esse debet: veluti domus, arbor, nauis, aliud imperfectum, quod per se non constat, sed alterius pars esse debet: veluti fundamentum per fe & quatenus fundamentum est, totum est: attamen non ita natura sua comparatum est, vt fit totum, & per fe constet: sed vt domus pars fit. Sic Ramus,quatenus ramus est, totü est:at natura sua pars esse arboris debet. Ité vt puppis,vt prora, vt sentina, partes esse nauis debent. eodémque modo & manus, & oculus, & auris, corporis humani sunt partes, neque per fe constant. Scitum est autem quod Ariftoteles libro Politicorum primo scribit, [illegible, ~6 letters] τῷ ἔργῳ ὠφέλησαι, ἐκ τῆς δυνάμει omnes ex fui muneris functione & efficientia æstimari, ac definiri. Itaque partem eam demum veré ac proprie dicendam esse, quæ in Toto est, fuóq; munere fungitur. Auulsam autem ac separatam, dici tantùm abusione & communione vocabuli,quam ὁμωνυμίαν appellat.Itaque manum & pedem tum demum veré dici,cùm suo munere funguntur.Vbi autem separata sunt, nihilo magis esse partes Totius,quàm cùm lapidea manus aut ænea, manus dicitur. Pars enim Totius pars dicitur, non totum partis totum. Itaque fundamentum dicitur domus fundamentum:& Tectum,domus tectum : nó contrà. quod idem scribit lib.4.Metheorön.
units.tr: What is the third division? A whole is either perfect, which stands by itself and need not be a part of anything else, such as a house, a tree or a ship; or imperfect, which does not stand by itself but must be a part of something else. For example, a foundation, as long as it is a foundation, is a whole; yet by its nature it is not so constituted that it is a whole and stands by itself, but it is made to be a part of a house. In the same way a branch, as long as it is a branch, is a whole; yet by its nature it must be a part of a tree. So too the stern, the prow and the bilge must be parts of a ship; and in the same way the hand, the eye and the ear are parts of the human body and do not stand by themselves. Aristotle rightly writes in the first book of the Politics that [τῷ ἔργῳ ὠφελεῖσθαι, ἐκ τῆς δυνάμεως] all things are to be judged and defined from the performance and efficacy of their function. Hence a part is properly and truly called a part only when it is in the Whole and performs its function. When it is detached and separated, it is called a part only by a misuse and loose application of the word, which he calls ὁμωνυμία [homonymia]. Thus a hand is truly called a hand only when it performs its function; when it is separated, a hand of stone or bronze is no more a part of the body than it is a hand. For a part is said to be a part of the Whole, not the whole of a part. So we speak of the foundation of a house and the roof of a house, not the reverse. He writes the same in the fourth book of the Meteorologica.

units.la: Quæ est quarta? Rerum aliæ sunt, viipfa tantùm: quod Græci τῇ δυνάμει dicunt: aliæ re ipsa,quod illi τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ. nos illas absolutas appellare possumus : has informes,fiue informatas,fiue etiā inchoatas. Vulgus dicit aliud esse actu, aliud potestate:
units.tr: What is the fourth division? Some things exist only potentially, which the Greeks call τῇ δυνάμει [te dynamei]; others actually, which they call τῇ ἐνεργείᾳ [te energeia]. We may call the former absolute and the latter unformed, or formed, or even inchoate. The common people say that one thing is actual and another potential.

units.la: Quæ sunt absolutæ? Quæ naturæ suæ persectionem, & quasi maturitatem quandam adeptæ sunt: quoniam in iis forma iam & finis inest, suisque omnibus numeris & partibus expletæ sunt. ut vinum, frumentum,oleum.
units.tr: Which things are absolute? Those which have attained the perfection of their nature and, as it were, a certain maturity, since their form and end are already present in them and they are complete in all their parts. Examples are wine, grain and oil.

units.la: Quæ sunt informes? Quæ vim in se nascendi & existendi cōtinent; verùm in spe tantùm atque expectatione sunt. In iis enim efficiens tantùm & materia est: veluti, Ovum quod à Gallina fouetur, vi & spe pullus est. Juglans lactea,quæ arboris succo alitur, expectatione nux est: seges,frumentum: uvæ pendentes, vinum:oliuæ,oleum. partus nondum editus, homo non recte dicitur: ait Papinianus in l. in Falcidia,9,D.ad leg.Falcid.
units.tr: Which things are unformed? Those which contain within themselves the power of coming into being and existing, but are so only in hope and expectation. In these there is only the efficient cause and the matter. For example, an egg being hatched by a hen is a chick in power and in hope. A milky walnut, fed by the sap of the tree, is a nut in expectation; a standing crop is grain; hanging grapes are wine; olives are oil. A child not yet born is not rightly called a man, says Papinian, in l. in Falcidia, 9, D. ad leg. Falcid.

units.la: Quæ est quinta diuisio? Totū aliud est natu-rale,quod natura non manu constant: ut Animal, Fūdus, Arbor.aliud artificiosum, quod hominis solertia atque arte confectum est. ut domus,nauis,currus,statua. Eiusque divisionis usus proximè intelligetur.
units.tr: What is the fifth division? A whole is either natural, which exists by nature and not by hand, such as an animal, a farm or a tree; or artificial, made by human skill and art, such as a house, a ship, a chariot or a statue. The use of this division will soon become clear.

units.la: Quæ est Partium distributio? Multiplex, sed illa primaria, ut aliæ sint principales, sine quibus constare res nō potest: velut in humano corpore, Caput, Humeri, Thorax. Aliæ minus principales, sine quibus res constat: ut auriculæ, crines, unguces[?], supercilia. Sic in Arbore, radix, truncus, rami, principales sunt partes: at folia, flores, baccæ, minus principales. Item in naue, prora, puppis, & sentina, partes sunt principales. at de malo & artemone disputatur. malū nauis esse partem, artemonem autem non esse, Labeo ait: quia pleraque naues sine malo inutiles sunt: artemo autē magis additamentum, quàm pars nauis est. Sic multæ naues sine gubernaculo sunt: ac prefertim exiguæ: vt scaphę, & scapharū similes.
units.tr: What is the distribution of parts? It is manifold, but the primary distinction is this: some parts are principal, without which the thing cannot exist, as in the human body the head, the shoulders and the chest. Others are less principal, without which the thing still exists, such as the ears, the hair, the fingernails and the eyebrows. Likewise in a tree the root, the trunk and the branches are principal parts, but the leaves, flowers and berries are less principal. Also in a ship the prow, the stern and the bilge are principal parts; but there is dispute about the mast and the artemon (the foresail). Labeo says the mast is a part of a ship but the artemon is not, because most ships are useless without a mast, whereas the artemon is more an addition than a part of the ship. Likewise many ships have no rudder, especially small ones such as skiffs and boats like them.

units.la: Quæ est altera diuisio? Vt alię sint cognatæ, quas Græci ὁμογενεῖς, siue ὁμοιομερεῖς appellant: aliæ vero extraneæ, quas iidem ἀνομοιομερεῖς, & ἑτεροφυεῖς, id est, alienigenas nominant.
units.tr: What is the other division? Some parts are kindred, which the Greeks call ὁμογενεῖς [homogeneis] or ὁμοιομερεῖς [homoiomereis]; others are foreign, which the same writers call ἀνομοιομερεῖς [anomoiomereis] and ἑτεροφυεῖς [heterophyeis], that is, of alien origin.

units.la: Quæ sunt Cognatæ? Quæ ex eodem quasi genere ortæ, totius nomen retinent: veluti lapidis partes omnes lapidis nomen retinent: Item fundi partes omnes, fundus dicuntur. l. plane. 3,4,§. vltim. D. de legat. j. quoniam, fundum Varro vocat, quę posis mittere funda: vt est in vetere prouerbio.
units.tr: Which parts are kindred? Those which arise from the same kind, as it were, and keep the name of the whole. For example, all the parts of a stone keep the name of stone, and likewise all the parts of a farm are called a farm. See l. plane, 3, 4, §. ultim., D. de legat. (1) Since Varro calls a farm "fundus", the word for what one can hurl with a sling, as in the old proverb.

units.la: Quæ sunt extraneæ? Quæ vel ex eodem capite ductæ, vel ei cohærentes, tamen quasi alienigenæ, variis nominibus appellantur. veluti, Arboris partes nullæ nomen Totius retinent, non magis quàm domus, aut nauis, aut corporis humani. Sic apud Iurisconsultos superficies omnis subiecti corporis pars est: vt vitis, vineæ: arbor, fundi: seges, arui: pictura, tabulæ: scriptura, membranæ: purpura, vestis. l. adeo, 7, §. cùm in suo, & seq. & l. qua ratione, 9, D. de acq. rer. dom.
units.tr: Which parts are foreign? Those which, though derived from the same source or cohering with the whole, are nevertheless called by various names as though they were of alien origin. For example, no parts of a tree keep the name of the whole, any more than the parts of a house, a ship or the human body do. Thus among the jurists every surface of a body is a part of that body: a vine is part of a vineyard, a tree of a farm, a crop of a field, a painting of a board, writing of parchment, purple of a garment. See l. adeo, 7, §. cum in suo, and following, and l. qua ratione, 9, D. de acq. rer. dom.

units.la: Quæ est tertia partium diuisio? Vt alię sint corporales, quæ pondere, numero, mensura fiunt: & quæ oculis cerni tangíque possunt. aliæ verò intelligi possunt. Corporalium exemplum est primùm in vulgatis diuisionibus, cùm ex vnâ re plures fiunt. nam quod pro diuiso nostrum est, id per se consideratum, iam non pars, sed totum est. l. recte dicimus, 25, D. de verb. signific. deinde exemplum est in generibus, & operis. nam genus numero tâtùm diuiditur. veluti si qui seruos duos stipulatus, duos heredes reliquerit, singulis heredibus singuli serui debebuntur. & si viginti, singulis deni: & si centum, singulis quinquageni. l. in stipulationibus, 54, l. si centum, 117, D. de verb. oblig. Sic si decem operas stipulatus, duos heredes reliquerit, numero diuidentur operæ, & singulis quinum dierum operæ debebuntur. l. stipulationes non diuiduntur, 72, & l. in stipulationibus, 54, §. 1. eod. l. libertus, 15, D. de oper. lib. Quod eodem modo de quantitatibus dicetur, id est iis rebus quæ numero, pondere, & mensura constant. l. cùm Stichus, 29, D. de solut. & liber. Intellectarum autem partium exemplum est, veluti cùm apud Mathematicos orbis diuiditur in partem concauam & conuexam: aut apud Iurisconsultos, cùm aliæ dicuntur partes pro indiuiso, aliæ pro diuiso. vt cùm duo vnius eiusdémque rei domini dicuntur. nam partes pro indiuiso, intellectu constant, & incertæ sunt, partes pro diuidiuisó corporales sunt, id est corpore & facto cóftant,ac certę sunt.l.placet,25, D.quib. mod.vfusfr.amitt. Seruus communis sic omnium est (inquit Vlpianus) non quasi fingulorum totus: sed pro partibus vtique indiuifis: vt intellectu magis partes habeat, quàm corpore.l.5,D.de ftip.feru.
units.tr: What is the third division of parts? Some parts are bodily, which are determined by weight, number and measure, and which can be seen and touched; others can only be understood. An example of bodily parts is first found in ordinary divisions, when several things arise out of one. For what is ours as a divided share, considered in itself, is no longer a part but a whole. See l. recte dicimus, 25, D. de verb. signific. Next, an example is found in genera and in services. For a genus is divided only numerically. For instance, if someone who has stipulated for two slaves leaves two heirs, a slave is owed to each heir; if he stipulated for twenty, ten are owed to each; if for a hundred, fifty to each. See l. in stipulationibus, 54, and l. si centum, 117, D. de verb. oblig. Likewise, if he stipulated for ten days' services and left two heirs, the services are divided numerically, and five days' services are owed to each. See l. stipulationes non dividuntur, 72, l. in stipulationibus, 54, §. 1, eod., and l. libertus, 15, D. de oper. lib. What is said in the same way of quantities applies to things that consist of number, weight and measure. See l. cum Stichus, 29, D. de solut. et liber. An example of intellectual parts is when mathematicians divide a sphere into a concave and a convex part, or when jurists say that some parts are undivided and others divided, as when two owners of one and the same thing are said to be owners. For undivided parts exist in the understanding and are uncertain; divided parts are bodily, that is, they consist in body and in fact and are certain. See l. placet, 25, D. quib. mod. usufr. amitt. The common slave belongs to all, says Ulpian, not as a whole to each individually, but in undivided parts, so that he is a part more in the understanding than in the body. See l. 5, D. de stip. serv.

units.la: Quid interest inter Totum & Genus? Genus, vniuersale est, & (vt ait Ariftoteles) ὅλως ὅλον[?]. Itaque & singulis suis formis inest, & de iisdem singulis dicitur. Totum vniuersale non est: nam neque in singulis partibus inest, neque ipsius nomen partibus singulis conuenit. Genus ex suis formis non constat. Totum suis partibus constat. Genus natura prius est formis, tempore posterius. Totum autem (vt mox dicemus) populari ratione suis partibus est posterius. Itaque generis interitu species intereunt. Toto perempto, partes tamen populari ratione non perimuntur. At contrà, specie perempta, genus nō interit: partis principalis interitu, Totum interit.
units.tr: What is the difference between a whole and a genus? A genus is universal and, as Aristotle says, wholly whole [ὅλως ὅλον]. So it is present in each of its species and is predicated of each of them. A whole is not universal: it is not present in each of its parts, and its name does not apply to each part singly. A genus does not consist of its species; a whole consists of its parts. A genus is prior to its species in nature but posterior in time. A whole, however (as we shall say shortly), is posterior to its parts in popular usage. So when the genus perishes, the species perish with it. When the whole perishes, the parts are not destroyed in popular usage. On the other hand, when a species perishes the genus does not, but when a principal part perishes, the whole perishes.

units.la: Quid interest inter Species & Partes? Species quidem subsunt generi, isque genus constat: & partes toti, isque Totum consistit. Verùm illarum numerus certus est, partium quandoque incertus. Species diuidendo non interit, sed in quoque indiuiduo permanet: partes autem secando intereunt. Illæ generis nomen recipiunt, hæ totius nomen non recipiunt. nam hominis pars homo non est:
units.tr: What is the difference between species and parts? Species fall under a genus, and the genus is made up of them; parts make up a whole, and the whole consists of them. But the number of species is fixed, while the number of parts is sometimes indefinite. A species does not perish when it is divided; it remains in each individual. Parts, however, perish when they are cut apart. Species receive the name of the genus, but parts do not receive the name of the whole: for a part of a man is not a man,

units.la: ait Paul. l.fi di&tū,s6,§.in stipulat.D.de evict.
units.tr: as Paulus says in the law cited above, D. de evictionibus, §.in stipulatu.

units.la: Cedo mihi exemplum aliquod, in quo harum differentiarum usus appareat. Summus ab eorum errore, qui Dialecticam aliam faciunt naturalem, aliam artificiosam: Ciceronis fortasse adducti exemplo, qui cùm adolescentulus Rhetoricam artem scriberet, putavit memoriam aliam esse naturalem, aliam artificiosam. Nā in eo error est, quòd Memoriam aut Dialecticā Genus esse putarunt, cū revera sit Totum: cuius hæ tres sunt partes, Natura, Ars, Exercitatio: quibus tanquā partibus omnis ea virtus constat. Quòd si Dialectica aut Memoria, genus essent, primùm arti soli, tanquam speciei suæ inessent: deinde arte posteriores essent, quorum utrùmque absurdum est. Præterea non duas tantùm, sed tres species constitui oporteret: Naturalem, Artificiosam,& Exercitatoriam. Quodeodē modo de Architectura posterius in diuisione ostendemus.
units.tr: Give me some example in which the use of these differences appears. I am very far from the error of those who make one kind of dialectic natural and another artificial, perhaps led by the example of Cicero, who, when still a young man writing a art of rhetoric, thought that memory was of two kinds, natural and artificial. For their error lies in thinking that Memory or Dialectic is a genus, when it is really a whole, of which these three are the parts: Nature, Art, and Practice, from which all such skill is composed as from its parts. If Dialectic or Memory were a genus, it would first be present only in art, as in its own species, and then would be posterior to art; both of which are absurd. Moreover, two species would not be the only ones to be posited, but three: natural, artificial, and practical. We shall show in the division that the same holds for architecture.

units.la: Superest illa quæstio: Totū & Partes, vtrùm prius aut posterius sint, anne simul? Rectè admones: neque leuis momenti quæstio illa est. Nā Aristoteles initio Politicorum scribit, ciuitatem quæ ex domibus constat, naturæ ordine prius esse quàm domum. [illegible, ~20 letters] (inquit) ἀναγκαῖον ἐ[?]τὰ μέρους, ἀναιρουμένου γὰρ [?] τοῦ ὅλου, οὐκ ἔσται ποῦς, οὐδὲ χείρ, εἰ μὴ ὁμωνύμως. Totum necesse est prius esse, quàm partem. sublato enim toto neque pes, neq; manus est, nisi nefi nominis communione: ut cùm lapidea manus dicitur in statua. Idem tamen libro Topicorum sexto scribit, Totum & partes non esse idem: &, si sint partes, nihil prohibere non esse Totum: atque interemptis partibus totū interire: interrempto vero toto, non necesse esse partes interire. ἀπὸ[?] μερῶν φθαρέντων,φθείρεσθαι τὸ ὅλον: τῷ ἢ ὅλου φθαρέντος[?], ἀναγκαῖον καὶ τὰ μέρη ἐφθάρθαι.
units.tr: There remains that question: whether the whole and the parts are prior or posterior to each other, or simultaneous? You rightly advise this, and the question is of no slight importance. For Aristotle, at the beginning of the Politics, writes that the city, which consists of households, is prior to the household in the order of nature. [illegible] he says, "it is necessary [ἀναγκαῖον] ... the part; for when the whole is destroyed there will be no foot, nor hand, except homonymously." So the whole must be prior to the part: with the whole taken away there is neither foot nor hand, except in name only, as when a hand of stone is spoken of in a statue. Yet in the sixth book of the Topics he writes the same, that the whole and the parts are not the same, and that, if there are parts, nothing prevents there being no whole; and that with the parts destroyed the whole perishes, but with the whole destroyed the parts do not necessarily perish [ἀπὸ μερῶν φθαρέντων φθείρεσθαι τὸ ὅλον· τοῦ δὲ ὅλου φθαρέντος ἀναγκαῖον καὶ τὰ μέρη φθαρῆναι].

units.la: Quidnam igitur in hac ambiguitate certi definiemus? Primùm distinctio superior adhibenda est: ut aliud sit Totum naturale, veluti arbor, fundus, avis, equus: aliud artificiosum: veluti domus, nauis, currus. si naturale totum est, verisimum est quod Aristoteles libro de Natura octauo scribit, Prius esse & naturæ, & temporis, & rationis ordine id quod perfectum est, eo quod est inchoatum: Sin autem artificiosum est, tum eiusdem Aristotelis monitu altera distinctio adhibenda est: utrum subtiliter ex artis ratione, an populariter ex sermonis consuetudine differatur. Nam quia subtili ratione ea demum pars verè proprieque dicitur, quæ suo munere fungitur: fungi autem suo muncre nisi suo toti cohærens non potest: certè Totum & Pars naturæ ac temporis ordine simul sint necesse est. nam ubi est domus, ibi necesse est esse tectum: & ubi tectum revera tegens, ibi necesse est esse domū. ubi currus: ibi rota: & ubi rota revera & actu volucns, ibi currus. Sin autem populariter loquamur, & homonymia, id est communione nominis abutamur,tum verò Pars dicetur esse prior: Totū verò posterius.ut area,quam Iurisconsulti posterius domus partem appellant, prior est ædificio: & fundus prior vitibus, aut arboribus,aut fruticibus.
units.tr: What then shall we define with certainty in this ambiguity? First the distinction above must be applied: a whole may be natural, such as a tree, a farm, a bird, a horse; or artificial, such as a house, a ship, a chariot. If the whole is natural, it is likely, as Aristotle writes in the eighth book of the Physics, that what is perfect is prior to what is incomplete in nature, in time, and in the order of reason. But if the whole is artificial, then, on Aristotle's advice, another distinction must be applied: whether the matter is distinguished subtly by the reason of the art, or popularly by the custom of speech. For since in strict reasoning that is properly and truly called a part which performs its function, and it cannot perform its function unless it cohere with its whole, the whole and the part must necessarily be simultaneous in the order of nature and of time. For where there is a house, there must be a roof, and where there is a roof that truly covers, there must be a house. Where there is a chariot, there is a wheel, and where there is a wheel that truly and actually turns, there is a chariot. But if we speak popularly, and abuse homonymy, that is, the sharing of a name, then the part will be said to be prior and the whole posterior: thus the yard, which the jurists call a part of the house posterior to the building, is prior to the building, and the farm is prior to the vines, or trees, or shrubs.

units.la: De quatuor causarum generibus.
units.tr: On the four kinds of causes.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: EINCEPS[?] de quinta notione sive Affectione videam'. Quid est caufa? Est id cuius vi rei cuiusque aut actionis euentus exitū habuit. Simul enim eodémque tempore vtriusque ratio habenda est, Euentus & Causæ. Rem autem appello,veluti nauigium,aut rhedam quam faber efficit. Actionem verò, veluti nauigationem,aut vectionem.
units.tr: Next I shall consider the fifth notion, or affection. What is a cause? It is that by whose power the outcome of a thing or of an action has come about. For the outcome and the cause must be taken into account together and at the same time. I call a "thing," for example a ship or a cart that a craftsman makes; and an "action," for example sailing or conveyance.

units.la: Quæ sunt in causis tractandis consideranda? Primùm ut Causa & Euentus tanquam inter se relata & respondentia perpetuò conferantur. Deinde ut in euentu & rerum & actionum ratio habeatur: postremò ut hæc eadem tum in iis quæ natura, tum ex iis quæ ex arte eueniunt, observentur.
units.tr: What must be considered in treating causes? First, that cause and outcome are always compared as things related to and corresponding with one another. Next, that account is taken of both things and actions in the outcome. Last, that these same points are observed both in those things which come about by nature and in those which come about by art.

units.la: Quotuplex est causa? Quadruplex. Efficiens, Sine qua non, Forma, & (quæ omnium principatū obtinet) Finis. sic Græci [illegible, ~4 letters] αἰτίων, alia ποιητικὰ[?] faciunt, alia [illegible, ~4 letters] ἐκ ἀρχῆς[?], alia μορφῆς[?] sive εἴδη[?], alia τελικά.
units.tr: How many kinds of cause are there? Four: efficient, without which not (sine qua non), form, and (which holds the chief place among them all) end. So the Greeks [illegible] some causes are productive [ποιητικά], some are from the beginning [ἐκ ἀρχῆς], some are forms or species [μορφῆς, εἴδη], and some are final [τελικά].

units.la: Quæ est Caussa efficiens? Quæ motus eius principium attulit, per quem euentus exitum habuit. velut in re naturali, Sol caussa est diei: Corpus in lumine, caussa est vmbræ. qua de caussa lunæ interpositus caussa est defectionis solis:& terræ interpositus, caussa defectionis lunæ. In artificio sutor caussa est calcei, sculptor numi. In actione naturali, ignis caussa est ardoris, cruditas morbi: in artificiosa, Auriga caussa est vectionis efficiés: & Gubernator nauigationis.
units.tr: What is the efficient cause? That which supplied the principle of motion through which the outcome came about. For example, in a natural thing, the sun is the cause of day; a body standing in the light is the cause of a shadow; for this reason the moon interposed is the cause of an eclipse of the sun, and the earth interposed is the cause of an eclipse of the moon. In a made thing, the shoemaker is the cause of the shoe, the sculptor of the coin. In a natural action, fire is the cause of heat, and a disordered state is the cause of disease; in an artificial action, the charioteer is the efficient cause of the journey, and the helmsman of the voyage.

units.la: Quæ est caussa sine qua non? Quæ natura efficiendi non habet, sed sine qua id quod faciendum est effici non potest. Hanc Latini vulgò materiā appellant: Græci ὕλη. ad naturarum quidem cognitionem, aptissimè: sed ad vsum Dialecticum, & actionum notationem, imperitissimè. Nam (vt Cicero in primo Academico scribit) de natura, inquit, ita dicebant, vt eam diuiderent in res duas: vt altera esset efficiens, altera autem quasi huic se præbens, ex qua efficeretur aliquid. In eo quod efficeret, vim esse cēsebant: in eo autem quod efficeretur, materiam quandam. At vbi de actionibus quæritur, longè alia ratio est.
units.tr: What is the cause without which not? That which has no power of producing, but without which that which is to be done cannot be effected. Latin writers commonly call this matter; the Greeks call it [ὕλη]. It is most apt for the knowledge of natures, but most unskilled for dialectical use and for the description of actions. For (as Cicero writes in the first book of the Academics) they spoke of nature in this way, dividing it into two things: one was the efficient, the other, as it were, offering itself to this, from which something is made. In what does the making they held there to be power; in what is made, a certain matter. But where actions are inquired into, the case is quite different.

units.la: Cedo vtrarumque exemplum. Primùm omnium ponatur, (vt antè monuimus) euentus, tum deinde caussa quæratur. nam hæc natura quidem prior est: at ille consideratione. In rebus igitur naturalibus, Quum materia est pulli:aqua est materia glaciei. In artificiofis,æs materia est statuæ: corium calcei. In a&ionibus verò naturalibus,caussa incendij sine qua non,est somes : in artificialibus,instrumentum caussa est sine qua non : ut nauigādi, nauis:vehendi,rheda:ambulandi, locus:accusandi,oratio.
units.tr: Let me give examples of both. First, let an outcome be set down (as we said before), and then the cause sought; for the cause is indeed prior in nature, but the outcome is prior in our consideration. In natural things, therefore: when there is a chick, water is the matter of ice. In artificial things, bronze is the matter of a statue, hide the matter of a shoe. In natural actions, the cause without which not of a fire is fuel; in artificial actions, an instrument is the cause without which not: for sailing, the ship; for conveying, the cart; for walking, the ground; for accusing, the speech.

units.la: Quæ est forma? Est naturalis cuiusque rei nota,per quam quæque vel res,vel actio,est id quod est, atq; ab altera discrépat. velut in rebus naturalibus,Ratio in homine,caussa est & quòd homo est, & quòd differt à bellua. vita in arbore, caussa est quòd & arbos est, & differt à trunco. In artificiosis, volubilitas in cylindro:at in actionibus naturæ , veluti incédij forma est,ardor. In artificiosis,motus mediocris forma est deambulationis : motus velox, forma est cursus. nam quæ sub eodem genere sunt,forma discrepant. Vsque ædeo autem verum est,formam esse per quam quæque res est id quod est,ut quanuis corpus maneat,tamen si forma mutata sit , nō eadē esse res videatur. veluti si ex scypho massa fa&a sit, Itaq; qui ad exhibēdum scyphũ tenetur,massam exhibēdo non liberatur. l. Iul. 9, s. siquis, D. ad exhib.
units.tr: What is form? It is the natural mark of each thing, by which each thing or action is what it is and differs from another. For example, in natural things, reason in man is the cause both of his being a man and of his differing from a beast; life in a tree is the cause both of its being a tree and of its differing from a trunk. In artificial things, roundness is the form of a cylinder; but in actions of nature, for example, the form of a fire is heat. In artificial things, a moderate motion is the form of walking, a swift motion is the form of running; for things that are under the same genus differ in form. Indeed it is so true that form is that by which each thing is what it is, that although the body remains, yet if the form has been changed, the thing does not seem to be the same. For example, if a cup has been made into a lump of metal, then one who is bound to produce the cup is not released by producing the lump. Digest, Julian, law 9, section "if anyone," title "on production."

units.la: Quæ est finis? Propter quàm quæque res & actio vel instituta, vel impedita est. Horum enim utrunque in fine considerandum est : ac propterea unum quodque eorum suam habet notam, ut, & xe. In rebus naturæ , veluti, Homo ere&us est, ut cœlum potius quàm terram contemplctur : vel,ne pecudum ritu perpetuò terram intueatur. In artificiosis, Naui instituitur, vt transmarinæ cómoditates parentur:& ne iis carere homines cogantur. Deambulaturà cœna, vt cibus in imum stomachum deprimatur: &, ne cibus fluitet in ore ventriculi. Domus finis est, ne tempestatibus lædamur, & vt seruari supellex possit, Jam in actionibus naturæ:veluti, Sol terram ambit, vt mortalibus luceat: néve mortales perpetuò sint in tenebris.in artificiosis, exercitatio suscipitur,vt valetudo côseruetur, néve morbi contrahantur.
units.tr: What is the end? That for the sake of which each thing or action is either undertaken or hindered. For both of these must be considered in the end, and therefore each of them has its own mark, as "and" and "xe" [sic]. In natural things, for example: man is upright so that he may contemplate the heavens rather than the earth, or so that he may not gaze perpetually at the earth in the manner of beasts. In artificial things: a ship is built so that the advantages of overseas may be obtained, and so that men are not forced to go without them. One walks after dinner so that the food may be pressed down into the lowest part of the stomach, and so that the food does not float in the mouth of the stomach. A house has as its end that we may not be harmed by storms, and that household goods may be kept safe. Now in actions of nature: for example, the sun circles the earth so that it may shine on mortals, and that mortals may not be perpetually in darkness. In artificial actions: exercise is undertaken so that health may be preserved, and that diseases may not be contracted.

units.la: Quis est causarum ordo? Duplex omnino est,naturæ & considerationis.naturæ,is quem secuti sumus. nã cùm efficiens mouendi principium sit, atque in eo vis infit efficiendi primaria,princeps ei debetur locus. Hunc sequitur causa sine qua non:mox species,qua quæque res ad exemplar in animo informatum fingitur.Postremò finis,quem constat esse bonum aliquod, cuius adipiscendi gratia res omnis efficitur. At ordo considerationis huic plane contrarius est: nam rei cuiusque contemplatio ex eo bono quod in fine inest,principium ducit: gradatimque ad ea quæ minus bona sunt,regreditur.
units.tr: What is the order of causes? It is twofold: of nature and of consideration. The order of nature is the one we have followed; for since the efficient cause is the principle of motion, and in it lies the primary power of producing, the first place is rightly given to it. The cause without which not follows this; then the form, by which each thing is shaped according to the pattern conceived in the mind; last, the end, which is agreed to be some good, for the sake of attaining which every thing is brought about. But the order of consideration is quite the opposite of this: for the contemplation of each thing takes its beginning from the good that is present in the end, and it proceeds step by step down to those things that are less good.

units.la: Quid? Materia corporis effecti, nónne prior est opifice? veluti, aurum annuli nónne prius est aurifice? & materia domus, quæ ex trabibus, calce & lateribus constat, nónne prius est naturæ ordine, quàm Architectus? Nequaquam. Idque facile tum ex naturalibus,tū ex artificialibus rebus, & nouatis materiis intelligi potest. nam & vitriarius prior est,quàm vitrum:& pistor prior est farina: architectus nauis prior est,quàm tabulæ: neque enim ita natæ tabulæ sunt, Atque ad hunc locum iocularis illa quæstio pertinet, de qua est apud Macrobium : Ouúmne prius fuerit, quàm Gallina. nam fi natura perfecta creauit animalia,vt Philosophi quoque ipsi statuunt, & Religio nos nostra docuit: prius certè Gallinam fuisse,quàm ouum necesse est.
units.tr: What then? Is the matter of a made body not prior to the craftsman? For example, is the gold of a ring not prior to the goldsmith? And is the matter of a house, which consists of beams, lime and bricks, not prior in the order of nature to the architect? By no means. And this can easily be understood both from natural things and from artificial things, and from newly devised materials. For the glassmaker is prior to the glass, and the baker is prior to the flour; the shipwright is prior to the planks, for planks are not born in that form. To this point pertains that playful question which is found in Macrobius: whether the hen or the egg was first. For if nature created perfect animals, as the philosophers themselves also hold, and our religion has taught us, then it is certainly necessary that the hen was before the egg.

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplū. Materia domus sunt trabes, calx, lateres,aut lapides excisi.annon igitur materiarius, prior fuit quàm trabes? aut coctor, quàm lateres? aut cementarius, quàm calx? aut faber, quàm lapis excisus, aptus & quadratus?
units.tr: Let me give another example. The matter of a house is beams, lime, bricks, or hewn stones. Is not then the timber-merchant prior to the beams? Or the brick-burner prior to the bricks? Or the mason prior to the lime? Or the workman prior to the hewn stone, fitted and squared?

units.la: De multiplici causarum efficientium genere.
units.tr: On the manifold kind of efficient causes.

units.la: CAP. IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: QVÆ[?] est causarum diuisio? Prima efficientium diuisio est, vt aliæ sunt absolutæ, perfectæ, & principales; aliæ adiuuantes, adiunctæ, & quasi sociæ. Illas Græci vocant αἰτία ἐνεργοῦντα καθ' αὑτὰ[?] : has verò συναίτια[?], vel ὑπεργοῦντα[?].
units.tr: What is the division of causes? The first division of efficient causes is that some are absolute, perfect and principal, while others are helping, accessory and, as it were, companions. The Greeks call the former αἰτία ἐνεργοῦντα καθ' αὑτά [aitia energounta kath' hauta], and the latter συναίτια [synaitia] or ὑπεργοῦντα [hypergounta].

units.la: Quæ est absoluta? Quæ per fe ac sua sponte vim habet efficiendi: velut, ignis per fe ac vi sua incendit. Sol vi sua lucet, colorat, incendit. hæc autem rursus bipartita est.
units.tr: What is an absolute cause? One that has the power of producing an effect by itself and of its own accord: for example, fire burns by itself and by its own power. The sun by its own power gives light, colours and heat. This kind of cause is in turn divided into two.

units.la: Quomodo? Ut alia sola in rerum natura efficiendi vim habeat; ideóque cum euentu reciprocetur. alia verò non sola in eo genere fit. veluti, Vbicunque ignis est, incendiù est: & vicissim vbicunque incendium, ibidem ignis est. Item; Vbicunque corpus in lumine est, ibi vmbra est, vicissimque vbicunque vmbra est, ibidem corpus in lumine est. Nihil est enim quod vel incendium efficiat, præter ignem: vel vmbram, præter corpus. At si aliud caussæ genus est, non reciprocantur: veluti, Si calet, ad ignem sese calefecit. Potest enim ex febri calere. Sol vi sua colorat: sed nō quicunque coloratus est, continuò à Sole est. Sol capitis dolorem vi sua facit: at non utique qui ex capite laborat, à Sole caussam habuit. Alia enim præter Solem eam vim & efficientiā habent. sic, Non si mulier nō peperit, iccirco cū viro non concubuit.
units.tr: How so? Some causes are the only ones in nature with the power to produce a given effect, and so they are convertible with that effect. Others are not the only cause of their kind. For example: wherever there is fire, there is burning; and conversely, wherever there is burning, there is fire. Likewise: wherever a body is in the light, there is a shadow; and conversely, wherever there is a shadow, there a body is in the light. For nothing produces a burning except fire, or a shadow except a body. But if the cause belongs to another kind, the two are not convertible. For example: if someone is warm, he has not warmed himself at a fire, since he may be warm from a fever. The sun by its own power colours things, but not everything that is coloured is coloured by the sun. The sun by its own power causes headache, yet not everyone who suffers from the head has the sun as his cause, for other things besides the sun have that power and efficacy. Thus: if a woman has not given birth, it does not follow that she has not lain with a man.

units.la: Quæ est adiuuans? Quæ non per se ac vi sua efficit: sed efficiendi socia est. veluti, Exercitatio caussa est eloquentiæ, non efficiens per se, sed adiuuans. Uinū febricitāti mortis caussam affert: labor in corpore impuro morbi caussam præbet. hæc verò vel propinqua est, vel remota.
units.tr: What is a helping cause? One that does not produce the effect by itself and by its own power, but is an associate in producing it. For example: exercise is a cause of eloquence, not an efficient cause by itself but a helper. Wine brings about death for one with a fever; labour in an unhealthy body provides the cause of disease. This helping cause is either proximate or remote.

units.la: Quæ est adiuuans propinqua?. Quæ efficienter antecedit: ut illa, quam modò posui, labor in corpore vitioso.
units.tr: What is a proximate helping cause? One that acts as an efficient cause immediately before the effect: such as the labour in a diseased body that I have just mentioned.

units.la: Quæ est Remota? Hæc duplex est. Nam aut consentanea est,aut aliena, Consentanea est, quæ naturam habet cum effectu ita congruentem, ut tamen hic & sequi, & non sequi potuerit: veluti, iurgium, aut inimicitia sæpe caussa est cædis antecedens,non tamen neceffaria. Collocutio sæpe caussa est coniugij antecedens,sed non necessaria.
units.tr: What is a remote cause? This is of two kinds. For it is either consonant or foreign. A consonant cause is one whose nature is so congruent with the effect that, although in this case it could both follow and not follow, it is nonetheless often its cause: for example, a quarrel or enmity often precedes and causes a killing, but not necessarily. A conversation often precedes and causes a marriage, but not necessarily.

units.la: Quæ est Aliena? Quæ cùm naturam habeat ab effectu dissentaneam, tamen propinquam caussam commouit. Itaque imperitè & abusiuè ex vulgi errore Caussa nominatur: cū[?] verius Opinata vel Pfeudocauffa dici possit: velut in illo, Veritas odium parit. Veritasenim ab odio alienissima, improbitatem quæ caussa est adiuuans,& propinqua,commouit, irritauit, exciuit. Sic negligentia patrisfam, vulgò dicitur caussa fuisse furi rem neglectam aufercendi: & viator bene vestitus (inquit Cicero)caussa grassatori fuisse dicitur,cur ab eo spoliaretur. Ex eodem genere illud Prouerbium est, Bonæ leges ex malis moribus procreantur. Itémque illa poëtarum iocularia & ab arte nostra longè abhorrentia, quæ Cicero in libro de Fato verius ad antecedentia retulit. veluti Hecuba Troianis caussa interitus fuit,quòd Alexandrum genuit.
units.tr: What is a foreign cause? One that, although its nature is dissimilar to the effect, nonetheless set in motion the proximate cause. Hence, carelessly and improperly, by the error of the common people, it is called a cause; but it could more truly be called an apparent or pseudo-cause. Take the saying "Truth breeds hatred." Truth, being most alien to hatred, has stirred up, provoked and roused wickedness, which is the helping and proximate cause. Thus it is commonly said that the negligence of a householder was the cause of a thief's carrying off the neglected property; and, as Cicero says, a traveller well dressed is said to have been the cause for a robber to strip him. To the same class belongs the proverb, "Good laws are born of bad morals." Also those jesting remarks of the poets, far removed from our art, which Cicero in his book On Fate more truly referred to antecedents, such as: "Hecuba was the cause of the destruction of the Trojans, because she bore Alexander."

units.la: Utinam ne in nemore Pelio securibus Cæsa cecidisset abiegna ad terram trabes,&c.
units.tr: Would that in the Pelian grove the fir beams had never fallen to the ground, cut down by axes, etc.

units.la: Quæ est altera Caussarum efficientium diuisio? Vt aliæ sint Procreatrices,quæ effentiâ & ortum significant: veluti superiores: aliæ
units.tr: What is the other division of efficient causes? Some are generative, which signify essence and origin, like those above; others

units.la: Peremptrices, quæ interitum afferunt. Illæ γεννητικαὶ[?] à Græcis, hæ φθαρτικαὶ[?] dicuntur. Et rursus aliæ per se, vt Aqua ignem extinguit: aliæ cum adiunctione, vt Vinum febricitanti mortis causam affert.
units.tr: are destructive, which bring about ruin. The Greeks call the former γεννητικαί [gennētikai], the latter φθαρτικαί [phthartikai]. And again, some act by themselves, as water extinguishes fire; others act with an addition, as wine brings death to one who has a fever.

units.la: Quæ est tertia Efficientium causarum diuisio? Vt aliæ in voluntate positæ sint, aliæ in fortuna, aliæ in necessitate, aliæ in imprudentia.
units.tr: What is the third division of efficient causes? Some lie in the will, others in chance, others in necessity, others in imprudence.

units.la: Quæ est voluntaria? Ea duplex est, aut Impulsiua, aut Ratiocinatiua. Impulsiuam Fortunatianus Rhetor & Iurisconsultus eam esse dicit, quam Græci ὁρμητικὴν[?] appellant, vt iram, odium. Ratiocinatiuam, quam iidem λογιστικὴν[?] vocant, vt lucrum, hereditatem. Quibus verbis significat, impulsiuam esse, quæ in impetu & perturbatione animi posita rationis expers est: qualis est ægritudo, iracundia, vinolétia[?], desperatio. Vt cùm Aiax, vbi resciuit quæ per insaniam fecerat, gladio incubuit: aut cùm Annibal, Themistocles, Cato Vticensis[?], odio vitæ adducti, necem sibi consciuerunt.
units.tr: What is a voluntary cause? It is of two kinds: either impulsive or rational. Fortunatianus, a rhetorician and jurist, says the impulsive kind is what the Greeks call ὁρμητική [hormētikē], such as anger or hatred. The rational kind, which the same writers call λογιστική [logistikē], is such as gain or inheritance. By these words he means that the impulsive cause is one which, rooted in the impetus and agitation of the mind, is devoid of reason: such are sickness, rage, drunken folly, despair. So when Ajax, on learning what he had done in madness, fell upon his sword; or when Hannibal, Themistocles and Cato of Utica, driven by hatred of life, brought death upon themselves.

units.la: Quam appellas Ratiocinatiuā? Quæ in ratione, consilio, & deliberatione posita, bonum aliquod tanquam finem propositum habet. Ita cùm animus noster[?] in duas distributus sit partes, quarum altera rationis est particeps, altera expers: ad hanc impulsiua, ad illam ratiocinatiua referenda est: in eáque differentia, momentum plerunque maximum est. Atque hoc eodem modo Cicero libro de Inuèt. II.vtranque hanc caussam explicauit.
units.tr: What do you call rational? That which, rooted in reason, counsel and deliberation, has some good as its proposed end. Since our mind is divided into two parts, one of which partakes of reason and the other lacks it, the impulsive cause is to be referred to the one and the rational cause to the other; and in this difference the weight is usually very great. In this same way Cicero, in Book II of On Invention, explained both these causes.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Ponatur lex, vt Tyrānicidæ præmium detur. Comprehēsus in adulterio à Tyranno, eum occidit. Quia Tyrannicida proprie est, qui liberandæ Reip. caussa Tyrannum interfecit, præmium non debebitur. caussa enim occidendi non ratiocinatio fuit, sed impulsio. Ponatur altera lex: Parricida in culeum insuatur: Cùm Tyrannus regno pulsus arma in Remp. ferret, prælio commisso, filius qui pro Repub. pugnabat, patrē qui à Tyranno stabat, interfecit. Hic parricida nō est. Rationem enim habuit patriæ liberationem.
units.tr: Give me an example. Let there be a law that a reward be given to the tyrannicide. A man caught in adultery by a tyrant kills him. Since a tyrannicide properly is one who kills a tyrant for the sake of liberating the commonwealth, no reward will be due, for the cause of the killing was not reasoning but impulse. Let there be another law: a parricide shall be sewn into a sack. When a tyrant, driven from his kingdom, took up arms against the state, in battle a son who was fighting for the republic killed his father, who was standing with the tyrant. This man is not a parricide, for he had regard to the liberation of his country.

units.la: Quæ est fortuita? Cuius caussa humanitus ignota est: veluti Piscatio caussa fuit fortuita Milefiis aurei tripodis reperiendi. Et fossio scrobis fuit caussa Timoni Misanthropo thesauri inueniendi: & apud Iurisconsultos pila à lusore percussa, & in nouaculam tonsoris adacta, caussa fuit hominis iugulandi.
units.tr: What is a chance cause? One whose cause is unknown to men: for example, fishing was by chance the cause of the Milesians' finding a golden tripod. And digging a pit was by chance the cause of Timon the Misanthrope's finding a treasure; and among the jurists, a ball struck by a player and driven onto a barber's razor was the cause of a man's having his throat cut.

units.la: Quæ est caussa ex necessitate efficiens? Cū quid alterius coactu, & vi aut metu factum est. vt siquis Potentioris imperio quempiam interfecerit. quo de genere illud est Laberij, qui Cæsaris coactu in scœnam prodiit.
units.tr: What is a cause that works by necessity? When something is done at another's compulsion, by force or by fear: for example, if someone kills a man by the command of a more powerful person. To this class belongs the line of Laberius, who came forward onto the stage at Caesar's compulsion.

units.la: Necessitas cuius aduersa impetum Voluerunt multi effugere, pauci potuerunt: Quò me detrusit pene extremis sensibus?
units.tr: Necessity, whose assault many wished to escape and few were able to: where has it thrust me, almost at my last breath?

units.la: Quæ est caussa ex imprudētia? Cùm quid neque confultò, neque casu, sed per errorem factum est. veluti : Siquis publico in ludo iaculans prætereuntem transfixerit : aut putator, ramum arboris in trâseuntem deiecerit: aut qui amphoram instituerat, currête rotam urceum effecerit : aut aliquis per ebrietatem flagitium admiserit.
units.tr: What is a cause from imprudence? When something is done neither deliberately nor by chance, but through error. For example: if someone, throwing a javelin in a public game, pierces a passer-by; or a pruner knocks a branch from a tree onto someone passing beneath; or someone who was carrying a jar, running, makes a wheel strike a pitcher; or someone commits a crime through drunkenness.

units.la: Quæ est quarta efficientium divisio? Ut alia adesse, alia vero abesse dicatur : cuius utriusque par eademque in contrarium vis atque efficientia est. quod enim præsens caussa, quoniam adest, efficit: eius contrarium absens, eo ipso quod abest, efficit.
units.tr: What is the fourth division of efficient causes? Some are said to be present, others to be absent; and each has an equal and the same power and efficacy, but in opposite directions. For what, being present, produces an effect because it is present, its opposite produces, being absent, by the very fact that it is absent.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Ut Gubernator cùm adest, recti cursus tenendi, caussa est: sic idē cùm abest, naufragij caussa esse dicitur. Quod idem in medico, in custode, & similibus dici potest. Mors Hectoris caussa fuit amittendæ Troiæ: cùm eā vivus conservaret. Sic fuga ducis ex prelio caussa est offensionis: cùm eiusdē præsentia victoriæ caussa fuisset. Itē, Negligentia præceptoris, caussa est inscitiæ puerorum: cùm eius diligentia eruditionis caussa esse potuisset. Sic accessus Solis, caussa est æstatis: recessus caussa hyemis.
units.tr: Give me an example. A helmsman, when he is present, is the cause of holding a straight course; likewise when he is absent he is said to be the cause of shipwreck. The same can be said of a physician, a guardian and the like. The death of Hector was the cause of the loss of Troy, since while he lived he preserved it. So a leader's flight from battle is the cause of defeat, whereas his presence would have been the cause of victory. Again, a teacher's negligence is the cause of the boys' ignorance, whereas his diligence could have been the cause of their learning. So the approach of the sun is the cause of summer, its withdrawal the cause of winter.

units.la: Quotuplex est Caussa sine qua nō? Duplex. altera quieta, & tanquam stolida: altera verò adiuvans.
units.tr: How many kinds are there of a cause without which not? Two: one quiet and, as it were, passive; the other helping.

units.la: Quæ est quieta? In rebus, materia: ut coriū calceolario: in actionibus, facultas, siue instrumentum. ut viatori, navis, equus, rheda. Instrumenti autem nomine, ferramenta, locum, tempus, & cetera generis eiusdem comprehendimus. Sic in Dialectica perdiscéda causfa fine qua non, est acumen ingenij: in Iurisprudentia, memoria fidelis. Sic Mathematicae scientiae cognitio causa est, fine qua non Aristotelis logica plane intelligitur. Itaque in ipsius vestibulo, recte vetus illud inscribi posset, ἀδὲς ἀγεωμέτρητος εἰς σέγγω. Ex eodem genere illud est Ciceronis, Tuscul. [?]. Si Numa Pompilius auditor fuit Pythagorae, necesse est eodem tempore utrunque vixisse. Et alibi: Si Sex. Roscius Romae patrem occidit, necesse est eum Romae fuisse.
units.tr: What is the quiet kind? In things, matter, as leather is for a shoemaker; in actions, the capacity or the instrument, as a ship, a horse or a carriage is for a traveller. Under the name of instrument we include tools, place, time and other things of the same sort. Thus in learning dialectic the cause without which not is a sharp wit; in jurisprudence, a faithful memory. Likewise a knowledge of the mathematical sciences is a cause without which Aristotle's logic is not clearly understood. And so at its very threshold that old saying could rightly be inscribed: "Let no one ignorant of geometry enter" [ἀγεωμέτρητος μηδεὶς εἰσίτω]. To the same class belongs Cicero's statement in the Tusculan Disputations [reference illegible]: "If Numa Pompilius was a hearer of Pythagoras, it is necessary that the two lived at the same time." And elsewhere: "If Sextus Roscius killed his father at Rome, it is necessary that he was at Rome."

units.la: Quae est adiuuans? Quae cùm antecessit, facultatem & opportunitate negotio præbuit. ut collocutio cū hoste, proditionis causa est: cohortatio Imperatoris, causa est virtutis in militibus. monitio Praeceptoris, causa eruditionis in adolescentibus. itē [?] diligentia, & excitatio in arte Dialectica, ceterisque disciplinis percipiendis.
units.tr: What is a helping cause? One that, having gone before, has provided the facility and the opportunity for an undertaking. Thus a conversation with the enemy is the cause of betrayal; an general's exhortation is the cause of courage in soldiers; a teacher's admonition is the cause of learning in young men; likewise diligence and encouragement are causes of mastering dialectic and the other disciplines.

units.la: De Effectis. CAP. X.
units.tr: On Effects. Chapter 10.

units.la: VAE sunt Effecta? Quae ex causarum concursu & quasi cōspiratione eueniunt. Itaque à Graecis αἰτίας [?]; à nostris Euenta nominatur. De quibus est illud Ciceronis: Causarum cognitio cognitionem euentorum facit. Nōnulli autē ἐκβάσις, id est exitus appellant: quod nihil in iis tractetur, nisi quid ex quoque euenerit.
units.tr: What are effects? Those things that come about from a concurrence, and as it were a conspiring together, of causes. Hence the Greeks call them αἰτίας [?], while ours name them events (Euenta). Of these Cicero says: "Knowledge of causes produces knowledge of events." Some, however, call them ekbasis [ἐκβάσις], that is, outcomes, because in them nothing is treated except what has resulted from each thing.

units.la: Quotuplex est Effectus? Quoniam effecta respondent caussis, eaque inter se referuntur; adaequantur, & parem rationem habet, sequitur vt Affectorum eadem plane quae caussarum diuisio sit. Alia enim Effecta sunt caussarum efficientium: alia causse sine qua non: alia formæ: alia finis.
units.tr: How many kinds of effect are there? Since effects correspond to causes and are related to them, and since they match and stand in the same relation, it follows that the division of effects is exactly the same as the division of causes. So some effects are of efficient causes, some of the cause without which the thing would not be, some of form, and some of end.

units.la: Quae est altera diuisio? Vt effectorum alia sint procreantia, alia interimetia. Illa ἀφύσεις[?], hæc φθοραὶ[?] nominantur. Prioris exempla sunt, velut in natura, flores, frondes, fruges. In artibus, opera effecta. Posterioris, velut in natura, deflorescere, arescere, defrondescere. in artibus, cædes, vastitates.
units.tr: What is the other division? Some effects are generative, others destructive. The former are called aphyseis [ἀφύσεις], the latter phthorai [φθοραί]. Examples of the former, in nature, are flowers, leaves and crops; in the arts, finished works. Examples of the latter, in nature, are shedding blossoms, withering, and losing leaves; in the arts, slaughters and devastations.

units.la: Quae est alia? Vt euentorum alia naturalia sint, quae naturalem caussam arguunt. vt defectio Lunae, arguit terrae interuentum: Tonitru arguit ignis restinctionem[?] in nube: frondium lapsus, arguit humoris concretionem. alia voluntaria, quae hominum iudicio & voluntate effecta sunt, vt opificum & artificum opera. alia fortuita, vt cum hostis vomicam Pharei Iafonis aperuit, quam sanare medici non potuerunt.
units.tr: What is another division? Some events are natural, indicating a natural cause: an eclipse of the moon indicates the interposition of the earth; thunder indicates the extinguishing of fire in a cloud; the falling of leaves indicates the condensing of moisture. Others are voluntary, brought about by human judgement and will, such as the works of craftsmen and artisans. Others are fortuitous, as when an enemy opened the abscess of Jason of Pherae, which the physicians could not heal.

units.la: Quae sunt Relata? Loco tu quidem quaeris. sed quia Relata sunt ex oppositorum, siue contrariorum genere (situ enim & positione adversantur: tametsi re & natura maximè consentanea sint) propterea satius videtur eorum explicationem ad contrariorum locum reseruare.
units.tr: What are relatives? You are indeed asking in the right place; but since relatives arise from the class of opposites, or contraries (for they are opposed in situation and position, although in substance and nature they agree most closely), it seems better to reserve their explanation for the place of contraries.

units.la: De Proprio. CAP. XI.
units.tr: Of the Proprium. CHAP. XI.

units.la: E Proprio igitur dicamus. Quid est Proprium? Vis & facultas rei cuiuspiam naturaliter, peculiariter, & inseparabiliter adhærescens. Græci ἴδιον[?] appellant. veluti, Proprium hominis est, ut sit rationis, sermonis, ordinis & disciplinæ capax. Hoc solum animal natum est, (inquit Cicero) pudoris & verecundiæ particeps. Proprium piscium est, ut aquarum sint incolæ: volucrium, ut cœlo libero fruantur: quadrupedum, ut gradiantur. Sic Animantium quarundam proprium est, ut sint cicures: aliarum, ut sint immanes: quarundam, ut sint soliuagæ: aliarum, ut congregatæ. Ridendi facultas hominí à natura peculiariter attributa est, sic ut neque alii ulli sit communis, neque adimi ei possit. Frugalitatis proprium est (inquit Cicero) motus animi appetentis regere & sedare. Proprium stultitiæ, aliorum vitia cernere, obliuisci suorum. Proprium sapientis, nihil quod pœnitere possit facere. Sic proprietatis quæstionem idem esse dicit, In hominémne solum cadat, an etiam in belluas ægritudo. Plura autem interdum eiusdem rei propria sunt: ut hominis, ratio, sermo, risus, verecundia[?], medicina, docilitas. Ignis lucere, calefacere, in sublime ferri.
units.tr: Let us therefore speak of the Proprium. What is the Proprium? It is the force or capacity of some thing, adhering to it naturally, peculiarly and inseparably. The Greeks call it idion [ἴδιον]. For example, it is proper to man to be capable of reason, speech, order and discipline. "This alone of animals," says Cicero, "is born to share in modesty and shame." It is proper to fish that they dwell in the waters, to birds that they enjoy the open sky, to four-footed animals that they walk. Thus it is proper to some animals to be tame, to others to be savage; to some to be solitary, to others to live in flocks. The faculty of laughter has been peculiarly bestowed on man by nature, so that it is shared with no other creature and cannot be taken from him. It is the proper mark of frugality, says Cicero, to govern and calm the movements of an appetitive mind. The proper mark of folly is to see the faults of others and forget one's own; the proper mark of the wise man is to do nothing he could repent of. In the same way, he says, the question of what is proper is whether sickness falls only upon man or also upon beasts. Moreover, several things are sometimes proper to the same thing: to man, reason, speech, laughter, modesty, medicine, teachability; to fire, to shine, to heat, and to be carried upward.

units.la: Quotuplex est Proprium? Duplex: alterum verè proprium, quod speciei soli convenit: ut homini ratione uti, loqui, mederi. cani,latratus: piscibus, aquatio. alterum quasi proprium, quod utique perpetuum est, sed non soli. ut cicurem esse, homini conuenit, sed non soli. Ignis calefacit: at non solus. Illud reciprocatur cum subiecto: hoc non reciprocatur. nam si quid ridet, homo est: & si homo est, ridet. si quid latrat, canis est: & si canis est, latrat. At, non ut si est ignis, calefacit: iccirco si calefacit, continuò ignis est. Sol enim etiam calefacit. Si est piscis, natat. At non si natat, cōtinuò piscis est: nam & homo & bos & canis natare possunt. si est auis, volat. sed non si volat, continuò auis est: quidam enim pisces volant.
units.tr: How many kinds of Proprium are there? Two. The one is truly proper, which belongs to the species alone: as for man to use reason, to speak and to heal; for the dog, to bark; for fish, to swim. The other is, as it were, proper: it is indeed perpetual, but not peculiar to one thing. For example, being tame belongs to man, but not to man alone; fire heats, but not fire alone. The first reciprocates with its subject, the second does not. For if a thing laughs, it is a man, and if it is a man, it laughs; if a thing barks, it is a dog, and if it is a dog, it barks. But it does not follow that if a thing is fire, it heats, and so if it heats, it is at once fire, for the sun also heats. If a thing is a fish, it swims; but it does not follow that if it swims, it is at once a fish, for man, ox and dog can also swim. If a thing is a bird, it flies; but if it flies, it is not at once a bird, for some fish fly.

units.la: Quæ est altera Proprii diuisio? Aristoteles fecit quadripartitam, ut primum sit illud verè proprium, [?]κυρίως ἴδιον, quod uni speciei soli & toti, hoc est omnibus eius indiuiduis & semper conuenit: ut ridere. alterum, quod uni speciei tantū conuenit, sed non toti. veluti iustum esse, & Aristidis similem, soli conuenit homini, sed non omnibus: tertium, quod universæ speciei conuenit, at non soli: ut bipedem esse. quartum, quod soli speciei conuenit, sed non semper: ut in senectute canescere. nam equi quoque canescunt.
units.tr: What is the other division of the Proprium? Aristotle made a fourfold one. The first is that which is truly proper [κυρίως ἴδιον], which belongs to one species alone, and to the whole of it, that is, to all its individuals, and always: such as laughing. The second belongs to one species only, but not to all of it: such as being just, and being like Aristides, which belong to man alone but not to every man. The third belongs to the whole species but not to it alone: such as being two-footed. The fourth belongs to the species alone but not always: such as growing grey in old age, for horses also grow grey.

units.la: De Antecedente. CAP. XII.
units.tr: On the Antecedent. CHAP. XII.

units.la: VIS est Antecedens? Quo vel posito, aliud quod ei cohæret, subsequitur: vel negato, non subsequitur. Græci [?] appellant.veluti:Si est ver,eftas subsequitur:fi est aurora,dies.Ex cótrario,Quod quis non habuit, non perdidit. Si non vixit poftumus (inquibat Crassus) nó est mortuus. Si amabat,non læsit sciens.Ex hoc genere sunt naturales affectiones,quæ à Græcis [?] nominantur.Si est mater,diligit filium. quod argumentum Salomon in illo nobili iudicio fequutus est. Item: Si filius est , parentem verebitur. Nam hæc consecutio naturæ ordine inftituta est:& quia caussam habet naturalé,non vitiosam , necessaria est. Sic Parentes suos liberos incolumes & beatos esse cupiunt : vicifsimque liberi suos parentes.
units.tr: What is an antecedent? It is that which, when it is posited, something else that coheres with it follows; when it is denied, that something does not follow. The Greeks [?] call it. For example: If it is spring, summer follows; if it is dawn, day follows. Conversely: What someone did not have, he did not lose. If the posthumous child did not live (Crassus used to say), it is not dead. If he loved, he did not harm knowingly. Of this kind are the natural affections, which the Greeks call [?]. If there is a mother, she loves her son. Solomon followed this argument in that famous judgment. Likewise: If there is a son, he will revere his parent. For this sequence was established by the order of nature, and because it has a natural and not a faulty cause, it is necessary. So parents desire their children to be safe and happy, and children in turn desire the same for their parents.

units.la: Quotuplex est antecedens? Duplex. Alterum proprium,quod necessario cohæret:alterum improprium,quod vel probabiliter tantum,vel fortuito cohæret. Illa reciprocantur inter fe,ac vicissim retróque commeant. hæc non reciprocantur.
units.tr: How many kinds of antecedent are there? Two. One is proper, which coheres necessarily; the other is improper, which coheres only probably or by chance. The former are reciprocal with one another, and pass back and forth in turn; the latter are not reciprocal.

units.la: Quæ sunt propria? Quæ inter fe pariter & necessario cohærent.veluti, Si viuit,morietur. &, fi mortu' est,vixit. Si est aurora,lucebit sol. &,fi Sol lucet, aurora antecessit. Si est ver,fuit hyems.&,fi est hyems,ver consequetur.
units.tr: Which are proper? Those that cohere with one another equally and necessarily. For example: If he is alive, he will die; and, if he is dead, he has lived. If it is dawn, the sun will shine; and, if the sun shines, dawn has gone before. If it is spring, winter has been; and, if it is winter, spring will follow.

units.la: Quæ sunt impropria? Quorum alterum necessario cohæret,alterum probabiliter,aut fortuito. Itaque hæc inter fe non reciprocantur. veluti : Satio arguit aratione necessario, aratio verò sationem probabiliter tantum. Exitum antecessit ingressus necessario. At nō siquis ingressus est, sequitur ut sit egressurus. Propterea autem Antecedentia aut consequentia haec dicuntur, non adiuncta, aut accidentia, quoniam eorum alterum proprium est. quod si neutrum est proprium, ad illum afsectionum locum hoc totum referendum est.
units.tr: Which are improper? Those of which one necessarily coheres, while the other coheres probably or by chance. Thus these do not reciprocate with one another. For example: Sowing necessarily implies ploughing, but ploughing implies sowing only probably. Going out is necessarily preceded by going in. But it does not follow that if someone has gone in, he is going to go out. These are therefore called antecedents or consequents, not "adjuncts" or "accidents", because one of each pair is proper. But if neither is proper, the whole matter must be referred to that place of affections.

units.la: Quid interest inter antecedens & caussam? Caussa & necessario & efficienter antecedit.
units.tr: What is the difference between an antecedent and a cause? A cause precedes both necessarily and efficiently.

units.la: Antecedes vero interdum necessario tantum, interdu aut probabiliter, aut fortuito tantum. non enim vis efficiendi in illo est. Itaque si Sol exortus est, dies est, quod ex caussis sumitur. At si lucifer exortus est, dies oritur, quod ex Antecedentibus ducitur.
units.tr: An antecedent, however, sometimes precedes only necessarily, and sometimes only probably or by chance, for there is no power of producing in it. So, if the sun has risen, it is day, and this is taken from causes. But if Lucifer (the morning star) has risen, day dawns, and this is drawn from antecedents.

units.la: De Consequentibus. CAP. XIII.
units.tr: On Consequents. CHAP. XIII.

units.la: Q[?]UID est Consequens? Quod cum eo quod antecessit necessario cohæret. Græci ἀκόλουθον appellant: velut in caussa Curiana, Si Postumus mortuus est, vixit. Quo in genere iocus est ille Parisiensium, Si mulierculæ vivæ sunt e monachorum claustris egredi, prius introierant. Item privantia omnia: Si amisit, habuerat. Si recuperavit, amiserat: si convaluit, ægrotarat. Ex quo illud est Fabij Maximi, qui Livio Salinatori, qui Tarento amisso fugerat in arcem, multaque ex ea prælia præclara fecerat, glorianti atque dicenti: Mea opera Q. Fabi Tarentum recepisti. Certè (inquit) ridens: nam nisi tu amisisses,ego nunquam recepissem.
units.tr: What is a consequent? It is that which coheres necessarily with what went before it. The Greeks call it ἀκόλουθον [akolouthon]. For example, in the Curian case: If Postumus is dead, he lived. To this kind belongs that joke of the Parisians: If the little women are alive and came out of the monks' cloisters, they had first gone in. Likewise all privatives: If he lost it, he had it. If he recovered it, he had lost it; if he got well, he had been sick. Hence that saying of Fabius Maximus, who, when Livius Salinator, having lost Tarentum, had fled into the citadel and fought many famous battles from there, boasted and said: "By my work, Q. Fabius, you recovered Tarentum." "Certainly," he replied with a laugh, "for unless you had lost it, I would never have recovered it."

units.la: Quid interest inter Caussam,Principium,& Antecedens? Locus est insignis apud Polybium lib.III, in quo sapienter admonet,permagni omnibus in vitæ partibus interesse, notum esse discrimen inter Caussam & Principium. Sed illa consideratio ad actiones,veluti ad rei militaris officia, de quibus eo loco agebat,tota pertinet. Caussas igitur ait esse, in rebus omnibus primas. principia vero vltima caussarum. Denique caussas esse,quę deliberationem antecedunt,vt consilia & ratiocinationes. Principia vero idem appellat primas hominum actiones in rebus,quæ decreta & deliberatæ sunt. Sed Antecedentium & Consequétium ratio nihil ad hoc genus pertinet, quod totum consilij est, cum illa sint necessitatis.
units.tr: What is the difference between cause, principle, and antecedent? There is a notable passage in Polybius, book 3, where he wisely points out that it matters greatly in every part of life to know the distinction between cause and principle. But that consideration applies entirely to actions, such as the duties of military affairs, which he was discussing in that place. So he says that causes are the first of all things, while principles are the last of causes. Finally, causes are those things which precede deliberation, such as plans and reasonings. Principles, on the other hand, he calls the first human actions in matters that have been decided and deliberated upon. But the account of antecedents and consequents has nothing to do with this kind, which is wholly a matter of counsel, since those are matters of necessity.

units.la: De Adiunctis. CAP. XIIII.
units.tr: On Adjuncts. CHAPTER 14.

units.la: AAE sunt Adiuncta? Quæ probabiliter communi hominum opinione rei attribuuntur. Græci τὰ κοινῶς συμ-βεβηκότα, τὰ ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ [?], τὰ μὴ ἀεὶ ἐ-πόμενα nominant: Id est plerunque & cómuniter contingentia: veluti, Adiunctum est viris,vt sint barbati: quamuis id non omnibus contingat. Item Agricola cùm florem olez videt, baccam quoque fe visurum putat. Item, Tyrannis adiunctum est , vt violenta morte intereant:,
units.tr: What are adjuncts? They are those things that are attributed to a thing by the common opinion of people, as probable. The Greeks call them things that commonly happen [τὰ κοινῶς συμβεβηκότα], things that happen for the most part [τὰ ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ], and things that do not always follow [τὰ μὴ ἀεὶ ἑπόμενα]; that is, things that generally and commonly happen. For example, it is an adjunct of men that they have beards, although this does not happen to all men. Likewise, when a farmer sees the olive in flower, he thinks he will also see the berry. Likewise, it is an adjunct of tyrants that they perish by a violent death:

units.la: Ad generum Cereris fine cæde & sanguine pauci Descendunt Reges, & sicca morte Tyranni. Itè: Iis qui facilè métiuntur, adiunctum est, vt facilè peierent. Has Iurisconsulti præsumptiones appellant. veluti cùm Ulyfles inventus est in sylva cruentum telum tenens, quod ex Aiacis inimici corpore extraxerat, quo se ille interfecerat.
units.tr: Of all the kings who go down to the realm of Ceres, few die without bloodshed and violence; and tyrants die by a dry death, far less often. Likewise, it is an adjunct of those who measure easily that they swear falsely easily. Jurists call these presumptions. For example, when Ulysses was found in the wood holding a bloody sword, which he had drawn from the body of his enemy Ajax, by which Ajax had killed himself.

units.la: Quænam Adiunctorum divisio est? Multiplex.nam alia ex naturæ habitu attribuuntur: veluti:attributū est iracundis, vt accepta contumelia commoveantur:quod in Aiace animadversum est. Item, mulieribus adiūctum est, vt sint avarae:Ingeniosis adiunctum est, vt sint iracundi(vt ait Plato)& melancholici. Auaris, vt iusiurandum negligant. Alia ex vitæ instituto:vt, Philosophis adiunctum est, vt pecuniā negligant: liberalibus, vt sint hospitales: Aulicis, vt sint vafri, palpatores, perfidiosi: militibus, vt sint gloriosi, rapaces, impij.
units.tr: What is the division of adjuncts? It is manifold. For some are attributed from the disposition of nature, for example: it is an attribute of the irascible that they are moved when they receive an insult, as was observed in Ajax. Likewise, it is an adjunct of women that they are greedy; of the clever that they are irascible (as Plato says) and melancholic; of the avaricious that they neglect oaths. Others come from the manner of life: for example, it is an adjunct of philosophers that they neglect money; of the liberal, that they are hospitable; of courtiers, that they are crafty, flattering, and treacherous; of soldiers, that they are boastful, rapacious, and impious.

units.la: Quid? nunquid etiam ex naturæ ordine Adiuncta attribuuntur, Veluti, Si mater est, diligit filium: Si filius est, veretur patrem? Hoc plerisque certè omnibus video placuisse: sed, vt opinor, non satis cõsiderantibus illum esse naturæ ordinem necessarium; ac proinde ad Antecedentia & Consequentia referendū esse: quæ non communi opinione, sed naturæ lege atque ordine necessariò eveniunt. In quibus autem naturæ ordo non valet, ea pro monstris habenda sunt. Sed quod de naturæ lege atque ordine dictum est, id ad vitia & depravationem transferri non oportet. quippe quæ disciplina emendari possit.vt de Socrate, Stylpone, & aliis traditum est, qui cum mulierosi natura essent, studio tamen, & disciplina naturæ vitium edomuerant. Præstat igitur naturæ propensiones, ad antecedentia: deprauationes autem, ad adiuncta referri.
units.tr: What then? Are adjuncts also attributed from the order of nature? For example: if she is a mother, she loves her son; if he is a son, he reveres his father? I see that this has certainly pleased almost everyone; but, as I think, they have not sufficiently considered that this is a necessary order of nature, and therefore must be referred to antecedents and consequents, which happen not by common opinion but necessarily by the law and order of nature. In those cases where the order of nature does not hold, such things are to be regarded as monstrous.
