But what has been said of the law and order of nature should not be transferred to vices and depravity, since these can be corrected by discipline, as is recorded of Socrates, Stilpo, and others, who, though naturally inclined to lust, subdued that vice by diligence and discipline. It is better, therefore, to refer natural propensities to antecedents, but depravities to adjuncts.

units.la: De Accidenti. CAP. XV.
units.tr: Of the Accident. CHAPTER XV.

units.la: QVID est Accidens? Quod per se cōstare non potest, sed ita subiecto adherescit, vt cùm accidēs sine hoc esse non possit, tamē hoc sine illo esse possit. veluti, Glacies, nix, grando, per se esse nō possunt. Ita autem in aqua insunt, vt neque fine aqua esse possint, & soluto gelu aqua nihilominus permaneat. potest igitur glacies & accedere & recedere, cùm aquæ natura semper maneat. Sic divitiæ & paupertas, ceteráque omnia quæ fortuita dicuntur, accidentia sunt. Eodémque in numero habenda censeo quæ rei principali sic adiuncta sunt, vt tamen pars eius non sint. veluti dos in matrimonio: pignus in mutuo: fideiussor in obligatione: Seruitus tum realis, tum personalis. nā omnia hæc neque per se, ac sine principali negotio cōstare possunt: & sine principalis interitu ab esse possunt.
units.tr: What is an accident? That which cannot exist on its own, but so clings to a subject that, although the accident cannot exist without this subject, the subject can exist without that accident. For example, ice, snow and hail cannot exist by themselves; they are in water in such a way that they cannot exist without water, yet when the frost melts the water remains nonetheless. So ice can both come and go while the nature of water always remains. Thus riches and poverty, and all the other things called fortuitous, are accidents. I think that in the same class should be counted those things which are joined to a principal thing in such a way that they are nonetheless not parts of it: for example, a dowry in marriage, a pledge in a loan, a surety in an obligation, and servitude, both real and personal. For none of these can exist on its own, apart from the principal transaction, and they can be absent without the destruction of the principal thing.

units.la: Quotuplex est Accidés? Triplex. nam aliud est naturale, ut adolescentia, senectus, aduncitas nasi[?], aut simitas[?]: aliud voluntarium, ut legere, ambulare, currerc[?]. aliud fortuitum, ut paupertas, diuitię, secunda vel aduersa navigatio.
units.tr: How many kinds of accident are there? Three. For one kind is natural, such as youth, old age, a hooked nose, or a snub nose; another is voluntary, such as reading, walking, running; another is fortuitous, such as poverty, riches, a favourable or an adverse voyage.

units.la: Quæ est altera diuisio Accidentis? Ut aliud sit separabile, quod & plerunque & facilè aut accedit, aut recedit: ut morbus in homine, frigus in aqua. aliud inseparabile: quod vbi accesserit, vix ac ne vix quidem diuelli potest: ut nigror à veste tinéta[?]: lepra à corpore: cæcitas, surditas, claudicatio, canities. Quod autem plerique omnes Dialectici accidens inseparabile definiunt, quod non re ipsa sed cogitatione tantùm diuelli potest: veluti candorem ab olore[?], & nigrorem, à coruo: id ego, quia natura insitum est, ad quasi proprium potius, quàm ad accidens referendum arbitror.
units.tr: What is the other division of accident? One kind is separable, which for the most part and easily either comes or goes, as disease in a man or cold in water. Another is inseparable, which, once it has come, can scarcely, or hardly at all, be detached: as blackness from dyed cloth, leprosy from the body, blindness, deafness, lameness, grey hair. But as to what almost all the dialecticians define as an inseparable accident, namely that which can be separated only in thought and not in fact, as whiteness from a swan and blackness from a raven: I think that this, because it is innate in the thing, should be referred to a property rather than to an accident.

units.la: Quid interest inter Proprium & Accidens? Illud insitum & naturale est: hoc fortuitum & aduentitium: illud vni tàtùm speciei cŏuenit: accidens, multis. Illud semper, hoc non semper. ut risus uni homini semper conuenit. morbus multis aliis præter hominẽ cŏuenit. Sic ator Indo & Aethiopi conuenit. Itémq; coruo, & carboni, & ebeno. sed cui sic conuenit, ab eo non auellitur.
units.tr: What is the difference between a property and an accident? The former is innate and natural; the latter is fortuitous and adventitious. The former belongs to one species only; the accident to many. The former is always present, the latter not always. For example, laughter always belongs to man alone. Disease belongs to many other things besides man. Thus whiteness belongs to the Indian and the Ethiopian; likewise to the crow, the coal and the ebony. But that which belongs to a thing in this way is not torn away from it.

units.la: Quid interest inter Proprium, Antecedens, Adiun-ctum, & Accidens? Proprium insitum est. Antecedens adhærescit necessariò. Adiunctum attributum est probabiliter: Accidens vero plane alienum & aduentitium est. Itaq; illa tria perpetua sunt, hoc vero fortuitum. & quo quidque illorum ordine posterius est, eo est a re ipsa disiunctius. Rursus neque Adiun&ta[?], neque Accidentia, vnquam necessario cohaerent. At vero Antecedentiū & Confequentium fi minus vtrunque necessario cohaeret, certe alterutrum cohaeret.
units.tr: What is the difference between a property, an antecedent, an adjunct and an accident? A property is innate. An antecedent clings necessarily. An adjunct is attributed probabilistically; an accident is plainly foreign and adventitious. Therefore the first three are perpetual, but the last is fortuitous. And the further along in this order each of them stands, the more it is separated from the thing itself. Again, neither adjuncts nor accidents ever cohere necessarily; but indeed, if antecedents and consequents do not both cohere necessarily, at least one of the two certainly does.

units.la: De Paribus, CAP. XVI.
units.tr: On Equals, CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: Q[?]VAE sunt Paria? Hæc Græci modò τὰ ἴσα, modò τὰ ὁμοίως ὑπάρχοντα no-minát.sunt autem (meo quidem iudicio) alia proprie paria, alia improprie.
units.tr: What are equals? The Greeks call these sometimes τὰ ἴσα [ta isa], sometimes τὰ ὁμοίως ὑπάρχοντα [ta homoiōs hyparchonta]. In my judgement some equals are equal properly, and others improperly.

units.la: Quæ sunt proprie Paria? Quorum æqualitas pondere, numero & mensura percipitur. qua de caussa Pariatores & paria fecisse olim dicebantur qui tantundē impenderant, quantum acceperant. Parium autem comparatio, nec elationem habet (vt ait Cicero) nec fubmifsionem: id est, nec magis, neç minus reciprocat, est enim æqualis.
units.tr: What are things equal properly? Those whose equality is perceived by weight, number, or measure. For this reason those who paid out exactly what they had received were once called equalisers, and their payments equal. The comparison of equals admits neither elevation nor depression (as Cicero says): that is, one does not exceed or fall short of the other, for it is equal.

units.la: Quibus modis paritas iudicatur? Sensu & ratione. Sēfu enim iudicatur paritas ex duorum collatione: vt duo bacilli inter fe collati æqualitatem ostendunt. Hinc pares soni, pares sapores, & odores, & colores, & frigora, & calores, sensibus & collatione iudicantur. Ratione autem iudicantur paria per tertij alicuius extrinsecus assumpti conuenientiam & proportionem. Geometrarum enim hoc axioma est, Quæ in tertio aliquo paria sunt, etiam inter se paria sunt.
units.tr: By what means is equality judged? By the senses and by reason. Equality is judged by the senses from the comparison of two things: as two rods placed side by side show their equality. Hence equal sounds, equal tastes, odours, colours, cold and heat are judged by the senses and by comparison. Things are judged equal by reason through the agreement and proportion of some third thing assumed from outside. For this is the axiom of the geometers: things which are equal to some third thing are also equal to one another.

units.la: Quæ sunt improprie Paria? Quæ à quantitate ad qualitatem transferuntur, quasi mensura, ratione appensa, numerata & dimensa essent. hanc autem comparationem quæ translationibus & abusionibus vocabulorum constat, meo iudicio, Rhetoricam appellare non incommodè possumus, veluti: noxiæ pœna par esto: id est æquè grauis: quasi eadem in vtraq; momenta sint. Itē si virtutes pares sunt inter se, paria esse etiam vitia necesse est. Item: Non minor est virtus, quam quærere parta tueri. Numerata: veluti cùm homines ætate pares dicuntur. Vnde illud vetus: Pares cum paribus facilè congregantur. Dimensa: veluti, mutuus animus in amicitia est, cùm par voluntas accipitur & redditur: id est æquè magna. Atque hoc modo parua magnis adhibita proportionibus, sæpè rectissimè conferuntur.
units.tr: What are things equal improperly? Those which are transferred from quantity to quality, as if they were weighed on a scale, counted, or measured. I may fairly call this comparison, which consists of transferred and abused words, Rhetorical, in my judgement. For example: "let the penalty for the offence be equal", that is, equally heavy, as though the weights in each case were the same. Likewise, if virtues are equal to one another, it is necessary that vices be equal too. Likewise: "It is no less a virtue to keep what has been won than to seek it." Counted: for example, when men are said to be equal in age. Whence the old saying: "Equals readily gather with equals." Measured: for example, mutual affection exists in friendship when an equal goodwill is received and returned, that is, equally great. And in this way small things, when brought alongside great ones by proportion, are very often compared most rightly.

units.la: De Similibus. CAP. XVII.
units.tr: On Similar Things. CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: Quæ[?] sunt Similia? Similia dicuntur quæ in eodem genere aut specie, eiusdem ferè qualitatis sunt. Proprium enim qualitatis est, vt ex ea simile aliquid, aut dissimile dicatur. Similitudo autem iisdem quibus paritas indicatur modis:collatione,& conuenientia.Collatio sensu iudicatur. Conuenientia verò, ratione : hoc est, tertij alicuius proportione. veluti, Sicut aspectus in oculo, sic mens in animo.nam utrunque in hoc tertio conuenit,quòd providet.Sicut in mari tràquillitas , ita serenitas in aëre.nam utrunque est quies vacuitásque ventorum. Varro autem simile sic definit : Simile est, quod res plerasque videtur habere easdē, quas illud cuius est simile. Itaque qui plura habent eadem,dicuntur similiores: ut vir viro similior est,quàm vir mulieri. quod plures habent easdem partes:&sic, Senex seni similior, quàm puero. qui verò proximè accedunt ad id,ut omnia habeant eadem, vocātur gemini, simillimi. Hæc Varro.
units.tr: What are similar things? Things are called similar when they belong to the same genus or species and are nearly of the same quality. For it is peculiar to quality that something is called similar or dissimilar on account of it. Similarity is indicated by the same means as equality: by comparison and by agreement. Comparison is judged by the senses. Agreement, however, is judged by reason, that is, by the proportion of some third thing. For example: as sight is in the eye, so mind is in the soul, since both agree in this third respect, that they perceive. As calm is in the sea, so serenity is in the air, since both are a rest and a stillness of the winds. Varro defines the similar thing thus: "A thing is similar to that of which it is a similar thing when it seems to have most of the same features as that thing. Hence those who have more features in common are called more similar: a man is more similar to a man than a man is to a woman, because he has more of the same parts; and an old man is more similar to an old man than to a boy. Those who come closest to having all things the same are called twins, or most similar." So far Varro.

units.la: Quamobrem in definitione addidisti Fere? Quia mira huius affectionis ratio est.nam certæ omnes vsquequaque sunt id quod sunt. Similia verò, ex parte tantùm : eadēmq; dissimilium ratio est.nam qua ex parte simile imperfectum est,dissimile est:vicissimque qua ex parte dissimile imperfectum est,simile est. unde natū in scholis proverbiū , Similia & dissimilia perpetuò claudicāt. Quinetiá animadverto eādem utrīque definitionem conuenire. cùm tamen posterius demōstraturi simus,quæ eadē definitione continentur, eadem à Dialecticis nominari. Vitiosa igitur similitudo est, cùm qua ex parte aliquid simile esse dicitur, ea ipsa in parte dissimile est: tametsi utique aliqua ex parte dissimile fit. Ac notádum illud est Ciceronis libro ad Heren. 4. Non res tota toti rei necesse est similis sit : sed ad ipsum ad quod conferetur similitudinē habeat oportet.
units.tr: Why have you added "nearly" (fere) to the definition? Because the nature of this affection is remarkable. For all certain things are wholly what they are, whereas similar things are so only in part, and the same reasoning applies to dissimilar things. For in the respect in which a thing is imperfectly similar, it is dissimilar, and conversely, in the respect in which it is imperfectly dissimilar, it is similar. Hence the proverb that arose in the schools: "Similar and dissimilar things always limp." Indeed, I observe that the same definition fits both, although we shall show later that things contained under the same definition are named differently by the dialecticians. Therefore a similarity is faulty when that in respect of which a thing is said to be similar is itself dissimilar in that very respect, even though it is in some respect dissimilar. And we must note what Cicero says in his book To Herennius, 4: "The whole thing need not be similar to the whole thing; but it must have a similarity to that to which it is compared."

units.la: Quotuplex est Similitudo? Quemadmodum qualitas alia insita est, alia externa: sic similitudo alia externa est, quæ oculis & aspectu iudicatur : alia vero insita, quæ ex vi & potestate ei innata æstimatur. Ex vtriusq; autem concursu tertia species conflatur, quæ mixta nominabitur.
units.tr: How many kinds of similarity are there? Just as one quality is inborn and another external, so one similarity is external, which is judged by the eyes and by sight, and another is inborn, which is estimated by the force and power innate in a thing. From the combination of both a third kind is formed, which will be called mixed.

units.la: Cedo exemplū Similitudinis externæ, & in rebus quæ in eodem genere sunt? Simia quàm similis turpissima bestia nobis? inquit Ennius,Homo igitur,& simia cùm genere,tum etiam exteriore aliqua specie quadantenus inter se cóueniunt.Interiore verò quæ cuiusque rei naturalis nota est, hoc est mente, longissimè dissident. Sic numus probus & adulterinus,specie exteriore similes sunt:interiore verò,longè dissimiles. Sic Aesopus Thersiti corpore fuit simillimus: animo dissimillimus.
units.tr: Give me an example of external similarity, among things of the same genus. "How like us is the ugliest beast, the ape?" says Ennius. Man and ape, therefore, agree with one another in genus, and also to some extent in some outward appearance. But in the inner nature, which is the natural mark of each thing, that is, in mind, they differ most widely. So a genuine coin and a counterfeit are similar in outward appearance, but very unlike in their inner substance. So Aesop was very like Thersites in body, but most unlike him in mind.

units.la: Cedo alterum de specie. Videsne (inquit Cicero) vt in prouerbio sit ouorum inter se similitudo? tamen hoc accepimus, Deli fuisse cõplures saluis rebus illis, qui gallinas alere permultas quæstus caussa solerent.hi cùm ouũ inspexerant, quæ id gallina peperisset, dicere solebant. sic mater geminos internoscit consuetudine oculorum. sic duo Seruilij gemini P.& Q. qui (vt idé ait)non cognoscebãtur soris, at domi: non ab alienis, at à suis. sic illi apud Plautum gemini Menahemi, qui ne ab uxore quidem internoscebantur.
units.tr: Give me another example, from appearance. "Do you see," says Cicero, "how there is a proverbial likeness between eggs?" Yet we have heard that at Delos there were several men, in comfortable circumstances, who used to keep very many hens for profit. When they had looked at an egg, they used to say which hen had laid it. So a mother distinguishes twins by long familiarity with their faces. So the two Servilii, twins, P. and Q., as the same writer says, were not recognised abroad but were recognised at home, not by strangers but by their own people. So in Plautus those twin Menaechmi, who could not even be told apart by their wife.

units.la: Cedo item aliud. Hercules & eius statua, non modò substantia conueniunt, corpora enim sunt: sed etiam eodem nomine continentur. qua de causa ὁμώνυμα (vt posterius cognoscēs) appellantur. Forma verò interiore, remotissimè discrepant.
units.tr: Give me another. Hercules and his statue agree not only in substance, since both are bodies, but are also included under the same name; for which reason they are called homonyms [ὁμώνυμα], as you will learn later. In inner form, however, they differ most widely.

units.la: Nunc de insita dicamus. Quod habes exemplum insitæ? Veluti, si gemina poma aut pira eiusdem sint succi, tametsi non eiusdem sint aut formæ, aut coloris. Sæpè gemina facie mala (inquit Varro) negant esse similia, si sapore sunt alio. Sic equos eadem facie, negamus esse similes, si natione, aut ætate dissimiles sint. Item alio loco: Neque enim forma collata (inquit) quærēdum solum, quid habeat in figura simile: sed etiam nonnunquam in eo, quem habeat effectum: Sic enim lana Gallicana & Ap-pula videtur imperito similis propter specie, cùm peritus Appulam emat pluris, quòd in usu firmior sit.
units.tr: Now let us speak of inborn similarity. What example of it do you have? For instance, if two apples or pears are of the same juice, though not of the same shape or colour. "Often," says Varro, "two apples of the same appearance are said not to be similar if they have a different taste." So we say that horses of the same appearance are not similar if they differ in breed or age. Again elsewhere Varro says: "For when comparing form, one must look not only at what similarity there is in shape, but sometimes also at the effect it has. Thus Gallic wool and Appulian wool seem alike to an unskilled buyer because of their appearance, whereas the skilled buyer pays more for the Appulian, because it is more durable in use."

units.la: Cedo exemplum mixtæ? Duo lapides magnetes (inquit Varro) vtrùm inter se similes sint necne perspicere poteris, si minutū prope apposueris ferrum, quòd similes lapides similiter attrahant. Eodem modo duo poma, aut pira similia dicuntur, cùm eiusdem & coloris & succi sint: eodemque modo duo numi aurei æquè probi, sintne vsquequaque inter se similes adhibita lydia coticula perspici poterit.
units.tr: Give me an example of a mixed similarity. "Two magnetic stones," says Varro, "you will be able to see whether they are similar to one another or not, if you bring near them a small piece of iron, since similar stones attract in a similar way. In the same manner two apples or pears are called similar when they are of the same colour and the same juice; and in the same way, two gold coins equally genuine can be seen, by applying a Lydian touchstone, whether they are wholly similar to one another."

units.la: Quæ est altera Similium divisio? Vt alia proprie, alia improprie similia sint. Proprie autem sic dicuntur, quæ (vt ante dixi) sub eodem genere aut specie, qualitatis eiusdem sunt.
units.tr: What is the other division of similar things? Some things are similar properly, others improperly. They are called properly similar, as I said before, when they are of the same quality within the same genus or species.

units.la: Quæ sunt improprie similia? Quæ cum diuersi generis & qualitatis sint, tamen Rhetorica translatione concinnè inter se conferuntur: quale illud est Ciceronis: Memoria est germana literaturæ quodammodo, & in dissimili genere persimilis. Nam vt illa constat ex notis literarum, & ex eo in quo imprimuntur illæ notæ: sic confectio memoriæ tanquam cera locis vtitur, & in his imagines, vt literas collocat. Item illud: Vt ager quamuis fertilis sine cultura fructuosus esse non potest: sic sine doctrina animus. Vt agri non omnes frugiferi sunt qui coluntur, sic animi non omnes culti, fructum ferunt. Vt aurum igne, sic benevolentia fidelis, periculo aliquo perspicitur. Eleganter (inquit Marcianus) Papyrius dicebat peculium simile esse homini: quoniam sicut homo, ita peculium nascitur, crescit, decrescit, moritur. l. peculium, 11, D. de pecul. Nā hæc omnia festinè & figuratè potius quàm vere Similia dicuntur. Itaque hanc Similitudinem Rhetoricam appellare possumus.
units.tr: What things are improperly similar? Those which, though of different genus and quality, are nevertheless compared with one another neatly by a rhetorical transfer, as in this saying of Cicero: "Memory is in some way a sister of writing, and in a different genus wholly like it. For as writing consists of the marks of letters and of that on which those marks are impressed, so the construction of memory uses places as if they were wax, and in these it arranges images as if they were letters." Likewise that: "Just as a field, however fertile, cannot be fruitful without cultivation, so neither can the mind be without learning. As not all fields that are tilled bear fruit, so not all minds that are cultivated bear fruit." "As gold is tested by fire, so faithful goodwill is tested by some danger." "Elegantly," says Marcianus, "Papirius used to say that a private fund is like a man, since just as a man is born, so a private fund is born, grows, diminishes and dies." (Digest, law "Peculium," 11, de peculio.) For all these things are called similar hastily and figuratively rather than truly. Therefore we may call this kind of similarity rhetorical.

units.la: De Eodem. CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: De Eodem. CAP. XVIII.

units.la: vir? Idem & Simile qua in re ins[?] ter se vel conueniunt vel differunt? Aristoteles Idem tripartitò distri- buit. Nam Eadem aliqua dici statuit, aut numero, aut specie, aut genere. Numero, quæ etiam si forte nominibus differant, tamen re & indiuiduo idem sunt. veluti Pallas, & Minerua: nam si materia & indiuiduo diuersa sunt, quamuis eadem nomine sint, tamē diuersa numerantur. vt siquis pro scypho, scyphum redderet, non idem, sed aliud pro alio redderet. specie, quæ cū numero diuersa sint, tamen vna specie continentur: vt in grege, oues: in familia, serui: in armento, boues. Genere, quæ cùm speciei diuersæ sint, tamen vno genere cótinentur: vt seruus, bos, equus, aquila. Quanquam, vt superius diximus Iurisconsul- tos Speciem plerunque pro indiuiduo & certo corpore, Genus, pro specie ima & postrema vsurpare: ita plerunque Genere diuersa esse dicunt, quæ Dialectici Specie diuersa facerēt. veluti Dauus & Pamphilus apud Dialecticos specie idem sunt: numero tantum differunt. nam Hominum siue Seruorum communi specie continentur. At Iurisconsulti eosdem genere illos faciunt: specie, diuersos. Sic eas res quæ pondere, numero, mensura constant, dicunt in suo genere potius solutionem recipere, quàm specie: pro, quàm ipso corpore mutuo dato, siue indiuiduo.l.2, D.si cert. petat. Sed quod vnum numero est, (inquit Ariftoteles) id demum verè ac proprie Idem appellatur. Superiora enim duo similia potius,quàm eadem dicenda sunt. Quanquam fi ad Platonis rationem hæc reuocetur quæftio,ne annulus quidem qui heri fuit,idem hodie dicetur: quoniam eo temporis spatio vetuftior est.quinetiam nullum esse aiunt pilum (inquit Cicero) omnibus rebus talem qualis est pilus alius.
units.tr: In what respect do the Same (Idem) and the Similar (Simile) agree with one another, or differ? Aristotle divides the Same into three kinds. He holds that some things are called the same in number, some in species, and some in genus. Things are the same in number, even if they sometimes differ in name, when they are identical in thing and individual, as Pallas and Minerva are. For if they differ in matter and individual, they are counted as different, even though they share a name. So if someone returned a cup (scyphus) in place of a cup, he would not return the same thing but another thing in place of another. Things are the same in species when, although they differ in number, they fall under one species, as sheep in a flock, slaves in a household, or oxen in a herd. Things are the same in genus when, although they differ in species, they fall under one genus, as slave, ox, horse, and eagle. Yet, as I said above, the jurists commonly use "species" for the individual and particular body, and "genus" for the lowest and last species. So they often call things different in genus what the dialecticians would call different in species. For example, Davus and Pamphilus are the same in species according to the dialecticians; they differ only in number, since both are contained under the common species of man or slave. But the jurists make these same men different in genus and say they differ in species. In the same way, they say that things which consist in weight, number, or measure are discharged in their kind rather than in their species, in that a loan of such goods is repaid with the same kind of thing rather than with the very body or individual given. But, says Aristotle, that which is one in number is properly and truly called the Same. The two former kinds should rather be called similar than the same. Yet if this question is referred to the reasoning of Plato, the ring that was yesterday will not even be called the same today, since it is older by that span of time. Indeed, they say there is no hair (says Cicero) in all things exactly like another hair.

units.la: Quid? Plato quidnā igitur proprie Idéappellat? Quod fèper est simplex, & vniufmodi, & vno ac perpetuo statu continetur. Hanc(inquit Cicero) Ideam Plato appellat: nos rectè Speciem dicere possumus. Sensus autem omnes hebetes & tardos esse arbitratur, nec percipere vllo modo res eas quæ subiectæ sensibus viderentur. quæ effent aut ita parua, vt sub sensum cadere non possent: aut ita mobiles & concitatæ, vt nihil vnquam vnum eflet constans, ne idem quidem: quia continenter laberentur & fluerent omnia. Item alio loco: Nihil Plato putabat esse verè, quod oriatur & intereat: idque solum esse, quod sèmper tale fit,qualem Ideam appellatille,nos Speciem.
units.tr: Well, what does Plato properly call the Idea? That which is always simple, uniform, and held in one and the same unchanging state. This, says Cicero, is what Plato calls the Idea; we may rightly call it the Species. Plato thinks the senses are dull and slow, and that they cannot in any way perceive those things that seem to lie under the senses: things either so small that they cannot fall under sense, or so mobile and restless that nothing ever remains one and constant, not even the same thing, because all things continually slip away and flow. Elsewhere again: Plato thought nothing truly is which comes into being and perishes; only that is, which is always such as that which he called the Idea, which we call the Species.

units.la: Sed omissa idearum subtilitate, quidnam ad vsum vitæ communis Idem proprie appellabimus? Dupliciter respondeo. primùm (vt modò dixisti) ex communi vitæ confuetudine: deinde ex arte Dialectica. Ergo ex vsu vitæ communis Idé proprie vereque dicitur, cuius & substantia & accidentia eadé manet: vel in rebus corporalibus, quorũ eadé & materia& forma est,quæ priùs fuit. nam alterius mutatio rem aliam ac diuersam efficit. De materia exemplum est in eo qui pro frumento, quod mutuum sumpsit, vinum reddit. Nam hic nõ idem, sed aliud pro alio reddere intelligitur. l.2, D.si cert. pet. De forma, exemplum est in eo,qui pro scypho commodato massam ex eo fuso redderet. nam mutata forma, res mutatur.l.Iulianus,9,f.2, D.ad exhibend. Quinetiam qui rem deteriorem,& deprauatâ offert, quam integram acceperat, non eandem rem reddere dicitur.l.3,f.3,D.commod.
units.tr: But setting aside the subtlety of the Ideas, what shall we properly call the Same in the use of common life? I answer in two ways: first (as you have just said) from common custom of life, and then from the art of dialectic. So in the use of common life, the Same is properly and truly said of that whose substance and accidents remain the same, whether in corporeal things whose matter and form are the same as before. For a change in either makes a different thing. An example of matter is the man who, having borrowed wheat, returns wine: for he is understood to return not the same thing but another in place of another. An example of form is the man who, for a lent cup, returns a lump melted from it: for when the form is changed, the thing is changed. Moreover, one who offers a worse and spoiled thing, instead of the whole thing he received, is said not to return the same thing.

units.la: Quid igitur si quis pro scypho, scyphum æquè bonũ,& materia,& forma reddat,idémne reddere intelligitur? Nequaquam. non magis, quàm si pro frumento, vino, vel oleo, tantundem æquè boni vini, olei, frumenti redderet: aut si pro numis aureis,alios eiusdem bonitatis vel aureos, vel argenteos. Itaque cùm Regula iuris esset, ne aliud pro alio inuito creditori redderetur, contrà istius artis subtilitatem communis vtilitatis caussa institutum est, vt in iisquæ pondere, numero, mensura constant,non tam corpus, quàm genus ipsum spectaretur. l. si is cui, 94, D. de solut.l.Titia, 87, D. de legat. 2. ac proinde vt quæ generè eadem essent, etiam si in specie atque indiuiduo differrent,tamen pro iisdem haberentur. l.cùm Stichus,29,D.de solut. vbi Vlpian. scribit,res istas vna & communi specie continerì cùm tamen stricta ratione Paulus scribat, specie nō easdem esse : & magis genere quàm specie functionem recipere.l.2,D.de reb.cred.
units.tr: What then, if someone returns a cup, equally good in both matter and form, in place of a cup: is he understood to return the same thing? Not at all. No more than if, in place of wheat, wine, or oil, he returned an equal quantity of wine, oil, or wheat of equal goodness; or if, in place of gold coins, he returned others of the same quality, whether gold or silver. Therefore, since the rule of law was that nothing different should be returned to an unwilling creditor in place of what was owed, the rule was contrary to the subtlety of this art, and was established for the sake of common utility, so that in things which consist in weight, number, or measure, one regards not so much the body as the genus itself. (Digest, on payment, 94; on legacies, 87.) And accordingly, things which are the same in genus, even if they differ in species and individual, are nonetheless held to be the same. (On payment, 29, where Ulpian writes that such things are contained in one common species; yet Paul writes, by strict reasoning, that they are not the same in species, and that they discharge the obligation more by genus than by species.)

units.la: Et ex arte Dialectica,quid proprie Idem appellabimus? Quod vna eadémque definitione continetur. Nam quæ definitione differūt, specie certè differunt. Itaque Cicero lib. de legib.1.disputat, homines omnes vnam atque eandem rem esse : quòd si qua in hominibus differentia sit,eam in numero esse, non in specie. Nihil (inquit) est vnum vni tam simile, tam par, quàm omnes inter nosmetipsos sumus. Quòd si deprauatio consuetudinum, si opinionum varietas, non imbecillitatem animorum torqueret & flecteret, quocunque cœpisset: sui nemo ipse tam similis esset, quàm omnes sunt omnium. Itaque quæcunque est hominis definitio, vna in omnes valet. quod argumenti satis est, nullam dissimilitudinem esse in genere : quæ si esset, non vna omnes definitio contineret.
units.tr: And from the art of dialectic, what shall we properly call the Same? That which is contained under one and the same definition. For things that differ in definition certainly differ in species. So Cicero, in the first book of the Laws, argues that all men are one and the same thing; and if there is any difference among men, it lies in number, not in species. Nothing, he says, is so like and equal to another thing as we all are among ourselves. But if the corruption of customs and the variety of opinions did not twist and bend the weakness of minds wherever they began, no one would be so like himself as all are like all. Therefore, whatever the definition of man is, it applies to all alike. This is sufficient proof that there is no dissimilarity in the genus; if there were, one definition would not contain them all.

units.la: De Rebus diuersis. CAP. XIX.
units.tr: On Diverse Things. CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: IDEO ista:redeóque in memoriam eius diuisionis quam superiùs attigisti, cùm alias dicerces esse res easdem, alias diuersas, siue differétes: pollicitúsque es, subtilius te deinceps de ea, dicturum. Quænam igitur diuersæ res sunt? Quemadmodum eędem res dicuntur, vel genere, vel specie, vel numero: similiter diversæ modis iisdem dicuntur: & rursus quemadmodum idem dicitur, cuius & materia & forma manet, sic aliud dicitur cùm vel utrunque vel alterutrum mutatum est.
units.tr: Therefore, let us return to the division you touched on earlier, when you said that some things are the same and others diverse or different, and promised to discuss it more carefully afterwards. What, then, are diverse things? Just as the same things are called the same either by genus, by species, or by number, so diverse things are called diverse in the same ways. And conversely, just as a thing is called the same when both its matter and its form remain, so a thing is called other when either both or one of them has been changed.

units.la: Quæ sunt genere differentes? Res de quibus cùm quæritur quid sunt, tot generum nominibus, quot ipsæ numeratæ sunt, respondetur. veluti quid sunt, homo, ferrum, aqua, platanus? Respondetur animal, metallum, elementum, arbor. quod contrà in eiusdem generis rebus fieri diximus. Atque hæc quidem definitio cum definitione generis Aristotelica reciprocatur.
units.tr: What things differ in genus? When we ask what things are, the answer is given with as many generic names as there are things in the list. For example, when asked what man, iron, water and the plane tree are, the answers are animal, metal, element and tree. This is the opposite of what we said happens with things of the same genus. This definition also agrees with Aristotle's definition of genus.

units.la: Quæ sunt specie differentes? Res quæ sub uno genere eóque infimo, proprietate tamen inter se discrepant. nam proprietas quæque speciem efficit. Cùm autem prima hominum ætate singulæ proprietates singulis nominibus designatæ essent: nunc tamen in tanta humanæ mentis caligine ut multarum proprietatum, sic nominum logè plurimorum ignoratio consecuta est. Exempli causa, Platanus, laurus, pinus, cupressus, quercus: non genere, sed proprietate ac nomine inter se disiuncta sunt. Item ut Leo, cervus, equus, asinus, elephas, camelus. Propterea autem genus infimum diximus, ut veram & infimam speciem intelligeremus, quæ genus esse non potest. nam avis, piscis, quadrupes inferiorum respectu genus sunt: animalis respectu, species. quod jam superius dictum ac demonstratum est;
units.tr: What things differ in species? Things that fall under one and the same lowest genus, yet differ from one another in property. For each property makes a species. In the first age of humankind, each single property was marked by a single name. But now, in such great darkness of the human mind, many properties and, even more, their names have become unknown. For example, plane tree, laurel, pine, cypress and oak are separated from one another not by genus but by property and name. So too are lion, stag, horse, donkey, elephant and camel. We called it the lowest genus so that we might understand the true and lowest species, which cannot be a genus. For bird, fish and quadruped are genera in relation to the lower things, but species in relation to animal. This has already been said and shown above.

units.la: Quæ sunt numero differentes? Res singulares, quæ sub eodem & genere & specie tamen inter numerandum discernuntur: velut in grege: prima, secunda, tertia ouis: in armento, primus, secundus, tertius bos. Sed in hominum genere comparatum est, ut in quoque numero ac multitudine singuli nota quadam propria & peculiari designarentur. velut nomine: ut C. Iulius, aut si commune cum aliis nomen esset, cognomine: ut C. Iulius Cæsar: aut si hoc quoque commune esset, tribus: C. Iulius Cæsar Quirina. item, Q. Seruius Sulpitius, Rufus, Lemonia. quod ex populi R. instituto sumptum exemplum est, unde fingere sibi quisque simile aliquod poterit.
units.tr: What things differ in number? Single things which, under the same genus and species, are nonetheless distinguished when counted: as in a flock, the first, second and third sheep, or in a herd, the first, second and third ox. But in the human race it has been arranged that, among any number or multitude, each individual is marked by some proper and peculiar sign: by a name, for instance Gaius Julius; or, if that name were shared with others, by a surname, as Gaius Julius Caesar; or, if this too were shared, by a tribe, as Gaius Julius Caesar of the Quirina tribe; likewise Quintus Servius Sulpicius Rufus of the Lemonia tribe. This example is taken from the institution of the Roman people, and from it anyone may devise a similar one for himself.

units.la: Et de materiæ aut formæ mutatione, quodnam exemplum affers? De utroque exemplo esto in eo, qui pro frumento vinum reddit: l.2, D.de reb. cred. de qualitate, velut in eo qui pro vino vetere nouum reddit. l.3, eod. item in eo qui e ciue, peregrinus: e libero, seruus: aut contra e seruo, liber factus est. nam hi alij homines appellantur, l. quoties, 4, D. de nouat. l. seruus, 27, D. de adim.legat. item si res deposita deterior reddatur l.1, §. si res, D. depof. aut res debita diminuta iure aliquo soluatur. l. etiam, aut ex domo factus sit hortus, aut ex loco domus, aut vinea. l. si fundus, 16, §.
units.tr: And as to change of matter or form, what example do you give? Let the example for both be the one who gives back wine instead of wheat (law 2, Digest, on loans, on quality), as in the one who gives back new wine instead of old (law 3, same title). Likewise, the one who from a citizen becomes a foreigner, from free a slave, or conversely from slave becomes free. For these are called other men (law "quoties", 4, Digest, on novation; law "servus", 27, Digest, on ademption of legacies). Likewise, if a deposited thing is returned in worse condition (law 1, §"si res", Digest, on deposit), or if a debt is reduced and discharged by some right (law "etiam"); or if a garden is made from a house, or from the site of a house, or a vineyard (law "si fundus", 16, §).

units.la: Sed quidnam interest inter Diuersa & Contraria? Quantum inter Genus & Speciem. nā quæ contraria sunt,quia specie differunt, certè diuersa sunt. Triplex autem ceteroqui differentia est.primùm enim verè & proprie cōtraria,dissentanea sunt: diuersa autem omnia dicuntur, etiam quæ consentanea sunt,& quæ quoquomodo inter se affecta,ac nó eadé sunt. Deinde cótraria omnia sub eodé genere cótinétur. Diuersa verò varij generis esse possunt. Tertiò contraria sunt quæ sub eodem genere longisimè & remotisimè disiuncta sunt. Diuersa,verò si sub eodem genere sunt,intermedia & interiecta sunt. veluti , Candidum & atrum contraria sunt :at Candidum & purpureum : rubrum aut ceruleum,diuersa sunt. Atque hæc quidem de contrariis generatim.
units.tr: But what is the difference between diverse and contrary? The same as between genus and species. For things that are contrary, because they differ in species, are certainly diverse. There is otherwise a threefold difference. First, things that are truly and properly contrary are those that are opposed to each other; but all things are called diverse, even those that agree, and those that are related in some way without being the same. Second, all contraries are contained under the same genus, whereas diverse things may belong to different genera. Third, contraries are those that, under the same genus, are most widely and remotely separated; diverse things, if they are under the same genus, are intermediate and lie between. For example, white and black are contrary, but white and purple, or red and blue, are diverse. This is enough about contraries in general.

units.la: De singulis autem sic habendum est. Relata non contraria sunt natura (vt superiùs diximus)sed situ & positione duntaxat. Itaque diuersa sunt proprie. Negantia verò & priuantia, diuersa dici non possunt. quia diuersa eodem tempore sunt. Illa simul esse non possunt. alterum enim ab altero pellitur. Quare sola aduersa diuersorum genere cotinentur : quorum vtrúnque vno eodémque tépore in rerü natura est. Verùm hæc sine contrariorum cognitione , qui locus iam proximè sequitur, intelligi non possunt. deinceps enim de assectionibus differendum est, in quibus Contraria primum locum obtinent.
units.tr: As for individual cases, the following should be held. Relatives are not contrary by nature (as we said above), but only by situation and position. Therefore they are properly diverse. Negating and privative things cannot be called diverse, because diverse things exist at the same time, whereas those cannot exist together, since one drives out the other. Hence only opposites are included under the genus of diverse things, both of which exist in the nature of things at one and the same time. But these cannot be understood without knowledge of contraries, which is the topic that follows next. For we must next discuss affections, in which contraries hold the first place.

units.la: De Contrariis. : CAP. XX. VAE sunt Contraria? Quæ sub eodé genere ita inter se affecta sunt, ut in unum idémq; subiectum eadé ratio ne,codémque tempore cócurrere nó possint.veluti,Virtus,vitium:atror & candor.
units.tr: On Contraries. CHAPTER XX. What are contraries? Those which, under the same genus, are so affected with respect to each other that they cannot meet in one and the same subject, in the same respect, and at the same time. For example, virtue and vice, black and white.

units.la: Ac veteres quidem Dialectici, atque in his Aristoteles, contraria intra duorum numerum paucitatémque reuocarunt:ut unum uni duntaxat opponeretur. Quorum sententiam quidam mirificè amplexati sunt. Contrariáque ita definierút: Opposita sunt quæ repugnát unum uni,sic ut neque alterum de altero,neque ambo de tertio dici possint. Quòd si ita est, certè contraria omnia paria sunt, neq; alterū altero magis cótrariū dici potest. Quod tamé Aristoteles ipse lib. Ethicorum11. cap. v111. falsum esse ostendit,vbi hanc regulam tradit: Quo quæque sub eodem genere longius inter se disiuncta sunt, eò magis inter sè contraria sunt.veluti,Auaritiæ liberalitas,contraria est. magis autem Prodigalitas.Ignauiæ contraria est fortitudo. magis autem Audacia. Tantū autem ea quæ longisimè remota sunt,inter se distant,quantum defectio distat ab exuperantia. Sic donare & non donare contraria sunt. Item,ut Donare & Carere aut Egere. Sed donare , & eripere longè magis contraria sunt. Sic Amare, non amare , odisse. In eodémque genere illa sunt, Nasci, viuere, mori. Ortus, essentia, interitus. Amare, non amare, odisse.
units.tr: The ancient dialecticians, and among them Aristotle, restricted contraries to a number of two and a pairing, so that one thing was opposed only to one. Some have embraced this opinion with great enthusiasm, and defined contraries thus: opposites are things that are repugnant one to one, such that neither can be predicated of the other, nor both of a third. If that is so, then all contraries are certainly equal, and one cannot be said to be more contrary than another. Yet Aristotle himself shows this to be false in the Ethics, book 11, chapter 8, where he gives this rule: the further apart things are separated within the same genus, the more contrary they are to each other. For example, liberality is contrary to avarice, but prodigality is more so. Courage is contrary to cowardice, but rashness is more so. Things that are most remotely separated are as far apart from each other as deficiency is from excess. Thus to give and not to give are contrary; likewise to give and to lack or to be in want. But to give and to snatch away are far more contrary. Likewise to love, not to love, and to hate. In the same genus are these: to be born, to live, to die; origin, essence, perishing; to love, not to love, to hate.

units.la: Quæ est Contrariorum diuisio? Re & natura tripertita est. Eorum enim alia sunt adversa, alia priuantia, alia negantia. At si figurā, situm, & oppositionem spectemus, in hunc numerum ea quoque adscribētur, quae cum alio conferuntur. ut Duplum, Simplum: Pater & Filius: quae vulgò Relata nominantur. Itaque Aristoteles non dixit πρὸς ἐναντίων[?] alia esse ἀντικείμενα, alia τὰ πρός τι, alia στερητικά, alia καταφατικά[?]: quod nonnulli falsò tradiderunt: sed hoc modo: λέγεται γὰρ ἕτερον ἑτέρῳ ἀντικεῖσθαι τρ-ισσῶς[?]. ἢ ὡς τὰ πρός τι, ἢ ὡς τὰ ἐναντία, ἢ ὡς στέρησις, ἢ ἕξις, ἢ ὡς κατάφασις, ἢ ἀπόφασις.
units.tr: What is the division of contraries? In reality and nature it is threefold: for some are adverse, others privative, others negative. But if we consider figure, position and opposition, those things that are referred to one another are also to be counted in this number, such as double and single, father and son, which are commonly called relatives. So Aristotle did not say that some things are opposed to contraries [πρὸς ἐναντίων], and that others are opposites, relatives, privatives, and affirmatives [ἀντικείμενα, τὰ πρός τι, στερητικά, καταφατικά], as some have falsely reported. He said it in this way: "For one thing is said to be opposed to another in three ways: either as relatives, or as contraries, or as privation and possession, or as affirmation and negation." [λέγεται γὰρ ἕτερον ἑτέρῳ ἀντικεῖσθαι τρισσῶς· ἢ ὡς τὰ πρός τι, ἢ ὡς τὰ ἐναντία, ἢ ὡς στέρησις, ἢ ἕξις, ἢ ὡς κατάφασις, ἢ ἀπόφασις.]

units.la: Quomodo igitur Relata in contrariis numerantur? Quia sunt inter se situ quidem & figura opposita; ut, Pater Filius, Dominus, Seruus: Donare, Recipere: sed notione & vi ipsa tanta inter ea necessitudo, atque amicitia est, ut alterum ab altero sustineatur: alterum alterius respectu fit id quod est: neutrum altero prius fit, sed utrunque natura simul. Ac propterea verè in consentaneorum numerum referri possunt. Et si autem in idem subiectum simul eodemque tempore cadere possunt, nō tamen eadē ratione conveniunt: nam Aeneas (verbi gratia) pater & filius verè dicitur, eodemque tempore: sed non eodem respectu & ratione. nam Ascanij respectu, pater est: Anchisae verò, filius.
units.tr: How, then, are relatives counted among contraries? Because they are opposed to each other in position and figure, as father and son, lord and slave, to give and to receive. But in meaning and in their very force there is such a close connection and friendship between them that each is sustained by the other: each becomes what it is with respect to the other. Neither comes before the other; both arise together by nature. And therefore they can rightly be referred to the number of things that agree. Although they can fall in the same subject at the same time, they do not agree in the same respect. For Aeneas, for example, is rightly called both father and son at the same time, but not in the same respect: with respect to Ascanius he is father, and with respect to Anchises he is son.

units.la: Quae sunt Adversa? Quae in eodem genere plurimū inter se differunt. vel hoc modo, Quae ita inter se infesta sunt, ut pariter alterum ab altero abhorreat: veluti,donare,eripere: desectio, exuperantia: graue,leue: atrum, candidum: rectum,inflexum: virtus, vitiū. Par enim utriusque in utrunque vis atque potestas est: pariter alterum ab altero abhorret: pariter inter se naturali odio dispellunt. quinetiam quo propius admouentur, eò magis pugnantiam declarant: vt Ariftoteles scribit in Rhetoricis,παραλλήλα τὰ ἐναντία μάλισα φαί-νεται: Aduersa proximè opposita maximè apparent. veluti cùm Aesopus (vt in eius vita scribitur) inter duos formosos pueros venalis ab hero expositus est.
units.tr: What are Adversa (contraries)? Those which differ most from each other within the same genus; or in this way: those which are so hostile to one another that each shrinks from the other equally. For example: to give, to snatch away; desertion, excess; heavy, light; black, white; straight, bent; virtue, vice. For the force and power of each against the other is equal: each shrinks from the other equally, and they drive each other off with equal natural hatred. Indeed, the closer they are brought together, the more clearly they show their opposition, as Aristotle writes in the Rhetoric: "Contraries appear most clearly when placed side by side" [παραλλήλα τὰ ἐναντία μάλιστα φαίνεται]: contraries set directly opposite are most apparent. This is so when Aesop (as his life is written) was put up for sale by his master between two handsome boys.

units.la: Quae sunt Relata? Graeci τὰ πρός τι hæc appellant: quorum ea vis atque affectio est, vt mutuò respondeant, seséque inuicem tueantur. vt dominus,seruus: paterfa.filiusfa.donare,recipere: locare,cõducere. Quanuis enim situ & positione (vt modò dixi) aduersantur, notione tamen par utriusque in utrunque naturalis amicitia ac necessitudo est. Itaque fem per inter fe reciprocantur: neque alterū altero natura prius est: sed utrunque simul sunt naturæ ordine. Quapropter non priùs donatio intelligitur quàm acceptio fit: neque priùs locatio,quàm conductio.
units.tr: What are Relata (correlatives)? The Greeks call them τὰ πρός τι. Their nature and condition is that they answer each other mutually and protect each other. For example: master, slave; father, son; to give, to receive; to let, to hire. For although they are opposed in position and placement (as I have just said), in meaning there is an equal natural friendship and mutual dependence of each on the other. Thus they are reciprocal to one another, and neither is prior to the other in nature; rather both exist together in the order of nature. Therefore a gift is not understood to come before a receipt is made, nor a letting before a hiring.

units.la: Quid? Nonne plures ferui vni domino,plures liberi vni parenti,pater item & mater,qui duo numero sunt,filio & filiæ qui totidem numero sunt,opponi possunt?
units.tr: What then? Can't several slaves be opposed to one master, several children to one parent, a father and a mother (who are two in number) to a son and a daughter (who are equally two in number)?

units.la: Quid igitur est, quod superiùs dixisti,con-
units.tr: What then is the meaning of what you said above, that contraries are only ever two, and one is opposed only to one?

units.la: traria bina esse tantummodo, & unū uni duntaxat opponi? Facilis solutio est. unum enim specie, non numero intelligitur: hoc est, una notio alteri de eodem genere distractæ, vel potius contractæ opponitur. Itaque quantumuis multi sint liberi: ut in fabulis Priami, vel Danai quinquaginta: tamen una omnes liberorum notione continentur. Pater autem & mater, cùm filio & filiæ opponuntur (veluti cùm Varro sic scribit: Ut est filius ad patrem, sic filia ad matrem) non bina, sed quaterna contraria sunt: ac proinde nō una oppositio, sed duæ: non duo respectus & affectiones: sed quatuor. Qua de causa non ratione, sed proportionem illam Varro nominatim appellat.
units.tr: The solution is easy. For "one" is understood in kind, not in number: that is, one notion is opposed to another drawn from or rather gathered into the same genus. Thus however many children there are, as in the stories of Priam or Danaus, with fifty, yet all are contained under one notion of "children." But father and mother, when they are opposed to son and daughter (as when Varro writes: "As the son is to the father, so the daughter is to the mother"), are not two contraries but four; and therefore there is not one opposition but two, not two relations and affections but four. For this reason Varro names that relation not a ratio but a proportion.

units.la: Quæ sunt Priuantia? Quæ ita inter se assecta sunt, ut unum tantum alterius pellēdi vim habeat. veluti, visus & cæcitas: dies & nox: honor & infamia: habere & carere: vestitus nuditas, vita & mors: valetudo & morbus. Quorum posterius duntaxat tollendi atque extinguendi prioris facultatem habet, illud cedendi tantummodo. Itaque nisi fit, quod cedendi vim habeat, non est quod habeat priuandi. Priuatio enim est, eius rei defectio in subiecto, quæ natura inesse in illo debuit. qua de causa neque infantes muti, calui, aut edentuli dicuntur, antequam per ætatem aut loqui, aut crines, & dentes habere possint: neque cæci catuli, ante diem nonum: neque talpa cæca: neque cornua perdidisse (ut in proverbio est) qui non habuit.priuatio verò non modò in habitus ademptione & detractione, verùm etiam in eiusdem inductione & restitutione intelligitur. veluti,nudus, tectus : amifsio,recuperatio : exilium, restitutio : morbus, valetudo : rudis,edoctus.
units.tr: What are Privantia (privatives)? Those which are so related to each other that one has only the power of driving out the other. For example: sight and blindness; day and night; honour and disgrace; to have and to lack; clothing and nakedness; life and death; health and sickness. Of these, the latter has only the power of removing and extinguishing the former, while the former has only the power of yielding. Thus, unless there is something that has the power of yielding, there is nothing that can have the power of depriving. For privation is the absence, in a subject, of a thing which by nature ought to be present in it. For this reason infants are not called dumb, bald, or toothless before they can by age either speak or have hair and teeth; nor are puppies blind before the ninth day; nor is a mole called blind; nor can one who never had horns (as the proverb says) be said to have lost them. Privation, however, is understood not only in the taking away and removal of a habit, but also in its introduction and restoration: for example, naked and clothed; loss and recovery; exile and restoration; sickness and health; untrained and taught.

units.la: Quæ sunt Aiétia& negátia? Quæ ita inter se affecta atque infesta sunt, ut tamen alterū alterius vicissitudinem ferre possit. deniq; quorū alterum subiecto habitum non detrahit, sed denegat. Eorum autem alia simplicia dicuntur,quæ nomine constant: ut Doctus, non doctus,indoctus:gratus,non gratus,ingratus:testatus,non testatus,intestatus. alia Copulata, quæ ex verbo constant: ut legere, non legere. ambulare, non ambulare.quæ propterea vulgò Contradicentia nominantur. ut, Illo tempore factum est: non illo tempore factum est. Illo loco,non illo loco.
units.tr: What are Affirmativa and Negativa (affirmatives and negatives)? Those which are so related and so hostile to each other that yet one can bear the alternation of the other. Finally, of these, one does not take away a habit from a subject, but denies it. Some of these are called simple, which consist of a single word: for example, learned, not learned, unlearned; grateful, not grateful, ungrateful; testate, not testate, intestate. Others are called compound, which consist of a verb: for example, to read, not to read; to walk, not to walk. These are therefore commonly called Contradictories: for example, "It was done at that time" and "It was not done at that time"; "in that place" and "not in that place."

units.la: Quid interest inter Priuationem & Negationem? Priuatio habitum fatetur,arguit,indicat,eúmque subiecto detrahit. negatio verò habitum inficiatur, non adimit. quod qui nō animaduertunt, imperitè duo illa genera cófundunt.
units.tr: What is the difference between Privation and Negation? Privation acknowledges, asserts and indicates a habit, and takes it away from the subject. Negation, however, denies a habit and does not remove it. Those who do not notice this confuse those two kinds unskilfully.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Indoctus,imò doctus,in eo homine priuantia sunt, qui antea rudis, nunc eruditus est. nam doctrina ignorantiæ priuatio est. At doctus, imò indoctus, in eo negantia sunt, qui nihil unquam didicit. sic impolitum argentū,imò politum, ad priuantia,refertur.Politum,imò impolitû ad negantia. Sic nitidus, maculosus, privantia sunt. Nitidus non nitidus,negantia. Sic formosus, deformatus, privantia sunt. At formosus, deformis,negantia sunt.vestitus,imò nudus, negantia sunt: vestitus, nudatus,privantia. Eadem insequentium ratio est: Armatus, inermis, dearmatus. crescere, non crescere, decrescere. florescere,non florescere,deflorescere. sævire, non sævire, desævire. frondescere, non frondescere,defrondescere.
units.tr: Give me an example. "Unlearned," or rather "learned," in a man who was formerly untrained and is now educated, are privatives; for lack of learning is a privation of knowledge. But "learned," or rather "unlearned," in one who has never learned anything, are negatives. So "unpolished silver," or rather "polished," is referred to privatives; "polished," or rather "unpolished," to negatives. So "bright" and "stained" are privatives; "not bright" is negative. So "handsome" and "disfigured" are privatives; but "handsome" and "ugly" are negatives. "Clothed" or rather "naked" are negatives; "clothed" and "stripped" are privatives. The same reasoning applies to the following: armed, unarmed, disarmed; to grow, not to grow, to cease growing; to flower, not to flower, to lose flowers; to rage, not to rage, to cease raging; to put forth leaves, not to put forth leaves, to lose leaves.

units.la: Cedo alia exempla. Habere & non habere, negantia sunt. At habere & carere privantia. Triste enim est, (ait Cicero)nomen ipsum carendi,quia subiicitur hæc vis: habuit, non habet. desiderat, requirit, indiget. Sic Pater & Orbus negantia sunt, si liberos nunquam habuit.Privantia, si iis orbatus est.
units.tr: Give other examples. "To have" and "not to have" are negatives. But "to have" and "to lack" are privatives. For the very word "to lack" is sad (says Cicero), because this force is implied: "he had, he does not have"; it longs for, seeks, needs. So "father" and "bereaved" are negatives, if he never had children; they are privatives if he has been bereaved of them.

units.la: Ecquanam igitur nota quatuor hæc inter se oppositorum genera internoscûtur? In adversis & relatis, par contrarii utriusque in utrunque vis ac natura est. verùm adversa inter se infesta sunt: privantia verò amica & necessaria. Rursus in privantibus & negantibus una tantùm ex parte pugna est, sed in privantibus subiectum depellitur: in his negatur. præterea quæ adversa sunt, eodem tempore in rerum natura sunt, mutuóque idipsum de se profitentur.at neque privantia, neque negantia eodem tempore sunt.
units.tr: By what mark, then, are these four kinds of opposites distinguished from one another? In contraries and correlatives there is an equal force and nature of each against the other; but contraries are hostile to one another, while privatives and correlatives are friendly and necessary to each other. Again, in privatives and negatives there is conflict on one side only; but in privatives the subject is driven out, while in negatives it is merely denied. Moreover, contraries exist at the same time in the nature of things, and mutually affirm the same of each other; but neither privatives nor negatives exist at the same time.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Annon plerique omnes Dialectici referūt in numerum aduersorum, valetudinem & morbum: diem & noctem? At qui inter Philosophos constat, morbum nihil aliud esse, quàm priuationem valetudinis, & noctem diei, nam corpus terrę soli oppositum umbram efficit. Cicero ipse in Topicis Sapientiā & stultitiam, bonitatem & malitiam inter aduersorum exempla posuit. At Boëtius homo acutissimus, & in hoc disciplinæ genere omnium iudicio singularis, rectè admonuit, stultitiam esse priuationem sapientiæ: malitiā bonitatis. sic multi inter aduersorum exempla referunt calorem & frigus: humorem & siccitatem: cùm tamen à Physicis, disputetur frigus priuationem esse caloris, & siccitatem humoris.
units.tr: Give an example. Do not almost all dialecticians place among contraries health and sickness, day and night? Yet it is agreed among philosophers that sickness is nothing other than the privation of health, and night the privation of day, for the body of the earth, placed opposite the sun, makes a shadow. Cicero himself, in the Topics, placed wisdom and folly, goodness and wickedness among examples of contraries. But Boethius, a most acute man and in this kind of discipline singular in the judgment of all, rightly warned that folly is a privation of wisdom, and wickedness of goodness. So many people likewise count heat and cold, moisture and dryness among examples of contraries, when yet by natural philosophers it is argued that cold is a privation of heat, and dryness of moisture.

units.la: De Medio in contrariis.
units.tr: On the Middle in Contraries.

units.la: CAP. XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI. Of the Middle in Contraries

units.la: VAE est altera Contrariorum summa diuisio? Vulgaris diuisio est huiusmodi, ut quædam tertium, siue medium, recipiant, quædā non recipiāt. nā in Aduersis, Relatis & Priuatibus, sunt quæ recipiāt: sunt & quæ nō recipiāt. In aientibus autem & negantibus, nulla mediū recipiunt.
units.tr: What is the second main division of contraries? The common division is this: some contraries admit a third thing, or middle, while others do not. Among Opposites, Relatives and Privatives, some admit a middle and some do not. But affirmations and negations never admit a middle.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de aduersis. In Aduersis hæc medium recipiunt: Candidum & atrum recipiunt fuscum, purpureum, viride, & alia nonnulla. Pulcher & deformis statam formā. Diuitiæ & Paupertas mediocritatem. At illa non recipiunt, Rectum & inflexum: Grauitas & leuitas: Status,motus:Vigilare & dormire. Omnis enuntiatio (inquiunt Dialectici) vel vera est,vel falsa. Omnis linea vel recta est, vel inflexa.Mulier aut amat,aut odit. nihil est tertium.In eodem genere sunt, Sacrum,profanum. Publicum,priuatum. Ciuis, Peregrinus. Maritus,cœlebs. Pater,orbus. Inter bellum & pacem medium nihil est : ait Cicero. nam induciarum,ita breue tempus est, vt earum ratio non ducatur.Imperium cupientibus, nihil medium inter summa, aut præcipitia: inquit Tacitus lib. xv.iii.[?]
units.tr: Let me give examples of Opposites. Among Opposites, these admit a middle: white and black admit grey, purple, green and several others; beautiful and ugly admit a moderate appearance; wealth and poverty admit a mean condition. But these do not admit one: straight and bent; heaviness and lightness; standing and moving; to be awake and to sleep. Every statement, the dialecticians say, is either true or false. Every line is either straight or bent. A woman either loves or hates; there is no third option. In the same class are sacred and profane, public and private, citizen and foreigner, husband and bachelor, father and orphan. Cicero says that between war and peace there is nothing in the middle, for a truce is so brief a time that it is not counted as a state of its own. Tacitus, book 15, says that for those who desire supreme power there is nothing in the middle between the highest summit and the precipice. [?]

units.la: Cedo exemplum de Relatis. Inter pauca & multa,longum & breue,est mediocritas.inter velocitatem & tarditatem,lenta sestinatio. Inter seruum & dominum est addictus. At inter patrem & filium, socerum & generum, nihil interie-ctum est.
units.tr: Let me give examples of Relatives. Between few and many, long and short, there is a mean. Between speed and slowness, there is a slow haste. Between master and slave there is the bondsman. But between father and son, or father-in-law and son-in-law, nothing is interposed.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de Priuantibus. Inter diē & noctem, diluculum & crepusculum interiectum est: vt inter calidum & frigidum, est tepidum. Inter visum & cæcitatem, lippitudo. Inter sanitatem & morbum Medicorum sententia aliquis status est interie-ctus. Inter vitam & mortem, Platonis sententia est, ἡ ἐξαίφνης φύσις,[?] vt in Parmenide loquitur: id est, momentum dissolutionis: quod tamen Iurisconsulti, vitæ attribuunt. At inter par & impar, humidum & siccum nihil interie-ctum est.
units.tr: Let me give examples of Privatives. Between day and night, dawn and dusk are interposed, just as between hot and cold there is the lukewarm. Between sight and blindness there is dimness of sight. Between health and sickness, the opinion of physicians places some intermediate condition. Between life and death, Plato's view is [ἡ ἐξαίφνης φύσις], as he speaks of it in the Parmenides; that is, the moment of dissolution, which nevertheless the jurists assign to life. But between even and odd, or moist and dry, nothing is interposed.

units.la: Quid? Aientia & Negantia cur tertium nō recipiunt? Quoniam cùm ceterorum contrariorum ea natura fit, vt alterum alterius habitum & essentiam fateatur: hæc sola contrariis sui habitum non fatentur. Itaque ex omnibus contrariis, hæc summè contraria nominantur. non quo aduersa non magis inter se infestafint, magísque inuicem abhorreant. nam hæc quoque Negantia sæpe aduersorum intermedia sunt. sed quia nihil inter Aientia & Negantia potest medium intercedere. veluti, donare & eripere aduersa sunt, magísque inter se abhorrent, quàm donare & non donare. cùm hoc posterius inter illa interiectum fit. Amicus & hostis aduersa sunt. inter quæ Non amicus aut Non hostis posset intercedere.
units.tr: Why do affirmations and negations not admit a third? Because, while the nature of the other contraries is such that each acknowledges the state and essence of the other, these alone do not acknowledge the state of their contrary. Therefore, of all contraries, these are called most absolutely contrary. Not that opposites are not hostile to one another or do not shrink from each other as much; for these negations too are often intermediate between opposites. Rather, it is because nothing can come between affirmation and negation. For example, to give and to take away are opposites, and they shrink from each other more than to give and not to give, since the latter is interposed between the former. Friend and enemy are opposites, between which the not-friend or not-enemy could come.

units.la: Quæ est altera Contrariorum diuisio? Eorū animaduerto esse quædam eiusmodi, vt aut vtrunque esse possit, aut alterutrum esse necesse sit, aut neutrum esse possit, aut denique vtrunque simul & neutrum esse possit.
units.tr: What is the other division of contraries? I observe that some of them are such that either both can be, or one of the two must be, or neither can be, or finally both can be together and neither can be.

units.la: Cedo exemplum eorum quorum vtrunque simul, non autem neutrum verum esse potest. Nullum animal est (inquit Proculus Iurisconsultus) quod nec faciat, nec patiatur. At potest simul & facere & pati. Sic Pater & filius idem diuerso respectu esse potest: Gener & Socer: duplum & dimidium. Eiusque doctrinæ visus posterius in coniunctiuis syllogismis apparebit. Vitiosa enim hæc conclusio est: Non & patitur animal & agit. Salamandra non & flammam alit, & restinguit.
units.tr: Let me give examples of those of which both can be together but neither cannot be true. No animal, says the jurist Proculus, neither acts nor is acted upon; yet a thing can both act and be acted upon at the same time. So a father and son can be the same thing under different respects; likewise son-in-law and father-in-law, double and half. The force of this doctrine will appear later in conjunctive syllogisms. For this conclusion is faulty: "The animal does not both suffer and act." The salamander does not both feed and extinguish the flame.

units.la: Cedo exemplum eorum, quorum esse alterutrum necesse est. Status, Motus: Actio, pe-fsio: Levis, gravis: Par, impar: Coelebs, maritus. Hinc illa sunt: Aut amat, aut odit mulier. nihil est tertium. Militi insitum est, aut vincere, aut emori. nihil est tertium. huius autē doctrinæ usus cùm alias ad res magnus est, tum verò ad illud, quòd syllogismi disiunctiui, de quibus posterius differemus, ex huius generis contrariis conficiuntur: veluti, Aut vigilat, aut dormit. Vigilat autem, non dormit igitur.
units.tr: Let me give examples of those of which one of the two must be. Standing and moving; acting and suffering; light and heavy; even and odd; bachelor and married man. From these come the sayings: a woman either loves or hates; there is no third. It is inborn in a soldier either to conquer or to die; there is no third. The use of this doctrine is great in many matters, but especially for this reason: disjunctive syllogisms, which we shall discuss later, are formed from contraries of this kind. For example: "Either he is awake or he is asleep. But he is awake; therefore he is not asleep."

units.la: Cedo exemplum eorum quorum neutrum esse potest? Ut nemo & sedere & ambulare simul potest (inquit idem Iurisconsultus) ita potest aliquis neutrum: velut is qui accumbit. Item Planities neque mons, neque vallis est. Tepidum neque calidum, neque frigidum est. Mediocris neque dives, neq; pauper est. Vxor stata forma, neque pulchra, neque deformis est. Sic habitus est mediocris inter Sanitatem & Morbum. Mediocritas inter multū & parū.
units.tr: Let me give examples of those of which neither can be? As no one can both sit and walk at the same time, says the same jurist, so someone can be neither; for example, one who is reclining at table. Likewise a plain is neither a mountain nor a valley. The lukewarm is neither hot nor cold. A moderate man is neither rich nor poor. A wife of middling beauty is neither beautiful nor ugly. So a condition is intermediate between health and sickness, and a mean between much and little.

units.la: Cedo exemplum eorum quorum & utrunque & neutrum simul esse potest. Lippitudo inter visum & caecitatem ita interiecta est, ut & utrunque & neutrum fit. Dilucululum & crepusculum ita inter diem & noctem, ut & utrunque & neutrum sint. Inducię inter bellum & pacem. Ambidexter inter dextra & sinistra recte utentem. Animantes ancipites inter terrenas & aquatiles.Hermaphroditus inter marem & fœminam.
units.tr: Let me give examples of those of which both and neither can be at the same time. Dimness of sight is interposed between sight and blindness in such a way that it is both and neither. Dawn and dusk are between day and night in such a way that they are both and neither. Truces are between war and peace. The ambidextrous person is between one who uses the right hand and one who uses the left. Amphibious creatures are between land animals and water animals. The hermaphrodite is between male and female.

units.la: De Repugnantibus. CAP. XXII.
units.tr: On Repugnant Things. CHAP. XXII.

units.la: QUONIAM de Cótrariis dixisti, deinceps de Repugnantibus videamus. Quæ sunt Repugnántia? Quæ non ex adverso, sed quasi ex transverso inter se opponuntur. Itaque disparata non incommodè á nonnullis appellátur, quasi comparata sint, quæ directò inter se opponuntur. Repugnátium enim alterum unum est è duobus contrariis: alterum verò non aliud contrarium, sed alterius contrarij consequens. quasi si duo gladiatores antagonistæ inter se commissi essent: quorum uterque auxiliarium sive συμμαχὸν haberet: & alter è gladiatoribus alterius auxiliatorem feriret. Denique Repugnans dicitur, quod contrarij est consequens. veluti Valetudo & morbus. Bonitas coloris & pallor.
units.tr: Since you have discussed contraries, let us next consider repugnants. What are repugnant things? They are things that are opposed to one another not directly, face to face, but as it were across the grain. So those that are set against each other not directly are not inappropriately called "disparate" by some, as if they were matched only in a side-on way. For one of two repugnants is one of two contraries, while the other is not simply another contrary but a consequence of the other contrary. It is like two gladiators pitted against each other, each with an ally or helper [σύμμαχον], where one of the gladiators strikes down the other's helper. In short, a thing is called repugnant when it is a consequence of a contrary: for example, health and sickness, a good colour and pallor.

units.la: Ecquænam Repugnantium inveniendorum ratio est? Cùm inter Antecedens & Cósequés negatio interiicitur, continuò ex consecutione Repugnantia efficitur. Ponantur primùm duo cótraria: Amicus, Hostis. tū subiiciantur eorundem consequentia: Juvádus, Lædédus: quæ inter se quoq; contraria sunt. Cōtrariorū enim (ut ait Cic.) cōtraria sunt cōsequētia. deinde amicus cū verbo lædendus cōmittatur: aut inimicus cum verbo iuuādus: Repugnantia existet,hoc modo: Nō & amicus est,& male meretur: Non & inimicus est, & benè meretur. Amicus Hostis Iuuandus Laedendus
units.tr: What is the method of finding repugnant things? When a negation is placed between an antecedent and its consequent, a repugnance is at once produced from the consequence. First let two contraries be set down: friend, enemy. Then let their consequences be placed under them: to be helped, to be harmed, which are also contrary to each other. For, as Cicero says, the consequences of contraries are contrary. Next, let "friend" be joined with "to be harmed", or "enemy" with "to be helped", and a repugnance will arise in this way: "He is not a friend and yet does ill by him"; "He is not an enemy and yet does well by him." Friend, enemy, to be helped, to be harmed.

units.la: De Disparibus. CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: On Disparates. CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: QVÆ sunt Disparia? Quæ cùm eiusdem naturæ sint, tamen propter elationem aut submisionē, id est, propter magis aut minus inæqualia sunt. Maius enim & minus in iis demū quæ generis eiusdem sunt, proprie vereque quæruntur. veluti Homo homine,& Bos boue, maior minorve dicitur:non Homo maior boue,vel camelo. μεῖζον (inquit Cedrenus) ἢ ἑαλ- τὴν δὲ τῆς ὁμοουσίων ζητεῖται ἢ κρίνεται.ἑτεροούσια δὲ ἀλλήλοις συγκρίνεσθαι ἢ δύνανται. quod tamē proprie strictéque intelligēdum est. cùm improprie atque abusiuē Comparatio etiam inter alterius generis res vsurpetur. vt cùm quæritur, an omnis stella maior fit terra: an vrus maior fit boue, & lupus cane. Vt autem Parium duæ sunt species: ita disparium quædā proprie sic dicuntur, quæ sensibus percipiuntur. veluti impares in libra lances: quædam improprie, quæ ad animum & rationem translata sunt: veluti dispares mores disparia studia sequuntur.
units.tr: What are disparates? They are things of one and the same nature which nonetheless differ by excess or deficiency, that is, by being more or less unequal. For "greater" and "less" are properly and truly sought only among things of the same kind. For example, a man is said to be greater or less than another man, and an ox than another ox, but a man is not said to be greater than an ox or a camel. Cedrenus says: μεῖζον ἢ ἔλαττον ἐν τοῖς ὁμοουσίοις ζητεῖται ἢ κρίνεται· ἑτεροούσια δὲ ἀλλήλοις συγκρίνεσθαι οὐ δύνανται. ("Greater or less is sought or judged only among things of the same substance; things of different substance cannot be compared with one another.") This must be understood strictly and properly, since comparison is also used loosely and improperly between things of different kinds, as when we ask whether every star is greater than the earth, or whether the aurochs is larger than the ox, or the wolf than the dog. Just as there are two kinds of equals, so some disparates are called such properly, namely those perceived by the senses, as unequal scales in a balance. Others are called such improperly, being transferred to the mind and reason, as when we say that dissimilar characters follow dissimilar pursuits.

units.la: Quid appellas Elationem & Submifsionem? Cùm ex comparatis alterum maius, alterum minus est. proprie quidem quantitate, vt modò dictum est. improprie verò, qualitate, vt ex pondere hoc modo: Grauior pœna est, quàm noxia. Præftabilior est gloria, quàm pecunia. Ex numero: veluti, Varro doctior est Cicerone, quia plura didicit. Ex mensura: veluti, Maior est victoria C. Cæsaris, quàm C. Marij. Ex hoc genere illæ sunt Rhetorum contentiones: velut apud Ciceronem Verrina III. Non enim furem, sed ereptorē: non adulterum, sed expugnatorem pudicitiæ: non facrilegum, sed hostem facrorū religionumq; : non sicarium, sed crudelisimum carnificicem ciuium sociorúmque in vestrum iudicium ad duximus.
units.tr: What do you mean by excess and deficiency? When, of things compared, one is greater and the other less. Properly, this is in quantity, as was just said; improperly, in quality. Thus, from weight: "A penalty is heavier than the offence." "Glory is more valuable than money." From number: "Varro is more learned than Cicero, because he has learned more." From measure: "The victory of Gaius Caesar was greater than that of Gaius Marius." To this kind belong the contrasts of the orators, such as in Cicero's Third Verrine: "We have brought before your judgment not a thief but a plunderer, not an adulterer but a violator of chastity, not a sacrilegious man but an enemy of sacred things and of religion, not an assassin but the most cruel executioner of citizens and allies."

units.la: Quid interest inter Contraria & Disparia? Contraria sunt, quorū vnum vni tantùm: Disparia, quorum vnum pluribus opponitur. Item Contraria ex toto inter fe pugnant: disparia verò ex parte tátùm: id est, (vt modò dicebamus) ex elatione & summissione. cuius rei exempla sunt in virtutibus & vitiis sanè insignia.
units.tr: What is the difference between contraries and disparates? Contraries are those of which one is opposed to only one; disparates are those of which one is opposed to several. Likewise, contraries fight each other wholly, whereas disparates do so only in part, that is (as we just said) by excess and deficiency. Examples of this are very clear in virtues and vices.

units.la: Quomodo inter virtutes & vitia disparitas ostenditur[?]? Philosophi veteres animaduerterunt, virtutem inter elationem & summissionem consistere: hoc est, inter nimium & parum: quasi cùm libra pari vtrinque pondere examinatur.Itaque cùm duo virtutis extrema vitiosa essent, rectè Horatius scripsisse creditur, Virtus est medium vitiorum vtrinquè redactum. Horum autem extremorum alterum virtuti contrarium est, eáque pugnantia per se elucet: alterum dispar : quæ disparitas obscura est, quia virtutem fallaciter imitans eam adulterat.
units.tr: How is disparity shown between virtues and vices? The ancient philosophers observed that virtue lies between excess and deficiency, that is, between too much and too little, as when a balance is weighed with equal weight on both sides. Therefore, since the two extremes of virtue are vicious, Horace is believed to have written rightly: "Virtue is the mean between vices, brought in on both sides." Of these extremes, one is contrary to virtue, and this opposition is plain in itself; the other is a disparate, and this disparity is hidden, because it imitates virtue deceptively and corrupts it.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Plutarchus in Camillo hæc inter se opponit, δεισιδαιμονίαν & ὀλιγωρίαν τῷ θεῶν. ἡ δὲ εὐλαβεία (inquit) καὶ τὸ μηδὲν ἄγαν, ἀεισον[?].
