Sic auaritia & prodigalitas vitia sunt aduersissima. Interponatur liberalitas, contraria erit auaritiæ : dispar prodigalitati. Rursus interponatur frugalitas,fiue parfimonia : contraria erit prodigalitati, dispar auaritiæ. Sic audacia & metus, duo vitia contraria sunt. his interiecta fortitudo est, quæ metui contraria est,audaciæ dispar. Rursus interponatur cautio:audaciæ cōtraria est, metui difpar.Ex eodem genere illa sunt,quæ ex Ciceronis Partitionibus proferemus: Nā & prudentiam(inquit)malitia,& temperantiam immanitas in voluptatibus aspernandis, & magnitudinem animi superbia in animis extollendis, & despicientia in contemnendis honoribus,&liberalitatem effusio,& fortitudinē audacia imitatur.& patiētiam duritia immanis, & iustitiam acerbitas, & religionem superstitio,& lenitaté mollitia animi, & verecundiam timiditas, & illam disputandi prudentiā concertatio captatióque verborum, & hanc oratoriā vim inanis quædā profluentia loquédi.
units.tr: Give an example. Plutarch, in the Life of Camillus, sets these against each other: δεισιδαιμονίαν and ὀλιγωρίαν τῶν θεῶν (superstition and contempt of the gods). "Caution," he says, "and the maxim 'nothing in excess' are the virtue between them." So avarice and prodigality are very opposed vices. If liberality is placed between them, it will be contrary to avarice and a disparate to prodigality. Again, if thrift or parsimony is placed between them, it will be contrary to prodigality and a disparate to avarice. Likewise, boldness and fear are two contrary vices; between them lies courage, which is contrary to fear and a disparate to boldness. Again, if caution is placed between them, it is contrary to boldness and a disparate to fear. Of the same kind are the examples we will give from Cicero's Partitiones: "For cunning imitates prudence, licentiousness imitates temperance in rejecting pleasures, arrogance imitates greatness of spirit in raising oneself up, and contempt of honours imitates the despising of honours; wastefulness imitates liberality, and rashness imitates courage; savage harshness imitates patience, bitterness imitates justice, superstition imitates religion, softness of mind imitates gentleness, timidity imitates modesty; and the contentiousness and hunting after words of that skill of disputing imitates prudence in argument, while a certain empty flow of talk imitates the power of oratory."

units.la: De Dissimilibus. CAP. XXIIII.
units.tr: On Dissimilars. Chapter 24.

units.la: VAE sunt Dissimilia? Superiùs dictum est, eandem esse similium & dissimilium definitionem: propterea quòd similia & dissimilia non ex toto dicuntur, sed ex parte tantùm. nihil enim simile est quod idem ex parte non fit dissimile: vicissimque nihil dissimile est, quod idem non aliqua ex parte fit simile.
units.tr: What are dissimilars? It was said above that the definition of similars and dissimilars is the same, because similar and dissimilar things are predicated not wholly but only in part. For nothing is similar which is not also in some part dissimilar; and conversely, nothing is dissimilar which is not in some part similar.

units.la: Quomodo dissimilitudo rerum internoscitur? Ex qualitatis aut insitæ aut externæ differentia: de qua superiùs in similium tractatione disseruimus. Itémque ex diversorum generum aut formarum demóstratione. nam vt aquarum varietas ex diversis fontibus cognoscitur, sic rerum differentia ex variorum generum & formarum demonstratione.
units.tr: How is the dissimilarity of things recognised? By a difference of quality, either innate or external, which we discussed above in the treatment of similars. Likewise by the demonstration of different kinds or forms. For just as the variety of waters is recognised from their different springs, so the difference of things is recognised by the demonstration of various kinds and forms.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de genere. Sumamus hoc familiare: Duo equi specie similes sunt, at natione dissimiles: quæ plerunque (vt ait Varro) pretium efficit. sic hinnulus dissimilis est mulo: quia mulus ex asino & equa est: hinnulus ex equo & asina. Formarum autem dissimilitudo in eo medio existit, quod superiùs dicebamus interdum interiectum esse inter duo aduersa. veluti, inter ignem & aquam, quæ proprie aduersa sunt, interiectus est aër, qui neutri extremo contrarius est,sed dissimilis.
units.tr: Give me an example of kind. Let us take a familiar one: two horses are similar in species but dissimilar in breed, and this, as Varro says, often makes the price. So a young hinny is dissimilar to a mule, because a mule is from a male ass and a mare, while a hinny is from a stallion and a she-ass. The dissimilarity of forms, however, lies in that middle ground which we said above is sometimes interposed between two opposites. For example, between fire and water, which are properly opposites, lies air, which is contrary to neither extreme but dissimilar.

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplum. Candor & atror aduersa sunt. at quinque colores intermedij, croceus, puniceus, purpureus, viridis, cerruleus,neutri è duobus extremis aduersi sut[?]:sed diuersi, &(vt de coloribus proprie veréque dicitur)varij. Item dulcis & amarus, duo sapores contrarij sunt: quorū illi quinque(eodem auctore) sunt intermedij: austerus, acerbus, aridus,acutus,falsus: qui neutri extremorum contrarij sunt,sed dissimiles.
units.tr: Give me another example. White and black are opposites. But the five intermediate colours, saffron, purple-red, purple, green and blue, are opposed to neither of the two extremes, but are different and, as is properly and truly said of colours, various. Likewise sweet and bitter are two opposite tastes; between them, according to the same authority, lie five intermediate tastes: astringent, sour, dry, sharp and salty, which are contrary to neither extreme but dissimilar.

units.la: Quomodo tractatur ea demoftratio? Non vt sacrificij, sic consilij dies expectandus est. Alia est enim sacrificij caussa, quod expectari potest:alia cosilij,quod interdum ex re & tempore sumi oportet. Non quemadmodum in paleftra qui tedas candentes accipit, celerior est in cursu continuo quam ille qui tradit: ita melior Imperator nouus qui accipit exercitum,quam ille qui decedit: propterea quod defatigatus cursor integro facem: hic peritus imperator imperito exercitum tradit. Non vt equis veteribus,teneros anteponere solemus, sic amici noui veteribus sunt anteponendi: non enim amicitiarum esse debent, sicut aliarum rerum, satietates: veterrima quaeque esse suauissima debent.nouitates tamē non repudiandae:vetustas autem suo loco conseruetur.
units.tr: How is this demonstration handled? One need not wait for the day of counsel as one waits for the day of sacrifice. For the reason for a sacrifice is one that can be awaited, but the reason for counsel is one that must sometimes be taken up from the circumstance and the moment. Just as in the wrestling-ground the runner who receives the burning torches is not swifter in continuous running than the one who hands them over, so a new commander who takes over an army is not better than the one who departs, since the exhausted runner hands over the torch to a fresh one; here a skilled commander hands over the army to an unskilled one. And just as we are accustomed to prefer young horses to old ones, so new friends are not to be preferred to old ones; for friendships, unlike other things, ought not to suffer satiety, and the oldest should be the sweetest. Yet novelties are not to be rejected, and antiquity is to be kept in its place.

units.la: Quid interest inter Disparia & dissimilia? Superius dictum est,Paria aut disparia,quantitate:Similia aut dissimilia,qualitate estimari: Quapropter in quibus ponderis, numeri, aut mensurae ratio habetur (diximus autem haec ad mentem & animum transferri) in iis est disparitas. in quibus autem forma spectatur, dissimilitudo.
units.tr: What is the difference between disparates and dissimilars? It was said above that equals or unequals are judged by quantity, and similars or dissimilars by quality. Therefore, in those things in which weight, number or measure is considered (and we have said that these are transferred to the mind and spirit), there is disparity. But in those in which form is regarded, there is dissimilarity.

units.la: De Dictione,& varijs ipsius diuisionibus.
units.tr: On Diction, and its various divisions.

units.la: CAP. XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: [?]GESIS, deinceps ad verba & dictiones accedamus. Sed primùm omnium velim, nisi molestum est, iterum mihi planius explices, annon tota de dictionibus, verbis, vocibus, nominibus, vocabulis, aduerbiis, participijs tractatio Grammaticorum potius, quàm Dialecticorum propria fit? Grammatici artis suae principia ferè à Dialecticis sumpserunt. quemadmodum Diogenes Laertius, cùm alijs multis locis; tum verò in Zenone dilucidè ostendit. Grammaticorum enim opera tum demùm usui esse coepit, cùm corrupti sermo coeptus est. quapropter & Quintilianus & idem Laertius à philosophis, ac maximè Stoicis, plurimas orationis partes constitutas scribunt. quinetiam Plato in Cratylo perspicuè statuit, Dialectici opus esse, aptè & cōmodè nomina rebus imponere: eáque imposita interpretari. Ubi enim divisa in partes quaestio est, tum singulae partes suis nominibus primùm designandae, pòst definitione explicandae sunt. [illegible, ~4 letters] τὰ πρᾶγμαζ[?] ὰ δ[?]ὲ τῆς ἐν λόγοις θεωρίας ὁρᾶταί[?]: ut Stoici (auctore Laertio) dicere solebant. Iam verò longè alia Dialecticorum, alia Grammaticorum de verbis & oratione disputatio est: quemadmodum superiùs dictum est: & deinceps ex huius institutionis progressu intelliges.
units.tr: Next, let us come to words and terms. But first, if it is no trouble, please explain to me again more plainly: is the whole treatment of terms, words, voices, names, vocables, adverbs and participles really the business of the Grammarians rather than the Dialecticians? The Grammarians took the principles of their art mostly from the Dialecticians, as Diogenes Laertius shows clearly in many places, and especially in his life of Zeno. For grammar only began to be useful once speech had begun to be corrupted. That is why Quintilian and the same Laertius write that most parts of speech were established by the philosophers, and especially the Stoics. Plato, moreover, states plainly in the Cratylus that it is the task of the Dialectician to impose names on things aptly and fittingly, and to interpret the names once imposed. For when a question has been divided into parts, each part must first be marked by its own name and then explained by definition. [τὰ πράγματα ... ἐν λόγοις θεωρίας] as the Stoics (according to Laertius) used to say. But the Dialecticians' discussion of words and speech is quite different from that of the Grammarians, as was said above, and you will understand this more fully as the course of this instruction proceeds.

units.la: Quotuplex est Dictio Dialectica? Dialectica dictio est aut nomen, aut verbū, aut aduerbium: ex quo quantum à Grammatica differat, cuius septem numerantur species, facilè intellectu est. Nam neque præpositio aut interiectio vim in illa vllam habent: & participium ac pronomen nominis locū obtinent. Quamuis autem omnis oratio dialectica minimùm ex duobus nominibus & verbo e s t conflet, tamen interdum aduerbium loci vel temporis alterum in ea momentum obtinet. ut Homines olim erant meliores; Homines nunc sunt deteriores, quàm olim.
units.tr: How many kinds of dialectical word are there? A dialectical word is either a noun, a verb or an adverb. From this it is easy to see how far it differs from grammar, which counts seven kinds. For neither the preposition nor the interjection has any force in it, and the participle and the pronoun take the place of a noun. Although every dialectical sentence is made up of at least two nouns and a verb, an adverb of place or time sometimes has a second role in it, as in: "Men were once better; men now are worse than they once were."

units.la: Quæ est altera diuisio? Hæc bipartita est, ut alia propria dictio sit, alia communis. Propria est, certa & rata cuiusque rei nota, quæ alteri non conuenit, videlicet, cùm singulæ res singulis nominibus appellantur. veluti: aër, ignis, aqua, terra. Communis est, quæ pluribus conuenit, ut concio, fraus, palma, familia. atque ex hac communitate ambiguitas nascitur, quam Poetæ Græci ἀμφιλογίαν nominarūt, & Nostis filiam, dixerunt: eandem Græci phi-losophi modò ἀμφιβολίαν, modò ἀμφιβολογίαν appellant. Iuris communionem explicant noftri in l.pen.& vlt.D.de iuftit.& iur,
units.tr: What is the second division? This one has two parts: one word is proper, another common. A proper word is a certain and fixed mark of each thing, which does not belong to another, namely when each thing is called by its own name, as: air, fire, water, earth. A common word is one that applies to many, as: assembly, fraud, palm, family. From this commonness ambiguity arises, which the Greek poets called ἀμφιλογία and called "the daughter of Strife"; the Greek philosophers call the same thing sometimes ἀμφιβολία and sometimes ἀμφιβολογία. Our jurists explain the communion of law in l. pen. and l. ult. D. de iustitia et iure.

units.la: Quid? Ambiguitatis verborum tractatio cur potius ad Dialecticos, quàm ad Grammaticos pertinet? Quia soli Dialectici vitádæ ambiguitatis artem tradunt, & Sophistis opponuntur, quorum instrumentum omne in ambiguitate & amphibolia positum est. Nam & multæ similes res dissimilibus verbis, & multæ rursus dissimiles similibus notatæ sunt.Itaque Cicero lib.de Orat.ıı, Ambiguorum(inquit) verborum complura genera sunt, quæ mihi videntur melius noffe,qui Dialecticiappellantur.
units.tr: Why? Why does the treatment of the ambiguity of words belong to the Dialecticians rather than the Grammarians? Because only the Dialecticians teach the art of avoiding ambiguity, and they are set against the Sophists, whose whole equipment rests on ambiguity and amphibology. For many similar things are marked by dissimilar words, and again many dissimilar things by similar words. So Cicero, in the second book of De Oratore, says: "There are several kinds of ambiguous words, which I think are better known to those called Dialecticians."

units.la: Velim igitur aliquanto dilucidius bipartitam illam dictionis[?] diuisionem explices. Rerum omnium aliæ ratione & nomine inter fe conueniunt:(Rationem autem appello quam Ariftoteles λόγον τῆς οὐσίας nominat,idest definitionem qua quid res fit tantùm, non etiá qualis res fit exponitur) vt bos & equus: quorum vterque & definitur & appellatur animal.hæc Dialectici συνώνυμα nominant.aliæ & ratione & nomine inter fe differunt,vt equus, argétum, quorum aliud animal est, aliud nó animal est, sed metallũ.Aliæ ratione conueniunt,nomine discrepant. de quibus hoc Ciceronis exemplum ex Tufcul.ı ıı.exponemus.Sed ratio(inquit) vna omnium eit ægritudinum, plura nomina.Nam & inuidere ægritudinis est,& ç-mulari,& obtrectare,& misereri,angi,lugere. hæc omnia definiunt Stoici, eáque verba quæ dixi singularum rerum sunt: non ( vt videntur) easdem res significant: sed aliquid differunt.Postremò aliæ nomine conueniūt,non ratione: vt Fraus fallaciam significat, & delictum & pœnam . Palma commune nomen est manus,arboris,baccæ,victoriæ . Hæc Dialecti ci ὁμώνυμα nominant . sed de synonymis & homonymis paulo vberius differendum est.
units.tr: Please explain to me, then, a little more clearly that twofold division of the word. Some things agree with one another both in definition and in name. (By definition I mean what Aristotle calls the λόγος τῆς οὐσίας, that is, the explanation which shows only what a thing is, not also what sort of thing it is.) For example, ox and horse: each is both defined and called "animal." The Dialecticians call these συνώνυμα. Others differ from one another both in definition and in name, as horse and silver: one is an animal, the other is not an animal but a metal. Others agree in definition but differ in name. For these we will set out this example from Cicero's Tusculan Disputations, book 3 (or 4): "But the definition of all the distresses is one, though the names are many. For to envy is a distress, and to emulate, to disparage, to pity, to be vexed, to mourn." The Stoics define all these, and the words I have mentioned belong each to a single thing; they do not, as they seem to, signify the same things, but differ in some respect. Lastly, others agree in name but not in definition: thus fraus means deceit, and also offence and punishment; palm is a common name for the hand, a tree, a berry and a victory. The Dialecticians call these ὁμώνυμα. But we must discuss synonyms and homonyms somewhat more fully.

units.la: De Synonymis, Homonymis & Paronymis.
units.tr: On Synonyms, Homonyms and Paronyms.

units.la: CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: VOTVPLEX igitur est dictionū cō-munitas? Duplex.quarum altera est in vniuersa dictione, quæ à Dialecticis nominatur Synonymia &Homonymia: altera in parte,quæ ab iisdem Paronymia dicitur.
units.tr: What, then, is the twofold community of words? It is twofold. One kind lies in the whole word, and the Dialecticians call it synonymy and homonymy. The other lies in a part of the word, and the same writers call it paronymy.

units.la: ·Quæ sunt Synonyma? Synonimorum sunt alia Dialectica, alia Grammatica. Dialectica sunt,quæ generis alicuiusfuperioris & nomē & rationē communem habēt: vt Bos & equus ex fui generis communione & nomen & rationem & definitionem essentialem (de qua posterius intelliges) communē obtinent.Nam vttunque dicitur animal : sed tamen in qualitate differunt.
units.tr: What are synonyms? Synonyms are of two kinds, dialectical and grammatical. Dialectical synonyms are those that share both a name and a common concept under some higher genus. Thus ox and horse share, by their common genus, both the name and the concept and the essential definition (which you will understand later). For each is called an animal, though they differ in quality.

units.la: - Quæ sunt Synonyma Grammatica? Plura vnius eiufdémque rei vocabula: vel,quæ re inter fe conueniunt,sono tantùm discrepant. quia sæpe (vt modò dixi) cùmvna res pluribus nominibus, tum etiam similes dissimilibus appellatur. veluti vestis, veftimentū: ensis, gladius: dialectica, logica: Prostrauit, afflixit, percu-lit, euertit. Sic apud Iurisconsultos, Pactum pactio, conuentum, conuentio, pactum conuentum. Gramatici hæc eadem & πολυώνυμα & ἰσο-δυναμοῦν[?] & nominant.
units.tr: What are grammatical synonyms? They are several words for one and the same thing, or words that agree in meaning and differ only in sound. As I said just now, one thing is often called by several names, and also similar things are called by dissimilar names. Examples are "vestis" and "vestimentum" (garment), "ensis" and "gladius" (sword), "dialectica" and "logica" (dialectic, logic), "prostravit," "afflixit," "percussit," "evertit" (knocked down, struck down, beat, overturned). So among the jurists: "pactum" and "pactio," "conventum" and "conventio," "pactum conventum" (agreement). Grammarians call these same things polyonyms [πολυώνυμα] and isodynamics [ἰσοδύναμα].

units.la: Quid? Dialectici ecquonam igitur nomine appellant, quæ ratione conueniunt, nomine discrepant, quam superiùs tertiam ambiguorū speciem faciebas? Hanc speciem Dialectici negligunt. quia vbi de notione conuenit, de voce nasci quæstio non potest. nam si cui ius est ensem gestare, dubium nemini est, quin eidem gladium gestare liceat.
units.tr: What then? What name do the Dialecticians give to those words that agree in concept but differ in name, which you called a third kind of ambiguity above? The Dialecticians pass over this kind, because where the concept agrees, no question can arise about the word. For if a man has the right to carry a sword, nobody doubts that he may carry a blade.

units.la: Quæ sunt homonyma? Homonyma dialectica dicuntur, quorum idem nomen, sed diuersa vel species est, vel genus. Specie autem modò specialissimā, hoc est primā substantiā intelligo. Specie igitur & substantia differunt, quæ tamen nomen vnū & commune habent. vt Alexander Magnus, & Alexander Cæsar: & duo Gracchi, & duo Cicerones, & omnes denique vel agnati, vel ceteri, qui eodem nomine sunt. vt duo Sempronij: in l. si fuerit, 10, D. de reb. dub. aut duo Titij: in l. quoties, 54. D. de vsuf. Si duo (inquit Iulianus) eiusdem nominis fuerint, & ita scriptum fuerit, Titijs vsumfructū alternis annis do lego: nisi consenserint vter eorum prior vtatur, inuicem sibi impedient. Genere autem differunt, cùm eodem nomine sunt, veluti Hercules, & eius signum, siue imago. Nam Hercules animal est, signū inanimatum. Hinc nata cōsuetudo, vt Deorum signa, dij appellarentur. Vt Verrina ii[?]: Deum deinqué nullum Siculis, qui ei paulo magis affabre atque antiquo artificio fa&us[?] videretur, reliquit. Sic equus Agamenonis, & equus Troianus. Equuleus pro equo tenello, & pro torméti genere. Scriptor historiæ, pro Thucydide & pro librario. Testamentū falsum, testamentum tamen dicitur (inquit Paulus) & modius iniquus, modius. l. Paulus, 221[?], D. de ver. fignif. l. 2, D. quemad. test. aper. Ex eodem genere est, quod Valerius scribit de Daphita, qui cùm Apollinis illudendi caussa quæsisset, an equum inuenire posset, cùm tamen nullum amisisset, respondsum tulit; equum inuenturum, sed quo deiectus periret, aliquanto post in Regem Attalum incidit, qui eum de saxo, cui nomē erat Equus, præcipitari iussit. Sic Philippus Macedo admonitus oraculo, vt quadrigas caueret, toto regno disiungi currus iussit: sed Pausanię gladio cuius capulus quadrigas celatas habebat, interfectus est. Ad hoc autē genus pertinent, & verborū ambiguitas, & metonymia.
units.tr: What are homonyms? Dialectical homonyms are those that have the same name but a different species or a different genus. By species I mean here the most specific species, that is, the first substance. Things that differ in species and substance, yet share one common name, are homonyms: for example Alexander the Great and Alexander Caesar, the two Gracchi, the two Ciceros, and in short all relatives or others who bear the same name, such as two Sempronii (in the law "si fuerit," D. de reb. dub., 10) or two Titii (in the law "quoties," D. de usufructu, 54). Julianus says: "If there are two of the same name, and it is written thus, 'I bequeath the usufruct to Titii in alternate years': unless they agree which of them shall use it first, they will hinder each other." They differ in genus when, though bearing the same name, they are such things as Hercules and his statue or image. For Hercules is an animal, but the statue is inanimate. Hence arose the custom of calling the statues of the gods "gods." Thus in Verres: he left the Sicilians no god, nor even one that seemed to have been made with more skill and in the old manner. So too the horse of Agamemnon and the Trojan horse. "Equuleus" means a young horse and also a kind of torture. A "scriptor historiae" means Thucydides or a copyist. A false will is still called a will (says Paulus), and an unjust bushel is still a bushel (law "Paulus," D. de verborum significatione, 221; law 2, D. quemadmodum testamenta aperiuntur). Of the same kind is what Valerius writes about Daphitas: when he asked, to mock Apollo, whether he could find a horse, and had lost none, he received the answer that he would find one, but that he would perish by being thrown down. Some time later he fell into the hands of King Attalus, who ordered him thrown from a rock called Horse. So also Philip of Macedon, warned by an oracle to beware of the four-horse chariot, ordered all chariots unyoked throughout his kingdom; yet he was killed by Pausanias with a sword whose hilt had a hidden four-horse chariot. To this kind belong also the ambiguity of words and metonymy.

units.la: Quæ sunt verba ambigua? Quæ in vtranque partem significatione ambigua dicuntur. veluti formidolosus, qui formidat, & formidatur: inuidiosus, qui inuidet, & cui inuidetur. infestus, qui malum infert, & cui infertur. ceteráque generis eiusdem, quæ Gellius commemorat lib.ix.ca.x11.&lib.xv.cap.xiii.Sic cùm in iure ciuili prouerbiû esset Filiofa. credi nō licere:Sceuola monuit, non ad verba referendum esse,sed ad numerationem.nam Credendi verbum erat ambiguum.
units.tr: What are ambiguous words? Those that are said to be ambiguous in meaning in either direction. For example "formidolosus," which can mean one who fears or one who is feared; "invidiosus," one who envies or one who is envied; "infestus," one who inflicts harm or one to whom harm is inflicted; and the others of this kind that Gellius mentions in book 9, chapter 12, and book 15, chapter 13. So, when the civil law had the maxim that a son under power may not be trusted (credi), Scaevola advised that it should not be referred to the words but to the counting, since the verb "credere" was ambiguous.

units.la: Quæ est metonymia? Est nominis pro nomine positio: idest, mutuatio alieni verbi, quod proprij loco subijcitur. verbū enim pro verbo summutatur: eóque nomine generatim complectimur quā Rhetores modò μεταφορὰν, modò ὑπαλλαγὴν, modò καταχρῆσιν, modò ἀλλὰ ἀγορίαν[?] appellant: vt benè morata ciuitas, orba Resp. parricida pro eo qui matré aut fratrem interfecit. sic gemma quæ proprie de lapillo dicitur, trāslatè de vitibus vsurpatur. Sic fratris nomine soror appellatur in l.tres fratr.35, D.de pact.l.Lucius,93,s.quæsitū, D.de lega.3. Sic qui chirographū legat, actione ipsâ legasse intelligitur.l.qui chirographū,59,D.de legat.3.
units.tr: What is metonymy? It is the placing of one name for another; that is, the borrowing of a word that is put in place of the proper one. For one word is exchanged for another, and by this name we embrace what the Rhetoricians call now metaphor [μεταφορά], now substitution [ὑπαλλαγή], now catachresis [καταχρῆσις], now allegory [ἀλληγορία]: for example, a well-mannered state, a bereaved commonwealth, or a parricide for one who has killed his mother or brother. So "gemma," which properly means a little stone, is used figuratively of vines. So "soror" (sister) is used for "frater" (brother) in the law "tres fratres," D. de pactis, 35, and in the law "Lucius," D. de legatis 3, 93 §quaesitum. So one who bequeaths a written acknowledgment of debt is understood to have bequeathed the action itself (law "qui chirographum," D. de legatis 3, 59).

units.la: Quæ sunt homonyma Grammatica? Quę res plures vno complectuntur nomine: quapropter &πολύσημα[?] dicuntur. Cùm enim plures sint res quàm dictiones, propter verborū penuriam ea cómunitas inducta est. vt Cócio (inquit Gellius) dicitur pro loco, vnde verba fiunt, pro cœtu populi audientis, & pro ipsa oratione. Ciuitas (inquit idem) pro oppido, pro multitudine hominum, & pro iure ciuiū, Fraus, pro delicto, pœna, deceptione. Ex eadē ratione Varro de Analogia scribens, homony miam esse ait nominis communionem, vt in voce Argus,quæ Latinè hominem,Græcè oppidũ significat. Item in voce Meto,quæ & meto,metonis,& meto metis efficit.
units.tr: What are grammatical homonyms? Things that embrace several things under one name; for this reason they are also called polysemes [πολύσημα]. For since there are more things than words, this sharing of names was introduced because of the poverty of words. Thus, as Gellius says, "concio" is used for a place where speeches are made, for an assembly of listening people, and for the speech itself. "Civitas" (he says) means a town, a multitude of men, and the law of citizens. "Fraus" means a crime, a penalty, and a deception. For the same reason Varro, writing On Analogy, says that homonymy is the sharing of a name, as in the word "Argus," which in Latin means a man and in Greek a town. So too "meto," which makes "metonis" and "metis."

units.la: Quæ sunt Paronyma? Hæc cognominata proprie dicere possumus,quæ ab eadem inflexa voce rationem inter se communem habét. veluti anima. vnde sunt (vt ait Cicero) animus,animare,animans,animal,animatus, animosus. Item honos,honestus,honestas, honoratus,honorabilis,honorificus . Equus,eques, equestris,equitare,equitatus, equitatio. Hæc Græci σύστοιχα quoque nominant,quæ orta ab vno varie commutatur: vt recte Cicero definit, melius fortasse quàm appellauit.nā latinè Cō-iugata nominat, quæ proprie sunt συζυγα & ἀμίζυγα [?].
units.tr: What are paronyms? We may properly call these "cognates," the words that are inflected from the same word and share a common meaning, for example anima (soul). From it come, as Cicero says, animus (mind), animare (to animate), animans (living thing), animal (animal), animatus (animated), and animosus (spirited). Likewise honos (honour), honestus (honest), honestas (honesty), honoratus (honoured), honorabilis (honourable), and honorificus (honorific). Equus (horse), eques (horseman), equestris (equestrian), equitare (to ride), equitatus (cavalry), and equitatio (riding). The Greeks also call these [σύστοιχα], words that arise from one word and vary in form. Cicero defines them well, perhaps better than he names them, for in Latin he calls them coniugata (conjugates), though those are properly what the Greeks call [συζυγα] and [ἀμίζυγα].

units.la: Quæ est altera Dictionum diuisio? Vt aliæ sint simplices, aliæ multiplices, aliæ dubiæ. & rursus simplicium aliæ sint voce & notione simul simplices, aliæ voce tantùm simplices, at notione multiplices.
units.tr: What is the other division of words? Some words are simple, some compound, and some doubtful. And again, of simple words, some are simple both in sound and in meaning, and others are simple in sound only but compound in meaning.

units.la: Quę sunt verè & perfectè simplices? Eę quas superiùs Proprias appellauimus,quę vna tantùm voce & notione constant: vt ignis, aër, aqua,terra. Hîc enim & vna vox est, & vna tantùm res significatur.
units.tr: What are truly and perfectly simple words? Those that I called proper above, which consist of one sound and one meaning: for example "ignis" (fire), "aer" (air), "aqua" (water), "terra" (earth). Here there is one word and only one thing is signified.

units.la: Quæ sunt voce simplices, notione multiplices? Quæ vel genere,vel toto constant: genere,vt quæ superiùs homonyma, & synonyma diximus. Totum autem vel diuiduum est,vel indiuiduum. Diuiduū, veluti Ciuitas, Senatus, Exercitus, Grex. nam vna voce multæ res significantur. Indiuiduum, veluti quæ mediæ & ancipites appellantur. hoc est, quæ duas contrarias recipere notiones possunt. veluti dolus: nam & bonus & malus dolus est. Item, Tempestas, valetudo, facinus, gratia, industria, venenum. quæ omnia cōtrariam notionem recipiunt. Item quæ simul & indiuiduè plures res significant: vt Eques cuius notione homo, & Equus indiuiduè intelliguntur. Sic Nautæ verbo, homo & nauis indiuiduè concipiuntur. Item vt Latomi vocabulo, homo, lapis, & incisio. quod eodem modo in Cerdone, fabro, sartore, fullone, sutore & tinctore, ceteríque opificibus intelligendum est.
units.tr: What are words simple in sound but compound in meaning? Those that consist either in their genus or in their whole. In genus, as the homonyms and synonyms we spoke of above. A whole is either divided or undivided. Divided wholes are, for example, "civitas" (state), "senatus" (senate), "exercitus" (army), "grex" (flock), for one word signifies many things. Undivided are those called middle and ambiguous, that is, those that can receive two contrary meanings: for example "dolus" (trickery), for it can be both good and bad; likewise "tempestas" (weather or storm), "valetudo" (health), "facinus" (deed), "gratia" (favour), "industria" (diligence), "venenum" (poison or remedy). All these take on contrary meanings. Also, those words that signify several things at once and undividedly: for example "eques," by whose meaning both a man and a horse are understood undividedly; so "nautae," by the word, a man and a ship are conceived undividedly; likewise "latomi," by the word, a man, a stone, and a cutting. The same must be understood of cobbler (cerdo), smith (faber), tailor (sartor), fuller (fullo), shoemaker (sutor), dyer (tinctor), and the other craftsmen.

units.la: Quæ sunt multiplices? Quæ ex pluribus compositæ, & quasi conflatæ sunt. veluti ex duobus integris, subterfugere, & supersedere. ex integro & corrupto, benevolus, Tyrannicida, sacrilegus. ex corrupto & integro, noctivagus[?], armipotens. ex duobus corruptis, veneficus, parricida, pedisequus.
units.tr: What are compound words? Those composed of several parts and, as it were, fused together. For example, from two whole words: "subterfugere" (to escape by stealth) and "supersedere" (to refrain from). From a whole and a corrupted word: "benevolus" (well-wishing), "tyrannicida" (tyrant-slayer), "sacrilegus" (temple-robber). From a corrupted and a whole word: "noctivagus" (night-wandering), "armipotens" (mighty in arms). From two corrupted words: "veneficus" (poisoner), "parricida" (murderer of a father or kin), "pedisequus" (attendant).

units.la: Quæ sunt dubiæ? Quæ utrius generis sint, simpliciter an multiplices, ambigitur: veluti, Postliminium, an ex Post & Limen: Testamentum ex testatio & mens: Aeditimus, ex æde & tuendo. Sacellum utrum à sacro deminutum, an ex sacro & fella iunctum. Auarus utrum simplex, vt Amarus: an iunctum ex auidus & ære.
units.tr: What are doubtful words? Those whose kind is uncertain, that is, whether they are simple or compound. For example, "postliminium" (right of return): is it from "post" and "limen"? "Testamentum" (will): from "testatio" and "mens"? "Aedituus" (temple-keeper): from "aedes" and "tueri"? Is "sacellum" (small shrine) diminished from "sacrum," or joined from "sacrum" and "fella"? Is "avarus" (greedy) simple, like "amarus" (bitter), or joined from "avidus" and "aes"?

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: Quot sunt affectiones, siue λόγοι, & comparationes verborum? Totidem quot superiùs rei ad disputandum propositæ esse diximus. Itaque ordinem prorsus eundem in iis exponendis, sequemur: ac primùm de genere & specie.
units.tr: How many affections, or [λόγοι], and comparisons of words are there? As many as we said above there are things proposed for disputation. So in setting them out we shall follow exactly the same order, and first take up genus and species.

units.la: Quod est cuiusque dictionis genus? Quod in quæstione quid est de quaque respondetur, semper autem superior de inferiore dicitur, ac pronuntiatur. veluti, Quid est gladius? est telum. quid platanus? est arbor.
units.tr: What is the genus of each term? To the question "what is each thing?" an answer is always given, and the superior is always predicated of the inferior. For example: "What is a sword?" It is a weapon. "What is a plane tree?" It is a tree.

units.la: Quid? Nónne hoc idem & eodem modo superiùs de rebus ipsis dixisti? Rectè interrogas. Sed sic habendum est: de re loqui & agere inter nos, nisi nomine ipsius pronuntiato, non possumus: non magis quàm sine calculis ratiocinari. ex quo intelligitur, inter rem & ipsius vocabulum quandam quasi concretionem existere. Hanc concretionem Dialectica dirimit, ac diducit: ut separatim & res & dictiones quasi auulsæ atque abstractæ considerentur. Liberæ enim sunt cogitationes nostræ (inquit in Miloniana Cicero) & quæ volunt sic intuentur, ut ea cernimus quæ videmus. veluti, si quis annuli signū in cera impressum per se & quasi abstractum consideraret: aut in orbe partem coexam à concava distingueret. Hanc autem animi notio separatam confiderationem efficit, de qua superiùs dictum est. Itaque vocabuli significationem Cicero multis locis notionem appellat.
units.tr: What? Did you not say this same thing above, in the same way, about the things themselves? You ask rightly. But it must be understood thus: we cannot speak or deal with one another about a thing unless its name is pronounced, any more than we can reckon without counters. From this it is clear that between a thing and its word there exists a kind of concretion. Dialectic divides and separates this concretion, so that things and words are considered separately, as if torn away and abstracted. For our thoughts are free (says Cicero in the Pro Milone), and they look at what they wish in such a way that we see what we see. For example, if someone were to consider the impression of a ring's seal in wax by itself, as if abstracted; or were to distinguish the concave part of a hollow sphere from the convex. Moreover, it is the notion of the mind that makes this separate consideration, of which we spoke above. Therefore Cicero in many places calls the meaning of a word a notion.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Substantiam superiùs appellauimus, non corpus (quod tamen sensuum iudicio verè & proprie subsistit) sed notam,qua genus rerum omnium, quæ per se subsistunt,demonstratur.
units.tr: Let me give an example. Above we called substance, not body (which nonetheless truly and properly subsists by the judgment of the senses), but a mark by which the genus of all things that subsist through themselves is shown.

units.la: Quot sunt dictionum omnium genera? Aristoteles eadem acie mentis, qua (ut Cicero scribit) rerum omnium vim naturamque viderat, decem esse dictionum omnium animadvertit prima ac summa genera, & veluti capita, quibus tanquam notis atque indicibus dictionum omnium naturæ, vires, significationes, & differentiæ demonstrantur, qua de causa categorias illas nominauit, quasi dicamus attributiones. quoniam quicquid alicui attribuitur, quicquid de quopiam dicitur, enuntiatur, prædicatur, id ex earum categoriarum aliqua sumitur. nam (ut ait Aristoteles lib. Analyt. prior. 1. cap. 21.) cùm dicimus aliquid de alio dici, id ex aliqua categoriarum dici intelligendum est.
units.tr: How many genera of words are there altogether? Aristotle, with the same keenness of mind by which (as Cicero writes) he had seen the force and nature of all things, observed that there are ten first and highest genera of all words, and as it were heads, by which, as by marks and indicators, the natures, powers, meanings and differences of all words are shown. For this reason he named them categories, as if we might say "attributions". For whatever is attributed to anything, whatever is said of anything, is stated and predicated, and this is taken from one of those categories. For (as Aristotle says in the first book of the Prior Analytics, chapter 21) when we say that something is said of another, it must be understood that it is said from one of the categories.

units.la: De Categoriis, unde attributa dicuntur.
units.tr: On the Categories, whence they are called attributes.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: VAE sunt ille decem attributionum notæ? Substantia, quantitas[?], qualitas, relatio, actio, passio, locus, tempus, situs, habitus. Et si autem una eademque res duarum esse Categoriarum non poteft,interdum tamé accidit, ut vario respectu, id est fecundum aliud atque aliud una eadém que species duarum ac plurium esse possit.
units.tr: What are those ten marks of predication? Substance, quantity, quality, relation, action, passion, place, time, position, and state (habitus). And although one and the same thing cannot belong to two categories, it sometimes happens that, in different respects, that is according to one aspect and another, one and the same species can belong to two or more.

units.la: Cur hæ notæ Categoriæ nominátur? Quia de omnibus aliis dicuntur, cùm de illis nihil aliud dici ac pronuntiari possit. quicquid enim (ut modò ex Ariftotele diximus) de altero dicitur; quicquid alteri in oratione attribuitur,id ex alicuius categoriæ ordinibus sumatur necesse est. veluti,quid est Platanus? est arbor, quæ substantiæ subiecta est. quid est linea? est longitudo. Decem quid sunt? sunt numerus,quæ ex quantitate sumptá sunt. Ité quid est candor, aut atror? est color:ex qualitate. Ut autem [illegible, ~9 letters] appellationem interpretatur : sic κατηγορία, πρὸς τὸ κατηγορούμενον[?] ficta videtur : quasi fuma[?] & prima dictio,cui ceterae omnes subiectae ac substratæ sunt.
units.tr: Why are these marks called categories? Because they are predicated of all other things, since nothing else can be said or predicated of them. For whatever is said of another (as we have just said from Aristotle), whatever is attributed to another in speech, must necessarily be taken from the orders of some category. For example: what is a plane tree? It is a tree, which is subject to substance. What is a line? It is length. What are ten? They are a number, taken from quantity. Again, what is whiteness or blackness? It is a colour, from quality. But as the word itself is explained, so the Greek term kategoria, in relation to what is predicated [pros to kategoroumenon], seems to have been coined, as if it were the summit and first term, to which all the others are subjected and placed beneath.

units.la: Quid est Substantia? Est nota quæ voces earum rerum omnium,quæ substantiæ nomine continétur,cóprehendit. Nunc enim Substantiâ (ut modò dixi) non tanquam οὐσία[?]: id est rem,corpus, natura, essentiam, quærimus: sed tanquam earum rerum omnium quæ sunt eius generis indicem & appellationem summam.
units.tr: What is substance? It is the mark that comprehends the words of all those things which are contained under the name of substance. For now we are seeking substance (as I have just said) not as ousia [οὐσία], that is, thing, body, nature, or essence, but as the general index and comprehensive name of all those things which are of that kind.

units.la: Expone istud,fi potes,planius. Ad hanc Categoriam non tam corpora ipsa pertinent (quorum in cognitione & natura peruestigáda omnis Physicorum ars consumitur ) quàm dictiones, quibus vel ipsa corpora appellantur,vel eorum qualitates designantur. veluti Pygmæus homo,non tâ pertinet ad hanc Dialecticam Categoriam,quàm hominis vocabulum : cùm quæritur an Pygmæo hominis nomen conueniat. De qualitate,veluti,Sapiens, eloquens, medicus, orator. quanquam ipsæ qualitates per se & quasi abstractæ consideratæ, alterius Categoriæ sunt. neque enim aut res aut substantiæ aut corpora sunt: neque dictiones,corpora aut substantias declarantes,sed eorum qualitatem significantes : quas tamen ad Substantiæ Categoriam pertinere, Cicero in Oratore ad Brutum planissimè ostendit. Eius enim vsus hic est verus, an Sapientis aut Eloquentis nomen Socrati conueniat.Similiter autem omnes corporū qualitates in hoc genere reponendæ sunt : veluti Aeger,claudus, cæcus, luscus, improbus, sceleratus. Itémque artificum nomina , ut medicus,faber,pictor,sculptor,scriptor,arator:ceteráque qualitatem corporis aliquam significantia.Denique, ut rem uno verbo coplectar[?], omnia nomina, quæ Grammatici tum substátiua,tum adiectiua nominant , ad hanc Categoriam pertinent.
units.tr: Explain this more plainly, if you can. To this category belong not so much the bodies themselves (on whose knowledge and investigation of nature the whole art of the natural philosophers is spent) as the words by which either the bodies themselves are named or their qualities are designated. For example, the word "pygmy man" belongs to this dialectical category not so much as the word "man", when it is asked whether the name man fits the pygmy. Of quality, for example: wise, eloquent, physician, orator. Although the qualities themselves, considered in themselves and as if abstracted, belong to another category; for they are neither things, nor substances, nor bodies, nor words declaring bodies or substances, but signifying their quality. Yet Cicero, in the Orator to Brutus, shows most clearly that these belong to the category of substance. For the use of the word is this: whether the name wise or eloquent fits Socrates. Similarly, all the qualities of bodies are to be placed in this genus: for example sick, lame, blind, one-eyed, wicked, criminal. Likewise the names of craftsmen, such as physician, smith, painter, sculptor, writer, ploughman, and other words signifying some quality of the body. Finally, to sum up the matter in one word, all the nouns which grammarians call both substantive and adjective belong to this category.

units.la: Quæ est substantiæ proprietas ? Primùm, ut contraria recipere in se possit. Homo enim ex indocto,doctus:ex calido frigidus fieri potest. deinde ut nec elationem nec summissionem recipiat.Homo enim magis aut minus est se homo non potest. Itaque nanus tam homo est,quàm gigas. scapha tâ navis est, quàm triremis.l.vlt.D.de inst.vel inst.
units.tr: What is the property of substance? First, that it can receive contraries into itself: a man can become learned from unlearned, or cold from warm. Second, that it admits neither intensification nor remission: a man cannot be more or less a man. Thus a dwarf is as much a man as a giant, and a skiff is as much a ship as a trireme (l. ult. D. de inst. vel inst.).

units.la: Quid est quantitas? Est nota earum dictionum quibus vel numerus,vel magnitudo pronuntiatur.Quantitas autem aut deiuncta est, quæ vel multitudo vel numerus appellatur: aut continua,quæ magnitudo dicitur. Quantitatis autem hoc proprium est, ut ex ea æquale aliquid aut inæquale nominetur.
units.tr: What is quantity? It is the mark of those words by which either number or magnitude is expressed. Quantity is either discrete, which is called multitude or number, or continuous, which is called magnitude. The proper feature of quantity is that something equal or unequal is named from it.

units.la: Quid est qualitas? Nota earum dictionum quibus qualis quæque res sit,declaratur:veluti Candor,ater,valetudo, imbecillitas:Sapiêtia [?],stultitiâ : quæ omnia per se considerantur. At Candidus,ater, sapiens , eloquens, quæ de subiecto(puta) Socrate dicuntur, nec tamen in eo insunt,neque per se considerari possunt, ad substantiam pertinent.Huius autem Categoriæ hoc proprium est, ut ex ea quædam vel similia,vel dissimilia dicantur.
units.tr: What is quality? It is the mark of those words by which what sort of thing each thing is, is declared: for example whiteness, blackness, health, weakness, wisdom, folly, which are considered in themselves. But white, black, wise, and eloquent, which are said of a subject (say, Socrates), and yet are not in him in the same way nor can be considered by themselves, pertain to substance. The proper feature of this category is that from it some things are said to be alike or unlike.

units.la: Quid est relatio? Nota earum dictionum quæ inter se conferuntur, atque invicem assectæ sunt:quarum hoc proprium est, ut semper inter se reciprocentur, neutra sit prior altera, sed utraque simul sit naturæ ordine. veluti Pater,filius:maritus,uxor:socer,gener.
units.tr: What is relation? It is the mark of those words which are compared with one another and are mutually dependent. The proper feature of these is that they always reciprocate: neither is prior to the other, but both exist together in the order of nature. For example: father, son; husband, wife; father-in-law, son-in-law.

units.la: Quid est actio? Nota earum dictionum, quibus quæcunque geruntur,agûtur,aut fiût, significantur:veluti Secare , urere, currere. In quo notandum est, quoniam contraria in eo-dem dem genere reponenda sunt, in hunc eundem ordinem referenda esse quæ ad quietem & cessationem pertinent. veluti negotium, otium: Bellum, pax: currere, consistere: turbare, sedare:movere,sistere,quiescere.
units.tr: What is action? It is the mark of those words by which whatever is done, carried on, or happens is signified: for example to cut, to burn, to run. Here it should be noted that, since contraries are to be placed in the same genus, those words which pertain to rest and cessation are to be referred to this same order: for example business and leisure, war and peace, to run and to stand, to disturb and to calm, to move, to halt, and to rest.

units.la: Quid est Passio? Nota earum dictionum, quibus quæcunque patiendo accidunt, designantur. veluti Secari, uri, calefieri.
units.tr: What is passion? It is the mark of those words by which whatever befalls by way of suffering is designated: for example to be cut, to be burned, to be heated.

units.la: Quid est Locus? Nota earum dictionū, quibus ubi quidque fit, demonstratur. veluti intra, extra, supra, infra, ante, post, domi, foris, ruri, peregri. At ubi de dictionibus nō agitur, Locus est (inquit Varro) ubi quid locatum esse potest, ubi quicquam consistit.
units.tr: What is place? It is the mark of those words by which where anything happens is shown: for example within, without, above, below, before, after, at home, abroad, in the country, away abroad. But where words are not in question, place is (says Varro) where something can be located, where anything stands.

units.la: Quid est Tempus? Nota earum dictionum, quibus pars temporis aliqua demonstratur. veluti annus, mensis, dies, hora, momētum: ut heri, cras, hodie, postridie, mane, vesperi.
units.tr: What is time? It is the mark of those words by which some part of time is shown: for example year, month, day, hour, moment; and such words as yesterday, tomorrow, today, the day after, morning, evening.

units.la: Quid est Situs? Nota earum dictionum, quibus quemadmodum quodque corpus positum est, demonstratur. veluti sedere, stare, iacere, rectum, pronum, curvum, supinum esse.
units.tr: What is position? It is the mark of those words by which the way in which each body is placed is shown: for example to sit, to stand, to lie, to be upright, prone, bent, or supine.

units.la: Quid est Habitus? Nota earum dictionum, quibus genus vestitus indicatur. veluti togatus, sagatus, palliatus, prætextatus, paludatus, tunicatus, penulatus.
units.tr: What is state (habitus)? It is the mark of those words by which the kind of dress is indicated: for example togate, in a military cloak (sagatus), in a Greek cloak (palliatus), wearing the purple-bordered toga (praetextatus), in campaign dress (paludatus), tunicked, or in a travelling cloak (penulatus).

units.la: Cedo mihi familiare aliquod exemplum, quo Categoriæ omnes una enuntiatione comprehensæ sint. Goliathus gigas ingens, robustus, hostis irruens in Dauidem, interfectus inter duas acies sub meridiem iacuit armatus. Horum enim decem nominum quę Goliatho attributa sunt, nullum est quod nó ab reliquis omnibus categoria & genere discrepet. ut nec in illo: Hector, vir magnus, fortis, bellator, pugnans, interfectus ad Troiam ętate[?] occubuit chlamydatus.
units.tr: Give me some familiar example in which all the categories are comprehended in a single statement. "Goliath, a giant, huge and robust, an enemy rushing upon David, slain, lay down armed at midday between the two armies." For of the ten words attributed to Goliath, there is none that does not differ in category and kind from all the rest. So also in this: "Hector, a great man, brave, a warrior, fighting, slain at Troy, in the prime of his age fell, clad in a cloak."

units.la: De vi & vsu Categoriarum.
units.tr: On the force and use of the Categories.

units.la: CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: CHAP. XXIX.

units.la: Q[?]VID? Nónne Categoriæ sunt ordo rerum omnium per genera, species & differentias compositus? Categoriarum disciplina, neque ad res, néque ad rerum ordinem describendum pertinet: quemadmodum vulgò in scholis traditur. sed ad dictiones tantum, & attributiones, & vocabula: ut eorum summa genera illis tanquam certis notis cognosci possint. quoniam (ut superius ex Aristotele docuimus) quicquid de alio dicitur id ex aliqua Categoria sumi, eíque attribui oportet. τὸ ͵ ὑπάρχειν τόδε τισὶ, ἢ τὸ ἀληθεύεσθαι τόδε κατά τῶν τόδε, τοσαυταχῶς λεγέον, ὅσαχῶς αἱ κατηγορίαι διήρηνται[?]. lib. prior. Analyt. 1. cap. 26. Caput autem Dialecticę artis est, ut qua ratione aliud de alio dici & pronunciari possit, demonstret. Itaque dictionum declinatione Categorias immutari constat: cùm tamen ob inflexionem verbi res non immutetur. veluti Iustus, est substantia. Iustitia, est qualitas. Eques substantia est, Equita-
units.tr: What then? Are the Categories not an arrangement of all things through genera, species and differences? The teaching of the Categories concerns neither the description of things nor their order, as is commonly taught in the schools, but only words, predications and terms, so that their highest genera may be recognised by them as by certain marks. For (as we showed above from Aristotle) whatever is said of something else must be taken from some Category and attributed to it. "To belong to this thing to that, or to be truly predicated of such a thing of such a thing, must be said in as many ways as the Categories are divided" [τὸ ὑπάρχειν τόδε τισὶ, ἢ τὸ ἀληθεύεσθαι τόδε κατά τῶν τόδε, τοσαυταχῶς λεγέον, ὅσαχῶς αἱ κατηγορίαι διήρηνται]. Prior Analytics, book 1, chapter 26. The chief task of the art of dialectic, however, is to show by what method one thing can be said and asserted of another. Thus it is plain that the Categories are altered by the inflection of words, although the thing itself is not altered by the inflection of the verb. For example: just (iustus) is a substance; justice (iustitia) is a quality. A horseman (eques) is a substance; horsema-

units.la: {Equita-} tus,qualitas:Equitatio, actio . Scribere,actio est:Scriptor substantia:Scriptura qualitas:Scriptor actio . Longus est substantia. longitudo, quantitas.
units.tr: {horsemanship} (equitatus) is a quality; horse-riding (equitatio) is an action. To write is an action; a writer (scriptor) is a substance; writing (scriptura) is a quality; the act of writing (scriptor) is an action. Long (longus) is a substance; length (longitudo) is a quantity.

units.la: Quisnam igitur praecipuus Categoriarum est usus? Omnis de verbis quaestio in eo versatur,an aliud de alio dici,aut non dici possit. Quod autem de altero dicitur, id aut superius est,aut par ei,de quo quaeritur.quia de superiore certè dici inferius nō potest . Ad hunc usum Categoriae pertinent. verborū enim genera demonstrant,ex quibus quodnam attributum sumi possit , hoc est , quodnam altero vel superius vel inferius,vel par fit:quid item summum, infimum,aut subalternū fit, intelligitur.
units.tr: What then is the chief use of the Categories? Every question about words turns on whether one thing can or cannot be said of another. What is said of something else is either superior to it, or equal to that about which the question is asked, for the inferior certainly cannot be said of the superior. To this use the Categories belong: they display the kinds of words from which one may take a given predicate, and so it is understood which predicate is superior, inferior or equal to the other, and likewise which is highest, lowest or subaltern.

units.la: Quaestiones de attributis vniúsne Categoriaesunt, an plurium? Quaestiones quaedam ad unam tantùm Categoriam pertinent:veluti,An Gigas fit homo,solius substantiae est.An bellum gerēdum fit,solius actionis. Quaedam ad plures:ut,An infans dum in utero eit,sit homo:substantiae est,& temporis.An bellū in Britannia sit gerēdum,& hyeme? actionis, loci & temporis.Utrum terra stet,an moueatur,substantiae,actionis & perpessionis.
units.tr: Are questions about predicates concerned with one Category only, or with several? Some questions concern only one Category: for example, whether a giant is a man belongs to substance alone; whether war ought to be waged belongs to action alone. Others concern several: for example, whether an infant in the womb is a human being belongs to substance and time; whether war ought to be waged in Britain in winter belongs to action, place and time; whether the earth stands still or moves belongs to substance, action and passion.

units.la: Sed vbi de verbis & vocabulis tantùm agebatur,quid erat opus tam altè ista è Philosophorum disciplinis eruere,quasi de natura rerum,& mundo,atque universitatis opificio instituta esset disputatio? Primùm quia nisi cognitis attributionum generibus , atq; ordinibus,perspici non potest, quid de quoque dici aut nō dici posit . deinde auctorem huius rei habemus Aristotelem,atque omnes qui ab eo sunt,Peripateticos,qui suas ætates in hiscè disciplinis exercendis contriuerunt . Quòd si Græcorum nihil nos mouet auctoritas,audiamus M. Varronem, Latinorum omnium facilè doctissimum, qui de latinis vocibus disputare ingressus,lib.de Lingua lat. [?]1 [?]1 [?]1,ita scribit:Pythagoras Samius ait,omnium rerum initia esse bina: ut status & motus: quod stat aut agitur,corpus:ubi agitatur, locus:dum agitatur,tépus:quod est in agitatu,actio. Quadripartitò magis sic apparebit : corpus est, ut cursor:locus, stadium quà currit:tempus, hora quà currit:actio,cursio. Qua re fit, ut ideo omnia ferè sint quadripartita, & ea externa, quòd neque unquam tempus, quin fuerit motus:eius enim interuallum,tempus:neque motus,ubi non locus &corpus,quod alterum est, quod mouetur:alterum ubi:neque ubi fit agitatus,non actio ibi.Igitur initiorum quadrigæ locus,& corpus,tépus,& actio. Quare quatuor genera prima rerū, totidem verborum. de his locis,&his rebus quæ in his videntur,in hoc libro summatim ponam. Totidem igitur Varro verbis utitur.
units.tr: But where only words and terms were under discussion, why was it necessary to dig up these matters so deeply from the doctrines of the philosophers, as if the disputation were established concerning the nature of things, the world and the workmanship of the universe? First, because unless the kinds and orders of predications are known, it cannot be seen what can or cannot be said of each thing. Second, we have Aristotle as the author of this matter, and all who follow him, the Peripatetics, who spent their lives in these studies. But if the authority of the Greeks does not move us, let us hear Marcus Varro, by far the most learned of all the Latins, who, beginning to discuss Latin words in his book on the Latin language, writes thus: "Pythagoras of Samos says that the beginnings of all things are twofold, as rest and motion: what stands or is driven is a body; where it is driven is a place; while it is driven is time; what is in the driving is action. It will appear more clearly in a fourfold scheme: the body is like the runner, the place the stadium where he runs, the time the hour in which he runs, the action the running. Hence it comes that almost everything is fourfold, and these are external, because there is never time without motion (for its interval is time), nor motion where there is no place and body, the one being what is moved, the other where it is; nor is there any action where a thing is not moved. Therefore the quadriga of beginnings is place and body, time and action. Hence four first kinds of things, as many kinds of words. About these places and these things which are seen in them I shall set out a summary in this book." So Varro uses as many words.

units.la: Superest unica de Categoriis quæstio.Cùm Varro institutam de vocabulis disputatione tam altè ex naturæ principiis ad Physicorum exemplum repetat, cur tu igitur superiùs vbi de Rebus dixisti,non tamen istas rerum notas & genera summa exposuisti? Ratio in promptu est.quia tractatio de generibus, vi & natura rerum, Physicorum ( vt ante dixi) propria est. At Dialectica in ea re vna occupata est, vt ex cuiusque rei dictionisue affectu & ratione doceat quemadmodū alterum de altero aptè dici & enuntiari possit: hoc est, quod cuique verbum conueniat aut non conueniat.Itaque proposita quæstione,si quid ambiguū est,continuò vtriusque verbi quod in questione positum est,definitio adhibęda est. Adhiberi autē definitio nō potest, nisi vtriusque genere perspecto.ItaqueCicero Tuscul.5,cùm hanc quæstionem posuisset,An omnes boni semper beati sint:cōtinuò sic infert: Quos dicam bonos, perspicuum est. Omnibus enim virtutibus in structos, & ornatos, tum sapientes, tum viros bonos dicimus. Videamus qui dicendi sunt beati.Equidem hos existimo, qui sunt in bonis:nulio adiuncto malo.nec vlla alia huic verbo,cùm beatum dicimus ,subiecta notio est. Sic lib.de Finib.2. Quærimus ( inquit) finem bonorum. Possumúsne scire hoc quale sit, nisi contulerimus inter nos quid finis,quid etiam sit ipsum bonum?
units.tr: One question about the Categories remains. Since Varro traces the discussion of words so deeply from the principles of nature, on the model of the natural philosophers, why then did you, when speaking earlier of things, not set out those marks of things and their highest genera? The reason is ready to hand: the treatment of genera, of the power and nature of things, belongs to the natural philosophers, as I said before. Dialectic, however, is occupied with this alone: to teach, from the affection and nature of each thing or term, how one thing may fittingly be said and asserted of another, that is, which word suits each thing and which does not. Therefore, once the question is proposed, if anything in it is ambiguous, the definition of each term in the question must be applied at once; and a definition cannot be applied unless the genus of each is clearly grasped. Thus Cicero, in the Tusculan Disputations book 5, having posed the question "Are all good men always happy?", immediately goes on: "It is plain whom I call good. For we call men good who are furnished and adorned with all the virtues, both wise men and good men. Let us see who should be called happy. Indeed I think those are happy who are in goods, with no evil added; nor is any other notion attached to this word when we say 'happy'." So too in De Finibus book 2: "We seek," he says, "the chief good. Can we know what this is, unless we have first compared among ourselves what the end is and what the good itself is?"

units.la: Reditus ad affectiones dictionum.
units.tr: Return to the affections of words.

units.la: CAP. XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX.

units.la: QVOD est Genus dictionis? Quod de multis subiectis dictionibus, in quaestione quid sint, responderi potest. veluti, Animal de rebus omnibus animatis, Corpus de corporeis, Sentiés de sentiétibus. vt Genus de suis formis aptè respondetur. Item vt Aqua de aqueis, & Terra de terrenis, & Lignum de ligneis.
units.tr: What is a genus of a word? It is that which can be given as the answer, in response to the question "what is it?", about many subjects. For example, Animal of all living things, Body of corporeal things, Sentient of sentient things, so that the genus is aptly given as an answer about its forms. Likewise Water of watery things, Earth of earthly things, and Wood of wooden things.

units.la: Quid est Totum dictionis? Quod partibus, id est, pluribus vocibus constat, aut pronuntiatis: veluti Subterfugere, Beneuolus, Tyrānicida: aut intellectis [?]: veluti, Eques autNauta: quibus verbis homo & equus, homo & nauis intelliguntur. Nam vtrarunque partiū ea natura est, vt totum partiendo intereat. neque enim homo per se eques est, neque nauta.
units.tr: What is the whole of a word? It is what consists of parts, that is, of several words either pronounced, as in Subterfugere, Beneuolus, Tyrannicida, or understood, as in Eques or Nauta, where the words man and horse, or man and ship, are understood. For the nature of each part is such that the whole perishes when it is divided, since a man is not by himself a horseman, nor a sailor.

units.la: Et caussam in dictionibus quānam appellas? Vetus est Philosophorum quaestio, quae à Platone in Cratilo luculenter explicatur, vtrùm vocabula sint natura, an instituto. ἢ φύσει, ἢ θέσει [?]. Quarum igitur dictionum materia gnota est, earum etiam causa ignota est: cuiusmodi multo maximam partem vocabulorum esse, Socrates in eo dialogo demonstrat. tametsi Stoici, artis dialecticae professores summi, omnium prope verborum origines peruestigare soleant [?].
units.tr: And what do you call the cause of words? It is an old question among the philosophers, clearly explained by Plato in the Cratylus, whether words exist by nature or by convention [ἢ φύσει, ἢ θέσει]. Therefore, the matter of those words whose material is known is also known, but their cause is unknown. Socrates in that dialogue shows that this is the case for by far the greater part of words. Yet the Stoics, the greatest professors of the dialectical art, are accustomed to investigate the origins of almost all words.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de cognitis. Audeamus (inquit Cicero) imitari Stoicos, qui studiosè exquirūt, vnde verba sint ducta: credamúsque quia fiat, quod dictum est, appellatā fidem. Sic Manius dictus putatur, qui mane natus est: Lucius, qui luce: Postumus qui post patris mortem: Proculus, qui patre procul absente. Item ex sono: Strepere, murmurare, boare, rugire, hinnire. Item ex habitu, Frontones, Claudij, Capitones, Rufi.
units.tr: Let me give an example of known causes. Let us venture (says Cicero) to imitate the Stoics, who carefully seek out whence words are derived, and let us believe, since it is done, that what was said has a reason. Thus Manius is thought to be named from being born in the morning (mane), Lucius from being born in the light (luce), Postumus from being born after his father's death, and Proculus from being born while his father was far away (procul). Likewise from sound: to strepere, murmur, boare, rugire, hinnire. Likewise from appearance: Frontones, Claudii, Capitones, Rufi.

units.la: Qua disciplina dictionum causæ & origines peruestigantur? Ea(inquit Varro) quam Philosophi ἐτυμολογίαν[?], id est notationem appellat: quæ(vt idem ait) demóstrat à qua re, & in qua re vocabulum fit impositum. Itaque à qua re fit pertinacia cùm quæritur, ostenditur esse à pertendendo. in qua re fit impositum, dicitur, cùm demonstratur in quo non debet pertendi & pertenditur, pertinacia esse: quod in quo oporteat manere, fi eo perstat, perseuerantia fit. Item alio loco: Docet (inquit) Etymologia non omnium verborum posse dici causas. ut quare ad medendum, medicina. Itaque Cicero in Academicis: Verborum (inquit) explicatio probabitur: id est, qua de causa quæque essent, & nominarentur, quod Etymologiam appellarunt. Sed tamen video veteres omnes Etymologiam non modo in causis, verum etiam in proprietate vocabulorum collocare, & notare.
units.tr: By what discipline are the causes and origins of words investigated? By that which (says Varro) the philosophers call etymology [ἐτυμολογίαν], that is, notation, which shows (as the same author says) from what thing and in what thing a word is imposed. So when we ask from what thing obstinacy (pertinacia) arises, it is shown to come from persisting (pertendendo). We say it is imposed in what thing when it is shown that persisting where one ought not to persist and doing so is obstinacy; whereas persevering (perseverantia) is persisting where one ought to remain. Elsewhere he says: Etymology teaches (he says) that not all words can be given their causes, as why medicine is so called from healing (ad medendum). So Cicero in the Academics: "An explanation of words (he says) will be approved, that is, for what reason each thing is called and named, which they called etymology." But I see that all the ancients place etymology not only in the causes but also in the proper meaning and notation of words.

units.la: Quis est Effectus verborum? Qui ex causarum concursu nascitur. hic autem in vita communi, longè maximus est. Nam unico verbulo maximis de rebus obligamur. ut in stipulationibus, siquis Spondeo dixerit, maximis se interdum de pecuniis obligat . Sic in testamento siquis Heres esto, vel Lego dixerit, maximas pecunias alienat. Sicverborum suorum Effecta Magi prædicant: cùm ex carminũ suorum euentis de vi verborum arguunt. Neque ab hoc loco aliena sunt bona nomina, quæ veteres notabant. Et Cicero in primo de Diuinat. Cùm Imperator (inquit) exercitum, Censor populum lustraret, bonis nominibus ; qui hostias ducerent, eligebātur : quod item in de leētu Consules obseruant, vt primus miles fiat bono nomine.
units.tr: What is the effect of words? It is what arises from the concurrence of causes, and in ordinary life this is by far the greatest. For we are bound by a single little word in the most important matters: in stipulations, if someone says Spondeo ("I promise"), he sometimes binds himself to very great sums of money. So in a will, if someone says Heres esto ("let him be heir") or Lego ("I bequeath"), he disposes of very large sums. Thus magicians proclaim the effects of their words, when they judge the power of words from the outcomes of their charms. Nor are good omens (bona nomina), which the ancients noted, foreign to this place. And Cicero in the first book of On Divination: "When the commander (imperator) was reviewing the army, or the censor the people, those were chosen to lead the victims who had good names." Likewise, in the levy the Consuls observe that the first soldier be one with a good name.

units.la: Quid appellas Proprium dictionis? Proprium dictionis, est vis vocabuli certa & natiua, & penè (vt ait Cicero) cum ipsa re nata: veluti Vagire proprium est infantium: plangere fœminarum : vlulare canum : hinnire equorum: rudere, asinorū: rugire leonum. Sic Orbus proprie dicitur, qui caret oculis. tranlatè qui liberis, aut qui parentibus, aut qui alia re chara priuatus est. Oracula (inquit Cicero) ex eo ipso appellata sunt, quia inest in his deorum oratio. Sic de Finib. 11. Varietas in disparibus coloribus proprie dicitur, sed transfertur in plura disparia. Morbus proprie dicitur in corpore: morbosos tamen veteres dicebant iracundos. Proprie (inquit Cicero) vt Aegrotatio in corpore, sic Aegritudo in animo nomen habet, non secundum à dolore. Et alibi: Vnde istud tam ἄχυρον[?], valetudini fideliter inseruiendo? cui verbo domicilium est proprium in officio:migrationes in alienû multæ. Nam & doctrina,& domus, & ars, & ager etiam fidelis dici potest: vt sit, quomodo Theophrasto placet, verecunda translatio. Proprietati enim opponitur tráslatio, quæ est tanquâ mutatio,cûm quod nô habeas,aliunde sumis:vt cûm gemmare vites, & lætæ segetes dicuntur.
units.tr: What do you call the proper meaning of a word? The proper meaning of a word is its certain and natural force, and almost (as Cicero says) born together with the thing itself. For example, to wail (vagire) is proper to infants, to lament (plangere) to women, to howl (ululare) to dogs, to neigh (hinnire) to horses, to bray (rudere) to asses, to roar (rugire) to lions. So orbus is properly said of one who lacks eyes, but figuratively of one who is bereft of children, or of parents, or of some other dear thing. Oracles (Cicero says) are so named from the very fact that the speech of the gods is in them. So in De Finibus book 2: variety (varietas) is properly said of differing colours, but is transferred to many differing things. Disease (morbus) is properly said of the body, yet the ancients called the irascible "morbosi." Properly (Cicero says), as aegrotatio ("sickness") has its name in the body, so aegritudo ("distress") has its name in the mind, not from pain. And elsewhere: "Whence that so chaff-like (ἄχυρον) devotion to serving health faithfully? For the word domicilium ("dwelling") is proper to the duty, but there are many transfers to other things. For doctrina, domus, ars, and even ager can be called faithful." Thus it is, as Theophrastus holds, a modest transfer. For translation is opposed to proper meaning: it is like a change, when you take from elsewhere what you do not have, as when vines are said to bud (gemmare) and fields to rejoice (laetae segetes).

units.la: Quid est antecedens aut cõsequens dictionis? Quod Grammatici primitiuum & deriuatiuum, Dialectici παρώνυμα[?], id est,cognominata nominant. Vt homo,humanus,homūcio,homunculus,humanè,humaniter, humanitas,humanitus. Aeger,ægrotus,ægritudo,ægrotatio. Hinc illud Terétij: Homo sum,huma ni à me nihil alienum puto. Et illa vulgata: Si Consul est,cōsulat Reip. Si Rex est,regat, non cuertat Remp. Quoniam verbum confidendi laudis est(inquit Cicero) sit etiam confidens: quod tamen mala consuetudine loquendi, in vitio ponitur. Item: Inuidia(inquit idē)tum est,cùm inuidetur:ab inuidendo autem inuidētia rectè dici potest, vt fugiamus ambiguū nomen inuidię: quod verbum ductū est à nimis intuêdo fortunam alterius. Ex eodem genere illud est eiusdem: Non enim pudēdo,sed non faciendo id quod non decet(id est impudenter) impudentię nomē effugere debemus. Itē illa quæstio: An sicarius dicatur tantū qui sica percussit,non etiam qui gladio. Est autem regula hoc loco seruanda, vt antecedentia & consequentia verborum non tam ex sono vocis,quàm ex notione æstimentur. Nulla enim coniugationis vis est, inter fortem & fortunâ, neque inter legem, legatum testamentarium, & legationem: neque inter liberum & librum: inter hominem bellum, & bellatorem, inter iustitiam & iustitium. Sic non si equus est, continuò erit equitatio. at si eques sit, hæc erit: & vicissim si hæc, etiam illa.
units.tr: What is the antecedent or consequent of a word? It is what the grammarians call the primitive and derivative, and the dialecticians call paronyms (παρώνυμα), that is, cognates. For example: homo, humanus, homuncio, homunculus; humane, humaniter, humanitas, humanitus. Aeger, aegrotus, aegritudo, aegrotatio. Hence that line of Terence: "I am a man; I think nothing human alien to me." And that common saying: "If he is a Consul, let him consult for the Commonwealth; if he is a King, let him rule, not overturn the state." Since the word for confiding is a term of praise (says Cicero), let one who confides be also confident, though by bad usage of speech this is put in the sense of a fault. Likewise: "Envy (invidia) is the thing itself, when one is envied; but from envying (invidendo) we can rightly say envious-ness (invidentia), so that we may avoid the ambiguous name of envy, a word derived from looking too hard at another's fortune." From the same class is this saying of his: "For we ought to escape the name of impudence not by being shameless, but by not doing what is unbecoming (that is, acting impudently)." Likewise that question: whether a sicarius ("assassin") is called only one who struck with a dagger (sica), and not also one who struck with a sword. In this matter the rule must be kept, that the antecedents and consequents of words are judged not so much by the sound of the voice as by their meaning. For there is no relation of derivation between fortis ("brave") and fortuna ("fortune"), nor between lex ("law"), legatum testamentarium ("testamentary legacy"), and legatio ("embassy"), nor between liber ("free") and liber ("book"), nor between bellum ("war") and bellator ("warrior"), nor between iustitia ("justice") and iustitium ("cessation of law"). So, if there is an equus ("horse"), it does not follow that there will be equitatio; but if there is an eques ("horseman"), there will be equitatio; and conversely, if equitatio, then also eques.

units.la: Quid est adiunctum vocabuli? Quod alicui propter nominis rationem probabiliter attribuitur: veluti, quia Ciceronis nomen est Tullius, probabile videri putauit se à Tullo Rege originem duxisse. Sic Plato iccircò Theagis nomen laudat in puero, ac parentibus suadet vt præclara nomina suis liberis imponant. Sic Orator Iulius lib de Orat.1 1. Numiū diuisorem illudens facetè dicebat, vt Neoptolemum ad Troiam, sic illum in campo Martio nomen inuenisse: quasi qui numos diuideret. Sic Aristoteles scribit in Rhetoricis, Thrasybulum audaci consilio hominem appellatum: & Draconis leges quòd duriores videbantur, non hominis leges fuisse, sed Draconis. & iure Venerè Aphroditem nominatâ, quòd Aphrosynes, id est, dementiæ dea esset. Sic in Phoenissis Euripidis, nomen Polynicis vt argumentum morû frater incessit, inquit Fabius. Nam, vt in prouerbio est, Conueniunt rebus nomina sæpe suis. Cicero Philipp. x 1: Caninium Cimbrum, Lysidici filium, Lysidicum ipsum, qui omnia iura dissoluit. Et in Oratore, Theophrastus, inquit, diuinitate loquendi nomen inuenit.
units.tr: What is an adjunct of a word? It is what is probably attributed to someone because of the reason of his name: for example, since Cicero's name is Tullius, he thought it probable that he traced his origin from King Tullus. So Plato praises the name Theages in a boy, and urges parents to give their children distinguished names. So the orator Julius, in his book On the Orator, mocking a distributor of coins (numi divisor) wittily said that, just as Neoptolemus found his name at Troy, so he had found his in the Campus Martius, as if he were one who divides coins (numi). So Aristotle writes in the Rhetoric that Thrasybulus was called a man of bold counsel, and that the laws of Draco, because they seemed harsher, were not the laws of a man but of Draco, and that Aphrodite is rightly named from Aphrosyne, that is, the goddess of folly. So in the Phoenissae of Euripides the name of Polynices, as Fabius says, marks the character of the man's brother. For, as the proverb has it, names often fit their things. Cicero in the Philippics: "Caninius Cimber, son of Lysidicus, and Lysidicus himself, who dissolved all laws." And in the Orator: Theophrastus, he says, found the name by a divine gift of speech.

units.la: Quod est accidens dictionis? Cùm casu factum est, vt nomen alicui impositum ei conueniat. vt si quis equorum studiosus Philippus dicatur, veluti in athleta Nicostrato vsuenit, qui certando & luctando quotidie coronabatur. Item in Verre qui Siciliam euerrit. Huc enim allusiones atque etiam omina pertinét. Cicero Verrina 1111: O praeclarè coniectum à vulgo in illam prouinciam omé communis famæ, atque sermonis: cùm ex istius nomine, quid in prouincia factypus esset, perridiculi homines augurabātur. Item in eadem: O Verrea praeclara! quò enim accessisti, quò non at tuleris tecū istum diem? Etenim quam tu domum, quam vrbem adiisti, quod fanum deni que, quod non euersum atque extersum reliqueris? Quare appellentur sanè ista Verrea, quæ non ex nomine, sed ex moribus naturáque tua constituta esse videātur. Ex eodé genere illa est Liuij disputatio lib.111: Fuere qui interpretarentur eadem hac Horatia lege, Cōsulibus quoque & Prætoribus, quia eisdē auspiciis quibus Consules crearētur, cautum esse. Iudicem enim Consulem appellari. quæ refellitur interpretatio: quòd his temporibus nondum Consulem, Iudicem: sed Prætoré appellari mos fuerit.
units.tr: What is an accident of a word? It is when a name imposed on someone by chance fits him. For example, if someone who is fond of horses is called Philip, as happened with the athlete Nicostratus, who was crowned daily for contests and wrestling. Likewise in Verres, who swept (everrit) Sicily. For allusions and even omens belong here. Cicero in the fourth Verrine: "O how well the common talk and rumour foretold of that province, when from that man's name men, very ridiculous, were predicting what would happen in the province!" Likewise in the same: "O splendid Verrine things! For wherever you went, did you not carry that day with you? For what house, what city did you enter, what temple finally, which did you not overturn and sweep clean and leave behind? Let these things indeed be called Verrine, which seem to be established not from the name but from your character and nature." From the same class is Livy's discussion in book 3: some interpreted that same Horatian law as providing that the Praetors too, since they were created under the same auspices as the Consuls, were covered. For they said the judge is called Consul. This interpretation is refuted, because in those times the custom was that the judge was not called Consul but Praetor.

units.la: Quæ dicuntur pares dictiones? Quæ rem vnam pluribus vocabulis declarant. vt Ensis, gladius,Logica,Dialectica:Pactio,conuentio, quæ(vt superiùs dictum est)Dialectici πολυώνυμα [?], Gramatici συνώνυμα [?] & ἰσοδυναμοῦντα [?] nominant.vt sepe,crebro, subinde,plerunque, identidem: olim,pridem, dudum, antiquitus.
