units.tr: What are paronyms? Those that express one thing by several words, such as sword and blade, Logic and Dialectic, bargain and agreement. Dialecticians call these (as said above) polyonyms [πολυώνυμα], and grammarians call them synonyms [συνώνυμα] or words of equal force [ἰσοδυναμοῦντα]. Examples are often, frequently, from time to time, commonly, again and again; long ago, formerly, of old, from antiquity.

units.la: Quæ dicuntur similes? Quod rogant(inquit Varro) ex qua parte oporteat simile esse verbum: à voce,an à significatione: respondemus,à voce. Sed hæc Varro de Analogia scribēs. Nam in Dialectica similes sunt dictiones quæ notione & voce inter se conueniunt, vtamen ex parte dissident, veluti Vallis & Vallus: Aestus,æstas: inuidia,& inuidentia. Seruitus,& Seruitium. Prohibere & inhibere.Demus operam Quirites, ne Patres Cóscripti, circumscripti putentur.In quo illud animaduertendum est, ne dictionum similitudo tam ex sono & voce, quàm ex notione æstimentur. velut Lepus, lepos,& lupus. Item Suis & Suis (inquit alio loco Varro) similia indiligenti videri possunt: cùm alterum Suem, alterum fuere significet.Scitum est autè quod VarroGrāmaticè hæc tractans, Similia(inquit) esse vocibus & syllabis confitemur. Dissimilia esse partibus orationis videmus. Nam Dialecticus non partibus orationis dixisset, sed qualitate, notione, vi & potestate. quoniam (vt superiùs ex Aristotele diximus) ex qualitate omnis vel similitudo vel dissimilitudo æstimatur.
units.tr: What are similar words? Varro asks in what respect a word ought to be like another: in its sound or in its meaning. We answer: in its sound. But Varro writes this in his work on Analogy. In Dialectic, similar words are those that agree with each other in meaning and in sound, yet differ in some respect, such as valley and vallus (a stake), tide and summer, envy and envying, servitude and slavery, to forbid and to inhibit. "Let us take care, citizens, that the Conscript Fathers are not thought to be circumvented" is an example. Here one must notice that words should not be judged similar by sound and spelling alone, but also by meaning, as with hare, pleasure and wolf. Likewise, Varro says elsewhere that the words suis (of a pig) and suis (of one's own) may seem similar to the careless, though one signifies a pig and the other one's own. Varro treats these matters as a grammarian, and he rightly says: "We admit that they are similar in their letters and syllables; we see that they are dissimilar in the parts of speech." A dialectician would not have spoken of parts of speech, but of quality, meaning, force and power, since, as we said above from Aristotle, all similarity or dissimilarity is judged by quality.

units.la: Quæ sunt quæ dicuntur dictiones aduersæ? Quas Græci ἀντίθετα [?] nominant, quæ vim habent inter se infestam atque contrariam: ut infrà, suprà: sursum, deorsum: totum, nihil: uterque, neuter: Omnis, nemo. Item Beneficium, maleficiù: Beneuolentia, maleuolentia. Quoniam misericordia (inquit Cicero) ægritudo est ex alterius rebus aduersis: sic inuidentia æ[?]-gritudo ex alterius rebus fecundis.
units.tr: What are opposed words, the ones called contrary? The Greeks call them opposites [ἀντίθετα]. They have a hostile and contrary force toward each other: below and above, up and down, whole and nothing, each and neither, everyone and no one. Likewise benefit and harm, goodwill and ill will. As Cicero says, pity is a distress at another's adversity; so envy is a distress at another's prosperity.

units.la: Quæ sunt Relatæ? Quæ inter se conferūtur, & sub eádem rationem cadunt: veluti duplum, simplum: cras, heri: hodie, pridie, postridie, perendie. Item cetera omnia rerum relatarum vocabula: dummodo meminerimus, quod iam sæpe diximus, ea seorsum ab ipsis rebus, & tanquam avulsa & abstracta cō- siderari oportere. Nam in his vocabulis, Pater, filius, Dominus, servus, Patronus, cliens, si rem & (ut Dialectici loquuntur) subiectum consideremus, neque ad rerum, neque ad dictionum relationem pertinebunt: sed ad Substantiam.
units.tr: What are relative words? Those that are compared with each other and fall under the same relation: double and single, tomorrow and yesterday, today, the day before, the day after, the day after tomorrow. So too all other names of relative things, provided we remember what we have often said, that these words must be considered apart from the things themselves, as if torn away and abstracted. For in such words as father, son, lord, servant, patron, client, if we consider the thing and (as the dialecticians say) the subject, they will belong not to the relation of things or of words, but to substance.

units.la: Quæ sunt Privantes? Quæ quod altera rei attribuit, id altera ei detrahit. ut semper, nunquam: ubíque, nusquam. Consül, consularis, vel exconsul. Prætor, prætorius, vel exprætor. heres, exheres: civis, exul: coniux, vidua. Divortium (inquiunt Iurisconsulti) propterea non dicitur in sponsa, quia divertere dicitur quæ à cōmuni habitatione discessit: sponsa autem nondum communem habitationem habuit. Ut frugalitas (inquit Cicero) dicitur à fruge: quia nihil melius è terra oritur: ita nequitia ab eo, quod nec quicquam est in tali homine:ex quo idem nihili dicitur.
units.tr: What are privatives? Those where what one word attributes to a thing, the other takes away from it: always and never, everywhere and nowhere; consul, consular, or ex-consul; praetor, praetorian, or ex-praetor; heir, disinherited; citizen, exile; spouse, widow. The jurists say that divorce is not used of a betrothed woman, because one is said to be divorced only if she has left the common dwelling, whereas a betrothed woman has not yet had a common dwelling. As Cicero says, frugality is named from fruit, because nothing better comes out of the earth; so worthlessness [nequitia] is named from the fact that there is nothing in such a man, whence the word for nothing is also used.

units.la: Quæ sunt Aientes & Negantes? Quarum quod ait altera,id altera inficiatur. veluti,furtum manifestum,furtum nec manifestum. scire, nescire. legere , negligere. otium, negotiū. gnarus,ignarus.sanitas,insania.
units.tr: What are affirming and denying words? Those where one affirms what the other denies: manifest theft and non-manifest theft; to know and not to know; to read and to neglect; leisure and business; knowing and ignorant; health and madness.

units.la: Quæ sunt Repugnantes? Quarum altera adversa est,altera adversæ alterius consequēs. ut Benevolentia, maleficium. Amicum esse & malè mereri. Non & deorsum suo pondere atomi feruntur,& paululum declinant.
units.tr: What are repugnant words? Those where one is adverse and the other is a consequence of the adverse thing: goodwill and wrongdoing; to be a friend and to deserve ill. "And atoms are carried downward by their own weight, and yet swerve a little."

units.la: Quæ sunt Dissimiles? Proprie quæ pondĕris,numeri, aut mensuræ inæqualitatem significant. ut As,semis:pondo,dupódius:medimnus,modius: bini,terni:quartarius,sextarius: Non enim hic vasa ( quæ ad Substantiam pertinēt) neque eorum mensuram , quæ ad Geometras: sed mensurarum vocabula per se , & tanquam abstracta consideramus.
units.tr: What are dissimilar words? Properly, those that signify inequality of weight, number or measure: as, semis (a whole and a half); pound, double-pound; medimnus, modius; a pair, a trio; quart, sixth. For here we consider not vessels (which belong to substance), nor their measure as the geometers do, but the names of measures by themselves, as if abstracted.

units.la: Quæ sunt dissimiles? Quæ ex eodem ductæ genere, qualitate inter se partim conveniunt, partim dissident. ut Gallus natione: Gallicus ex Gallia:Atheniensis,Atticus: Hispanus, Hispaniensis. Corinthium æs, Corinthiaca vasa. Sic apud Iurisconsultos aliud est Servum esse, aliud servire:aliud in libertate,aliud liberum esse.aliud Prætorē esse, aliud Prætura fungi.aliud est mentiri, aliud mendacium dicere, inquit Gellius lib.ii.cap.ii.
units.tr: What are dissimilar words in another sense? Those derived from the same kind, which partly agree and partly differ in quality: a Gaul by birth, Gallic from Gaul; Athenian, Attic; Spaniard, Hispanic. Corinthian bronze, Corinthian vessels. So among the jurists, to be a slave is one thing, to serve another; to be in liberty is one thing, to be free another; to be praetor is one thing, to discharge the praetorship another. "To lie is one thing, to tell a falsehood another," says Gellius, book 2, chapter 2.

units.la: INSTITUTIONIS DIALECTICAE LIBER II. De Triplici Methodo. CAP. I.
units.tr: THE DIALECTIC INSTITUTES, BOOK II. On the Threefold Method. CHAPTER I.

units.la: ACTENUS primam Dialectica artis partem videmur absoluisse. deinceps ad diuisionem accedamus. sed utri prior debetur locus, diuisioni, an definitioni? Huic quæstioni responderi commodè antequam de Methodo, & docendi ratione disseruerimus, satis non poterit. Nam ad huius artis cognitionem ea præmunitione est opus.
units.tr: Thus far we seem to have completed the first part of the art of Dialectic. Next let us come to division. But which should come first, division or definition? This question cannot be answered properly before we have discussed Method and the manner of teaching, for knowledge of this art requires that preliminary groundwork.

units.la: Quid est Methodus? Ars quæ quemadmodum disciplina omnis redigi in artem & certam rationem possit, demonstrat. hoc est, quemadmodum ex iis rebus, quarum ars nondum est, effici ars possit.
units.tr: What is Method? It is the art which shows how every discipline can be reduced to an art and a fixed system; that is, how an art can be made out of those subjects for which no art yet exists.

units.la: Quid est Ars? Antonius apud Ciceronem lib.de Orat.II, sic definit: Ars est, quæ cognitis penitusque perspectis, & in unum exitum spectantibus, & nunquam fallentibus rebus continetur. Aristoteles autem, Artem dicit esse rei per suas causas cognitionem, quæ aliter se habere non possunt. Apud Lucianum vero sic definitur: σύστημα ἐκ καταληψεων ἐγγεγυμνασ-μένων πρὸς τι τέλος εὔχρηστον τῆς ἐν τῷ βίῳ. Est coa-ceruatio multarum de unare perceptionum usu & exercitatione collectarum ad finem aliquem vitæ utilem accommodata. Ars enim (ut ait Cicero lib. Acad. iii.) quæ potest esse, nisi quæ non ex una aut ex duabus, sed ex multis animi perceptionibus constat? quam fi subtraxeris, qui distinguës artifice ab inscio?
units.tr: What is Art? Antonius, in Cicero's De Oratore Book II, defines it thus: "Art is that which is contained in things known, thoroughly perceived, aimed at a single outcome, and never deceptive." Aristotle says that art is knowledge of a thing through its causes, which cannot be otherwise. Lucian defines it thus: "a system of practised comprehensions directed to some useful end of life" [σύστημα ἐκ καταληψεων ἐγγεγυμνασμένων πρὸς τι τέλος εὔχρηστον τῆς ἐν τῷ βίῳ]. That is, it is an accumulation of many perceptions, gathered from use and practice, adapted to some useful purpose in life. For (as Cicero says in the third book of the Academica) what can art be unless it consists not of one or two but of many perceptions of the mind? Take these away, and how will you distinguish the artist from the unskilled?

units.la: Quis est huius disciplinæ usus? Ut qua de caussa, quoque ordine quicque in præcipiendo tradatur, notari atque animaduerti possit.
units.tr: What is the use of this discipline? It is so that one may note and observe for what reason, and in what order, each thing is taught in precepts.

units.la: Quodnam Methodi fundamētum est? Finis eius disciplinæ, cuius ars instituitur. Suus enim cuique arti finis est propositus: ut medicinæ, valetudo: architecturæ, domus: rei militari, victoria: Rhetoricæ, persuasio. Quare primùm omnium constituendum est, quis sit eius quā tractes disciplinæ finis: hoc est, quod bonum, quò spectare ac referri omnia oporteat: ut ad eum quasi viæ & progressiones omnes dirigantur.
units.tr: What is the foundation of Method? It is the end of the discipline for which the art is set up. For every art has its end set before it: for medicine, health; for architecture, a house; for military affairs, victory; for rhetoric, persuasion. Therefore the first thing of all to be settled is what the end of the discipline one is treating is; that is, what good it is to which everything ought to look and be referred, so that all the steps and progress are directed towards it as to a goal.

units.la: Quotuplex est Methodus? Triplex. Analysis, Synthesis & Dierefis. id est dissolutio, compositio, & diuisio. Sed analysis ad inuentionē, synthesis & dierefis ad explicationem pertinent.
units.tr: How many kinds of Method are there? Three: Analysis, Synthesis and Diairesis, that is, resolution, composition and division. Analysis, however, belongs to invention, while synthesis and diairesis belong to explanation.

units.la: Quid est Analysis? Est Methodus quæ finem in sua principia per ea quæ intermedia sunt, resoluit: hoc est, via & ratio quæ à fine retexendo ad media, à mediis ad indiuidua, quæ cuiusque rei minutissimæ partes sunt, progreditur. Hæc autem (vt dixi) ad artium inuentionem pertinet. nam vbi finis artis cōstitutus est, tum quibus ad eam modis perueniri posset, excogitatur.
units.tr: What is Analysis? It is the method which resolves the end into its principles through the intermediate steps; that is, a way and reasoning which proceeds by tracing back from the end to the means, and from the means to the indivisible elements, which are the smallest parts of each thing. This, as I have said, belongs to the discovery of arts. For once the end of an art has been fixed, one then considers by what means it can be attained.

units.la: Quid est Synthesis? Est methodus, quæ à principiis per media paulatim ad finem progreditur: vel hoc modo: Synthesis est, multarum singularum rerum confimiliū in vnam aliquā notionem, & rursus huius & aliarum generis eiusdem in aliam communem notionem tantisper cōtinuata coaceruatio, dum ad summum genus perueniatur. Itaque ratio hæc superiori planè contraria est. quod enim in deliberando primū fuerat, id in agendo est postremum. Siue autem Totum integrum sit, à partibus progressio fit: siue vniuersum, à formis & speciebus. Atque Aristoteles quidē lib. Ethicorum primo scribit, Platonem studiose quæsisse, ac dubitasse vtra methodus præstaret, eáne quæ à principiis ad finem progrederetur: an quæ ad principia perduceret. veluti cùm in curriculo præmia proponuntur iis qui à carceribus ad calces, & contrà à calce ad carceres decurrerint. In Politicis autem, postea quam ostendit ex familiis vicinitatem, ex vicinitatibus ciuitatem constare, ordine de singulis explicat.
units.tr: What is Synthesis? It is the method which proceeds gradually from the principles through the means to the end. Or, put another way: Synthesis is a continued gathering of many individual things that are alike into one notion, and again of this and other notions of the same kind into another common notion, continued until the highest genus is reached. Thus this method is quite the opposite of the former: what came first in deliberation comes last in action. Whether the whole is complete, progress is made from the parts; or whether it is universal, from the forms and species. Aristotle, in the first book of the Ethics, writes that Plato eagerly sought, and hesitated over, which method was better: the one that proceeds from principles to the end, or the one that leads back to the principles. It is like a race in which prizes are offered to those who run from the starting-gates to the turning-post, and conversely from the turning-post back to the gates. In the Politics, after showing that the family is the neighbourhood and the neighbourhood the state, he then explains each matter in order.

units.la: Cedo familiare aliquod exemplum. Nónne qui ædificandi artem inuenerunt, primùm de tecto cogitarunt, quod tempestatis vitandæ caussa subirent: tum deinde quia per se stare tectum non poterat, de parietibus: ac postremò de fundamentis, quibus parietes niterentur. At in agendo, primùm omnium fundamenta iaciuntur: tum parietes extruuntur: ad extremum tectum imponitur. Ita ex fundamento, pariete, & tecto domus componi dicitur: cùm ex inuentione tecti, paries: ex parietis, fundamentum ortum fit.
units.tr: Let me give a familiar example. Did not those who invented the art of building first think of the roof, which they put up to ward off the weather; then, because the roof could not stand by itself, of the walls; and last of all of the foundations on which the walls rest? But in actual building, the foundations are laid first of all, then the walls are raised, and at last the roof is put on. Thus a house is said to be composed of foundation, wall and roof, while in the order of invention the wall arises from the roof, and the foundation from the wall.

units.la: Cedo item aliud. Quoniam Grammaticæ finis est propositus, rectè loqui: prima deliberatio est, de orationis probitate: secunda, de verbis, quibus constat oratio: tertia de syllabis, earúmque pronuntiatione. At in arte tradenda prima de literis præcepta sunt: secúda, de syllabis: tertia, de dictionibus: postrema, de oratione.
units.tr: Let me give another example. Since the aim of grammar is set down as speaking correctly, the first consideration is the correctness of speech; the second, the words of which speech consists; the third, the syllables and their pronunciation. But in teaching the art, the precepts come first concerning letters, second concerning syllables, third concerning words, and last concerning speech as a whole.

units.la: Quid est diæresis? Methodus distributionis quæ à primo & summo genere instituta, eoúsque per genera intermedia producitur, dum ad species infimas perveniatur. Itaque primo loco, qua de re agatur proponit, ac definit: tum deinde partes ipsius singulas diuidendo, nominando, definiendo, & notandis cuiusque proprietatibus exponit. Partium enim singularum nomina singulis definitionibus & proprietatibus aperienda sunt: quandoquidem omnis, (ut ait Aristoteles) scientia per definitionem aperitur. propterea quòd idem est scire, & per definitionem intelligere. Itaque diæresis partes sunt quatuor: propositio,diuisio,nominatio,& definitio. Sic Grammatica in arte tradenda primùm proponitur esse ars recte loquendi,& scribendi:tum deinde diuiditur in literam,syllabam, dictionem, & orationem. Nam diuidendo simul nominantur partes. Rursus literæ diuidûtur in vocales & cõsonantes:hę rursus in mutas,& semiuocales.Syllabæ postea diuiduntur in longas, & breues:dictiones in nomina,verba,ceterásque orationis partes. Oratio verò in planam & figuratam. Singulis autem partibus sua definitio, & proprietatis cuiusq; declaratio adhibetur.
units.tr: What is diairesis? It is the method of distribution which begins from the first and highest genus and is carried on through intermediate genera until the lowest species are reached. Accordingly, it first sets out and defines the subject under discussion; then it expounds it by dividing its individual parts, naming them, defining them, and noting the properties of each. For the name of each part must be explained by its own definition and properties, since, as Aristotle says, all knowledge is disclosed through definition, because to know and to understand through definition are the same thing. Thus there are four parts of diairesis: proposition, division, naming, and definition. So in teaching the art, grammar is first presented as the art of speaking and writing correctly; then it is divided into letter, syllable, word and speech. For in dividing, the parts are named at the same time. Again, letters are divided into vowels and consonants, and these in turn into mutes and semivowels. Syllables are then divided into long and short, words into nouns, verbs and the other parts of speech, and speech into plain and figured. A definition is applied to each part, and a declaration of the property of each.

units.la: Cedo aliquod huius tertię Methodi exemplum. ab antiquo aliquo scriptore vsurpatũ. Extat longè apertissimum in eo libello quem ex hac methodo Cicero Partitiones inscripsit, vbi Rhetoricam artem à summo ad minutissimas quasque partes paulatim partiendo exposuit.Sed nusquàm hæc methodus luculentius explicatur,quàm apud eundem lib.de Orat.1. vbi Crassus ita loquitur: Omnia ferè quæ sunt conclusa nunc artibus, dispersa & disipata quondam fuerunt,vt in Musicis numeri & voces & modi. in Geometria,lineaméta,formæ, interualla, magnitudines.in Astrologia,cœli conuersio, ortus, obitus, motúsque syderum. In Grammaticis, poëtarum pertractatio, historiarum cognitio, verborum interpretatio, pronuntiandi quidam sonus.in hac denique ipsa ratione dicendi excogitare,ornare,disponere,meminisse,agere,ignota quondam omnibus & diffusa latè videbantur. Adhibita igitur est ars quædam extrinsecus,ex alio genere quodam, quod sibi totum Philosophi affumunt,quæ rem dissolutam divulsámque conglutinaret, & ratione quadam constringeret. Sit ergo in iure ciuili finis hic,legitimæ atque vsitatę in rebus caussísque ciuium æqualitatis conseruatio. Tum sunt notanda genera, & ad certum numerum, paucitatémque reuocanda. Genus autem est,id quod sui similes communione quadam, specie autem differentes, duas aut plures complectitur partes. Partes autem sunt, quæ generibus iis,ex quibus emanant,subiiciuntur:omniáque quæ sunt vel generum, vel partium nomina, definitionibus, quam vim habeant,est exprimendū. Est enim definitio earum rerum,quæ sunt eius rei proprię quam definire volumus,breuis & circunscripta quædam explicatio. Hisce ego rebus exempla adiungerem, nisi apud quos hæc haberetur oratio, cernerem. nunc complectar, quod propositi, breui[?]. Si enim aut mihi facere licuerit, quod iam diu cogito, aut alius quispiam, aut me impedito occuparit, aut mortuo effecerit, ut primum omne ius ciuile in genera digerat, quæ perpauca sunt: deinde eorum generum quasi quædam membra dispartiat, tum propriá cuiusque vim definitione declaret, perfectam artem iuris ciuilis habebitis; magis magnam atque uberem, quàm dissicilem & obscuram.
units.tr: Let me give an example of this third method, used by an ancient writer. It stands out most clearly in that little book which Cicero entitled Partitiones, in which by this method he set out the art of rhetoric, dividing it gradually from the highest parts down to the smallest. But nowhere is this method explained more brightly than in the same author's De Oratore, Book I, where Crassus speaks thus: "Almost everything that is now enclosed in arts was once scattered and dispersed: as in music, rhythms, notes and modes; in geometry, lines, shapes, intervals and magnitudes; in astronomy, the revolution of the heavens, risings, settings and the motions of the stars; in grammar, the study of the poets, knowledge of history, interpretation of words, and a certain sound of delivery; and finally in this very art of speaking, to invent, to adorn, to arrange, to remember, and to deliver, all these once seemed unknown to everyone and widely spread about. Therefore a certain art was brought in from outside, from another kind of thing, which philosophers claim entirely for themselves, which would bind together the loose and scattered matter and constrain it by some reasoning. So let the aim of civil law be this: the preservation of a lawful and customary equality in the affairs and causes of citizens. Then the genera must be noted and reduced to a fixed number, and a small one. A genus is that which embraces two or more parts that resemble one another in some common respect but differ in species. Parts are those which are subordinate to the genera from which they spring. And the definitions of all the names of genera or parts, and what force they have, must be stated. For a definition is a brief and bounded explanation of those things which belong properly to the thing we wish to define. I would add examples to these matters, were I not to see before whom this discourse is held. Now I will sum up briefly what I propose. For if I am permitted to do what I have long been thinking of, or if someone else takes it up, or if death or hindrance prevents it, and if the whole civil law is first arranged into genera, which are very few, then the parts of those genera are set out, and then the proper force of each is declared by definition, you will have a complete art of civil law: one that is great and rich rather than difficult and obscure."

units.la: Cedo item aliud exemplū. Sumatur ex eiusdem libro de Finib.11. Omnis in quærendo, quæ via quadam, & ratione habetur, oratio, præscribere primùm debet (ut quibusdam in formulis ea res agatur) ut inter quos disseritur conueniat,quid sit id,de quo differatur. hoc positum in Phædro à Platone, probauit Epicurus, sensitque in omni disputatione,id fieri oportere. sed quòd proximum fuit, non vidit: negat enim definiri ré placere: sine quo fieri interdum non potest,ut inter eos qui ambiguunt, conueniat quid sit, id de quo agatur. velut in hoc ipso de quo nūc disputamus. quærimus enim finem bonorum possimúsne scire hoc quale sit,nisi contulerimus inter nos,cùm finem bonorum dixerimus,quid finis,quid etiam sit ipsum bonum? Eodémque insignis ille locus pertinet,ex lib.de Orat.1, ubi Crassus ita loquitur:Sin autem ea quæ observata sunt in usu ac ratione dicendi, hæc ab hominibus callidis animaduersa ac notata, verbis defignata, generibus illustrata, partibus distributa sunt,non intelligo,&c.Itémque ille alter ex lib.de Orat.11. ubi Antonius ita loquitur: Ego vero(inquit)pergam, & id faciam quod in principio fieri in omnibus disputationibus oportere censeo:ut quid illud sit,de quo disputetur,explanetur.ne vagari & errare cogatur oratio, si ij qui inter se dissenserint, non idem esse illud de quo agitur,intelligét.Nam si fortè quæreretur, quę esset ars Imperatoris: constituendum putarem, principio quis esset Imperator. qui cùm esset constitutus administrator quidam belli gerendi: tum adiungeremus de exercitu, de castris, de agminibus, de signorum collationibus, de oppidorum oppugnationibus, de commeatu, de insidiis faciendis, atque vitandis, de reliquis rebus, quæ essent propriè belli administrădi. quarum qui essent animo & scientia compotes, eos esse Imperatores dicerem. utérque exemplis Africanorum, & Maximorum: Epaminondā atque Annibalem atque eius generis homines nominarem.
units.tr: Let me cite another example. Take the same author's book on the Ends of Goods, book 1: "Every discourse on inquiry that proceeds by some method and reason ought first to set out (as is done in certain formulas) that those who are debating agree on what the subject of discussion is." Epicurus approved of this, as Plato had put it in the Phaedrus, and he judged that it ought to be done in every debate. But he did not see the next point, for he denies that it is right to define the thing. Yet sometimes this cannot be done without it: those who dispute must agree on what the matter under discussion is. Take the very question we are now debating. We ask whether we can know what the end of goods is, unless we first agree among ourselves, when we say "the end of goods," what an end is and what the good itself is. That famous passage also belongs here, from book 1 of On the Orator, where Crassus speaks thus: "But if those things that have been observed in the practice and method of speaking, noted and marked by clever men, have been designated in words, illustrated by kinds, and divided into parts, I do not understand, etc." Likewise that other passage from book 2 of On the Orator, where Antonius speaks thus: "I shall indeed proceed," he says, "and do what I think ought to be done at the outset of every debate: that what the subject of discussion is should be explained, so that the speech is not forced to wander and err, if those who disagree do not understand that they are not talking about the same thing. For if it were asked what the art of the general is, I would think it necessary first to establish who the general is. When he has been established as a certain administrator of waging war, we would then add: concerning the army, the camp, the marches, the gathering of standards, the storming of towns, supplies, laying and avoiding ambushes, and the other matters which properly belong to the conduct of war. Those who had mastery of these both in mind and knowledge, I would call generals." He would name as examples of both kinds the Africani and the Maximi, and men of that sort such as Epaminondas and Hannibal.

units.la: De Dialogorum & Dialecticorum Methodo.
units.tr: On the Method of Dialogues and Dialecticians.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: ENEO ista. Sed quæro ecquamnam harum methodorum trium veteres illi Dialectici suis in dialogis tenerent. nam eorum institutum nosse, permagni (ut video) ad Dialecticæ cognitione interest. Cicero lib. de Finib. 1 r.[?]scribit, primum Sophistarum omnium Gorgiam Leontinum, ausum esse in conventu quæstionem poscere, id est iubere dicere qua de re quis audire vellet. Tum deinde Academicos instituisse, ut qui philosophum audire vellent, primum dicerent quid sentirent. veluti, Malum mihi videtur esse mors. Voluptas mihi videtur esse summum bonum.Quod cùm dixissent,ille contrà:sic tamen,vt qui audiebant, quoad possent, defenderent sententiam suam. Apud Stoicos verò, & Peripateticos, atque etiam ad extremum apud Academicos, eum qui quæsiuit aliquid tacere solitum. vbi enim qui audire vult,ita dixit, Voluptas mihi videtur esse summum bonum:perpetua oratione cótrà disputabatur.
units.tr: I have said enough on these. But I ask which of these three methods those ancient dialecticians followed in their dialogues, for knowing their practice is, as I see it, of very great importance for a knowledge of dialectic. Cicero, in the first book of De Finibus, writes that Gorgias of Leontini, first of all the Sophists, dared to call for a question in an assembly, that is, to order someone to say on what subject he wished to be questioned. Then the Academics instituted the practice that those who wished to hear a philosopher should first state what they thought, for example: "Death seems to me to be an evil," or "Pleasure seems to me to be the highest good." When they had said this, the philosopher answered them in the opposite sense, yet in such a way that the listeners defended their opinion as far as they could. But among the Stoics and Peripatetics, and even at the end among the Academics, the questioner was accustomed to keep silent. For when the one who wished to hear had said, "Pleasure seems to me to be the highest good," the argument was conducted against him in a continuous speech.

units.la: Atlib. Tusc.1. scribit veterem & Socraticam rationem differendi hanc fuisse , vt cùm is qui audire vellet dixisset quid sibi videretur, tum Philosophus cótradiceret . Atlib.de Fin. v.scribit,ab Aristotele principe de singulis rebus in vtranque partem dicendi exercitationem esse institutâ: vt non cótra omnia semper diceret : & tamen vt in omnibus rebus quicquid ex vtraque parte dici posset,exprimeret.
units.tr: Again, in the first book of the Tusculan Disputations, he writes that the ancient and Socratic method of arguing was this: when the one who wished to hear had said what seemed true to him, then the philosopher contradicted him. Again, in the fifth book of De Finibus, he writes that from Aristotle, the chief of them, the practice was instituted of speaking on single matters on either side, so that one would not always speak against everything, and yet in every matter would set out whatever could be said on each side.

units.la: Quid? ipse Aristoteles de suo instituto & docendi ratione quid scribit? Multis in Logicæ suæ locis profitetur, se ita suos discipulos instituisse, vt in vtráque partem parati essent: vt siue Etiam,siue Non aduersarius respon-deret,tum cui, ETIAM responsum esset,refelleret:cui verò,NON,confirmaret: contráque aduersarius ipse quoque pro sua parte disputaret,eámque tueretur.Itaque libro de Captionibus sophisticis extremo testatur suum hoc inuentum esse , vt facultate traderet differédi de quaque re proposita, ex iis quæ essent in re proposita quâ maximè probabilia. vnde sine dubio illa Dialectice definitio sumpta est:vt fit ars probabiliter in vtranque parte de quaque re proposita differendi.
units.tr: What, then? What does Aristotle himself write about his own practice and method of teaching? In many places of his Logic he declares that he trained his disciples so that they were ready on either side: so that, whether the opponent answered "Yes" or "No," the one to whom "Yes" had been answered would refute, and the one to whom "No" had been answered would confirm; and conversely the opponent himself would also argue for his own side and defend it. Accordingly, at the end of the book On Sophistical Refutations, he testifies that this invention of his is meant to give the faculty of arguing on any proposed matter from those things which, within that matter, are most probable. Whence, without doubt, that definition of dialectic was taken: that it is the art of arguing probably on either side about any proposed matter.

units.la: Sed definitionis & diuisionis quodnam apud disputatores illos veteres institutū fuit? Omnium quidē commune fuisse video, vt primum inter se constituerent quid esset illud de quo disputādum esset. tum deinde vt illud vel definirent, vel diuiderent. (neque enim magnopere vtrum prius, an posterius facerent, laborabant) vt illa dialogorum ratio magis ad methodum diuisionis, quàm ad alias duas accedere videretur. Sed definiendi verbo video Ciceronem dupliciter esse vsum. primùm pro eo quod modò dicebam, constituere & ponere, qua de re disputandum esset. veluti, Malum mihi videtur esse mors. deinde pro breui & dilucida controuersæ rei explicatione. Nam in lib. de Off. 1. sic scribit, Omnis quæ à ratione suscipitur de aliqua re institutio, debet à definitione proficisci: vt intelligatur quid sit id, de quo disputetur. At in lib. de Finib. 11. perspicuè demonstrat, definitionē eo loco vsurpatā, pro enuntiato ad disputandum proposito. Omnis (inquit) in quærendo, quæ via quadam & ratione habetur oratio, præscribere primùm debet, vt inter quos disseritur, cōueniat quid sit id, de quo differatur. Hoc positum in Phædro à Platone, probauit Epicurus, sensitque in omni disputatione id fieri oportere: sed quod proximum fuit, non vidit. negat enim definiri rem placere: sine quo fieri interdum non poteft, ut inter eos, qui ambigunt conveniat, quid sit id de quo agatur. Locus autem Platonis quē Cicero protulit, perspicuè hoc ipsum ostendit ἀεὶ πάντος, ὥπαι, μία ἀρχὴ τοῖς μέλλουσι καλῶς βουλεύεσθαι, εἰδέναι δεῖ ἀεὶ ὃ ἂν ἦ, ἢ βλάπτ[?]ειν ἀμαρτάνειν ἀνάγκη.
units.tr: But what was the practice of those ancient disputants regarding definition and division? I see that it was common to all of them first to settle among themselves what the thing was that was to be disputed, and then either to define it or to divide it. (For they did not greatly labour over whether they did this first or later.) So that form of dialogue seems to belong more to the method of division than to the other two. But I see that Cicero used the word "to define" in two ways. First, in the sense I was just describing, to set down and lay out what was to be disputed: for example, "Death seems to me to be an evil." Second, for a brief and clear explanation of the matter in controversy. For in the first book of De Officiis he writes thus: "Every plan of action undertaken by reason concerning some matter ought to proceed from definition, so that it may be understood what that is of which one is disputing." But in the second book of De Finibus he clearly shows that "definition" is there used for the statement put forward for disputation. "Every speech (he says) which is held in inquiry by some method and reason ought first to set down that those between whom one argues agree on what that is about which one is arguing." Epicurus approved this, which Plato had placed in the Phaedrus, and he felt that it ought to be done in every disputation; but what came next he did not see. For he denies that it pleases him to define a thing, though without it it can sometimes not happen that those who dispute agree on what the matter is. But the passage of Plato that Cicero cited shows this very thing clearly: ἀεὶ πάντως, ὦ παῖ, μία ἀρχὴ τοῖς μέλλουσι καλῶς βουλεύεσθαι, εἰδέναι δεῖ ἀεὶ ὃ ἂν ᾖ, ἢ βλάπτειν ἀμαρτάνειν ἀνάγκη. [Always, my boy, for those who are going to deliberate well there is one beginning: one must always know what each thing is, or it is necessary to err and do harm.]

units.la: Et de Aristotele, quid habes dicere? Primū in lib. de interpretatione ita scribit: Τί ἐστιν ἐρώτησις ὅτι ἀλεξ[?]ικὴ· δεῖ γὰρ δεδόσθαι ἐν τῆς ἐρωτήσεως ἑλέσθαι, ὁπότερον βούλεται τῆς ἀντιφάσεως μόριον, ἀλλὰ δεῖ τὸν ἐρωτῶντα προσδιορίζεσθαι πότερον τόδε ἐστὶν ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἢ ἵ τόδε. id est: Quid est, non est quæstio Dialectica. oportet enim dari ex interrogatione optionem, utram velit contradictionis partem declarare. Sed oportet interrogantem definire, utrum homo sit hoc, an illud. Deinde lib. Analyt. priorū primo: Δεῖ ὃ τὰς προτάσεις ἀεὶ ἕκαστον τούτων ὅτως ἐπιλαμβάνειν, ἐπὶ τιθέμενον αὐτὸ πρῶτον ἢ τῆς ὁρισμὸς, ἐδοσαίδια τὸ πράγματος. Id est: Oportet propositiones de horum unoquoque ita sumere: subiiciente primum id de quo agitur, deinde definitiones, tum omnes rei proprietates. Post lib. Topic. v iii. cùm dixisset facilem differendi rationem non esse, nisi prius intelligatur, quid sit id de quo disputatio instituitur: maximeque id principiis artium contingere, quibus cetera probantur, tum ita infert: ἀλλ' ἀναγκαῖον ὁρισμῷ τῆς τοιῶν ἕκαστον γνωρίζειν. id est, definitione unumquodq; eorū necessario aperiendum est. quoniam autem formula, quid est,nő est anceps, propterea paucis antè versibus monuit quæstionem definitionis ita proponendam esse:Homo éstne animal rationis particeps,an non? Quod eodem modo in libro de interpretatione admonuerat,eo loco quem superiùs protulimus.
units.tr: And what have you to say about Aristotle? First, in the book On Interpretation he writes thus: τί ἐστιν, οὐκ ἔστιν ἐρώτησις διαλεκτική· δεῖ γὰρ δεδόσθαι ἐν τῇ ἐρωτήσει αἵρεσιν, ὁπότερον βούλεται τῆς ἀντιφάσεως μόριον ἀποφαίνειν· ἀλλὰ δεῖ τὸν ἐρωτῶντα προσδιορίζεσθαι πότερον τόδε ἐστὶν ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἢ οὔ. [What is it? It is not a dialectical question. For in the question there must be given a choice of which part of the contradiction it wishes to declare; but the questioner must specify whether this is man or not.] Then in the first book of the Prior Analytics: δεῖ δὲ τὰς προτάσεις ἀεὶ ἕκαστον τούτων οὕτως ἐπιλαμβάνειν, ὑποτιθέμενον αὐτὸ πρῶτον ἢ τὸν ὁρισμόν, ἔπειτα τὰ συμβεβηκότα τοῦ πράγματος. [One must always take the propositions about each of these thus, setting down first the subject itself or its definition, then the properties of the thing.] Afterwards, in the Topics, when he had said that there is no easy method of arguing unless one first understands what the thing is that the disputation is about, and that this comes about most of all with the principles of the arts, by which the rest are proved, he then infers: ἀλλ' ἀναγκαῖον ὁρισμῷ τῶν τοιούτων ἕκαστον γνωρίζειν. [But it is necessary to make each of these known by definition.] Since the formula "what is it?" is not ambiguous, therefore a few lines earlier he had advised that the question of definition should be put thus: "Is man a rational animal, or not?" which he had likewise laid down in the book On Interpretation, in the passage I cited above.

units.la: Potésne harum rerum omnium exemplum aliquod ex veterum libris proferre? Sumatur Ciceronis illa disputatio quæ est sub initium lib.Tuscul.quarti: vbi & quæstio ponitur, & post quæstionem diuisio singularum partium definitur. planissimēque vetus istud de quo iam diximus institutum observatur.
units.tr: Can you produce any example of all these things from the books of the ancients? Let Cicero's disputation at the beginning of the fourth book of the Tusculan Disputations be taken: there both the question is posed, and after the question the division of its parts is defined, and that ancient practice we have just mentioned is observed most plainly.

units.la: De artis & libelli huius Methodo.
units.tr: On the Method of the Art and of this Little Book.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: CQVAMNAM igitur Methodum in hac Dialecticæ artis institutione sequemur? Analyticam. cuius in meditando hic ordo est: primùm vt finem nobis Dialecticæ proponamus eum, quem superiùs diximus, Demonstrationem: id est veri & falsi diiudicationem: tum vt è sex consequentibus quod finì proximum est, proximè consideremus: hoc est, primo loco rationis conclusionem, siue argumentationum formulas: secundò vim & firmamentum argumentorum, ex quibus quid quodque valeat, intelligitur: tertiò enuntiationes, quibus argumenta constant: quartò partis cuiusque nomen, & & definitionem: quintò eiusdem materiæ cõfufæ distributionem : postremò affectionem rerum & vocabulorum, ex quibus Enũtiationes constant.Et quoniam longius à fine regredi non possumus, ab eo artem nostram componere instituemus. Id autem operis nostri fundamentum iam ante iactum est,cùm ab eo quod vltimum inuenimus, exorsi fumus : nimirum ab affectionibus. Deinceps igitur de diuisione, tum de definitione, de argumento, & de argumentatione differemus. Nam etsi in omni methodo, primùm (vt modò dixi-mus) locum obtinet definitio, tamen in hac arte tradenda, priora sunt diuisionis præcepta, quàm definitionis. quia definitio eo inftrumento conficitur, quod in diuisionis arte traditur:nimirum genere,partitione, & differentia. deinde chaos cuiusque quæstionis isto modo,certissimè distingui, atque in ordinem redigi potest. Idémque video Ciceronem & in Officiis & in Tufc.quarta fecisse[?].
units.tr: By what method, then, shall we proceed in this institution of the art of dialectic? The analytic. Its order in meditation is this: first, we set before ourselves as the aim of dialectic the one we named above, demonstration, that is, the distinguishing of true from false. Next, of the six consequents, we consider first the one nearest to that aim: namely, in the first place, the conclusion of reasoning, or the forms of argument; second, the force and firmness of arguments, from which it is understood what each one is worth; third, the propositions of which arguments consist; fourth, the name and definition of each part; fifth, the distribution of each confused matter; and last, the affections of things and words, of which propositions consist. And since we cannot go back further from the end, we shall set out to compose our art starting from it. Indeed, the foundation of our work has already been laid, since we began from what we found last, namely the affections. Hence we shall next discuss division, then definition, the argument, and argumentation. For although in every method definition holds the first place (as I have just said), in teaching this art the precepts of division come before those of definition, because a definition is made with that instrument which is taught in the art of division: namely, genus, partition and difference. Then, too, the chaos of any question can be distinguished most certainly in this way and reduced to order. And I see that Cicero did the same in the Offices and in the Tusculans, book four.

units.la: Quodnam appellas chaos quæstionum? Quia proposita quæstione protinus vniuersi generis confusio, & quasi chaos quoddam animo & menti obiicitur. Quare vt in opificio mundi, cùm eiffet confusa naturarum moles, primùm lux est adhibita:tum singulæ materiæ secretæ ac definitæ sunt : dein vnaquæque fuû in locum ac tãquam sedem ordine collocata: pòst earum omnium vsus atque fructus hominibus concessus est : similiter proposita quæstione principio rationum notitia tanquam lucerna in tenebris adhibenda est, atque ita dispersæ ac dissipatæ quæstionis partes (de quibus superiùs ex Cicerone dicebamus) sub oculos subiiciendæ sunt: earúmque certa genera notanda: id est, nominibus suis appellanda, atque ad angustum numerum paucitatemque reuocanda sunt. Tum singulæ quæstionis partes distinguendæ, atque in ordinem distribuendæ. pòst singulæ partes definitionibus, & argumentatione tractandæ, ex quibus operis totius fructus, vtilitásque percipitur. At quoniam finis omnis Dialecticæ in ratiocinatione & syllogismo positus est, quod verbum à ratiocinatoribus sumptum esse constat, venit mihi in mentem totam huius artis structuram ratiocinationibus calculatorum similem facere.
units.tr: What do you call the chaos of questions? Because once a question is proposed, at once a confusion of the whole kind, and as it were a certain chaos, is thrown before the mind and intellect. Therefore, just as in the making of the world, when the mass of natures was confused, light was first introduced; then the individual kinds of matter were separated and defined; next each was placed in order in its own place, as if in its seat; and afterwards the use and fruit of all of them was granted to men: so, once a question is proposed, the knowledge of the principles of reasoning must be brought in like a lamp in darkness, and so the scattered and dissipated parts of the question (about which we spoke above, following Cicero) are to be set before our eyes. Their definite kinds are to be noted, that is, named by their own names, and reduced to a narrow number and few in number. Then the single parts of the question are to be distinguished and arranged in order. Afterwards the single parts are to be treated by definitions and argumentation, from which the fruit and usefulness of the whole work is perceived. But since the whole end of dialectic lies in reckoning (ratiocinatio) and the syllogism, a word which is known to be taken from accountants (ratiocinatores), it has come into my mind to make the whole structure of this art similar to the reckonings of accountants.

units.la: Quomodo? Quoniam qui societatem aliquot annos exercuerunt, cùm de ea dirimenda cogitant, primùm omnium finem sibi rationum distractionem proponunt. deinde numerationem, quam ego argumentationibus comparo. pòst numerandi artem, vt quid quisque numerus valeat, intelligatur. tum calculos, qui enuntiationibus aptissimè conferuntur. Inde temporum quibus societas fuit, aut negotiationum diuisarum titulum siue definitionem: pòst eiusdem temporis, earundémque rerum partitionem. Et quoniam regredi vlterius non possunt, ab eo incipiunt, quod vltimum mum invenerät:ac tum deinde ab hoc postremo gradatim progredientes ad id quod sibi finem statuerant,hoc est,rationum distractionem,peruenerunt.
units.tr: How so? Those who have carried on a partnership for some years, when they think of dissolving it, first of all propose to themselves as their aim the settling of the accounts. Then comes the numbering, which I compare with argumentations. After that comes the art of numbering, so that it is understood what each number is worth. Then come the calculations, which are most aptly compared with propositions. Next come the title or definition of the period during which the partnership lasted, or of the business that was divided; and afterwards the partition of that same period and of those same matters. And since they cannot go back any further, they begin from what they had found last, and then, progressing gradually from this last step, they arrive at what they had set as their aim, that is, the settling of the accounts.

units.la: De Divisione. CAP. IIII.
units.tr: On Division. CHAP. IIII.

units.la: EINCEPS[?] igitur de Divisione disseramus: Quid est Divisio? Divisio summo genere est, partium quæstionis ad disputandum propositæ distributio. sed eius species duæ sunt, quarum prior proprie dispositio dicitur, altera generis sui nomine divisio appellatur.
units.tr: Next, then, let us discuss Division. What is Division? Division, taken in the highest genus, is the distribution of the parts of a question proposed for discussion. It has two species: the first is properly called arrangement (dispositio), and the other takes the name of its genus, division.

units.la: Quid est dispositio? Prima maiorum partium distributio, per quam summa quæstionis genera, non solùm ordine, sed etiam momento quodam, perexiguo numero, notantur. Est enim quasi operis futuri designatio, atque(ut pictores loquuntur,) rudis quædam informatio:ut cū in Officiis Cicero ita scribit, Omnis de officio duplex est quæstio: unum genus est, quod pertinet ad finem bonorum, alterum ad institutionem vitæ communis. Atque etiam alia divisio est officij: nam & medium quoddām officium dicitur & perfectum. Sed nullum eius rei vel dilucidius vel luculentius exemplũ statui potest: quàm ex initio Partitionum Ciceronis: ubi summatim omnem dicendi doctrinam tripartitò distribuit, in vim orationis, orationem, & quæstionem: quarum singulas pofterius subtiliter explicat.
units.tr: What is arrangement? It is the first distribution of the larger parts, by which the main kinds of a question are marked out, not only in order but also with a certain weight, by a very small number of divisions. For it is, as it were, a sketch of the work to come and, to use the language of painters, a rough outline. So Cicero writes in the Offices: "Every question about duty is twofold: one kind concerns the end of goods, the other the arrangement of common life." And there is also another division of duty, for one duty is called intermediate and another perfect. But no example of this matter can be set out more clearly or more brilliantly than the beginning of Cicero's Partitions, where he divides all the teaching of speaking into three parts, namely the power of speech, the speech itself, and the question; and afterwards he explains each of these carefully.

units.la: Quid est diuisio? Notio quæ rem vniuersam in cognatas partes singulas adhibita cuiusque differentia distinguit. Nam omnis res vniuersalis per adiunctionem differentiæ in singularem contrahitur.
units.tr: What is division? It is a notion which, applying the difference of each part, separates a whole thing into its related parts. For every universal thing is narrowed into a particular one by the addition of a difference.

units.la: Quod est officiū diuisionis? Vt & species à suo genere distrahat, & eas distractas adhibita differētia inter se opponat. Eius autem artis cùm maximis in disciplinis omnibus est vsus: tum verò laus plané singularis. Nam Socrates in Phædro Platonis profitetur, siquè natus esset diuidēdi peritū, eius se quasi Dei alicuius vestigia secuturū. τῆτον Διὸς (inquit) κα- [?]ιςτ μετ' ἴχνιον θεοῖο. Atque ad eum locum allusisse Ciceronem arbitror in lib.1 1.de Oratore, cùm in illo Antonius ait, Crassū semper in dicendo sibi videri Deū, cuius vestigia Cæsar & Catulus adolescentes persequi cupiant: in hoc autem, Qui ordo(inquit)Antonio Catulus,tibi placet, & quæ dispositio argumé-torum:in qua tu mihi semper Deus videri soles.
units.tr: What is the function of division? To separate a species from its genus and, once separated, to set them against one another by means of a difference. This art is used in all the major disciplines, but its praise is truly unique. For Socrates, in Plato's Phaedrus, declares that if he were born skilled at dividing, he would follow in the footsteps of that god, as it were: "I shall follow him, as the footsteps of a god [κατ' ἴχνιον θεοῖο]." I think Cicero alluded to this passage in the first book of the De Oratore, where Antonius says that Crassus always seemed to him a god whose footsteps Caesar and the young Catulus desired to follow; and in the same place Catulus says to Antonius, "What order and arrangement of arguments do you approve? In which you always seem to me a god."

units.la: Quid interest inter differentiam & diuisionem? Superius dictum est, differentia species insigniri, vt secernātur. Hoc igitur inter diuisionem & differētiam interest, quòd in rebus insignitis interest inter instrumentum & signum. nam exempli caussa, quod in iudendis numis materia est: id in hac re est species: quod illic instrumentum: hîc, diuisio: quod illic signum, siue nota publica:hîc, differētia.
units.tr: What is the difference between a difference and a division? It was said above that difference is used to mark a species so that it may be distinguished. The relation between division and difference is therefore like that between an instrument and a sign. For example, what the material is in striking coins, that is the species in this matter; what the die is there, that is division here; and what the public mark or stamp is there, that is difference here.

units.la: Quotuplex differentia est? Quoniam diuisio & differentia ita inter se affectæ sunt, vt instrumentum & signum: sequitur, vt diuisionum ac differentiarum eadem plane distributio fit: & quod de illis, idem de his dicatur.
units.tr: How many kinds of difference are there? Since division and difference are related to one another as instrument and sign, it follows that the distribution of divisions and of differences is exactly the same, and what is said of the one is said of the other.

units.la: De multiplici Diuisionum genere.
units.tr: On the Manifold Kinds of Division.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: QVOT VPLEX igitur Diuisionum ac differentiarū distributio est? Earum tot ferè genera sunt, quot superiùs sectionum locos exposuimus. Nam (vt ante monuimus) ex iis locis tanquam thesauris Diuisionum & definitionum materia omnis eruitur. Itaq; remotis genere, specie, to[?] & partibus: reliquos omnes locos ordine, si voles, persequi possumus. Quatuor autem illos propterea remouemus, quia Genus communis omnium diuisionum materia est: Species autem, quæ quidem infima est, iccirco nō diuiditur, quia indiuidua tantùm complectitur: quæ (vt iam persæpe diximus) infinita, caduca, & fluxa sunt. quæ verò infinita sunt, percurri animo non possunt: ad totum autem & partes, non diuisio (vt paulo ante diximus) sed partitio adhibetur.
units.tr: What, then, is the full range of the distributions and differences of division? There are about as many kinds as the places of section we set out above. For, as we said before, all the material of divisions and definitions is drawn from those places as from storehouses. So, setting aside genus, species, the whole and its parts, we can, if you like, go through all the remaining places in order. We set those four aside for these reasons: genus is the common material of every division; species, the lowest kind, is not divided, because it embraces only individuals, which (as we have said very often) are infinite, perishable and fluid. What is infinite cannot be run through by the mind. For the whole and its parts, the procedure is not division (as we said a little earlier) but partition.

units.la: Quæ est diuisio generis? Hæc vniuersalis est, & fusa per omnes locos. Itaque reliquæ omnes sumi ex locis dicuntur: at hæc sumi ex generis loco dici nō potest. Generis igitur diuisio est,quæ Genus aliquod in certas & finitas species distribuit, quarum singulæ generis nomen retinent: siue illud summum fit, siue medium, siue infimum. Summum: veluti, Corpus aliud est animatum, aliud inanimatum. Medium: veluti, Animal aliud est rationale, aliud irrationale. Infimū: veluti, Homo alius est Gallus, alius Germanus, alius Italus. Hæc autem distributio duplex, dicitur à Græcis διαίρεσις & ὑποδιαίρεσις: à Latinis, Diuisio & Subdiuisio. Omnes autem illæ species distributæ, summi generis, quod est corpus, nomen retinent.
units.tr: What is division of a genus? It is universal and spread through all the places. So all the other kinds are said to be taken from places, but this one cannot be said to be taken from the place of genus. Division of a genus, then, is that which distributes some genus into definite and finite species, each of which keeps the name of the genus, whether that genus is the highest, the middle or the lowest. Highest: for example, Body is one thing animate, another inanimate. Middle: for example, Animal is one thing rational, another irrational. Lowest: for example, Man is one thing a Gaul, another a German, another an Italian. This distribution is twofold: the Greeks call it διαίρεσις and ὑποδιαίρεσις, the Latins division and subdivision. All those distributed species, however, retain the name of the highest genus, which is body.

units.la: Quotuplex generis diuisio est? Duplex. Nã altera certâ cuique speciei ex sua differentiâ nota attribuit: altera propter differentiæ ignorationem & nominum penuriam non attribuit: sed vel contrariam speciem ex contradictionis particula notat, vel sui generis nomine appellat.
units.tr: How many kinds of division of a genus are there? Two. One assigns to each species its own known difference. The other, because the difference is unknown or the names are lacking, does not assign it, but either marks the opposite species with the particle of contradiction or names it by the name of its own genus.

units.la: Cedo exemplum contradictionis. Superiùs vbi de differentia disseruimus, hæc vulgata protulimus: Animal aliud est rationale, aliud irrationale. Rerum aliæ sunt corporales, aliæ incorporales. Ius aliud scriptum, aliud nō scriptum. Furtum aliud manifestum, aliud nec manifestum.
units.tr: Let me give an example of contradiction. Above, when we discussed difference, we set forth these common examples: Animal is one thing rational, another irrational. Some things are corporeal, others incorporeal. Law is one thing written, another unwritten. Theft is one thing manifest, another not manifest.

units.la: Cedo exemplū speciei, quæ pro differentia generis nomen obtinet. Fruges commune nomen est & terræ & arborum. Baccæ tamen de arboribus proprie: de terra fruges dicuntur, vt apud Ciceronem in Catone Maiore. Tanquam in arborum baccis, terræque frugibus. Sic apud Cæsarem: Gallorum alii dicuntur Belgæ, alii Aquitani, alii proprie Galli. Sic apud Iuriscósultos[?] Cognatio quædam propriè dicitur Agnatio, eorum videlicet qui per patrem coniunguntur: quædam tantummodo Cognatio, eorum qui per matrem. Solétque hæc species voce & nota illa Tantùmodo plerùnque designari. Vt apud Ciceronem in Topicis. Genus est vxor. Eius sunt duæ formæ: vna matrumfamilias[?], hæ sunt quæ in manum conuenerunt. altera earum quæ tantummodo vxores habentur. Scitum est autem illud eiusdem eodémque loco: Species à genere, quoad suū[?], id est ipsius, nomen retinet, nunquam fciungitur. Sic Aristoteles initio Topicorum Proprii duas dicit esse species: vnam, quæ rei vim & naturam declarat, quæ Definitio dicitur: alteram, quæ non declarat, & communi nomine Proprium vocatur. Et lib. Politicorum 11 r. cùm Reip. tres esse species dixisset, vnam quæ vnius dominatu regeretur, quæ Monarchia diceretur: altera, quæ paucorum, quæ Aristocratia: tum verò tertiam subiunxit, quæ populi imperio ac potestate contineretur: quæ communi nomine Resp. Græce πολιτεία[?] dicitur. Eodémque modo Iuriscósulti[?] doni duas species constituunt: vnam, quæ cum causa fit, quæ proprie Munus appellatur: alteram, quæ sine causa, quæ generis nomine Donum vocatur. Sed vsum huius differentiæ posterius ex locis argumentorum cognosces.
units.tr: Let me give an example of a species which takes the name of the genus in place of a difference. Fruits is a common name both of the earth and of trees. Yet berries are properly said of trees, and fruits of the earth, as in Cicero's Cato Maior: "as in the berries of trees and the fruits of the earth." So in Caesar: some Gauls are called Belgae, others Aquitani, others properly Gauls. So among the jurists, one kind of kinship is properly called agnation, namely that of those joined through the father; another is called only cognation, that of those joined through the mother. This species is usually marked by the word and the particle "only." As in Cicero's Topics: "Genus is wife. Of this there are two forms: one of matrons of families, who have come into the hand (manus); the other of those who are regarded merely as wives." There is also that saying in the same passage: "A species keeps the name of its genus, as far as its own name goes, and is never separated from it." So Aristotle at the beginning of the Topics says that Proprium has two species: one which declares the force and nature of a thing, and is called definition; the other, which does not declare it, and is called by the common name proprium. And in the Politics, after saying that the commonwealth has three species, one ruled by the domination of one, which is called monarchy, another of the few, which is aristocracy, he then added a third, contained under the power and authority of the people, which is called by the common name commonwealth, in Greek πολιτεία. In the same way the jurists establish two species of gift: one made with a cause, which is properly called a munus; the other without a cause, which by the name of the genus is called a donum. But you will learn the use of this difference later, from the places of arguments.

units.la: Quæ est diuisio ex caussa Efficiente? Quæ genus in species ex causarum efficientium varietate diuidit.veluti, Arborum alię spóte nascuntur (ait Plinius) alię ex semine, alię ex traducę. Animalium aliud ex parente, aliud à sole, aliud ex putredine nascitur.
units.tr: What is division from the efficient cause? It is that which divides a genus into species according to the variety of efficient causes. For example, some trees arise of themselves, says Pliny; others from seed, others from a cutting. Some animals are born from a parent, others from the sun, others from putrefaction.

units.la: Quæ est ex Materia? Quæ genus in species pro cuiusq; materię varietate distribuit: veluti, Metallorum aliud est aurum, aliud argentum, aliud æs, aliud ferrum. Prædium aliud est urbanum, aliud rusticum.nam urbanum (inquiunt Iurisconsulti) non locus facit, sed materia. Vasorum quædam sunt ærea, quædam vitrea, quædam fictilia.
units.tr: What is division from matter? It is that which distributes a genus into species according to the variety of each matter. For example, of metals, one is gold, another silver, another bronze, another iron. An estate is one thing urban, another rural; for, say the jurists, it is not the place but the material that makes an estate urban. Some vessels are bronze, some glass, some earthenware.

units.la: Quæ est ex Forma? Quæ genus in species ex formarum varietate distribuit: veluti, navium aliæ sunt constratæ, aliæ aperte, aliæ turritæ, aliæ rostratæ, aliæ biremes, aliæ triremes, aliæ quadriremes. Linearum alia recta est, alia obliqua.
units.tr: What is division from form? It is that which distributes a genus into species according to the variety of forms. For example, ships are some decked, others open, others towered, others beaked, others two-banked, others three-banked, others four-banked. Of lines, one is straight, another oblique.

units.la: Cedo exemplum ex fine. Navium aliæ sunt actuariæ, aliæ piscatoriæ, aliæ onerariæ, aliæ speculatoriæ. Seruorum alij sunt atrienses, alij dispensatores, alij topiarij, alij amanuenses, alij scriptores. Vasorum alia sunt vinaria, quædam escaria, quædam aquaria, quedā vnguentaria.
units.tr: Let me give an example from the end (purpose). Some ships are for coasting, some for fishing, some for carrying loads, some for scouting. Some slaves are hall-attendants, some stewards, some gardeners, some secretaries, some scribes. Some vessels are for wine, some for food, some for water, some for ointments.

units.la: Quæ est diuisio ex effectis? Quæ genus in species pro effectorum varietate dispertit. veluti herbarum quedā calefaciendi vim habent,
units.tr: What is division from effects? It is that which divides a genus into species according to the variety of effects. For example, some herbs have the power of warming,

units.la: Stray mark at the bottom centre is not text and is left out. quædam refrigerandi.aër alius est salubris,alius pestilens.
units.tr: some of cooling. Air is one thing healthy, another pestilential.

units.la: Quæ est diuisio ex Proprio? Quæ genus in species pro cuiusque proprietate partitur.veluti,Beluarum aliæ sunt volatiles,aliæ terrenę, aliæ natatiles. Item,aliæ cantant, alię latrant, aliæ hinniunt,aliæ vlulant,alie rudent,aliæ rugiunt.Item aliæ sunt cicures,aliæ ferę.
units.tr: What is division from the property? It is that which partitions a genus into species according to each one's property. For example, of beasts, some are flying, some land-dwelling, some swimming. Likewise, some sing, some bark, some neigh, some howl, some bray, some roar. Likewise, some are tame, some wild.

units.la: Quæ est diuisio ex Antecedente? Locus ex antecedente necessarió cum illo ex consequente coniungendus est. Nam diuisio hæc alias species antecedentes constituit, alias consequentes. veluti, Ætas hominis diuiditur in pueritiam, adolescentiam, iuuentutę, & fene&tutem.Illa autę anni partitio est potius quàm diuisio. Annus diuiditur in ver, æstatem, autumnum,& hyemen.
units.tr: What is division from the antecedent? A place drawn from the antecedent must necessarily be joined with one drawn from the consequent, for this division makes some species antecedent and others consequent. For example, the age of man is divided into boyhood, youth, young manhood and old age. But that division of the year is a partition rather than a division: the year is divided into spring, summer, autumn and winter.

units.la: Quæ est diuisio ex Adiunctis? Quæ genus pro adiunctorum varietate distribuit.vt,Senŭ alij sunt creduli, alij suspiciosi, alij iracundi, alij inertes,alij loquaces.vel hoc modo : Senŭ alij facilè lippitudinem contrahunt, alij podagram,alij in surditatem facilius incidunt, alij in delirium.
units.tr: What is division from adjuncts? It is that which distributes a genus according to the variety of adjuncts. For example: of old men, some are credulous, some suspicious, some irascible, some sluggish, some talkative. Or in this way: of old men, some easily contract bleary eyes, others gout, others fall more readily into deafness, others into delirium.

units.la: Quę est diuisio ex Accidenti? Quæ genus in species pro accidentium varietate diftinguit.veluti, Equorum alij sunt gradarij, alij afturcones,alij veredi,alij fuccuffatores.Flores alij sunt hyberni, alij verni, alij eftiui, alij autumnales.
units.tr: What is division from accident? It is that which distinguishes a genus into species according to the variety of accidents. For example: of horses, some are pacers, some Asturian ponies, some post-horses, some hacks. Of flowers, some are wintry, some spring, some summer, some autumn.

units.la: Quæ est diuisio ex Comparatione? Quæ genus ex formarum aut paritate aut imparitate diftibuit.veluti,Magistratuum alij sunt maiores,alij minores.Item,alij sunt maiorum , alij minorum gentium.Militum alij sunt præpofiti,alij gregarij.
units.tr: What is division from comparison? It is that which distributes a genus according to the equality or inequality of the things compared. For example: of magistrates, some are greater, some lesser. Likewise, some belong to the greater peoples, some to the lesser. Of soldiers, some are commanders, some common soldiers.

units.la: Quæ eit diuisio ex Similitudine? Quein[?] diftribuêdo varias similitudines aucupatur: veluti apud Ciceronem in ea pro Sex,Rofcio: Simillima est accusatorum ratio. Alii vestrûm anseres sunt,qui tantummodo clamant,nocere nó possunt:alij canes,qui & latrare & mordere possunt.Et Tufcul.v.Vt in ludis Olympi cis alij corporibus exercitatis gloriam & nobilitatem coronæ petunt, alij emendi aut vendendi quæstu ducuntur , alij visendi caussa veniunt: sic in vita quidam gloriæ seruiunt , alij pecuniis, alij rerum naturam studiosè intuentur.Item, Hominum alij sunt tanquam apes, vt patresfa.nauiatque industrij:alij tanquam fuci,qui alieno labore victitant.
units.tr: What is division from similitude? It is that which, in distributing, seeks out various likenesses. For example, in Cicero's speech for Sextus Roscius: "The case of the accusers is very like. Some of you are geese, who only cackle and cannot do harm; others dogs, who can both bark and bite." And in the Tusculan Disputations, book 5: "As at the Olympic games, some men with trained bodies seek glory and the renown of the crown, others are drawn by the profit of buying and selling, others come only to watch; so in life some serve glory, others money, others study the nature of things with attention." Likewise: of men, some are like bees, the diligent and industrious householders; others like drones, who live on another's labour.

units.la: Quæ est diuisio ex Aduersis? Quæ genus in maximè dissidentes atque infestas species diftribuit.veluti,Elementorum aliud est calidû, aliud frigidum , aliud leue , aliud grane,aliud humidum,aliud siccum. Enuntiationum aliæ sunt veræ,aliæ falsæ.
units.tr: What is division from opposites? It is that which distributes a genus into species that are most sharply at odds and hostile. For example: of the elements, one is hot, another cold, one light, another heavy, one moist, another dry. Of statements, some are true, others false.

units.la: Quæ est diuisio ex Relatis? Quæ species interse relatas exponit . vt , Hominum alij sunt patresfa.alij filiifa.alij tutores,alij pupilli:alij domini,alij ferui.
units.tr: What is division from relatives? It sets out the species that stand in relation to one another, as: of men, some are fathers of families, some sons; some are guardians, some wards; some are masters, some slaves.

units.la: Quæ est diuisio ex Priuantibus? Quæ genus in eas species distribuit,quarum aliæ habitum,aliæ priuationem significét.veluti, Hominum alij sunt fapiétes, alij stulti.alij valentes, alij imbecilli.Instrumentorum(inquit Aristo teles in Politicis)alia sunt animata,vt ferui:alia inanimata,vt securis,aut dolabra.
units.tr: What is division from privatives? It divides a genus into species, of which some signify a possession of a quality and others its privation, as: of men, some are wise, some foolish; some are strong, some weak. Of instruments (says Aristotle in the Politics), some are animate, such as slaves; others inanimate, such as an axe or an adze.

units.la: Quæ est diuisio ex Aientibus & Negatibus? Quæ genus in eas species diuidit, quarum aliæ affirmét,aliæ negent:veluti,Furtum aliud est manifestum,aliud necmanifeftum.Animal aliud est rationale,aliud irrationale.Ius aliud scriptum,aliud non scriptum.Res aliæ corporeæ,aliæ incorporeæ.
units.tr: What is division from affirmatives and negatives? It divides a genus into species, of which some affirm and others deny, as: theft is one thing if it is manifest, another if it is not manifest. Animal is one thing if rational, another if irrational. Law is one thing if written, another if unwritten. Things are some corporeal, some incorporeal.

units.la: Quæ est diuisio ex Repugnantibus? Quæ species ita distribuit, vt vna contrarium oftédat,altera alterius contrarij consequens.veluti, Rerum quædã bonæ sunt,quædam fugiendæ.Ciuium alij sunt vtiles Reip . alij ciuitate exterminandi . Nam fugiendum consequens est mali: & Eiiciendum inutilis,
units.tr: What is division from opposites? It divides in such a way that one member shows the contrary, and the other shows what follows from the contrary of the first, as: some things are good, some are to be avoided. Some citizens are useful to the commonwealth, others are to be banished from the state. For what is to be avoided follows from what is bad, and what is to be cast out follows from what is useless.

units.la: Quæ est diuisio ex Disparibus? Quæ difpa res species constituit. veluti , Genus aliud est summum, aliud medium,aliud infimum. Capitis diminutio alia est maxima,alia media,alia minima. Elementorum aliud est graue , aliud leue . Aetas apud Romanos alia erat iuniorum,vsque annum x 1 v[?]:alia seniorum.Officium(inquit Cicero)aliud medium est,aliud perfectum.
units.tr: What is division from unequals? It constitutes species that are unequal, as: a genus is one thing if highest, another if middle, another if lowest. A loss of civil status (capitis diminutio) is one thing if greatest, another if middle, another if least. Of elements, one is heavy, another light. Among the Romans, age was one thing for the juniors, up to forty-five years, and another for the seniors. Duty (says Cicero) is one thing if middle, another if perfect.

units.tr: What is division from dissimilars? It is that which, within each species, marks out some dissimilarity between

units.la: De arte & praeceptis Diuidendi.
units.tr: On the Art and Precepts of Dividing.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: Q[?]uot sunt Diuisionum praecepta? Vnum & summum diuisionis praeceptum est, quo cetera omnia continentur: vt vis vniuersi generis in species cognatas diducatur. Sed perspicuitatis causa quatuor exponenda sunt. primum, vt cognatae species ab vno eodémque genere diftrahantur. alterum, vt inter fe ex aduerso & tanquâ è regione refpódeant: id est semper ex aliquo contrariorum genere sint. tertiû, vt ne vel species generi, vel genus speciei exequetur. quartum, ne qua species vel redundet, vel prętermittatur: sed paria specierum & generis vniuersi momenta sint.
units.tr: What are the rules of division? There is one chief rule of division, which contains all the others: the force of the whole genus should be drawn apart into kindred species. For the sake of clarity, four points must be explained: (1) the kindred species should be drawn from one and the same genus; (2) they should answer one another face to face, as if from opposite regions, that is, they should always belong to some genus of contraries; (3) neither should a species exceed its genus, nor a genus its species; (4) no species should be superfluous or omitted, but the species and the whole genus should carry equal weight.

units.la: Quid est cognatas species diduci? Est non modò ex eodé affectuum loco, sed etiā ex eodem genere omnes partes inter fe cognatas, ac non aliunde ascitas proponi. Sic enim Zeno (vt Laertius testatur) διαίρεσιν definiebat: ἡ εἰς τὰ πρῶτα εἴδη τομή[?]. vt fiquis Herculeorum genus, verbi gratia, diuideret in eos demum, qui eodem sanguine prognati effent, neque alienos vllos admisceret. nam genus est id demum, quod de pluribus communione quadam inter se coniunctis, & continentibus, dicitur: ut superius docuimus. veluti, Quicquid in deliberationem cadit, id vel honestum est, vel turpe. Nam si quis ita diuideret, id vel honestum est, vel vtile, ex altero genere speciem sumeret. Caput igitur diuisionis est, ut cognatae species ex eodem genere ducantur: quasi cum riuuli ex eodem fonte & capite derivantur.
units.tr: What does it mean for kindred species to be drawn apart? It means that all the parts set out should be kindred with one another, not only in the same place of the affections but also in the same genus, and not brought in from elsewhere. Zeno, as Laertius reports, defined division in this way: "the cutting into the first species" [ἡ εἰς τὰ πρῶτα εἴδη τομή]. So if someone divided the genus of the Herculeans, for example, only into those who were born of the same blood, admitting no outsiders, he would be dividing correctly. For a genus is that which is predicated of several things joined and held together by some common bond, as we taught above. For example: "Whatever falls under deliberation is either honourable or shameful." But if someone divided it thus: "it is either honourable or useful," he would be taking a species from another genus. The essence of division, then, is that kindred species be derived from the same genus, just as streams are derived from the same spring and head.

units.la: Quid est species ex aliquo genere contrariorum esse? Non est id quidem dubium, quin species ex eadem animi notione distractae inter se contrariae sint. Nam vna posita, continuo altera e regione occurrit. Itaque quae ex eodem genere, quasi ex altera parte, diuidendo referuntur, simul natura esse dicuntur: neutrum autem prius, aut posterius, ex quo accidit (quemadmodum posterius intelliges) ut quod vni speciei proprie conceditur, id alteri denegatur. Atque haec nimirum illa est διχοτομία[?], siue bipartita sectio, quam veteres tantopere commendarunt, atque in primis Plato: qui in dialogo de Regno statuit, diuisionem aut ad eam paucitatem, aut certe ad quamproximum licebit numerum accommodanda esse. Tametsi Aristoteles saepenumero testetur, rei naturam ferre id non semper posse. Nam (ut superius dictum est) in contrariis saepe intermedia reperiuntur: ut necesse sit, multo plures species duabus exponere.
units.tr: What does it mean for species to belong to a genus of contraries? There is no doubt that species drawn apart from the same notion of the mind are contrary to one another. For once one is posited, the other immediately meets it from the opposite region. Therefore those that are referred to the same genus, as if from the other side, in dividing, are said to be simultaneous in nature; neither is prior or posterior, and so it follows (as you will understand later) that what is properly granted to one species is denied to the other. This is certainly that dichotomy [διχοτομία], or two-part section, which the ancients commended so highly, and Plato above all, who in his dialogue on the Kingdom laid down that division should be adapted to two parts, or at least to as small a number as possible. Yet Aristotle often testifies that the nature of things cannot always allow this. For, as said above, between contraries there are often intermediates, so that it is necessary to set out many more than two species.

units.la: Cedo exemplū. Elementorū aliud est ignis, aliud aqua, aliud aer, aliud terra. Nā duæ priores qualitates è regione inter se adversantur. Ignis enim est calidus & siccus: aqua frigida & humida. at cetera duo ab utroque participant. Sed tamen nullum eorum vel natura, vel tempore prius est: sed omnia natura simul sunt & ortu, & tempore. Philosophia (inquit Cicero) in tres partes est distributa, in naturæ obscuritatem, in differendi subtilitatem, in vitâ atque mores. Bonorum (inquit Aristoteles) alia sunt animi, alia corporis, alia externa. Item: Metallorum aliud est ferrum, aliud aurum, aliud argentū, aliud æs. Bestiarum aliæ sunt volucres, aliæ terrenæ, aliæ natatiles. Nullum horum altero prius est: sed simul natura sunt. Sic Hominum alii sunt magni, ut gigantes: alii breves, ut nani: alii mediocres. Item alii sunt Indi, alii Britanni, quamplurimi interiecti. Colorum alius est albus, alius niger, alius ceruleus, alius ruber, alius viridis, alius purpureus: qui ab utroque adverso participant, & ex aliis permixtis constant.
units.tr: Let me give an example. Of the elements, one is fire, another water, another air, another earth. For the first two qualities are opposed to each other from opposite regions: fire is hot and dry, water cold and moist; but the other two partake of both. Yet none of them is prior either in nature or in time, but all are simultaneous in nature, origin and time. Philosophy, says Cicero, is divided into three parts: the investigation of nature, the subtlety of reasoning, and life and conduct. Of goods, says Aristotle, some are of the soul, some of the body, some external. Likewise: of metals, one is iron, another gold, another silver, another bronze. Of beasts, some are birds, some land animals, some swimmers. None of these is prior to another; they are simultaneous in nature. So too among men, some are large, like giants; some short, like dwarfs; some of middling stature. Likewise some are Indians, some Britons, and very many in between.
