Of colours, one is white, another black, another blue, another red, another green, another purple, which partake of both opposites and are made up of mixtures of others.

units.la: Quid est speciem generi exæquare? Est partem speciei pro specie, id est partem subdivisionis in divisione ponere. veluti, Gallorum alii sunt Aquitani, alii Celtæ, alii Belgæ, alii Hedui. nam Hedui sub Celtarum specie continetur. Item, si quis dicat, Hominum alii sunt liberi, alii servi, alii liberti. Nam liberti species est eius generis, quod est liberi. Ita species suo generi adæquatur. Tria sunt (ait Cicero lib. de Orat. i 1.[?]) genera, quæ in controversiâ cadere possunt:quid sit,quale sit,&quomodo nominetur.Nam illud quod quidā Græci adiungunt, recténe factum sit, totum in eo est,quod quale sit,quæritur. Simile vitium est, cum apud Iurifconsultos Res ita dividuntur, ut aliæ dicantur corporales, aliæ incorporales, aliæ immobiles.vel aliæ mobiles,aliæ immobiles, aliæ incorporales.l.1,§, cum autem sC.de[?] rei vx.act. l.2, & l.3, C. de quad. præscript. quanquam id brevitatis causa fieri intelligitur:ut cum Ulp, ait Conventionum tres esse species: publicas privatas, legitimas, & iurisgentium.l.5,D.de pact.
units.tr: What does it mean to make a species equal to its genus? It means to put a part of a species in place of the species, that is, to put a part of a subdivision in the division. For example: some of the Gauls are Aquitanians, some Celts, some Belgians, some Aedui, for the Aedui are contained under the species of the Celts. Likewise, if someone says: "Some men are free, some slaves, some freedmen," for a freedman is a species of the genus that is "free." So the species is made equal to its genus. Cicero (in book 1 of the De Oratore) says there are three kinds of questions that can arise in dispute: what a thing is, what kind it is, and how it is named. For what some Greeks add, whether it was done rightly, is entirely included in the question of what kind it is. A similar fault occurs when lawyers divide things so that some are called corporeal, some incorporeal, some immovable, or some movable, some immovable, some incorporeal (Dig. 1.§ cum autem; C. de rei vx. act. l. 2 and l. 3; C. de quad. praescript.), although this is understood to be done for brevity's sake, as when Ulpian says there are three species of agreements: public, private, legitimate, and of the law of nations (D. de pact. l. 5).

units.la: Quid est Genus speciei exæquare? Est genus pro specie ponere:id est,in dividendo genere verbum aliquod æquè latum ut genus ipsum, aut etiā latius vsurpare. veluti Liberorū alij sunt ingenui, alij liberti,alij patressa.[?] vel sic: Hominum alij sunt docti,alij indocti,alij philosophi.
units.tr: What does it mean to make a genus equal to its species? It means to put the genus in place of a species: that is, in dividing a genus, to use some word as broad as the genus itself, or even broader. For example: "Some free persons are freeborn, some freed, some patrons." Or thus: "Some men are learned, some unlearned, some philosophers."

units.la: Quomodo paria specierum & generis momenta efficiuntur? Cum neque species ulla præter generis universitatem additur, neque ulla prætermittitur. Nam ut divisio generis universi vim omnem explicare debet, sic etiam nullam omittere. Abesse autem poterit hoc modo: Bonorū alia sunt animi, alia corporis. deest enim tertia species,quæ est fortunæ. Redundabit autem siquis addiderit, Alia externa:vel,Alia naturæ.
units.tr: How are the species and the genus made equal in weight? When no species is added beyond the universality of the genus, and none is omitted. For just as the division of the whole genus ought to explain its entire force, so it should omit nothing. It will be defective in this way: "Some goods are of the soul, some of the body." For a third species is lacking, that of fortune. It will be redundant if someone adds, "some external," or "some of nature."

units.la: CAP. VII. De Partitione Totius.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII. On the Partition of the Whole.

units.la: QVONIAM de Diuisione dixisti, deinceps de Partitione differam. Quid est Partitio? Est Totius in partes vel singulas, vel plerasque distributio. Nā si certę ac finitæ sunt, omnes enumerandæ sunt. At non est vitiosum (ait Cicero) in re infinita nonnihil prætermittere. Scitum est autem illud Platonis in Phædro, cauendū esse in partiendo, ne coquorum imperitorum ritu offa frangantur: cùm artus & membra prius diuidenda sint: actum deinde singulorum membrorum articulos sciungi oporteat.
units.tr: Since you have spoken of division, I shall next take up partition. What is partition? It is the distribution of a whole into either all of its parts or most of them. For if the parts are certain and finite, all of them must be enumerated. Yet, as Cicero says, it is not faulty to leave out something in a matter that is infinite. Plato's remark in the Phaedrus is well known: one must take care in partitioning not to break up the pieces like a clumsy cook carving meat; rather, the limbs and members must first be divided, and only afterwards the joints of each member are to be separated.

units.la: Quænam est ars Partitionis? Eadem fere quæ diuisionis: dummodo partium (vt ante dixi) finitus sit numerus. Itaque quæ notio diuisionem, eadem quoque Partitionem efficit: nimirum differētia: qua quæque pars tanquam certa & propria nota insignitur.
units.tr: What is the art of partition? It is almost the same as that of division, provided the number of parts is finite, as I said before. Therefore the notion that makes a division also makes a partition: namely, the difference by which each part is marked out as a definite and proper note.

units.la: Vnde Partium differentiæ sumuntur? Aliæ ex forma, aliæ ex materia. Ex forma, veluti, domus apud Philosophos partitur in fundamentum, parietes, cōtignationem & tectum. apud Iurisconsultos, tantū in solum & superficiem. Ex materia sic: domus partitur in lapides, trabes, cæmenta, & tegulas. Item, Corpus hominis partitur in caput, pectus, vētrem, & tibias: aut partitur in ossa, carnem, sanguinem & neruos.
units.tr: From what are the differences of the parts taken? Some from form, others from matter. From form, for example: a house is divided by the philosophers into foundation, walls, floors and roof; by the jurists only into ground and surface. From matter, thus: a house is divided into stones, beams, mortar and tiles. Likewise the human body is divided into head, chest, belly and shins, or divided into bones, flesh, blood and sinews.

units.la: Quid interest inter Diuisionem & Partitio nem? Diuisio adhibetur ad genus. Partitio ad totum. Illius differentiæ semper generis nomen retinent. Partes verò totius nomen non retinent. Eorum tamen hoc commune est, quòd & partes diuiduntur in species, & species vicissim in partes : cùm aut illæ generis vim obtinent, aut hæ totius.
units.tr: What is the difference between division and partition? Division is applied to a genus, partition to a whole. The parts of a division always keep the name of the genus; the parts of a whole do not keep the name of the whole. Yet they have this in common: parts are divided into species, and species in turn into parts, since the one either have the force of a genus or the other of a whole.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Sumatur ex eo libello quem hoc ipso Partitionū nomine Cicero appellauit. Nam primo loco Rhetoricam tanquam totum proposuit. tum eius tres fecit partes : vim oratoris, orationem, & quæstionem. deinde vbi ad quæstionem ventum est, eius non partes, sed species distribuit. Quæstio (inquit) alia finita est, alia infinita.
units.tr: Let me give an example. Take it from that little book which Cicero called by this very name of Partitions. For at the first place he set out Rhetoric as a whole, then he made three parts of it: the power of the orator, the speech, and the subject of inquiry. Then, when he came to the subject of inquiry, he distributed not its parts but its species: "One inquiry," he says, "is finite, another infinite."

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplum. Domus partitur in fundamentum, parietes, contignationem, tectum. tectum autem aliud est planum, aliud fastigiatum.
units.tr: Let me give another example. A house is divided into foundation, walls, floors and roof; and the roof is either flat or pitched.

units.la: Sed quæ cautio est ne vel diuisionem pro partitione, vel hanc pro illa vsurpemus? Si distracte partes vniuersi nomen retinent, diuisio est: sin minus, partitio. eiúsque rei exemplum superius in affectione partium ex Dialectica & Memoriæ partitione ostendimus, in naturalem & artificiosam. nunc etiam ex Architecturæ partitione à Vitruuio tradita sumere possumus. non enim dixit aliam esse naturalem, aliam artificiosam. Sed hoc modo: Nascitur ex fabrica & ratiocinatione. Fabrica est continuata usus meditatio, quæ manibus perficitur. Ratiocinatio quæ res fabricatas ratione proportionis demonstrat. Sic Ariftoteles in Politicis scribit, Mercaturæ tres esse partes, non species: navigationem, invectionem,& negotiationem.
units.tr: But what caution is there lest we use division for partition, or partition for division? If the parts when separated keep the name of the whole, it is division; if not, it is partition. We showed an example of this above in the affections of the parts, from the partition of Dialectic and of Memory into natural and artificial. Now we may also take one from the partition of architecture handed down by Vitruvius. For he did not say that one kind is natural and another artificial; rather he put it this way: it arises from building and reasoning. Building is the continued practice of thought which is carried out by the hands; reasoning is that which demonstrates the made things by the rule of proportion. So Aristotle in the Politics writes that trade has three parts, not species: navigation, importing, and selling.

units.la: Quoniam divisionis & partitionis præceptâ expositi, velim eius distributionis rationem exponas, qua principio huius artis in Dialectica partiêda es usus. Id verò superiùs in Methodo exponenda præstitimus, cùm artis huius Analysin; & quasi operis totius formam, & definitionê propositimus: & ratiocinatorum similitudine usi sumus. Sed quoniam plerique divisionem & definitionem nō summas Dialecticæ artis partes constituunt, sed quasi Partium subdivisionem faciunt, neque de iis nisi cùm ad argumentorum locos ventum est disputant: quasi argumentationis tantūm partes essent (quod non immerito quifpiam à Cicerone in Topicis factum existimaret) confirmandum est, divisionem & definitionem argumentationis partes propterea dici non posse, quoniam & per hanc, illæ duæ probátur: & per illas duas, hæc tractatur. To-tum autem neque ad partes confirmandas adhibetur, neque partes ad Totum tractandum, sed tertium quippiam extrinsecus assumptû. Quod cùm ita sit, perspicuum est, tres illas effe pari feré momento Dialecticæ artis partes: ac falsò duas illas huius tertiæ partes numerari. Sed quod de illarum mutua probatione & tractatione breuiter attigi, deinceps cùm eò ventum erit planius dabitur exponendi locus.
units.tr: Since you have explained the rules of division and partition, I should like you to set out the method of distribution by which you used, at the beginning of this art, to partition Dialectic. I did indeed take care to explain this earlier, in the exposition of Method, when I set out the analysis of this art and, as it were, the form of the whole work, and the definition; and I made use of the likeness of reasoned arguments. But since most men do not make division and definition the chief parts of the art of Dialectic, but treat them as a sort of subdivision of the parts, and discuss them only when they come to the places of arguments, as if they were merely parts of argumentation (which, not unreasonably, someone might think Cicero did in the Topics), it must be maintained that division and definition cannot be called parts of argumentation, since both are proved through it and those two prove it; and the whole is neither used to confirm the parts nor the parts to treat the whole, but something third, assumed from outside. Since this is so, it is plain that those three are parts of Dialectic of almost equal weight, and that those two are falsely counted as parts of this third. But what I have touched on briefly about their mutual proof and treatment, the place for explaining it more fully will be given when we come to it.

units.la: Quid verò? Cuiusmodi peruulgatam illam Dialecticæ partitionem esse censes, cùm ita distribuitur: Dialecticæ partes duæ sunt, inuentio & dispositio? Vitium huius partitionis perspicuum est in eo, quod pars subpartitionis in partitione ponitur. nam cùm veteres (in his Cicero) hanc distributionem posuerunt, nequaquam summam artis totius partitionem esse voluerunt: sed quartæ partis, quæ Argumentatio est, subpartitionem: quod postea dilucidius intelliges.
units.tr: And what? What do you think of that commonly received partition of Dialectic, when it is distributed thus: the parts of Dialectic are two, invention and arrangement? The fault in this partition is plain, in that a subpartition is put in the partition: for when the ancients (Cicero among them) set out this distribution, they did not at all mean it to be the partition of the whole art, but the subpartition of the fourth part, which is Argumentation; as you will understand more clearly later.

units.la: De vocabulis Definitionis & Enuntiationis.
units.tr: On the terms of Definition and Enunciation.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: UID [?] sequitur nunc? Vt de Enuntiatione & Definitione dicamus: quarum, si vocabuli notionem spectemus [?], par eadémque vis, natura, & ratio est. Quanquam enim omnis definitio enuntiatio est, tamen ea demum enuntiatio hoc proprio definitionis nomine signata est, quæ inter Enuntiationes principatum obtinet. propterea autem princeps & Regina Enuntiationum omnium definitio est, quia sola veram propriámque reciprocationem & conuersionem recipit, cū cetera aut non recipiāt omnino, aut impropriam & abusiuam recipiant. quemadmodum posterius ex conuerfionum disciplina cognosces. Itaque vt iustitia est virtus,quæ suum cuique tribuit:ita virtus quæ suum cuique tribuit,est iustitia.
units.tr: What follows now? Let us speak of enunciation and definition. If we consider the meaning of the words, they have the same force, nature and reason. For although every definition is an enunciation, only that enunciation which holds the first place among enunciations is marked with the proper name of definition. Definition is therefore the prince and queen of all enunciations, because it alone admits a true and proper reciprocation and conversion, whereas the others either admit none at all or admit only an improper and abusive one, as you will learn later from the doctrine of conversions. Thus, as justice is the virtue that gives each their due, so the virtue that gives each their due is justice.

units.la: Quid est Enuntiatio? Enuntiatio generali nomine est oratio, quæ aliud de alio quoquomodo pronuntiat: siue indicandi modo: veluti, Titius est heres meus: siue imperandi, Titius heres meus esto: siue optandi, Vtinam Titius hæres meus effet: siue coniungendi, si Titius heres meus fit. Itaque nullæ in hominum vita verius hoc nomine appellãdæ sunt, quàm quæ legum scita & sanctiones continent. veluti, Salus populi suprema lex esto. Periurij pœna diuina, exitium: humana, dedecus esto.
units.tr: What is an enunciation? In general terms, an enunciation is a speech which affirms something of something in some way: in the indicative mood, for example, "Titius is my heir"; in the imperative, "Let Titius be my heir"; in the optative, "Would that Titius were my heir"; or in the subjunctive, "if Titius becomes my heir." Hence no utterances in human life are more truly called by this name than those which contain the decrees and sanctions of laws, for example: "Let the safety of the people be the supreme law." "Let the penalty for perjury be divine destruction, and human disgrace."

units.la: Quod eodem modo de regulis & præceptis artium intelligēdum est, quæ Græci ἀξιώματα [?] nominant. veluti, Omnes anguli recti inter se sunt æquales. Quæ tertio alicui paria sunt, etiam inter se paria sunt. Si æqualibus addantur æqualia, omnia erunt æqualia. Si æqualibus detrahantur æqualia, reliqua erunt æqualia. sed alia est Enuntiatio communis, alia dialectica.
units.tr: The same must be understood of the rules and precepts of the arts, which the Greeks call axioms [ἀξιώματα]. For example: "All right angles are equal to one another." "Things that are equal to a third thing are also equal to one another." "If equals are added to equals, the wholes are equal." "If equals are taken from equals, the remainders are equal." But one enunciation is common, another dialectical.

units.la: Quæ est Enuntiatio Dialectica? Est oratio quæ aliud de alio pronuntians, verù falsumve aliquid complectitur. nam (vt Cicero in Lucullo scribit) fundamentum omnis Dialecticæ est, quicquid enuntietur aut verum esse, autfalsum. veluti, Voluptas est bonum, Voluptas est malum. Virtus sola expetenda est. Dolor est summum malum. Itaque ex multis Enuntiationum modis nulla est ad difputandum & conclusiones componendas apta, nisi quæ indicandi modo concepta est. Hæc enim sola verũ falsũmve aliquid pronuntiat. Idque intelligi licet primùm ex illa Dialecticorum consuetudine, de qua superiùs diximus: vt in circulis & conuentu ponerent, qua de re difputari vellent. veluti, Malum mihi videtur esse mors. Voluptas mihi videtur esse fummũ bonum. deinde ex eo quòd Syllogismi quibus cõcludendæ rationis artificium continetur, nullis aliis Enuntiationibus cõsici & exponi possunt, nisi quæ indicandi modo conceptæ sunt.
units.tr: What is a dialectical enunciation? It is a speech which affirms one thing of another and embraces something either true or false. For (as Cicero writes in the Lucullus) the foundation of all dialectic is that whatever is enunciated is either true or false. For example: "Pleasure is a good." "Pleasure is an evil." "Virtue alone is to be sought." "Pain is the greatest evil." Thus, of the many modes of enunciation, none is fit for disputing and composing conclusions except the one cast in the indicative mood. Only this mood states something true or false. This may be understood first from the custom of the dialecticians mentioned above, that in their circles and assemblies they would set forth the matter they wished to dispute: for example, "Death seems to me to be an evil," "Pleasure seems to me to be the highest good." Second, it may be understood from the fact that syllogisms, by which the art of concluding reasoning is contained, can be formed and expounded by no enunciations except those cast in the indicative mood.

units.la: Positiones autem illas, hoc est sententias quæ ad difputandũ positæ θέσεως[?] appellátur à Græcis, definitionis nomine appellari superiùs ex aliquot Ciceronis locis probauimus.
units.tr: Those positions, that is, opinions laid down for disputation, which the Greeks call theses [θέσεως], we proved above from several passages of Cicero to be called by the name of definition.

units.la: Etde regulis, quodnam habes testimonium? Extat in Cluetiana Ciceronis apertissimum, vbi quam vulgo Regulam dicimus, Definitionis nomine perspicuè appellat. Denique (inquit) illa definitio iudiciorum quæ nobis à maioribus tradita est, retineatur, vt in iudiciis & fine inuidia culpa plectatur, & fine culpa inuidia ponatur. Item in Lucullo, cùm ita scripsit: Fundamentum Dialecticæ est, quicquid enuntiatur aut verum esse, aut falsum: paucis versibus interiectis sic infert: Vbi est illa definitio, Effatum esse id, quod aut verum, aut sal-. sum est? Hinc illud vulgatum apud Iurisconsultos: Omnis in iure definitio periculosa est: quod iidem Grecè sic convertunt πᾶς μορικὸς λόγος ἀκριβὴς σαφῶς ἔστιν[?]. Eodemque pertinet, quod ἀφοριστικοὶ[?] Graeci artium summa praecepta & regulas appellant: cùm Galenus ἀφοριστικὸν definiat, ὅπερ διὰ βραχυτάτων τῶν ἀπαντῶν τὰ τῶν πραγμάτων ἰδία ἀφορίζει[?].
units.tr: And for rules, what testimony do you have? There is a very clear one in Cicero's Pro Cluentio, where he calls by the name of definition what we commonly call a rule: "Finally," he says, "let that definition of judgments handed down to us by our ancestors be retained: that in trials a fault is punished without hatred, and hatred is not imposed without fault." Likewise in the Lucullus, when he wrote, "The foundation of dialectic is that whatever is enunciated is either true or false," he then infers a few lines later: "Where is that definition, that an utterance is what is either true or false?" Hence the common saying among jurisconsults, "Every definition in law is dangerous," which they render in Greek thus: [πᾶς μορικὸς λόγος ἀκριβὴς σαφῶς ἔστιν]. To the same point belongs the fact that the Greeks call the highest precepts and rules of the arts [ἀφοριστικοὶ], aphoristic, since Galen defines the aphoristic as [ὅπερ διὰ βραχυτάτων τῶν ἀπαντῶν τὰ τῶν πραγμάτων ἰδία ἀφορίζει], that which by the briefest statements marks off the particular features of things; and he uses the word [ἀφοριστικὸν] for it.

units.la: De Subiecto & Attributo. CAP. IX.
units.tr: On Subject and Predicate. CHAP. IX.

units.la: X quibus constat Enuntiatio? Ex iisdem partibus, ex quibus à Grammaticis dicitur oratio cōstare: sed quæ minima est, aut ex nomine & verbo, ut Socrates ambulat: aut ex duobus nominibus, & verbo inter ea interiecto, ut Homo est beatus. Homo est miser. Mors est terribilis. Mors est expetenda. Enuntiationem autem Peripatetici ἀπόφανσιν[?], Stoici ἀξίωμα, nonnulli ἐπαγγελίαν appellárunt: propterea quòd mentis interpres & quasi internuntia quædam est oratio.
units.tr: What are the constituents of a proposition? The same parts out of which grammarians say speech is made up. The smallest proposition consists either of a noun and a verb, as "Socrates walks," or of two nouns with a verb placed between them, as "Man is happy," "Man is wretched," "Death is terrible," "Death is to be desired." The Peripatetics called the proposition apophansis [ἀπόφανσιν], the Stoics axioma [ἀξίωμα], and some epangelia [ἐπαγγελίαν], because speech is the interpreter of the mind and, as it were, a kind of messenger.

units.la: Quomodo definitur ἀξίωμα? Graeci (inquit Gellius) ita definiunt: λεκτὸν αὐτοτελὲς ὅπερ φαντὸν ἔσον ἐφ' ἑαυτῷ: id est, dictum per se constans, & quantum in ipso est, enuntians. Quam definitionem Chrysippo Laertius in vita Zenonis attribuit. Cicero modò Effatum, modò Enuntiationem, modò Pronuntiatum, modò etiam Pronuntiationem appellat. M. Var-roro modò profatum, modò proloquium: atque ita definit: Proloquium est sententia in qua nihil desideratur. ut, Cæsar Tyrannidé occupauit. Scipio Numantiā deleuit. Aristoteles autem hoc modo: Quæ aliquid vel ait, vel negat, pro ratione & varietate temporum: id est, provt tempora distincta sunt. Affirmat enim aut negat, aliquid vel esse, vel fuisse, vel futurū esse.
units.tr: How is axioma defined? The Greeks (says Gellius) define it thus: a thing said that is complete in itself, which states what it states as far as it lies in itself [λεκτὸν αὐτοτελὲς ὅπερ φαντὸν ἔσον ἐφ' ἑαυτῷ]: that is, a statement that stands on its own and, so far as it is concerned, asserts something. Laertius attributes this definition to Chrysippus in the life of Zeno. Cicero calls it now effatum, now enuntiatio, now pronuntiatum, and now also pronuntiatio. Varro calls it now profatum, now proloquium, and defines it thus: a proloquium is a sentence in which nothing is lacking, as "Caesar seized the tyranny," "Scipio destroyed Numantia." Aristotle defines it in this way: that which either affirms or denies something, according to the reckoning and variety of times; that is, as the times are distinguished. For it affirms or denies that something either is, or was, or will be.

units.la: De vtra igitur definitione prius dicemus? De Enuntiatione: idque duabus de caussis. primùm quoniā (vt paulò ante posui) Dialecticorum ratio ita ferebat, vt primo loco sententia disputabilis proponeretur: tum vt eius sententiæ vtraque pars definiendo aperiretur: deinde quia definitio Enuntiatione,id est oratione perfecta conficitur.
units.tr: Which of these definitions shall we discuss first? The proposition, and for two reasons. First, because (as I set out a little above) the method of the dialecticians required that a disputable statement be put forward first, and then that both parts of that statement be opened up by definition. Second, because definition is made by means of the proposition, that is, by a complete sentence.

units.la: Quot sunt partes Enuntiationis? Duę.Inferior, de qua aliquid dicitur, & superior, quæ de alio dicitur. Illam Græci ὑποκείμενον[?], Latini subiectū appellant: hanc κατηγορούμενον[?], id est attributum. neque vlla Enūtiatio est, quæ pluribus constet partibus. qua de causa, ὅρος[?], id est termini, vel extrema dicūtur: quorū illud minus appellatur, hoc maius. Subiectū est dictio, cui altera impositā conuenire aut non conuenire dicitur. Attributum, dictio quæ alteri imposita conuenire, vel non conuenire dicitur. Κατηγορούμενον[?] autem hoc appellatur, quoniam (vt superiùs diximus) quicquid de altero dicitur, enuntiatur, prædicatur, id totum ex Categoriarū ordinibus sumitur. Veluti, virtus est expetenda. Voluptas fugienda est.
units.tr: What are the parts of a proposition? Two: the lower, of which something is said, and the upper, which is said of another. The Greeks call the former hypokeimenon [ὑποκείμενον], the Latins subiectum; the latter katēgoroumenon [κατηγορούμενον], that is, attributum. And there is no proposition that consists of more parts. For this reason the terms, which are called horoi [ὅρος], that is, termini, or extremes, are so named: of these, the former is called the lesser and the latter the greater. The subject is the term to which another term, placed upon it, is said to agree or not to agree. The predicate is the term which, placed upon another, is said to agree or not to agree. The latter is called katēgoroumenon because (as we said above) whatever is said of another is predicated or asserted, and that whole idea is taken from the orders of the Categories. For example: virtue is to be desired; pleasure is to be avoided.

units.la: Quid? Suntné igitur Enuntiationis partes substantiuū & adiectiuum? Sunt, qui hoc affirment, ac statuant, nihil apud Dialecticos aliud esse Subiectum & Attributum, quàm apud Grammaticos Substantiuum & Adiectiuum. quod sanè cuiusmodi fit, cōiectura assequi non possum. Sepè enim vel ex duobus substantiis, vel ex duobus adiectiuis enūtiatio conficitur. veluti, Iustitia est virtus. Laudabile est expeten-dum. Platanus est arbor. Expetendum est honestum.
units.tr: What then? Are the parts of a proposition the substantive and the adjective? Some affirm this and maintain that among the dialecticians subject and predicate are nothing other than what the grammarians call substantive and adjective. What sort of thing this is, I cannot grasp by conjecture. For a proposition is often made up of two substantives, or of two adjectives. For example: "Justice is a virtue"; "The praiseworthy is to be desired"; "The plane tree is a tree"; "The honourable is to be desired."

units.la: Quid igitur proprie Subiectum appellas? Nomen habitum significans, cui aliud quodpiam in oratione imponitur: quasi cùm in structura lapis lapidi superiniicitur. Ars enim Dialecticorū tota in eo (vt sæpe iam diximus) occupata est, vt quod cuique verbum alteriapte & conuenienter imponi possit, demōstret: quasi si verborum aceruus construatur. vnde frequetissimè Stoicorum disputationes Graecè σωρίτες[?], Latinè Aceruales (vt posteriùs intelliges) appellatæ sunt. veluti, Quod bonum est, expetendum est. quod expetendum, placens. quod placens, diligendum. quod diligendum, probandum. quod probandum, laudabile. quod laudabile, honestum. ergo quod bonum est, id etiam honestū est. Hic septem sunt Enuntiationes, in quibus quod in priore attributum fuerat, id in posteriore subiectū est.
units.tr: What then do you properly call the subject? A noun signifying a possession (habitus) to which something else is added in the sentence, as when in building one stone is laid upon another. For the whole art of the dialecticians is occupied with this (as I have often said already): to show which word may be placed with which other word aptly and suitably, as if a heap of words were built up. Hence the very frequent arguments of the Stoics were called in Greek sōrites [σωρίτες], in Latin acervales (as you will understand later). For example: What is good is to be desired. What is to be desired is pleasing. What is pleasing is to be loved. What is to be loved is to be approved. What is to be approved is praiseworthy. What is praiseworthy is honourable. Therefore what is good is also honourable. Here there are seven propositions, in each of which what was the predicate in the former is the subject in the latter.

units.la: Quid appellas Nomen habitum significās? Quod subiectam rem aliquam completitur, ac priuatio non est. Priuationis autem illę notæ sunt, nihil,nemo,nullus. Nam cùm ex negatione nihil constituitur, quæ ex eiusmodi nominibus Enuntiationes conceptæ sunt,necefsario in affirmationē conuertendæ sunt: veluti, Nemo est iustior Aristide. Aristides iustior est omnibus. Omnia nemo potest. Vnus omnia efficere non potest. Nihil diuturnum est,in quo est aliquid extremum. Omne in quo est aliquid extremum, non est diuturnum. Nemo potest non beatus esse, qui totus aptus est ex sese. Omnis qui totus aptus est ex sese,necessarió est beatus. Nihil est dulcius otio literato. Otium literatum omnibus rebus est dulcius. Sed hac de re postea commodior incidet differendi locus.
units.tr: What do you mean by "a noun signifying a possession"? One that completes some subject thing and is not a privation. The marks of privation are nothing, no one, none. For when something is constituted by a negation, the propositions formed from such nouns must necessarily be converted into affirmations. For example: No one is more just than Aristides; Aristides is more just than all. No one can do everything; one alone cannot do everything. Nothing that has an end is lasting; whatever has an end is not lasting. No one who is wholly fitted out of himself can fail to be happy; everyone who is wholly fitted out of himself is necessarily happy. Nothing is sweeter than literary leisure; literary leisure is sweeter than all things. But a more suitable place for discussing this matter will come up later.

units.la: Quid appellas Attributum? Idem prorsus, quod subiectum.nomen per quod habitus,nō priuatio,significatur. Non enim notione & definitione differūt: sed ordine, & situ: quoniam alterum subiectum, alterum impositum est. Itaque sæpè ( vt modò dixi ) quod in prima Enuntiatione attributum est, id in secunda est subiectum. Quòd si nomine tantùm & verbo immutatio cóstet,veluti, Socrates philosophatur,Aristoteles disputat, tum ex vi & notione verbo nomen cum verbo ES T perspicuitatis causa est exprimendum: atque ita resoluendum:Socrates est Philosophus, Aristoteles est disputans: Veritas odium parit : Veritas odij causa est. Cæsar vicit Pompeium: Cæsar fuit victor Pompeij.
units.tr: What do you call the predicate? Exactly the same as the subject: a noun through which a possession, not a privation, is signified. For they do not differ in notion and definition, but in order and position, since the one is the subject and the other is placed upon it. So often (as I have just said) what is the predicate in the first proposition is the subject in the second. But if the change consists only of a noun and a verb, as "Socrates philosophises," "Aristotle disputes," then for the sake of clarity the noun, by its force and meaning, must be expressed together with the verb "is" and resolved thus: Socrates is a philosopher; Aristotle is disputing. "Truth produces hatred": truth is the cause of hatred. "Caesar conquered Pompey": Caesar was the victor over Pompey.

units.la: Quid igitur de iis quæ de futuro aliquid dicunt, deque eo quod possit fieri, aut non possit: de quibus Cicero in libro de Fato quæstionem logicæ artis obscurissimam esse scribit? Sanè disputari posset, non verè & proprie illas Enuntiationes esse. primùm quia non sunt habitus: deinde quia Medij, quod est quasi norma diiudicandæ conuenientiæ inter subiectũ & attributum, de quo in Argumentationibus intelliges: adhiberi ad ea quæ non sunt, non potest. Sed quoniam rerũ naturalium certus quidam ordo est à Deo constitutus, cuius propterea certus videtur euétus, vt in Solis & Lunæ defectionibus, quarum causæ naturales sunt: propterea satius est, illas Philosophorum argutias non attingere,
units.tr: What then about those propositions which say something about the future, and about what can or cannot happen? Cicero, in his book on Fate, writes that this question is the most obscure in the art of logic. One could certainly argue that these are not true and proper propositions. First, because they do not signify a possession; then because the middle term, which is as it were the norm for judging the agreement between subject and predicate (as you will understand in the treatment of arguments), cannot be applied to things that do not yet exist. But since there is a certain fixed order of natural things established by God, whose outcome therefore seems certain, as in eclipses of the sun and moon, whose causes are natural, it is better not to touch those subtleties of the philosophers.

units.la: Diuisio Enuntiationum. CAP. X.
units.tr: Division of Propositions. CHAP. X.

units.la: VOTVPLEX[?] est Enuntiatio? Duplex. Vna quæ est simplex, quâ Græci ti[?] κατηγορικῶ[?] vocant: altera copulata, quâ iidem συνθετικῶ[?] appellant.
units.tr: How many kinds of proposition are there? Two. One is simple, which the Greeks call categorical [κατηγορικῶς]; the other is compound, which they call synthetic [συνθετικῶς].

units.la: Quæ est Simplex? Quæ de uno tantùm, idque purè & absolutè vel affirmat, vel negat. vt Iuti, Mors est horribilis, mors non est horribilis, Filius heres esto. Filius exheres esto.
units.tr: What is a simple proposition? One that affirms or denies something, purely and absolutely, of one thing only: for example, "Death is terrible," "Death is not terrible," "Let the son be heir," "Let the son be disinherited."

units.la: Quæ est prima diuisio simplicis Enuntiationis? Vt alia sit affirmatiua, quæ vnum aliquid & de vno affirmat.vt, Olor est cādidus. altera negatiua, quæ vnū aliquid & de vnonegat. vt Coruus non est candidus. Qua in diuisione quanta vis sit, veteris poetæ versus ostendunt,quos propter elegantiam proferemus.
units.tr: What is the first division of simple propositions? Some are affirmative, which affirm one thing of one thing, for example, "The swan is white." Others are negative, which deny one thing of one thing, for example, "The raven is not white." The force of this division is shown by the verses of an old poet, which we quote for their elegance.

units.la: Est & non cunctis monosyllaba nota frequentant. His deptis,nihil est hominum quod sermo volutet. Omnia in his,& ab his sunt omnia:siue negoti, Siue oti quicquam est.seu turbe,siue quietis. Si consentitur,mora nulla interuenit Est Est. Si controuersa est dissensio subiiciet Non.
units.tr: "Yes and no, the monosyllables that all know, are the words everyone uses. With these said, there is nothing men's talk turns over. In these, and from these, are all things, whether of business or of leisure, whether of tumult or of quiet. If there is agreement, no delay intervenes: Yes, yes. If the dispute is contested, it will bring in No."

units.la: Quæ est secunda Diuisio? Vt alia sit vniuersalis,alia particularis,alia indefinita, alia singularis.
units.tr: What is the second division? Some propositions are universal, some particular, some indefinite, and some singular.

units.la: Quæ est vniuersalis? Quæ de omni subiecto ait quid,aut negat. Itaque notæ ipsius hæ sunt:Omnis,nullus:semper,nunquam.veluti, Omnis coruus est niger.Nullus coruus est candidus.Semper verum dicendum est. Nunquā boni viri est mentiri.Omnia sunt hominum tenui pendentia filo. Græci autem notas illas modò συγκατηγορήματα[?] nominant, quia sine adiunctione nihil significat:modò ἀποδιορίσματα[?], quia quemadmodum attributum subiecto cóueniat,definiunt,ac demonstrant.
units.tr: What is a universal proposition? One that says something, or denies something, of every subject. Its signs are therefore: all, none; always, never. For example, "Every raven is black," "No raven is white," "One must always tell the truth," "It is never the part of a good man to lie," "All things of men hang by a slender thread." The Greeks call these signs sometimes συγκατηγορήματα [predicate-signs], because they signify nothing without an addition, and sometimes ἀποδιορίσματα [determinations], because they define and show how the attribute belongs to the subject.

units.la: Quodnam huius firmamentum ac præceptum est? Vt vera sit vniuersalis, necesse est singulas eius partes esse veras.vt eadem falsa sit,satis est vnicam ipsius partem esse falsam. veluti:Omnes apes sunt aculeatæ.Solus rex aculei expers , falsam enuntiationem efficit. Titius heres esto, si omnes mei liberi impuberes decesserint. Unus pubes decessit, Titius heres non erit. Id accidit (inquit Iulianus) quia significatio, id est, enuntiatio. ἀπόφανσις[?], fumitur ex universo: in qua si aliquid falsum est, totam enuntiationem falsam efficit. l. si is qui, 13, D. de reb. dub. Et hinc natum est proverbium, Qui omne dicit, nihil excipit. l. testatorem, 68. D. de legat. 3.
units.tr: What is the rule and principle for this? For a universal to be true, every one of its parts must be true; for it to be false, it is enough that one part of it be false. For example: "All bees have stings" is a false proposition, because the one king bee lacks a sting. "Titius shall be heir if all my children die without reaching puberty. One child reached puberty and died; Titius will not be heir." This happens, says Julian, because the meaning, that is the proposition [ἀπόφανσις], is taken from the universal; if anything in it is false, it makes the whole proposition false (law "si is qui," D. de reb. dub., 13). Hence the proverb arose: "He who says everything excepts nothing" (law "testatorem," D. de legat. 3, 68).

units.la: Quæ est Particularis? Quæ de subiecti parte ait quid, aut negat. Itaque notæ ipsius hæ sunt: Aliquis, quidam, non omnis, interdum, aliquādo, nonnunquam. vt Quidam homines sunt Gigantes, nonnulli, pumiliones. Vt non omne vinum, sic non omnis natura vetustate coacescit. Boni viri est aliquando mentiri. Aliqua pecunia soluta non est.
units.tr: What is a particular proposition? One that says something, or denies something, of part of the subject. Its signs are: some, certain, not all, sometimes, at times, now and then. For example, "Certain men are giants, some are dwarfs." "As not all wine, so not every nature sours with age." "It is sometimes the part of a good man to lie." "Some money has not been paid."

units.la: Quodnam huius firmamentū est? Vt particularis vera fit, satis est vel singularem esse veram: vt eadem falsa fit, necesse est singulas esse falsas. veluti: Quidā homines sunt sapientes. Solus Socrates veram orationem efficiet, quoniam, (vt Iulianus ait) cùm significatio id est, ἀπόφανσις[?], enuntiatio, non ex universo, sed ex aliquo sumitur, si veri aliquid inde fit, verā efficit totam orationem. d.l. si is qui, D. de reb. dub. at falsum esse non potest, nisi homines nulli sint sapientes.
units.tr: What is the rule for this? For a particular to be true, it is enough that even a single instance be true; for it to be false, every instance must be false. For example: "Some men are wise." Socrates alone makes this true, since (as Julian says) when the meaning, that is the proposition [ἀπόφανσις], is taken not from the whole but from some part, if something true follows from it, it makes the whole statement true (the same law, D. de reb. dub.). But it cannot be false unless no men are wise.

units.la: Quæ est Indefinita? Quæ nulla vel totius, vel partis adiunêta nota, de subiecto aliquid vel affirmat,vel negat.ut, Voluptas est bonum. Dolor est malum. Pecunia soluta non est. Hæc autem in necessariis idem quod universalis valet:ut,Homo est doctrinæ capax.Idem enim valet acsi additum esset, Omnis.At in fortuitis idem valet,quod particularis: quoniam ut ea vera sit, satis est veram esse particularem. veluti, Homo deambulat.Satis est enim si Socrates deambulet. Unde ioculare illud Aesopi,qui iussus ab hero lentem coquere,granum lentis unicum coxit. Notam autem appellamus etiam circumstantiam aut loci, aut persone,aut téporis. nam(ut ait Aristeles libro Topicorum fecundo extremo ) τὸ ἁπλῶς Θεῖον [?] μηδ' ἑνὸς ὁμοίως Θεῖος ἐρεῖς [?] id esse indefinitè & omnino dicitur,quod sine circunstantie adiectione dicitur.veluti,Colere religionem, honestū est, etiam loco nullo designato. At parentem immolare,honestum esse,indefinitè non dicitur:quamuis apud Tribalos laudi & gloriæ ducatur.
units.tr: What is an indefinite proposition? One that, with no sign of the whole or of a part attached, affirms or denies something of the subject: "Pleasure is good," "Pain is evil," "Money is not paid." In necessary matters an indefinite has the same force as a universal, as in "Man is capable of learning," for it is as if "all" had been added. In contingent matters it has the same force as a particular, since for it to be true it is enough that it be true of some: for example, "A man walks," for it is enough if Socrates walks. Hence Aesop's joke, of the man who, ordered by his master to cook lentils, cooked a single lentil. We also call a circumstance of place, person or time a sign. For, as Aristotle says at the end of the second book of the Topics, what is said without the addition of any circumstance is said indefinitely and absolutely. For example, "To worship religion is honourable," even with no place specified. But "To sacrifice a parent is honourable" is not said indefinitely, although among the Tribali it is counted praise and glory.

units.la: Cedomihi coniunctum aliquod indefinite & particularis exemplum: ut illarum usum dispiciam. Veluti,si convenerit ut sors annua bima trima die soluatur. deinde adiecta pactio sit,utnisi pecunia sua quaque die soluatur,pignus vendere liceat. vel,Si qua pecunia sua die non soluatur. Nam inter illas hoc interest,quòd in illa vox Pecunia, indefinitè positā enuntiationem efficit universalem: ut de summa universa intelligatur. in hac pronomé QUÆ[?] definitè propriéq; positum enuntiationem efficit particularem:ut de partibus fingulis intelligatur.l.fi necessarias,8,ʃ.fi annua,D. de pignerat.a&.
units.tr: Let me add a connected example of an indefinite and a particular, so that I may examine their use. Suppose it has been agreed that a yearly sum is to be paid within two or three days, and a condition is then added that, unless the money is paid on each day, it shall be lawful to sell the pledge; or, "If any money is not paid on its day." The difference between these is this: in the first, the word "money" used indefinitely makes the proposition universal, so that it is understood of the whole sum; in the second, the pronoun QUÆ, placed definitely and specifically, makes the proposition particular, so that it is understood of the single parts (law "si necessarias," 8, and law "si annua," D. de pignerat. act.).

units.la: Quodnam huius est firmamentum? Ut vera fit indefinita, fatis est veram esse particularem. Ut eadem falsa fit, necesse est singulas esse falsas.veluti: Heres meus damnas esto dare aureos quinq;. Plures instituti sunt. fi unus dederit,satisfiet testatori. neque illi non fatisfiet,nisi nemo omnium dederit. l. fi pluribus, 44,D.de legat.2.l.fi plures,98,deleg.3.
units.tr: What is the rule for this? For an indefinite to be true, it is enough that a particular be true; for it to be false, each of its singular instances must be false. For example: "My heir shall be bound to give five gold pieces." Several are appointed. If one of them gives, the testator is satisfied; nor is he unsatisfied unless none of them gives (law "si pluribus," 44, D. de legat. 2; law "si plures," 98, D. de legat. 3).

units.la: Quæ est singularis? Quæ defingulari,fiue indiuiduo ait quid,aut negat. ut,Aristides est iustus. Phalaris fuit Tyrannus. Quantū unus heres habebit, tantum Ti-thafo dari volo. Sæpè tamen singularis pro uniuersali usurpatur. ut,Quantum heres meus habebit,tantum Tithafo dari volo:id est,quantum omnes. l.fi ita reliétum, 43, D. de legat. 2. Item, Heres meus damnas esto dare aureos quinque. Omnes dānati sunt.l. fi plurib. 44,eod.l. fi plures,98.D. de legat.3.
units.tr: What is a singular proposition? One that says something, or denies something, of an individual or single thing: "Aristides is just," "Phalaris was a tyrant," "As much as one heir shall have, I want the same given to Titius." Yet a singular is often used for a universal, as in "As much as my heir shall have, I want given to Titius," that is, as much as all of them. Likewise, "My heir shall be bound to give five gold pieces. All are condemned" (law "si ita relictum," 43, D. de legat. 2; law "si plures," 44, eod.; law "si plures," 98, D. de legat. 3).

units.la: Quod est huius firmamentum? Ut singularis vera aut falsa fit, fatis est indiuiduū ipsum quo de agitur verū aut falsum esse. in quo dubitandi caussa nulla est.
units.tr: What is the rule for this? For a singular proposition to be true or false, it is enough that the individual it concerns be true or false. There is no room for doubt in this.

units.la: Quæ est Tertia diuisio? Ut alia fit Enuntiatio necessaria,alia contingens, alia impofsibilis.vel hoc modo,Alia necessariò vera,quædam necessariò falsa,quædam fortuita.
units.tr: What is the third division? Some propositions are necessary, some contingent, and some impossible. Or in this way: some are necessarily true, some necessarily false, and some fortuitous.

units.la: Quæ est Necessaria? Cuius subiectum & attributum ita inter se necessariò cohærent, vt disiungi non possint.veluti,Nemo pogeft[?] non beatissimus esse,qui totus aptus est ex sese.Necesse est ligneam materiam vri flamma. necesse est hominem aliquo tempore interire.
units.tr: What is a necessary proposition? One whose subject and attribute cohere with each other so necessarily that they cannot be separated. For example: "No one can fail to be most blessed who is wholly fitted from himself." "Wooden matter must burn in flame." "Man must die at some time."

units.la: Quæ est Impossibilis? Cuius extrema itä inter se abhorrét, vt cóiungi nisi absurdè non possint: veluti,Arbor est Platanus: Pariesest domus. Homo digito cœlum attigit. Ignis est frigidus.nã cùm aut inferiora de superiorib*, aut dissentanea de dislentaneis dicuntur,tum absurda & impossibilis enuntiatio nascitur.
units.tr: What is an impossible proposition? One whose extremes so repel each other that they cannot be joined except absurdly: for example, "A tree is a plane tree," "A wall is a house," "A man touched heaven with his finger," "Fire is cold." For when lower things are predicated of higher, or discordant things of discordant, an absurd and impossible proposition arises.

units.la: Quæ est Contingés? Cuius extrema ita inter se affecta sunt,vt casu & coniungi,& difiungi possint. itaq; à Græcis ἐνδεχόμενα[?] nominātur:veluti,Figulus inuidet figulo. Iracúdus accepta cótumelia cómouetur. Maior pars vincit meliorem. Mulier prægnans tres pariet.nã in ventre, incerta re,terni concepti numerantur.l.sed & si,28,s.vlt.D.de iudic.Sed in argumentorum tractatione planius hæc intelligentur.
units.tr: What is a contingent proposition? One whose extremes are so disposed that by chance they can both be joined and separated. Hence the Greeks call them ἐνδεχόμενα [things that may be]: for example, "A potter envies a potter," "An angry man is moved when insulted," "The greater part overcomes the better," "A pregnant woman will bear three." For in the womb, while the outcome is uncertain, three conceptions are counted (law "sed et si," 28, s. vlt., D. de iudic.). But these will be explained more clearly in the treatment of arguments.

units.la: Quæ est quarta diuisio? Hæc modificatoria est,& vulgò modalis appellatur:cùm illius generis Enuntiationes non simpliciter & absolutè , sed adiuncta modi siue generis illius nota proferuntur. Modi autem sunt,Necesse est, oportet, fortasse,fieri potest,possibile est, impossibile est. Enuntiationum igitur alię hoc modo,alię illo,vel illo modo proferuntur.Eatúmque hæc vis est, vt quid necessario fortuitóve accidat, demonstret : & semper de futuro pronuntiatur. veluti, Fieri potest, vt tergemini nascantur. l. 3, D. si pars heredit. Fieri non potest, vt mortuus conditionem impleat. Nō prius certum est nō dedisse, quàm sit mortuus. l. ita stipulatus, 115, D. de verb. oblig. Ac de hoc genere mirificæ Philosophorum contentiones fuerunt. nam Academici Enuntiationes omnes quæ de futuro aliquid dicebant, veras esse aut falsas putabant. Stoici nec veras, nec falsas, sed veras & falsas esse posse. Non enim rerum naturam intuendam, in quâ omnia certa essent, cùm futura vtique fierent: sed nostram inscientiam aspici debere. d. l. sed etsi, De iudic. Nonnulli disputabãt id demum fieri posse, quod verum futurum esset: quod non esset, fieri nō posse. veluti, Cras moriere. Si verum est, euenier. Sin falsum, non eueniet. Quinetiam negationis adiectæ translatio momentum discriminis ostendit. veluti, Non impossibile est Troiam à Græcis capi. Impossibile est Troiam à Græcis non capi.
units.tr: What is the fourth division? This is the modificatory division, commonly called modal, and it applies when propositions of that kind are put forward not simply and absolutely, but with the addition of a sign of mode or kind. The modes are: it is necessary, it is fitting, perhaps, it can happen, it is possible, it is impossible. Some propositions are therefore put forward in this mode, others in that. The force of this is to show whether something happens necessarily or by chance, and it is always pronounced of the future. For example: "It can happen that triplets are born" (law 3, D. si pars hereditatis). "It cannot happen that a dead man fulfils a condition. It is not yet certain that he has not given, until he is dead" (law "ita stipulatus," 115, D. de verb. oblig.). There were remarkable disputes among the philosophers about this kind. The Academics thought that all propositions which said something about the future were either true or false. The Stoics held that they were neither true nor false, but could be true and false: for one should look not at the nature of things, in which all would be certain since they will certainly come to pass, but at our ignorance (law "sed etsi," D. de iudic.). Some argued that only what would be true in the future can happen, and what would not be true cannot happen. For example: "You will die tomorrow. If it is true, it will come to pass; but if false, it will not." Moreover, the shift of an added negation shows the weight of the distinction: "It is not impossible that Troy be taken by the Greeks" differs from "It is impossible that Troy not be taken by the Greeks."

units.la: Quæ est quinta diuisio ? Alia directa est, quæ [?]so & naturali verborum ordine concepta est. veluti, Deus cōsulit rebus humanis. Formæ dignitas aut morbo deflorescit, aut vetustate: alia conuersa, alia traiecta.
units.tr: What is the fifth division? One kind is direct, conceived in the natural and ordinary order of words, for example: "God takes thought for human affairs." "The beauty of a form fades either through disease or through age." Another kind is converted, and another is transposed.

units.la: Quæ est conuersa? Quæ id quod directè, sicuti natura fert, dictum erat, idem quasi sursum versus retróque pronuntiat : velut in Læbio : Cùm iudicaueris , diligere oportet : non cùm dilexeris,iudicare. Et alibi: Esse oportet, vt viuas : non viuere, vt edas . Magistratus est lex loquens:lex,magistratus mutus.Si poema, loquens pictura est: pictura, tacitum poema debet esse. Seruus (inquit Aristoteles) est instrumentum animatum:instrumetum , seruus inanimus. Quia stultus es, ea re taces : non quia taces,ea re stultus es. Sic, Homo non est conditus vt coelum & solem contempletur: sed coelum & sol & astra condita sunt, vt homini luceant. Ex eodem genere illud fuit Pafquilli ioculare , quod animi caussa subscribemus.
units.tr: What is a converted proposition? It is one that states in reverse, as it were turning back upward, what was stated directly, as nature bears it. Thus in Laelius: "When you have judged, you ought to love; not, when you have loved, to judge." And elsewhere: "One must exist in order to live; not live in order to eat." "The magistrate is a speaking law; the law is a silent magistrate." "If poetry, then painting is speaking poetry; painting ought to be silent poetry." "A slave, says Aristotle, is an animate instrument; an instrument is an inanimate slave." "Because you are foolish, therefore you are silent; not because you are silent, therefore you are foolish." Likewise: "Man was not made to contemplate heaven and sun; rather, heaven and sun and stars were made so that they might shine for man." Of the same kind was that jesting Pasquil saying which we will append for amusement:

units.la: Pauperibus sua dat gratis,nec munera curat. Curia Papalis,quod modo percipimus. Laus tua,non tua fraus, virtus non copia rerum. Scandere te scit hoc decus eximium. Hic Deus omnipotens faciat te viuere longo Tempore,nec labilis sit tua conditio.
units.tr: He gives freely to the poor, and does not care for gifts. The Papal Curia, as we now perceive it. Your praise, not your fraud; virtue, not an abundance of wealth. He knows how to climb to this outstanding honour. May Almighty God make you live a long time, and may your condition never be unstable.

units.la: Quæ est Traiecta? Quæ præpostero vel dictionum , vel sententiæ ordine concepta est. Hanc Cicero permistam & intercisam appellat in Partitionibus.veluti,Humanis Deus rebus consulit. Deflorescit formæ dignitas aut morbo,aut vetustate. Aut morbo aut vetustate formæ dignitas deflorescit.Item illud:Crescentem sequitur cura pecuniam. Instabilis in omnes plurimum fortuna valet. Nam in oratione non modò verba, sed etiam eorũ notio ita inversa est, ut quod subiectū videatur, sit attributum:& contrà,quod attributum,id subiectum sit. Sic,Nihil est præstabilius virtute, pro Virtus est præstabilior rebus omnibus.
units.tr: What is a transposed proposition? It is one conceived in a preposterous order of words or of the sentence. Cicero calls this "mixed and interrupted" in the Partitions. For example: "God takes thought for human affairs" becomes "Human affairs God takes thought for." "The beauty of a form fades through disease or age" becomes "Through disease or through age the beauty of a form fades." Likewise: "Care follows growing money"; "Unstable fortune has great power over all." For in speech not only the words but also their meaning is so inverted that what seems to be the subject is the predicate, and conversely what seems to be the predicate is the subject. Thus, "Nothing is more excellent than virtue" stands for "Virtue is more excellent than all things."

units.la: Quorsum hæc divisio? Quia cùm in posita quæstione naturalis & verborum & sententiæ ordo est, nomina quæ verbum antecedunt, subiecti locum obtinent: quæ verò sequuntur,attributi. At si conversus ordo est, ad naturalem ita revocãdus est, ut hoc ipsum appareat: quãuis res naturæ ordine prior sit.
units.tr: Why this division? Because when, in the question posed, the order of both words and sentence is natural, the nouns that precede the verb hold the place of subject, and those that follow hold the place of predicate. But if the order is converted, it must be restored to the natural order, so that this very thing becomes apparent, even though the thing is prior in the order of nature.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. In hac Enũtiatione,Umbra sequitur corpus, quamuis Corpus notione prius sit,ut Causa notione & intelligentia prior est Effectu: tamen umbra in quæstione prius est extremum, posterius est quod subiecto attribuitur. Itaque sic invertēda est: Corpus in luce est causa efficiens umbræ. Sicin[?] illa:Crescentem sequitur cura pecuniam: Pecunia, etsi natura prior est,tamen non est subiectum,ut quibusdam placuisse video. Revocãdaenim est oratio ad ordinem naturalem, & ponenda quæstio,An curæ conveniat,quod ei attributur. Pecunia crescens est causa curarum & solicitudinum.
units.tr: Give an example. In this proposition, "The shadow follows the body," although the body is prior in notion, just as a cause is prior in notion and understanding to its effect, nevertheless in the question the shadow comes first as the extreme term, and what is attributed to the subject comes after. It must therefore be inverted thus: "The body in the light is the efficient cause of the shadow." Similarly in that case, "Care follows growing money": money, although it is prior by nature, is nevertheless not the subject, as I see some have thought. For the statement must be brought back to the natural order, and the question posed: whether care belongs to that to which it is attributed. Growing money is the cause of cares and anxieties.

units.la: Deinceps de copulata videamus. Quid est Copulata Enuntiatio? Quæ neque de uno, neque purè & absolutè, sed depluribus vel sub conditione,vel disiunctiuè, vel coniunc-tiuè affirmat aut negat. veluti, Si sol lucet, dies est.Aut dies est,aut nox est.Et sol lucet,& dies est. Si mihi filius nascatur, heres esto. Aut Titius heres esto,aut Mæuius. quæ institutionis & substitutionis vis est. Et Titius & Mæuius heredes funto.
units.tr: Next let us look at the conjoined proposition. What is a conjoined proposition? It is one that affirms or denies, not of one thing, nor purely and absolutely, but of many things, either under a condition, or disjunctively, or conjunctively. For example: "If the sun shines, it is day." "Either it is day or it is night." "The sun shines and it is day." "If a son is born to me, let him be heir." "Let Titius be heir, or Maevius," which is the force of institution and substitution. "Let Titius and Maevius be heirs."

units.la: Quæ est Conditionalis? Quæ per notam cõditionis elata,de nulla parte purè affirmat, sed vel antecedens ex consequenti, vel consequens ex antecedenti pollicetur. Notæ autem conditionis sunt Si,vel Nisi. veluti:Si dies est, sol lucet. Si sol lucet,dies est. Nisi dies est, sol non lucet. Nisi sol lucet,dies non est.
units.tr: What is a conditional proposition? It is one that, expressed by a sign of condition, affirms nothing purely of any part, but promises either the antecedent from the consequent, or the consequent from the antecedent. The signs of condition are "if" or "unless." For example: "If it is day, the sun shines." "If the sun shines, it is day." "Unless it is day, the sun does not shine." "Unless the sun shines, it is not day."

units.la: Si fortuna volet,fies de Rhetore Consùl.
units.tr: If fortune wills it, you will become consul from being a rhetorician.

units.la: Si volet hæc eadem,fies de Consule Rhetor. Sed conditionalis alia rursus est simplex,quæ simplicem adiúctionem habet, vt ea quam modò exposuimus,altera mixta.
units.tr: If the same fortune wills it, you will become a rhetorician from being consul. But the conditional is again of another kind: the simple, which has a simple addition, like the one just set out, and the mixed.

units.la: Quod est firmamentum istius enuntiationis? Vt verum fit antecedens, necesse est confequés verum esse:vicissímque vt hoc fit, illud esse necesse est.
units.tr: What is the foundation of this kind of proposition? For the antecedent to be true, it is necessary that the consequent be true; and conversely, for this to hold, it is necessary that the antecedent be true.

units.la: Quæ est Códitionalis mixta? Quæ adiun&ionem habet,aut ex coniunctiua, aut ex difiunctiua. veluti:Si stertit, & cubat, & dormit. Si ciuis est,aut natus est,aut factus. Si filiusfa. est,aut natura,aut adoptione est.
units.tr: What is a mixed conditional? It is one that has a conjunctive or a disjunctive addition. For example: "If he snores, and lies down, and sleeps." "If he is a citizen, he is either born or made one." "If he is a son, he is either so by nature or by adoption."

units.la: Quæ est Enuntiatio disiunctiua? Quæ per disiunctionis notâ concepta de incerta parte affirmat.Notæ autè disiunctionis sunt, Aut & Vel.veluti,Aut dies est, aut nox est.Aut amat, aut odit mulier. nã disiunctiua dicûtur, quorum posito uno necesse est tolli alterum : item sublato altero poni alterum. l. hæc verba, 1124, [?] D.de verb. signif. Gellius ἀπεζευγμένον [?] ἀξίωμα Græcè, Latinè disiunctum proloquium appellat.
units.tr: What is a disjunctive proposition? It is one conceived with the sign of disjunction, which affirms something of an uncertain part. The signs of disjunction are "either" and "or." For example: "Either it is day or it is night." "A woman either loves or hates." For those are called disjunctive of which, when one is posited, the other must be removed; and likewise, when the other is removed, the one must be posited. Gellius calls it in Greek [ἀπεζευγμένον ἀξίωμα], and in Latin a disjunct utterance.

units.la: Quid est Disiunctio? Quæ vel per divisionem, genus in species, vel per partitionem, totum in partes distribuit. Duplex autem disiunctio est: una duarum partium: veluti, Aut vigilat, aut dormit: altera plurium: veluti, Beluæ sunt aut aëriæ, aut terrenæ, aut aquatiles.
units.tr: What is disjunction? It is that which either divides a genus into its species, by division, or distributes a whole into its parts, by partition. Disjunction is of two kinds: one of two parts, for example, "Either he keeps watch or he sleeps"; the other of several, for example, "Beasts are either aerial, or terrestrial, or aquatic."

units.la: Quæ est natura disiuncti pronuntiati. Ut una pars vera, universam orationem veram efficiat. nam cùm disiunctiva sit particularis (ut Iulianus docet in l. si is qui, 13, §. utrum, D. de reb. dub.) satis constat subcontrarias simul veras esse posse. veluti, Aliquis homo est albus. Non omnis homo est niger. Quanvis igitur quidam sint nigri, vera tamen erit enuntiatio, Homines aut sunt albi, aut nigri. Itaque iussus illud aut illud dare, alterutrum dando liberatur. l. cùm pupillus, 78, D. de cond. & demonst. l. 5, D. de cond. instit. Gellius autem copiosius rem sic explicat: Omnia (inquit) quæ disiunguntur, pugnatia esse inter sese oportet: eorumque opposita, ἀντικείμενα Græci dicunt, ea quoque ipsa inter sese adversa esse. Exomnibus quæ disiunguntur, unum esse verû debet: falsa cetera. Quòd si aut nihil omnium verum, aut omnia, pluráve quàm unum, vera erunt: aut quæ disiuncta sunt, non pugnabunt: aut quę opposita eorum sunt, contraria inter se non erunt: tũc id disiunctũ mendacium est, & appellatur ἀσυνδιαζευγμένον[?]: sicuti hoc est, in quo quę opposita, non sunt contraria: aut curris, aut stas, aut ambulas. Nam ipsa quidē inter se adversa sunt, sed opposita eorum non repugnant. Non ambulare enim, & non stare, & non currere, contraria inter sese non sunt: quoniam contraria ea dicuntur quę simul vera esse non queunt. Possis enim simul eodémque tempore, neque ambulare, neque stare, neque currere.
units.tr: What is the nature of a disjunctive utterance? That one true part makes the whole proposition true. For since the disjunctive is particular (as Julian teaches in the law "si is qui"), it is well established that subcontraries can be true together. For example: "Some man is white. Not every man is black." Although some men are black, the proposition "Men are either white or black" will nevertheless be true. Therefore one who is ordered to give this or that is freed by giving either one. Gellius explains the matter more fully as follows: "All things that are disjoined (he says) must be at odds with one another, and their opposites, which the Greeks call [ἀντικείμενα], must also be mutually opposed. Of all the things disjoined, one must be true and the rest false. But if none of them is true, or all of them, or more than one, are true, then either those that are disjoined will not clash, or their opposites will not be contrary to one another. In that case the disjunction is a falsehood, and it is called [ἀσυνδιαζευγμένον]. Such is this one, in which the opposites are not contraries: 'Either you run, or you stand, or you walk.' For indeed these are mutually opposed, but their opposites do not conflict. For not walking, not standing, and not running are not contrary to one another, since those are called contrary which cannot be true together. For you could, at one and the same time, neither walk, nor stand, nor run."

units.la: Quę est Coniunctiua? Quę per coniunctionis notam cōcepta, de partibus omnibus aliquid aut affirmat, aut negat. Notę autem coniunctionis sunt, Et, Nec. veluti, Cicero & eloquens fuit, & bonus ciuis. Cicero nec bellicosus fuit, nec magnanimus.
units.tr: What is a conjunctive proposition? It is one that, conceived with the sign of conjunction, affirms or denies something of all its parts. The signs of conjunction are "and" and "nor." For example: "Cicero was both eloquent and a good citizen." "Cicero was neither warlike nor magnanimous."

units.la: Quod est firmamētū istius? Ut cōiunctiua vera sit, singulas partes veras esse oportet. ut eadē falsa sit, unica falsam esse satis est. Hęc enim universalis est: ut Julianus scribit in l. si is qui, 13, §. utrũ D. de reb. dub. Quare cui legatum est si & illud & illud fecerit, utrunque facere cogitur. l. si quis ita, 129, D. de verb. signif. Gellius hanc enuntiationem scribit à Græcis nominari συμπεπλεγμένον ἀξίωμα: id est, cōiunctum vel copulatum. veluti, Scipio bis Consul fuit, & triumphavit, & Censura functus est, & collega in Censura Mummij fuit. Eius autē hoc esse proprium, ut si unum est mendacium, etiam fi cetera vera sint ; totum esse mendacium dicatur, nā si ad ea omnia quæ de Scipione illo vera dixi(inquit) addidero, Et Annibalem in Africa superauit, quod est falsum : vniuersa quoque illa quæ coniunctè dicta sunt, propter hoc vnum quod falsum accesserit, vera non erunt.
units.tr: What is the foundation of this? For a conjunctive proposition to be true, each of its parts must be true; for it to be false, one falsehood is enough. For it is universal, as Julian writes in the law "si is qui": "Wherefore one to whom a legacy is left, if he does both this and that, is compelled to do both." Gellius writes that the Greeks call this kind of proposition [συμπεπλεγμένον ἀξίωμα], that is, conjoined or coupled. For example: "Scipio was consul twice, and triumphed, and held the censorship, and was colleague in the censorship of Mummius." It is peculiar to this kind that if there is one falsehood, even though the rest are true, the whole is said to be false. For if to all those things that I have said are true of that Scipio I add (he says) "and he defeated Hannibal in Africa," which is false, then all those things said conjointly will not be true, on account of this one falsehood that has been added.

units.la: De Comparatione Enuntiationum per contrad- ictionem. CAP. XI.
units.tr: Of the Comparison of Propositions by Contradiction. CHAP. XI.

units.la: SACTENVS de Enuntiationibus per se confideratis satis videtur dictum. deinceps de ipsarum inter se ratione & affectione differamus.
units.tr: Enough has now been said about propositions considered in themselves. Next let us discuss how they stand to one another, in their relation and their affections.

units.la: Quot modis Enuntiationes inter se coparantur? Tribus. per contradictionem, per pariationé, & per couerfioné: ex quibus vtrum inter se conueniant, an disideant intelligitur. Has Græci vocant ἀντίθεσιν, ἰσοδυναμίαν, & ἀντιστροφὴν[?].
units.tr: In how many ways are propositions compared with one another? In three: by contradiction, by parity, and by conversion. From these we understand whether they agree with one another or disagree. The Greeks call these antithesin [ἀντίθεσιν], isodynamian [ἰσοδυναμίαν], and antistrophen [ἀντιστροφὴν].

units.la: Quid est Contradictio? Vnius eiusdem rei affirmatio & negatio. vel, Oratio quæ idem de eodem & affirmat, & negat.
units.tr: What is contradiction? The affirmation and denial of one and the same thing. Or, a statement that both affirms and denies the same thing of the same thing.

units.la: Quotuplex est Contradictio? Quadruplex. aut enim contrariæ sunt enuntiationes, aut subcontrariæ, aut subalternæ, aut disparatæ. Græcè sic: ἐναντίαι,ὑπεναντίαι[?],ὑπαλλήλαι,ἀντιφατικαί. quarum figuram Græci in quadrato sic constituunt. Omne verbum est ambiguum. | Contrariæ ἐναντίαι. | Nullum verbum est ambiguum. Contradicentes Per diametrum Subalternæ ὑπαλλήλαι [?] Subalternæ ὑπαλλήλαι [?] Subcontrariæ ὑπεναντίαι [?] Aliquod verbum est ambiguum. | Subcöntrariæ ὑπεναντίαι | Nõ omne verbũ est ámbiguum.
units.tr: How many kinds of contradiction are there? Four. For propositions are either contrary, or subcontrary, or subalternate, or contradictory. In Greek they are enantiai [ἐναντίαι], hypenantiai [ὑπεναντίαι], hypallelai [ὑπαλλήλαι], and antiphatikai [ἀντιφατικαί]. The Greeks set out their arrangement in a square, as follows. Top: "Every word is ambiguous." Left: "Contrary" and right: "No word is ambiguous," with "Contradictories" along the diagonal, and "Subalternate" on each side, with "Subcontrary" at the bottom, between "Some word is ambiguous" and "Not every word is ambiguous."

units.la: Quę sunt Cōtrariæ? Duæ vniuersales, quarum quod affirmat altera, idem ipsum de eodem altera negat. Itaque verè simul esse non possunt: at falsæ possunt. veluti, Omnis homo est beatus. Nullus homo est beatus. Vtraque falsa est.
units.tr: What are contraries? Two universal propositions, of which the one affirms what the other denies of the same thing about the same thing. Therefore they cannot be true together, but they can be false together. For example: "Every man is happy." "No man is happy." Both are false.

units.la: Quę sunt Subcontrariæ? Duæ particulares, quarum quod altera affirmat, id altera de eodem negat. Hæ falsæ simul esse non possunt: at verè possunt. Aliquis homo est beatus. Non omnis homo est beatus.
units.tr: What are subcontraries? Two particular propositions, of which the one affirms what the other denies of the same thing. These cannot be false together, but they can be true together. For example: "Some man is happy." "Not every man is happy."

units.la: Quæ sunt Subalternæ? Duæ de eodem Enuntiationes, quarum una universalis est, altera particularis. Cum tamen utraque vel affirmativa sit, vel negativa. Veluti, Omnis homo est miser. Quidam homo est miser. Nullus homo est beatus. Non omnis homo est beatus. Itaque si vera universalis est, erit & particularis vera: at non contrà, si haec vera est, illa crit: veluti, Quidam homines sunt caeci. Omnes homines sunt caeci. Subalternae autem dicuntur, quia sunt ὑπαλλήλων[?], id est, quoniam altera alteri subiecta est.
units.tr: What are subalternates? Two propositions about the same thing, of which one is universal and the other particular, while both are either affirmative or negative. For example: "Every man is wretched." "Some man is wretched." "No man is happy." "Not every man is happy." Therefore, if the universal is true, the particular will also be true; but not conversely: if the particular is true, the universal need not be. For example: "Some men are blind." "All men are blind." They are called subalternate [hypallelai] [ὑπαλλήλων], that is, because the one is subordinate to the other.

units.la: Quae sunt Contradicentes? Quarum una universalis affirmativa est, altera particularis negativa. vel contrà, quarum una universalis negativa, & altera particularis affirmativa est. Haec autem adeo inter se pugnant, ut simul neque vere, neque falsè esse possint. Veluti, Omnes homines sunt miseri: Quidam homines non sunt miseri. vel contrà: Nulli homines sunt atri: Quidam homines sunt atri. Ac scitum est quod in quadrato superiore Dialectici notant, in solis diagonicis enuntiationibus contradictionem esse. Est autem διαγώνιος, quae & Diameter dicitur, linea quae in quadrato ab angulis ad angulos ea parte ducitur, qua longissimè quadratum patet.
units.tr: What are contradictories? Those of which one is a universal affirmative and the other a particular negative, or conversely, one a universal negative and the other a particular affirmative. These are so opposed to one another that they cannot be true together or false together. For example: "All men are wretched; some men are not wretched." Or conversely: "No men are black; some men are black." And the point that the Dialecticians note in the square above is well known: contradiction exists only in the propositions on the diagonals. A diagonal [diagōnios, διαγώνιος], also called the diameter, is the line drawn in a square from corner to corner, along the direction in which the square extends furthest.

units.la: Quid? Oppositionis, quaenam praecepta sunt? Ut in re, vocabulo & tempore eodem, oppositio committatur. Nam si in iis varietas est, committi non potest. In re, veluti: Cato sibi mortem conscivit. Cato sibi mortem non conscìuit. Prius de Vticési[?] verum est: alterum autem de Censorino. Item Aethiops est niger: Aethiops non est niger. Non comittuntur, si alterum de cute, alterū de dentibus enûtictur[?]. In vocabulo, veluti, Scriptor huius historię est eloquentissimus: idem scriptor est infantissimus. Non comittuntur si prius de auctore, alterum de librario pronunciētur. In tempore, veluti Clodius illo die visus est Romæ. Clodius illo die visus est Interamnæ. non comittuntur si diei fiat partitio: non magis quàm in illo: Cesar interfe&' est Idibus Martiis. Cesar Idibus Martiis non est interfe&us. Nam manè nondum interfe&us erat.
units.tr: What then are the rules of opposition? That the opposition be made in the same thing, the same word, and the same time. For if there is variation in these, the opposition cannot be made. In the thing: for example, "Cato killed himself"; "Cato did not kill himself." The first is true of Cato of Utica, the second of Censorinus. Likewise, "The Ethiopian is black"; "The Ethiopian is not black." They are not opposed if one is said of the skin and the other of the teeth. In the word: for example, "The writer of this history is most eloquent"; "The same writer is most foolish." They are not opposed if the first is said of the author and the second of the copyist. In the time: for example, "Clodius was seen at Rome on that day"; "Clodius was seen at Interamna on that day." They are not opposed if the day is divided into parts, no more than in this case: "Caesar was killed on the Ides of March"; "Caesar was not killed on the Ides of March." For in the morning he had not yet been killed.

units.la: De Pariatione. CAP. XII.
units.tr: On Pariation. CHAP. XII.

units.la: Quæ[?] est Pariatio? Est duarum enunciationum quæ inter se dissident, cōciliatio. Hāc (ut dixi) ἰσοδυναμίαν Græci vocant, vulgus Aequipollentiam: nos Pariationem ex accepti & expensi rationibus non incommodè appellari posse putavimus: quoniā tum in quātitate, tum in qualitate ea comparatio fit. Quantitas autem de universalibus,& particularibus dicitur: Qualitas de affirmatiuis & negatiuis.
units.tr: What is pariation? It is the reconciliation of two propositions that disagree with each other. The Greeks call it [ἰσοδυναμίαν], as I said, and the common people "equipollence." I thought "pariation" could fairly be named from the accounts of receipts and expenditures, since the comparison is made both in quantity and in quality. Quantity belongs to universal and particular propositions; quality to affirmative and negative ones.

units.la: Quot modis Pariatio conficitur? Duobus: adiun&ione negationis,& verborum conversione . Sed negatio interdum una est, interdum gemina. Itaque de utriusque vi separatim exponendum est.
units.tr: By how many methods is pariation effected? By two: by adding a negation, and by converting the terms. But the negation is sometimes single and sometimes double, so the force of each must be explained separately.

units.la: Quotuplex est vis unius Negantie? Qua-
units.tr: How many-fold is the force of a single negation? Fourfold.

units.la: [Note: the initial of "Quæ" is a large decorated letter, read here as Q with [?].] druplex. Nam aut totum partémve ponit:aut totum partémve tollit. Itaque modos omnes Enuntiationum conturbat, quia ex varietate situs & positionis potestas eius variatur.
units.tr: For it either posits the whole or a part, or removes the whole or a part. So it upsets all the forms of propositions, because its power varies with the variety of its position and placement.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de Parte per negantiā posita. Sumamus huiusmodi: Homo est bipes: Non homo est bipes: hîc negantia partem ponit: quia declarat aliud quippiam esse bipes, præter hominem, ut aves. Ergo ad illam indefinitam enuntiationem: Homo est bipes, partem addit: Etiā quod non homo est, bipes est. Sic Homines natant, Non homines natant: id est, etiam non homines. Item: Civis est liber: non civis est etiā liber. Reges sunt beati. Non Reges sunt etiam beati. Hostis est peregrinus. non hostis est etiam peregrinus.
units.tr: Give me an example of a part posited by negation. Let us take this: Man is two-footed. Not-man is two-footed. Here the negation posits a part, because it declares that something other than man is two-footed, such as birds. So to the indefinite proposition "Man is two-footed" it adds a part: that what is not a man is also two-footed. Likewise: Men swim; non-men swim, that is, even non-men. Also: A citizen is free; a non-citizen is also free. Kings are happy; non-kings are also happy. An enemy is a foreigner; a non-enemy is also a foreigner.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de Toto per negantiā pofito. Sumatur huiusmodi: Homo est animal docile: Homo est animal non docile. Canis est cicur: Canis est non cicur. Omnes Elephanti sunt feroces. Omnes Elephanti sunt non feroces. Hîc negantia propterea Totum ponere dicitur, quia novum attributum & superioris contrarium inducit: id est, novam qualitatem subiecto attribuit.
units.tr: Give me an example of a whole posited by negation. Let us take this: Man is a teachable animal; Man is a non-teachable animal. The dog is tame; the dog is non-tame. All elephants are fierce; all elephants are non-fierce. Here the negation is said to posit the whole because it introduces a new attribute, contrary to the previous one; that is, it assigns a new quality to the subject.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de Negantia quæ partem tollit. Ponatur huiusmodi: Omnis homo est albus: Non omnis homo est albus: vel, Omnis homo non est albus. Hîc negantia parté propterea detrahere dicitur, quoniam ex universali enuntiatione particularem efficit. Cedo exemplum de Negantia, quę Totum tollit. Ponatur huiusmodi: Homo est animal docile. Homo non est animal docile. Balbus est musicus. Balbus non est musicus. Leo est ferox. Leo non est ferox. Hic Negantia perspicuè est ἀπόφανσις τινὸς ἀπόφασις[?] (vt Ariftoteles loquitur) ac proprie vim suam exerit, Totum enim attributum remouet atque auertit à subiecto.
units.tr: Give me an example of a negation that removes a part. Let it be put thus: Every man is white; not every man is white, or, every man is not white.
