Here the negation is said to remove a part, because it turns a universal proposition into a particular one. Give me an example of a negation that removes the whole. Let it be put thus: Man is a teachable animal; Man is not a teachable animal. Balbus is a musician; Balbus is not a musician. The lion is fierce; the lion is not fierce. Here the negation is plainly a denial of something by a denial [ἀπόφανσις τινὸς ἀπόφασις], as Aristotle puts it, and exerts its force properly, for it removes and turns the whole attribute away from the subject.

units.la: Quomodo Negantia modos Enuntiationis variat? Quoniam ex affirmatiuis negativas, ex negatiuis affirmativas, & ex universalibus particulares efficit: veluti, Homo est animal sociale. Homo non est animal sociale. Ex aiente & negante effecta est. At cum dicimus, Nulli homines sunt atri: Nonnulli homines sunt atri: ex negante cōficimus affirmantem. Quòd si dicamus, Omnis homo est albus: Nō omnis homo est albus: ex universali particulare efficimus.
units.tr: How does negation vary the forms of a proposition? Because it makes negative propositions from affirmative ones, affirmative from negative, and particular from universal. For example: Man is a social animal; Man is not a social animal. This is made from an affirming and a denying. But when we say, No men are black, and then, Some men are black, we make an affirming from a denying. And if we say, Every man is white, and then, Not every man is white, we make a particular from a universal.

units.la: Quo pacto varius negantiæ situs vim ipsius variat? Quia cūm vis eius propria & naturalis hæc sit, ut avertat & removeat, sæpe tamen ex ratione positionis & situs ponēdi atque inducendi vim obtinet. veluti, Homo est bipes, Non homo est bipes. Homo natat, Non homo natat. Hæc negantiæ præpositio vim affirmationis quādam ei attribuit, ac facit vt aliquid ab ea ponatur atque inducatur, quod præter hominem bipes sit, aut natet. ut canis, equus.
units.tr: In what way does the varying position of a negation vary its force? Although its proper and natural force is to turn away and remove, it often takes on the force of affirmation from the placement of its position and from the way it is set down and introduced. For example: Man is two-footed; not-man is two-footed. Man swims; not-man swims. This placement of the negation gives it a certain force of affirmation, and makes something posited and introduced by it, which is two-footed besides man, or swims, such as the dog or the horse.

units.la: Item, negantiæ post verbum es t collocatio vim affirmationis ei tribuit: ut Greci loquuntur ἐκ μεταθέσεως. veluti, Concubina est non iusta vxor. Spurius est non iustus filius. Crudelitas est non virtus. Prudentia est nihil temere credere. Ex eodem genere illa sunt: Agricola non plantat, pro, Est non plantans: cùm arat. Studiosus non legit: pro, Est non legens: cùm scribit. Sic Cato in otio est, non otiosus. Christiani locupletes (inquit Paulus) debent esse vt non locupletes: quod valet, inopes. Ex eodē[?] quoque genere illa sunt: Nulli homines sunt nigri: nonnulli homines sunt nigri. Genus enim hominum inducitur, quod nigrum esse affirmatur. Item: Quidam homines sunt claudi: Quidam homines non sunt claudi. Nihil superiori posterior adimit: sed cùm ex toto cum illa congruat, affirmationis locum obtinet.
units.tr: Likewise, placing the negation after the verb "is" gives it the force of affirmation, as the Greeks speak of it, by transposition [ἐκ μεταθέσεως]. For example: A concubine is not a lawful wife. A bastard is not a lawful son. Cruelty is not virtue. Prudence is to believe nothing rashly. Of the same kind are: A farmer does not plant, meaning he is a non-planter while he ploughs. A student does not read, meaning he is a non-reader while he writes. So Cato is at leisure, not idle. Christians who are rich (says Paul) ought to be as not rich, which means poor. Of the same kind also are: No men are black; some men are black. For a class of men is introduced, which is affirmed to be black. Likewise: Some men are lame; some men are not lame. The later proposition takes nothing away from the earlier, but since it agrees with it as a whole, it holds the place of an affirmation.

units.la: Quotuplex est vis geminæ negationis. Triplex. nam aut totum tollit, quippe quæ totum inficiatur: aut totū partémve ponit, cùm aut totum aut partem duntaxat affirmat. Partis enim tollendæ vim non habet: quia particulam negatiuam efficere non potest.
units.tr: How many-fold is the force of a double negation? Threefold. For either it removes the whole, since it denies the whole; or it posits the whole or a part, when it affirms either the whole or only a part. It does not have the force of removing a part, because it cannot make a particular negative.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de Toto per geminam negantiā sublato. Per geminam negantiā Totum tollitur, cùm vniuersalis negatiua cócipitur: veluti, Non homo nó ridet. Non miles, nó belligeratur. Non liber, non est ciuis. Non ciuis, non agit lege. Non Senator, non admittitur in curiam. Valet enim idem quod vniuersalis negatiua huiusmodi: Nullus nō senator in curiam admittitur.
units.tr: Give me an example of the whole removed by a double negation. The whole is removed by a double negation when a universal negative is conceived. For example: The non-man does not laugh. The non-soldier is not waging war. The non-free man is not a citizen. The non-citizen does not act under the law. The non-senator is not admitted into the senate. For this has the same force as the universal negative: No non-senator is admitted into the senate.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de Toto per geminam negantiam inducto. Cùm geminata negatione universalis affirmativa conficitur. veluti, Nemo non est improbus. Nemo est non improbus. Nullus civis non est liber. Nullus civis est non liber. Nullus leo non est ferox. nullus leo est non ferox. Nulla gemma non est lucida. nulla gemma est non lucida. Nam hæc idem valet atque illa, Omnis gemma est lucida.
units.tr: Give me an example of the whole introduced by a double negation. When a universal affirmative is made by a doubled negation. For example: No one is not wicked; no one is non-wicked. No citizen is not free; no citizen is non-free. No lion is not fierce; no lion is non-fierce. No gem is not shining; no gem is non-shining. For these have the same force as that: Every gem is shining.

units.la: Cedo exemplū de parte per geminam negantiam posita. Cùm geminata negatione universalis in affirmationem particularem convertitur. veluti, Nulli sunt Centauri. Nonnulli sunt Cétauri. Nusquā sunt Pygmæi: Non nusquam sunt Pygmæi. Nemo senator est maculosus. Non nemo Senator est maculosus.
units.tr: Give me an example of a part posited by a double negation. When a universal is turned by a doubled negation into a particular affirmative. For example: There are no centaurs; some are centaurs. Nowhere are there Pygmies; not nowhere are there Pygmies. No senator is stained; not no senator is stained.

units.la: Quamobrem gemina negantia partis tollendæ vim non obtinet? Quia secunda negatio particulari negatiuæ adhibita, universalem affirmativam efficit. veluti, Quidam Senatores non sunt divites. non quidam Senatores non sunt divites. Quidã Tyranni non sunt interficiendi. non quidam Tyranni non sunt interficiendi. Nam idem valet atque illa, Omnes Tyranni sunt interficiendi.
units.tr: Why does a double negation not have the force of removing a part? Because the second negation, added to a particular negative, makes a universal affirmative. For example: Some senators are not rich; not-some senators are not rich. Some tyrants are not to be killed; not-some tyrants are not to be killed. For this has the same force as: All tyrants are to be killed.

units.la: De Conversione. CAP. XIII,
units.tr: On Conversion. Chapter 13,

units.la: QVID est Conuersio? Est attributi in subiectum, & vicissim subiecti in attributum commutatio. Itaque singularis eius vis ac praestantia in eo cernitur, quòd cùm ars dialectica in eo potissimum versetur, ut ostendat qua ratione aliud de alio dici atque enuntiari possit: tum verò Conversionis disciplina demonstrat, quemadmodum duo diversa de uno, id est subiectum de attributo, & attributum de subiecto praedicari possit: simúlque de duobus in Enuntiatione positis utrù fit subiectum, aut attributum. Haec à Graecis ἀντιστροφὴ [?] quasi ἰσοστροφὴ [?] nominatur: quasi quis dicat vicissitudinem, aut reciprocationem: cùm id quod directè dictum est, invertitur, & idem quasi sursum versus retròque dicitur. veluti, nulla voluptas est bona. nihil quod bonum sit, est voluptas. Hoc enim ex Aristotele vulgò traditur exemplum. Deinde, quoniam superiùs diximus, subiectum nunquam esse privationem, si negatiua concepta enuntiatio fit, demonstrat quomodo ita commutari possit, ut aliquid in subiecto insit. veluti, Nihil est praestabilius virtute. Virtus est praestabilior omni re. Nullum honestum est non utile. Omne honestum est utile. Nulla crudelitas est virtus. Omnis crudelitas est vitiū. Nulla voluptas est bonum. Omnis voluptas est malum. Nihil est insipiente fortunato intolerabilius. Insipiés fortunatus omnibus hominibus est intolerabilior.
units.tr: What is conversion? It is the interchange of the attribute into the subject and, conversely, of the subject into the attribute. Its unique force and excellence lies in this: dialectic is chiefly concerned to show by what reasoning one thing can be said and asserted of another, and the discipline of conversion shows how two different things can be predicated of one, that is, the subject of the attribute and the attribute of the subject, and, of two terms placed in a proposition, which is the subject and which the attribute. The Greeks call this antistrophē [ἀντιστροφὴ], as it were isostrophē [ἰσοστροφὴ], as if one said interchange or reciprocation, since what was stated directly is inverted and the same thing is said as it were upward and back again. For example: No pleasure is good; nothing that is good is pleasure. This example is commonly handed down from Aristotle. Then, since we said above that the subject is never a privation, the proposition, if framed negatively, shows how it can be changed so that something inheres in the subject. For example: Nothing is more excellent than virtue; virtue is more excellent than everything. No honourable thing is not useful; every honourable thing is useful. No cruelty is virtue; every cruelty is vice. No pleasure is good; every pleasure is bad. Nothing is more intolerable than a foolish fortunate man; a foolish fortunate man is more intolerable than all men.

units.la: Quotuplex conuersio est? Duplex. Propria & impropria. Propria est, cùm & subiectum de attributo, & attributum de subiecto, quasi idem de eodem pronuntiatur. Itaque unius tantum generis Enuntiationum propria hæc conuersio videtur: eius videlicet, quæ idem de eodem enùtiat[?], ut superiùs diximus, Contradictionem esse, cùm idem de eodem & affirmatur & negatur. Nam quæ sunt eadem, necessarió inter se reciprocantur, vicissimque commeāt: veluti, Ut bis bina sunt quatuor, sic quatuor sunt bis bina: & ut quater quinque sunt viginti, sic viginti sunt quinquies quater. Quo argumento Genus & species cunctæ, Totum item & partes coniunctæ inter se reciprocantur: ac proinde etiam definitum & definitio: quia definitio (ut paulo post intelliges) nihil aliud est, quàm singularum partium inuolutarum euolutio. Itaque ut Rhetorica est facultas copiosè loquendi, ita facultas copiosè loquendi, est Rhetorica. Dolor, ægritudo crucians. Aegritudo crucians, dolor.
units.tr: How many kinds of conversion are there? Two: proper and improper. The proper conversion is when both the subject is predicated of the attribute and the attribute of the subject, as if the same thing were said of the same. Thus this proper conversion seems to belong to only one kind of proposition, namely those which say the same of the same; as we said above, this is contradiction, when the same thing is both affirmed and denied of the same. For things that are the same necessarily reciprocate with one another and pass back and forth: for example, as twice two are four, so four are twice two; and as four times five are twenty, so twenty are five times four. By this argument genus and all species, and likewise whole and joined parts, reciprocate with one another, and consequently also the defined and the definition; for a definition (as you will understand shortly) is nothing other than the unfolding of the individual parts folded up together. Thus, as rhetoric is the faculty of speaking copiously, so the faculty of speaking copiously is rhetoric. Pain is a tormenting sickness; a tormenting sickness is pain.

units.la: Quænam eius disciplinæ præceptio & formula tradi potest? Ut omnis enuntiatio vniuersalis quæ de paribus pronuntiat, siue affirmatiua, siue negatiua sit, reciprocationem recipiat hoc modo: Quicunque habet bis bina, idem habet quatuor: & vicissim qui quatuor, idem habet bis bina. In quo est mœror, in eo est ægritudo flebilis: in quo est ægritudo flebilis, in eo est mœror. Et ex contrario: in quo non est angor, in eo non est ægritudo premés: & in quo non est ægritudo premens, in eo nō est angor. In his exemplis idem de eodem dicitur : quemadmodum in contradictione factum est. Definitum enim & definitio re sunt paria: verborum solo numero differunt.
units.tr: What precept and formula of this discipline can be given? That every universal proposition which predicates of equals, whether affirmative or negative, admits reciprocation in this way: whoever has twice two has four; and conversely, whoever has four has twice two. In whoever there is sorrow, there is grievous distress; in whoever there is grievous distress, there is sorrow. And conversely: in whom there is no anguish, in him there is no oppressive distress; and in whom there is no oppressive distress, in him there is no anguish. In these examples the same is said of the same, as happened in contradiction. For the defined and the definition are equal in fact; they differ only in the number of words.

units.la: Quæ est impropria Conuersio? Quæ non idem de eodem enuntiat, sed alterum alterius æquè vel consentaneum vel dissentaneum esse declarat. veluti: Omne honestum est vtile. & vicißim, Omne vtile est honestum. Nihil honestum, quod non vtile. Nihil vtile, quod non honestum. Item: Omnis sapiens est dies : Omnis dies est sapiens. Nemo dies nisi sapiens: & nemo sapiens, nisi dies. Vtraq; est, vt paulō post intelliges, argumentatio ex antecedentibus & consequentibus. Nam vt honestas antecedens vtilitatis est, sic sapiétia diuitiarum. Eiusdémque generis illud est: Magistratus est Lex loquens: Lex est magistratus mutus.
units.tr: What is improper conversion? That which does not say the same of the same, but declares that one thing is equally either consistent or inconsistent with another. For example: Every honourable thing is useful; and conversely, every useful thing is honourable. Nothing honourable which is not useful; nothing useful which is not honourable. Likewise: every wise man is a day; every day is a wise man. No day except a wise one; and no wise man except a day. Both are, as you will understand shortly, arguments from antecedents and consequents. For as honesty is antecedent to usefulness, so wisdom is to riches. Of the same kind is this: The magistrate is the law speaking; the law is the magistrate mute.

units.la: Quænam eius rei præcepta Aristoteles tradidit? Omnis quæ de hoc genere est Aristotelis disputatio, ad improprias pertinet. Itaque non eodem libro hanc, quo contradictionem tradauit, vt cùm eò peruéneris, intelliges. Primum autem eius præceptum est huiusmodi: Omnis enuntiatio quæ vniuersalis negatiua est, necessariam conuersionem efficit : veluti, Nulla voluptas est bona. Nihil quod bonum fit, est voluptas. Sed nihil mirum est, si hæc nō reciprocentur, cum ex repugnantium numero rofint. Aequè autem absurdum est de Repugnantium conuersione disputare, ac de Contrariorum. veluti, Vt nulla virtus vitium est, sic nullum vitium est virtus. de quo fanus nemo dubitarit.
units.tr: What precepts did Aristotle hand down on this matter? All of Aristotle's discussion of this kind pertains to the improper conversions. Therefore you will understand it not in the same book in which he taught contradiction, but when you arrive there. His first precept is of this kind: every universal negative proposition produces a necessary conversion. For example: No pleasure is good; nothing that is good is pleasure. But it is no wonder if these do not reciprocate, since they belong to the class of opposites. It is equally absurd to dispute about the conversion of opposites as about that of contraries. For example, as no virtue is vice, so no vice is virtue; no one in his senses would doubt this.

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplum. Simillima ratio est eorum quę passim in scholis proferuntur. Nulla crudelitas est virtus. Nulla virtus est crudelitas. Nullum iustum malum est. Nullum malum iustum est. Nam hæc omnia ex Repugnantium habitu & affectione sumpta sunt. sic, Nullum animal est cordis expers: Nullum cordis expers est animal. Apertifsima est argumentatio ex Toto ad Partem affirmatiuè: & vicifsimà Partibus ad Totum negatiuè. Nam Cor præcipua pars est Animalis, vt Rota vehiculi: de quo fi sic dicerem, Vt nullum vehiculum rota vacuum est, sic nullum rota vacuum est vehiculum: absurdisfimè argumentatione ex Toto & Partibus ad Enuntiationis naturā & habitum trásferrem.
units.tr: Give me another example. The reasoning is very similar for those things commonly put forward in the schools. No cruelty is virtue; no virtue is cruelty. No just thing is evil; no evil thing is just. For all these are taken from the state and condition of opposites. So too: No animal is without a heart; nothing without a heart is an animal. This is a most evident argument from whole to part affirmatively, and conversely from parts to whole negatively. For the heart is the chief part of an animal, as a wheel is of a vehicle. If I were to say of this, "As no vehicle is wheel-less, so nothing wheel-less is a vehicle," I would most absurdly transfer an argument from whole and parts to the nature and condition of the proposition.

units.la: Quod est alterum Ariftotelis præceptum? Vt Enúntiatio vniuersalis affirmatiua reciprocetur illa quidem, sed in parte tantùm, nö vniuerse. veluti: Si voluptas omnis est bona, quoddam bonum est voluptas. Sed ex generis & speciei habitu hæc couerfio ducitur: & per-spicuè, non ad Enuntiationum naturam, sed ad locos argumentorum pertinet: in quibus traditur, Cui conuenit genus, eidem conueni-re speciem. sed cui conuenit species, eidem genus ex parte tantùm convenire. Eadem ratio est illius, Si omne iustum bonum est, quoddā bonum, iustum est. Si omnis homo est animal, quoddam animal est homo.
units.tr: What is Aristotle's other precept? That a universal affirmative proposition does reciprocate, but only in part, not universally. For example: If all pleasure is good, some good thing is pleasure. But this conversion is drawn from the condition of genus and species, and it clearly pertains not to the nature of propositions but to the topics of arguments, in which it is taught that what the genus belongs to, the species belongs to as well; but what the species belongs to, the genus belongs to only in part. The same reasoning applies to: If every just thing is good, some good thing is just; if every man is an animal, some animal is a man.

units.la: Quod est Tertium? Ut Enuntiatio particularis affirmatiua necessariò reciprocetur. veluti, Si quędam voluptas est bona, quoddā bonum est voluptas. Est enim hæc non Enuntiationis natura, sed Argumentatio ex genere & specie superiori simillima. non secus atque illæ in scholis usitatę: Si quędam fortitudo virtus est, quædam virtus est fortitudo. Si quoddam iustum bonum est, quoddam bonum iustum est. Si quidam amor est obscœnus, quiddam obscœnum est amor. quasi vero alterum de altero eodem modo prædicetur, quomodo Attributum de subiecto prædicari dicitur.
units.tr: What is the third? That a particular affirmative proposition reciprocates necessarily. For example: If some pleasure is good, some good thing is pleasure. For this is not the nature of the proposition but an argument from genus and higher species, very like those commonly used in the schools: If some courage is a virtue, some virtue is courage; if some just thing is good, some good thing is just; if some love is obscene, some obscene thing is love. As if, indeed, one thing were predicated of another in the same way as an attribute is said to be predicated of a subject.

units.la: Quid? Nónne superiùs dixisti, Affectiones quasdā reciprocationem admittere? Dixi. sed hoc nihil adhanc [?] nostrā subiecti in attributū, aut attributi in subiectum vicissitudine. quę est eiusmodi, ut cùm quæritur, quid fit Subiectū, aptè respondeatur Attributū: & vicissim hoc de illo. At in illis reciprocatio nihil aliud est quàm unius ad alteram affectio, relatio, habitus. veluti, Ut pater dicitur pater filij: sic filius dicitur filius patris. At neque qui pater est, dicitur filius: neque hic, ille. Sic discendi facultas est hominis proprium. sed neque homo præcisè definitur doctrinæ capax: neque doctrinæ capax homo. Proprium enim nō est totum, sed pars duntaxat. Itaque doctrinæ capax non adæquat vocabulum homo: sed cōiunctè definitur Animal doctrinæ capax. Sic rectè dicetur: Si sol lucet, dies est. Si dies est, sol lucet. Sed non natura Enuntiationis reciprocantis illa est, verū argumentatio ex cauffis & effectis. Et quamuis urgeri possit, hæc inter fe conuerti: Vt lux solis, est dies: sic dies est lux solis: tamen perspicuum est, hanc esse definitionem, & definitum: sed eam non verā & solidam, sed ex caussis & effectis adumbratam: de quarum vtraque nunc est differendi locus.
units.tr: What then? Did you not say above that certain affections admit reciprocation? I did. But this has nothing to do with our interchange of subject into attribute or attribute into subject, which is of such a kind that when one asks what the subject is, the attribute is aptly given in answer, and conversely. In those other cases, however, reciprocation is nothing other than the affection, relation, or condition of one thing to another. For example: as one is called father of a son, so the son is called son of the father. Yet neither is whoever is a father called a son, nor the other way round. So the capacity for learning is a property of man; but man is not defined precisely as capable of learning, nor is the capable of learning man. For a property is not the whole but only a part. Hence "capable of learning" does not match the word "man"; rather it is defined jointly as "animal capable of learning." So it will rightly be said: If the sun shines, it is day; if it is day, the sun shines. But this is not the nature of a reciprocating proposition; it is an argument from causes and effects. And although it could be urged that these convert with one another, as the light of the sun is day, so day is the light of the sun, it is nevertheless clear that this is a definition and the defined, but not a true and solid one; it is only sketched out from causes and effects. Of both of these we must now discuss the place.

units.la: De vera & propria Definitione.
units.tr: On the true and proper Definition.

units.la: CAP. XIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIV.

units.la: Q[?]VONIAM igitur de priore Enuntiationum genere fatis dixisti, deinceps de ea dicamus, quam principem & Reginam omnium superiùs appellasti.
units.tr: Since you have said enough about the first kind of proposition, let us next speak of the one you called the prince and queen of them all.

units.la: Quid est Definitio? Oratio (inquit Cicero) quæ id quod definitur explicat quid fit. Et alibi, Oratio quæ quid fit id de quo agitur explicat quàmbreuissimè. Item, Oratio quæ complicatam animi notionem euoluit. Item, quæ inuolutæ rei notionem aperit. Item, quæ quasi inuolutum euoluit, id de quo quæritur. Item, quæ inuolutam animi notionem explicat. Ité, est quasi patefactio rerum opertarū, cùm quid quidque fit, aperitur. Item,quæ aperit notionem nostram quam habemus, de re definiéda tectam atque inuolutam. Itaque sæpe ab Aristotele dicuntur omnes scientiæ ex definitione oriri. ἄσσα αἱ ὁρισμοῖ (inquit) δὲ ὁρισμὸς γίνονται.
units.tr: What is a definition? "A speech," says Cicero, "which explains what the thing defined is." And elsewhere: "a speech which explains, as briefly as possible, what the matter under discussion is." Likewise: "a speech which unfolds a complex notion of the mind"; "which reveals the notion of a thing that is enfolded"; "which unfolds, as it were, what is enfolded and under inquiry"; "which explains a notion of the mind that is wrapped up"; and again, it is "as it were an unveiling of hidden things, when it is disclosed what each thing is"; and "which reveals our notion of the thing to be defined, which is covered and enfolded." So Aristotle often says that all sciences arise from definition: "all the sciences," he says, "arise from definitions" [ἐκ τῶν ὁρισμῶν αἱ ἐπιστῆμαι γίνονται].

units.la: Quæ est materia Definitionis? Quoniam definitio mentis & rationis opus est, ratio autem & scientia in rebus singulis non versatur, in quibus sensus occupati sunt: sequitur vt definitio ad species tantùm aut certè ad ea genera quæ intermedia sunt, adhiberi possit: ἀεὶ γὰρ ὅρος καθόλου, inquit Aristoteles. In diuiduorum verò & singularum rerum nulla definitio est. quippe cùm earũ (vt modò dixi) scientia nulla fit. nulla autem idcirco scientia est, quia & infinitę & fluxę atque caducæ sunt. Itaq; quæ de Socrate fingi definitio potest, eadem etiam in omnes homines valet. Summa autem genera idcircò definiri non possunt, quia quæque res (vt mox intelliges) ex suo genere definitur.
units.tr: What is the matter of a definition? Since definition is the work of the mind and reason, and reason and science do not deal with individual things, which the senses occupy, it follows that a definition can be applied only to species, or at least to those genera that are intermediate. For Aristotle says: "A definition is always of the universal" [ἀεὶ γὰρ ὅρος καθόλου]. There is no definition of individuals and single things, since, as I have just said, there is no science of them. And there is no science of them because they are infinite, fluctuating and perishable. Thus whatever definition can be framed of Socrates holds also for all men. The highest genera, however, cannot be defined, because each thing (as you will soon understand) is defined through its own genus.

units.la: Quotuplex definitio est? Prima diuisio hæc est, vt alia sit rei, alia dictionis. nam cùm definitio sit oratio, quæ declarat τί ἐστι, sequitur (inquit Aristoteles) vt etiam sit oratio demonstrans, quid nomē significet: aut λόγος ἕτερος ὀνο-ματώδης: id est altera oratio nomen explicans: cuiusmodi est qua docetur quæ sit vis & significatio verbi Triangulum: quam tamen ad notationem propius quàm ad definitionem pertinere, fatis alio loco demonstratum est.
units.tr: How many kinds of definition are there? The first division is this: one kind is of a thing, another of a word. For since a definition is a speech that declares what a thing is [τί ἐστι], it follows, as Aristotle says, that there is also a speech that shows what a name signifies, or "another speech explaining a name" [λόγος ἕτερος ὀνοματώδης]. Such is the speech which teaches what the word "triangle" means and signifies. This, however, has been sufficiently shown elsewhere to belong more to notation than to definition.

units.la: Quæ est altera definitionis diuisio? Hæc bipartita quoque est: vt altera fit solida (quæ à Græcis οὐσώδης, vulgò Essentialis dicitur: qua de caussa sola substantia, nullum accidens definiri potest) altera adumbrata, quæ ab illis {*} συμβεβηκὸς dicitur, à nostris accidentalis.
units.tr: What is the other division of definition? This too is twofold. One kind is solid, which the Greeks call οὐσώδης and which is commonly called essential; for this reason only a substance, and no accident, can be defined by it. The other is sketched or outlined, which the Greeks call συμβεβηκός and we call accidental.

units.la: Quæ est solida definitio? Ariftoles sic explicat, ὅρος μὲν λόγος ὁ τὸ, τί ἐστι σημαίνων. quod Boëtius ita cóuertit. Est oratio quid fit, esse significans. fortasse planius ita poterit: Oratio quæ demonstrat, quid fit esse hoc. Quod ab illo acutissimè dictum sic accipiendū est, quasi dixisset: Oratio respondens ad quæstionem quid fit esse hoc. Nam qui quærit quid fit, vi ipsa quærere videtur, quid fit esse hoc. Quære autem quid fit esse hoc, nihil aliud est, quàm quærere cur ita res fit. Itaque (vt idem alio loco docuit) definitio quæ docet quid res fit, & ea quæ docet caussam cur res fit, eadem est. nofle enim quid fit, & cur res fit, idem sunt.
units.tr: What is a solid definition? Aristotle explains it thus: "A definition is a speech signifying what a thing is" [ὅρος μὲν λόγος ὁ τὸ τί ἐστι σημαίνων]. Boethius translates this: "a speech signifying what it is to be." It may perhaps be put more plainly: "a speech which shows what it is to be this." This must be understood as the most acute saying of his, as if he had said: "a speech answering the question, what is it to be this." For he who asks what a thing is seems by the very force of the question to ask what it is to be this. But to ask what it is to be this is nothing other than to ask why the thing is so. Hence (as he teaches elsewhere) the definition which tells what a thing is and the one which tells the cause why a thing is are the same. For to know what a thing is and why it is are the same.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Sumatur illud ipsum quo Ariftoteles vtitur: Quid est Eclypfis lunæ? Desectio luminis ex terræ interpofitu. Quamobrem luna deficit? quia lumen eius terræ interceptu obscuratur. Item, Quid est Tonitru? Est restinctio ignis innube. Cur tonat? quoniam ignis in nube oppressus extinguitur.
units.tr: Let me give an example. Take the very one Aristotle uses: What is an eclipse of the moon? A loss of light caused by the interposition of the earth. Why does the moon fail? Because its light is cut off and darkened by the interception of the earth. Again: What is thunder? It is the extinguishing of fire in a cloud. Why does it thunder? Because the fire, pressed down in the cloud, is put out.

units.la: Quin tu igitur planius Ariftotelis definitioné explicas? Definitio est oratio, quæ quid fit, & quale fit id de quo ambigitur, proprie, aperte, ac breuiter enuntiat. Neque enim ex sola essentia satis intelligitur, quid sit esse hoc, vel cur ita sit: sed qualitas insuper exponenda est. Itaque veteres eam veram esse definitionē dixerunt, quæ ex genere & differentia constaret: quoniam genus respondetur ad quæstionem quid est: differentia vero ad quæstionem quale est. Ea vero demum differētia sunt, quæ definitione differunt. Scitū est enim illud Aristotelis, neque diuersarū rerum vnā definitionem, neque vnius rei diuersas definitiones, esse posse. ὅτε γὰρ ἕν ἐστι δυοῖν, ὅτε δύο τῶν ἀπλῶν [?] [?] Denique genus non est tota speciei substantia. non enim solum genus sine differentia speciem format, vt neque sola differentia sine genere: sed tamen interdum accidit, vt qualitates aliunde quam ex differentijs exponendæ sint: cum aut vera qualitas ignota est, aut non sufficit. tum igitur aut proprietates aut accidentia, aut caussas, pro supplemento adhibemus.
units.tr: Why not explain Aristotle's definition more plainly, then? A definition is a speech which states, properly, clearly and briefly, what a thing is and what sort of thing it is, about which there is doubt. For from essence alone it is not sufficiently understood what it is to be this, or why it is so; the quality must be set out as well. Accordingly the ancients said that the true definition is the one that consists of genus and difference, since the genus answers the question "what is it?" and the difference answers the question "what sort of thing is it?" Those are differences which distinguish one definition from another. Aristotle's saying is apt: there cannot be one definition of different things, nor different definitions of one thing. [ὅτε γὰρ ἕν ἐστι δυοῖν ...] Finally, the genus is not the whole substance of the species. For the genus alone does not form the species, any more than the difference alone does without the genus. Yet it sometimes happens that qualities must be explained from elsewhere than from the differences, when either the true quality is unknown or it is not sufficient. Then, as a supplement, we use either properties, or accidents, or causes.

units.la: Quid? Definitionis quæ ratio est, & quæ via? Non dubium est (inquit Cicero) quin definitio genere declaretur, & proprietate quadam, aut etiam communium frequentia (id est multitudine) ex quibus proprium quid sit, el[?] ceat. Genus igitur primum quærendum est, dein quæ in eo genere aliorum erunt communia definitione circunscribenda sunt, vt quasi definita regio sit, quæ terminis septa teneatur. Nā quæ definitione conueniunt, i. quorū eadem definitio est, eadem omnino sunt. Itaque quia Cicero in libro de Fato Logicam definit artem differendi, aliis autem locis Dialecticā totidem verbis definit: rectè concludetur, Dialecticam & Logicam idē esse, ac solo vocis sono differre.
units.tr: What, then, is the method and the way of definition? "There is no doubt," says Cicero, "that a definition is declared by genus and by some property, or even by a number of common features [that is, a multitude], from which it may be gathered what is proper to the thing." So first the genus must be sought; then whatever else in that genus is common to others must be marked off by the definition, so that the thing is like a defined region, enclosed by boundaries. For things that agree in definition, that is, whose definition is the same, are altogether the same. Therefore, since Cicero in his book On Fate defines logic as the art of disputing, and elsewhere defines dialectic in the same words, it will be rightly concluded that dialectic and logic are the same and differ only in the sound of the word.

units.la: Vnde dicitur definitio? Quoniam id de quo ambigitur certis finibus, & quasi cancellis circunscribit, ut à reliquarum communitate disiungatur, & proprium efficiatur. Itaque à Græcis ὅρος & ὁρισμός dicitur: quia definitio in disputationibus sic adhibetur, ut in agris & regionibus limites sive termini, aut sepes undique circumscriptæ. Nanque definitio, Geographorum & Agrimensorum propria est.
units.tr: Whence is the word "definition" derived? Because it marks off, by fixed boundaries, as it were by a lattice, the matter in question, so that it is separated from the community of the rest and made its own. Hence the Greeks call it horos and horismos, because in disputations definition is used as limits or boundaries in fields and regions, or hedges fenced around on all sides. For definition is properly the business of geographers and land-surveyors.

units.la: Cedo exemplū. In Geographia peruulgatum est huiusmodi. Italia est regio quæ terminatur & à septentrione & ab occasu, Alpiū iugis: ab ortu Adriatico, mari: à meridie, mari Siculo. Sicilia est insula, cinēta à septentrione & occasu mari Thyrreno, à meridie Afro, ab ortu Adriatico. Sardinia,quæ ab occasu mari Thyrreno, à meridie Africo ab occasu & septentrione Sardo cingitur.
units.tr: Let me give an example. In geography this sort of thing is very common: Italy is a region bounded on the north and the west by the ridges of the Alps; on the east by the Adriatic Sea; on the south by the Sicilian Sea. Sicily is an island, surrounded on the north and west by the Tyrrhenian Sea, on the south by the African Sea, and on the east by the Adriatic. Sardinia is girt on the west by the Tyrrhenian Sea, on the south by the African Sea, and on the west and north by the Sardinian Sea.

units.la: Cedo exemplum definitionis Dialecticæ.
units.tr: Let me give an example of a dialectical definition.

units.la: Homo est animal rationis particeps, mortale. Nam animal,genus: mortale,differētia est hominem ab Angelis separans. Rationale, item altera,eundē à belluis distinguens. Quod si ad sepimentū absoluendū substantialis differētia non sufficit,tum supplementum(vt ante dixi) vel ex proprio, vel ex accideti, vel ex utroque sumendum est.
units.tr: Man is a mortal animal partaking of reason. For "animal" is the genus; "mortal" is the difference separating man from the angels. "Rational" is another difference, likewise distinguishing him from the beasts. But if the substantial difference is not enough to complete the enclosure, then, as I said before, the supplement must be taken from the property, or from the accident, or from both.

units.la: Cedo itē aliud exemplū: Equus est animal quadrupes, quod collo & dorso domatur. Hæc Enuntiatio in asinos & mulos convenit. Itaque quod sæpimento deest, ex proprietate sumendum erit: Hinniendi vim habens.
units.tr: Let me give another example: The horse is a four-footed animal, tamed by the neck and back. This statement also fits asses and mules. So what the enclosure lacks must be taken from a property: having the power of neighing.

units.la: Cedo exemplum ex Accidenti. Pygmæus est homo perexiguæ staturæ. Hæc Enuntiatio etiam in Nanos & Pumiliones valet. Itaque ex accidenti supplementum quærendum est: Qui in vltimis Indiç[?] finibus nascitur: vel, Qui dorsis hircorum insidens, cum gruibus belligeratur. Item ex cōtrario: Gigas est homo ingenti corporis magnitudine. Hoc idem Germanis Cæsar tribuit. supplementum ergo ex Accidenti petendum est: præter vsitatam naturæ consuetudinem.
units.tr: Let me give an example from an accident. The pygmy is a man of very small stature. This statement also holds for dwarfs and little men. So the supplement must be sought from an accident: one who is born at the farthest limits of India; or, one who sits on the backs of goats and fights with cranes. Likewise by contrast: a giant is a man of enormous bodily size. Caesar attributes this same thing to the Germans. So the supplement must be sought from an accident, beyond the customary course of nature.

units.la: Cedo exemplū ex utroque. Asinus est animal quadrupes, quod collo & dorso domatur, rudendi vim habens. Hæc definitio etiā in mulos conuenit. Quorum autem eadem definitio est, eadem iudicantur.
units.tr: Let me give an example from both. An ass is a four-footed animal, tamed by the neck and back, having the power of braying. This definition also fits mules. But things that have the same definition are judged to be the same.

units.la: Quid igitur si ex accidenti supplementum addatur: Quadrupes vegrandibus auriculis? At hoc ipsum in mulos quoque conueniet. Ad datur[?] igitur illud, Fœcūdum. à communione recessum erit. illa autem quæ à nonnullis traditur: Animal solidis pedibus auritū & fœcun-dum dum:fi quidem auriti equi non sunt, propria fortasse iudicabitur.
units.tr: What then if a supplement is added by way of accident: "a four-footed animal with long ears"? But this too would apply to mules. Therefore that addition "fertile" would be a departure from what is common; while the definition given by some, "an animal with solid hooves, eared and fertile," will perhaps be judged a proper one, provided that eared horses do not exist.

units.la: Quomodo ex Caussis supplementum quaeritur? Tyrannicida est percussor, qui Tyrannum interfecit: hoc idem in carnificem conuenit, qui traditum sibi Tyrannum interfecerit: aut in eum qui deprehensus ab eo in adulterio ipsum interfecerit. Ergo praeter genus & imperfectam differentiam, caufla adhibenda est, Qui cofulto Tyrannum occidit, ut Remp. liberaret.
units.tr: How is a supplement sought from causes? A tyrannicide is one who kills a tyrant: the same applies to the executioner who kills a tyrant handed over to him, or to the man who kills someone caught in adultery with his wife. Therefore, besides the genus and the incomplete difference, a cause must be added: one who deliberately kills a tyrant in order to free the commonwealth.

units.la: Quid? In genere asciscendo, ecquanam uti arte debebimus? Illa notionum disciplina ac serie, quam superius demonstrauimus: quae cum naturalem gradationem habeat, fatis erit primam asciscere, neque altius a capite, repetere oportebit. Nam (ut Ariftoteles in Topicis admonuit) qui proximum genus posuit, is etiam superiora omnia posuisse intelligitur. quadoquidem (inquit) in inferioribus ea quae supra sunt, intelliguntur. vis autem & natura cuiusque rei cum proximo genere, coniuncta est.
units.tr: What of the choice of genus: what art should we use here? The discipline and order of notions which we demonstrated above; since it has a natural gradation, it will be enough to take the first, and it will not be necessary to go back further from the head. For (as Aristotle warned in the Topics) whoever has posited the nearest genus is understood to have posited all the higher ones too, since (he says) in the lower things those that are above are understood. The force and nature of each thing, moreover, is joined to its nearest genus.

units.la: Et in qualitate reperienda quanam utemur arte? Sicuti sursum ad Categoriam afcenden do, effentia reperitur, sic vicissim deorsum defcendendo reperitur qualitas. veluti, fiquis de Murena quaerat, qualis haec substantia fit, refpondebitur corporata. tum quale est corpus? animatum, quale animal? piscis. qualis piscis? murena. Quis est definiendi modus? Cùm ea sumuntur quæ sunt ei rei, quam definire volumus, cũ aliis communia: idque usque cò persequimur, dum proprium efficiatur, quod nullam in aliam rem transferri possit. sic enim Aristotelis præceptum, Latinè Cicero expressit: quod etiam Plato in Theeteto tradiderat. Exemplum autem superiùs exposuimus.
units.tr: And in finding the quality, what art shall we use? Just as the essence is found by ascending upward to the category, so conversely the quality is found by descending downward. For example, if someone asks what kind of substance a moray eel is, the answer will be: a body endowed with life; then, what kind of body? an animate one; what kind of animal? a fish; what kind of fish? a moray. What is the mode of defining? It is this: one takes those things which belong to the thing we wish to define, even those shared with others, and pursues this until it becomes proper, so that it cannot be transferred to any other thing. For Cicero expressed in Latin the precept of Aristotle in this way, which Plato had also handed down in the Theaetetus. We have set out an example above.

units.la: Quid? Nunquámne genus prætermitti potest? Tum demum omitti genus potest, cùm ex definitionis verbis satis intelligitur. Sed ea nõ exacta & limata definitio est, veluti, Orator est qui quacunque de re copiosè disserit. Subauditur enim, homo. Procurator est, qui aliena negotia mãdatu domini administrat: pro, Est administrator negotiorum alienorum.
units.tr: What then? Can the genus never be omitted? The genus can be omitted only when it is sufficiently understood from the words of the definition. Yet such a definition is not exact and polished, as for instance: "An orator is one who speaks copiously on any subject." For "man" is understood. "A procurator is one who administers the affairs of another by mandate of the owner," in place of "is an administrator of the affairs of others."

units.la: De Definitione adumbrata, sive minus propria. CAP. XV.
units.tr: On the Adumbrated, or Less Proper, Definition. CHAP. XV.

units.la: QVAE est Definitio adumbrata? Quæ non solidam rei naturam ex genere & differentiis, sed extrinsecus notas ipsius quasi demonstrat: quasi cùm pictores imaginem informât. Itaque σκιαγραφία[?] Plato in Theæteto appellat. alij etiam [illegible, ~14 letters], ὑπογραφῶ[?]. Latini autem Descriptionem nominant. Sed Boetius omnes eius modi descriptiones aptè Allusiones appellat.
units.tr: What is an adumbrated definition? It is one that does not set out the solid nature of a thing through genus and differences, but only sketches its external marks, as painters do when they outline an image. For this reason Plato, in the Theaetetus, calls it skiagraphia [σκιαγραφία]. Others also call it hypographē [ὑπογραφή]; [illegible]. The Latins, however, call it descriptio. Boethius, though, aptly calls all such descriptions allusions.

units.la: Quænam illæ externæ notæ sunt? Quæ ex aliis affectionibus, quàm ex genere sumptæ sunt.Nam quæ per translationem & aliis ludicris modis fiunt, vt cùm Adolescentia definitur flos ætatis: Induciæ, feriæ belli: Peccare, trâfire lineas:nos eas Allusiones potius,quàm Definitiones appellamus.
units.tr: What are those external marks? They are drawn from affections other than the genus. For things done by metaphor and other playful devices, as when adolescence is defined as the flower of life, a truce as a holiday from war, or sinning as crossing the lines, we call these allusions rather than definitions.

units.la: Quæ est Definitio ex formis? In qua species omnes continentur, quæ sub eo genere sunt, quod definitur. velut apud Ciceronem: Iniuria est quæ aut pulsatione corpus, aut conuicio aures,aut aliqua turpitudine vitam alicuius violat. Item, Gloria est illustris ac peruagata multorum & magnorum vel in suos ciues, vel in patriam, vel in omne genus hominum fama meritorum. Item,Ineptus dicitur, qui aut tempus quid postulet, non videt:aut plura loquitur: aut se ostentat, aut eorū quibuscumeft vel dignitatis, vel commodi rationem non habet:aut denique in aliquo genere aut inconcinnus,aut multus est. Item, Nothus est,qui vel ex concubina, vel ex meretrice, vel ex virgine, vel ex vidua honestæ existimationis, vel ex adultera, vel ex cognata susceptus est.Item,Sacrilegium est surripere aliquid sacri,aut ex sacro.
units.tr: What is a definition by forms? It is one that contains all the species that fall under the genus being defined. For example, in Cicero: "Injury is whatever violates a person's body by a blow, his ears by abuse, or his life by some disgrace." Likewise: "Glory is the far-spread and widely known praise of great and many deserts, earned either towards one's fellow citizens, one's country, or the whole human race." Likewise: "A person is called inept who either does not see what the time requires, or talks too much, or shows off, or pays no regard to the dignity or advantage of those with whom he deals, or, in short, is either clumsy or overdone in some kind of conduct." Likewise: "A bastard is one born of a concubine, of a prostitute, of a maiden, of a widow of good repute, of an adulteress, or of a cousin." Likewise: "Sacrilege is stealing something sacred, or from what is sacred."

units.la: Quæ est definitio ex Toto & Partibus? Definitio per Partitione fit (inquit Cicero) cùm res proposita quasi in membra discerpitur: id est cùm Totius partes enumerātur, ex quibus res definita constat.veluti: Domus est,quæ fundamento, parietibus, contignatione, & tecto constat. Orator est (inquit Cicero) qui quæcunque res inciderit,quæ fit dictione explicanda, prudenter,& compositè & ornatè & memoriter dicat, cum quadam etiam actionis dignitate. Senator est,qui quibus rebus Reipu.utilitas paretur, augeatúrque, tenet, iisque utitur.Dialectica est,quæ ex cuiusque rei & vocabuli affectione diuidendi, definiendi & argumentandi rationem commonstrat. Hic enim genus omissum est. Eodem pertinet definitiones quæ partium enumeratione & remotione fiunt,veluti:Plebs est(inquiunt Iurisconsulti) ceteri ciues sine senatoribus.Argentum factum (inquit Vlpianus) recte quis ita definierit,quod neque in massa,neque in lamina, neq; in signato, neque in suppellectili, neque in mundo,neque in ornamentis fit.
units.tr: What is a definition from the whole and its parts? Cicero says a definition is made by partition when the thing proposed is, as it were, torn into its limbs; that is, when the parts of the whole are listed, of which the thing defined consists. For example: "A house is that which consists of foundations, walls, floor-beams, and roof." Cicero says: "An orator is one who, whatever matter comes up that must be explained in speech, speaks wisely, in an orderly and ornate way, and from memory, and with a certain dignity of delivery as well." "A senator is one who holds and uses those means by which the welfare of the commonwealth is secured and increased." "Dialectic is that which sets out the method of dividing, defining and arguing, from the properties of each thing and of each word." Here the genus has been left out. To the same kind belong definitions made by enumerating and removing parts, for example: "The commons are (the jurists say) the other citizens apart from the senators." Ulpian says: "One may rightly define silver as that which is made neither in a mass, nor in a plate, nor in coin, nor in household furniture, nor in ornament."

units.la: Quæ est definitio ex Causis? In qua pro genere & differentia causla[?] vna plurésve pronuntur. veluti ex Efficiente: Sonus est collisio duorum corporum. Item,Dies est sol super terrā, Lex est mes[?] à cupiditatibus libera. Ex materia:Ira est ebullitio sanguinis. Vox est ictus sensibilis qui auditur quantū in ipso est.Dialectica est ars eius sermonis qui in interrogando & respondendo versatur, vt Stoici definiebat. Ex forma: Homo est,quod animo præditum, ratione utitur,Ex fine:Homo est, quod ad colendum in terris Deum, natum est. Domus est tectum, quo & frigorum vis pellitur, & calorum molestiæ sedantur. Dialectica est ars vera & falsa diiudicandi:ut Zeno definiebat.
units.tr: What is a definition from causes? It is one in which one or more causes are stated in place of the genus and the difference. For example, from the efficient cause: "Sound is the collision of two bodies." Likewise: "Day is the sun above the earth." "Law is reason free from desires." From the matter: "Anger is the boiling of the blood." "Voice is a sensible impulse which is heard, so far as it is in itself." "Dialectic is the art of that discourse which is conducted by question and answer," as the Stoics defined it. From the form: "Man is that which, endowed with a soul, uses reason." From the end: "Man is one born to worship God on earth." "A house is a roof by which the force of cold is driven off and the discomforts of heat are soothed." "Dialectic is the art of distinguishing the true from the false," as Zeno defined it.

units.la: Quid? Definitio ex materia & forma simul nonnè solida & essentialis est: cùm & illæ formæ sine controuersia rei substantiâ attingant: & quemadmodum superius ex Aristotele dixisti, definitio quid res sit, & cur res sit, idem sint?Ita vulgò traditur. sed non si essentia demonstratur, continuò etiam qualitas exponitur, deinde plerunque aut genus aut differentia prætermittitur, aut certè non proximum genus,
units.tr: What then? Is a definition from matter and form together not solid and essential? For those forms too touch the substance of the thing beyond dispute; and, as you said earlier from Aristotle, the definition of what a thing is and of why it is are the same. So it is commonly taught. But if the essence is shown, the quality is not therefore also set out at once; and then, for the most part, either the genus or the difference is omitted, or at least the nearest genus is not given.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Glacies est aqua gelu concreta. hæc definitio est ex materia, forma & efficiente, in qua tamen genus non demonstratur: cùm aqua substantia sit, glacies accidens, glacies igitur est cóncretio aquæ congelatæ. sic Homo est corpus animatū. Hæc descriptio materiam quidem & formam demonstrat: sed & remotius genus assciuit, & differentiam prætermisit. Item vt illa Ciceronis in Academicis: Dialectica est oratio ratione conclusa. Et illa Aristotelis: Tonitru est restinctio ignis in nube, cùm paulò pòst plenius ita definiat: Est strepitus oppressi & extincti ignis in nube. Item illa, Nix est aqua congelata & concreta. Cœnum terra humore temperata. nam neque cœnum terra est (inquit idé) neque nix aqua.
units.tr: Give me an example. "Ice is water congealed by frost." This definition is from matter, form and efficient cause, yet the genus is not shown in it; since water is a substance and ice an accident, ice is therefore a congealing of frozen water. So too: "Man is an animate body." This description does indeed show matter and form, but it assumes a more remote genus and leaves out the difference. Likewise is that of Cicero in the Academics: "Dialectic is discourse closed by reason." And that of Aristotle: "Thunder is the extinguishing of fire in a cloud," though a little later he defines it more fully thus: "It is the noise of fire pressed down and quenched in a cloud." Likewise that: "Snow is water congealed and frozen." "Mud is earth tempered with moisture." For, says the same author, mud is not earth, nor snow water.

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplum. Panis est farina aquæ mixta, & à pistore vescendi causa coćta. Hæc descriptio & materiam & formam, & efficientem, & finem complectitur. at non genus neque differentiam. Vera enim hæc definitio est,Panis est cibus ex farina & aqua coctus. Item :Cervisia est aqua cum hordeo & lupulo decocta:cùm fit potus ex iis rebus confectus.
units.tr: Give me another example. "Bread is flour mixed with water and baked by the baker for the sake of eating." This description takes in the matter, the form, the efficient cause and the end, but not the genus or the difference. The true definition is: "Bread is food baked from flour and water." Likewise: "Beer is water boiled with barley and hops," since it is a drink made from those things.

units.la: Cedo item aliud. Eloquentia (inquit Cicero) nihil aliud est, nisi copiosè loquens sapientia. Ex efficiente, materia & forma hæc definitio est. At illa ex genere: Est facultas sapienter & copiosè loquendi.
units.tr: Give me yet another. "Eloquence," says Cicero, "is nothing other than wisdom speaking copiously." This definition is from efficient cause, matter and form. But the one from the genus is: "It is the faculty of speaking wisely and copiously."

units.la: Quæ est definitio ex Effectis? Quæ ex eventu rem arguit. veluti: Pater est, qui filium procreauit. Rhetorica est, vis persuadendi, & animos auditorum in quam velis partem contorquendi. Homicida est, qui fecit quid sciens, per quod perire homini necesse esset: ait Fabius. Honestum est, ait Cicero, quod per seipsum potest iure laudari. Dialectica est (inquit idem) quæ efficit, ne cui falsò assentiamur, neve unquam captiosa probabilitate fallamur.
units.tr: What is a definition from effects? It is one that proves a thing from its outcome. For example: "A father is one who has begotten a son." "Rhetoric is the power of persuading, and of turning the minds of hearers towards whatever side you wish." "A murderer is one who knowingly does something through which a man must necessarily die," says Fabius. "The honourable," says Cicero, "is that which can rightly be praised for its own sake." "Dialectic," says the same author, "is that which keeps us from assenting to anything falsely, and from ever being deceived by captious plausibility."

units.la: De reliquis generibus definitionum.
units.tr: On the other kinds of definitions.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: QVAE est Definitio ex Proprio? Hæc duplex est, quarum prior ad rem pertinet, altera ad notationem. Ad rem, veluti: Magnes est lapis, qui ferrum ad se allicit. Hæmatites lapis, qui sanguinem sistit. Homo est animal pudoris ac verecundiæ particeps. Adamas est gemma, quæ neque ferro, neque igne, neque vetustate consumitur. nam[?] in his omnibus abest differentia. Atque ex hoc genere omnes propè sunt definitiones apud Medicos, arborum, herbarum, & fruticum.
units.tr: What is a definition from the property (ex Proprio)? It is of two kinds. The first concerns the thing itself, the second concerns the name. A definition concerning the thing: for example, "The magnet is a stone that draws iron to itself." "Haematites is a stone that stops blood." "Man is an animal that shares in modesty and shamefastness." "The diamond is a gem that is consumed neither by iron, nor by fire, nor by age." For in all these examples the differentia is lacking. And almost all definitions of trees, herbs and shrubs in the medical writers belong to this kind.

units.la: Quænam ex Notatione definitio est? Quæ vocabuli originem exponit per ἐτυμολογίαν, quam Cicero veriloquiū appellat: veluti, Seruus est qui seruitutem feruit. Sic enim veteres definiebant. Item, Præuaricator est (inquit Cicero) qui in contrariis caussis, quasi varié positus esse videtur, quoniam à varicibus nomen deductum est. Item, Philosophia est studium sapientiæ. Assiduus dicitur ab ære dando, is qui locuples est. Quid est aliud tumultus (inquit Cicero) nisi perturbatio tanta, vt maior timor oriatur? vnde etiam nomen ductum est Tumultus. Pratū est (inquit Vlpian.): in quo ad fructum percipiendum, falce duntaxat opus est, quasi paratum.
units.tr: What is a definition from the name (ex Notatione)? It is one that sets out the origin of a word by etymology [ἐτυμολογία], which Cicero calls the "true-speaking." For example: "A slave is one who endures servitude (servitus)." For this is how the ancients defined. Likewise: "A prevaricator (praevaricator) is," says Cicero, "one who, when he is in opposite causes, seems to be placed in a crooked way (varie), since the name is derived from varices (swollen veins)." Likewise: "Philosophy is the study of wisdom." "The assiduus is so called from giving money (aes dando), that is, the one who is wealthy." "What else is a tumult (tumultus)," says Cicero, "except such a great disturbance that a greater fear arises? Whence the word tumultus is also derived." "A meadow (pratum) is," says Ulpian, "that in which only a scythe is needed to gather the crop, as if it were prepared (paratum)."

units.la: Cedo exemplum ex Antecedéti[?]. Seruus est qui vel ex hostibus captus, vel pretio emptus est. Lata culpa est, non intelligere id quod omnes intelligunt. Postliminio reuersus dicitur, qui in bello ab hostibus captus fuerat. Bonum est (inquibat[?] Cicero) quod natura est absolutum.
units.tr: An example from the antecedent: "A slave is one who has been taken captive from the enemy or bought for a price." "Gross negligence is failing to understand what everyone understands." "One is said to have returned by postliminium who had been taken captive by the enemy in war." "Good," says Cicero, "is that which is complete in its nature."

units.la: Cedo exemplum ex consequenti. Cicero in Partitionibus hoc exemplum profert: Præuaricator dicitur, qui cùm accusator esset, ab reo corruptus est. nàm ea litera de accusatore dari soletiudici[?]: hoc est notæ in tabella A. P. Accusator præuaricatus est. Ex eodem genere illa definitio est, Hereditas est successio in universum ius defuncti. Prius enim ius est succedendi, quàm ipsa successio. Seruus est, qui si manumittatur, fiet libertinus. Addictus est, qui si libertatem accipiat, erit ingenuus.
units.tr: An example from the consequent: Cicero in the Partitiones offers this example: "A prevaricator is one who, when he was the accuser, was bribed by the defendant." For that letter (A) is usually given to the judge concerning the accuser; that is, the mark on the tablet, A. P., "The accuser has prevaricated." From the same kind is the definition: "An inheritance is succession to the whole right of the deceased." For the right of succeeding comes before the succession itself. "A slave is one who, if he is manumitted, will become a freedman." "An addictus is one who, if he receives his liberty, will be freeborn."

units.la: Cedo exemplum ex Adiunctis. Pirata (inquit Cicero) non est ex perduellium numero definitus: sed communis hostis omnium. Tyrannus est, cuius manus contra omnes, & cotra quem manus omnium.
units.tr: An example from adjuncts: "A pirate," says Cicero, "is not defined as one of the number of public enemies, but as the common enemy of all. A tyrant is one whose hand is against all, and against whom the hand of all is raised."

units.la: Cedo exemplum ex Accidenti. Homo est animal bipes, implume, quod erectum ingreditur. Itaque cùm hanc Plato definitione protulisset, postridie Diogenes, gallum gallinaceum implumem in conuentum attulit. Item illud: Homo est in quo pietas & impietas, probitas & improbitas inesse possunt.
units.tr: An example from an accident: "Man is a two-footed, featherless animal that walks upright." And so when Plato had put forward this definition, the next day Diogenes brought a plucked cockerel into the assembly. Likewise that: "Man is one in whom piety and impiety, uprightness and wickedness can be present."

units.la: Cedo exemplum ex paribus. Cicero ad Herennium hoc protulit: Modestia est in animo continens moderatio cupiditatum. At alibi: Iustitia est aequitas, ius unicuique tribuens. Item alibi: Amare nihil aliud est nisi eum ipsum diligere, quem ames, nulla utilitate quaesita. Item: Par est quod in omnes aequabile est. Item: Pax est tranquilla libertas. Atque haec quidem omnia Ciceronis sunt. Illa autem Iurisconsultorum: Intestatus est non tantum qui testamentum non fecit, sed etiam cuius ex testamento hereditas adita non est. Paria enim sunt testamentum non fecisse, & irritum atque inane fecisse.
units.tr: An example from equals: Cicero put forward this in his To Herennius: "Moderation is a steady restraint of the desires in the mind." But elsewhere: "Justice is equity, giving each person his right." Likewise elsewhere: "To love is nothing other than to cherish the very person whom you love, with no advantage sought." Also: "Equality is that which is even among all." Also: "Peace is free tranquillity." All these are of Cicero. But this one is from the jurists: "One is intestate not only who has not made a will, but also one whose inheritance under a will has not been entered upon." For not having made a will and having made one that is void and null are equivalent.

units.la: Cedo exemplum ex Simili. Stulte quid est somnus, gelidæ nisi mortis imago? inquit Ouidius. Magistratus est lex loquens. Lex magistratus mutus. Ira furor breuis est. Tyrānus est, lupus rabiosè ouiculas dilanians. Amicus est alter idem.
units.tr: An example from the similar: "Foolishly, what is sleep, if not an image of chill death?" says Ovid. "The magistrate is a speaking law; the law is a silent magistrate." "Anger is a brief madness." "A tyrant is a wolf savagely tearing the little sheep."  "A friend is another self."

units.la: Cedo exemplum de Contrariis. Cicero in Partitionibus hoc profert: Quoniam Accusator is dicitur verus, qui ab reo corruptus non est: præuaricator quoque dicatur is accusator, qui ab reo corruptus est. Item, Nothus est, qui iustus filius non est. Concubina est, quæ iusta vxor non est. Virtus est vitium sugere: & Sapientia prima stultitia caruisse. Purus locus est (inquit Vlpianus) qui neque sacer, neque sanctus, neque religiosus est.
units.tr: An example from contraries. Cicero in the Partitiones offers this: "Since he is called a true accuser who has not been bribed by the defendant, so also that accuser should be called a prevaricator who has been bribed by the defendant." Likewise: "A bastard is one who is not a lawful son." "A concubine is one who is not a lawful wife." "Virtue is to flee vice," and "Wisdom is first to have been free from folly." "A pure place," says Ulpian, "is one that is neither sacred, nor holy, nor religious."

units.la: Cedo exemplum ex Relatis. Pater est, cui est filius. Dominus est, cui serui subsunt. Imperator, cui exercitus paret.
units.tr: An example from correlatives: "A father is one who has a son." "A master is one to whom slaves are subject." "A commander (imperator) is one whom an army obeys."

units.la: Cedo exemplum ex Priuantibus. Securitas est vacuitas ægritudinis. Nox est defectio lucis. Voluptas est vacuitas doloris. Quoniã misericordia est (inquit Cicero) ægritudo ex alterius rebus aduersis: sit inuidentia ægritudo ex alterius rebus secundis.
units.tr: An example from privatives: "Security is the absence of distress." "Night is the failure of light." "Pleasure is the absence of pain." For since pity is (says Cicero) distress at another's adverse circumstances, so envy is distress at another's prosperous circumstances.

units.la: Cedo exemplum ex Aientibus & Neganti-bus. Virtus est quod in vitio non est. Lauda-bile est, quod vituperari non potest. Ciuis est, qui peregrinus non est.
units.tr: An example from affirmatives and negatives: "Virtue is what is not in vice." "Praiseworthy is what cannot be blamed." "A citizen is one who is not a foreigner."

units.la: Cedo exemplum ex Repugnantibus. Natus est qui non mortuus editus est: inquit Iurifcõfultus. nam ut viuens mortui contrarium est, sic viuentis natus est consequens. Amicus est, qui non male de quopiam meretur. Hostis est, qui non bene de quopiam mcretur[?]. Peregrinus est, cui honorum capiendorum ius nō est. nam honores capere, civis est consequens.
units.tr: An example from opposites: "One who has been born is one who was not born dead," says the jurist. For just as being dead is the contrary of living, so being born is the consequence of living. "A friend is one who does not deserve ill of anyone." "An enemy is one who does not deserve well of anyone." "A foreigner is one who does not have the right to hold offices." For to hold offices is the consequence of being a citizen.

units.la: Cedo exemplum ex disparibus. Virtus est medium vitiorum utrinque reductum: quod in habitu disparium exposuimus. Liberalitas est quæ inter avaritiam & prodigalitatem interiecta est.
units.tr: An example from unequals: "Virtue is the mean between vices, brought back on both sides; which we set out in the treatment of disparates in the habit." "Liberality is that which lies between avarice and prodigality."

units.la: Cedo exemplum ex Dissimili. Inducię sunt (inquit Varro) pax castrensis paucorum dierum[?]. Bellum enim manet, pugna cessat.
units.tr: An example from the dissimilar: "A truce," says Varro, "is a camp peace of a few days. For war remains, while the fighting ceases."

units.la: De præceptis Definitionis. CAP. XVII.
units.tr: On the Precepts of Definition. CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: QVOT[?] sunt præcepta Definitionis Tria. Ut sit propria, brevis & aperta. Nam (ut Cicero scribit) Definitio est earum rerum quæ sunt eius rei propriæ quam definire volumus, brevis & circumscripta quædam explicatio. ac sæpe commemorandum est axioma illud Aristotelis in hoc genere præstantissimum: neque una duarum rerum, neque unius rei duas definitiones esse posse. ἔτε γὰρ ἕνα δυοῖν, ἔτε δύο τῷ αὐτῷ ὁρι[?]σμὸν δυνατὸν εἶναι[?]. Nam cum unius rei una natura lit[?], quæ definitione explicatur, rectissimè à Galeno scriptum est: ἐνεςι ϖαμπόλλης ὁεισμὸς ϖοιεῖ[?] ἑνὸς πράγματος ἐν ταῖς φωναῖς μόνον ἃ [?] ἐν τοῖς νοήμασι [?] διαφέροντας. licet plures vnius rei definitiones conficere vocibus tantum differentes, non notionibus.
units.tr: There are three precepts of definition: that it be proper, brief and clear. For, as Cicero writes, a definition is a brief and bounded explanation of those things which belong to the thing we wish to define. And that saying of Aristotle, most outstanding in this kind, should often be recalled: that one thing cannot have two definitions, nor two things one definition [ἔτε γὰρ ἕνα δυοῖν, ἔτε δύο τῷ αὐτῷ ὁρισμὸν δυνατὸν εἶναι]. For since one thing has one nature, which is explained by its definition, Galen wrote most rightly that it is possible to make many definitions of one thing which differ only in words and not in meanings [ἔνεστι πολλοὺς ὁρισμοὺς ποιεῖν ἑνὸς πράγματος ἐν ταῖς φωναῖς μόνον διαφέροντας].

units.la: Quomodo propria efficitur Definitio? Cùm ei soli quod definitur, peculiariter cõuenit, neque in aliud vllum transferri potest. Quorum enim eadem definitio est, hæc nimirû eadem sunt. Veteres hoc appellarùt Definitum & definitionē inter se conuerti, & reciprocari: cùm de quo vnum dicitur, de eodem quoque alterum dici potest. quia neque definitio aliud est, quàm definitum: neque definitum, aliud quàm definitio. Itaque quod Zeno de Dialectica & Rhetorica dixit, cùm illam pugno, hanc palmæ similem esse demonstrabat, idem de definito & definitione statuere possumus. Re namque sunt eadem, sed alterum inuolutum, alterum evolutum est, veluti: Quatuor sunt bis bina: & vicissim, Bis bina sunt quatuor. Quatuor sunt tanquam pugnus: Bis bina sunt tanquam manus diducta & dilatata.
units.tr: How is a definition made proper? When it belongs peculiarly to the thing defined alone and cannot be transferred to anything else. For things whose definition is the same are certainly the same. The ancients called this the definiendum and the definition as being convertible and reciprocal: whatever is said of the one can also be said of the other, since a definition is nothing other than the thing defined, and the thing defined is nothing other than its definition. So what Zeno said about dialectic and rhetoric, when he showed that the one was like a clenched fist and the other like an open palm, we may also apply to the definiendum and the definition. They are the same in substance, but one is folded up and the other unfolded, as: "Four is twice two," and conversely, "Twice two is four." Four is like a closed fist; twice two is like a hand opened and spread out.

units.la: Cedo item aliud. Aemulatio est ægritudo, ex eo quod alter potiatur eo, quod ille ipse cupierit. Hæc Enuntiatio etiam alterius speciei communis est, quæ est Obtrectatio. Itaque non reciprocantur inter se. Non enim quicquid est ægritudo, id continuò est æmulatio. Addendum est igitur, ut eo ipse careat. Sic Equus est quadrupes, qui dorso & collo domatur. commune mulorum, asinorum, elephantorum & Camelorum. Adde, Et hinniendi vim habet: reciprocabitur. quia quicquid erit quadrupes eiusmodi, erit equus. & vicis-sim quicquid erit equus, erit huiusmodi quadrupes. Sic illa definitio, Diuinatio est earum rerum prædictio & præsensio quæ sunt fortuitæ: reprehenditur apud Ciceronem lib. de Diuin. i r.[?]quia & medici & imperatoris & gubernatoris est præsensio rerum fortuitarum. Sic definitio illa generis ex schola Stoicorum à Laertio tradita, Genus est plurium notionum collectio: minus plena videtur. Deest enim Communium, aut Cognatarum: vt superiùs in Generis definitione diximus.
units.tr: Here is another example. Envy is distress arising from the fact that another enjoys what that very person has desired. This statement also applies to another species that is common to it, which is detraction; so they do not reciprocate. For not everything that is distress is at once envy. So it must be added that the envious person lacks that thing himself. Thus: "A horse is a four-footed animal, tamed by the back and neck," is common to mules, asses, elephants and camels. Add "and has the power of neighing," and it will reciprocate: whatever is a four-footed animal of this kind will be a horse, and conversely whatever is a horse will be a four-footed animal of this kind. Likewise that definition, "Divination is the foretelling and foreknowing of those things which are chance events," is criticised in Cicero, De divinatione, book 1, because the foreknowing of chance events also belongs to the physician, the general and the helmsman. Likewise the definition of genus handed down by Laertius from the school of the Stoics, "A genus is a collection of several notions," seems less complete. For it lacks "of common or related [notions]," as we said above in the definition of genus.

units.la: Quomodo breuis efficitur definitio? Cùm ita pressa & angusta est, vt nullum in ea verbū otiosum, aut redundans appareat. Stulta est tamen breuitatis affectatio (vt Aristoteles in Rhetoricis monuit) nisi quantū satis est adhibeatur. nam & breuitas est (ait Cicero) cū tantum verborum est, quantum necesse est. Id autem fiet si & è proximo finitimum genus petatur (nam proximo sumpto, inquit Aristo-teles, satis constat, superiora antecedere) & vbi satis processum erit, ibi consistatur, neque vlterius prodeatur.
units.tr: How is a definition made brief? When it is so compressed and tight that no word in it appears idle or superfluous. Yet an affectation of brevity is foolish (as Aristotle warned in the Rhetoric) unless it is used only as far as is enough. For brevity, Cicero says, is when there are only as many words as are necessary. This will happen if the nearest neighbouring genus is sought (for, as Aristotle says, when the nearest is taken, it is clear enough that the higher ones come before it), and when enough progress has been made, one stops there and does not go further.

units.la: Cedo exemplum ex Genere. Vt si Equus non definiatur, corpus animatum, sed animal. Iustitia non habitus animi, sed virtus.
units.tr: Here is an example from the genus. If a horse is defined not as an animated body but as an animal. Justice is not a habit of the mind but a virtue.

units.la: Cedo exemplum ex Productione. Homo est animal rationis particeps, natum ad disciplinam.Nam hoc Proprio sublato, plena erit definitio, reíque naturam omnem complectetur. Equus est(inquit Quintilianus) animal,mortale, irrationale,hinnies. Nam Quadrupes quæ dorso & collo domatur,erat præsius.Sic idem ita Dialecticam definit: Est rei propositæ propria,dilucida, & breuiter comprehensa verbis Enuntiatio.Nam cùm Enuntiatio nihil aliud sit,quàm verborum comprehensio,duo illa verba superuacanea sunt. Sic Equus est (inquit idem)animal mortale,irrationale,hinniens: nam & altius genus repetitum est, & quadrupedum prætermissa differentia.
units.tr: Here is an example from the production (of the definition). "Man is an animal partaking of reason, born for learning." For when this proper feature is removed, the definition will be complete and will embrace the whole nature of the thing. "A horse," says Quintilian, "is a mortal, irrational, neighing animal." For "a four-footed animal tamed by the back and neck" was superfluous. Likewise the same writer defines dialectic in this way: it is a statement proper to the matter proposed, clear, and comprehended in few words. For since a statement is nothing other than a comprehension of words, those two words are superfluous. Thus, he says, "A horse is a mortal, irrational, neighing animal": for both the genus was repeated too high up, and the difference of four-footed was omitted.

units.la: Quomodo apertà efficitur Definitio? Cũ inuoluta rei notio sic euoluitur, vt nihil non apertum atque explicatum remaneat. Nam cùm definitio cognoscéde[?] rei causa tradatur, vt ad breuitatem nihil redundare oportet, sic ad perspicuitatem nihil deesse. Itaque dilucida & illustris definitio tum efficitur, cùm definitio & definitũ pariter inter se respondent, & alterum alteri sic adæquatur, vt paria in vtranque partem momenta sint. Vitium autem admittitur, cùm aut obscura interpretatio ponitur,aut minus quàm necesse est, adhibetur.quod tum fit, cùm pro totius definitione partis definitio ponitur.
units.tr: How is a definition made clear? When the notion of the thing, which is folded up, is so unfolded that nothing remains unclear or unexplained. For since a definition is handed down for the sake of knowing the thing, it ought to contain nothing superfluous for brevity, and nothing lacking for clarity. So a definition is made lucid and illustrious when the definition and the definiendum correspond equally to each other, and the one is so matched to the other that the weights are equal on both sides. A fault occurs, however, when either an obscure explanation is given, or less is used than is necessary, which happens when a definition of a part is put in place of a definition of the whole.

units.la: Cedo exemplum obscuritatis in definiendo vitádæ.Sumatur illud Pacuuij, apud quem cùm quæsitũ esset, quid esset Testudo, respondetur,Quadrupes,tardigrada,agrestis, humilis,aspera,capite breui,ceruice anguina, aspe &tu truci,Euiscerata,inanima,cum animali sono.vel illud : Quid est Cochlea? est bestia terrigena, herbigrada, domiportă, & sanguine cassa.
units.tr: Here is an example of obscurity to be avoided in defining. Take that passage of Pacuvius, in which, when it was asked what a tortoise is, the answer was: a four-footed slow-walking, rustic, low, rough creature, with a short head and a snake-like neck, a viper and a fierce asp, disembowelled, lifeless, with the sound of an animal. Or that one: What is a snail? It is an earth-born beast, creeping on herbs, carrying its house, and bloodless.

units.la: Cedo exemplum Partis pro Toto definitæ. Aristoteles hoc profert : Grammatica est ars bene scribendi:addendū est enim ( inquit ille)& legendi. Ex hoc genere illa vulgata est Dialectica est ars bene differédi,& vera ac salsa diiudicádi. Sic énim Cicero de Oratore 11. definit. At hæc definitio eius est solius partis propria,quæ ad componendam argumentū conclusionem pertinet,idest ad iudicium& dispositionē:quod Cicero libro de Fini.111, his ostendit verbis : Cúmque duæ sint artes, quibus perfectè ratio & oratio compleatur, vna inueniendi,altera differendi,&c. Differendi autem verbum Stoicorum Dialecticæ proprium fuisse videtur : qui(vt posterius intelliges)longa verborum serie & cōtinuatione argumentationes suas texebant ac retexebant quam formam Soritem,id est aceruum appellabant. quanquam rectè differendi artem Cicero dixisse Latinè videtur,pro eo quod Grædicere solebăt [illegible, ~7 letters] ὀρϑῶς διαλέγεσθαι[?]. Sed rursus idem in Topicis Artem diligenter differendi generatim ad utrãque Argumentationis partem retulit. Cùm omnis ratio difgens differendi(inquit)duas habeat partes:vnam inveniendi, alteram judicandi.
units.tr: Here is an example of a part defined for the whole. Aristotle offers this: "Grammar is the art of writing well"; for, he says, "and reading" must be added. From this kind is the commonly quoted: "Dialectic is the art of disputing well, and of distinguishing the true from the false." For so Cicero defines it in De oratore, book 2. But this definition belongs peculiarly to only one part, that which concerns the composition of the argument and its conclusion, that is, to judgement and arrangement. Cicero shows this in book 3 of De finibus, in these words: "And since there are two arts by which reason and speech are completed perfectly, one of discovering and the other of disputing," and so on. Now the word "disputing" seems to have been peculiar to the Stoic dialectic, who wove and rewove their arguments in a long series and continuous chain of words, and called this form the Sorites, that is, the heap. Although Cicero seems to have said in Latin "the art of disputing" rightly, in place of what the Greeks used to call "to converse correctly" [ὀρθῶς διαλέγεσθαι]. But again, in the Topics the same Cicero carefully referred the art of disputing, in general, to each part of argumentation: "Since all method of disputing," he says, "has two parts: one of discovery, the other of judgement."

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplū. Aemulatio est ægritudo ex eo quod alter potiatur eo quod ille ipse concupierit: Nam hæc in obtrectatione convenit definitio. Itaque nondum satis explicatum est quod erat involutum. Addendum igitur, Cùm ipso careat. Sacrilegium est surripere aliquid sacri. Nondum satis explicatum est, deest enim, Aut ex sacro. Ex eodem genere illa Ciceronis in Partitionibus: Argumentum est probabile inventum ad faciendam fidem. Nam in lib. de Invét. II. plenius definierat, inventum aliquam in rem probabile, aut necessarium.
units.tr: Here is another example. Envy is distress arising from the fact that another enjoys what that very person has desired. For this definition agrees with detraction.
