So what was involved has not yet been explained enough. Therefore add: "while himself lacking it." "Sacrilege is the stealing of something sacred." This has not yet been explained enough: for "from what is sacred" is lacking. Of the same kind is Cicero's definition in the Partitions: "An argument is a probable invention for producing belief." For in book 2 of De inventione he had defined it more fully, as an invention, probable or necessary, concerning some matter.

units.la: De materia Dialectica. CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: On the Matter of Dialectic. Chapter XVIII.

units.la: M[?]ULTAS vero & varias definitionum formas exposuisti: sed tamen ad certum affectuum numerum accommodatas. Quid deinceps sequitur? Superest ut de Argumentatione differamus. Sed antequam longius abeamus, monendus mihi videris, vitandam eorum esse opinionem, qui scripserunt definitionem & divisionem esse opus Physici, & eius scientiæ proprium, quæ prima rerum principia tradit. à quo definiendi & dividendi artem Dialectica mutuatur. Quasi vero Theologi aut Jurisconsulti artis suæ divisiones ac definitiones ex Physicorum disciplinis hauriant. Intelligendum est igitur, Dialecticam non aut materiam vllam esse, aut certum aliquod habere ac definitū genus, in quo solo versetur, atque occupata sit: sed instrumentum esse, quo artium omnium materiæ ordine ac ratione certa tractentur. qua de causa ὄργανον[?] à Græcis appellatur. quoniam neque Theologi, neque Physici, neque Medici, neque Iurisconsulti, neque aliarum artium professores suas disciplinas sine illius adiumento tractare possunt. Quod ex Grammaticæ artis similitudine intelligi s. Nam vt illa nullam sibi propriam habet subiectam materiam, sed ceteris disciplinis omnibus orationem atque ptam verborum consecutionem suppeditat, sine qua mutæ omnino essent: ita Dialectica non in vna aliqua re versatur, sed artibus reliquis omnibus instrumenta suppeditat: quibus vel confusa diuidere, vel infinita definire, vel ambigua diiudicare possint.
units.tr: You have set out many and varied forms of definition, but all of them fitted to a fixed number of kinds. What follows? It remains for us to discuss argumentation. But before we go further, I think I must warn you to avoid the opinion of those who have written that definition and division are the work of the natural philosopher and belong to that science which delivers the first principles of things, and from which Dialectic borrows its art of defining and dividing. As if theologians or jurists drew the divisions and definitions of their art from the teachings of the natural philosophers! We must understand, then, that Dialectic is neither some matter nor has a certain defined kind of its own in which it alone is engaged and occupied. Rather, it is an instrument by which the matters of all the arts are handled in an orderly and sound method. For this reason the Greeks call it ὄργανον [organon]. Neither theologians, nor natural philosophers, nor physicians, nor jurists, nor practitioners of the other arts can handle their disciplines without its help. This can be understood from the likeness of the art of grammar. For just as grammar has no subject matter of its own, but supplies all the other disciplines with speech and the correct arrangement of words, without which they would be altogether mute, so Dialectic does not engage with any one thing, but supplies the other arts with instruments by which they can divide what is confused, define what is infinite, and decide what is ambiguous.

units.la: Teneo ilta: viderisque eandem fere materiæ infinitatem Dialecticæ tribuere, quam Crassus Rhetoricæ tribuit apud Ciceronem in lib. de Orat. 1. vbi disputat Oratoris opus se omni de re, quæcunque fit proposita, ornate copioséque dicere. vt siue Physicus de natura, siue Architectus de ædificando, siue Medicus de curandis morbis, siue Astrologus de syderibus, siue Iurisconsultus de ciuili iure disputet, si modo id ornatè copioséque faciat, verborum quidem proprietatem à Grammatica, ornatum verò & splendorem orationis
units.tr: I grasp those points. And you seem to assign to Dialectic almost the same boundless range of matter that Crassus assigns to Rhetoric in Cicero's De Oratore book 1, where he argues that it is the task of the orator to speak on any subject that is put before him, and to speak with ornament and fullness: so that whether the natural philosopher discourses on nature, or the architect on building, or the physician on the curing of diseases, or the astrologer on the stars, or the jurist on civil law, provided he does so with ornament and fullness, he borrows from Grammar the correct use of words, but from Rhetoric the ornament and brilliance of speech.

units.la: Rhetorica mutuentur. Atque ut de nostra hac dicamus, ordinem ac certam rationem à Dialectica recte accipies: quare licet jam ad cetera quæ consequuntur, pergamus.
units.tr: Rhetoric. But, to speak of this our own art, you will rightly take the order and sound method from Dialectic. Therefore, let us now proceed to the remaining matters that follow.

units.la: FINIS II. LIBRI.
units.tr: END OF BOOK II.

units.la: INSTITVTIONIS DIALECTICAE LIB. III.
units.tr: The Third Book of the Dialectical Institution

units.la: De argumento, & Argumentatione.
units.tr: Of the argument and of argumentation.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAP. I.

units.la: QUID est Argumentatio? Regula qua vera & falsa diiudicātur. Est enim ratio qua utrum vera an falsa enuntiatio fit, idest utrum attributum in enuntiatione subiecto cōveniat, an non conveniat, ostenditur: quasi cùm adhibita lydia coticula aurum ab ære, probus numus ab adulterino discernitur.
units.tr: What is argumentation? It is the rule by which true and false are judged. For it is the reasoning by which it is shown whether a statement is true or false, that is, whether the attribute in the statement agrees with its subject or does not. It is like gold being distinguished from copper, and genuine coin from counterfeit, when the Lydian touchstone is applied.

units.la: Quotuplex est Argumentatio? Prima & summa diuisio est huiusmodi: Argumentatio altera est simplex, quæ una ratiocinatiua enuntiatione constat. Ratiocinatiuam appello, quæ implicatam in se ratione complectitur. veluti: Quia spiritum ducit, vivit. Si lac habet, perit. altera composita, quæ ex pluribus Enuntiatis evidentem rationem demonstrantibus coniuncta est. veluti: Qui spiritum ducit, vivit. Hic spiritum ducit-vivit igitur. Sicenim Cicero libro de Inventione primo scribit. Argumentatio nomine uno duas res significat:ideo quod & inuentum aliquam in rem probabile aut necessarium, Argumentatio vocatur. & eius inuenti artificiosa expolitio. quando igitur proferent aliquid huiusmodi: Quoniam peperit, cum viro concubuit: inuentum proferent,non expolitionem. Et aliquanto post, Simplex autem conclusio reprehenditur, siid quod sequitur, non videatur necessario cum eo quod antecessit,cohærere.nam hoc quidé, Si spiritum ducit,viuit: Si dies est, lucet:eiufmodi est, ut cum priore necessario posterius cohærere videatur,&c. Sic Antonius lib. de Orat.II. Nam & omne quod eloquimur, sic, ut aut esse dicamus,id,aut non esse: & si simpliciter dictum sit,suscipiũt Dialectici, ut iudicet, verúmne sit an falsum. & si coniunctè sit elatum, & adiuncta sint alia, iudicent recténe adiuncta sint, & veráne sit summa uniuscuiusque rationis.Sed distinguendi & vitandae ambiguitatis causa placuit illam priorem Argumentum,hanc Argumentationem appellari. :
units.tr: How many kinds of argumentation are there? The first and chief division is this. One kind is simple, consisting of a single reasoning proposition. I call a proposition "reasoning" when it contains an implied reason within it, as: "Because he draws breath, he lives"; "If he has milk, he perishes." The other kind is composite, joined together from several propositions that set out an evident reason, as: "He who draws breath lives; this man draws breath; therefore he lives." For so Cicero writes in the first book of On Invention. The word "argumentation" signifies two things: both the discovered matter, probable or necessary, that is established about some question, and the artful elaboration of that discovery. So when people put forward something like "Since she has given birth, she has lain with a man," they are putting forward the discovery, not the elaboration. A little later he says: a simple conclusion is faulted if what follows does not seem to cohere necessarily with what went before. For this kind of thing, "If he draws breath, he lives; if it is day, it is light," is such that the latter seems necessarily to cohere with the former, and so on. So Antonius, in the second book On the Orator: "For whatever we utter, we say either that a thing is or that it is not. If it is stated simply, the dialecticians undertake to judge whether it is true or false; if it is uttered in conjunction with other things added, they judge whether the additions are rightly made and whether the sum of each reasoning is true." But for the sake of distinction and avoiding ambiguity, it has been agreed that the former is called the argument and this the argumentation.

units.la: Quomodo? Quoniam idem in Topicis & Partitionibus scribit: Argumentum esse probabile inuentum ad faciendam fidem: vel rationem,quae rei dubiae facit fidem. Argumentationem autem esse argumenti expositionem, tractationem, conclusionem,expolitionem. Aristoteles ἀποδείξιν[?], hoc est demonstrationem, appellat: opinor, quia suppressam & inuolutā: in argumento rationem demonstrat, patefacit,& in lucem profert, vt euidenter eluceat. Itaque quoties aliqua earum particularū quibus ratio exponitur, in oratione sumitur: veluti, Quia,quoniam,cùm,quando,quádoquidem:toties argumentum vsurpatum intelligitur.item,cùm particula Si,apponitur. nam in veris Enuntiationibus,Si pro Quia(vt in proverbio est)positum intelligitur.
units.tr: In what way? Because he writes the same in the Topics and the Partitions: an argument is a probable discovery for producing belief, or a reason that makes a doubtful matter believable. Argumentation, however, is the setting out, handling, concluding and elaborating of the argument. Aristotle calls it demonstration [ἀπόδειξιν], I suppose because it brings out and reveals the reason that is hidden and folded up within the argument, so that it shines forth clearly. Therefore, whenever one of those particles by which a reason is expressed is used in speech, as quia, quoniam, cum, quando, quandoquidem, the argument is understood to be in use. Likewise when the particle si is added; for in true statements si is understood as standing for quia, as the proverb has it.

units.la: Velim hæc aliquanto planius adhibita definitione & certa aliqua regula exponas. Esto igitur argumentum omnis enuntiatio,quæ rationis vnius firmamento nititur. Argumentatio verò enuntiatio duplex:quæ non modò ratione, sed etiam rationis ratione constat.meministi enim illud Ciceronis: Cuius rationis ratio reddi non potest, ei rationi ratio non est fidem habere.Vnius autem rationis in vnica & simplici enuntiatione quinque notæ sunt: Quia,Cùm,Si,Aut nō Aut,Non & Non. veluti:Quia Callicles homo est,necessario animal est. Hæc autem nota omnes eiusdē generis rationales particulæ comprehenduntur. veluti, Quando,quandoquidem,quoniam &similes. Item, Cùm Callicles sit homo, necesse est esse animal.Si Callicles est homo, necessariò animal est.Aut Callicles homo non est, aut certè est animal. Non & Callicles homo est, & animal non est.'
units.tr: I would like you to explain these things a little more plainly, with a definition applied and some fixed rule. Let an argument, then, be any statement that rests on the support of a single reason. An argumentation, however, is a double statement, one that consists not only of a reason but of the reason of that reason. For you remember that saying of Cicero: "For a reason of which no reason can be given, there is no ground for trusting that reason." Now a single reason in a single simple statement has five marks: quia, cum, si, aut non aut, and non et non. For example: "Because Callicles is a man, he is necessarily an animal." All the rational particles of this same kind are comprehended under this mark, for example quando, quandoquidem, quoniam and similar words. Likewise: "Since Callicles is a man, it is necessary that he is an animal." "If Callicles is a man, he is necessarily an animal." "Either Callicles is not a man, or he certainly is an animal." "Not: Callicles is a man, and he is not an animal."

units.la: Cedo exemplum Argumentationis. Quia Callicles homo est,necessario animal est.quicquid enim homo est, necessario animal est. Si Callicles ratione utitur, animal est. quicquid enim ratione utitur, idé est homo. Cicero autem Argumentationem ita definit, Rationem quæ ex rebus perceptis id quod nō percipiebatur adducit. Multis autem locis conclusionis componendæ rationem appellat: vel orationem ratione coclusam: vel necessariam aut probabilem consecutionem.
units.tr: I give an example of an argumentation: "Because Callicles is a man, he is necessarily an animal, for whatever is a man is necessarily an animal. If Callicles uses reason, he is an animal, for whatever uses reason is a man." Cicero defines argumentation thus: "a reasoning which, from things perceived, brings forward what was not perceived." In many places he calls it the reasoning by which a conclusion is composed, or a speech concluded by reason, or a necessary or probable sequence.

units.la: Quæ est secunda diuisio Argumentationis? Hæc, Aristotelis sententia, quadruplex est. διδασκαλικὴ [?], quæ ad docendum & demonstrandum accommodata est, & constat ex propriis cuiusque disciplinæ principiis. ἐλεγκτικὴ [?], quæ utranque contradictionis partem ex probabilibus concludit. πειραστικὴ [?], quæ ad alterum tentandum instituta est, & ex iis quæ aduersario probantur concludit. & ἐριστικὴ [?], id est contentiosa, quæ ex iis quæ probabilia videtur, nec sunt, concludit: quæ tota Sophistarum & impostorum propria est. Trium autem superiorum eadem propemodum ars atque disciplina est, quæ in Dialectica traditur. quare de Dialectica & Sophistica tantum differemus.
units.tr: What is the second division of argumentation? According to Aristotle's view it is fourfold. There is the didactic [διδασκαλικὴ], which is adapted to teaching and demonstrating and consists of the proper principles of each discipline. There is the elenctic [ἐλεγκτικὴ], which concludes both parts of a contradiction from probable premises. There is the peirastic [πειραστικὴ], which is designed for testing another person and concludes from things the opponent grants. And there is the eristic [ἐριστικὴ], that is, contentious, which concludes from things that seem probable but are not; this is wholly the property of sophists and impostors. Of the three former the art and discipline are almost the same, and these are taught in Dialectic. Therefore we shall treat only of Dialectic and Sophistic.

units.la: De Materia, Fine & partibus Argumentationis.
units.tr: On the Matter, End and Parts of Argumentation.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAP. II.

units.la: QUOTUPLEX est Argumentatio Dialectica? Duplex. Altera necessaria, quæ id quod vult efficit necessario: altera probabilis, quæ nihil necessario,
units.tr: How many kinds of dialectical argument are there? Two. One is necessary, and brings about what it aims at by necessity. The other is probable, and concludes nothing necessarily, only probably.

units.la: sed probabiliter tantùm concludit. Sed quæ necessaria est, ea vel Ratiocinatio est, quæ à Græcis συλλόγισμος appellatur: vel inductio, quæ ab isdē ἐπαγωγὴ[?]. quæ verò nihil necessariò concludit, totáque est (meo quidem iudicio) Rhetorica, ea vel exemplo, vel sententia constat: quorum illud à Græcis παράδειγμα, hoc ἐνθύμημα[?] nominatur.
units.tr: Of the necessary kind, one is reasoning, which the Greeks call syllogism [συλλόγισμος], and the other is induction, which they call epagoge [ἐπαγωγή]. What concludes nothing necessarily, and is (in my judgement at least) wholly rhetorical, consists either of example or of maxim. The former the Greeks call paradigm [παράδειγμα], the latter enthymeme [ἐνθύμημα].

units.la: Quæ est materia Argumentationis? Quadruplex. illud quæstionis genus de quo superiùs commemorauimus an sit, quid sit, quale sit, & quæ eius causa sit. Iam verò (eodem auctore Aristotele) quicquid in disputationem cadit, in eo vel generis, vel definitionis, vel proprii, vel accidentis quæstio versatur. Speciei apud Dialecticos quæstio nulla est, quia Species de indiuiduis dicitur, quorum iccirco nulla scientia est, quia (vt superiùs diximus) infinita fluxa & caduca sunt. Differentia autem, quia generis natura imitatur, ad generis quæstionem accommodanda est. Ergo si quæstio est, An sit, aut an ita sit, generis ac differentiæ quæstio est: ac prior ad resolutionem, idest, Analysim, posterior ad diuisionem pertinet: si quid sit, definitionis: si cur ita sit, proprij. Accidentis autem quæstiones ad res externas & fortuitas pertinêt, quæ & accidere & decedere possunt, vt suo loco dictum est.
units.tr: What is the matter of argumentation? It is fourfold. It is that kind of question which we mentioned above: whether a thing is, what it is, what sort it is, and what its cause is. Now (on the same authority of Aristotle) whatever falls into disputation turns on a question of genus, definition, property, or accident. There is no question of species among the dialecticians, because species is predicated of individuals, and there is no science of these, since (as we said above) they are infinite, fleeting and perishable. A difference, however, since it imitates the nature of the genus, is to be treated in the question of genus. So if the question is whether a thing is, or whether it is so, it is a question of genus and difference: the first belongs to resolution, that is analysis, the second to division. If the question is what a thing is, it belongs to definition; if why it is so, to property. Questions of accident concern external and chance things, which can both come and go, as was said in its proper place.

units.la: Quamobrem quatuor tantùm quæstionum genera constituuntur? quia quicquid de alio quæritur, id est quæritur an alteri conueniat, id vel superius est, ac magis universum eo de quo quaeritur: vel certè par eidem. dici enim superius de inferiore non potest. Si superius atque amplius est, generis quaestio est, cùm de rei natura ambigitur: sin minus, accidentis. sin par est, tûc vel proprij est, vel definitionis. Nam si convenire rei nulli alteri potest, vel definitio est, vel proprium: si potest, vel genus est, vel accidens.
units.tr: Why are only four kinds of question set up? Because whatever is asked about something, that is, whether it belongs to another thing, either is superior to and more universal than that about which it is asked, or is equal to it. For what is inferior cannot be said of what is superior. If the predicate is superior and wider, the question is one of genus, when the nature of the thing is in doubt; if not, it is one of accident. If it is equal, then it is either of property or of definition. For if the predicate can belong to no other thing, it is either definition or property; if it can, it is either genus or accident.

units.la: Quæ est altera quæstionum divisio? Ut alia sit infinita, quæ generatim aliquid sine ulla circûstantia interrogat. veluti: An Dialectica sit utilis: An eloquentia sit expetenda: alia finita, quæ de negotio certa aliqua circunstantia definito proponitur. veluti, An Dialectica historico sit utilis. An Bellû hyeme sit gerendum, & in Britannia.
units.tr: What is the other division of questions? One kind is infinite, which asks in general about something without any circumstance, for example: Whether dialectic is useful; whether eloquence is to be sought. The other is finite, which is put about a particular matter with some defined circumstance, for example: Whether dialectic is useful to the historian; whether war is to be waged in winter, and in Britain.

units.la: Quis est finis Argumentationis? Quæstionis explicatio. instrumentum autem explicandæ quæstionis est (ut sæpe jam dixi) ratio cur attributum subiecto cõuenire vel affirmetur, vel negetur. Hæc enim ratio duo quæstionis extrema necessariò inter se vel connectit, vel disparat. Itaque quoniam ad utriusque vel convenientiam vel discrepantiam diiudicandam, quasi Arbiter honorarius adhibetur, Medium appellatur. ut Argumentatio vera ea fit, quæ ea de quibus ambigitur, utrum inter se conveniant an dissideant, necessariò vel convenire vel dissidere ostendit ex eo, quod illa in tertio aliquo, vel conveniunt, vel dissisunt, illustrantur. qua de causa passim argumétatio definitur ratio,quæ ex perspicuis dubia illustrat.
units.tr: What is the end of argumentation? The explanation of the question. The instrument for explaining the question is (as I have often said already) the reason why the attribute is affirmed or denied of the subject. For this reason necessarily connects or separates the two extremes of the question. Therefore, since it is brought in as a kind of honorary arbiter to judge whether the two agree or disagree, it is called the middle term. Thus an argument is true when it shows that the things in doubt, whether they agree with one another or disagree, necessarily either agree or disagree, because they are both illustrated by their agreement or disagreement with some third thing. For this reason argument is commonly defined as a reason which makes clear doubtful things by means of evident ones.

units.la: Ecquænam igitur de Medio axiomata & summæ leges ac regulæ tradi possunt? Nos ad illius Mathematici axiomatis normā has quatuor direximus. I. Cui conuenit mediū, eidem,quod medio cohæret, necessariò conuenit. II. Quod medio cohæret, ei cui medium cōuenit, necessariò cōuenit. III. Quod medio non conuenit, ei cui medium conuenit, non conueniet. IIII. Cui medium non conuenit , ei quod medio conuenit , non conueniet.
units.tr: What axioms, and what supreme laws and rules, concerning the middle term can then be handed down? Taking as our norm that mathematical axiom, we have drawn up these four. I. What the middle agrees with necessarily agrees with whatever the middle coheres with. II. What coheres with the middle necessarily agrees with that to which the middle agrees. III. What the middle does not agree with will not agree with that to which the middle agrees. IV. That to which the middle does not agree will not agree with what agrees with the middle.

units.la: Cedo istarum regularum familiare aliquod exemplum.Esto hoc familiarissimum,ac penè puerile : sed tamen aptissimum. Ponantur in tabula gemini annuli inter se conserti & catenati. proximè alterutrum, magnes. nunquid verum erit,quod modò dicebamus : Cui magneti is annulus qui iam medius est cōueniet, eidem is qui illi cohæret necessariò cōueniet. Simillima est argumētationis ratio. ponatur enim quæstio an Callicles sit animal. Tū quia Callicles est subiectum , animal attributum: Callicles in imo , animal in summo scribatur. Medium interponatur, Homo. Tum ratio ita ineatur:Si Medium , quod homo est, Callicli cōuenit,etiam id quod medio cohæret, nimirum animal,conueniet.
units.tr: Let me give a familiar example of these rules. Let it be a very familiar one, almost childish, but nonetheless most apt. Let two rings, linked and chained together, be placed on a table, with a magnet close to one of them. Will it not be true, as we were just saying, that the ring which is now in the middle agrees with the magnet, and that what cleaves to it will necessarily agree with the same magnet? The method of argument is very similar. Let the question be whether Callicles is an animal. Then, since Callicles is the subject and animal the predicate, write Callicles at the bottom and animal at the top. Interpose a middle term, man. Then the reasoning is set out thus: If the middle, which is man, agrees with Callicles, then that which coheres with the middle, namely animal, will also agree with him.

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplum. Retineatur eadem & quæstio, & verborum trium collocatio directa, malè nanque alij duos terminos in plano collocât, vt medium inter eos interponât. Nam subiectum à Græcis dicitur ὑποκείμενον[?], non autem ἀντικείμενον[?]. Scribátur ergo, Callicles, homo, animal. nónne tria hæc eádem inter se rationem habent, quam habét illi numeri 1. 2. 3? sunt enim indiuiduum, species & genus. Quod igitur notio communis valet in illis numeris, vt in maiore summa minor infit, & pars in toto: idem quoque in illa valeat. vt si vnum est in duobus, duo in tribus, necessario vnum erit in tribus. eodem modo, si Callicles in homine, homo in animali fit, Calliclem quoque in animali esse concludatur. Atque hoc nimirum est quod superius diximus, quæcunque de aliquo dicuntur, ea vel superiora esse, vel paria.
units.tr: Let me give another example. Let the same question and the same direct arrangement of the three terms be kept; for others badly place two terms on a level and interpose a middle between them. For the subject is called in Greek hypokeimenon [ὑποκείμενον], not antikeimenon [ἀντικείμενον]. Write therefore: Callicles, man, animal. Do not these three stand to one another in the same relation as those numbers 1, 2, 3? For they are individual, species and genus. Therefore what the common notion holds good for in those numbers, namely that in a greater sum the lesser is contained, and the part in the whole, let it hold good equally here: so that if one is in two, and two in three, one will necessarily be in three. In the same way, if Callicles is in man, and man is in animal, it is concluded that Callicles is also in animal. And this is indeed what we said above: whatever is said of something is either superior to it or equal to it.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de Pari. Ponatur quæstio, An Pygmęus sit homo. Medium interponatur hominis proprium, vt Rationis particeps. Tū ratio ita ineatur: Si Pygmęus rationis est particeps, quicquid autem rationis est particeps, idem est homo, certè Pygmęus homo est. Cui enim proprium convenit, ei etiam illud cuius id erat proprium, necessario convenit.
units.tr: Let me give an example of the equal. Let the question be: Is a pygmy a man? Interpose a property of man, namely being a partaker of reason. Then the reasoning is set out thus: If a pygmy is a partaker of reason, and whatever is a partaker of reason is a man, then certainly a pygmy is a man. For to whatever a property belongs, to that also whose property it is necessarily belongs.

units.la: De Acernali Stoicorum Conclusione.
units.tr: On the Acernal Conclusion of the Stoics.

units.la: CAP. IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: VID igitur si longior illa verborum catena fit, hoc est longa verborum series & continuatio, quasi catena ex multis annulis inter se cohaerentibus & contextis? Eadem omnino ratio sutura est. Ac nimirum illa ipsa est Stoicorum propria differendi ratio consectaria, de qua pleni sunt Philosophici Ciceronis libri: quam illi propterea Soritem (ut posterius dicemus) id est quasi verborum consequentium acervum ac struem appellabant. Synthesim quoque non minare possumus. Cicero quidem Confectarium appellat. quod etsi Aristoteles secutus non est, eius tamen hanc magneti & catenae nostrae regulam consentaneam initio artis suae Logicae tradidit: Quoties alterū de altero vt de subiecto dicitur, quaecunque de prædicato dicūtur, ea omnia de subiecto quoque dicuntur. ac paulo post breuius: ὅσα κ̓ τῶ καθηγορουμένου λέγεται, ὅσα ... ὑποκειμένου ὑπάρχει [?]
units.tr: Do you see, then, whether that longer chain of words is made, that is, a long series and continuation of words, like a chain of many rings linked and joined together? The method is entirely the same. Indeed, this is the very method of reasoning peculiar to the Stoics, which Cicero's philosophical books are full of. Because of it they called it the sorites (as we shall say later), that is, as it were, a heap and pile of consequent words. We may also not omit the synthesis. Cicero calls it the "confectarium" (conclusion). Although Aristotle did not follow this, he nevertheless delivered at the beginning of his logic this rule, which agrees with our magnet and chain: Whenever one thing is said of another as of a subject, whatever is said of the predicate is said of the subject as well. And a little later, more briefly: [ὅσα κατὰ τοῦ καθηγορουμένου λέγεται, ὅσα ... ὑποκειμένου ὑπάρχει [?]].

units.la: Cedo aliquod longae istius catenae ac synthesis exemplum. Sumatur illa Ciceronis ex Tusc.5. Omne bonum laetabile est: quod laetabile, id praedicandum: quod praedicandum, id gloriosum: quod gloriosum, id laudabile: quod laudabile, id honestum: Ergo quod bonum, honestum. Nam ista ratiocinatione firmamentum illud nostrum comprobatur: Cui magneti annulus unus cohaeret, ei etiam omnes alii qui una cum illo conferti sunt, cohaerebunt: id est, Cui medium convenit, eidem omnia quæ medio cohærent, siue genus, siue species, siue totum, siue pars, siue proprium, siue alius affectus aliquis consentaneus conueniet.
units.tr: Let me give one example of this long chain and synthesis. Take that one of Cicero's from the Tusculan Disputations, book 5: Every good thing is delightful; what is delightful is to be praised; what is to be praised is glorious; what is glorious is laudable; what is laudable is honourable; therefore what is good is honourable. For by this reasoning that little structure of ours is proved: if one ring clings to the magnet, then all the other rings that are linked together with it will cling too. That is: whatever agrees with the middle term, to the same thing will agree all those things that cohere with the middle, whether genus, species, whole, part, property, or some other consequent affection.

units.la: Quidnam igitur inter Aristotelicã & Stoicam argumentandi formam interfuit? Hoc nimirum, quòd Stoici in disputando, synthesin: Peripatetici verò, analysin obseruarunt. Nam Stoici semper ab imo incipiêtes, quam quasi ædificationis totius basim constituebãt, quasi gradibus sursum versus progrediebantur. unde illud Ciceronis: Iam argumenti ratione conclusi caput esse faciũt[?] ea, quæ perspicua dicunt. deinde ordinem sequuntur: tũ quod verum sit in singulis: extrema conclusio est. Aristoteles verò maiorem Medij ratione ducebat, & semper ab eo in quo momentum omne positum est, initium faciebat.
units.tr: What, then, was the difference between the Aristotelian and the Stoic form of arguing? Surely this: that in disputing the Stoics observed synthesis, while the Peripatetics observed analysis. For the Stoics, always beginning from the bottom, which they set down as the base of the whole structure, advanced upwards as if by steps. Hence that saying of Cicero: they make the head of the conclusion those things which they call self-evident; then they follow the order, so that what is true in each part becomes the final conclusion. Aristotle, however, took the major premise from the middle term, and always began from that in which the whole force of the argument lies.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Sumatur ex Cicerone, cuius animadverto longè plures plurésque Stoicas esse argumētationes, quàm Aristotelicas. Is igitur lib.de Fin.iii.ita cócludit: Quod est bonũ, omne laudabile est. quod autem laudabile est, omne honestum est. bonum igitur quod est, honestum est. hæc vera est Synthesis, ab imo, & tanquam basi ad summum fastigiũ progrediens. At illa proprie Analysis, cuius à medio tanquam momento, initium nascitur: Quod est laudabile, est honestum. Quod bonum, est laudabile. Ergo quod bonum est, honestum est. Sed de Medij collocatione plus satis. Posterius enim proprius nobis constitutus est de ea differendi locus. Tantùm harum progressionum figuram hîc describemus, ut earum imaginem animo conceptam memoria tenere possis.
units.tr: Let me give an example. Take one from Cicero, whose works I notice contain far more Stoic arguments than Aristotelian ones. So in book 3 of the De Finibus he concludes thus: What is good is wholly praiseworthy; what is praiseworthy is wholly honourable; therefore what is good is honourable. This is the true synthesis, proceeding from the bottom, as if from the base, up to the summit. But that one is properly analysis, whose beginning arises from the middle, as from the pivot: What is praiseworthy is honourable; what is good is praiseworthy; therefore what is good is honourable. But enough about the placing of the middle term. For we shall have a proper place to discuss this method of arguing later on. Here we shall only set out the figures of these progressions, so that you may keep their image, once conceived in the mind, in your memory.

units.la: Stoica synthesis: quæ est progressio ab imo:
units.tr: Stoic synthesis, which is the progression from the bottom:

units.la: Ariftotelica Ana-lysis à summo progrediens. Honestum 4 Laudabile 3 Bonum Honestum Laudabile 4 Bonum 3 Item: Animal 4 Homo 3 Callicles Animal Homo 4 Callicles 3
units.tr: Aristotelian analysis, proceeding from the top: Honourable 4, Praiseworthy 3, Good; Honourable, Praiseworthy 4, Good 3. Likewise: Animal 4, Man 3, Callicles; Animal, Man 4, Callicles 3.

units.la: In quibus argumentationibus Medium adhibeatur.
units.tr: In which arguments the middle term is to be employed.

units.la: CAP. V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: QVID? Medium in omnibúsne quæstionibus & argumentationibus adhibetur? Nequaquam. sed in iis demum quæstionibus, quæ mente & ratione explicantur: non iis quæ sensibus diiudicantur. Medium enim (ut modò dixi) nihil aliud est, quàm rationis & notionis quæ in hominis mente insita, & mente percepta est, expositio. Itaque Medii natura prius & notius est eo, quod in quæstione ponitur. At quæstionesquæ sensibus iudicantur, nullam in mente notionem, & quasi regulam ante perceptam habent. Quarum autem rerum positum in sensibus iudicii est, ad eas argumentatio non adhibetur: sed ex posterioribus omnes iudicatur.
units.tr: But is the middle term used in all questions and arguments? By no means. It is used only in those questions that are explained by the mind and reason, not in those that are judged by the senses. For the middle (as I have just said) is nothing other than the exposition of a reasoning and notion that is innate in the human mind and perceived by it. So the nature of the middle is prior to and better known than what is put in the question. But questions judged by the senses have no notion in the mind and, as it were, no rule perceived beforehand. Argument is not applied to matters whose judgement lies in the senses; all judgement of them is made from what comes later.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Sumatur aliquod facillimum, & pene puerile. Esto posita quaestio: An ubicunque est arbor, ibi sit radix. Medium est in hac quaestione regula, quae animi notione comprehenditur: Toto concesso partes concedantur. Si est arbor, etiam radix subest. Item, Posito proprio etiam id cuius proprium est, poni intelligitur. Si sermo hic auditur, necessario hic sunt homines: Si lapis iste ferrum allicit, necessario est magnes.
units.tr: Let me give an example. Take some very easy one, almost childish. Let the question be posed: wherever there is a tree, is there a root? The middle term in this question is a rule grasped by the notion of the mind: if the whole is granted, the parts are granted. If there is a tree, a root lies beneath it. Likewise, when a thing is posited, that to which it belongs is understood to be posited too. If this speech is heard, men are necessarily here. If this stone attracts iron, it is necessarily a magnet.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de quaestione fine Medio: Ponatur quaestio, An imperii aliquod sit sempiternum. Assyriorum imperii concidit. Persarum imperium concidit. Medorum item. Graecorum item. Romanorum item. Nullum igitur imperium est sempiternum. Sic Religionē Christianam extinguere non potuerunt, nes commentitiae: non ullae Imperatorum & Regum opes: non Philosophorum doctissimorum disputationes & argutiae: non tyrannorum se[?]va crudelitas. Nullae igitur humanae vires delere Religionem Christianam potuerunt.
units.tr: Let me give an example of a question with no middle term. Let the question be posed: is any empire everlasting? The empire of the Assyrians has fallen. The empire of the Persians has fallen. So too the empire of the Medes. So too the empire of the Greeks. So too the empire of the Romans. Therefore no empire is everlasting. So too, they could not extinguish the Christian religion: neither by fabricated fables, nor by the resources of emperors and kings, nor by the disputations and subtleties of the most learned philosophers, nor by the savage cruelty of tyrants. Therefore no human powers have been able to destroy the Christian religion.

units.la: Quaenam argumentationes Medio adhibito tractantur? Syllogismus & Enthymema. Sorites vero, inductio & exemplum medio non concluduntur.
units.tr: Which arguments are treated with the middle term applied? The syllogism and the enthymeme. The sorites, induction and example, however, are not concluded by means of a middle term.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: JAM profecto Medij istius vim praedicas. Sed unde tandé,cùm usus venerit,eius sumendi nobis facultas erit? Ex iisdem Affectuũ thesauris, ex quibus divisionis & enuntiationis materiam sumpsimus. Iis enim adhibitis intelligitur, quemadmodum quaestionis cuiusque subiectum & attributum inter se affecta sint: & conueniántne inter se, an dissideat: nam quęcunque & quacunque de re poni quaestio potest, eam necesse est per Regulas ex illis locis sumptas diiudicari. & quaecunque & quacunque de re concipi Enuntiatio potest, eam necesse est per illas Regulas vel confirmari vel refutari. Atque ob eam causam τόποι, siue loci, à Dialecticis appellantur, quasi sedes, ex quibus omnium quaestionū argumenta promuntur. Qua eadem de causa Argumentorum fontes à Cicerone appellantur: adeo ut una eademque enuntiatio per illos duos & viginti locos vel cō firmari vel infirmari possit.
units.tr: Now indeed you are praising the power of this Middle. But whence, when the need arises, will we get the means of taking it? From the same storehouses of affections from which we took the matter of division and enunciation. For when these are applied, it is understood how the subject and attribute of any question stand in relation to each other, and whether they agree or disagree. Whatever question can be raised, and about whatever matter, must necessarily be decided by rules taken from those places. And whatever enunciation can be conceived, and about whatever matter, must necessarily be either confirmed or refuted by those same rules. For this reason the dialecticians call them topoi, or places, as it were seats from which the arguments of all questions are drawn. For the same reason Cicero calls them the sources of arguments, so that one and the same enunciation can be either confirmed or weakened through those twenty-two places.

units.la: Quæ est divisio locorum? Aristotelis partitio illa est (inquit Quintilianus) ut alij sint insiti in eo, de quo ambigitur, qui artificiales sunt: nimirum habitus illi, de quibus differendum est: alij assumpti, qui extrinsecus, & non ex arte depromuntur. veluti, Tabulę, testimónia,pacta,conuenta,queftiones,leges, senatusconsulta. Sed hæc nihil ad Dialecticam.Sensibus enim iudicantur, qui rationis sunt expertes.Itaque diuisionem hanc nusquam in logicis libris tradidit Aristoteles, sed in Rhetoricis dūtaxat: vnde,si vsus venerit,depromētur.
units.tr: What is the division of places? Aristotle's partition is this (says Quintilian): some are inherent in the matter under dispute, and these are artificial, namely those habits about which one must discourse; others are assumed, which come from outside and not from art, such as documents, testimonies, pacts, agreements, questions, laws, and decrees of the senate. But these have nothing to do with dialectic, for they are judged by the senses, which have no share in reason. Hence Aristotle never handed down this division in his logical books, but only in the Rhetoric, from which it will be drawn if the need arises.

units.la: Quot in partes tota hæc de Argumentatione doctrina distribuitur? Duas:in artem inueniendi & concludendi:quarum illā Græ-ci Συνθετικῶ[?], vel ὑπερτικῶ[?] : hāc κεςτικῶ[?], vel ἀναλυ-τικῶ appellant.Earum autē qui auctores fuerint,Cicero in Topicis,sed præcipuè in lib.de Finib.4 .demonstrat : Cūmque duæ sint artes (inquit)quibus perfectè ratio & oratio compleatur,vna inueniendi,altera differēdi : hanc posteriorem & Stoici & Peripatetici:priorem autem illi egregiè tradiderunt: hi omnino ne attigerunt quidem.Nam è quibus locis quasi thesauris argumēta depromerentur, vestri ne suspicati quidem sunt:superiores autem artificio & via tradiderunt. Sic Antonius lib.de Orat.I I.In hac(inquit) Stoici Diogenis arte Dialectica nullum est præceptum , quomodo verum inueniatur , sed tantùm est quomodo iudicetur.Hic nos igitur Stoicus iste nihil adiuuat : quoniam quemadmodum inueniam quid dicam, non docet.Quare istam artem totam dimittamus, quæ in excogitandis argumentis muta nimium est:in iudicandis, nimium loquax. Critolaum puto plus huic studio prodesse.Erat enim ab Aristotele.ac paulò ante antè eodem libro Catulus locorum inventionem Aristoteli apertissimè tribuit.
units.tr: Into how many parts is this whole doctrine of argumentation divided? Into two: the art of finding and the art of concluding. The Greeks call the former synthetic [συνθετικῶς] or hypothetic, and the latter critical [κριτικῶς] or analytic [ἀναλυτικῶς]. Cicero demonstrates who the authors of these were in the Topics, but especially in book 4 of De Finibus. Since there are two arts (he says) by which reason and speech are completed, one of finding and the other of disputing, the Stoics and the Peripatetics both handled the latter, while the former was handled admirably by those others (the Peripatetics); the Stoics did not touch it at all. For as to the places from which arguments are drawn, as from storehouses, your people did not even suspect them, whereas the earlier philosophers taught them by method and technique. So Antonius, in book 2 of De Oratore: "In this dialectic of the Stoic Diogenes there is no precept for how the true is found, but only for how it is judged. That Stoic therefore does nothing to help us, since he does not teach how I am to find what to say. Let us then dismiss that whole art, which is too mute in devising arguments and too talkative in judging them. I think Critolaus contributes more to this study, for he came from Aristotle's school." Shortly before, in the same book, Catulus openly attributes the invention of places to Aristotle.

units.la: Quid est ars Inveniendi? Quæ quid quisque affectus ad disputandum valeat, aut non valeat, ostendit. Non enim satis est locos assectuum digito commonstrasse, nisi quæ cuiusque vis & facultas sit, quam in partem valeat, & qualis eorum sit usus,demonstretur. ut medico non satis est magnam aliquam bonorum simplicium (ut vulgò loquuntur) copiam indicasse, nisi quæ cuiusque vis & proprietas sit, & quemadmodum iis uti conveniat, demonstret.
units.tr: What is the art of finding? It shows how much each affection is worth for disputing, or not worth. For it is not enough to point with a finger to the places of the affections, unless it is also shown what the power and faculty of each is, in which direction it is effective, and what its use is. Likewise for a physician it is not enough to have indicated a large supply of simple remedies (as people commonly say), unless he also shows what the power and property of each is, and how it is proper to use them.

units.la: Quid est ars Iudicandi? Quæ quemadmodū queque affectio in argumentatione accommodanda sit, declarat.
units.tr: What is the art of judging? It declares how each affection is to be applied in argumentation.

units.la: Quænam igitur Medii inveniendi ars est? Notatio proprietatis cuiusque loci atque argumenti, quæ longo usu & exercitatione percepta certis regulis comprehensa est. ut cùm ex observatione proprietatis cuiusque stirpis longa experientia notatæ & perceptæ, certæ regulæ colliguntur, quæ literis mandatæ facilem ad condiscendū viam prębent. Nam quæ multis eiusdem generis morbis profuisse stirps animadversa est, eam omnibus consimilibus profuturam inducitur.
units.tr: What, then, is the art of finding the Middle? It is the noting of the property of each place and argument, which, grasped through long use and practice, is comprehended in fixed rules. This is like the way that, from observing the property of each plant, long experience noted and perceived, fixed rules are gathered, which, once committed to writing, offer an easy path to learning. For a plant observed to have helped many diseases of one kind is taken to be going to help all similar ones.

units.la: De Firmamentis, quæ vulgò Maxima ap- pellantur.
units.tr: On the Firmaments, which are commonly called Maxims.

units.la: CAP. VII.
units.tr: CAP. VII.

units.la: VID Simile in locis Dialecticis? Ex multis eiusdem generis, id est eodem ex loco ductis argumentis animadversum est, vim & proprietatem eo loco quandā inesse, quæ certis regulis, & quasi legibus comprehensę sunt. has nonnulli Maximas propositiones, alij Elementa, quidam Locos communes appellarunt. nos vitādæ ambiguitatis caussa Firmamēta nominare voluimus, quòd iis solis quasi fundamentis argumētatio sustineatur, quæ iis subductis corrueret. qua de caussa Cicero in libris Oratoriis eam rationem qua sola caussa nititur, & sine qua stare non potest, passim eodem Firmamēti nomine appellavit.
units.tr: What is the similar thing in the dialectical places? From many arguments of the same kind, that is, drawn from the same place, it has been observed that this place contains a certain force and character, which has been set out in fixed rules, as it were laws. Some have called these the maxim propositions, others the elements, others the common places. For the sake of avoiding ambiguity, I have chosen to call them firmaments, because argument is supported only by these, as by foundations, and would collapse if they were removed. For this reason Cicero, in his books on oratory, often called by the name of firmament that principle on which a case alone rests and without which it cannot stand.

units.la: Cedo aliquod exemplum. Superiūs dictū est, ex innumerabilibus indivi-duis quæ sensū percipiuntur, generis notionem animo concipi: quam ἰδέαν Græci appellant: ut cùm ex multis natantibus animalibus generalis piscis notio concipitur. Eadem harum notionum, & regularum generalium ratio est. Nam siquis totius puta grégis aut armenti dominus est, eum singulorum quoque capitum esse dominum: & qui nauefli totam conduxit, eum navis malum, & transtra & remos, & gubernaculum conduxisse: & cui totus fundus est venditus, ei arbores quoque esse venditas. cui totius frumenti aceruus donatus est, eidem singulos modios esse donatos. Ex infinitis eiusdē modi particularibus, singularibus, individuis,tádem similium inductione (quæ species quædam argumentationis est) generalis hæc regula concepta est : Quod toti convenit, id parti cuique convenit. Cuique totum convenit,ei pars quæque convenit. Itaque cū quæreretur, An ei cui domus oppignerata esset,incensa domo, penitúsque sublata superficie, area tamé oppignerata maneret: eo firmamento adhibito respondebitur,manere. Eius autem notionis(ut itadicam)igniculus in hominis mente propemodum sopitus hoc præceptorum genere accéditur,ut ad Dialecticæ artis usum luceat : nimirum ut cur quidque hoc vel illo modo concludatur, intelligatur. Continet enim,(ut Aristoteles loquitur)τὸ διότι.
units.tr: Let me give an example. It was said above that from the countless individuals perceived by the senses, the notion of a genus is conceived in the mind, which the Greeks call the idea [ἰδέαν]: as when from many swimming animals the general notion of fish is formed. The reasoning behind these notions and general rules is the same. For if someone is the owner of a whole flock or herd, he is also the owner of each single head; and whoever has leased a whole ship has leased its mast, its benches, its oars and its rudder; and to whom a whole estate has been sold, to him the trees also have been sold; to whom a whole heap of grain has been given, to him each single bushel has been given. From infinite particulars, singulars and individuals of this kind, by induction of like cases (which is a certain kind of argument), this general rule is formed: what belongs to the whole belongs to each part; what belongs to every whole belongs to every part of it. Thus, when it is asked whether, if a house has been pledged to someone and the house is burned and its superstructure entirely destroyed, the site nevertheless remains pledged, the answer is given by applying this firmament: it remains. Now the spark of this notion, almost smothered in the human mind, is kindled by this kind of precept so that it shines for the use of the dialectical art, namely so that one understands why each thing is concluded in this or that way. For it contains, as Aristotle puts it, the why [τὸ διότι].

units.la: Suntné certa & rata hæc firmamenta omnia? Non tam profectò quàm cōmunes notiones, aut Mathematicorum theoremata, sive præcepta. Sed tamen non iccirco prætermittenda sunt. non enim regulæ ullæ tā universales sunt, quin exceptione aliqua vitientur: ut Iurisconsulti longo usu periti tradiderunt. sed ut Anaxagoras dicere solebat nomina rebus imponi, non ut usquequaque, sed ut maxima ex parte valeant: sic Regulæ non omni ex parte, sed ex maiore & potiore æstimādæ sunt. Itaque haud scio maiórne sit eorū amétia, qui regulas illas propterea omittēdas censent, an impudētia, qui scribere ausi sunt, nullam earum ab Aristotele mentionem esse factam: cuius in Topicis tam sæpe inculcatæ & decantatę[?] sunt, ut facilè appareat,damnatum ab iis Aristotelem,qui eius libros nunquam aspexerant.
units.tr: Are all these firmaments certain and fixed? Not so surely as common notions or the theorems or precepts of the mathematicians. Yet they are not on that account to be passed over. For no rules are so universal that they are not subject to some exception, as the jurists, skilled through long practice, have taught. But just as Anaxagoras used to say that names are imposed on things not so as to hold good in every respect, but so as to hold good for the most part, so rules are to be judged not as valid in every respect, but by what is greater and more powerful. Accordingly I do not know whether the madness or the impudence is greater of those who think these rules should be omitted for that reason, or who have dared to write that Aristotle made no mention of any of them. In his Topics they are so often inculcated and repeated that it is easily apparent that Aristotle was condemned by men who had never looked at his books.

units.la: Quotuplex singulorum locorum firmamētum est? Omnium ferè locorum triplex est. primum est essentiæ,quam οὐσίαν Græci dicūt, qua respondetur ad quæstionem an sit.sic enim esse in rerum natura,quod quæritur, ex alterius comparatione confirmatur.binorū quippe inter se collatio utriusque essentiam ostendit. Alterum est convenientiæ, quam Græci ἀναλογίαν,Latini proportionem nominat [?]: qua respondetur vel ad quæstionem, quale sit: vel quæ eius causa sit.Tertium est reciprocationis,quam iidem ἀντιστροφῶ dicunt.Primum in binis tantùm affectionibus versatur, alterum in ternis aut quaternis:tertium in utrisque.
units.tr: How many firmaments does each single place have? Almost every place has three. The first is that of essence, which the Greeks call substance [οὐσίαν]; by it one answers the question whether a thing is. For that which is asked, whether a thing exists in nature, is confirmed by comparison with another thing; indeed, the comparison of two things shows the essence of each. The second is that of agreement, which the Greeks call analogy [ἀναλογίαν] and the Latins proportion; by it one answers either the question of what sort a thing is, or what its cause is. The third is that of reciprocation, which the same writers call convertibility [ἀντιστροφῶ]. The first operates only in pairs of attributes, the second in threes or fours, the third in both.

units.la: De quadruplici locorum quæstione.
units.tr: On the fourfold question concerning places.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: IDEO ista: sed quæro nonne quæstio an sit,potius ad Physicos,& naturæ indagatores,quàm ad Dialeticos pertinet, qui solam verborum consecutionem inquirunt? Dialectici non nudam verborum consecutionem exquirunt:sed consecutionem rerum & verborum in eloquendo.Itaque quicquid tota philosophia quæri & dubitari potest,quicquid denique ullo in genere cadere in disquisitionem potest,id omne à Dialecticæ artis instrumento diiudicatur. quod vel ex eo licet intelligi, quia quicquid vllo in genere demonstratur, id Medio demonstratur: neque vlla alia est certa probandi ratio. Medium autē solius artis Dialecticæ proprium instrumentum est: quo si qua alia ars vti volet, id ab illa mutuetur, oportet.
units.tr: So far, that is what I have to say. But I ask whether this question, whether a thing is at all, belongs rather to the natural philosophers and investigators of nature than to the dialecticians, who inquire only into the order of words. Dialecticians do not inquire into the bare order of words, but into the order of things and words in speech. So whatever can be asked and doubted in all of philosophy, and in short whatever can come under investigation in any kind of subject, is all judged by the instrument of the dialectical art. This can be understood even from the fact that whatever is demonstrated in any kind is demonstrated by the middle term, and there is no other sure method of proof. The middle term is the proper instrument of the dialectical art alone, and if any other art wishes to use it, it must borrow it from dialectic.

units.la: Cedo aliquod exemplum de quæstione An sit. Ponatur quæstio inter Philosophos peruulgata, An sit Deus. Tum si quis hoc concludat modo: Quia hæc rerum vniuersitas, hic astrorum cursus, cœli temperatio, terrarum fœcũditas, hæc rerum vicissitudo, tot iam seculorũ ætatibus rata permanet: apparet esse Deũ, qui hæc regat & gubernet: an non perspicuum est, medium ex loco ab Effectis sumptum esse, vt causa tanta ista opera efficiens arguatur. non secus atque illud argumentum, quod ex fulminibus, tempestatibus, vastitate, & pestilentia, bellis aut externis aut ciuilibus, & manifestis irati Dei effectis depromitur. Rursus cùm Plinius ex eo arguat esse hippocentauros, quia ĩ principatu Claudij Cæsaris vnum vidit in melle ex Aegypto allatum: nunquid perspicuè medium demonstrationis sumit ex similibus. nam si vnus allatus est, alij erant consimiles. quemadmodum nostris temporibus cùm ex orbis noui regionibus Reges adducti sunt, ex Relatis concludebamus, quia Reges sunt, ciues etiam eorum ditioni, atque imperio sub-iectos suisse Gigantes, ex eo quòd dentem vidit quatuordecim librarum pódere: nónne & ex partis proportione ad totum,& ex similium comparatione concludit?
units.tr: Let me give an example of the question whether a thing is. Let the question be one commonly debated among the philosophers: whether God exists. Suppose someone concludes in this way: because this universe of things, this course of the stars, the temperate heavens, the fertility of the earth, and this succession of things remain fixed through so many ages of time, it is evident that there is a God who rules and governs these things. Is it not plain that the middle term is taken from a place drawn from effects, so that so great a cause is inferred as the efficient cause of these works? It is no different from that argument which is drawn from thunderbolts, storms, devastation and pestilence, wars both foreign and civil, and the manifest effects of an angry God. Again, when Pliny argues that hippocentaurs exist because under the principate of the Emperor Claudius one was seen in honey brought from Egypt, does he not plainly take the middle term of his demonstration from similar cases? For if one was brought, there were others like it. Just as in our own times, when kings were brought from the regions of the New World, we concluded from these reports that there are kings, and that giants also were subject to their rule and dominion, because someone saw a tooth weighing fourteen pounds: does he not also conclude from the proportion of a part to the whole, and from the comparison of like things?

units.la: Sed cùm omnis Dialectica quæstio posita in eo fit, vt intelligatur an attributū subiecto in oratione conueniat,quidnā hīc vel subiectū vel attributum est? Natura rerum Subiectū est, id quod esse vel dicitur, vel negatur attributum. Itaque ad eam quæstionem Cicero lib. de Orat. 3. exemplum hoc accommodat: Sítne in humano genere sapientia: id est conueniátne humano generi. Similiter cùm quæritur,An sint Centauri, aut Blemiæ, aut Pygmæi: vi ipsa quæri videtur,Conueniátne illud naturæ rerum,an non.
units.tr: But since every dialectical question consists in asking whether an attribute agrees with its subject in a statement, what here is the subject and what the attribute? The subject is the nature of things, and the attribute is that which is said either to be or not to be. Therefore Cicero, in book 3 of De Oratore, applies this example to that kind of question: whether there is wisdom in the human race, that is, whether it agrees with the human race. Similarly, when we ask whether there are centaurs, or Blemmyes, or Pygmies, the question seems to be whether this agrees with the nature of things or not.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de quæstione quid fit. Dictum est superiùs, definitionem nō modo demonstrationis ministram esse, atque ad eius perspicuitatem adhiberi: verùm etiam à demonstratione probari ac iudicari. Definitionis autem medium est vel genus & differétia, in plerisque: vel, in nonnullis caussa, quoniā nosse quid sit, & quæ caussa fit (vt ex Aristotele superiùs dictum est) idem omnino est. Sic igitur cùm dicimus Rhetoricam esse arte copiosè loquendi, attributum subiecto nomini ex medij conuenientia concludimus,quia genus & species aptisimè conueniunt. Sic Tonitru est strepitus ignis in nube restincti,quia caussa effectui respondet.
units.tr: Let me give an example of the question what a thing is. It has been said above that a definition not only serves demonstration and is employed to make it clear, but is also proved and judged by demonstration. The middle term of a definition is either the genus and difference in most cases, or in some the cause; for, as was said above from Aristotle, to know what a thing is and to know its cause are entirely the same. So when we say that rhetoric is the art of speaking copiously, we conclude that the attribute agrees with the subject-name from the agreement of the middle term, because genus and species agree most fittingly. Likewise thunder is the noise of fire quenched in a cloud, because the cause corresponds to the effect.

units.la: Cedo exemplū de quæstione quale fit? Veluti, si quæratur an hic lapis sit Magnes, adhibito minuto ferro argumentatio ab effectis sumetur. itémque in lapide Aëthite,qui «λεκ-τέλεγχος dicitur, si furem deprehendat. & remora si nauem remoretur: ceterísque generis eiusdem innumerabilibus.
units.tr: Let me give an example of the question of what sort a thing is. For instance, if it is asked whether this stone is a magnet, the argument will be drawn from its effects, when fine iron is brought near it. So too with the aetites stone, called [ἐλεγκτέλεγχος], if it detects a thief; and with the remora, if it holds back a ship; and with countless others of the same kind.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de quæstione, Cur ita sit? Huius tot sunt exempla quot posterius in loco ex effectis enumerabimus. veluti, Cur fit tonitru? Quia ignis in nube oppressus extinguitur,
units.tr: Let me give an example of the question why a thing is so. Of this there are as many examples as we shall list later in the place on effects. For instance, why does thunder occur? Because fire pent up in a cloud is extinguished.

units.la: De Proportione. CAP. IX.
units.tr: On Proportion. CHAP. IX.

units.la: QVID est Proportio? Superiùs dictum est, primum opus Dialecticæ esse notationem λόγου, & rationis, quam bina quæque generis eiusdem habent inter se: qua de causa separatim dicuntur analoga. ut quatuor & quatuor pares sunt numeri. quatuor & duo sunt impares. duo cubiti pares: cubitus & pes, impares. At plurium pro cuiusque portione comparatio, analogia dicitur: & à Latinis proportio: quæ (ut ait Varro) in omnibus eiusdem generis rebus locum habet: & ab Euclide definitur rationum similitudo. Magnitudines autem eandem habentes rationem, proportionales. hâc vulgò in scholis Proportionalitatè appellant. Eius etiam in Architectura & operibus omnibus vis permagna est: ut partes inter se & cum toto respondeant. Itaque Vitruuius:Proportio, inquit, 'est ratæ partis membrorum in omni opere totiúsque commodulatio : id est partium cum toto pro rata parte consensiout in corpore humano, proportio est apta compositio membrorum, quæ tum interit, cū pes trium est cubitorum, reliquum corpus duorū palmorum.
units.tr: What is proportion? It was said above that the first task of dialectic is the notation of λόγος and of the ratio which any two things of the same kind have to one another; for this reason they are called analogous separately, as four and four are equal numbers, four and two are unequal, two cubits are equal, and a cubit and a foot are unequal. But the comparison of several things according to the share of each is called analogy, and by the Latins proportion, which (as Varro says) applies to all things of the same kind, and which Euclid defines as the similarity of ratios. Magnitudes that have the same ratio are proportional, and in the schools this is commonly called proportionality. Its force is also very great in architecture and in all works, so that the parts correspond with one another and with the whole. Hence Vitruvius: "Proportion," he says, "is the fitting relation of the parts of the members in every work, and the commensurability of the whole; that is, the agreement of the parts with the whole according to a fixed part. In the human body, proportion is the apt composition of the limbs, which exists when the foot is three cubits long and the rest of the body two palms."

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Vt octo se habet ad quatuor, sic quatuor ad duo: & duo ad vnum. Quā rationem (inquit Varro) in ære habet as ad semissem, eandem habet in argento libella ad sembellam. Sicut est ad vnum victoriatum denarius: sic ad alterum victoriatum alter denarius. Vt est filius ad patrem, sic filia ad matrem. Vt est in temporibus meridies ad diem, sic media nox ad noctem. his enim Varro exemplis vtitur.
units.tr: Give an example. As eight is to four, so four is to two, and two is to one. Varro says: the ratio that the as has to the semis in bronze, the libella has to the sembella in silver. As the denarius is to one victoriatus, so is the other denarius to the other victoriatus. As the son is to the father, so the daughter is to the mother. As midday is to the day in time, so midnight is to the night. For these are the examples Varro uses.

units.la: Quid interest inter Rationem & Proportionem? Ratio est duarum inter se quantitatum comparatio. Proportio vero minimum est trium: quarum media est, quato vnam superat, tanto ab altera superatur. veluti I. II. III. I.quorum medius vt primum vno superat, sic à postremo superatur. Item III. V. VII. quorum medius vt binario primum exsuperat, sic à postremo superatur. Ac scitum est illud Aristotelis in Ethicis: Aequale id esse, quod medium est inter id quod superat, & id quod superatur. vt si decem nimium multa sint: quo vero non satis: tum sex capiatur pro rei medio. quia medium hoc sicut quaternario vnum extremum superat, sic eodem quaternario ab altero superatur.
units.tr: What is the difference between ratio and proportion? Ratio is the comparison of two quantities with one another. Proportion, however, requires at least three terms, of which the middle exceeds one as much as it is exceeded by the other: for example, 1, 2, 3, where the middle exceeds the first by one just as it is exceeded by the last; likewise 3, 5, 7, where the middle exceeds the first by two just as it is exceeded by the last. And that saying of Aristotle in the Ethics is apt: that the equal is that which is the mean between what exceeds and what is exceeded. For example, if ten is too much and six is not enough, then take six as the middle of the thing, because this middle exceeds one extreme by four, just as it is exceeded by the other by the same four.

units.la: Cedo aliquod Geometricæ proportionis exemplum. Ponatur in A.gemma. In B. silex. Pòst dücatur altera linea, & in C. ponantur centum aurei. in D.obolus. Tum ita ratio ineatur. Vt est A. ad B. sic C.ad D. Deinde fi vt A.est ad B.ita C. ad D. necessariò A. est ad C. sicut B. ad D. postremò vt est Totü ad Totü, ita altera pars totius ad alterã alterius.veluti, vt est A C ad B D,ita A ad B & C ad D.Nã(vt ait in Ethicis Ariftoteles) Geometrica proportio est, in qua sicut tota cum totis, sic vtraque cum vtrisque conferuntur.
units.tr: Give some example of geometric proportion. Let a gem be placed at A and a flint at B. Then let another line be drawn, and let a hundred gold coins be placed at C and an obol at D. Then let the ratio be reckoned thus: as A is to B, so C is to D. Next, if as A is to B, so C is to D, then necessarily A is to C as B is to D. Lastly, as the whole is to the whole, so the other part of the whole is to the other part of the other: for example, as AC is to BD, so A is to B and C is to D. For (as Aristotle says in the Ethics) geometric proportion is that in which, as the whole is compared with the wholes, so each of the two is compared with each of the two.

units.la: De Reciprocatione. CAP. X.
units.tr: On Reciprocation. CHAP. X.

units.la: VID est Reciprocatio? Affectio locorü eiusmodi, vt fi cöfentanei sint, vno concessó vel negato, alterü concedatur, vel negetur: fi dissentanei, contrà vno posito, vel sublato, alterum ponatur, vel tollatur. Nam in eos demum locos reciprocatio conuenit, quorum paria in vtranque partem momenta sunt. quorum naturæ ordine neutrü altero prius aut posterius est, sed vtrunque simul. veluti, Proprium & species: canfla[?] & effectus. At genus cum specie non reciprocatur: nec totum cum parte. quoniam illa priora sunt naturæ ordine, vt suo loco diximus. Huius autem difcipline maximus contra Sophistas est vsus, quemadmodum in Elenchis sophisticis Aristoteles docuit.
units.tr: What is reciprocation? It is a property of places such that, if they are consonant, when one is granted or denied the other is granted or denied; and if they are dissonant, when one is posited or removed the other is posited or removed. Reciprocation applies only to those places whose members carry equal weight in either direction, and whose natural order is such that neither is prior or posterior to the other, but both are together: for example, property and species, cause and effect. Genus and species do not reciprocate, nor do whole and part, because those are prior in natural order, as we said in its place. The use of this doctrine against the Sophists is very great, as Aristotle taught in the Sophistical Refutations.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Reciprocatur hæc inter se: Si sol lucet, dies est: & si dies est, sol lucet. Si quid ridet, homo est: & si homo est, ridet. At illa non reciprocantur: Siquis habet febrem, calet. At non, si quis calet, continuò habet febrem. Si pluit, madefacta terra est. At non si madefacta terra est, pluit. Si peperit, cum viro concubuit. At non si concubuit, continuò verò est parituram. Ex hoc genere illud est festiuũ Iphicratis, quod ab Aristotele commemoratur lib. Rhetor. 2. nam cùm filium haberet statura magnum: ætate verò puerũ: Aediles autem propter magnitudinem eum ad onera ciuitatis compelleret: Si magnos, inquit, pueros existimatis viros esse: necesse est vt viros paruos, pueros esse decernatis.
units.tr: Let me give an example. These reciprocate with each other: If the sun is shining, it is day; and if it is day, the sun is shining. If anything laughs, it is a human being; and if it is a human being, it laughs. But these do not reciprocate: If someone has a fever, he is warm; but it does not follow that if someone is warm, he necessarily has a fever. If it rains, the ground is wet; but it does not follow that if the ground is wet, it is raining. If she has given birth, she has lain with a man; but it does not follow that if she has lain with a man, she will certainly give birth. Of this kind is the witty remark of Iphicrates, which Aristotle mentions in the second book of the Rhetoric. He had a son who was big for his stature but still a child in years, and the aediles, because of his size, were trying to press him into the city's burdens. Iphicrates said: "If you think big boys are men, then you must decide that small men are boys."

units.la: De loco generis. CAP. XI.
units.tr: On the place from the genus. CHAP. XI.

units.la: [?]EINCEPS igitur de singulis locis videamus. Quod est firmamentũ loci à genere, cùm quæritur an fit species? Primum est huiusmodi: Posito genere vniuerso, quæuis continuò ponitur species. Nam qui omne dicit (vt in proverbio est) nihil excipit. Locus igitur ex genere vniuerso ad quanuis speciem probandã valet. nam semper in generalibus specialia insunt:vt est in regula iuris ciuilis : veluti : Si omnis arbor in illo fundo est, est etiam plantanus. Si omnes ciues in vrbe sunt, sunt etiam senatores. Sequitur I I. Sublato genere vniuerso, quæuis continuo species tollitur:Nam hic quoque locus ad speciem refellendam valet..Si nulla in hoc fundo arbor est, ne laurus quidem. Si telum in armamentario nullum est, ne fustis quidem. Sequitur III. Concesso genere indefinito,non continuo certa species conceditur. Locus enim ex genere indefinito ad probandam certam speciem non valet: quoniam (vt in Enuntiationibus dictum est) vt indefinita Enuntiatio vera fit, fatis est veram esse vel particularem, vel singularem. Indefinitè autem, fiue ἀπλῶς[?], id est simpliciter & omnino enûtiariea diximus, quæ fine circunstantia vlla,hoc est,fiue temporis,loci,aut persone adiectione pronuntiatur. Non valebit igitur hoc modo: Si est arbor,'est laurus. Si est animal,est homo.Si est telum,est gladius. Sequitur IIII. Negato genere indefinito , quæuis species negatur. quasi indefinita negatio vniuersalis negationem efficiat. itaque locus hic ad refutādum valet. nam à quo genus abest,necesse est formam abesse.veluti, Quod nõ est arbor,vtique non est laurus.Quod non est animal,non homo. Quod omnino non est,id nec ex parte,nec interdum,nec vspiam est: inquit Ariftoteles.Sequitur V.Posito genere indefinito,speciesincerta ponitur.Nam iccirco locus hic ad confirmandum valet: quoniam ut vera indefinita fit,satis est particularem aut singularem esse veram. Tractatur autē hic locus per diuisionem specierum hoc modo: Si sunt Centauri, aut sunt expertes rationis, aut participes.Si est Phoenix,aut est mas, aut fœmina.Quod indefinitè & omnino est,id aut ex parte est,aut interdum,aut uspiam.
units.tr: Next, then, let us look at each place. What is the support of the place from the genus, when we ask whether something is a species? The first is of this kind: given the whole genus, any species is at once posited. For whoever says "every" (as the proverb goes) excepts nothing. The place from the whole genus is therefore valid for proving any species. For in general statements the specific cases are always contained, as in the rule of civil law: If every tree is on that estate, there is also a plane tree. If all citizens are in the city, there are also senators. It follows II. With the whole genus removed, any species is at once removed, for this place is also valid for refuting a species. If there is no tree on this estate, not even a laurel. If there is no weapon in the armoury, not even a club. It follows III. Granting an indefinite genus, a certain species is not at once granted. For a place from an indefinite genus is not valid for proving a certain species, since (as was said in the discussion of propositions) an indefinite proposition is true if a particular or singular one is true. By indefinite, or simply [ἀπλῶς], that is, absolutely and without qualification, we mean a proposition pronounced without any circumstance, that is, without any addition of time, place or person. So this will not hold: If it is a tree, it is a laurel. If it is an animal, it is a man. If it is a weapon, it is a sword. It follows IV. Denying an indefinite genus, any species is denied, as if an indefinite negation produced a universal negation. So this place is valid for refutation. For from what the genus is absent, the species must necessarily be absent: e.g., What is not a tree is certainly not a laurel. What is not an animal is not a man. What altogether is not, that neither in part, nor sometimes, nor anywhere is, says Aristotle. It follows V. Positing an indefinite genus, an uncertain species is posited. For this place is valid for confirming, because for an indefinite to be true it is enough that a particular or singular one be true. This place is handled by division of the species, in this way: If there are Centaurs, they are either without reason or endowed with it. If there is a phoenix, it is either male or female. What is indefinitely and absolutely, that is either in part, or sometimes, or somewhere.

units.la: Quod est firmamentum loci à genere,cùm de speciei convenientia quæritur? Quod generi universo cõvenit, omni speciei quæ suum ac proprium nomen non habeat, convenit:vicissimque cui genus omne cõvenit, ei species omnes quæ proprium ac separatū nomen non habent,non conveniunt.Magna enim cautio adhibenda hoc loco est, de qua in speciei Affectu dictum est:quasdam esse species, quæ generis nomen retinent, quasdam quæ suū proprium & à genere separatum nomen adeptæ sunt. Cuius distinctionis ac differentiæ cùm tantum in usu momentum fit, mirum est nullam in scholis mentionem fieri. Priùs autē vulgaris firmamenti exempla proponemus. Id est huiusmodi:Quod omni generi convenit,omni speciei convenit. Locus enim ex convenientia generis universi propter vim proportionis ad cuiusuis speciei convenientiam probandam valet. Nã (ut ait Cicero lib.de Orat.iii.) Quod in genere universo probatum est, id in parte probetur necesse est.Veluti, Si omnis arbor vere florescit,etiam platanus florescit.Etenim quam habet rationem omnis arbor ad ver,eandem habet platanus pro sua portione. Sic omnium rerum satietas vitæ facit fatietatem:ait idem in Catone maiore. Ex illo genere iocus est ille Cafcellij Iurifcófulti, qui cùm Aedilesedixiffent, nequis prebente lúdos Va tinio aliquid praeter pomum mitteret,consùltus per eos dies ,an nux pinea pomum effet, respóndit : Si in Vatinium missurus es, pomü est.Si omnia quę sunt(inquit Cicero)mutabilia sunt, nullũ èorpus esse potest nó mutabile; mutabilia autè sunt illa ex quibus omnia constant.omne igitur corpus mutabile est. Ethuc pertinet Regula Iurifcófultorũ:Cui genus debetur,eidè species debetur.de qua in l.fiquid; 47,ʃ.1,D.de legat.3.
units.tr: What is the support of the place from the genus, when we ask about the agreement of a species? What agrees with the whole genus agrees with every species that does not have its own proper name; and conversely, what no genus agrees with, neither do all those species agree with which do not have a proper and separate name. Great caution must be used in this place, about which we spoke under the affection of a species: some species retain the name of the genus, others have obtained their own proper name, separate from the genus. Since so much depends on this distinction and difference in practice, it is strange that no mention is made of it in the schools. First, however, we will set out examples of the common support. It is of this kind: What agrees with every genus agrees with every species. For the place from the agreement of the whole genus is valid for proving the agreement of any species, on account of the force of proportion. For (as Cicero says in the first book of On the Orator) what has been proved in the whole genus must necessarily be proved in the part. For example: If every tree flowers in spring, the plane tree also flowers. For the plane tree has, for its part, the same relation to spring that every tree has. So, says the same author in Cato Major, the satiety of all things makes the satiety of life. There is a joke of this kind by the jurist Cascellius, who, when the aediles had decreed that no one should send anything to Vatinius, who was giving the games, besides an apple, was consulted over those days whether a pine nut was an apple. He answered: If you are going to send it to Vatinius, it is an apple. If all things that exist (says Cicero) are changeable, no body can be unchangeable; but those things out of which all things are made are changeable. Therefore every body is changeable. To this belongs the rule of the jurists: To whom the genus is owed, to him the species is owed; on which see the law Si quid, 47, §1, D. de legatis 3.

units.la: Cedo planius aliquod exemplû de próportione.Sumantur illa quæ tamenAriftoteles ad locum ex maiore retulit.Si voluptas bonû est; maior voluptas eftmaius bonum. Si iniuriam facere malum est,maiore iniuriam facere maius malum est. Nam certè maius & minus generis species sunt. Ex eodem genere illud:est Ciceronis: In quo fallit eos quod audierunt, dicendo homines vt dicant efficere solere. verè enim illud dicitur,Peruersè vt dicant homines, peruersè dicendo facillimè consequi. Sic enim locum illum corrigendum arbitror.
units.tr: Come, let me give a plainer example of proportion. Take those which Aristotle himself cited for the place from the greater: If pleasure is a good, a greater pleasure is a greater good. If to do injury is an evil, to do a greater injury is a greater evil. For certainly the greater and the lesser are species of the genus. From the same genus is that of Cicero: In which he deceives them by what they have heard, that by speaking men usually bring about what they say. For it is truly said, that men say perversely, and by speaking perversely they very easily attain it. For thus I think that passage should be corrected.

units.la: Age: quis est nouæ illius distinctionis vsus? Species à genere (inquit Cicero in Topicis) quoad suum nomen retinet non seiungitur; Quod sic interpretor : quasi dixisset, Quoad ipsius generis nomen retinet. Sic enim aliis quoque locis Suum pro Ipsius vsurpauit. Hoc cùm ita fit,illud quoque sequitur, specié quæ proprium & separatū à genere nomen habet, à suo genere seiungi:cuius præceptionis vis ex eo ipso quod à Cicerone tractatur exemplo intelligetur. Quoniâ(inquit)argentū omne mulieri legatum est,non potest ei pecunia quæ numerata domi relicta est, nō esse legata. numerata enim pecunia(inquit) nomen argenti retinet.hoc Cicero ex sui temporis cósuetudine & sermone vsitato cóstituit.Itaq; & apud Plautũ,& apudTerentiũ,Argenti nomine pecuniã quoque numeratã appellari videmus. Multis autè post annis Vlpian. Iurisconsultus ita locutus est,An cui argentum omne legatum est, ei nūmi quoque legati esse videantur, quæritur:& ego puto non cōtineri. non facilè enim quisquam argenti numero nummos cōputat.
units.tr: Come now, what is the use of that new distinction? Cicero says in the Topics: a species is not separated from its genus so long as it retains the genus' name.
