I interpret this as if he had said: so long as it retains the name of the genus itself. For in other places too he used "suum" for "ipsius". Since this is so, it also follows that a species which has a proper and separate name from its genus is separated from that genus. The force of this precept will be understood from the example Cicero himself treats. Since (he says) all silver has been left to a woman, money which was left counted at home cannot not be included in the bequest; for counted money, he says, retains the name of silver. Cicero established this from the custom and ordinary speech of his own time. And so in Plautus and in Terence we see that counted money too is called by the name of silver. But many years later the jurist Ulpian spoke thus: It is asked whether, if all silver has been bequeathed to someone, coins also seem to be bequeathed; and I think they are not included. For no one easily counts coins among the kind of silver.

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplum. Supellectilis legato , eas res contineri puto (inquit Alphenus) quæ ad vsum communē patrisfa.parate essent, quæ nomen sui generis seperatim non haberet. (vulgo enim corruptè legitur Separatim) quare quæ ad artificij genus aliquod pertinebunt,neque ad communem vsum patrisfa.accomodatæ essent, supellectilis nō esse: sed nec pugillares,& codices in supellectili sunt.
units.tr: Let me give another example. For a bequest of household goods, I think (says Alphenus) that those things are included which were made ready for the common use of the household, but not those which have their own name as a separate kind. (For commonly the text is read corruptly as "separatim".) Therefore things which belong to some kind of craft, and are not fitted to the common use of the household, are not household goods. But writing tablets and codices are among household goods.

units.la: Cedo aliquod planius & familiarius. Ponatur[?] legatum esse omnibus cognatis: non dubium est,quin agnatis nihil debeatur. Forma enim a genere, si proprium nomen habet, seiungitur. Sic lex Pompeij,ut qui Pontica matre natus est,ciuis sit Ponticus:ad spurios (inquit Vlpianus) qui separatum nomē habent, & iam materna origine censentur,nihil pertinet. Sequitur I I. Quod generi vniuerso non conuenit,nulli speciei conuenit. vel potius isto modo: Quod generi vniuerso repugnat, id ab unaquaque specie disidet. valet enim hic locus ad refellendam speciei conuenientiam. veluti, Si homo est animal, quod non est animal, id non est homo. Si nulli homines ante mortem beati sunt,ne Reges quidem. Si malum in sapientem non cadit, dolor autem cadit, dolor non est malum.ut in lib. de Finib. II[?]. Qui in summo malo est,iste cum in eo est, nō est beatus. Sapiens autem semper beatus est: & est aliquando in dolore. Non est igitur summum malum dolor. Sequitur III. Quod generi indefinito cōuenit, non cōtinuò certæ speciei conuenit. Itaque nihil ad confirmādum valet. cuius rei caussam superiùs exposuimus. veluti Non si arbor frugifera est, cōtinuò etiā tamarix frugifera est. Nō si homo indefinitē legat°[?] est,continuò optimus debetur, ait Cassius. Sequitur IIII. Quod generi indefinitò non conuenit,nulli speciei conuenit. Itaque locus hic ad refutandam speciei conuenientiam valebit. veluti, Si pisces non sunt cicures,ne murena quidem. Si homines non sunt ante mortem beati,ne Reges quidem. Sequitur V. Quòd generi indefinito conuenit, continuò etiam speciei incertæ conuenit. Cuius rei caussa superiùs explicata est. Tractatur autem, hic locus per disiunctionem specierū: hoc modo: Si Philosophi sapientes sunt, necesse est aut Stoicos, aut Academicos, aut Peripaticos, aut Epicureos fuisse. Si ciuis est, aut natus, aut factus est.
units.tr: Let me give something plainer and more familiar. Suppose a legacy is left to all relatives: there is no doubt that nothing is owed to agnates. For a form is separated from its genus if it has a proper name. So too the law of Pompey, that one born of a Pontic mother is a citizen of Pontus, does not apply to bastards, who (says Ulpian) have a separate name and are already reckoned by maternal origin. It follows II. What does not agree with the whole genus agrees with no species. Or rather, in this way: What is repugnant to the whole genus differs from every species. For this place is valid for refuting the agreement of a species. For example: If man is an animal, what is not an animal is not a man. If no men are blessed before death, neither are kings. If evil does not befall the wise man, but pain does befall him, then pain is not evil, as in the book On Ends II. He who is in the greatest evil, while he is in it, is not blessed. But the wise man is always blessed, and is sometimes in pain. Therefore pain is not the greatest evil. It follows III. What agrees with an indefinite genus does not at once agree with a certain species. Therefore it is of no use for confirming. The reason for this we explained above. For example: It does not follow that because a tree is fruitful, a tamarisk too is at once fruitful. If a man is indefinitely a legatee, the best is not at once owed to him, says Cassius. It follows IV. What does not agree with an indefinite genus agrees with no species. Therefore this place will be valid for refuting the agreement of a species. For example: If fish are not tame, neither is the moray. If men are not blessed before death, neither are kings. It follows V. What agrees with an indefinite genus at once agrees also with some uncertain species. The reason for this was explained above. This place is handled by division of the species, in this way: If philosophers are wise, they must have been either Stoics, or Academics, or Peripatetics, or Epicureans. If a citizen is, he is either born or made.

units.la: De loco Speciei. CAP. XII.
units.tr: On the Place from the Species. CHAP. XII.

units.la: Q[?]VÆ fiunt firmamenta ex Specie, cùm quæritur, An fit genus? Primùm est huiusmodi: Posita vna specie, non continuò ponitur genus vniuersum. Plus enim in genere vniuerso est, quàm in specie. Itaque locus ex specie ad genus vniuersum probandū non valet. veluti: Si in illo agro cupressus est, est omnis arbor. Sequitur II. Posita vna specie, continuò ponitur genus indefinitum: quoniam vt vera indefinita fit, satis est verâ esse particularem. Itaque locus ex specie ad genus indefinitum probandum valet: veluti, Si Platanus est, est arbor. Si murena est, piscis est. Si gladius est, telū est. Sequitur III. Sublata vna specie, neutrum genus iccirco tollitur. plus enim in genere vniuerso remanet. Itaque locus ex vna specie ad refellendum genus non valet. Non enim quadrat: Si non est cupressus, non est arbor, aut nulla est arbor. Si non est iustitia, non est virtus. Potest enim esse sortitudo,constantia,continentia.Sequitur IIII. Pofitis formis omnibus cōtinuò succedit genus, non tātùm indefinitum,sed etiam universum. Valet enim hic locus & ad confirmandum & ad refutādum. Tractatur autem hic locus per cōiunctionem:veluti,Si & aues sunt, & pisces, & quadrupedes, omnis generis beluæ sunt.Si sunt Senatores,equites,& plebeij:sunt omnes ciues.Sequitur V.Remotis formis singulis, cō tinuò utrumque remouetur genus. valet enim ad refutandum:& per remotionem tractatur, cùm species omnes quæ generi subiectę sunt, remouentur. Si in eo loco neque mortale est, neque immortale,animal non est.Si neque na tus est,neque factus ciuis,nullus est ciuis.
units.tr: What are the strong arguments from the species, when it is asked whether there is a genus? The first is this: once one species is posited, the universal genus is not thereby posited. For there is more in the universal genus than in the species. So the place from the species does not prove the universal genus. For example: If there is a cypress in that field, every tree is there. Second: once one species is posited, the indefinite genus is posited at once, since for an indefinite proposition to be true it is enough that the particular is true. So the place from the species does prove the indefinite genus. For example: If it is a plane tree, it is a tree. If it is a moray eel, it is a fish. If it is a sword, it is a weapon. Third: once one species is removed, neither genus is thereby removed, for more remains in the universal genus. So the place from one species does not serve to refute the genus. For this does not follow: If it is not a cypress, it is not a tree, or no tree exists. If it is not justice, it is not virtue; for there can be fortitude, constancy, and temperance. Fourth: once all the forms are posited, the genus follows at once, not only the indefinite but also the universal. For this place serves both to confirm and to refute. This place is handled by conjunction, for example: If there are birds, and fishes, and quadrupeds, then they are all kinds of living creatures. If there are senators, knights, and commoners, then they are all citizens. Fifth: once the single forms are removed, both genera are at once removed, for the place is good for refuting, and it is handled by removal, when all the species that are subordinate to the genus are removed. If in that place there is neither a mortal nor an immortal thing, there is no animal. If he was neither born nor made a citizen, he is no citizen.

units.la: Quæ sunt firmamenta loci ex specie,cùm de generis conuenientia quæritur? Primum est huiusmodi: Quod uni speciei conuenit, non continuò generi universo conuenit. veluti: Si homo doctrinæ capax est, non continuò animal omne disciplinæ capax est. Quod legatum est Fabiæ matrifa.si ea simpliciter vxor est, neque in manum conuenit,nihil debetur.Sequitur II.Quod uni speciei conuenit,etiam indefinito generi cōuenit.Si smaragdus est viridis, gemma est viridis.Si Platanus florescit verè,arbor vere florescit.Nam particularis verè efficit indefinitam veram. in quo videndum est diligenter,ne indefinita dicantur , quæ necessariam circunstantiæ adiectionem habent.veluti, Apud Tribalos laudi & gloriæ ducitur, patrem immolare. Ergo patrem immolare ho neftum est. non valet. Nam & si quod aliqua ex parte est, aut alicubi, aut interdum, id certè omnino est: vicissimque quod omnino nō est, id nec aliqua ex parte, nec interdum, nec vsquam est: tamē id demum esse omnino & absolutè, & infinitè, & simpliciter dicitur, quod sine vlla circunstantiæ adiectione necessaria pronuntiatur. Nam (vt ait Aristoteles secundo Topico extremo) τὸ ἁπλῶς ἕστιν, ὁ μὴ ἐνδεχόμενος ἐπεῖς[?]. Sequitur III. Quod vnispeciei non conuenit, non continuò generi indefinito non conuenit. Non enim reciprocatio est. veluti: Si homo est animal, quod non est animal, id non est homo. Sed non siquid non sit homo, id continuò sequitur non esse animal. Ex eo quod prohibet lex Iulia damnatam adulterii mulierem testimonium dicere, colligitur etiam mulieres testimonij in iudicio dicendi ius habere. Sic, Si salix non est frugifera, non continuò arbores sunt infrugiferæ. Et si autē disputari posset, videri hæc inter se pugnantia, quia contrariorum (vt postea dicemus) contraria sunt consequentia: tamen intelligendum est, differentiæ caussam in negatione esse positam, quæ cùm priuatio sit, affirmatione, quæ habitus est, semper est deterior: neque parē cum illa vim habet. Sequitur IIII. Quod vnicuique speciei cōuenit, vtrique generi cōuenit. qui locus per enumerationem & affirmationem formarum tractatur: de qua poste-rius rius differemus. Si & rationis particeps & rationis expers mortale est, omne animal mortale est. Sequitur V. Quod nulli speciei convenit, generi non convenit. Qui locus per Enumerationem formarum tractatur. Si Archias neque natus, neque factus est civis, non est civis.
units.tr: What are the strong arguments from the species, when the agreement of a genus is asked? The first is this: what belongs to one species does not at once belong to the universal genus. For example: If man is capable of learning, it does not follow that every animal is capable of learning. A legacy was left to Fabia, a materfamilias: if she is simply a wife and has not passed into manus, nothing is owed. Second: what belongs to one species also belongs to the indefinite genus. If the emerald is green, a gem is green. If the plane tree blooms in spring, a tree blooms in spring. For the particular makes the indefinite true. In this matter one must take care that those are not called indefinite which have a necessary addition of circumstance. For example: Among the Triballi it is counted a matter of praise and glory to sacrifice one's father. Therefore to sacrifice one's father is honourable. This does not hold. For if something is in some respect, or somewhere, or at some time, it certainly is absolutely; and conversely what is not absolutely is neither in some respect, nor at some time, nor anywhere. Yet that alone is said to be absolutely, and unconditionally, and simply, which is affirmed without any addition of a necessary circumstance. For (as Aristotle says at the end of the second book of the Topics) what simply is, is what cannot not be [τὸ ἁπλῶς ἐστιν, ὃ μὴ ἐνδέχεται μὴ εἶναι]. Third: what does not belong to one species does not therefore fail to belong to the indefinite genus. For this is not a reciprocal relation. For example: If man is an animal, what is not an animal is not a man. But it does not follow that if something is not a man, it is therefore not an animal. From the fact that the Julian law forbids a woman condemned for adultery to give testimony, it is gathered that women also have the right to give testimony in court. So: If the willow is not fruitful, it does not follow that trees are unfruitful. And although it might be argued that these seem to conflict with each other, because contraries have contrary consequences (as we shall say later), yet it must be understood that the difference lies in the negation, which, since it is a privation, is always worse than an affirmation, which is a habit, and does not have an equal force with it. Fourth: what belongs to each single species belongs to both genera. This place is handled by enumeration and affirmation of the forms, which we shall discuss later. If a thing that partakes of reason and a thing that lacks reason are both mortal, then every animal is mortal. Fifth: what belongs to no species does not belong to the genus. This place is handled by enumeration of the forms. If Archias was neither born nor made a citizen, he is not a citizen.

units.la: Restat ut de Reciprocatione videamus. Quæ sunt regulæ Reciprocationis inter genus & speciem? Omnes ex superiore disputatione & colligi & confirmari possunt. Itaque regulas enumerare contenti ab earum exemplis supersedebimus. Prima est huiusmodi: Ut posito genere universo quævis succedit species: ita positis formis omnibus, continuo succedit genus. Sequitur II. Ut sublato genere universo, quævis continuo species tollitur: sic remotis formis omnibus, continuo removetur genus. Sequitur III. Ut quod generi universo convenit, omni speciei convenit: ita quod singulis formis convenit, generi convenit. Sequitur IIII. Ut quod generi universo non convenit, nulli speciei convenit: ita quod nulli speciei convenit, generi non convenit. Sequitur V. Non ut posito genere universo, quævis succedit species: ita quavis posita specie, continuo succedit genus. Sequitur VI. Non ut sublato genere universo, quævis continuo species tollitur: ita sublata una specie, continuo genus tollitur. Sequitur VII. Non ut quod generi universo posito convenit, omni speciei conuenit, ita quod uni formæ cōvenit, continuò generi conuenit. Sequitur VIII. Non ut quod generi universo non conuenit, nulli speciei conuenit: ita quod uni alicui speciei non conuenit, continuò generi non conuenit.
units.tr: It remains to see what concerns reciprocation. What are the rules of reciprocation between genus and species? All of them can be gathered and confirmed from the preceding discussion. Therefore, being content to list the rules, we shall pass over their examples. The first is this: as, once the universal genus is posited, any species whatever follows, so, once all the forms are posited, the genus follows at once. Second: as, once the universal genus is removed, any species whatever is at once removed, so, once all the forms are removed, the genus is at once removed. Third: as what belongs to the universal genus belongs to every species, so what belongs to each of the forms belongs to the genus. Fourth: as what does not belong to the universal genus belongs to no species, so what belongs to no species does not belong to the genus. Fifth: not as, once the universal genus is posited, any species whatever follows, so, once any species whatever is posited, the genus follows at once. Sixth: not as, once the universal genus is removed, any species whatever is at once removed, so, once one species is removed, the genus is at once removed. Seventh: not as what belongs to the universal genus when posited belongs to every species, so what belongs to one form belongs at once to the genus. Eighth: not as what does not belong to the universal genus belongs to no species, so what does not belong to some one species does not at once belong to the genus.

units.la: Quid sequitur nunc? Ut de specie & de individuo differamus. Sed quoniam eadem speciei ad individuum ratio est, quæ generis ad speciem: vicissimque eadem individui ad speciem, quæ speciei ad genus: propterea subtilior horum disputatio superuacanea videtur.
units.tr: What follows now? That we should discuss the species and the individual. But since the relation of the species to the individual is the same as that of the genus to the species, and conversely the relation of the individual to the species is the same as that of the species to the genus, a more subtle discussion of these matters seems superfluous.

units.la: Itaque in quæstionibus de Specie & individuo iisdem ut firmamentis licebit, quæ superiùs exposita sunt. Veluti: Si quæratur an Callicles sit animal, Firmamentum hoc adhibebitur: Quia quod speciei conuenit, individuo conuenit: si animal homini conuenit, etiā Callicli, qui homo est, conueniet. Contrà si quæratur an Callicles sit lapis, eodē adhibito firmamento concluditur: quia quod speciei repugnat, etiam individuo repugnat: si lapis homini non conuenit, etiam Callicli, qui homo est, non conueniet. Quare proximum est, ut ad locum de Toto transeamus.
units.tr: Therefore, in questions about the species and the individual, the same arguments as were set out above will be admissible. For example: If it is asked whether Callicles is an animal, this argument will be applied: because what belongs to the species belongs to the individual; if animal belongs to man, it will also belong to Callicles, who is a man. On the contrary, if it is asked whether Callicles is a stone, the same argument being applied, it is concluded: because what is incompatible with the species is also incompatible with the individual; if stone does not belong to man, it will not belong to Callicles either, who is a man. Wherefore it is next in order that we pass to the place from the whole.

units.la: De loco Totius. CAP. XIII.
units.tr: De loco Totius. CAP. XIII.

units.la: QVOD[?] est firmamentum loci ex Toto, cùm quæritur an sint partes? Ponatur hoc I. Toto concesso conceduntur partes principales, Totum enim sine principalibus partibus non consistit: sive illud naturale fit, sive artificiosum. Itaque locus ex Toto ad probandas principales partes valet. veluti: Si est arbor, est etiam truncus, & radix, & rami. Si est currus, etiam rota est. Si nauis est, etiam puppis est, & prora, & sentina. Eiusdémque loci est illud: Posito toto, nihil extrinsecus relinquitur. Nam qui omne dicit, nihil excipit. Ut in illo Aesopi ridiculo, qui cum venalis conseruus interrogatus quid sciret, respondisset se scire omnia: posset eadé de re interrogatus, respondit se nihil scire: quòd alter omnia se scire dixisset. Sequitur II. Posito toto, non continuò partes minus principales ponuntur, quia totum sine iis potest consistere. Itaque locus ex toto non valet ad probandam partem minus principalem, veluti: Si est, arbor, sunt etiam folia, aut flores. Si est nauis est & artemo. Nam (ut superius ex Labeone diximus) artemo pars nauis non numeratur, nisi ne cessaria. l. malũ, 242, D. de verb. signi. Sequitur III. Sublato toto, subtili ratione partes continuò tollùntur: popularí verò ratione, propter homonymiam non tolluntur. Sic enim superius in affectionum tractatu distinguendum esse ostendimus ex Aristotele, qui libro Politicorum primo statuit, eas demùm verè ac proprie partes dici, quæ munere suo funguntur, & sunt in actu. Separatas verò, abusiuè & improprié tantùm sic appellari. Quare cùm id demum fundamentum dicatur, quo sustinetur domus, euersa domo fundamentum subtili & limata ratione nullum est: ut nec tectum, quod non tegit: nec rota, quę nō voluitur: nec remus, qui non impellitur. Sed vitæ communis ratio necessariam homonymiam induxit: ut etiam sublata superficie area pars domus dicatur: & rota nominetur, quæ non voluitur: & remus, qui nō impellitur. Amiculum apud mercatore, quamuis non amiciat: & toga quáuis non tegat: & ramus, quamuis ex arbore excisus.
units.tr: What is the warrant of the topic from the Whole, when it is asked whether there are parts? It is laid down thus. Once the whole is granted, its principal parts are granted too, for a whole does not subsist without its principal parts, whether it is natural or made by art. So the topic from the whole is valid for proving principal parts. For example: if there is a tree, there is also a trunk, and roots, and branches. If there is a chariot, there is also a wheel. If there is a ship, there is also a stern, and a prow, and a bilge. Of the same topic is this: once the whole is posited, nothing outside it is left over, for whoever says "all" excepts nothing. Thus in that joke of Aesop, when a fellow slave who was up for sale was asked what he knew and answered that he knew everything, he was then asked the same question and answered that he knew nothing, because the other had said he knew everything. It follows, second, that once the whole is posited, the less principal parts are not thereby posited, because the whole can subsist without them. So the topic from the whole is not valid for proving a less principal part. For example: if there is a tree, there are also leaves or flowers. If there is a ship, there is also a rudder-oar. For (as we said above from Labeo) the rudder-oar is not counted as a part of the ship, unless it is necessary. l. malum, 242, D. de verb. signi. It follows, third, that when the whole is removed, the parts are immediately removed in a strict reckoning, but in a popular reckoning they are not removed, on account of homonymy. For as we showed earlier in the treatment of affections, following Aristotle, who in the first book of the Politics laid down that those things are truly and properly called parts which perform their function and are in act, while separated ones are called parts only abusively and improperly. Hence, since that is called the foundation by which a house is held up, when the house has been overthrown there is no foundation in a subtle and refined reckoning, just as there is no roof that does not cover, no wheel that does not turn, no oar that does not propel. But the practice of common life has introduced a necessary homonymy, so that even when the surface is removed the bare ground is called a part of the house, and a wheel is named as one that does not turn, and an oar as one that does not propel. A wrap kept by a merchant, though it does not wrap anyone, and a toga, though it covers no one, and a branch, though cut from the tree.

units.la: Quod est firmamentum loci ex Toto, cùm de conuenientia quæritur? Primum est huiufmodi: Quod Toti conuenit, partibus coniunctis pro rata conuenit: disiunctis non conuenit. Itaque ad probandam partium concretarum conuenientiam valet. veluti: Si nauis nauigat, & prora & puppis, & malus, & gubernaculum, & transtra, & remi, & anchora pro rata parte nauigant. At disiunctæ nullo modo: unde illa Iurisconsultorum regula: Cuius est totū, eius sunt partes. Si domus oppignerata est, est etiam area. Cui legatus est anulus, eidem gemma quoque legata est. Qui fur est totius, fur est singularum partiū. Quæ de tota re vindicanda dicta sunt, eadem & de tota parte intelligenda sunt. Cui pater se in adoptionem dedit, eidem quoque filium datus intelligitur. Totius enim nomine non modò continuum corpus, sed etiam deiunctum intelligimus: veluti familia: ut superius in To-tius tius affectu dictum est. Ex hoc eodem fonte ducta est vera illa & Christiano digna homine, Ciceronis argumentatio in lib. de nat. deor. II. extremo: Si Deus consulit omnibus hominibus, qui in orbe terrarum sunt, etiam iis consulit, qui eius partes tenent, Asiam, Africam, Europam. Si iis, etiam universis qui Romæ sunt, & Athenis & Rhodi. Si universis, etiam singulis. Sequitur II. Non si cui totum non convenit, iccirco pars non convenit. Itaque nihil ad refellendam partem, totius refutatio valet: veluti, Non si totus fundus meus non est, iccirco nulla eius pars mea est. Non si quis integrum bouem gestare, ut Milo Crotoniates, non poterit, continuò partem eius non poterit. Non si quis universum exercitum regere non poterit, iccirco partem eius non poterit. Non si vas aliquod totum illud frumentum capere non potuit, iccirco partem eius aliquam non poterit.
units.tr: What is the warrant of the topic from the Whole, when agreement is asked about? The first is of this kind: what agrees with the whole agrees with the parts taken together in proportion, and does not agree with them when separated. So the topic is valid for proving the agreement of parts taken together. For example: if a ship sails, then the prow and the stern, and the mast, and the rudder, and the thwarts, and the oars, and the anchor all sail in their proper proportion. But separated they do so in no way. Hence that rule of the jurists: whose the whole is, his the parts are. If a house is pledged, the courtyard is pledged too. If a ring is bequeathed to someone, the gem is bequeathed to the same person as well. Whoever is a thief of the whole is a thief of the individual parts. What has been said about claiming the whole thing is to be understood also of the whole part. When a father has given himself into adoption, the son is understood to be given to the same person as well. For by the name of "whole" we understand not only a continuous body but also one that is disjoined, as with a family, as was said above in the treatment of the affection of the whole. From this same source is drawn that true argument of Cicero's, worthy of a Christian man, at the end of the second book of On the Nature of the Gods: If God cares for all men who are on the earth, he also cares for those who hold its parts, Asia, Africa, Europe. If for those, then also for all who are at Rome, and at Athens and at Rhodes. If for all, then also for each single one. It follows, second, that if the whole does not agree with someone, it does not follow that the part does not agree with him. Hence the refutation of the whole is of no use for refuting a part. For example: it does not follow that, if my whole estate is not mine, no part of it is mine. It does not follow that if someone cannot carry a whole ox, as Milo of Croton could, he cannot carry a part of it. It does not follow that if someone cannot rule the whole army, he cannot rule a part of it. It does not follow that if some vessel could not hold all that grain, it cannot hold some part of it.

units.la: De loco Partium. CAP. XIIII.
units.tr: On the Place from Parts. CHAP. XIV.

units.la: QVOD est firmamentum loci ex Partibus, cùm quæritur An sit Totum? Locus hic bipartitò tractatur. Aut enim ex parte vna, aut ex pluribus, & rursus ex omnibus aut coniunctis, aut disiunctis, argumentamur. Primum est huiusmodi: Posita parte, sive necessaria sit, sive redundans, non continuò ponitur Totum. Itaque locus ex partibus nullo modo valet ad probandum Totum. nam siue vna pars est, siue plures tätùm, siue omnes disiunctæ, nihil prohibet non esse totum. Totum enim & partes non idem sunt, vt ait Aristoteles in Topicis. Non igitur si est truncus, continuò est arbor: non si est truncus, & ramus, continuò est arbor. Sic, Nó si est & truncus & radix,& hæc inter se disiuncta sint, continuò cst arbor. Nō si trabes sunt,& cementa,& lapides,& tegulæ, continuò domus est: nisi forma cóiunctæ sint. Separatis enim corporibus ex quibus ædes constant,universitas ædium intelligi non potest.l.eũ qui.23,D.de vsurpat.Sequitur 11. Positis partibus omnibus compositis; totum cōceditur.Differtè autem addendum fuit Compositis. Non enim partibus omnibus positis (vt modò diximus )si conipositio,id est forma desit,Totum continuò sequitur, Itaque,bona venia quorundam hominum eruditorum dictum sit,non valet hoc argumentum : Si & radix est,& caudex,& cortex, & frondes [?], & rami, arbor est. Possunt enim esse omnia eiulsa & ruta cæsa,cùm tamen arbor non sit. Hoc autē argumentum partiū enumeratione tractatur, de qua posterius differemus. veluti: Si & invenire & disponere, & memoria tenere, & eloqui potest, orator est. Si & leges, & edicta, & senatusconsulta,& constitutiones, & responsa prudentum,& consuetudinem civitatis tenet, ius civile universum tenet. Sequitur 11 1.Sublata parte, si ea principalis est, Totum tollitur: si minus principalis, non continuò tollitur. nam locus ex parte principali ad refellendum Totum valet: ex minus principali, non valet: veluti: Si rota non est, non est currus. At non si non est artemo, continuò non est nauis.
units.tr: The support of the place from parts, when it is asked whether something is a whole, is treated in two ways. We argue either from one part, or from several, and then from all of them, whether they are joined or separated. The first form is this: once a part is posited, whether it is necessary or superfluous, the whole does not necessarily follow. So the place from parts is in no way valid for proving a whole. For whether there is only one part, or only several, or all of them separated, nothing prevents the thing from not being a whole. The whole and the parts are not the same, as Aristotle says in the Topics. So it does not follow that if there is a trunk, there is a tree; nor, if there is a trunk and a branch, there is a tree. Likewise, if there is a root and a trunk, and these are separated from one another, a tree does not follow. If there are beams, mortar, stones and tiles, it does not follow that there is a house, unless they are joined in a form. For when the bodies from which a building is made are separated, the whole of the building cannot be understood. See the law "Qui eum" 23, D. de usurpationibus. The second form: once all the parts are posited as composed, the whole is granted. But it was necessary to add carefully "composed." For if all the parts are posited (as we have just said) but the composition, that is the form, is lacking, the whole does not follow at once. So, with due respect to certain learned men, this argument is invalid: If there is a root, and a stock, and bark, and leaves [?], and branches, then there is a tree. For all these things can be torn off and cut down, while there is still no tree. Yet this argument is handled by enumeration of parts, which we shall discuss later. For example: If someone can invent, arrange, retain in memory and deliver, he is an orator. If he holds laws, edicts, decrees of the senate, constitutions and the responses of the learned, and the custom of the state, he holds the whole civil law. The third form: when a part is removed, if it is a principal part, the whole is removed; if it is less than principal, the whole is not removed at once. For the place from a principal part is valid for refuting the whole; from a less than principal part it is not valid. For example: If there is no wheel, there is no chariot. But it does not follow that if there is no rudder, there is no ship.

units.la: Quod est firmamentum loci ex partibus, cùm de Totius cóuenientia quæritur? Primum est huiusmodi: Quod parti coniunctæ conuenit, vbi proportio seruatur, etiam toti conuenit. Itaque ex partis ratione de totius ratione argumentum sumitur, hoc est, de quantitate & qualitate: cuius argumenti vis omnis in proportione sita est: vt cùm ex vngue, leonis magnitudo æstimatur: quo' argumento Phidias vsus dicitur, cùm inspecto vngue leonem integrum effinxit. Itémque Pythagoras, qui Herculis magnitudinè ex eo stadio, quod Hercules suis pedibus admensus erat, æstimauit. veluti: Si rota est volubilis, totus currus pro rata est volubilis. Si velum vento pellitur, tota nauis pro rata pellitur. Ex hoc genere illud est ex lib. Ciceronis de nat. deo. 2. Nullius sensu carentis pars aliqua potest esse sentiens. Mundi autem partes sentientes sunt, non igitur caret sensu mundus. Et lib. 3. Si ea intereunt, ex quibus constat omne animal, nullum est animal sempiternum. Et lib. de Orat. 1. Mirari desinamus, quæ caussa sit eloquentiü paucitatis: cùm ex illis rebus vniuersis eloquentia constet, quibus in singulis elaborare permagnum est. At si proportio nulla est, nulla convenientia est. Itaque non si Aethiopis dentes sunt candidi, iccirco Aethiops est candidus. non si contignatio domus lignea est, iccirco domus est lignea. Sequitur II. Quod parti disiunctæ convenit, non iccirco toti pro rata convenit. Non si separatim quisque horum puerorum bene canit, iccirco coniuncti symphonia canere poterunt. nam plerunque voces coniunctæ discrepant. non si separatim quisque horum equorum velox est ad currum, iccirco ad bigas aut quadrigas aptisunt. Non si rota separata volui potest, iccirco reliqua pars currus voluetur. Sequitur III. Quod parti coniunctæ non convenit, ubi proportio est, toti pro rata non convenit. Si tunicæ virilis manica puero non convenit, nec tota tunica conueniet. Sequitur IIII. Quod parti disiunctæ non convenit ubi proportio nulla est, non iccirco toti non convenit. veluti: non si prora aut transtrum separatum non fluctuat, iccirco coniunctū non fluctuabit. nō si solus equitatus vincere non potuit, iccirco cum exercitu coniunctus vincere non poterit. Sed in his omnibus (ut ante dixi) magna proportionis ratio adhibenda est.
units.tr: What is the support of the place from parts, when the agreement of the whole is asked? The first form is this: what agrees with a part joined to others, where the proportion is kept, agrees also with the whole. So an argument about the whole's nature, that is its quantity and quality, is drawn from the nature of the part; the entire force of this argument lies in proportion. Thus from a lion's claw its size is judged; Phidias is said to have used this argument when, having inspected a claw, he fashioned the whole lion. Likewise Pythagoras, who estimated the size of Hercules from the stadium that Hercules had measured with his own feet. For example: If the wheel is able to turn, the whole chariot, in proportion, is able to turn. If the sail is driven by the wind, the whole ship, in proportion, is driven. Of this kind is that passage from Cicero's De natura deorum, book 2: "No part of anything without sense can be sentient. But the parts of the world are sentient; therefore the world is not without sense." And book 3: "If those things perish of which every animal consists, no animal is everlasting." And from De oratore, book 1: "Let us cease to wonder what the cause is of the scarcity of eloquence, since eloquence consists of all those things, each of which it is very hard to labour at in isolation." But if there is no proportion, there is no agreement. So it does not follow that because the teeth of an Ethiopian are white, the Ethiopian is white; nor that because the beams of a house are wooden, the house is wooden. The second form: what agrees with a part separated from the others does not for that reason agree with the whole, in proportion. It does not follow that because each of these boys sings well separately, they will be able to sing in harmony when joined; for often joined voices clash. Nor, because each of these horses is swift for a chariot separately, are they therefore fit for a two-horse or four-horse team. Nor, because a wheel separated can be turned, will the rest of the chariot be turned. The third form: what does not agree with a part joined to others, where there is proportion, does not agree with the whole in proportion. If a man's sleeve does not fit a boy, neither will the whole tunic fit. The fourth form: what does not agree with a separated part, where there is no proportion, does not for that reason fail to agree with the whole. For example: it does not follow that because a prow or a crossbeam separated does not float, the joined whole will not float; nor that because the cavalry alone could not conquer, the cavalry joined with the army will not be able to conquer. But in all these cases (as I said before) a great regard for proportion must be applied.

units.la: Quæ sunt firmaménta Reciprocationis? Primum est huiusmodi, Ut toto concesso partes principales conceduntur, sic concessis partibus omnibus compositis, totum conceditur. Sequitur II. Ut posito toto non cōtinuò partes redundantes ponuntur : sic posita parte a‐ liqua non continuò totum conceditur. Sequitur III. Neque sublato toto, continuò partes tolluntur: neque sublata redundáte parte,totum tollitur. nam necessaria quidem certè tollitur. Sequitur IIII. Ut quod toti conuenit, compositis partibus pro rata conuenit : ita quod parti coniunctæ conuenit, vbi proportionì locus est, etiam toti conuenit. Sequitur V. Ut cui Totum non cóuenit,vbi proportio est, partes non conueniunt : ita cui pars non conuenit,totum similiter non conueniet.
units.tr: What are the supports of reciprocation? The first is this: as the principal parts are granted when the whole is granted, so when all the composed parts are granted, the whole is granted. The second: as, once the whole is posited, the superfluous parts are not posited at once, so, once some part is posited, the whole is not granted at once. The third: neither, once the whole is removed, are the parts removed at once; nor, once a superfluous part is removed, is the whole removed. For a necessary part is certainly removed. The fourth: as what agrees with the whole agrees in proportion with the parts when composed, so what agrees with a part joined to others, where there is room for proportion, also agrees with the whole. The fifth: as the parts do not agree with that to which the whole does not agree, where there is proportion, so likewise the whole will not agree with that to which a part does not agree.

units.la: De loco Caussarum. CAP. XV.
units.tr: On the place from causes. CHAPTER XV.

units.la: VOD est firmamentum loci ex Cauffis,cū quæritur an sint Esse&a? Quoniam effectus is demum dicitur,qui ex caussarum cócurfu nascitur,de eo tantum breuitatis caussa præcipiemus,neque singulas persequemur. Caussarum autem concursum intelligimus,cùm caussæ sunt absolutè vi sua efficientes. Primum igitur firmamentum fit huiusmodi I.Posita caussa,ponitur Effectus.Secundum illud:II.Sublata caussa,tollitur Effectus. Caussa enim à suis effectis(vt ait Cicero) non seiungitur.Et,vt ait Ariftoteles lib.Rhetor.2.cap.42 : Si caussa est, etiam est id,cuius ea caussa est:& fi hoc non fit, ne illud quidem. Simul enim & caussa & euenta sunt. ἐὰν τι ὑπάρχῃ, ὅτι ἐστὶ, κἂν μὴ ὑπάρχῃ, ὅτι οὐ[?] ἔστιν. ἅμα γὰρ τὸ ἄρτιον ἢ ἕ [?]ἄρτιον. ἢ ἄνευ αὐτῆς, ᾧδ' ἐν [?]
units.tr: What is the foundation of the place from causes, when it is asked whether something is an effect? Since an effect is properly said to be that which arises from a concurrence of causes, we will teach only briefly about this and will not pursue each cause individually. We understand a concurrence of causes when the causes are each absolutely efficient by their own power. The first foundation is therefore of this kind: (1) When the cause is posited, the effect is posited. The second follows from it: (2) When the cause is removed, the effect is removed. For a cause is not separated from its effects (as Cicero says). And, as Aristotle says in Rhetoric book 2, chapter 4: If the cause is, then that of which it is the cause also is; and if this is not, neither is that. For cause and effect exist together [ἐὰν τι ὑπάρχῃ, ὅτι ἐστί, κἂν μὴ ὑπάρχῃ, ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν. ἅμα γὰρ τὸ αἴτιον].

units.la: Valet igitur locus ex caussis, tum ad confirmandum, tum ad refellendum effectum. Veluti: Si sol lucet, dies est: si non lucet, dies non est. Cùm conciliatrix amicitiæ virtutis opinio fit, difficile est amicitiam manere, si à virtute defeceris: ait in Lælio Cicero. Eodémque pertinet regula, cuius magnus in disciplinis est usus: Cui caussa sine qua non adimitur, ei res principalis adimitur. veluti: Quoniam illi acumen defuit, Dialecticus esse non potuit. nam in Dialecticæ studioso caussa sine qua non, est acumen ingenij. unde illud Ciceronis in Academicis: Faciunt pueriliter. quo enim omnia iudicantur, sublato, reliqua se negant tollere. ut siquis quem oculis priuauerit, dicat, ea quæ cerni possent, nō se ei ademisse. Hinc illud populi Rom. institutum, ut aqua & igni interdicerent iis, quibus ciuitate verbo adimere nolebat. Hinc Iulianus Apostata cognominatus non se Christianæ religionis ministris conuentum habendorum potestatem eripere dicebat, sed usum rhedarum & vehiculorum adimebat. Huc illud Iurisconsultorum pertinet: Quod per se esse non potest, rapit secum in accessionis locum id, sine quo esse non potest.
units.tr: The place from causes is therefore valid both for confirming and for refuting an effect. For example: If the sun shines, it is day; if it does not shine, it is not day. When the opinion of virtue, which brings about friendship, is present, friendship finds it hard to last if you have departed from virtue: so Cicero says in the Laelius. The rule that is of great use in the disciplines also belongs here: when the cause without which a thing cannot be is taken away, the principal thing is taken away. For example: since he lacked keenness, he could not be a dialectician; for for a student of dialectic the cause without which he cannot be one is keenness of wit. Hence that saying of Cicero in the Academics: "They talk childishly. For when that by which all things are judged is removed, the rest cannot be said to be removed either," just as if someone deprived a man of his eyes and then said that the things which could be seen had not been taken away from him. Hence the custom of the Roman people of forbidding water and fire to those whom they did not wish to deprive of citizenship in words. Hence Julian, surnamed the Apostate, said that he was not taking from the ministers of the Christian religion the power of holding assemblies, but only the use of carriages and vehicles. To this belongs the lawyers' saying: What cannot exist by itself draws with it, into the place of accession, that without which it cannot exist.

units.la: Quod est firmamentum loci ex caussis, cùm cõuenientia quæritur? Hæc sunt huiusmodi. I. Cui conuenit causa, eidem etiam effectus conuenit: vicissimque, Quod causæ conuenit, essectui conuenit. veluti: Si bona sapientia est bonos sapientes efficit. Item, Libidinosa & intemperans adolescentia effœtum corpus tradit senectuti. Si quod generauit bonum est, etiam quod generatur, est bonum. Si quod corrumpit, bonum: malum, quòd corrumpitur. Item de natur. deor. 3. Vt si omnis cera commutabilis esset, nihil esset cereū quod commutari non posset: item, nihil argentum, nihil aeneum, si commutabilis esset natura argenti & aeris: similiter si omnia quæ sunt, ex quibus cuncta constât, mutabilia sunt; nullum corpus esse potest non mutabile. Sequitur II. Cui non conuenit causa vnica efficiens, eidem nec effectus conuenit. vicissimque quod causæ nō conuenit, nec effectui conuenit. veluti, Potest bonum cuiquam malo esse? Potéstne quisquā in abundantia bonorum ipse esse non bonus? Item: Quicquam bonum est, quod non eum qui posidet, meliorem faciat? Huius autē generis est argumentatio ex causa sine qua non: quæ cùm abest, poni effectus non potest. vnde illud Anacharsis ioculare, Quia vites apud Scytas nullę sunt, nullas esse tibicines: a quo illud Ciceronis non abhorret: quia ebriosus Muræna non sit, saltatorem non esse. Intempestiui conuiuij, amœni loci multarum deliciarum comes est extrema saltatio. Videndum autem erit diligenter quæ causæ ponentur, aut negabuntur. qua de re quoniam in affectuum explicatione disseruimus, illinc assumentur, quæ ad hunc locum pertinebunt.
units.tr: What is the foundation of the place from causes, when agreement is sought? These are of this kind: (1) What agrees with a cause, the effect also agrees with; and conversely, what agrees with the effect, agrees with the cause. For example: If good wisdom exists, it makes men wise. Likewise: A lustful and intemperate youth hands down a worn-out body to old age. If that which produced something is good, that which is produced is also good; if that which corrupts is good, that which is corrupted is bad. Likewise in On the Nature of the Gods, book 3: If all wax were changeable, there would be no waxen thing that could not be changed; likewise there would be no silver and no bronze, if the nature of silver and bronze were changeable; similarly, if all the things that exist, from which everything is composed, are changeable, no body can be unchangeable. (2) What the single efficient cause does not agree with, the effect does not agree with either; and conversely, what does not agree with the cause does not agree with the effect. For example: Can a good thing be bad for anyone? Can anyone, amid an abundance of goods, himself fail to be good? Likewise: Is anything good which does not make its possessor better? Of this kind is also the argument from a cause without which, when it is absent, the effect cannot be posited. Hence that jesting saying of Anacharsis: Because there are no vines among the Scythians, there are no flute-players; and Cicero's remark is not far from this: because Murena is not drunk, he is not a dancer; and the final dance is the companion of an unseasonable banquet and a pleasant place of many delights. We must, however, carefully consider which causes are posited or denied. Since we have discussed this in the explanation of the affections, what pertains to this place will be taken from there.

units.la: Quod est Firmamentum loci ex essectis, cùm queritur an causæ subsint?
units.tr: What is the foundation of the place from effects, when it is asked whether causes are present?

units.la: Primum est huiusmodi : Posito essectu ea causa ponitur, quæ sola & absolutè efficiens est. Itaque hic locus ad confirmandam causam valet. veluti: Si est incendiū, est ignis. Si dies est, follucet. Si peperit, cum viro concubuit. Si cinis est, fuit incendium. Sequitur II. Sublato effectu ea demum causa tollitur, quæ sola & absolutè efficiens est. Itaque ad refellendam causam valet. Veluti : Si dies non est, sol non lucet. Nihil enim est quod diem efficiat, præter solis lumen. Si est vmbra, corpus est in sole. At si aliud causarum genus fit, nihil valebit. veluti: Si non peperit, cum viro non concubuit. Si non est Dialecticus, non studuit, aut non præceptorem bonum habuit. Potest enim vtrunque habuisse, cùm in illo vel acumen ingenij, vel diligentia desset.
units.tr: The first is of this kind: When the effect is posited, that cause is posited which alone and absolutely is efficient. So this place is valid for confirming a cause. For example: If there is a fire, there is flame. If it is day, the sun shines. If she has given birth, she has lain with a husband. If there is ash, there was a fire. (2) When the effect is removed, only that cause is removed which alone and absolutely is efficient. So this place is valid for refuting a cause. For example: If it is not day, the sun is not shining, for nothing makes the day except the light of the sun. If there is a shadow, a body is in the sun. But if the cause is of another kind, nothing will be proved. For example: If she has not given birth, she has not lain with a husband. If he is not a dialectician, he did not study, or did not have a good teacher; for he may have had both, since in him either keenness of wit or diligence was lacking.

units.la: Quod est Firmamentum de conuenientia?
units.tr: What is the foundation of the argument from agreement?

units.la: Esto hoc 1. Cui conuenit effectus, ei causa conuenit: vicissimque quod effectui congruit, etiam causæ cōgruit ἀεί γὰρ δὴ ᾧ ὑπάρχει ἕκαστον[?], ἐκείνῳ μᾶλλον ὑπάρχει[?] inquit Ariftoteles: quod vulgò sic effertur, Propter quod aliquid tale est, id quoq; magistale est. Velut ex li.Cic.de sin.2.Qui probari potest, vt is qui propter me aliquid gaudeat, plus, quàm ego ipse, gaudeat? Ité lib.de nat.Deor.2. Nihil quod animi & rationis est expers,generare ex fe potest animätem compotémque rationis. mundus autem generat animantes , compotésque rationis. Animans est igitur mundus,compósque rationis.Item:Si ex oliua modulatè canentes tibiæ nascerentur,non dubitares quin effet in oliua tibicinis quædam scientia.quid fi plantani tibias ferrent numerosé sonantes? Idem etiam censeres in platanis inesse musicam? Cur igitur mundus non animans, sapiénsque iudicetur, cùm ex fe procreet animátes atque fapiétes?Sequitur II. superiori confentancü: Qualis effectus est,talis caussa est.Eóqueillud pertinet peruulgatum,Ex baccis arboré agnosci. Item illud:Magistratus virum ostendit.Quod est maius argumentum nihil prodesse philofo phiam (inquit Cicero Tufcul. 2.) quàm quofdam perfectos philosophos turpiter viuere?
units.tr: Let this be the first: (1) What agrees with an effect, the cause also agrees with; and conversely, what agrees with the effect, agrees also with the cause. "For that by which each thing belongs to something belongs more to that thing," says Aristotle; which is commonly rendered thus: because of which something is of such a kind, that also is more so [ἀεὶ γὰρ δὴ ᾧ ὑπάρχει ἕκαστον, ἐκείνῳ μᾶλλον ὑπάρχει]. From the second book of Cicero's On Ends: Can it be proved that one who rejoices because of me rejoices more than I myself do? Also from On the Nature of the Gods, book 2: Nothing that is devoid of mind and reason can generate from itself an animate being possessed of reason; but the world generates animate beings possessed of reason. Therefore the world is animate and possessed of reason. Likewise: If flutes playing tunefully were born from an olive tree, you would not doubt that there was some skill of the flute-player in the olive tree. What if plane trees bore flutes sounding in rhythm? Would you think music too was in the plane trees? Why then is the world not judged to be animate and wise, since it produces animate and wise beings from itself? (2) In accordance with the above: What kind of effect it is, such is the cause. Hence the widely known saying: a tree is recognised by its berries. Likewise that: The magistrate shows the man. What is a greater proof that philosophy profits nothing (says Cicero in the Tusculan Disputations, book 2) than that some perfect philosophers live shamefully?

units.la: Atque huc, meo iudicio , locus ex adie&tione pertinet, quem Ariftoteles appellat ἐκ τῆς προ-θέσεως[?]: veluti:Siquidem alteri adie&tū, id bonum efficit:etiam illud bonum esse necefle est.
units.tr: And here, in my judgment, belongs the place from addition, which Aristotle calls from the proposition [ἐκ τῆς προσθέσεως]: for example: if something added to another makes it good, it must necessarily be that that thing too is good.

units.la: Valet etiam ad proportionem hic locus: utcu[?] iusmaior & præstantior est esse&us , ea caussa maior& præstantior habeatur.Unde illud Ciceronis in lib.de natur.Deor. 3.Si aliquid est, quod homo efficere non potest: qui id efficit, melior est homine . Homo autem hæc quæ in mundo sunt efficere non potest.qui potuit igitu,is præstat homini. Homini autem præstare quis posit, nisi Deus? Item illud in Philip.
units.tr: This place is also valid for proportion: when the effect is greater and more excellent, the cause is held to be greater and more excellent. Hence that saying of Cicero in On the Nature of the Gods, book 3: If there is something which man cannot produce, whoever produces it is better than man. Man, however, cannot produce those things which are in the world; therefore whoever could produce them is superior to man. But who could be superior to man, except God? Likewise that in the Philippics, book

units.la: XI. Ut maior est vis animi quàm corporis, sic sunt graviora quæ cócipiuntur animo, quàm illa quę corpore. Seq. III. Cui effectus nō conuenit, ei causa nō cōuenit: vicisimque quod effectui non conuenit, id causæ non conuenit. Si fruges ex eo agro non nascantur bonæ, nec bonus fundus est. Verùm (ut superiùs monui) videndum est diligenter ut vel causarum omniū fit concursus, vel certè causa necessaria & absolutè efficiens: non autem socia & adiutrix. Ut illa προσθέσεως[?], de qua loquitur Aristoteles: Nō enim, inquit, si id quod additur, nō facit id cui adiunctū est bonū, propterea id nō bonū est. veluti: Non si discipulus indoctus abiit, iccirco præceptor fuit indoct[?]. nō enim præceptor eruditionis causa fuit absolutè efficiēs. Ex eodem genere lubricū illud est argumentandi genus vulgò usurpatum: Ut res secundæ Imperatori auctoritate conciliāt, sic res aduersæ minuunt. Item illud Lucani:
units.tr: XI. As the power of the mind is greater than that of the body, so the things conceived by the mind are weightier than those conceived by the body. Next, third: (1) What the effect does not agree with, the cause does not agree with; and conversely, what does not agree with the effect, does not agree with the cause. If good crops do not spring from that field, the soil is not good. But (as I warned above) one must carefully see that there is either a concurrence of all the causes, or certainly a necessary and absolutely efficient cause, and not merely a companion and helper. As in that of addition, of which Aristotle speaks: For, he says, if what is added does not make that to which it is joined good, it is not therefore not good. For example: If an untaught pupil departed, it does not follow that the teacher was untaught; for the teacher was not the absolutely efficient cause of his learning. From the same kind is that slippery way of arguing commonly used: As prosperous events win an Emperor authority, so adverse events diminish it. Likewise that of Lucan:

units.la: -- Quis iustius induat arma, Scire nefas: magno se iudice quisque tuetur. Victrix causa diis placuit, sed victa Catoni.
units.tr: -- Who would rightly take up arms is unknown to know: each man defends himself with a great judge. The winning cause pleased the gods, but the losing cause pleased Cato.

units.la: Non enim consilia ex euentis iudicanda sunt. Et quod Cæsar, Cicero veteréque omnes rerum euentis coacti toties inculcant, multùm cùm in omnibus rebus, tum in re militari fortunam valere: id nos de moderatore rerum omnium Deo verè affirmare possumus: ut non tam euenta, quàm auctorem spectemus.
units.tr: For plans are not to be judged by their outcomes. And although Caesar, Cicero and all the others, forced by events, so often insist that fortune counts for much in all affairs, and especially in war, we can truly affirm this of God, the governor of all things: that we should look not so much at outcomes as at the author.

units.la: Quæ sunt firmamenta Reciprocationis?
units.tr: What are the supports of Reciprocation?

units.la: Primū est huiusmodi: Ut posita cau-sa effectus sequitur: sic posito effectu causa absolutè efficiens ponitur. Sequitur II. Ut sublata causa, effectus tollitur: sic sublato effectu, causa absolutè efficiés tollitur. Sequitur III. Ut cui causa conuenit, effectus conuenit: sic cui conuenit effectus, ei causa conuenit. Sequitur IIII. Ut cui non conuenit causa absolutè efficiens, ei effectus non conuenit: sic cui non conuenit effectus, nec causa conuenit. Quorum omniū exempla quiuis mediocriter eruditus excogitare poterit.
units.tr: The first is this: as, when a cause is posited, its effect follows, so, when an effect is posited, the efficient cause is posited absolutely. The second: as, when a cause is removed, its effect is removed, so, when an effect is removed, the efficient cause is removed absolutely. The third: as what a cause belongs to, its effect belongs to, so what an effect belongs to, its cause belongs to. The fourth: as what an efficient cause does not belong to, its effect does not belong to, so what an effect does not belong to, its cause does not belong to either. Anyone of moderate learning will be able to think up examples of all of these.

units.la: De loco Relationis. CAP. XVII.
units.tr: On the Place of Relation. CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: VOD[?] est Firmamentum ex Relatione, cùm quæritur, an alterū relatum sit? Unum hoc erit: Ut posito uno Relatorum, alterū necessariò ponitur: ita negato uno, alterum necessariò negatur. Tanta enim inter hæc necessitudo à natura est, ut alterum esse sine altero non possit, atque adeo naturæ ordine alterum altero prius non fit. Itaque locus hic ad probandum & refellendum valet. Reciprocationem enim admittit, veluti in illa Socratis: qui cùm à Melito accusaretur, quasi Deos esse negaret: primùm ex illo percontatus est, an etiam Dæmonas esse inficiaretur: deinde negante Melito, sic intulit: Nónne dæmones ex diis nati sunt? Annuente illo: Si sunt deorū liberi, sunt dij, & si non sunt dij,non sunt deorum liberi.Ex eodem genere illa sunt: Si est Imperator,est exercit'.Et si exercitus , est Imperator. vicissimque si non est Imperator,non est exercitus:si non est exercitus,non est Imperator . Si tu illi cognatus es, vicissim ille tibi.si nō ille tibi,nec tu illi.Hinc illud Crassi in Philippum: Si[?] tibi ego Senator non sum,nec tu mihi Consul. Et libr.de natu. deor,3.Age porro: Iovem & Neptunū Deum numeras.ergo etiam Orcus frater eorūDeus. Si nó est Orcus Deus,quid dicitis ergo de fratribus? Et si ij fratres sunt in numero Deorū, num de patre eorum Saturno negari potest? qui si est Deus, patrem quoque eius cœlū esse Deum confitendū est.Ex eodé genere illud est vetus, quia fine acceptione donatio nulla est. Mācinus qui à Numātinis acceptus nō est,nō fuit deditus.Vnde illa iuris regula,Non videtur data quæ eo tempore quo dantur accipietis non fiunt.
units.tr: What is the argument from relation, when it is asked whether the other correlative is also so? It runs thus: as, when one of two correlatives is posited, the other is necessarily posited, so when one is denied, the other is necessarily denied. For such is the necessary connection between them by nature that one cannot exist without the other, and so by the order of nature neither is prior to the other. Hence this place is valid both for proving and for refuting. For it admits of reciprocation, as in that saying of Socrates. When Meletus accused him of denying that there are gods, Socrates first asked him whether he also denied that there are demons. Meletus denying it, Socrates inferred: Are not demons born of the gods? When Meletus assented, he said: If they are children of the gods, they are gods; and if they are not gods, they are not children of the gods. Of the same kind are these: If there is an Imperator, there is an army; and if there is an army, there is an Imperator. Conversely, if there is no Imperator, there is no army; if there is no army, there is no Imperator. If you are a kinsman of him, he is conversely a kinsman of you; if he is not a kinsman of you, neither are you of him. Hence that saying of Crassus against Philippus: If I am not a senator to you, neither are you a consul to me. And in the book On the Nature of the Gods, book 3: Come now, you count Jupiter and Neptune as gods; therefore Orcus, their brother, is also a god. If Orcus is not a god, what do you say then about his brothers? And if they are brothers in the number of the gods, can it be denied of their father Saturn? If he is a god, his father Caelus must also be confessed to be a god. Of the same kind is the old saying: there is no gift without acceptance. Mancinus, who was not accepted by the Numantines, was not surrendered to them. Hence that rule of law: those things are not regarded as given which, at the time they are given, do not become the recipient's.

units.la: Quod est Frmamentum de convenientia? Sepenumero dictum est,Relata nequaquā esse vi & natura contraria:sed figura tantùm, & situ, & positione inter se opponi. Itaque longè alia relatorum , quàm contrariorum ratio & facultas est . Non enim si unum contrarium uni ex relatis convenit, eius contrarium alteri relato conveniet.ut,Non si pater est doctus, iccirco filius doctus nō est. Aut nō si dominus est robustus, iccirco servus robustus non est.
units.tr: What is the argument from agreement? It has often been said that relatives are not contrary by their force and nature, but are opposed to one another only in form, position and placement. So the reasoning and capacity of relatives is quite different from that of contraries. For if one contrary belongs to one of two relatives, its contrary does not therefore belong to the other relative. For example: it does not follow that because the father is learned, the son is learned; or because the master is strong, the slave is strong.

units.la: Firmamentum igitur hoc est, Quod uni relatorum conuenit ; alteri etiam necessario conuenit: & vicissim, quod vni non conuenit, nec alteri conuenit. Si discere Dialecticam honestum est, docere honestum est. Et si hoc non est, ne illud quidé. Si fœnori pecuniâ accipere honestum est, dare honestum est. Et si dare fœnori æquum non est, nec accipere rectum est. Si portorium locare honestum est, conducere quoque honestum est. Si non hoc, ne illud quidem. Ex hoc genere illud est Aristotelis libr. Rhetor.2. Si tu iuste & honeste supplicio assectus es, ego iuste & honeste supplicio te affeci. Quod ad carnificum existimationem defendendam valet.
units.tr: The argument is therefore this: what belongs to one of the relatives necessarily belongs also to the other; and conversely, what does not belong to one does not belong to the other either. If it is honourable to learn dialectic, it is honourable to teach it; and if the latter is not honourable, neither is the former. If it is honourable to take money at interest, it is honourable to lend it at interest; and if it is not fair to lend at interest, neither is it right to receive it. If it is honourable to farm out the customs duties, it is also honourable to contract for them; if not the one, then not the other either. Of this kind is that passage of Aristotle in Rhetoric 2: If you have been justly and honourably subjected to punishment, I have justly and honourably punished you. This is useful for defending the reputation of executioners.

units.la: Quæ sunt firmamenta Reciprocationis? Relationis effectus naturalem reciprocationē habet: quæ in superioribus firmamentis necessario exposita est. Itaque ad affectum locúque Proprij transfeundum est.
units.tr: What are the arguments of reciprocation? The effect of relation has a natural reciprocation, which was necessarily set out among the foregoing arguments. Therefore we must pass to the affect and to the place of the Proprium.

units.la: De loco Proprij. CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: On the place from the proper (property). CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: QUOD[?] est Firmamentum ex Proprio, ad id cuius proprium est? Locus hic tantum ad convenientiam & reciprocationem pertinet. nam posito proprio, dubitari de subiectę speciei essentia non potest. Unum autem hoc Firmamentum est: Ut posito proprio, species ponitur: sic sublato proprio, tollitur species: si modo verum illud proprium est, de quo in Affectuum præceptione disseruimus Itaque locus ex Proprio ad speciem & confirmandam & refellendam valet.veluti:Si lapis hic ferrum allicit,est magnes.Si non allicit,non est magnes.Si à natura volandi vim habet,est auis. Si non habet, non est auis, Si hinniedi vim habet, est equus. Si non habet,non est equus. Si ratione vtitur, est homo.Si non vtitur,non est homo. Si est olor,est candidus. Si non est candidus, non est olor.Si est coruus, est niger.Si non est niger, non est coruus.
units.tr: What is the firmament from the proper, to that whose proper it is? This place pertains only to agreement and reciprocation. For once the proper is posited, there can be no doubt about the essence of the species that is its subject. This is one firmament: as, when the proper is posited, the species is posited; so, when the proper is removed, the species is removed; provided that the proper in question is true, the proper of which we spoke in the teaching on affections. So the place from the proper is valid both for confirming and for refuting a species. For example: If this stone attracts iron, it is a magnet. If it does not attract, it is not a magnet. If it has the power of flying by nature, it is a bird. If it does not have it, it is not a bird. If it has the power of neighing, it is a horse. If it does not have it, it is not a horse. If it uses reason, it is a man. If it does not use it, it is not a man. If it is a swan, it is white. If it is not white, it is not a swan. If it is a raven, it is black. If it is not black, it is not a raven.

units.la: Quod ést Firmamentum reciprocationis? In veré propriis, vt specie concelsa[?] proprium conceditur:sic proprio concelsio[?],species sequitur.Itémque, Vt sublata specie tollitur proprium,sic sublato proprio,species tollitur. At in eo quod veré proprium non ést, nulla reciprocatio ést:quod quia in affectibus explicatum ést,actum (quod proverbio[?] vetamur) nó agemus.
units.tr: What is the firmament of reciprocation? In truly proper attributes, just as the proper is granted when the species is granted, so when the proper is granted, the species follows. And likewise: just as, when the species is removed, the proper is removed, so when the proper is removed, the species is removed. But in that which is not truly proper, there is no reciprocation; since this has been explained in the discussion of affections, we will not do the thing (which we are forbidden by the proverb to do) and go over it again.

units.la: De loco Antecedentis. CAP. XIX.
units.tr: On the Place of the Antecedent. CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: Non[?] est Firmamentum ex antecedente? Primum & secundum sunt huiusmodi: Vt necessaria antecedente concesso, quod consequens est, subsequitur:sic negato antecedente, consequens tollitur.Sed videndum est diligenter,vt necessaria consecutio fit. Valet enim hic locus ad necessarium consequens & confirmandum & re-felfellendum.Veluti:Si uesperi coelum rubet, postridie sudum erit.Si Lucifer exortus est, mox solis ortus subsequetur. Si nondum ortus est, sol nondum propinquat. Si pleuritide correptus est,febri uexabitur.Si non est natus postumus(inquibat orator Antonius) non est mortuus. Ex quo illud est in oratione pro Sylla: Neque enim princeps ad salutem esse potuisem , si esse alij comites noluissent. At si nulla necessaria inter Antecedens & Consequens cohærentia est, neutram in partem argumentum valet. veluti : Si aratio facta est, sementis fiet.Si arbores florescunt,ver propinquat. Interdum enim præmaturè arbores florescunt. Eadémque conuenientiæ ratio est.Nam si cui conuenit Antecedens, eidem necessarium cósequens conuenict: & si cui illud non conuenit,ne hoc quidé.Ut in illo peruulgato:Qualem sementem feceris,ita & metes. Et pro Muræna:Nemo fere saltat sobrius,nisi forte infanit : neque in solitudine , neque in conuiuio moderato atque honesto.Intempestiui conuiuij; amoeni loci,multarum delitiarum,comes est extrema saltatio. tu mihi arripis id quod necesseest omnium vitiorum esse postremum. relinquis illa, quibus remotis hoc vitium omnino esse non potest. Itaque huc illa Iuris regula pertinet:Cùm principalis caussa non confistit , ne eà quidem quæ sequuntur locum habent.Ex eodem genere illud est: Quò quisque est ingeniosior, eò magis acutis disputationibus delectatur: quò quisque tardior eò minus. Ex quo intelligi potest, quamobrem nōnulli Aristotelis lectione magis aut minus delectentur. Indidem illud est Ciceronis lib.de nat.Deor.3. Si nullum corpus immortale est, nullum est corpus sempiternum. corpus autem immortale nullum est,ne indiuiduum quidem.nullum igitur sempiternum est. Item:Si omne animal dolorem capit, id accipiat etiā interitum necesse est.Atque hic quidem argumenti ex antecedentibus locus est, eáque firmamentorum formula. Cicero autem in Topicis septuplicem formam ac rationem horū trium locorum tractandorum exponit: Antecedentium,Consequentium,& Repugnantiū: quæ ad locorum præceptionem nihil omnino pertinet: sed ad formas argumentationū, de quibus posterius differemus.
units.tr: What is the strength of an argument from the antecedent? The first and second forms are these: just as, when the antecedent is granted, the consequent that is necessarily connected with it follows, so when the antecedent is denied, the consequent is removed. But one must look carefully to see whether the consequence is necessary. This place is useful both for confirming and for refuting a necessary consequent. For example: If the sky is red in the evening, it will be clear the next day. If Lucifer has risen, the rising of the sun will soon follow. If it has not yet risen, the sun is not yet near. If he is seized with pleurisy, he will be troubled by fever. If he was not born posthumous (said the orator Antonius), he is not dead. Hence that passage in the speech for Sulla: "For the leader could not have been safe, if the others had not been willing to be his companions." But if there is no necessary connection between antecedent and consequent, the argument is valid in neither direction, as in: If the ploughing has been done, the sowing will be done; if the trees are in flower, spring is near. For trees sometimes flower too early. The rule of agreement is the same: if the antecedent belongs to someone, the necessary consequent belongs to him too; and if the antecedent does not belong to him, neither does the consequent. So in the well-known saying: "As you sow, so shall you reap." And in the speech for Murena: "Hardly anyone dances while sober, unless perhaps he is mad; neither in solitude nor at a moderate and respectable dinner. Dancing is the last thing that follows an ill-timed dinner, pleasant places and many delights. You snatch up what is, as you say, the last of all vices, and you leave aside those things without which this vice cannot exist at all." To this belongs the rule of law: "When the principal cause does not exist, neither do the things that follow from it have any place." From the same kind is this: The more clever someone is, the more he delights in subtle disputations; the duller he is, the less he does. From this it can be understood why some people take more or less pleasure in reading Aristotle. From the same source is Cicero's argument in the third book of On the Nature of the Gods: If no body is immortal, no body is everlasting. But no body is immortal, not even an indivisible one; therefore none is everlasting. Likewise: If every animal feels pain, it must also undergo death. This is indeed a place of argument from antecedents, and a form of proof of this kind. But Cicero, in the Topics, sets out a sevenfold form and method of treating these three places: of the antecedent, the consequent, and the repugnant. This has no bearing at all on the teaching of the places, but on the forms of argument, which we shall discuss later.

units.la: De loco Consequentis. CAP. XX.
units.tr: On the Place of the Consequent. CHAPTER XX.

units.la: QVOD est firmamentū ex consequente ad antecedens? Ponatur hoc I. Cōcesso necessario consequente, antecedens conceditur. Itaque locus ex consequente valet ad necessarium antecedens confirmandum. Veluti: Si satio est, fuit aratio. Si reuertit, abierat. Sequitur II. Sublato consequente, necessarium antecedens tollitur. nā (vt Cicero de Finib. 4. scribit) cū consequens aliquod falsum est, illud cuius id consequens est non potest esse verum. Si nondum dies est, nondum Lucifer exortus est. Si excusso sacco patera non excidit, non fuerat imposita. Eodē illud pertinet ex oratione pro Sylla: Cuius vicarius qui velit esse, inueniri nemo potest: lōgè ab eo abest regni suspicio. Item illud ex lib. de nat. deor. 3. Si dij sunt, sunt etiam Nymphæ deæ. Si nymphæ, panifci etiam, & satyri. hi autem non sunt: ne nymphæ quidem deæ igitur. Item in lib. de Amicitia: Si curam fugimus, virtus fugienda est: quæ necesse est, ut cū aliqua cura res sibi contrarias aspernetur, atque oderit. Ex eodem genere sunt, quæ ex tempore sumuntur. velut illud Ciceronis: Si Numa fuit auditor Pythagoræ, necesse est eo tempore illum fuisse, quo Pythagoras docuit: At aliquanto ante Pythagoram fuit, auditor igitur ipsius esse non potuit. Item quæ ex loco: Si Sextus Roscius Romæ illo die patrem interfecit, Romæ certè illo die fuit. At illo die Ameriæ visus est. Si Clodius eo die Romæ in opertum Bonæ deæ ingressus est, illo die Romæ fuit. At illo die Interannæ visus est. Ex eodem genere sunt illa Jurisconsultorum: Cui quid propter aliud cōceditur, eidem illud ipsum concedatur necesse est. Quod vulgò sic effertur: Concesso fine, omnia quæ ad eum necessaria sunt, concededuntur. Veluti: Cui jurisdictio data est, ei quoque concessa esse videntur, sine quibus explicari jurisdictio non potest. Item, Quod per se esse non potest, rapit secum in accessionis locum id fine quo esse non potest. Nam (ut ait Aristoteles in libro de cœlo) Propositis duobus extremis, si posterius fine priore convenire non potest, prius autem convenire non potest, certè nec posterius poterit. At si necessarium non est, non valebit. veluti: Si satio non est, non fuit aratio. Si non rediit, non abierat. Potuit enim ibi manere, aut mori. Quod eodem modo de Convenientia iudicandum est.
units.tr: What is the argument from the consequent to the antecedent? Let this be the first rule: if the necessary consequent is granted, the antecedent is granted. So the place from the consequent serves to confirm a necessary antecedent. For example: If there is sowing, there has been ploughing. If he has returned, he had gone away. It follows, second: if the consequent is removed, the necessary antecedent is removed. For (as Cicero writes in De Finibus 4) when some consequent is false, that of which it is the consequent cannot be true. If it is not yet day, Lucifer has not yet risen. If, when the sack is shaken, the dish does not fall out, it had not been put in. To this same point belongs the passage from the speech For Sulla: "No one can be found who would be his deputy; suspicion of kingship is far from him." Likewise that from the third book of On the Nature of the Gods: "If there are gods, there are also nymphs, goddesses. If there are nymphs, there are also Panisci and satyrs. But these do not exist; therefore not even nymphs are goddesses." Likewise in the book On Friendship: "If we flee from care, virtue must be fled, which, since it is bound to some care, necessarily spurns and hates things contrary to it." Of the same kind are those drawn from time, such as Cicero's: "If Numa was a hearer of Pythagoras, he must have been alive at the time when Pythagoras taught. But he lived some time before Pythagoras; therefore he could not have been his hearer." Likewise those drawn from place: "If Sextus Roscius killed his father at Rome on that day, he was certainly at Rome on that day. But on that day he was seen at Ameria." "If Clodius entered the rites of the Good Goddess at Rome on that day, he was at Rome on that day. But on that day he was seen at Interamna." Of the same kind are those of the jurists: "To whom something is granted for the sake of something else, that same thing must necessarily be granted to him." This is commonly expressed thus: "When the end is granted, all things necessary to it are granted." For example: "To whom jurisdiction is given, the powers without which jurisdiction cannot be exercised seem to be granted as well." Likewise: "What cannot exist by itself carries with it, as an accessory, that without which it cannot exist." For (as Aristotle says in the book On the Heavens): when two extremes are proposed, if the latter cannot agree with the middle, and the former cannot agree with it either, then the latter certainly cannot agree with the former. But if the antecedent is not necessary, the argument will not hold. For example: If there is no sowing, there has not been ploughing. If he has not returned, he had not gone away; for he could have remained there, or died. The same judgement must be made of agreement in the same way.

units.la: Quod est firmamentum reciprocationis? Primum est huiusmodi: Ut concesso antecedente, necessario consequens succedit: ita cōcesso consequente, necessario antecedens cōceditur. Sequitur II. Ut sublato necessario antecedente, consequens tollitur: ita sublato consequente necessario antecedens tollitur. Sequitur III. Ut cui antecedens convenit, ei consequens necessarium convenit: ita cui hoc convenit, etiam illud convenit. Sequitur IIII. Ut à quo necessarium antecedens dissidet, etiam consequens dissidet: sic à quo consequens dissidet, etiam antecedens dissidet. Quod cum ita sit, non dubito quin ad hunc locum aptissime conveniant, quæ Aristoteles secúdo Topico extremo ad Aientia & negantia retulit, hoc modo: Si quod honestum est, id iucundum est: etiam si quid non sit iucundum, id honestum non est. At si quod iucundum non est, id non est honestum: certè quod honestum est, etiam iucundum est. Eodémque ex fonte ducta illa Ciceronis acerrima disputatio est in Officiis. Si quod honestum est, idem est utile: quod utile non est, id honestum non est. Et si quod utile non est, id honestum non est: etiam quod honestum est, utile est.
units.tr: What is the argument of reciprocation? The first is of this kind: just as, when the antecedent is granted, the necessary consequent follows, so, when the consequent is granted, the necessary antecedent is granted. It follows, second: just as, when the necessary antecedent is removed, the consequent is removed, so, when the consequent is removed, the necessary antecedent is removed. It follows, third: just as what the antecedent belongs to, the necessary consequent also belongs to, so what this belongs to, that also belongs to. It follows, fourth: just as, where the necessary antecedent is absent, the consequent is absent too, so where the consequent is absent, the antecedent is absent too. Since this is so, I do not doubt that those arguments which Aristotle, in the last chapter of the second book of the Topics, related to affirmative and negative propositions fit this place most aptly, in this form: If what is honourable is pleasant, then whatever is not pleasant is not honourable. But if what is pleasant is not honourable, then certainly what is honourable is pleasant. And from the same source comes that most keen disputation of Cicero in On Duties: If what is honourable is also useful, then what is not useful is not honourable. And if what is not useful is not honourable, then what is honourable is useful.

units.la: De loco Adiunctorum. CAP. XXI.
units.tr: On the Place of Adjuncts. CHAP. XXI.

units.la: QVOD[?] est firmamentum ex adiunctis? Locus hic ad Rhetores potius, quam ad Dialecticos pertinet. Adiuncta enim esse ostendimus, quae plerunque quidem eveniunt, sed tamen nulla necessitate rem comitante. Itaque cum ad confirmandum hic locus infirmus est, tum vero ad refellendum infirmissimus: sive essentiam, sive convenientiam, sive reciprocationem spectemus. veluti:Si est avarus, iusiurandum negligit.
