Si non est avarus, non negligit. Si negligit iusiurandum, est avarus. Si nō negligit, non est avarus. Si Tyrannus est, interficietur. Si non est Tyrannus, non interficietur. Si interficietur, est Tyrannus. Si non interficietur, non est Tyrannus. Quae omnia levia & infirma sunt. Ex hoc genere sunt, quas Praesumptiones Iurisconsulti appellant: velut illa Ciceronis ex lib. de Orat. 3. Si & ferro interfectus ille, & tu inimicus eius cum gladio cruento deprehensus es in illo ipso loco, & nemo praeter te ibi visus est, & causa nemini, & tu semper audax, quid est quod de facinore dubitare possimus?
units.tr: What is the strength of an argument from adjuncts? This topic belongs more to the Rhetoricians than to the Dialecticians. For we have shown that adjuncts are things which generally happen, but which do not accompany the thing by any necessity. Therefore this topic is weak for confirming, and very weak for refuting, whether we look at essence, agreement, or reciprocation. For example: If he is a miser, he neglects his oath. If he is not a miser, he does not neglect it. If he neglects his oath, he is a miser. If he does not neglect it, he is not a miser. If he is a tyrant, he will be killed. If he is not a tyrant, he will not be killed. If he is killed, he is a tyrant. If he is not killed, he is not a tyrant. All of these are slight and weak. Of this kind are those things which the jurists call presumptions, such as that example of Cicero from the third book On the Orator: "If that man was killed with a sword, and you, his enemy, were caught with a bloody sword in that very place, and no one but you was seen there, and there was no motive for anyone else, and you are always bold, what is there that we can doubt about the crime?"

units.la: QVOD est firmamentum ex Accidente? Esto primum huiusmodi: Posito quocunque accidente, ponitur substantia. Posito vero accidente inseparabili, sequitur perpetuitas. Itaque ut locus de quocunque accidenti ad substantiam probandam valet: ita locus ex accidente inseparabili ad perpetuitatem probandam valet. Prioris exempla hæc sunt: Si dos est, etiam matrimonium est. Si est pignus, est principalis obligatio. Si glacies est, etiam aqua est. Quod pertinet ad quæstionem, an vsufructus legatus alicui quo ad filius testatoris pubescat, mortuo ante pubertatem puero extingua[?] tur: quia si pupillus non est, pubertas intelligi non potest. l. ambiguitatem, 12, C. de vsufr. Itè ad illam, Cùm Titius annorum triginta erit, illi dato centum. l. si ita scriptum, 16, D. de manumiss. test. Sic nemo potest mortem liberari intelligitur. l. qui libertinus, 37, §. vlt. D. de operis libert. Posterioris exemplum est hoc: Si lepra aut podagra correptus est, nunquam curabitur: Si pannus atrore tinctus est, nunquam albescet. Ex separabili verò non valet: ut, Si æ-grotat, non convalescet. Si convaluit, nonæ-grotabit. Sequitur II. Negato accidenti, non continuò substantia negatur. Itaque locus ex accidente ad refellendam substantiam non valet, ne si inseparabilis quidem sit. Nam argumentum illud, Si non est albus,nō est olor: Sinon est niger,non est corvus: quia non fortuita & adventitia sunt, ad Proprij locum referenda sunt.
units.tr: What is the strength of an argument from an accident? Let the first case be of this kind: Given any accident, the substance is posited. But given an inseparable accident, perpetuity follows. Therefore, just as the topic of any accident is valid for proving the substance, so the topic of an inseparable accident is valid for proving perpetuity. Examples of the first are these: If there is a dowry, there is also a marriage. If there is a pledge, there is a principal obligation. If there is ice, there is also water. This bears on the question whether a usufruct bequeathed to someone, until the testator's son reaches puberty, is extinguished when the boy dies before puberty, because if he is not a ward, puberty cannot be understood (l. ambiguitatem, 12, C. de usufructu). Likewise with that case: "When Titius shall be thirty years old, let a hundred be given to him" (l. si ita scriptum, 16, D. de manumissis testamento). Thus no one is understood to be able to be freed from death (l. qui libertinus, 37, §. last, D. de operis libertorum). An example of the second is this: If he is seized with leprosy or gout, he will never be cured. If a cloth is stained with black, it will never be whitened. But from a separable accident the argument does not hold: for instance, "If he is sick, he will not recover. If he has recovered, he will not be sick." The second point follows: when an accident is denied, the substance is not at once denied. Therefore the topic from an accident does not hold for refuting a substance, not even if the accident is inseparable. For the argument, "If it is not white, it is not a swan; if it is not black, it is not a raven," because these features are not chance and adventitious, must be referred to the place of the Proprium.

units.la: Quod est firmamentū convenientiæ?Quoniam accidens, nihil aliud est, quàm id quod fortuitò convenit, nullus hic disputationi de convenientia locus est. Reciprocationis autem hoc primum firmamentum est: Non ut posito antecedente,ponitur substantia:ita posita substantia, continuò succedit accidens. Potest enim & matrimonium sine dote,& mutuum sine pignore consistere. Sequitur II.Nō ut negato accidente substantia non tollitur, ita negata substantia,non tollitur accidens. Sublata enim substantia (utiampridem superiús dictum est) continuò tollitur accidens.
units.tr: What is the strength of agreement? Since an accident is nothing other than what happens to belong to something by chance, there is no place here for a disputation about agreement. Of reciprocation, however, this is the first strength: it is not the case that, as the antecedent being posited posits the substance, so, the substance being posited, the accident immediately follows. For marriage can exist without a dowry, and a loan without a pledge. The second point follows: it is not the case that, as the accident being denied does not remove the substance, so the substance being denied does not remove the accident. For when the substance is removed (as was said earlier), the accident is removed at once.

units.la: De loco Parium. CAP. XXIII.
units.tr: On the Place of Equals. CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: Q[?]VOD est firmamentum de Paribus? Primum hoc esto: Ut posito uno pari,alterum conceditur: ita negato uno, alterum negatur. Paritas enim ex Relatorum numero est: quorum eam esse naturam diximus, ut alterum sine altero esse non possit,sed utrumque simul esse & incipiat & desinat. Itaque Reciprocationis nulla omninò dubitatio est. Quæ igitur duo in tertio aliquo pariter conveniunt, etiam inter se paria sunt.omnis enim huius loci vis proportione continetur.veluti:Si drachma decé assibus Romanis valuit : pares fuerunt drachma & denarius.Eáque ratione exterarũ gentium mensuræ & pondera omnia inter fe conferentur. Si duo nũmi vni momento pares sunt, etiã inter fe sunt pares. Si duæ magnitudines tertiæ alicui,puta perticæ, sunt pares, etiam inter fe sunt pares.Sequitur II, Quorum alterum tertio alicui par non est, ea inter fe non sunt paria. Quod ex alterius collatione facilè intelligitur.
units.tr: What is the first rule concerning equals? Let this be the first: as, when one equal is granted, the other is granted, so, when one is denied, the other is denied. For equality belongs to the class of relatives, whose nature, as we have said, is such that one cannot exist without the other, but both begin and cease to exist together. Therefore there is no doubt at all about reciprocation. Whatever two things agree equally in some third thing are also equal to each other, for the whole force of this place rests on proportion. For example: if a drachma was worth ten Roman asses, the drachma and the denarius were equal. In this way the measures and weights of foreign nations are all compared with one another. If two coins are of equal value at one time, they are also equal to each other. If two magnitudes are equal to some third, say a pole, they are also equal to each other. Second: of two things, if one is not equal to some third, those two are not equal to each other. This is easily understood from comparing each with the third.

units.la: Quod est Firmamentum de conuenientia[?] Primum est hoc.I. Quod vni pari conuenit,etiam alteri conuenit.valeat æquitas(inquit Cicero) que in pari caussa paria iura defyderat. Si parricida in culeum insuendus est,etiã matricida. par enim sceleribus paribus supplicium debetur. Si liberto impuberi patronus tutor esse debet,etiam filio impuberi pater tutor sit oportet . Si finem edicto Prætoris asseruntb Kalendæ Ianuarij,cur non initiũ quoque nascitur à Kalendis Ianuarij. Nam Kalendæ Ianuarij vtrique extremo annui imperij conueniunt.Sequitur II. Quod vni pari non conuenit,alteri non conuenit. Veluti: Si hæc forma illi calceo non cóueuit,huic qui par illi est, non cõueniet.Sequitur III.Vt paria paribus, sic imparibus imparia conueniunt. Vnde illud præclarũ Aristotelis , qui lib.Ethic.5.scribit, contentiones , bella , inimicitias ex eo nasci, quòd vel æqualibus nó æqualia: vel non æqualibus æqualia tribuuntur. Ex eodem genere illud est Quintiliani: Quemadmodum vascula oris angusti superfusam hu[?]moris respuunt copiam, sensim autem instillantibus replentur: sic tenera puerorum ingenia grandia non percipiunt: modica & viribus suis apta commodius addiscūt. Atque hæc quidem hactenus de proportione, quæ in tribus versatur. deinceps de quadruplici videamus.
units.tr: What is the rule concerning agreement? The first is this: what agrees with one equal also agrees with the other. Let equity prevail, says Cicero, which in an equal case demands equal rights. If a parricide is to be sewn into a sack, so is a matricide, for equal crimes deserve equal punishment. If a patron must be guardian of an under-age freedman, a father too ought to be guardian of his under-age son. If the Praetor's edict sets the end of the year at the Kalends of January, why does the beginning not also arise from the Kalends of January? For the Kalends of January belong to both extremes of the annual magistracy. Second: what does not agree with one equal does not agree with the other. For example: if this shape does not fit that shoe, it will not fit the one that is equal to it. Third: as equals agree with equals, so unequals agree with unequals. Hence that famous saying of Aristotle, in Ethics book 5, that quarrels, wars and enmities arise from giving unequal things to equals or equal things to unequals. From the same kind is Quintilian's: just as narrow-necked vessels refuse a poured-in flood of liquid but fill up when it trickles in slowly, so tender young minds do not take in great things, while moderate things suited to their strength are learned more readily. So much for proportion, which involves three terms. Next let us look at the fourfold proportion.

units.la: Quod est Firmamentum Reciprocationis? Quod in ceteris omnibus paribus convenit, etiam in unum conveniat necesse est. Quo firmamento vis eius argumentationis, quæ Inductio appellatur, tota consistit. veluti: Summum imperium fuit apud Assyrios. Assyriorum potiti sunt Medi. Medos superauere Persæ. Persis Græci dominati sunt. Græcos Spartiatæ sub imperium suum redegerunt. Spartiatas superauere Thebani. Thebanorum potiti sunt Macedones. Macedonas Romani subegerunt. Romanos Gotti. Non dubium est, quin Gottorum imperium non sit perpetuum futurum.
units.tr: What is the rule of reciprocation? What agrees with all the other equals must necessarily agree with the one as well. On this rule the whole force of that argument rests which is called induction. For example: supreme power was held by the Assyrians. The Medes gained mastery of the Assyrians. The Persians overcame the Medes. The Greeks ruled the Persians. The Spartans brought the Greeks under their rule. The Thebans overcame the Spartans. The Macedonians gained mastery of the Thebans. The Romans subdued the Macedonians. The Goths overthrew the Romans. There is no doubt that the empire of the Goths will not be perpetual.

units.la: Quid sequitur nunc? Ordo quidem consentaneorum habituum postulabat, ut de comparatione minoris hoc loco diceremus: sed quia divelli maioris & minoris comparationes nisi difficillimè non possunt, propterea satius est eam ad locum de disparibus referre, ac iam de Similitudine differere.
units.tr: What follows now? The order of related habits required that we speak here about the comparison of the less. But since comparisons of the greater and the less can hardly be separated, it is better to refer it to the place of unequals, and now to discuss similarity.

units.la: Quod[?] est Firmamétum de Similibus? Vt paritas, sic etiam similitudo rerum, ex tertio aliquo foris ascito, cognoscitur. Itaque huius quoque loci vis omnis proportione consistit. Primum igitur hoc esto: Quatenus duo in tertio aliquo conueniunt, eatenus inter se similia sunt. Nam posito uno simili, alterum ponitur. veluti, Si lapis ille qui ferrum allicit, est Magnes, hic qui ferrū similiter attrahit, eodem nomine est. Huc illud pertinet ridiculū de Nerone qui matrem Agrippinā interficiendā curarat.
units.tr: What is the rule concerning similars? As with equality, so also the similarity of things is recognised through some third thing brought in from outside. So the whole force of this place too rests on proportion. Let this be the first: insofar as two things agree in some third, so far they are similar to each other. For once one similar is posited, the other is posited. For example: if that stone which attracts iron is a magnet, then this one which likewise draws iron has the same name. To this belongs the ridiculous saying about Nero, who had arranged the killing of his mother Agrippina.

units.la: Quis neget Aeneas magna de stirpe Neronem? Sustulit hic matrem, sustulit ille patrem..
units.tr: Who would deny that Aeneas and Nero come of a great stock? One of them took his mother's life, the other his father's.

units.la: Tertium in quo Aeneas & Nero conueniunt est sublatio parentum. Cuius ex verbi ambiguitate luditur. Locatio & conductio ea re emptioni & venditioni similis est, quia ut hæc sine pretio, sic illa sine mercede constare non potest. In quo perspicua proportionis ratio est.
units.tr: The third thing in which Aeneas and Nero agree is the killing of parents. The joke plays on the ambiguity of the word. Letting and hiring is like buying and selling, because just as the latter cannot exist without a price, so the former cannot exist without a fee. Here the proportion is plain.

units.la: Sequitur II. Quatenus duo in tertio aliquo non conueniunt, eatenus inter se similia non sunt. Nam ut in Affectuum doctrina diximus: Simile & dissimile nō vsquequaque, sed tantum ex parte dicuntur. Sed de dissimilibus inferius suo loco differemus.
units.tr: Second: insofar as two things do not agree in some third, so far they are not similar to each other. For, as we said in the doctrine of the affections, similar and dissimilar are not said in every respect but only in part. But we shall treat of dissimilars lower down, in their proper place.

units.la: Quod est Firmamentum de conuenientia? Primum est huiusmodi: Quod in vna re simili valet, etiam in ceteris valebit. veluti: Vt tutela,sic procuratio Reip. ad vtilitatem eorum qui commisi sunt,non ad eorum quibus commissa est,gerenda est:ait inOffic.Cicero.Vt remiges fine gubernatore,ita milites fine imperatore nihil valent : inquit idé apud Quint.li. 5.ca.11.Vt ager quáuis fertilis,fine cultura fructuosus[?] esse non potest: sic fine doctrina animus.apud eundē Tusc.2. Item lib. de Natur. Deor.3. Vt in iure ciuili, qui est de matre libera liber est,item iure naturæ qui de dea matre est,Deus fit necesse est. Sequitur II. Quod in re simili non valet, nec in ceteris valebit.ve luti:Si quod medicamentū nihil in vnius morbo depellendo valuit, ne in alterius quidem consimili morbo valebit.
units.tr: What is the rule concerning agreement? The first is of this kind: what holds good in one similar thing will hold good in the others too. For example: as with guardianship, so the management of public affairs must be carried on for the benefit of those who have entrusted it, not of those to whom it is entrusted, says Cicero in De Officiis. As rowers without a helmsman, so soldiers without a commander are worth nothing, says the same author in Quintilian, book 5, chapter 11. As a field, however fertile, cannot be fruitful without cultivation, so neither can the mind be without learning; the same author in the Tusculan Disputations, book 2. Likewise in De Natura Deorum, book 3: as, under civil law, one born of a free mother is free, so under the law of nature one born of a goddess mother must become a god. Second: what does not hold good in a similar thing will not hold good in the others either. For example: if a medicine did nothing to drive out one disease, it will not work against another similar disease either.

units.la: Quod est Firmamentum reciprocationis? Quod in ceteris rebus similibus valet, etiam in vna valeat necesse est. Nam ex hoc fonte ea nascitur argumentatio, quam inductionem appellant:quæ similitudini reciprocatur . Nam similitudo illa est,si socius fidem debet,debet etiam mandatarius,depositarius,tutor, & pro curator. Illa autem inductio:Si socius,mādatarius, &.depositarius fidem praestant, etiam procurator praestat. Sequitur II. Quod ceteris similibus non conuenit, etiam vni alicui non conuenit. veluti : Si quod medicamentū nihil in multorū morbis consimilibus depellendis valuit, nihil in huius consimili morbo valebit.
units.tr: What is the rule of reciprocation? What holds good in the other similar things must necessarily hold good in the one as well. For from this source arises the argument which they call induction, which reciprocates with similarity. The similarity is this: if a partner owes good faith, so do a mandatary, a depositary, a guardian and a procurator. The induction runs: if a partner, a mandatary and a depositary render good faith, so does a procurator. Second: what does not agree with the other similar things does not agree with any one of them. For example: if a medicine did nothing to drive out many similar diseases, it will do nothing against this similar disease.

units.la: QUOD est Firmamentum ex aduersis, cùm de essentia quæritur? Esto hoc I. Posito vno contrario, siue quod medium habeat, siue quod non habeat, alterum tollitur. Tantùm enim ad refellendū hic locus valet. Veluti: Si stat, non mouetur. Si mouetur, non stat. Si par est numerus, non est impar. Si impar, non est par. Mediati autem contrarij hoc exemplum est: si pulchra mulier est, non est deformis. Si dives est, non est pauper. quorum utrumque reciprocatur. Sequitur II. Sublato cōtrario, quod medium non habeat, continuò alterum ponitur. Veluti: Si levis nó est, est grauis: & vicisim. Item: Si paritas non est, est imparitas: & vicisim. Item, Aut amat, aut odit mulier: nihil est tertium. Ergo, si non amat, odit: si non odit, amat. Sequitur III. Sublato contrario, quod medium habeat, non continuò alterum ponitur. Potest enim intermedium aliquod succedere. non si nó est dies, continuò nox est: aut ex cótrario. Potest enim esse vel diluculum, vel crepusculum. Non si nó est atror, continuò est candor: aut vicisim. Potest enim esse color aliquis intermedius, ut suscus, aut ceruleus.
units.tr: What is the rule from contraries, when the essence is in question? Let this be the first: once one contrary is posited, whether it has a middle or not, the other is removed. For this place serves only for refuting. For example: if it stands, it does not move; if it moves, it does not stand. If a number is even, it is not odd; if odd, it is not even. Of contraries with a middle, this is an example: if a woman is beautiful, she is not ugly; if rich, she is not poor. Both of these reciprocate. Second: with a contrary removed which has no middle, the other is at once posited. For example: if not light, then heavy, and conversely. Likewise: if not equal, then unequal, and conversely. Likewise: a woman either loves or hates; there is no third. Therefore, if she does not love, she hates; if she does not hate, she loves. Third: with a contrary removed which has a middle, the other is not at once posited, for some intermediate may come in. If it is not day, it is not at once night, or conversely, for there may be either dawn or twilight. If it is not black, it is not at once white, or conversely, for there may be some intermediate colour, such as grey or blue.

units.la: Quod est Firmamentum de convenientia? Huius loci præcepta de convenientia & reciprocatione communia sunt. Aduersa enim simul sunt natura. Itaque simul ea duo tracta-buntur. buntur. Primum igitur hocefto. I. Quod uni contrario conuenit,alteri non cōuenit, sed potius eius contrarium. Nam contraria de contrariis dicta probabilia sunt:vt ait Aristoteles:&(vt Cicero scribit) Contrariis contraria conueniunt.Itémque alio loco : Omnium rerum in contrarias partes facultas ex iisdem suppeditatur locis.veluti:Si bonum liberi,mi fera orbitas.Si bonum patria,miserum exilii. Si bonū valetudo, miserum morbus. Si bonū integritas corporis,misera debilitas.Si bonū, incolumis acies,misera cæcitas:ait Cicero,de Finib.5.Ex eodem genere illud est in Milonia na:Non fuisset iusta causa restituendi mei,ni si fuisset iniusta eiiciendi. Item illud Aristotelis in Rhetoricis,quod Quintilianus protulit: Si malorum causa bellum fuit, erit remedatio pax. Siqui imprudens nocuit,nullam poenam meretur: qui imprudens profuit (vt qui Phæreo Iasoni vomicam aperuit) præmium nullū meretur. Si mulieri adulterij damnatæ testimonij dictio adimitur, honestæ matrifa.conceditur. Si quem ex iudicum numero Prætor iudicare vetat,ceteris id concedit.Cicero pro Sylla:Neque verò quid mihi irascare,intellige re possum,si quòd eum defendo, quem tu accusas;cur tibi quoque ipse non fuccenseam, qui accuses eum, quem ego defendo? Inimicū (inquis) accusò meum.Et amicum ego defendo meum. Sequitur II. Quod uni contrario non conuenit, eius contrarium alteri contrario non convenit. Contrariorum enim contraria sunt cóse-quentia: inquit Cicero: id est, Consequentia contrariorum æquè sunt inter se contraria, ut ipsa contraria. veluti: Si ebrietas turpis non est, sobrietas non est honesta. Si vitium non est fugiendum, virtus non est expetenda. Si præmiũ bene meritis civibus non debetur, neque pœna male meritis debetur. Ac præclara hæc convenientiæ ratio est, quæ proportionem & analogiam ostendit. Nam positis binis adversis, quam rationem habet prima pars primi ad primam secundi, eandē habet secunda pars primi ad secundam partem secundi. Itaque locus hic ex Contrariorū convenientia & ad confirmandum & ad refellendū valet. veluti: Ponatur in A sobrietas. in B temulétia. Subter altera ducatur linea: & in C ponatur honesta. in D turpis. Tum ita ratio ineatur: Si ut A est ad B, ita C ad D: necessariò ut est A ad C: ita B ad D. Ex eodem genere illud est Stoicorum: Si virtutes pares sunt inter se, paria etiam esse vitia necesse est. quòd si hæc paria non sunt, ne illę quidem. Et ex hac eadē proportione quæstio illa explicabitur: An præmium propositum ei debeatur, qui Tyrannum imprudens necarit. Si veniam meretur, qui imprudens nocuit: etiam merétur præmium qui imprudens profuit. At nulla inter Veniam & Præmiũ proportio est. sunt enim disparia. Sic igitur ad proportionem revocanda res est: Ut veniam, id est nullam pœnam meretur, qui imprudens nocuit: sic nullum premium meretur, qui profuit imprudens. Nam positis binis aduersis quam rationem habet prima pars primi ad partem primam secundi, eandem habet secunda pars primi ad secundam partem secundi. Itaque locus hic & confirmandi & refellēdi vim habet.
units.tr: What is the rule concerning agreement? The precepts of this place concerning agreement and reciprocation are common to both, for contraries are naturally bound together, so these two will be treated together. First, then, let this be: what agrees with one contrary does not agree with the other, but rather with its contrary. For things said of contraries are probable, as Aristotle says, and, as Cicero writes, contraries agree with contraries. And elsewhere he says: the means of arguing both ways on any matter are supplied from the same places. For example: if children are good, childlessness is wretched; if one's country is good, exile is wretched; if health is good, sickness is wretched; if bodily soundness is good, weakness is wretched; if sound sight is good, blindness is wretched, says Cicero, De Finibus, book 5. From the same kind is that in the speech for Milo: my recall would not have been a just cause unless my expulsion had been unjust. Also Aristotle's in the Rhetoric, which Quintilian cites: if war was the cause of evils, peace will be the remedy. If someone harmed unwittingly, he deserves no punishment; whoever benefited unwittingly (like the man who lanced Jason's boil for Phereus) deserves no reward. If a woman condemned for adultery is denied the right to give evidence, an honest mother is granted it. If the praetor forbids one of the judges to sit in judgement, he permits the others. Cicero, for Sulla: "Nor indeed can I understand why you should be angry with me because I defend the man you accuse; why should I not likewise be angry with you, who accuse the man I defend?" "I accuse my enemy," you say. "And I defend my friend." Second: what does not agree with one contrary, its contrary does not agree with the other contrary. For the consequences of contraries are contrary, says Cicero; that is, the consequences of contraries are as contrary to one another as the contraries themselves. For example: if drunkenness is not shameful, sobriety is not honourable. If vice is not to be avoided, virtue is not to be sought. If a reward is not owed to citizens who have deserved well, neither is a punishment owed to those who have deserved ill. This is a clear and excellent ground of agreement, which shows proportion and analogy. For when two opposites are posited, the relation the first part of the first bears to the first part of the second, the second part of the first bears to the second part of the second. So this place has force both for confirming and for refuting. For example: let sobriety be placed in A and drunkenness in B. Let another line be drawn beneath, and in C let honourable be placed, in D shameful. Then the reasoning runs: if as A is to B, so C is to D, then necessarily as A is to C, so B is to D. From the same kind is that of the Stoics: if the virtues are equal to one another, the vices must also be equal; but if these are not equal, neither are those. By the same proportion that question will be resolved: whether the reward offered should be owed to one who unwittingly killed a tyrant. If he who unwittingly harmed deserves pardon, then he who unwittingly benefited deserves a reward. But there is no proportion between pardon and reward; they are unlike. So the matter must be brought back to proportion thus: as he who unwittingly harmed deserves pardon, that is, no punishment, so he who unwittingly benefited deserves no reward. For when two opposites are posited, the relation the first part of the first bears to the first part of the second, the second part of the first bears to the second part of the second. So this place has force both for confirming and for refuting.

units.la: Cedo planius aliquod exemplum de Reciprocatione.Ponatur in A virtus: in B vitium. Subter altera ducatur linea, & in C ponantur expetenda, in D fugienda. Tum ita ratio inearur:Si vt est A ad B,ita est C ad D:necessariò vt est A ad C:ita B.ad D.Itaque si hoc fugiendum non est,ne illa quidem expetenda. Et si illa non expetenda,ne hoc quidem fugiendum. Si qui imprudens nocuit, nullam poenam meretur (id est veniam) is qui profuit imprudēs, nullum praemium meretur. Item,si qui imprudens nocuit,veniam meretur:iccirco qui imprudens profuit,premium meretur. Nam premium non est contrarium veniæ,sed nulla poena,nullum praemium. Si virtutes pares sunt inter se, paria esse etiam vitia necesse est. Quòd si haec paria non sunt,ne illa quidem.
units.tr: I give a plainer example of reciprocation. Let A be virtue and B vice. Beneath them draw another line, and in C place the things to be desired and in D the things to be avoided. Then the inference runs thus: if, as A is to B, so C is to D, then necessarily, as A is to C, so B is to D. Therefore if this is not to be avoided, neither is that to be desired; and if that is not to be desired, neither is this to be avoided. If one who has harmed unwittingly deserves no punishment (that is, pardon), then one who has benefited unwittingly deserves no reward. Likewise, if one who has harmed unwittingly deserves pardon, then one who has benefited unwittingly deserves reward. For reward is not the opposite of pardon; rather, no punishment corresponds to no reward. If virtues are equal to one another, vices must also be equal. But if these are not equal, neither are those.

units.la: De loco Priuantium. CAP. XXVI.
units.tr: On the place from privatives. CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: QVOD est Firmamentum ex Priuantibus, cùm de habitus essentia quaeritur? Primum est huiusmodi: Posita priuatione vt habitus tollitur, ita aliquádo affuisse arguitur. Nam locus hic ad habitum & confirmandum & refellendum valet.veluti,Si est nox , dies non est,nunc quidé, sed prius fuit.Si est morbus,valetudo non est, nunc quidem , sed prius fuit. Sequitur II. Sublato priuante quod medium non recipit,habitus cóceditur : sublato eo quod recipit,non conceditur.veluti:Si non est mors,est vita. At non sequitur,fi non est calidum, est frigidum. poteftenim effetepidum.neque rursus,Si non est morbus,est valetudo. nam medicorü sententia quidam habitus interiectus est. Sequitur III. Negato habitu poni priuatio non poteft. Itaq; nó potest videri desiisse habere,qui nunquam habuit:inquit Paulus Iurifconsultus.neque sponsa diuortium fecifle, quæ nunquam simul cum viro habitauit. neque quifquam plus iuris in alterum transferre , quàm ipse habuit. neque rem amittere , quorü propria non fuit.In hoc genere illa Curiana caufa est apud Ciceronem de poftumo, qui cùm natus non effet,mortuus dici non poterat. Sic in Paradox. Itaque pulsus ego è ciuitate non sum,quæ tum nulla erat. accersitus in ciuitatem sum,cùm effet in Rep.Consul, qui tü nullus fuerat:eflet Senatus, qui tum occiderat.
units.tr: What is the argument from privatives when the essence of a habit is in question? The first is this: once the privation is posited, the habit is taken away, and so it is shown to have been present at some earlier time. For this place is useful both for confirming and for refuting a habit. For example: if it is night, it is not day, at least now, but it was before. If there is sickness, there is not health, at least now, but it was before. The second: when the privative that admits no middle is removed, the habit is granted; when the privative that admits a middle is removed, the habit is not granted. For example: if it is not death, it is life. But it does not follow that if it is not hot, it is cold, since it may be lukewarm. Nor again: if it is not sickness, it is health, for in the opinion of physicians there is a certain intermediate habit. The third: when the habit is denied, the privation cannot be posited. So one who never had something cannot be said to have ceased to have it, says the jurist Paul. Nor has a betrothed woman who never lived with a husband made a divorce. Nor can anyone transfer more right to another than he himself had, nor lose a thing that was never his own. In this kind belongs the Curian case in Cicero about the posthumous son, who, since he was not yet born, could not be said to be dead. So too in the Paradoxes: "Therefore I was not driven out of the state, which at that time did not exist. I was summoned back into the state when there was a consul in the republic, who at that time had not existed; there was a senate, which at that time had perished."

units.la: Quod est Firmamentum de Conuenientia? Hic videndum est diligeter, vt præceptum de Conuenientia ad hunc locum accommodemus,quatenus priuatio spectatur,non quatenus est oppofitio & ἀντίθεσις[?] .Nam firmamentum de oppositorum convenientia proprie non pertinet, nisi ad locum adversorum. Non enim ut contrariorum contraria sunt consequentia, sic privantium consequentia sunt contraria. Nam in privantibus non est æqua proportio, veluti, Visus & cæcitas & privátia sunt & opposita. At locus de convenientia non est accommodádus tanquá ad opposita, sed tanquam ad privantia. Nam si dicamus, Ut cçcitas est malum, sic aspectus est bonum: recté quidé argumétabimur: sed nó ex privantibus verùm ex contrariis. Idque ex altero exemplo apparebit. Virgo & nupta privantia sunt. At non si virgo casta est, iccirco nupta erit non casta. non si illa honesta, iccirco hæc inhonesta. Non si cœlibatus honestus est, iccirco conjugium inhonestum est. Privátium enim consequentia non sunt inter se contraria: sed interdum consentanea. Et quamuis prima specie videantur, tamé illa pugnantia non est privantium, sed contrariorum. Itaque locus ex Privantibus nunquam ad contrariorum convenientiam probandam valét. non enim in illo æqua proportio est, veluti, Vita & Mors privantia sunt. Non autè si vita beata est, iccirco mors misera est. nec ex contrario, si mors misera est, iccirco vita est beatá. multi enim & in vita & post viram sunt miserrimi. Firmamentú igitur est huiusmodi. I. Cui privatio convenit eidem habitus non convenit, nunc quidem, sed antea convenisse arguitur. veluti: Siquid amisisti,id non habes:nunc quidem:sed antea certè habuisti. Si in ciuitatem restitutus est, nunc quidem exul non est,sed certè priùs fuit. Si conualuit ,ægrotauit. Ex hoc genere illud est Ciceronis in lib.de nat.Deor.3. Temperātia constat ex prætermittendis voluptatibus corporis,cui si locus in cœlo est, est etiam voluptatibus. Sequitur II. Cui priuatio non cōuenit,eidem contrarium conuenire arguitur.veluti:Sinon ægrotat, valet.Si non est cæcus,videt.Si non est surdus,audit.
units.tr: What is the confirmation from agreement? Here we must take care to adapt the precept of agreement to this place insofar as privation is considered, not insofar as it is opposition and antithesis. For the confirmation from the agreement of opposites properly pertains only to the place of contraries. Just as the consequences of contraries are contrary, so the consequences of privatives are not contrary. For in privatives there is no equal proportion: sight and blindness are both privatives and opposites. But the place of agreement is not to be applied to opposites as such, but to privatives. For if we say, As blindness is an evil, so sight is a good, we argue rightly, but not from privatives; rather from contraries. This will appear from another example. Virgin and married woman are privatives. But it does not follow that if a virgin is chaste, a married woman is therefore unchaste; nor that if the former is honourable, the latter is dishonourable; nor that if celibacy is honourable, marriage is therefore dishonourable. For the consequences of privatives are not contrary to one another, though sometimes they are consistent. And although at first sight they may seem to conflict, that conflict belongs not to privatives but to contraries. Thus the place from privatives never avails to prove the agreement of contraries, since in it there is no equal proportion. Life and death are privatives, yet it does not follow that if life is blessed, death is therefore wretched; nor conversely, that if death is wretched, life is therefore blessed. For many are most wretched both in life and after life. The confirmation therefore runs as follows. I. Where a privation agrees with a subject, the habit does not agree with the same subject now, but it is argued that it agreed earlier. For example: If you have lost something, you do not have it now, but certainly you had it before. If he has been restored to the city, he is not now an exile, but certainly he was one before. If he has recovered, he was sick. Of this kind is that passage of Cicero in the third book of On the Nature of the Gods: "Temperance consists in setting aside bodily pleasures; if it has a place in heaven, then pleasures have one too." It follows II. Where a privation does not agree with a subject, the contrary is argued to agree with the same subject. For example: If he is not sick, he is well. If he is not blind, he sees. If he is not deaf, he hears.

units.la: Quod est Firmamentum de Reciprocatione? Esto hoc I: Non vt posita priuatione affuisse habitus arguitur, ita posito habitu affutura priuatio arguitur. Sequitur II. Vt negato priuante immediato, habitus conceditur: ita negato habitu,locus priuationi nullus est. Sequitur III.Non vt cui priuatio conuenit,eidem habitus antea conuenisse arguitur : ita cui habitus conuenit, in idem casura priuatio arguitur.
units.tr: What is the confirmation from reciprocation? Let this be I: just as, when a privation is posited, the earlier presence of the habit is argued, so, when the habit is posited, the future occurrence of the privation is argued. It follows II. As, when the immediate privative is denied, the habit is conceded, so, when the habit is denied, there is no place for the privation. It follows III. Not as, where a privation agrees with a subject, the same habit is argued to have agreed with it earlier, so, where a habit agrees with a subject, the privation is argued to fall upon the same subject later.

units.la: De loco Aientium & Negantium.
units.tr: On the Place from Affirming and Denying.

units.la: CAP. XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: Q[?]VOD est firmamentum de Ajentibus & Negantibus? Argumentum hoc simul & essentiam & conuenientiam,& reciprocationem complectitur. Itaque primum erit huiusmodi: Vt posito aiente negans,sic posito negante aiés tollitur.
units.tr: What is the foundation of the argument about affirming and denying? This argument embraces at once the essence, the agreement and the reciprocation. First, then, it will be of this kind: as the affirmative being posited the negative is posited, so the negative being posited the affirmative is removed.

units.la: Omnium enim contrariorum hæc summè contraria sunt. Itaque medium non recipiunt: ut in affectuum præceptione diximus. veluti: Siquis legit, non potest dici nō legere. vicissimque, siquis non legit, dici non potest legere. Siquis dies est, non potest dici non dies: vicissimque siquis non est dies, dici dies non potest. non enim medium, quod est mediocritas, recipit. Sequitur II. Vt sublato negante, aliens conceditur: sic aliente sublato, negans conceditur. Ergo siquis non est indoctus, sequitur vt idé sit doctus: vicissimque si doctus non est, etiam indoctus est. Siquis non est ingratus, sequitur vt sit gratus: vicissimque si quis gratus non est, idem est ingratus. In hoc genere illud est Iurisconsultorum: Quem sine liberis esse dicere non possumus, hunc necesse est dicamus liberos habere: quanuis vnū tantum habeat. Aristoteles autem reciprocationis exemplum profert acutissimum: quod tamen ad antecedentis & consequentis locum pertinere superiùs diximus. Si quod honestū est, id laudabile est: etiam quod laudabile non est, id honestum non est. Et si quod laudabile non est, id honestum non est: etiam quod honestum est, id laudabile est. Si quod homo est, id animal est: etiam quod animal non est, homo non est, etiam quod homo est, necessario animal est. Eodem modo: Si virtus est expetenda, etiam quod expetendum non est, virtus non est : vicissimque quod virtus est, expeten-dum est.
units.tr: For the most contrary of all contraries are these. So they admit no middle, as we said in the teaching on the affections. For example: if someone reads, he cannot be said not to read; and conversely, if someone does not read, he cannot be said to read. If something is a day, it cannot be said not to be a day; and conversely, if something is not a day, it cannot be said to be a day. For it does not admit a middle, which is mediocrity. Second, as the negative being removed the affirmative is granted, so the affirmative being removed the negative is granted. Therefore, if someone is not unlearned, it follows that he is learned; and conversely, if he is not learned, he is also unlearned. If someone is not ungrateful, it follows that he is grateful; and conversely, if someone is not grateful, he is ungrateful. To this kind belongs the lawyers' saying: whom we cannot call without children, we must say has children, even though he has only one. Aristotle, however, gives a most acute example of reciprocation, which we said earlier belongs to the place of antecedent and consequent: If what is honourable is praiseworthy, then what is not praiseworthy is not honourable; and if what is not praiseworthy is not honourable, then what is honourable is praiseworthy. If what is a man is an animal, then what is not an animal is not a man, and what is a man necessarily is an animal. In the same way: if virtue is to be sought, then what is not to be sought is not virtue; and conversely, what is virtue is to be sought.

units.la: De eadem Contrariorum disciplina.
units.tr: On the same discipline of contraries.

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: QVID[?] sequitur nunc? Vt de repugnantium loco differamus. sed prius peruulgatum illud axioma explicandum est, quo traditur, Contrariorum artem ac disciplinam eandem esse. [?]ἡ ἐναντίων [?]τῷ αὐτῷ ἐπιστήμῃ[?] Et alio loco, Contrariorum eandem vim ac potestatem esse.
units.tr: What follows now? Let us deal with the topic of things that repugn one another. But first the widely known axiom must be explained, by which it is handed down that the art and discipline of contraries is one and the same: [ἡ ἐναντίων τῷ αὐτῷ ἐπιστήμῃ]. And elsewhere it is said that contraries have the same force and power.

units.la: Quotuplex contrariorum facultas est? Duplex. Efficiens, & (vt ita dicam) patiens.
units.tr: How many kinds of capacity do contraries have? Two: the efficient and, so to speak, the receptive.

units.la: Quae est efficiens? Quae parem in vtroque contrario efficiendi caussam ostendit. Itaque firmamentum ipsius non sic exponendum est, quasi contrariorum eadem potestas esset: sed hoc modo: Contrariorum par potestas atque efficientia est. non enim eadem illorum vis est, sed contraria. veluti: Si calor laxat, frigus astringit. si ignis exsiccat, aqua madefacit. si bellum exitiale est, pax est salutaris. Vt creditor aliud pro alio incommodo suo accipere: sic debitor aliud pro alio soluere non cogitur. Contrariorum enim contraria vis atq; potestas est. Vt quod testator legato adiecit, legatario accrescit: sic quod detraxit, legatario decrescit. Et hoc est quod dici solet: Quod operatur propositum in proposito: idem operatur oppositum in opposito. l. si ex toto, ff.D.de legat.prim.l.ult.in sin. D.de legat.tert. Ex eodem genere illa est regula: Secundū naturam est commoda cuiusque rei eum sequi, quem sequuntur incommoda.
units.tr: What is the efficient capacity? It is that which shows an equal cause of producing effects in each of two contraries. So the foundation of this should not be stated as if contraries had the same power. It should be put like this: the power and efficacy of contraries are equal, but their force is not the same, it is opposite. For example: if heat loosens, cold binds; if fire dries, water moistens; if war is deadly, peace is healthful. As a creditor cannot be made to accept one thing in place of another to his own disadvantage, so a debtor is not compelled to pay one thing in place of another. For contraries have contrary force and power. As what a testator adds to a legacy accrues to the legatee, so what he takes away diminishes it for the legatee. This is what is commonly said: what the proposition brings about in the proposition, the opposite brings about in the opposite. l. si ex toto, ff. D. de legat. prim.; l. ult. in sin. D. de legat. tert. From the same kind comes that rule: by nature, the advantages of a thing belong to the one whom its disadvantages follow.

units.la: Quæ est Contrariorum facultas patiens? In qua hominum artes contrarios effectus parirunt. non enim in ipsis rebus vis illa inest, sed potius in hominibus, qui eas res tractant, & in quibus elaborant. Artes autem aliæ sunt cognitionis, aliæ actionis: quarum ambarum unum idemque axioma illud est, Contrariorum eadem vis atque potestas est.
units.tr: What is the receptive capacity of contraries? It is that in which the arts of men produce contrary effects. For that power does not inhere in the things themselves, but rather in the people who handle those things and work upon them. Some arts concern knowing, others acting; and of both the one and the same axiom holds: the force and power of contraries is the same.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de cognitione. Aristoteles initio lib. Ethic. 5. scribit, quoniam eadem contrariorum est δύναμις [?] eum qui bonam corporis constitutionem norit, eadem facultate malam quoque cogniturum. Sic cuius musici est nosse fidium consonantiam: eiusdem est earundem dissonantiam intelligere. Cuius medici est nosse ex arteriæ pulsu, aut urinæ colore bonam valetudinem, eiusdem est nosse morbum.
units.tr: Let me give an example from knowing. Aristotle, at the beginning of Ethics book 5, writes that since the power of contraries is the same, whoever knows a good bodily constitution will by the same faculty know a bad one as well [δύναμις]. So whoever's art it is to know the harmony of strings, it is his to understand their discord. Whoever's art it is for a physician to know good health from the pulse of the artery or the colour of urine, it is his to know disease.

units.la: Quæ igitur ars unius contrarij cognoscendi, eadem alterius quoque intelligendi facultatem præbet. Cognoscendi enim contraria una eademque ars, scientia, & facultas est. Ex eodem genere illud quoque firmamentum est: Contrarij unius qualitate cognita, simul alterius qualitas contraria esse intelligitur. Nam (ut superiùs dictum est) contraria contrariis conveniunt. Itaque cùm vel è genere duæ species vel è toto duæ partes diuisæ atque inter se oppositæ sunt, si vni certa qualitas vel attribuatur, vel denegetur, simul alteri contraria qualitas conuenire intelligitur. vnde illud Iurisconsultorum: Qui accusare possunt, intelligemus, si scierimus, qui non possunt. Item illud: Si cognouerimus quæ personæ alieno iuris subiectæ sunt, simul intelligemus, quæ iurissunt. Sed non iccirco firmamentum ita concipiendum est: Vno contrario cognito, simul alterum cognoscitur. non enim contrarium simul cognoscitur: sed eius qualitas alteri contraria. Ex eodem genere illa regula est, Quod sub conditione iubetur, deficiente conditione non iussum intelligitur. veluti: Si mater mea moritur, dato: Nisi moritur, ne dato. l. quibus, 11, §. 2, D. de cond. & demonst. Sic qui sic legat: Pamphilus si rationes reddiderit, liber esto: ita statuisse intelligitur: Si nō reddiderit, ne esto. Sic qui sic pacisci-tur: Si filia in matrimonio sine liberis moriatur, dote reddi: pacisci intelligitur, si superstitibus liberis moriatur, non reddi. l. inter socerum, 26, §. 1, D. de pact. dotal. Atque huc pertinet vis omnis exceptionum.
units.tr: Therefore whatever art gives the knowledge of one contrary also gives the faculty of understanding the other, for the art, the knowledge and the faculty of knowing contraries is one and the same. From the same kind comes this foundation too: once the quality of one contrary is known, the contrary quality of the other is understood at the same time. For (as was said above) contraries agree with contraries. So when two species of a genus, or two parts of a whole, are divided and opposed to each other, if a definite quality is either ascribed or denied to one of them, the contrary quality is understood to belong to the other at the same time. Hence that saying of the jurists: "We shall understand who can bring an accusation, if we know who cannot." Likewise: "If we know which persons are subject to another's authority, we shall at the same time understand which are not." But the foundation should not on that account be conceived thus: once one contrary is known, the other is known at the same time. For the contrary is not known at the same time; rather, its quality is contrary to the other's. From the same kind comes the rule: what is ordered under a condition is understood not to be ordered when the condition fails. For example: "If my mother dies, give; if she does not die, do not give." l. quibus, 11, §. 2, D. de cond. & demonst. So too whoever bequeaths thus, "Pamphilus, if he renders accounts, let him be free," is understood to have decided thus: if he does not render them, let him not be free. And whoever agrees thus, "If the daughter dies in marriage without children, the dowry is to be returned," is understood to agree that if she dies leaving surviving children, it is not to be returned. l. inter socerum, 26, §. 1, D. de pact. dotal. And all the force of exceptions belongs here.

units.la: Ecquamnam Exceptionum vim appellas? Effectus exceptionis hic est, ut cùm ex vniuerso partem exemit, contrarias in seiunctis partibus conditiones demonstret. Si exceptio facit ne liceat (inquit Cicero in ea pro Balbo) ibi necesse est licere, vbi non est exceptum. quam enim relictis conditionem attribuit, eius contrariam in exemptis ostendit : vicissimque quam istis, eius contrariam illis. adeo vt etiam in partibus non exemptis suam conditionem illustrare & confirmare videatur. Et hoc est quod dici solet, Exceptio in casibus non exceptis regulam confirmat.l. Tribunus, 20,§.1,D.de militit.test.
units.tr: What force do you call the force of exceptions? The effect of an exception here is that when it removes a part from the whole, it shows contrary conditions in the separated parts. "If an exception makes something not permitted," says Cicero in his speech for Balbus, "it is necessary that it be permitted where there is no exception." For the condition it assigns to the things left out, it shows the contrary of that in the things removed; and conversely, what it assigns to those, it shows the contrary of in these. So much so that even in the parts not excepted it seems to illustrate and confirm its own condition. And this is what is commonly said: an exception in cases not excepted confirms the rule. l. Tribunus, 20, §. 1, D. de militit. test.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Cùm miles factus in testamento quod ante militiam fecerat, quaedã delet, ius eorũ quæ non deleuit militari privilegio confirmat. Eodémque illud pertinet, cùm prætor vnum ex pluribus iudicare vetat, ceteris id permittit.l. cùm prætor,12,D.de iudic. Ex eo quod prohibet lex Iulia testimonium dicere mulierem adulterij condemnatam, colligitur etiá mulieres testimonij etiá in iudicio dicendi ius habere.l .ex eo,18, D.de testib. Eodémque præterea regula illa referéda est, In toto iure generi per speciem derogatur.l. in toto, 80, D. de reg.iur. quæ tamen planius & fortasse verius ita conciperetur: Et pars toti derogat: & res singularis Vniuersitati. veluti, si cùm Titio penum omne legatum esset, Mæuio postea vinum legetur: Mæuio vinum debebitur.l.2,D.de tritic.vin. &, si Titio fundi instrumentum vniuersum legatum sit, post mácipium quoddam Mæuio legetur, huic mancipium illud: illi reliquum omne debebitur.l.legatum,24,§.1,D.de adim.legat.
units.tr: Give an example. When a man who has become a soldier deletes certain things in a will he made before his military service, he confirms by military privilege the validity of those things he did not delete. To this also belongs the case where the praetor forbids one of several to judge and permits it to the rest. l. cum praetor, 12, D. de iudic. From the fact that the Julian law forbids a woman condemned for adultery to give testimony, it is gathered that women also have the right to give testimony in court. l. ex eo, 18, D. de testib. To this rule also should be referred: "In the whole law, the species derogates from the genus." l. in toto, 80, D. de reg. iur. Yet this would be conceived more plainly, and perhaps more truly, thus: a part derogates from the whole, and a particular thing from the universal. For example, if the whole pantry was bequeathed to Titius, and wine is afterwards bequeathed to Maevius, wine will be owed to Maevius. l. 2, D. de tritic. vin. And if the entire equipment of a farm was bequeathed to Titius, and afterwards a certain slave is bequeathed to Maevius, that slave will be owed to Maevius, and all the rest to Titius. l. legatum, 24, §. 1, D. de adim. legat.

units.la: Cedo iam exemplum de Actione. Sumatur illud pervulgatum: Qui condemnare potest, is absoluendi quoque potestatem habet. Item, Eius est nolle, qui potest & velle. Vicissim autem, Qui adire hereditatem nō potest, repudiare nō potest. Item, Pater captiuus qui consentire filij nuptiis non potest, nec dissentire potest. Item, Eiusdem est artificis ex arte dissoluere, cuius est ex arte constrvere. Sic, Faber, qui domum aut nauem ædificauit, eandē ex arte dissoluet. & artifex qui horologiū confecit, idem arte dissoluet: quod artis imperitus non poterit.
units.tr: Now let me give an example from action. Take the widely known one: whoever can condemn also has the power of acquitting. Likewise: it belongs to one who can will also to be unwilling. Conversely: whoever cannot enter upon an inheritance cannot renounce it. Likewise: a captive father, who cannot consent to his son's marriage, cannot dissent from it either. Likewise: it belongs to the same craftsman to dissolve by his craft what it belongs to him to construct by craft. Thus a carpenter who built a house or a ship will take it apart by his craft, and a craftsman who made a clock will by his art take it apart, which one unskilled in the art will not be able to do.

units.la: De loco Repugnantium. CAP. XXIX.
units.tr: On the Place of Opposites. CAP. XXIX.

units.la: Quod est Firmamentum de Repugnantibus? Locus hic & essentiam & conuenientiam, & Reciprocationem simul complectitur. Primum autem est huiusmodi. I. Posito vno ex Repugnantibus, alterum tollitur. Valet enim idem quod illud, Cui vnum è Repugnantibus conuenit, ei repugnat conuenire alterum. Repugnans enim aliud nihil est, nisi aduersi vel consequens, vel antecedens. Itaque ad refellendum hic locus valebit. Si amicus est, non est laedendus. Si hostis est, non iuuadus. Si mortuus est, non est natus. Si proba vxor est, non est exigenda. Si improba, non retinenda. Laedendum enim est consequens aduersi, quod est Hostis: vt Exigendum, improbae. Consequentia autem Contrariorum sunt etiam ipsa per se contraria. Sequitur II.Negato uno ex Repugnantibus, alterum succedit. Valet enim idem quod illud: Cui unum e Repugnantibus non convenit, eidem alterum quod quidem in eodem genere necessario convenit. Itaque ad confirmandum & refellendum hic locus valet: Si non est socius, lædendus est.Si est hostis, non est iuvandus.Sic Cicero in Parad.Potes aute m esse tu civis, propter quem aliquando civitas non fuit? Repugnant enim Civem esse, & Civitate opprimere. hoc modo: Non & civitatem oppressisti[?], & idem es civis. Si honestum est,non est inutile.Siturpe,nō est utile. Reciprocationis autem exemplum est huiusmodi: Ut non imaginaria venditio est, pretio accedente: sic non vera venditio est, pretio non accedente. Ut tyrannus non est,qui civium commodis consulit: sic Rex non est, qui non consulit: Ut impius non est, qui toto pectore Deum colit: ita pius non est,qui eum non colit.
units.tr: What is the strength of the topic of Opposites? This topic embraces at once essence, agreement, and reciprocation. The first form is as follows. I. If one of two opposites is posited, the other is removed. For this amounts to the same as saying: to whom one of the opposites belongs, to him the other opposite does not belong. For what opposes something is nothing other than either its contrary, or its consequence, or its antecedent. So this topic will be useful for refutation. If he is a friend, he must not be harmed. If he is an enemy, he must not be helped. If he is dead, he was not born. If she is a good wife, she must not be sent away. If she is wicked, she must not be kept. For what must be harmed is the consequent of the contrary, namely the enemy; so too what must be sent away is the wicked wife. The consequences of contraries are also themselves contrary in their own right. It follows II. If one of two opposites is denied, the other follows. For this amounts to the same as saying: to whom one of the opposites does not belong, to him the other necessarily belongs within the same genus. So this topic is useful both for confirming and for refuting: If he is not a companion, he must be harmed. If he is an enemy, he must not be helped. So Cicero, in the Paradoxa: "Can you be a citizen, you through whom the state at some time did not exist? For to be a citizen and to oppress the state are opposites. In this way: you have not oppressed the state, and you are a citizen." If it is honourable, it is not useless. If it is shameful, it is not useful. An example of reciprocation is of this kind: as a sale is not a sale in appearance when the price is added, so it is not a true sale when the price is not added. As he is not a tyrant who consults the good of the citizens, so he is not a king who does not consult it; as he is not impious who worships God with his whole heart, so he is not pious who does not worship him.

units.la: Deloco Disparium. CAP. XXX.
units.tr: Of Unlike Things in Place. CHAPTER XXX.

units.la: VOD[?] est Firmamentum ex disparibus, cùm de eorum essentia quaeritur? Ut paritas rerum, sic etiā disparitas ex aliquo tertio intelligitur. Itaque primum Firmamentum hoc erit: Quæ[?] in tertio aliquo disparia sunt, quorúmque alterutrum dūtaxat dispar est, eadem inter fe disparia sunt. veluti: Si è duobus frumenti aceruis alterum medimno, alterü modio conueniat,etiam inter fe sunt dispares.Id quod ex illo Mathematicorum precepto sumptum est:Si æqualium alterum tertio inæquale fuerit, etiam erit alterum. Sed de imparium effentia facilis ex Parium loco diiudicatio est.
units.tr: What is the argument from unlike things when their essence is under inquiry? Just as likeness of things is understood through some third thing, so too is unlikeness. Hence the first argument will be this: those things which are unlike some third thing, where only one of them is unlike it, are unlike each other. For example: if of two heaps of grain one matches a medimnus and the other a modius, they are also unlike each other. This is taken from that precept of the mathematicians: if one of two equals is unequal to a third, the other is also unequal to it. But from the place of likeness, the judgement about the essence of unlike things is easy.

units.la: Quod est firmamentum de conuenientia? Locus de conuenientia implicitam reciprocationem habet. Itaque vno firmamento vtranque complectemur: Quod vni disparium conuenit,alteri non cõuenit. veluti:Si Giganti toga quædam conuenit,pumilioni nón conueniet. Si pro frumeti medimno tot asses debetur,pro modio non tot debentur. Si Gigas & pumilio vinciendi sunt, illi catenis opus est:huic funiculus fatis erit. Et eo pertinet regula Iuris,vt quemadmodum valere debet æquitas quæ in pari caussa paria iura desiderat: sic ea valeat, quæ in caussa dispari, difparia iura constituit. Sequitur II.Quod vni difpari non conuenit, non continuò alteri eius dispari non conuenit. veluti: Non fi toga paruula Giganti non conueniet , iccirco pumilioni non conuenit. Sequitur III. Neque paria disparibus,neque disparia paribus conueniunt. Eóque illud Geometrarum præceptũ pertinet, Si inæqualibus æqualia vel addatur, vel detrahantur ,omnia erunt inæqualia. veluti:Si pari poena furem & sacrilegum afficere iniquum est, dispari poena duos eiusdem furti socios afficere iniquum est. Si par præmium forti & ignauo tribuere iniustum est, dispar eiusdem præclari facinoris sociis tribuere iniustum est. Locus autem de conuenientia duplex est. Nam quæ disparia sunt, aut maiora sunt, aut minora. Itaque duplex Comparatio nascitur: quarum altera ex maiore, altera ex minore appellatur.
units.tr: What is the argument from agreement? The topic of agreement carries an implicit reciprocation, so we shall embrace both sides in one argument: what agrees with one of two unlike things does not agree with the other. For example: if a certain gown suits a giant, it will not suit a dwarf. If so many asses are owed for a medimnus of grain, not so many are owed for a modius. If a giant and a dwarf are to be bound, the giant needs chains, while the dwarf will be sufficiently bound by a little cord. To this belongs the rule of law, that just as equity, which requires equal rights in an equal case, ought to hold good, so equity should hold good when it establishes unequal rights in an unequal case. It follows (1) that what does not agree with one unlike thing does not necessarily fail to agree with its unlike. For example: if a little gown does not suit a giant, it does not follow that it does not suit a dwarf. It follows (2) that neither equal things agree with unequal things, nor unequal things with equal things. This is the point of the geometers' precept: if equals are added to or taken from unequals, all the results will be unequal. For example: if it is unjust to punish a thief and a sacrilegious person with the same penalty, it is unjust to punish two accomplices in the same theft with unequal penalties. If it is unjust to give the same reward to a brave man and a coward, it is unjust to give unequal rewards to the associates of the same notable deed. The topic of agreement is twofold, for unlike things are either greater or smaller. Thus a twofold comparison arises: one is drawn from the greater, the other from the smaller.

units.la: De Comparatione Maioris & Minoris.
units.tr: On the Comparison of Greater and Less.

units.la: CAP. XXXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXI.

units.la: QVID appellas Maius & Minus? Maiuseft, non quod Cicero, Quintilianus, & alij innumeri crediderunt, id quod præstantius, aut quod difficilius est: neque Minus id vere est, quod facilius & expeditius est: sed (quemadmodum Ari-ftoteles & in Topicis & in Rhetoricis ad Theodectem docuit) Maius hic appellatur, quod maiorem rationem habet ad aliquid, quod magis probabile est, quod vero propius est, quod maiore ratione conuenire posse videbatur. Minus autem, quod à vero & probabili disiunctius est, quodque minorem rationem habet ad aliquid: quod minore ratione alicui conuenire videbatur. Alioqui vis argumenti nulla prorsus existeret: vt ex firmamentis constabit. quorum hoc prius est, I: Quod in re maiore non valet, etiam in minore non valet ἔ ὥμαλλον εἰκὸς ὑπάρχειν, μὴ ὑπάρχει,ὑδ' ὁ ἥττον. Nam si quae ( inquit Aristoteles ) multo maiore ratione res aliqua conuenire potest,ei non conuenit , ne ei quidem conueniet , cui multo minus videtur posse conuenire. Itaque locus ex maiore tantum ad refellendum valet. vt recte fine dubio sentiant, qui regulam in Topicis Ciceronis sic emendant: Quod in re maiore non valet , non valeat in minore. Plerunque autem per has notas Nedum , vel Tantum abest,hoc argumentum tractatur.velut apud Terentium:Satrapes si fiet, nūquam sufferre eius sumptus queat:nedum tu possis. In eodem genere illud est: Tantum abes à persectione maximorum operum, vt fundamenta quae cogitas nondum ieceris. Item illud: Faminiam regere non potuit : tantùm abest, vt Remp. posit. Quo argumento Paulus Apostolus vtitur in eo qui familiae suae praeesse nō poterat, tantùm abeit vt Ecclesiae praeesse possit. quod tamen ex minore sumptum nonnulli falsò existimarunt. nam maiorem habet rationem paterfa. ad suam familiam , quàm ad Ecclesiam aut Rempub. Ex hoc genere illud est Ciceronis lib.de Orat.1. Illa verò deridenda arrogantia est, in minoribus nauigiis rudé esse se confiteri : quinqueremes autem , aut etiam maiores gubernare didicisse. Item : Citius is qui duorum scalmorum nauiculam in portu euerterit,in Euxino ponto Argonautarum nauem gubernarit.
units.tr: What do we mean by the greater and the lesser? The greater is not, as Cicero, Quintilian and countless others believed, that which is more excellent or more difficult, nor is the lesser truly that which is easier and more convenient. Rather, as Aristotle taught both in the Topics and in the Rhetoric to Theodectes, the greater is that which has a greater ground for something: that which is more probable, or closer to the truth, or which seems able to belong to something on a greater reason. The lesser is that which is further from the true and the probable, and which has a smaller ground for something: that which seems to belong to someone on a lesser reason. Otherwise the force of the argument would not exist at all, as will be clear from the grounds. The first of these is this: what is more likely to belong and does not, the less likely does not belong either [ἃ μᾶλλον εἰκὸς ὑπάρχειν, μὴ ὑπάρχει, οὐδ' ὁ ἧττον]. For, as Aristotle says, if something which could belong to a thing on a much greater ground does not belong to it, then it will not belong to that to which it seems much less able to belong. So the argument from the greater works only for refutation. Those who emend the rule in Cicero's Topics to read, "What does not hold in the greater thing should not hold in the lesser," surely think rightly. Mostly, however, this argument is handled through the expressions "much less" (nedum) or "far from it" (tantum abest). Thus in Terence: "If he becomes a satrap, he can never bear his expenses, much less you could." In the same kind is this: "You are far from completing the greatest works, so much so that you have not yet laid the foundations you are planning." Likewise: "He could not rule his household; far less can he rule the state." Paul the Apostle uses this argument against a man who could not govern his own family: far less can he govern the Church. Some have wrongly thought this was drawn from the lesser, for the head of a household has a greater ground for his own household than for the Church or the commonwealth. To this kind belongs also that passage of Cicero in the first book of On the Orator: "That arrogance is to be laughed at, which confesses itself inexperienced in small boats, yet claims to have learned to steer quinqueremes or even larger ships." Likewise: "He who has overturned a little boat with two oars in harbour would sooner have steered the Argo's ship on the Euxine Sea."

units.la: Quod est firmamentum ex comparatione minoris? Quod in minore valet, valeat in maiore. Nam sicut minus conuenire videbatur, conuenit tamen: etiam ei conueniet, cui maioris conuenire videbatur. εἰ τὸ ἧττον ὑπάρχει, ἢ τὸ μεῖζον ὑπάρχει[?]. Itaque locus hic tantum ad confirmandum valet. Veluti: Si ferae partus suos diligunt, qua nos in liberos nostros indulgentia esse debemus? Nam minorem habet rationem fera rationis expers ad suos partus, quam homo qui & rationis & doctrinae est particeps ad suos liberos. Si singulas discipulas percipere magnum est, quanto maius omnes? Si bellum pro patria susceптum pium & iustum est, quanto magis illud quod pro religione suscipitur? Qui mentiri aut fallere infuerit patrem, aut audebit, tanto magis audebit ceteros. Itaque recte Cicero in lib. de Orat.2. ex minore exemplum hoc profert:
units.tr: What is the ground from the comparison of the lesser? What holds in the lesser should hold in the greater. For as the lesser seemed to belong, and yet does belong, so it will also belong to that to which the greater seemed to belong [εἰ τὸ ἧττον ὑπάρχει, ἢ τὸ μεῖζον ὑπάρχει]. Hence this argument has force only for confirming. For example: "If wild beasts love their young, with how much more indulgence ought we to love our children? For a wild animal, lacking reason, has a lesser ground for its young than a man, who shares in both reason and learning, has for his children." "If it is a great thing to receive single disciples, how much greater is it to receive them all?" "If war undertaken for one's country is pious and just, how much more so is war undertaken for religion?" "He who has dared or will dare to lie to or deceive his father will dare much more to do so to others." Thus Cicero, in the second book of On the Orator, rightly brings forward this example from the lesser:

units.la: -hic parua consuetudinis Caussa huius mortem fert tam familiariter. Quid si ipsi amasset? quid mihi hic faciet patri?
units.tr: Here a man dies, of little acquaintance with him, and yet he takes it so much to heart. What if he had loved him? What will he do for me, his father?

units.la: Sed ex maiore non recte: Si bona exiltimatio diuitiis praeflat, & pecunia tantoperè expetitur, quanto gloria magis est expetenda? Nam ex minore hoc quoque exemplum esse ex eo intelligitur, quòd minorem habet rationem pecunia ad hominem, quàm gloria. Quod autem ibidem similitudinem illum attribuit, Si ferae partus suos diligunt: perspicuè falsum & absurdum est. Idque est totidem propè verbis in Lælio. Quòd si hoc (inquit) apparet in bestiis, vt requirant atque appetant ad quas fe applicét,eiusdem generis animantes,quanto magis in homine fit natura, vt alterum acquirat, cuius animum ita cum suo commisceat,vt efficiat penè vnum ex duobus?
units.tr: But the argument from the greater is not valid in the same way: "If a good reputation is preferred to riches, and money is so eagerly sought, how much more should glory be sought?" For it is clear that this example also comes from the lesser, since money has a lesser ground in relation to a man than glory has. Moreover, the comparison he draws there, "If wild beasts love their young," is plainly false and absurd. The same thing is said in almost the same words in the Laelius: "But if this appears in beasts, that they seek out and desire those of their own kind to whom they may attach themselves, how much more is it in the nature of man to acquire another, whose mind he so mingles with his own that they become almost one out of two?"

units.la: Quid? Regula illa peruulgata, vtro ex loco sumpta est? Non debet cui plus licet, quod minus est non litere. Ex comparatione minoris. Minus enim dicitur, quod minus conuenire & licere posse videbatur.At illud, Qui fidem in re parua non præstitit,is in magna nó præstabit : ex maioris comparatione sumptum est: id est eius quod magis conuenire videbatur.
units.tr: And what of that common rule: from which place is it taken? "He to whom more is permitted may not do what is less." This comes from the comparison of the lesser, for what seemed less able to belong and be permitted is called "less." But the saying, "He who has not kept faith in a small matter will not keep it in a great one," is taken from the comparison of the greater, that is, of what seemed more likely to belong.

units.la: De loco Dissimilium. CAP. XXXII.
units.tr: On the Place of Dissimilars. CHAPTER XXXII.

units.la: VOD[?] est firmamentum de Difsimilibus? Vt rerum disparitas, sic etiam dissimilitudo ex tertio aliquo exquiritur. Itaque primum firmamentum est huiusmodi. I: Quæ in tertio aliquo dissimilia sunt, quorúmque item alterum duntaxat simile est, etiam inter fe difsimilia sunt. Itaque locus hic ad probandam dissimilitudinem valet. veluti cùm quæritur, An asinus & mulus dissimiles sint: sic concludetur:Si asinus ex asino & asina, mulus ex afino & equa genitus est, sunt dissimiles . Itémque fi quæratur,An mulus & hinnulus sint difsimiles: dissimiles, etiam inter se sunt dissimiles. mulus autem ex asino & equa, hinnulus ex equo & asina generatur.
units.tr: What is the argument from dissimilars? As the unlikeness of things is sought from some third thing, so dissimilarity too is sought from something third. The first argument of this kind is therefore as follows: Things which are unlike in some third thing, and of which only one is like it, are also unlike each other. So this place serves to prove dissimilarity, as when it is asked whether the ass and the mule are unlike: the argument runs, If the ass is born of an ass and a she-ass, and the mule of an ass and a mare, they are unlike. Likewise, if it is asked whether the mule and the hinny are unlike: they are unlike, since [the ass and the horse] are also unlike each other. The mule, however, is born of an ass and a mare, and the hinny of a horse and a she-ass.

units.la: Quod est firmamentum de Conuenientia? Idem quod de reciprocatione. Itaque una eadem regula utrunque concludemus. Quod uni dissimili conuenit, alteri non conuenit. veluti: Si lachrymæ mulieribus conueniunt, viris non conueniunt. Si viris arma conueniunt, mulieribus non conueniunt. Sequitur III. Quod uni dissimili non conuenit, non continuò alteri eius dissimili non conuenit. veluti: Non filufiones[?] senibus nō conueniūt, iccircò pueris non conueniunt. Non ut ex improbo patre probus filius nascitur, sic ab indocto præceptore doctus discipulus efficitur. SequiturIIII: Neque similia dissimilibus, neque dissimilia similibus conueniunt. Si similem priuato & Consuli togam permitti iniquum est, etiam dissimilem duobus Consulibus attribuere iniquum est.
units.tr: What is the argument from agreement? It is the same as the argument from reciprocation, so we shall conclude both by one and the same rule: What agrees with one of two unlike things does not agree with the other. For example: If tears belong to women, they do not belong to men; if arms belong to men, they do not belong to women. It follows, second: What does not agree with one of two unlike things does not necessarily fail to agree with the other unlike thing. For example: Games do not suit old men, therefore they do not suit boys. Just as a good son is not born of a wicked father, so a learned pupil is not made by an unlearned teacher. It follows, thirdly: Neither like things agree with unlike things, nor unlike things with like. If it is unjust to grant a toga of one kind to a private citizen and a consul alike, it is also unjust to assign a toga unlike that of two consuls.

units.la: De loco Definitionis. CAP. XXXIII.
units.tr: On the Place of Definition. CHAPTER XXXIII.

units.la: ERGE porro: ac deinceps de dictionū ratione & mutuis affectionibus differamus. Nihil verò attinet eum laborem capere, cùm ex rerum locis quiuis mediocri ingenio prædītus facilè de dictionum locis existimare poffit. Quatuor tantùm locorum specimen edemus,Generis, Totius, Caussæ, & Antecedentis:quorum primus & fecundus per definitionem , tertius per notationem, quartus per coniugationem tractatur.
units.tr: Next, then, let us deal with the nature of words and their mutual relations. There is no need to take that trouble, since anyone of moderate intelligence can easily work out the places of words from the places of things. We will give a sample of only four places: Genus, Whole, Cause and Antecedent. Of these, the first two are treated through definition, the third through notation, and the fourth through conjugates.

units.la: Quid? non igitur separatos facis tres locos ex definitione,notatione, & coniugatis? Fieri quidem id vulgo in libris & scholis dialecticorum solet. Sed,vt opinor, ab iis qui non fatis videntur animaduertisse, neque affectiones esse illas tres, neque argumenta, neque argumentationes: sed argumenti tantùm tractandi formas, vt cùm diximus argumenta ex partibus & formis per Partium enumerationem tractari: aut ea quæ ex Antecedentibus, consequentibus,& repugnantibus, iis tribus tractari modis, quos Cicero in Topicis exposuit. Absurdum enim effet, locos ex partibus & ex partium enummeratione, quasi diuersos separare:quemadmodum posteriusintelliges. Harum verò trium rationem in præfentia fatis erit ex sola definitione cognofcere.
units.tr: Why, then, do you not separate three places from definition, notation and conjugates? Indeed, that is what is commonly done in books and in the schools of the dialecticians. But, as I think, those who do so have not sufficiently noticed that these three are neither affections, nor arguments, nor argumentations, but only forms of treating an argument. Thus when we said that arguments from parts and forms are treated by enumerating the parts, or that those drawn from antecedents, consequents and repugnants are treated in the three ways Cicero set out in the Topics. It would be absurd to separate places drawn from parts and from the enumeration of parts as if they were different, as you will understand later. For the present, it will be enough to know the method of these three from definition alone.

units.la: Quomodo? Quia definitioné non esse affectum,vel hinc licet intelligatur,quòd ea ex afsectionum locis vel omnibus,vel plerisque( vt superiùs demonstratum est) conficitur. Iam argumentum non esse ex eo constat, primum quòd cùm definitio per argumentum probetur,perspicuum est,aliud esse quod probatur, aliud medium per quod probatur. Deinde quod singuli affectus argumenta singula fuppeditant: neque vllum vnum ex pluribus sumitur.At definitio necessariò ex pluribus coiunctis conficitur. veluti ex genere & specie per differentiam distracta, aut, fi per diuisionem fit, ex genere & formis omnibus: fi per Partitionē ex Toto & Partibus. Postremò definitionem dici argumentationem non posse, hinc perspicuum est, quòd vnica enuntiatione definitio constat, cùm argumentatio minimum ex tribus componatur.
units.tr: How so? That definition is not an affection can be seen from this: it is composed from the places of affections, either all of them or most of them (as was shown above). Now, that it is not an argument is clear, first, because when a definition is proved by an argument, it is obvious that what is proved is one thing and the middle through which it is proved is another. Second, because each single affection supplies a single argument, and no one argument is taken from several, whereas a definition is necessarily made up of several things joined together: for example, of a genus and a species distinguished by a difference, or, if it is made by division, of a genus and all its forms, or, if by partition, of a whole and its parts. Lastly, that a definition cannot be called an argumentation is clear from this: a definition consists of a single proposition, whereas an argumentation consists of at least three.

units.la: Quænā igitur erroris peruulgáti caussa est? Creditum est Ciceronis eam fuisse fententiam,cùm tamē & in Topicis & in Partitionibus & inlib. de Oratore 3. nō dicat argumenta fumi ex definitione, neque definitionem in locis numeret:sed ad id totum de quo disseritur,adhiberi.Si res tota(inquit)quaeritur, definitione vniuersa vis explicanda est: quippe, cum vniuersa vis & notio vel subiecti, vel attributi.definiendo explicetur. Ex quo perfpicuum est, locum qui vulgo Ex definitione appellatur,esse,fi subtilior definitio fit,vel ex genere & formis, vel ex toto & partibus: sin rudius exposita est, ex aliquo reliquorum affectuum sumptum esse.
units.tr: What, then, is the cause of this widespread error? It was believed that this was Cicero's view, although in the Topics, in the Partitions and in book 3 of On the Orator he does not say that arguments are taken from definition, nor does he count definition among the places. Rather, he says it is applied to the whole thing under discussion. "If the whole matter (he says) is in question, the whole force must be explained by definition: since the whole force and notion of either the subject or the predicate is explained by defining." From this it is clear that the place commonly called "from definition" is, if the definition is more refined, drawn either from genus and forms or from whole and parts; but if it is set out more crudely, it is taken from one of the other affections.
