units.la: Cedo aliquod exemplū. Ponatur illa quaestio, An Rhetorica fit laudabilis:dein ratiocinatio,Ars copiosè dicendi est laudabilis:Rhetorica est ars copiosè dicendi:Ergo Rhetorica est laudabilis.Mediū perspicuè sumitur ex genere & specie per differentiam distracta: id est, ex genere & differentia. At si sic concludatur: Rhetorica est ars inveniendi, quæ ad persuadendum valet, eáque disponendi eloquendi & memoriter pronuntiandi: horum autem unumquodque laudabile est: Rhetorica igitur laudabilis: si sic, inquam, concludamus, ex Toto & Partibus erit argumentatio. Definitio igitur non argumenti locus est, sed argumenti tractatio, vel argumenti tractandi forma.
units.tr: Let me give an example. Take the question, whether rhetoric is praiseworthy, and then the reasoning: the art of speaking copiously is praiseworthy; rhetoric is the art of speaking copiously; therefore rhetoric is praiseworthy. The middle term is clearly taken from genus and species distinguished by a difference, that is, from genus and difference. But if we conclude thus: "Rhetoric is the art of finding what is useful for persuading, and of arranging, expressing and delivering from memory; each of these is praiseworthy; therefore rhetoric is praiseworthy," then, I say, the argumentation will be from whole and parts. Definition, therefore, is not a place of argument, but a treatment of an argument, or a form of treating it.

units.la: Nullâne igitur de Definitione firmamenta traduntur? Tradi certè possunt, sed non tanquam loci alicuius proprij, verùm tanquã generis, aut totius. Veluti I: Cui convenit definitio, eidem nomen convenit: vicissimque quod definitioni convenit, id nomini convenit. Hoc enim perinde est, ac si dictum esset: Cui genus totúmve convénit, ei species pársve convenit: vicissimque quod generi totius convenit, id speciei partive convenit. Valet autem ad confirmandum. veluti: Si iustitia est habitus ratio-ni consentaneus, recte virtus appellabitur. Si Davus servitutem servit, est servus. Quoniam (inquit Cicero de Finib. 1.) cùm privamur dolore, ipsa liberatione ac vacuitate omnis molestiæ, gaudemus: omne autem id quo gaudemus, voluptas est: ut omne quo offendimur dolor: doloris omnis privatio recte nominata est voluptas. De conversa autem convenientia exemplum extat eiusdem in Topicis: Si Ius ciuile est æquitas constituta iis, qui eiusdem ciuitatis sunt, ad res suas obtinendas, eius autem æquitatis notitia est utilis: certè Iuris ciuilis cognitio est utilis.
units.tr: Are no supports, then, handed down concerning definition? They certainly can be handed down, but not as the place of some particular thing, rather as the place of genus or whole. For example: "What the definition fits, the name fits too; and conversely, what fits the definition, fits the name." For this is just the same as saying: "What fits the genus or whole, fits the species or part; and conversely, what fits the genus or whole of a thing, fits its species or part." It is used for confirming, for example: "If justice is a habit in accordance with reason, it will rightly be called virtue." "If Davus serves a slavery, he is a slave." Cicero says in On Ends, book 1: "Since, when we are freed from pain, we rejoice in that very release and freedom from all discomfort; and everything in which we rejoice is pleasure; just as everything by which we are offended is pain; so the absence of all pain is rightly called pleasure." An example of the converse agreement is found in the same author's Topics: "If civil law is the fairness established for those who belong to the same state, for the sake of keeping their own property, and knowledge of that fairness is useful, then certainly knowledge of civil law is useful."

units.la: Quod est secundum? Cui non conuenit definitio, eidem nec nomē conuenit. Valet enim ad refellendum. Cicero in Parad. Si nemo dies est, nisi qui exercitum alere potest suis fructibus, hoc proposito nunquam eris dies, antequam ex tuis possessionibus tantum reficias, vt ex eo tueri sex legiones possis. Iam fateris igitur non esse te diuitem, cui tātum defit, vt expleas id quod exoptas? In eodē genere illud est: Si neque sacrum, neque de sacro quicquam surripuit, non est sacrilegus. itéque illud Iurisconsultorum: Si stipulatio est verborum conceptio, qua qui interrogatus est, daturum se respondet: neque mutus, neque surdus stipulari possunt.
units.tr: What is the second? What the definition does not fit, the name does not fit either. This is used for refuting. Cicero in the Paradoxes: "If no one is rich except the man who can feed an army from his own revenues, then at this rate you will never be rich, unless you draw so much from your estates that you can keep six legions from them. Do you therefore admit that you are not rich, since you still lack so much of what you long for?" In the same kind is this: "If he has stolen neither a sacred thing nor anything from a sacred thing, he is not a sacrilegious person." Likewise the jurists' saying: "If a stipulation is a form of words by which one who is asked replies that he will give, then neither a mute nor a deaf person can stipulate."

units.la: Quæ est Regula de Reciprocatione? Vt cui nomen conuenit, eidem definitio conuenit: sic cui definitio conuenit, eidem nomen conuenit. Et contrà, cui vnum non conuenit, nec alterum conuenit. veluti: vt qui in vniuersum de defuncti ius successit, heres est: ita qui heres est, in defuncti ius omne successit.
units.tr: What is the rule of reciprocation? As the name fits one thing, so the definition fits it; and so, to whatever the definition fits, the name fits too. And conversely, what one does not fit, the other does not fit either. For example: as whoever succeeds to the whole right of the deceased is heir, so whoever is heir succeeds to the whole right of the deceased.

units.la: Quoniam paulo ante dixisti definitionem Argumentatione & Syllogismo probari: quæro quænam definitionis probandæ ars est? Aristoteles duobus locis hanc tradit, vt non tota oratio pro extremis collocetur, sed eius ea pars duntaxat, ad quam probatio pertinet. Nam cùm definitio rei naturam explicet, si quis ea sola sumat, quæ de natura rei dici debent, definitionem cõficiet. veluti: Si quis(inquit) probare velit, Aquam esse humorem potabilé, Aqua & potabilis pro extremis collocanda sunt: humor autem pro medio. Quod eodem modo in illis Ciceronis definitionibus ostendi potest. Odium est ira inveterata: Inimicitia est ira ulciscendi tempus observans: Discordia est ira acerbior, intimo odio & corde concepta: Indigentia libido inexplebilis. Nam cùm intermedium nomen utrique extremo conveniat, necessariò ambo extrema inter se convenient.
units.tr: Since you said a little while ago that definition is proved by argumentation and syllogism, I ask: what is the art of proving a definition? Aristotle gives this in two places: the whole speech should not be placed under the extremes, but only that part to which the proof pertains. For since a definition explains the nature of a thing, if someone takes only those things which ought to be said about the nature of the thing, he will make a definition. For example: "If someone (he says) wishes to prove that water is a drinkable liquid, then 'water' and 'drinkable' are to be placed as the extremes, and 'liquid' as the middle." The same can be shown in Cicero's definitions: "Hatred is long-standing anger. Enmity is anger watching for a time to take revenge. Discord is a more bitter anger, conceived in the innermost hatred and heart. Covetousness is an insatiable desire." For since the middle term agrees with each extreme, the two extremes must necessarily agree with each other.

units.la: De loco Notationis. CAP. XXXIIII.
units.tr: On the Place of Notation. CHAPTER 34

units.la: QVONIAM[?] superiùs quid Notatio esset[?] definiti, quæro nunc quotuplex notatio est? Triplex: alia enim verborum est simplicium, alia iunctorum: & rursus simplicium, alia naturalium, alia factorum. Itaque ad tres affectuum locos notatio pertinet, Causarū, Proprij, & Totius. Naturalium, veluti: cùm propria cuique vocabuli notio exquiritur, vt cùm quæritur cur Vultus nullo in animante ponatur præter hominem: cur Morbus in corpore, Vitiū in animo ponatur: cur Rapiendi verbo vis infit: Furandi non infit. Factorum, vt, Fides dicitur, quia quod promissum est,fiat. Nequitia ab eo quod necquicquam est in tali homine. Coniunctorum verò : vt,An Tumultus nó dicitur,nisi cùm timor multus est.Benè (inquit Cicero)maiores nostri accubationem epularem amicorum, quia vitæ coniunctionem haberet,conuiuium nominarunt. meliùs quàm Græci, qui hoc idem tum compotationem tum concœnationem vocant.
units.tr: Since I have already defined what notation is, I now ask: how many kinds of notation are there? There are three. One kind belongs to words that are simple, another to words that are joined together, and the simple kind is again divided into natural and made. Notation therefore pertains to three places of the affections: causes, what is proper, and the whole. Natural notation is, for example, when the proper meaning of each word is sought out, as when we ask why "vultus" (face) is applied to no living thing except man, why "morbus" (disease) is applied to the body and "vitium" (vice) to the mind, why the verb "rapere" (to snatch) carries force but "furari" (to steal) does not. Made notation is, for example, "fides" (faith) is so called because what has been promised is done; "nequitia" (worthlessness) is named from the fact that a man of that kind is good for nothing. Joined notation is, for example, "tumultus" (uproar) is not said unless great fear is present. Cicero says: "Our ancestors rightly called the couch-gathering of friends at a feast a 'convivium' (living together), because it has the fellowship of life; better than the Greeks, who call the same thing by the names 'compotatio' and 'concoenatio'."

units.la: Quænam de Notatione firmamenta ponemus? Eadem quæ de caufla aut proprij conuenientia posuimus.Itaque primum erit huiufmodi:Cui conuenit notatio,eidē nomen conuenit.Valet enim ad confirmandum. Si Reip. consulit,est Consul.Si edes tuetur,est edituus.
units.tr: What firmaments of notation shall we lay down? The same ones we laid down for cause and for what is proper. So the first will be of this kind: whatever a notation fits, the name fits the same thing as well. For it serves to confirm. If someone looks after the commonwealth, he is a consul. If someone guards a building, he is an aedituus (temple-keeper).

units.la: Quoniam vidua dicta est fine duitate [?] (ait Labeo)quemadmodū vecors & vesanus fine corde & sanitate :sequitur vt ea quoque mulier quæ virū nunquam habuit, vidua dici possit.
units.tr: Since a widow (vidua) is so called from being without a husband, as Labeo says, just as a senseless man (vecors) and a madman (vesanus) are named from being without heart and sanity, it follows that a woman who has never had a husband may also be called a widow.

units.la: Sequitur 11:Cui notatio non conuenit,eidem nomen non conuenit. Valet enim ad refellendum.veluti : Si non est timor multus ,non est tumultus.nisi consilium,ratio,& sententia effent in senibus (ait Cato apud Ciceronem) non summum consilium maiores nostri appellassent Senatum.Eiusmodi argumentū fuit Friderici Imperatoris aduersus Adrianum Papam de quo est in Radeuici historia : Si vrbis Romæ dominus non sum , Romanus Imperator nō sum. Cùm diuina(inquit) ordinatione ,ego Imperator Romanus & dicar , & gnus putetur? cui tandem hic libero imperabit, qui non potest suis cupiditatibus imperare: cùm ipse improbissimis dominis dedecori & turpitudini parere desierit. Item, Præclarè dictum est, nisi sapientem liberum esse neminem. Quid est enim libertas? Potestas viuedi vt velis. quis igitur viuit vt vult, nisi profecto, qui recta sequitur?
units.tr: The second follows: whatever a notation does not fit, the name does not fit the same thing either. For it serves to refute. For example: if there is no great fear, there is no tumult. Unless there were counsel, reason and judgement in the old men, as Cato says in Cicero, our ancestors would not have called the highest council the Senate. An argument of this kind was used by the Emperor Frederick against Pope Adrian, which is recorded in the history of Radevicus: "If I am not lord of the city of Rome, I am not Roman emperor. When by divine ordinance I am called and believed to be Roman emperor, to whom at last will this man rule freely, who cannot rule his own desires, since he himself has ceased to submit to the most wicked masters, to his shame and disgrace?" Likewise, it is well said that no one is free except the wise man. For what is liberty? The power of living as you wish. Who, then, lives as he wishes, except surely the one who follows what is right?

units.la: Quod est firmamentum de conuenientia? Esto hoc I. Quod vni ex necessariis coniugatis conuenit, alteri conuenit. veluti: Si sapientia laudanda est, Socrates, qui sapiens est & sapienter viuit, laudandus est. Si ebrietas vituperanda est, etiam ebriosi vituperandi sunt. & si ebrij, etiam ebrietas. Si Regulus Tyrannidem in suos exercet, Tyrannus est. Si Reges Tyrannorum nomen oderunt, oderint Tyrannidem. § quod recte fit (inquit Cicero) & honeste, & cum virtute, id benefieri verè dicitur: & quod recte, & honestum, & cum virtute est, id solum opinor bonum. Sequitur II. Quod vni ex necessariis coniugatis non conuenit, alteri non conueniet. veluti: Si non continenter viuit, nō est continens. Si non est continens, non continenter viuit. Si non est laudanda crudelitas, nec crudeles laudandi sunt. At hoc non reciprocatur. Si fuit intestabilis, testamentum non fecit. Non si testamentum non fecit, fuit intestabilis.
units.tr: What is the firmament of fitting? Let this be the first: whatever fits one of the necessarily conjugated things, fits the other as well. For example: if wisdom is to be praised, then Socrates, who is wise and lives wisely, is to be praised. If drunkenness is to be censured, then drunkards too are to be censured; and if they are drunk, then drunkenness too. If Regulus exercises tyranny over his own people, he is a tyrant. If kings hate the name of tyrants, let them hate tyranny. Cicero says: "What is done rightly, honourably, and with virtue, is truly said to be done well; and what is right, honourable and virtuous, that alone, I think, is good." The second follows: whatever does not fit one of the necessarily conjugated things, will not fit the other. For example: if he does not live continently, he is not continent. If he is not continent, he does not live continently. If cruelty is not to be praised, neither are cruel men to be praised. But this does not reciprocate. If he was incapable of making a will (intestabilis), he did not make a will. But it does not follow that if he did not make a will, he was incapable of making one.

units.la: Quid sequitur nunc? Vulgò exponi solent loci probationum inartificialium ex locis af-sumptis: sumptis : ut ex testimonio, auctoritate, iurciurando ; praeiudiciis, rumoribus, tabulis. Sed hæc (ut superius monui) quæ non in ratiocinatione, sed in sensibus posita sunt, & facti sunt non artis, nihil ad Dialecticam pertinent. Itaque ex Rhetorum disciplina, in qua sola hæc Aristoteles tradidit, eruenda sunt. Fides enim disputando non ex testibus, sed ex argumentis eruitur. non enim tam auctores in disputando, quàm rationis momenta quærenda sunt:
units.tr: What follows now? It is usual to set out the places of inartificial proofs drawn from assumed places: from testimony, authority, oath; from precedents, rumours, documents. But these things (as I warned above), which rest not on reasoning but on the senses, and are matters of fact rather than of art, have nothing to do with dialectic. Therefore they must be drawn from the teaching of the rhetoricians, in which alone Aristotle handed these down. For faith in disputation is not won from witnesses, but from arguments. For in disputing one must seek not so much the authorities as the weight of reason:

units.la: ait Cicero libro de nat.Deor.1
units.tr: says Cicero in the first book of De natura deorum.

units.la: FINIS LIBRI TERTII.
units.tr: END OF THE THIRD BOOK.

units.la: INSTITVTIONIS DIALECTICAE LIBER IIII.
units.tr: THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE DIALECTICAL INSTITUTION

units.la: De Analytice,siue arte iudicandi.
units.tr: On Analytic, or the Art of Judging.

units.la: CAP. I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: QUONIAM de inuetione Medij Syllogistici satis dixisti, deinceps de ipsius collocatione videamus: quam iudicandi artem superius Analyticen appellabas. Sed primum quæro, quid est Analytice? Est ars, quæ medij ad utrunque quæstionis extremum adhibendi rationem commonstrat.
units.tr: Since you have said enough about the discovery of the syllogistic middle term, let us next consider its arrangement, the art of judgement which above you called Analytic. But first I ask: what is Analytic? It is the art which shows the manner of applying the middle term to each extreme of the question.

units.la: Quisnam eius artis est usus? Probatio cōsecutionis, qua pronuntiata omnia vel ut vera recipiuntur, vel ut falsa repudiantur. Nam ut in ædificiis, alius est faber, qui lapides lapidibus adiungit: alius peritus, cuius arbitrio effectum opus probatur: sic oratio verba verbis adiungit: sed Analyticæ artis probatio est, utrum ea inter se rectè coniuncta sint, an secus.
units.tr: What is the use of this art? The proof of sequence, by which, once propositions are stated, all of them are either accepted as true or rejected as false. For just as in buildings, one man is the builder who joins stones to stones, and another is the skilled judge by whose decision the finished work is approved; so speech joins words to words, but the proof belongs to the art of Analytic: whether those words are rightly joined together or not.

units.la: De Syllogismo, & variis Syllogismi generibus.
units.tr: On the Syllogism, and the various kinds of syllogism.

units.la: CAP. II.
units.tr: CHAP. II.

units.la: Q[?]VONIAM fuperiùs diuifione argumentationis expofuisti, deinceps fingulas eius species videamus: ac primùm de syllogismo. Quid eft Syllogismus? Ariftoteles duobus locis ita definit, συλλόγισμός ὅτι λόγος ἐν ᾧ τεθέντων τινῶν ἕτερόν τι τῶν κειμένων ἐξ ἀνάγκης συμβαίνει, ὅτι διὰ τῶν κειμένων[?].
units.tr: Since you explained the division of argument above, let us now look at its individual kinds, beginning with the syllogism. What is a syllogism? Aristotle defines it in two places: a syllogism is a discourse in which, certain things being laid down, something other than those things follows of necessity from them, through those things that are laid down [συλλόγισμός ἐστι λόγος ἐν ᾧ τεθέντων τινῶν ἕτερόν τι τῶν κειμένων ἐξ ἀνάγκης συμβαίνει, τὸ διὰ τῶν κειμένων].

units.la: Gellius autem Latinè ita conuertit: Oratio in qua confesis quibusdam atque concessis, aliud quid;atque ea quæ concessa sunt, per ea quæ concessa sunt, neceffariò conficitur. Sed Ariftoteles initio priorum Analyticorum pro clausula ὅτι τῶν κειμένων: hàc posuit τὸ μὲν ταῦτα εἶ[?]. λέγω δ’ (subiungés) τὸ μὲν ταῦτα εἶ[?], τὸ δὲ ταῦτα συμβαίνει. quoniâ nullo externo eget extremo, vt neceffaria fiat confecutio. Itaque planius hæc definitio cóuerti fic poterit: Eft oratio, in qua quædam ita ponuntur, vt aliud quippiam diuerfum ab iis quæ pofita funt iccirco efficiatur neceffariò, quoniam ea ita funt. quanquam eandem vtriufque vim effe, verbum ἐξ ἀνάγκης oftendit.
units.tr: Gellius translates it into Latin thus: "A speech in which, certain things having been agreed and conceded, something else follows of necessity from those things that were conceded, through those same things." But at the beginning of the Prior Analytics Aristotle, after the clause about what is laid down, puts the phrase "that these things being, something else necessarily results" [τὸ μὲν ταῦτα εἶναι, τὸ δὲ ταῦτα συμβαίνει], adding: "I mean that these things being, those other things follow," since the syllogism needs no external term in order for the consequence to be necessary. So this definition can be turned into Latin more plainly thus: It is a discourse in which certain things are so posited that something different from what is posited is necessarily brought about, because those things are so. Although the words ἐξ ἀνάγκης show that the force of both is the same.

units.la: Quomodo? Quoniam non ad cóclufione ea verba pertinent, fed ad necefsariâ medij & extremorum coniunctionem. nam (vt idem alio loco declarat) quando medium neceffario cohæret, etiam conclufio neceffariò fequitur. ὅταν τὸ μέσον ἐξ ἀνάγκης, ᾗ[?] τὸ συμπέρασμα ἐξ ἀνάγκης. Nonenim (vt alio item loco docuit) ex omnibus propositionibus veris Syllogismus efficitur: sed ex duabus necessario consequentibus, & inter fe non minus cohærentibus, quàm annuli in cathena conferti inter fe cohærent. Oportet enim conclusionem ex superiorum propositionum consecutione exprimi: quemadmodum paulò post intelliges.
units.tr: How so? Because those words do not refer to the conclusion but to the necessary connection of the middle term with the extremes. For, as he explains elsewhere, when the middle necessarily coheres, the conclusion also necessarily follows [ὅταν τὸ μέσον ἐξ ἀνάγκης ᾖ, καὶ τὸ συμπέρασμα ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἐστίν]. For (as he taught in another passage too) a syllogism is not made from all true propositions, but from two propositions that necessarily follow from one another and cohere no less closely than the rings of a chain linked together. For the conclusion must be drawn from the succession of the premises above, as you will understand shortly.

units.la: Vnde dicitur Syllogismus? Idem Ariftoteles translatum esse verbum ostendit, ex calculatorum ratiocinationibus: cùm ait esse tanquam συλλογισμὸς ἢ ἐπαγωγή [?], hoc est collectionem summæ, quæ initis subductisque rationibus conficitur: qua de caussa ratiocinatio Latinè à Cicerone appellatur. veluti, Callicli data sunt primùm quinque: post eidem septẽ data sunt:duodecim igitur ad summam data sunt. Quanquam in tam exiguis numeris fridgidius exemplum est.
units.tr: Whence is the word syllogism taken? Aristotle himself shows that the term was transferred from the reckonings of calculators, when he says that it is like a syllogismos or epagoge [συλλογισμὸς ἢ ἐπαγωγή], that is, a collection of a sum, which is made by bringing together and subtracting the accounts. For this reason Cicero calls it in Latin ratiocinatio. For example: Callicles was first given five; afterwards he was given seven more; therefore twelve were given in total. Although, with such small numbers, the example is rather flat.

units.la: Quotuplex est Syllogismus? Duplex. Estenim (vt idem scribit) aut καταγορικὸς [?], aut ὑποθετικὸς [?]: id est, aut simplex, aut copulatus. Simplex est, qui ex puris enuntiatis constans, purè concluditur. veluti, Omnis arbor vere florefcit. Platanus est arbor. Ergo vere florescit. Copulatus autem, qui non purè, sed vel per conditionem, vel per disiunctionem, vel per coniunctionem cócluditur. veluti: Si dies est, sol lucet. Item, aut dies est, aut nox est. Non & dies est, & nox est. Simplicem solum Ariftoteles tractauit, quoniam ad demonstrationem omnem omnem suam artem dirigit. Copulatū, Theophraftus, Eudemus, & Stoici cóplures, quemadmodum Boëtius testatur.
units.tr: How many kinds of syllogism are there? Two. For (as the same writer says) it is either categorical or hypothetical [καταγορικὸς or ὑποθετικὸς], that is, either simple or compound. The simple syllogism consists of pure propositions and is concluded purely. For example: Every tree flowers in spring. The plane tree is a tree. Therefore it flowers in spring. The compound syllogism is concluded not purely, but by a condition, or by a disjunction, or by a conjunction. For example: If it is day, the sun shines. Again: either it is day or it is night. It is not the case that it is both day and night. Aristotle treated only the simple syllogism, since he directs his whole art to demonstration. The compound syllogism was treated by Theophrastus, Eudemus, and several of the Stoics, as Boethius attests.

units.la: Quibus in rebus omne Syllogismi artificiū versatur? In ratiocinationis figura & modo. Est autem figura medij collocādi forma. Modus autem, qui in enuntiatorum qualitate & quantitate cernitur.
units.tr: In what does the whole art of the syllogism consist? In the figure and the mood of the reasoning. The figure is the form in which the middle term is placed; the mood is seen in the quality and quantity of the propositions.

units.la: Quot sunt huius artificij regulæ? Vulgò hæ quinque traduntur : quarum hæc 1. est: Quod de omni dicitur, de singulis ei subiectis dicitur. unde illud Ciceronis lib. de nat.deor. 3. Si omne animal mortale est, nullum est animal immortale. Et si omne animal secari ac diuidi potest, nullum est eorum indiuiduum. Et, si esset corpus aliquod immortale, non esset omne mutabile. Sequitur II, Quod dicitur de nullo, à singulis ei subiectis remouetur. Sequitur III. Ex solis negatiuis nihil concluditur: qua de caussa propositionum alterutrā affirmatiuam esse oportet. IIII. autem est hæc. Ex solis particularibus nihil conficitur. quapropter propositionum alterutram universalem esse oportet. Superest V. Conclusio semper ad deteriorem se partem applicat. nam si propositionum alterutra negatiua est, ipsa erit negatiua: si particularis, erit particularis.
units.tr: What are the rules of this art? Commonly five are handed down. The first is this: What is said of all is said of each of the things subsumed under it. Hence that passage of Cicero in book 3 of De natura deorum: If every animal is mortal, no animal is immortal; and if every animal can be cut and divided, none of them is indivisible; and if there were some immortal body, not every body would be changeable. The second follows: What is said of none is removed from each of the things subsumed under it. The third: nothing is concluded from negative premises alone; for this reason one of the premises must be affirmative. The fourth is this: nothing is concluded from particular premises alone; for this reason one of the premises must be universal. The fifth remains: the conclusion always follows the weaker part. For if one of the premises is negative, the conclusion itself will be negative; if one is particular, it will be particular.

units.la: De partibus Syllogismi,& vi conclusionis.
units.tr: On the parts of the syllogism, and the force of the conclusion.

units.la: CAP. III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: Quot sunt Syllogismi partes? Superius dictū est, ratiocinationem aliam fuisse Stoicorum propriam, aliam Peripateticorum. ac Stoici quidem syllogismi partes infinitæ sunt. tandiu enim verborum feries texitur, dum is qui disserit, quod intendit, efficiat. Aristoteles autem primùm acutissimè perspexit, nullamin iis verâ medij vim apparere. nam id demum medium dici, quòd æquè ab vtroque extremo abest. deinde vim & necessitatem conclusionis nequaquam in illis longis verborum continuationibus ita esse perspicuam, vt in paucis. Quapropter Aristoteles ad eam quam potuit paucitatem ac breuitatè Syllogismi partes redegit: trésque tâtummodo effecit. quarū prima Propositio, altera Assumptio, tertia Conclusio Latinè appellatur. Græci verò πρό-τασιν [?], λῆμμα, & συμπέρασμα nominant.
units.tr: How many parts does a syllogism have? It was said above that the Stoics had one kind of reasoning and the Peripatetics another. The Stoics made the parts of a syllogism unlimited, since the chain of words went on as long as the speaker needed to reach what he intended to prove. Aristotle, however, first saw very acutely that no true force of the middle term appears in such chains. For a term is called middle only if it is equally distant from each of the extremes. Next, he saw that the force and necessity of the conclusion are not nearly as clear in those long continuous strings of words as they are in short ones. For this reason Aristotle reduced the parts of the syllogism to the fewest and briefest possible, and made them only three. The first is called the proposition, the second the assumption, and the third the conclusion in Latin. The Greeks call them πρότασιν, λῆμμα and συμπέρασμα.

units.la: Quid est propositio? Superius dictum est, Analysin Aristoteli in argumentando placuisse contrariam ei synthesi, quam Stoici sequuti sunt. Itaque quod illi postremum collocabant, Aristoteles primum sumpsit. veluti (vt in peruulgato exemplo consistamus) si ponatur quæstio, an Callicles sit animal: medium adhibebitur ex specie, homo. ac tum ita ratio inibitur, non vt ab imo ad summum ascendamus: quemadmodum Stoici faciebant: Callicles est homo: homo est animal: ergo Callicles est animal. Sed primo loco medium sumetur. De homine verò pronuntiatur animal, quippe genus de specie. hæc propositio est. deinde hoc modo : De Callicle verè pronuntiatur homo. quippe species de indiuiduo. vnde necessaria conclusio sequitur:Ergo animal verè de Callicle pronuntiabitur.. Superiùs enim legem illam posuimus:Quod medio conuenit, ei quoque cui medium conuenit, necessariò conuenit. Conuenire autem dicuntur,quæ subiectorum attributa sunt.
units.tr: What is the proposition? It was said above that Aristotle preferred an analysis in reasoning, opposed to the synthesis that the Stoics followed. So what they placed last, Aristotle took first. For example, to stay with the well-known instance: if the question is whether Callicles is an animal, the middle term will be taken from the species, man. The reasoning then runs not from the bottom up to the top, as the Stoics did: Callicles is a man, a man is an animal, therefore Callicles is an animal. Instead the middle term is taken first. Animal is predicated of man, since the genus is predicated of the species. This is the proposition. Next, in this way: man is truly predicated of Callicle, since the species is predicated of the individual. From this a necessary conclusion follows: therefore animal will be truly predicated of Callicle. For we laid down above this rule: whatever agrees with the middle, that also to which the middle agrees necessarily agrees. Things are said to agree when they are attributes of their subjects.

units.la: Quamobrem fecunda Enuntiatio dicitur assumptio? Quoniam in argumento pro iam concesso sumitur:vt cùm dicimus:Si homo est animal,Callicles est animal. Illud pro concesso sumitur: Calliclem esse hominem.In quo illud obseruandum est,hoc inter Stoicum & Ariftotelicum argumentum intercesse,quòd quâ partem Stoici propositionem faciunt, eam Ariftoteles assumptionē facit : vicissímque quâ illi assumptionem, hic propositionem. Nam in quæstione,An Callicles fit animal,Stoici sic disputant:Si Callicles homo est, Callicles est animal.vbi illud pro concesso sumunt:Omnis homo est animal. Ariftoteles verò hoc modo: Si homo est animal:Callicles est animal. quasi iam concessum illud fuisset, Callicles est animal.
units.tr: Why is the second statement called the assumption? Because in the argument it is taken as already granted, as when we say: if man is an animal, Callicles is an animal. This is taken as granted: that Callicles is a man. In this we must notice that the difference between the Stoic and the Aristotelian argument is this: what the Stoics make the proposition, Aristotle makes the assumption, and conversely what they make the assumption, he makes the proposition. For in the question whether Callicles is an animal, the Stoics argue thus: if Callicles is a man, Callicles is an animal, where they take as granted: every man is an animal. Aristotle, however, puts it this way: if man is an animal, Callicles is an animal, as if that had already been conceded, namely that Callicles is an animal.

units.la: Quænam igitur est Conclusionis istius necessitas? Quia necesse est ex antecedentibus necessariis consecutionem effici necessariam. Quod Ariftoteles in definitione dixerat,ἐξ ἀἀνάγκης[?]. Necessitatem enim non ad conclusionem duntaxat (ut superiùs diximus) sed communiter ad propositionem & assumptionem retulit. ut planè demirer esse, qui contra definitionem Aristotelis illud obiiciunt: Venti incubuere mari: Crebris micat ignibus æther: Densi fundūtur ab æthere nimbi: Ergo tempestas est. Hic enim & veras esse propositiones, & necessariam consecutionem: neque tamen syllogismum existere. ac proinde falsum esse quod dictum est, Syllogismum esse, qui ex pluribus veris propositionibus efficitur. quasi verò Virgilianæ istæ propositiones eiusmodi sint, cuiusmodi Aristoteles posuit: nimirū necefsitate ita inter se connexas, & cohærescentes, ut annuli in cathena cōferti adhærēscunt. ὅταν τὸ μέσον ἐξ ἀνάγκης, ἢ τὸ συμπέρασμα ἐξ ἀνάγκης[?]: & (ut alibi scribit) ἀεὶ γὰρ ἢ ὅλη, ἢ μέρος αἱ ἀποτάσεις ἐξ ἑνὸς συλλογισμός[?]. Semper propo-fitiones debent ita esse inter se affectæ, quasi aut totum, aut pars. Argumentum autem illud Virgilianum est ex caussis efficientibus sumptum: sed non inter se consequentibus, ac necessario cohærentibus. nam ut venti mari incubuerint, tempestas effecta erit: quāvis neque nimbi, neque fulgura coniuncta sint.
units.tr: What, then, is the necessity of this conclusion? Because a necessary consequence must arise from necessary antecedents. Aristotle had said this in his definition, ἐξ ἀνάγκης [from necessity]. For he referred necessity not merely to the conclusion (as we said above) but in general to the proposition and the assumption. So I am quite surprised that there are those who object to Aristotle's definition with this: the winds have fallen upon the sea; the sky glitters with frequent fires; dense storm clouds pour forth from the sky; therefore there is a storm. Here the propositions are true and the consequence is necessary, and yet there is no syllogism. And so they conclude that what was said, that a syllogism is one made of several true propositions, is false. As if those Virgilian statements were of the kind Aristotle laid down, namely joined together and cohering by necessity, as the links of a chain fitted together cling to one another. Aristotle writes: ὅταν τὸ μέσον ἐξ ἀνάγκης, ἢ τὸ συμπέρασμα ἐξ ἀνάγκης [when the middle is from necessity, the conclusion is also from necessity]; and (as he writes elsewhere) ἀεὶ γὰρ ἢ ὅλη, ἢ μέρος αἱ ἀποτάσεις ἐξ ἑνὸς συλλογισμός [for the premises always, whether wholly or partly, make one syllogism]. The propositions must always be related to one another as whole and part. That Virgilian argument, however, is drawn from efficient causes, but these do not follow from one another or cohere with necessity. For although the winds may have fallen upon the sea, a storm will be produced, yet the storm clouds and lightning are not connected with them.

units.la: Ecquonam igitur pacto Syllogismus ex illo Virgiliano exemplo concludi potest: Aestus maris navē impellit. Ventorum impetus stū[?] efficit. Ergo ventorum impetus nauis iactationem efficit. Nam posita quæstione, An ventorum impetus nauis iactatione efficiat, medióque interposito, Aestus maris: facilè concludetur, quod medio adhærescit, ei quoque cui medium conuenit, necessariò conuenire.
units.tr: In what way, then, can a syllogism be concluded from that Virgilian example? The swell of the sea drives the ship. The force of the winds produces the swell. Therefore the force of the winds produces the tossing of the ship. For if the question is posed, whether the force of the winds produces the tossing of the ship, and the swell of the sea is interposed as the middle term, it will easily be concluded that whatever adheres to the middle also necessarily belongs to that to which the middle belongs.

units.la: De tribus Syllogismorum Figuris.
units.tr: On the Three Figures of the Syllogism.

units.la: CAP. IIII.
units.tr: CHAP. IIII.

units.la: VOT sunt Medij collocandi formæ? Tres. Nam aut inter duos quæstionis terminos interponitur, qui locus Medio maximè conuenit: aut supra utrunque, aut sub utroque. unde tres Syllogismi figuræ ab Aristotele factæ sunt: prima ex loco Medij dignisimo: secunda ex eo qui minus dignus est: tertia ex infimo.
units.tr: How many forms is the middle term to be placed in? Three. For it is either interposed between the two terms of the question, which place suits the middle most, or above both, or below both. Hence Aristotle made three figures of the syllogism: the first from the most worthy place of the middle, the second from the place that is less worthy, and the third from the lowest.

units.la: Quomodo medium inter utrunque extremum interiicitur? Cum primo loco maius extremum de ipso dicitur: pòst ipsum de minore. Nam propositio fit ex medio & attributo: assumptio ex subiecto & medio. unde subiecti & attributi cōuenientia perspicitur. Scitum est autem, quod Aristoteles scribit, ex figuris omnibus hanc esse ad docendum accommodatissimā, & mathematicas omnes scientias, veluti Arithmeticā, & Geometriam, suas in hac figura demōstrationes concludere: propterea quòd omnes quæ caussa rei fit, declarant. certissimum autem & exquisitissimū sciendi genus esse, per quod rei cuiusque caussa intelligitur.
units.tr: How is the middle interposed between each extreme? When the major extreme is predicated of it in the first place, and afterwards it is predicated of the minor. For the proposition is formed from the middle and the predicate, and the assumption from the subject and the middle. Hence the agreement of subject and predicate is perceived. It is worth knowing what Aristotle writes: of all the figures this is the most suitable for teaching, and all the mathematical sciences, such as arithmetic and geometry, conclude their demonstrations in this figure, because they all show the cause of the thing. And the most certain and exquisite kind of knowing is that through which the cause of each thing is understood.

units.la: Cedo exemplum primæ figuræ. Esto posita quæstio, An sobrietas fit laudabilis, Sobrietas minus extremum est.laudabilis,maius. Adhibeatur medium ex genere minoris, Virtus. Tum ita disseratur. Virtus est laudabilis 2 laudabilis Sobrietas est virtus 1 virtus 4 Ergo sobrietas est lau-dabilis. Sobrietas 3
units.tr: Let me give an example of the first figure. Let the question be posed: Does sobriety become laudable? Sobriety is the minor extreme, laudable the major. Let a middle be taken from the genus of the minor: Virtue. Then the argument runs thus: Virtue is laudable. Sobriety is virtue. Therefore sobriety is laudable. Sobriety 3

units.la: Nam genus Subiecti quæsitum est, Virtus:que inter duo quæstionis extrema ita interiicitur,vt in propositione sit subiectum attributi,&in assumptione attributū subiecti. quod autem generi conuenit , etiam speciei conueniat necesse est.Itaque ad hunc locū illud quoque pertinet : Quæ mulier lac habet,ea peperit.Hæc mulier lac habet.ergo peperit.
units.tr: For the genus of the subject is what is sought, Virtue; and it is interposed between the two extremes of the question so that in the proposition it is the subject of the predicate, and in the assumption the predicate of the subject. What belongs to the genus must necessarily belong to the species too. So to this place also belongs this: Whatever woman has milk has given birth. This woman has milk. Therefore she has given birth.

units.la: Quomodo Medium supra vtrumque extremum collocatur? Cùm de ambobus extremis pronuntiatur:id est,cùm & in propositione & in assumptione vtriusque extremi attributū est.veluti,Ponatur quæstio, an aliqua ebrietas sit laudabilis.Deinde sumatur Medium,ex repugnantibus attributi,nimirum Turpe. Nihil quod dementat est laudabile 1 Laudabilis Omnis ebrietas est demen-tans 2 Dementās 4 Nulla igitur ebrietas est lau-dabilis. Ebrietas 3 In hac autem figura hoc perpetuum est, ut nulla ex ea colligi affirmatio possit.
units.tr: How is the middle placed above both extremes? When it is predicated of both extremes, that is, when the predicate belongs to each extreme in both the proposition and the assumption. For example, let the question be posed: Is some drunkenness laudable? Then let a middle be taken from what is repugnant to the predicate, namely Base. Nothing that makes one mad is laudable. Every drunkenness makes one mad. Therefore no drunkenness is laudable. In this figure it is always the case that no affirmative conclusion can be drawn from it.

units.la: Quomodo medium sub utroque extremo collocatur? Cùm de Mediũ utrunque extremum pronuntiatur. Cùm & in propositione & in assumptione Mediũ utriusque extremi subiectum est, veluti, Ponatur quæstio, An aliqui homines sint atri, deinde sumatur Mediũ ex specie: nimirum, Aethiopes. Aethiopes sunt atri Aliqui homines sunt Aethiopes Ergo aliqui homines sunt atri.
units.tr: How is the middle placed below both extremes? When the middle is predicated of each extreme. When the middle is the subject of each extreme, in both the proposition and the assumption. For example, let the question be posed: Are some men black? Then let a middle be taken from the species, namely Ethiopians. Ethiopians are black. Some men are Ethiopians. Therefore some men are black.

units.la: 2 Atri | A 1 Aethiopes 3 | C Aliqui homines 4 | B
units.tr: 2 Black | A 1 Ethiopians 3 | C Some men 4 | B

units.la: Huius autem figurae hoc proprium est, ut conclusio semper sit particularis, veluti, Socrates est probus Socrates est Philosophus Ergo aliqui Philosophi sunt probi.
units.tr: It is peculiar to this figure that the conclusion is always particular. For example: Socrates is upright. Socrates is a philosopher. Therefore some philosophers are upright.

units.la: Possumusne, quoniam hæ Figurae appellantur, & ex Mathematicorum consuetudine sumptę sunt, descriptionem earum aliquam ob oculos ponere? Licet vero, idque Aristotelis exemplo, qui cum adolescentibus in mathematicis artibus eruditis Logicam traderet, accuratè istam figurarum & descriptionum consuetudinem seruauit. Prima igitur figura hæc esto. | Secunda hæc. | Tertia huiusmodi. Si de B dicitur A, B autem de C. Certè de C dicitur A. | Si de A nō dicitur B. De C autē dicitur A. Certè de C non dicitur B. | Si de C dicitur A. De B autē dicitur C. Certè A dicitur de B.
units.tr: Since these are called figures and were taken from the custom of the mathematicians, can we also set a depiction of them before the eyes? We may indeed, and this follows the example of Aristotle, who, when he taught logic to young men trained in the mathematical arts, carefully kept this custom of figures and diagrams. So let the first figure be this. | The second this. | The third of this kind. If A is said of B, and B of C, then certainly A is said of C. | If B is not said of A, and A is said of C, then certainly B is not said of C. | If A is said of C, and C is said of B, then certainly A is said of B.

units.la: Ita B, quæ medij nota est, in prima suum locum obtinet: in secunda summum, in tertia infimum. A. | B. | A. B. | A. | C. C. | C. | B.
units.tr: So B, which is the mark of the middle, holds its place in the first figure; in the second, the highest; in the third, the lowest. A. | B. | A. B. | A. | C. C. | C. | B.

units.la: De Modis prima figura. CAP. V.
units.tr: On the Modes of the First Figure. CHAP. V.

units.la: Quot sunt modi primæ figuræ? Quatuor tantūm modis variari prima figura potest, qua de causa quatuor eiusmodi numerātur. quoniam autem eorum modorum fluxa memoria est, iccirco adiuuandæ memoriæ causa, vulgò in scholis receptum est, vt quatuor primis vocalibus hi quatuor disignētur modi. nam A vniuersalis affirmatiuæ nota est. E vniuersalis negatiuæ. I particularis affirmatiuæ. O particularis negatiuæ. vnde ficta vocabula, χεάμμακα[?], ἐκαλε[?], χεαφίδι[?], τεχνικὸς[?], ἐκαλε[?], καταχε[?], μέπειον[?], ἀχολον[?], ἀπαπ[?], χέναρος[?], ἰσάκις[?], ἀσνιδὶ[?], ὁ μαλὸς[?], φέεισος[?]. Et latini versiculi:
units.tr: How many modes does the first figure have? The first figure can be varied in only four modes, and for that reason four such modes are counted. Since the memory of these modes is slippery, and to aid the memory, it has become customary in the schools that these four modes be marked by the first four vowels. Thus A is the sign of a universal affirmative, E of a universal negative, I of a particular affirmative, and O of a particular negative. From this come the invented words [χεάμμακα, ἐκαλε, χεαφίδι, τεχνικὸς, ἐκαλε, καταχε, μέπειον, ἀχολον, ἀπαπ, χέναρος, ἰσάκις, ἀσνιδὶ, ὁ μαλὸς, φέεισος, as printed, garbled in the scan]. And the Latin verses:

units.la: Barbara,celarent,prima:darij,ferióque, Cafare[?],camestres,festino,baroco, secunda: Tertia grande sonans dedit,darapti,felapton. Adiungens,disamis,datisi,bocardo,firizon.
units.tr: Barbara, Celarent, first; Darii and Ferio; Cesare, Camestres, Festino, Baroco, second. The third has sounded Darapti and Felapton, adding Disamis, Datisi, Bocardo and Ferison.

units.la: Primæ autem figuræ hæc ratio est, vt Barbara valeat ad rem ex toto confirmandam: Celarent ad rem ex toto refellendam: Darij ad rem ex parte cōfirmandam : Ferio ad rem ex parte refellendam.
units.tr: The rationale of the first figure is this: Barbara serves to confirm a thing wholly; Celarent to refute a thing wholly; Darii to confirm a thing in part; Ferio to refute a thing in part.

units.la: Age, quis est primus primæ figuræ modus? Cùm è propositione & assumptione vtraque & vniuersali,& affirmatiua,vniuersalis & affirmatiua conclusio cogitur. atque hoc quidem primo modo genus omne quæstionis tractari potest: sed cautio adhibenda est, vt propositio sit vniuersalis,& assumptio affirmatiua. Bar Omne animal est mortale 2 ba Omnis homo est animal 1.4 3 ra Ergo omnis homo est mortalis. 3
units.tr: Come now, what is the first mode of the first figure? When both the proposition and the assumption are universal and affirmative, a universal and affirmative conclusion follows. This first mode can be used to treat every kind of question, but care must be taken that the proposition be universal and the assumption affirmative. Barbara: Every animal is mortal. Every man is an animal. Therefore every man is mortal.

units.la: Quodnam huius syllogismi firmamentum est? Medium est ex genere ad speciem, cuius hoc firmamentum est: Quod generis proprium est, idem speciei quoque proprium est. Nam propositio proprij affectione continetur. Proprium enim animalium est mori. quod cùm de inanimatis dicitur, veluti de stirpibus, tráslatè dicitur. assumptionem verò generis affectio sustinet.
units.tr: What is the foundation of this syllogism? The middle term passes from genus to species, and its foundation is this: What belongs to the genus belongs also to the species. For the proposition is supported by a property (proprium) of the genus. Thus it is a property of animals to die; when this is said of inanimate things, such as plants, it is said figuratively. The assumption, however, is sustained by the genus's attribute.

units.la: Quis est secundus? Cùm è propositione vniuersali negatiua & assumptione vniuersali affirmatiua conclusio universalis negatiua cogitur: Semper enim (ut ante diximus) ad deteriorem se partem applicat conclusio. veluti, Ce Nullus sapiens est avarus 2 la Omnis Philosophus est sapiens 1 4 rent Ergo nullus Philosophus est avarus. 3
units.tr: What is the second mode? When a universal negative proposition and a universal affirmative assumption are taken, a universal negative conclusion follows, for the conclusion (as we said before) always takes the worse part. For example: Celarent. No wise man is avaricious. Every philosopher is wise. Therefore no philosopher is avaricious.

units.la: Quod est huius Syllogismi firmamentum? Locus est ex genere ad speciem, cuius hoc firmamentum est. Quod generi repugnat, idem speciei quoque repugnat. Nam propositio repugnantium affectione continetur: assumptio generis.
units.tr: What is the foundation of this syllogism? It is a topic from genus to species, and its foundation is this: What is repugnant to the genus is also repugnant to the species. For the proposition is sustained by the principle of things that are repugnant; the assumption concerns the genus.

units.la: Quis est tertius? Cùm è propositione universali affirmativa, & assumptione particulari affirmativa, conclusio particularis affirmativa cogitur. Semper enim (ut dixi) deteriorē partem conclusio sequitur. veluti, Da Omne inutile est fugiendum 2 ri Quædam artes sunt inutiles 1 4 j Ergo quædam artes sunt fugienda. 3
units.tr: What is the third mode? When a universal affirmative proposition and a particular affirmative assumption are taken, a particular affirmative conclusion follows; for, as I have said, the conclusion always follows the worse part. For example: Darii. Every useless thing is to be avoided. Some arts are useless. Therefore some arts are to be avoided.

units.la: Quodnam huius firmamentum est? Locus est ex genere ad speciem, cuius hoc firmamétum est: Quod generis est consequens, idem quoque speciei est consequens. Nam propositio consequentiū ratione continetur: assumptio, generis.
units.tr: What is the foundation of this? It is a topic from genus to species, and its foundation is this: What follows from the genus also follows from the species. For the proposition is sustained by the reason of things that follow; the assumption concerns the genus.

units.la: Quis est quartus? Cùm ex proportione universali negativa, assumptione particulari affirmativa, conclusio particularis negativa cogitur. veluti: Nullus sapiens mærore conficitur Quidam Philosophi sunt sapientes Quidam igitur Philosophi mærore non conficiuntur.
units.tr: What is the fourth mode? When a universal negative proposition and a particular affirmative assumption are taken, a particular negative conclusion follows. For example: No wise man is worn down by grief. Some philosophers are wise. Therefore some philosophers are not worn down by grief.

units.la: Locus est ex genere ad speciem, cuius hoc firmamentum est: Quod generi repugnat, idē speciei repugnat. Nam propositio repugnantium ratione sustinetur: assumptio generis.
units.tr: It is a topic from genus to species, and its foundation is this: What is repugnant to the genus is also repugnant to the species. For the proposition is sustained by the reason of things that are repugnant; the assumption concerns the genus.

units.la: De quatuor secunda figura modis.
units.tr: On the Four Modes of the Second Figure.

units.la: CAP. VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: QVOT sunt Modi secūde figure? Quatuor: quorū primus est cùm ex propositione vniuersali negatiua, & assumptione vniuersali affirmatiua, sequitur conclusio vniuersalis negatiua. veluti, Nullus perturbatus ratione bene utitur Omnis sapiens ratione bene utitur Nullus ergo sapiens est perturbatus.
units.tr: How many modes does the second figure have? Four. The first is when a universal negative major premise and a universal affirmative minor premise yield a universal negative conclusion, as: No one disturbed by reason uses reason well; every wise man uses reason well; therefore no wise man is disturbed.

units.la: Locus est ex proprio: cuius hoc firmamentum est, Quod proprio non conuenit, speciei non conuenit. Nam propositio repugnantium ratione animatur: assumptio proprij. Repugnat autem sapientem esse, & non bene ratione uti.
units.tr: The place is from the property, and its foundation is this: what does not belong to the property does not belong to the species. For the major premise is grounded in the repugnance of the terms, and the minor in the property. Now it is incompatible for a wise man to be someone who does not use reason well.

units.la: Quis est secundus? Cùm ex conuersis superioribus propositionibus conuersa conclusio efficitur. Sola enim propositionum inuersione à superiore discrepat. veluti, Ca Omnis Tyrannus est crudelis 1 mef Nullus vir bonus est crudelis 2 4 tres Nullus vir bonus est Tyrannus. 3
units.tr: What is the second mode? When a converted conclusion is produced from the converted premises above. For it differs from the previous mode only by the inversion of the propositions, as: Every tyrant is cruel; no good man is cruel; therefore no good man is a tyrant.

units.la: Locus est ex Repugnantibus, cuius hoc firmamentum est: Quod uni Repugnantium convenit, alteri non convenit. Nam propositionem proprij affectio continet: assumptionem repugnantia.
units.tr: The place is from repugnants, and its foundation is this: what belongs to one of two repugnant things does not belong to the other. For the major premise contains the affection of the property, and the minor the repugnance.

units.la: Quis est Tertius? Cùm ex propositione universali negativa, & assumptione particulari affirmativa, sequitur cóclusio particularis negativa: veluti · Fe Nulli sapientes secum ipse diffident 1 fti Quidam Philosophi secum ipsi diffident 2 4 no Quidam igitur Philosophi non sunt sapientes. 3
units.tr: What is the third mode? When a universal negative major premise and a particular affirmative minor premise yield a particular negative conclusion, as: No wise men distrust themselves; some philosophers distrust themselves; therefore some philosophers are not wise.

units.la: Locus est ex genere: cuius hoc firmamentum est, Quod generi repugnat, id speciei quoque repugnat. Nam propositio est ex repugnantibus: assumptio ex genere.
units.tr: The place is from the genus, and its foundation is this: what is repugnant to the genus is repugnant to the species as well. For the major premise is from repugnants, and the minor from the genus.

units.la: Quis est Quartus? Cùm ex propositione universali affirmativa, & assumptione particulari negativa, particularis negativa conclusio sequitur. veluti, Ba Omnis sapiens virtute contentus est 1 ro Quidam Philosophi virtute conten-ti non sunt 2 4 co Quidã igitur Philosophi sapientes nō sunt. 3 Locus est ex Repugnantibus, cuius hoc firmamentum est. Quod uni convenit, alteri non convenit. propositio est ex proprio, assumptio ex repugnantibus.
units.tr: What is the fourth mode? When a particular negative conclusion follows from a universal affirmative major premise and a particular negative minor premise, as: Every wise man is content with virtue; some philosophers are not content with virtue; therefore some philosophers are not wise. The place is from repugnants, and its foundation is this: what belongs to one does not belong to the other. The major premise is from the property, the minor from repugnants.

units.la: De sex tertiæ figuræ Modis. CAP. VII.
units.tr: On the Six Modes of the Third Figure. CHAPTER VII.

units.la: Q[?]uot sunt modi tertiæ figuræ? Sex. quorum primus est cum ex propositione & assumptione universalibus affirmativis, particularis affirmativa conclusio conficitur. Da Omnes fœnatores sunt auari 2 rap Omnes fœnatores sunt pecuniosi 1 3 ti Aliquis igitur pecuniosus est auarus. 4
units.tr: How many modes are there of the third figure? Six. The first is when a universal affirmative major premise and a universal affirmative minor premise yield a particular affirmative conclusion. For example: All moneylenders are greedy. All moneylenders are wealthy. Therefore some wealthy men are greedy.

units.la: Locus est ex causa sine qua non, cuius hoc firmamentum est: A quo abest causa sine qua non, ab eo abest effectus necesse est. Propositio est ex proprio, assumptio ex causa.
units.tr: The topic is from a cause without which not, and its foundation is this: From that which lacks a cause without which not, the effect necessarily also lacks. The major premise is from the proper, the minor from the cause.

units.la: Quis est Secundus? Cùm ex propositione universali negativa, & assumptione universali affirmativa, particularis & negativa conclusio sequitur. veluti, Fe Nullus filiusfa.est sui iuris 2 lap Omnis filiusfa.est liber 1 3 ton Ergo non omnis liber est sui iuris. 4
units.tr: What is the second? When a universal negative major premise and a universal affirmative minor premise yield a particular negative conclusion. For example: No son under power is sui iuris. Every son is free. Therefore not every free man is sui iuris.

units.la: Locus est ex specie ad genus, cuius hoc firmamentum est: Quod speciei convenit, generi convenit. Propositio est ex consequentibus: assumptio ex specie.
units.tr: The topic is from species to genus, and its foundation is this: What belongs to the species belongs to the genus. The major premise is from consequents; the minor from the species.

units.la: Quis est Tertius? Cùm ex propositione particulari affirmativa, assumptione universali affirmatiua particularis affirmatiua conclusio sequitur.veluti, Di Aliquis fœnerator est improbus 5 2 fa Omnis fœnerator est pecuniosus 2 1 3 mis Aliquis ergo pecuniosus est improbus. 4 5
units.tr: What is the third? When a particular affirmative major premise and a universal affirmative minor premise yield a particular affirmative conclusion. For example: Some moneylender is dishonest. All moneylenders are wealthy. Therefore some wealthy man is dishonest.

units.la: Locus est ex caussa fine qua non: cuius idé firmamentum, est quod paulo ante commemorauimus. Propositio sumitur ex adiunctis: assumptio ex caussa.
units.tr: The topic is from a cause without which not, and its foundation is the one we mentioned a little earlier. The major premise is taken from accidents; the minor from the cause.

units.la: Quis est quartus? Cùm ex propositione vniuersali affirmatiua, assumptione particularis affirmatiua cóclusio conficitur. qui modus à tertio sola propositionum disposition discrepat.veluti, Da Omnis fœnerator est improbus 5 2 ti Aliquis fœnerator est pecuniosus 2 1 3 fi Ergo aliquis pecuniosus est improbus. 4 5
units.tr: What is the fourth? When a universal affirmative major premise and a particular affirmative minor premise yield a conclusion. This mode differs from the third only in the arrangement of the premises. For example: All moneylenders are dishonest. Some moneylender is wealthy. Therefore some wealthy man is dishonest.

units.la: Locus & firmamëtum eiusdem modi quē proximè exposuimus.
units.tr: The topic and foundation are of the same kind as those we have just set out.

units.la: Quis est quintus? Cùm ex propositione particulari negatiua, assumptione vniuersali affirmatiua, particularis negatiua conclusio colligitur.veluti, Bo Aliquis mercator non est improbus 2 1 car Omnis mercator est pecuniosus 1 5 3 do Aliquis igitur pecuniosus non est improbus 4 5
units.tr: What is the fifth? When a particular negative major premise and a universal affirmative minor premise yield a particular negative conclusion. For example: Some merchant is not dishonest. Every merchant is wealthy. Therefore some wealthy man is not dishonest.

units.la: Locus est ex caussa fine qua non. Propositio verò ex accidenti.
units.tr: The topic is from a cause without which not. The major premise, however, is from an accident.

units.la: Quis est sextus? Cùm ex propositione vniuersali negatiua, assumptione particulari af-firmatiua, particularis negatiua conclusio efficitur.veluti: Fe Nullus sapiens est improbus {2 ri Aliquis sapiens est pecuniosus {1 3 son Non omnis igitur pecuniosus est 4 } improbus.
units.tr: What is the sixth? When a universal negative major premise and a particular affirmative minor premise yield a particular negative conclusion. For example: No wise man is dishonest. Some wise man is wealthy. Therefore not every wealthy man is dishonest.

units.la: Locus est ex Accidenti: firmamentum propositionis ex Repugnantibus.
units.tr: The topic is from accident; the foundation of the major premise is from incompatibles.

units.la: De Syllogismo copulato, & primùm de figuris conditionalis.
units.tr: On the Copulated Syllogism, and first on the figures of the conditional.

units.la: CAP. VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: VIp[?] sequitur nunc? Quoniam ad mediocrē Dialecticę cognitionem satis de puro & simplici Syllogismo dictum est, vt deinceps de hypothetico siue copulato differamus. Est autem Syllogismus copulatus, Oratio quæ ex hypothetica propositionis, parte altera, eîve opposita, partem alteram eîve oppositam cócludit. Quoniam autē vis omnis huius syllogismi in superiore inest, neque tantus ipsius est vsus, vt eum Aristoteles tractatione fit dignatus (omnes enim suos syllogismos Aristoteles ex simplicibus pronuntiatis confecit, nullos ex disiunctionibus & coniunctionibus) modicè nos quoque genus hoc disputationis attingemus.
units.tr: What follows now? Since enough has been said about the pure and simple syllogism for an intermediate knowledge of dialectic, we shall go on to treat the hypothetical or conjunctive syllogism. A conjunctive syllogism is an argument which, from a hypothetical proposition, concludes one part, or the opposite of one part, from the other part, or the opposite of the other. But since all the force of this syllogism lies in the earlier one, and since its use is not so great that Aristotle thought it worthy of treatment (for Aristotle built all his syllogisms from simple propositions, and none from disjunctions and conjunctions), we too shall touch on this kind of reasoning only briefly.

units.la: Quotuplex est Syllogismus copulatus? Triplex : ex conditione , disiunctione , & coniunctione.Atque hic nimirum est,de quo tam valde & tam sæpe Cicero commemorat:cuius logè plurimæ(vt superius diximus) argumentationes magis Stoicæ sunt , quàm Aristotelicæ.
units.tr: How many kinds of conjunctive syllogism are there? Three: from a conditional, from a disjunction, and from a conjunction. This is certainly the one of which Cicero speaks so often and so emphatically, and most of whose arguments, as we said above, are more Stoic than Aristotelian.

units.la: Quot sunt figuræ Syllogismi conditionalis? Tres:quarum prima est cùm propositionis conditionalis affirmatiuæ vel ponitur antecedēs, vt consequens ponatur : vel negatur antecedens,vt consequens negetur.Appellant autem Dialectici(inquit Cicero) eam conclusionem argumenti,in qua cùm primum sumpseris, consequitur id quod connexum est, primum conclusionis modum.veluti : Si sol lucet,dies est. sol autem lucet. dies est igitur. Ipsa enim ratio connexi(vt ait alio loco Cicero)cùm concesseris superius,cogit inferius concedere.Posterioris autem hoc exemplum est . Si sol non lucet,dies non est. sol autem non lucet. dies igitur non est.
units.tr: How many figures does the conditional syllogism have? Three. The first is when, in an affirmative conditional proposition, the antecedent is affirmed so that the consequent is affirmed, or the antecedent is denied so that the consequent is denied. Dialecticians (says Cicero) call the form of argument in which, once you have granted the first part, the connected part follows, the first mode of conclusion. For example: If the sun is shining, it is day; the sun is shining; therefore it is day. For the nature of the connection (as Cicero says elsewhere) forces you, once you have conceded the first, to concede the second. An example of the latter is: If the sun is not shining, it is not day; the sun is not shining; therefore it is not day.

units.la: Quæ est secunda? Cùm propositionis conditionalis vel affirmatiuæ negatur consequens, vt antecedens negetur : vel negatiuæ consequens affirmatiuè pronûtiatur, vt antecedens ponatur.veluti:si sol lucet,dies est:non est autem dies:sol igitur non lucet.Item : Si sol non lucet,dies non est.Est autem dies. sol igitur lucet. Vtranque figurâ Cicero lib. de Diuinatione 2.coniunxit : Si dij sunt , est diuinatio, sunt autem dij. est ergo diuinatio. Multo est probabilius: Nó est autem diuinatio:nō sunt dij. ergo dij. Nam cùm id quod annexū est negaris,vt id quoque cui fuerit annexum,negetur, secundus appellatur concludendi modus: inquit Cicero in Topicis. In lib. autem de Finib. 4.Huius conclusionis firmamentum hoc profert: Docent (inquit) Dialectici, si ea quæ rem aliquam consequantur, falsa sint, falsam illam ipsam esse quam sequantur. Ita fit illa conclusio non solùm vera, sed ita perspicua, vt Dialectici ne rationem quidem reddi putét oportere. Si illud, hoc: non autem hoc: ne illud quidé. Et paulo post: Teneamus enim illud necesse est, cùm consequens aliquod falsum est, illud cuius id consequens sit, non posse esse verum. Ex eodem genere illa Ciceronis conclusio est: Si pares sunt omnes virtutes, paria etiam omnia vitia sunt. Non sunt autem vitia paria, neç virtutes igitur.
units.tr: What is the second figure? When the consequent of an affirmative conditional proposition is denied, so that the antecedent is denied; or when the consequent of a negative conditional is affirmed, so that the antecedent is affirmed. For example: If the sun is shining, it is day; but it is not day; therefore the sun is not shining. Likewise: If the sun is not shining, it is not day; but it is day; therefore the sun is shining. Cicero, in the second book of the De Divinatione, combined both forms: If there are gods, there is divination; but there are gods; therefore there is divination. Much more probable is this: But there is no divination; therefore there are no gods. For when what is attached is denied, so that what it was attached to is also denied, this is called the second mode of concluding, says Cicero in the Topics. In the fourth book of the De Finibus he offers the following support for this conclusion: Dialecticians teach (he says) that if the things which follow from something are false, then that from which they follow is itself false. Thus that conclusion is not only true but so evident that dialecticians think it unnecessary to give any reason for it. If the first, then the second; but not the second; nor therefore the first. And a little later: For we must hold that when some consequence is false, that of which it is the consequence cannot be true. Of the same kind is Cicero's conclusion: If all virtues are equal, then all vices are also equal. But the vices are not equal; nor therefore the virtues.

units.la: Quæ est tertia? Cùm propositionis conditionalis negatiuę sumitur antecedens, vt tollatur consequês. veluti: Non & sol lucet, & dies non est. Sol autem lucet. Non igitur dies non est. Nam cùm aliqua coniuncta negaris, & his alia negatio rursus adiungitur: & ex his primum sumpseris, vt quod relinquitur tollendum sit:istertius[?] appellatur conclusionis modus: inquit Cicero in Topicis. Ubi meminisse illud te oportet, quod superius monuimus, quo loco Cicero hæc tractat, quamuis Antecedentia, Consequëtia, & Repugnantia nominet, tamen non quasi argumentorum locos, sed tanquam eorū tractandorū formam & ratiotionem exponi. quod ipse quoque disputationis illius initio his profitetur verbis: Cùm tripartitò distribuatur locus hic, reperiendi argumenti locus simplex est, tractandi triplex.
units.tr: What is the third figure? When the antecedent of a negative conditional proposition is assumed so that the consequent is removed. For example: It is not the case that both the sun is shining and it is not day; but the sun is shining; therefore it is not the case that it is not day. For when some conjoined things are denied, and another negation is added to them, and you assume the first of these so that what remains must be removed, this is called the third mode of conclusion, says Cicero in the Topics. Here you must remember what we noted above, that in the passage where Cicero treats these matters, although he names Antecedents, Consequents and Incompatibles, these are not set out as places of arguments but as the form and method of treating them. He himself professes this at the beginning of that discussion in these words: Since this topic is divided into three parts, the place for finding an argument is single, while the handling of it is threefold.

units.la: De Syllogismo disiunctiuo. CAP. IX.
units.tr: De Syllogismo disiunctiuo. CAP. IX.

units.la: EINCEPS de disiunctione videamus. Quotuplex est syllogismus disiunctiuus? duplex. Nā aut duabus tantùm partibus constat, aut pluribus. verùm ille proprie dicitur per disiunctionem tractari, hic verò per partium enumerationem. Rursus syllogismus disiunctiuus duplex est. nam aut ad partem alterutram vel confirmādam, vel refellendam adhibetur: aut ad vtranque. Atque hic posterior proprie Dilemma nominatur.
units.tr: Next let us consider disjunction. How many kinds of disjunctive syllogism are there? Two. For it either consists of only two parts or of more. The former is properly said to be treated by disjunction, the latter by enumeration of its parts. Again, the disjunctive syllogism is of two kinds. For it is used either to confirm or to refute one of the alternatives, or else to deal with both. This latter is properly called the dilemma.

units.la: Quot sunt figurae syllogismi disiunctiui? Duę·quarum prior est, cùm propositionis disiunctiuę altera pars sumitur, vt altera tollatur. Nam in disiunctione plus vno verum esse non potest. Atque hic quartus connexę conclusionis modus appellatur. veluti, Aut stat, aut mouetur. Stat autem, non mouetur igitur. Sic enim (vt Cicero scribit) Dialectici statuunt, omne quod ita disiunctum sit, quasi aut etiā, aut non, non modò verum esse, sed etiam necessarium. & lib. de Nat. deor. r.[?] In omnibus disiunctionibus, in quibus, aut etiam, aut non ponerctur[?] retur, alterutrum verum esse.
units.tr: How many figures does the disjunctive syllogism have? Two. The first is when one part of a disjunctive proposition is taken so that the other is removed, for in a disjunction only one part can be true. This is called the fourth mood of the connected conclusion. For example: Either it stands or it moves. It stands; therefore it does not move. For thus (as Cicero writes) the dialecticians hold that everything disjoined in the form "either it is or it is not" is not only true but necessary. And in the book On the Nature of the Gods: in all disjunctions in which "either... or not" is set down, one of the alternatives is true.

units.la: Quæ est secunda? Cùm propositionis disiunctiuæ altera pars tollitur, vt altera ponatur: qui copulatæ conclusionis quintus est modus. veluti: Numerus aut par est, aut impar. Impar autem hic non est. Par est igitur.
units.tr: What is the second? When one part of a disjunctive proposition is removed so that the other is posited. This is the fifth mood of the conjoined conclusion. For example: A number is either even or odd. But this one is not odd. Therefore it is even.

units.la: Quodnam huius est axioma? In syllogismo disiunctiuo necesse est alterum ex duobus quæ disiungūtur verum, alterum falsum esse. Nam eæ demum disiunctiones ad has conclusiones valent, quæ ex iis contrariis sumuntur, quæ neque medium habent, & quorum alterutrum esse necesse est: de quibus suo loco diximus. velut illa quæ modò posuimus. Item illud: Aut dormit, aut vigilat. Aut cœlebs est, aut maritus. Omne animal aut agit, aut patitur. Itaque si inter diem & noctem est diluculum, vulgata conclusio non valeret: Aut dies est, aut nox est. Illa autem perspicuè vitiosa est, Aut stat, aut sedet. potest enim cubare. quod neutrum est. Aut albʾ est, aut niger. potest enim fuscus esse: qui est vtriusque particeps. Aut mas est, aut fœmina. Potest enim esse hermaphroditus. Item, mulier est aut pulchra, aut deformis. Potest enim stata esse forma.
units.tr: What is the axiom of this syllogism? In a disjunctive syllogism it must be that one of the two things disjoined is true and the other false. For those disjunctions hold for these conclusions which are taken from contraries that have no middle and of which one of the two must necessarily be the case; about these we spoke in their proper place, as with the examples just put forward. Likewise this: Either he sleeps or he is awake. Either he is unmarried or he is married. Every animal either acts or is acted upon. So if there is dawn between day and night, the usual conclusion would not hold: Either it is day or it is night. But that one is plainly faulty: Either he stands or he sits, for he can lie down, which is neither. Either he is white or black, for he can be dusky, which partakes of both. Either he is male or female, for he can be a hermaphrodite. Likewise: a woman is either beautiful or ugly, for she can be of middling appearance.

units.la: De figuris Syllogismi coniunctiui. CAP. X.
units.tr: On the figures of the conjunctive syllogism. CHAPTER X.

units.la: I[?]NTEQVAM dealiis disiunctiuis differamus, locum hunc de Copulato syllogismo absolui oportet. Quot sunt figurae coniunctiui syllogismi? Duæ:quarum prior est cùm propositionis conexæ negatiuæ altera pars sumitur, vt altera tollatur:qui sextus numeratur modus. veluti, Non & dies & nox est. at nox non est. dies est igitur.
units.tr: Before we turn to the other disjunctives, this discussion of the copulative syllogism must be finished. How many figures does the conjunctive syllogism have? Two. The first is when one part of a negative conjunctive proposition is taken so that the other is removed; this is counted as the sixth mood. For example: "It is not the case that both day and night exist. But night does not exist. Therefore day exists."

units.la: Quæ est secunda? Cùm propositionis conexæ negatiuæ altera pars tollitur, vt altera ponatur. qui septimus censetur modus. veluti.
units.tr: What is the second? When one part of a negative conjunctive proposition is removed, so that the other is posited. This is counted as the seventh mood. For example:

units.la: Terra non & grauis est, & leuis.
units.tr: The earth is not both heavy and light.

units.la: At non est leuis. grauis est igitur.
units.tr: But it is not light. Therefore it is heavy.

units.la: Nam hic syllogismus ex coniunctionum negantia conficitur.
units.tr: For this syllogism is formed from the negating of conjunctions.

units.la: In quibus contrariis coniunctiuus syllogismus valet? In iis quæ neque medium habent, & quorum vtrunque verum esse non potest: sed quorum vno sumpto vel negato, alterum vel tollitur, vel sequitur. veluti: Non & vigilat, & dormit. At quæ sunt huiusmodi, vt vel eorū vtrunque verū esse possit, vel vtrunque simul & neutrum, non valet. Itaque longè difsimilis disiunctiui & coniunctiui syllogismi ratio est.
units.tr: With what kinds of contraries does the conjunctive syllogism hold? With those that have no middle, and of which both cannot be true; but of which, when one is taken or denied, the other is either removed or follows. For example: Not both is he awake and is he asleep. But where the terms are of such a kind that both may be true, or both at once and neither, it does not hold. So the reasoning of the disjunctive and the conjunctive syllogism is very different.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Vera illa disiunctiua est: Omne animal aut facit,aut patitur. At hæc coniunctiua non valet: Non & agit,& patitur. Potest enim facere & pati simul: vt ait Proculus Iurisconsultus. Similiter illa vitiosa est, Non & aspectus est, & cæcitas. Lippitudo enim interiecta est. Item illa: Non & mas & fœmina est. Potest enim hermaphroditus esse. Non & terrenum animal est, & aquatile. potest enim esse anceps.
units.tr: Give an example. That disjunctive is true: Every animal either acts or is acted upon. But this conjunctive does not hold: Not both does it act and suffer. For it can act and suffer at the same time, as the jurist Proculus says. Likewise that one is faulty: Not both is he seeing and blind; for a bleariness lies between. Also that one: Not both male and female is it. For it can be a hermaphrodite. Not both land animal and water animal is it; for it can be amphibious.

units.la: De Dilemmate. CAP. XI.
units.tr: On the Dilemma. CHAP. XI.

units.la: EINCEPS de Dilémate videamus. Quid est dilemma? Conclusio, per quam ex duobus propositis, utrum aduersarius vel concesserit, tollitur: vel negarit,confirmatur . Itaque & ad confirmandum , & ad refellendum valet. Atque ex necessariarum conclusionum numero est. nā si vera est, reprehendi non potest: & ea demū vera est,quæ neque conuersione, neque partis infirmatione reprehendi potest. Verbum ex δὶς & λαμβάνειν[?] fictum est: quoniam ambæ species utrinque sic collocantur, ut elabi adversarius quasi circumuentus non possit. qua de causa Cicero Complexionem illam appellat. nam quocunque se adversarius verterit, tenetur. Itaque ad hanc conclusionem illud Ciceronis in Verrina Diuinatione pertinet, ubi de Q. Hortensio loquitur: Quoties ille tibi potestatem optionémque facturus sit, ut eligas utrum velis: factum esse, necné: verum esse, an falsum: utrum dixeris,id contra te futurum.
units.tr: Next, let us look at the dilemma. What is a dilemma? It is a conclusion drawn from two propositions, such that whichever of them the opponent has either granted, it is overturned, or has denied, it is confirmed. So it serves both to confirm and to refute. It also belongs to the class of necessary conclusions, for if it is true it cannot be censured; and a conclusion is true only when it can be censured neither by conversion nor by weakening one of its parts. The word is formed from the Greek words meaning "twice" and "taking" [δὶς λαμβάνειν], because both alternatives are set up on either side in such a way that the opponent, as if surrounded, cannot slip away. For this reason Cicero calls it the complexio. Whichever way the opponent turns, he is held fast. Accordingly, Cicero's words in the Divinatio against Verres apply to this kind of conclusion, where he speaks of Quintus Hortensius: "Whenever he is about to give you the power and choice of selecting whether you wish that a thing has happened or not, that it is true or false: whatever you say, it will turn against you."

units.la: Cedo exemplū veri dilemmatis. Si quis Cæsari insidiatur, est aut ex amicis, aut ex inimicis. At neque ex amicis, neque ex inimicis quisquam insidiatur. nullus igitur insidiatur. quo argumento Cicero in ea pro Marcello est usus. Sic, Si ciuis est, aut natus est, aut factus. at neque factus, neque natus est. non est igitur ciuis. Simile illud est in Academicis: Quodcunque videtur, id aut falsum est, aut verum. at neque verum, neque falsum potest percipi. nullum igitur est visum, quod percipi possit. Item illud in lib.de Diuin.2. Si prouideri nihil potest futurum esse eorum quæ casu fiunt, quia esse certè nō possunt, diuinatio nulla est. Sin autem iccirco possunt prouideri, quia certa sunt & fatalia: rursus diuinatio nulla est. eam enim tu fortuitarum rerum esse dicebas.
units.tr: Give me an example of a true dilemma. If anyone lies in wait for Caesar, he is either a friend or an enemy. But no friend and no enemy lies in wait for him. Therefore no one lies in wait for him. Cicero used this argument in his speech for Marcellus. Likewise: If someone is a citizen, he was either born one or made one. But he was neither made one nor born one. Therefore he is not a citizen. Similar is the argument in the Academica: Whatever seems to be, is either false or true. But nothing can be perceived as either true or false. Therefore there is no appearance that can be perceived. Likewise that passage in the second book of On Divination: If nothing that happens by chance can be foreseen, because such things certainly cannot be, there is no divination. But if they can be foreseen because they are fixed and fated, then again there is no divination, for you were saying that it concerns fortuitous things.

units.la: Quod est dilemma vitiosum? Vitium dilemmatis est triplex: in vtraque parte, in alterutra duntaxat, aut in pluribus. In vtraque vitiū est, cùm per cōuerfionem retorqueri potest: hoc est, cùm eadem disiunctione id affirmatur, quod erat eadem disiunctione negatum. quod reprehensionis genus est acutifsimum. In alterutra verò, cùm alterutra pars infirmatur. In pluribus, cùm pro pluriū partium disiunctione duæ tantummodo expofitæ sunt.
units.tr: What makes a dilemma faulty? The fault of a dilemma is threefold: it lies either in both parts, in one part only, or in more than two parts.
