There is a fault in both parts when the dilemma can be turned back by conversion, that is, when the same disjunction affirms what the same disjunction had denied. This is the sharpest kind of refutation. The fault lies in one part when that one part is weakened. It lies in the number of parts when, of the several parts of the disjunction, only two have been set out.

units.la: Cedo exemplum conuersionis. Sumatur illud Ennij éx Herennianæ Rhetoric.lib.II.
units.tr: Give me an example of conversion. Take the passage of Ennius from the Rhetorica ad Herennium, book 2.

units.la: Iniuria abste[?] afficior indigna.pater. Nam si improbum Trefphontem existimaueras, Cur me huic locabas nuptiis? sin est probus; Cur talem inuitam inuitum cogis linquere?
units.tr: I am wronged by you, father, in an unworthy way. For if you thought Tresphontes wicked, why did you give me in marriage to him? But if he is upright, why do you force me, unwilling, to leave one who is unwilling?

units.la: Huic dilemmati vitioso Pater ita ex cōtrario respondet,
units.tr: To this faulty dilemma the father replies in the opposite way:

units.la: Nulla te indigna nata afficio iniuria. Si probus est,bene locaui:sin est improbus, Diuortio te liberabo incommodis.
units.tr: I do you no unworthy wrong, my daughter. If he is upright, I have married you well; but if he is wicked, I will free you from the trouble by divorce.

units.la: Cedo exemplum partis infirmatæ. Sumatur ex eodem:Nam ad illud vitiosum:
units.tr: Give me an example of a weakened part. Take it from the same passage, namely the faulty one:

units.la: Nam si improbum Tresphontem existimaras, Cur me huiclocabas nuptiis? Duxi probum. Erraui,post cognoui,& fugio cognitum.
units.tr: For if you thought Tresphontes wicked, why did you give me to him in marriage? I took him to be upright. I was mistaken; afterwards I came to know him, and I flee from what I know.

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplum de conuersione. Nō est ducenda uxor : quoniam uxore mortua, in luc-tum:liberis mortuis, in orbitatem incidimus.imo est ducenda: quia uxore mortua, ex liberis solatium capitur: mortuis liberis, ex coniuge.Extat etiam apud Gellium lib.9.cap. ult. ubi lex hæc proponitur : Vir fortis præmio quod optauerat donetur. Qui fortiter fecerat, petiit alterius uxorē in matrimonium, & accepit.Is deinde cuius ea uxor fuerat, fortiter fecit. repetit eandem. Dilemma est actoris. Si placet lex,redde : si non placet, reddo. Conuersio defensoris : Si placet lex, non reddo : si non placet,non reddo. Cùm autem hoc sit acutissimum argumentum, falli certè absurdissimè videntur, qui hanc conuersionem ad Sophismata retulerunt.
units.tr: Give me another example of conversion. One should not take a wife: for if the wife dies, we fall into mourning; if the children die, into bereavement. Rather one should take a wife: for if the wife dies, solace is found in the children; if the children die, in the spouse. There is also the passage in Gellius, book 9, final chapter, where this law is set out: "A brave man shall be given as a reward the thing he had desired." A man who had acted bravely asked for another man's wife in marriage and received her. Then the man whose wife she had been also acted bravely and demands her back. The dilemma is the plaintiff's: "If the law stands, give her back; if it does not stand, I give her back." The conversion by the defendant: "If the law stands, I do not give her back; if it does not stand, I do not give her back." Since this is a most acute argument, those who have counted this conversion among the sophisms seem to me to be wholly mistaken.

units.la: Cedo item aliud. Sumatur illud ex eodem Gellio lib. 5. cap. 10. Quod etiam vulgò inter Sophismata referri solet. Euathlus adolescés, diues, eloquentiæ discendæ, causarúmque orandi cupiens fuit. Is in disciplinam Protagorae sese dedit:datur úmque promisit mercedem, grandé pecuniam, quantam Protagoras petiuerat. dimidiúmque eius dedit iam tunc statim prius, quàm disceret. Pepigítque ut reliquum dimidium daret, quo primo die causam apud iudices oraret & vicisset. Post-ea, quû diutius auditor affectatórque Protagorae fuisset: & in studio quidem facundiæ abundè promouisset: causas tamen non reciperet, tempúsque iam longum transcurreret, & facere id videretur, ne reliquum mercedis daret: consilium capit Protagoras, ut tum existimabat, astutû. Petere instítit ex pa&o mercedem. litem cum Euathlo contestatur. Etcû ad iudices coniiciendæ consistendæque causæ gratia venisset, tum Protagoras sic exorsus est: Disce, inquit, stultissimè adolescens utroque id modo fore, ut reddas quod peto, siue contra te pronuntiatum erit, siue pro te. Nam si contra te lis data erit, merces mihi ex sententia debebitur, quia ego vicero. Sin verò secundum te iudicatum erit, merces mihi ex pa &o debebitur, quia tu viceris. Ad ea respondit Euathlus: Potui, inquit, huic tuæ tam ancipiti captioni isse obuiam, si verba non ipse facerem, sed alio patrono uterer. Sed maius mihi in ista victoria proludium est: cum te non in causa tantùm, sed in argumento quoque isto vinco. Disce igitur, tu quoque magister sapientissime, utroque modo fieri, ut non reddam quod petis: siue contra me pronuntiatum fuerit,siue pro me. Nam si iudices pro caussa mea senserint, nihil tibi ex sententia debebitur: quia ego vicero. Sin contra me pronuntiauerint, nihil tibi ex pacto debebo: quia ego non vicero. Tum iudices dubiosum hoc,inexplicabiléque esse, quod vtrinque dicebatur, ratione[?] sententia sua vtrancunque in partem dicta esset ipsa sese rescinderet: rem iniudicatam reliquerunt, caussámque in diem longissimam distulerunt. Sic ab adolescente discipulo magister disciplina eloquentiæ inclytus suo sibi argumento confutatus est, & captionis versutè excogitatæ frustratus fuit.
units.tr: Give me another example. Take the one from the same Gellius, book 5, chapter 10, which is also commonly listed among the sophisms. The young man Euathlus, rich and desiring to learn eloquence and the art of pleading causes, gave himself up to the teaching of Protagoras. He promised a reward, a large sum of money, as much as Protagoras had asked, and paid half of it at once, before he began to learn. He agreed to pay the remaining half on the first day on which he pleaded a case before the judges and won it. Afterwards, when he had been a long-time listener and admirer of Protagoras, and had indeed advanced greatly in the study of eloquence, yet did not accept any cases, and a long time was passing, and he seemed to be doing this so as not to pay the rest of the fee, Protagoras took a plan which he thought clever. He began to demand the fee under the agreement, and brought a lawsuit against Euathlus. When he had come before the judges to begin and join the case, Protagoras began thus: "Learn, most foolish young man, that in either way it will come about that you pay what I ask, whether the verdict is given against you or in your favour. For if the suit is decided against you, the fee will be owed to me under the judgment, because I have won. But if the judgment goes in your favour, the fee will be owed to me under the agreement, because you have won." Euathlus replied to this: "I could have met your so two-edged trap, had I not pleaded myself but used another advocate. But in this victory there is a greater prelude for me: I defeat you not only in the case but in this very argument. So learn, you too, most wise teacher, that in either way it will come about that I do not pay what you ask: whether the verdict is given against me or in my favour. For if the judges have judged in favour of my cause, nothing will be owed to you under the judgment, because I have won. But if they pronounce against me, I owe you nothing under the agreement, because I have not won." Then the judges, judging that this matter, which was argued on both sides, was doubtful and could not be resolved, and that whichever way they gave their verdict, it would undo itself, left the case undecided and postponed the hearing to a very distant day. Thus the master of eloquence, famous for his teaching, was refuted by his young pupil with his own argument, and was foiled by the trap he had cunningly devised.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de vitio in numero partium. Extat apud eundem Gellium lib.5.cap. 12. quo Bias concludebat vxorem non esse ducendam: quia qui habet pulchram, habet κοσμῷ[?]: qui deformen, [illegible, ~6 letters]. At rectè Phauorinus docuit,vitium esse in eo, quod pars omissa est. Potest enim stata & mediocri forma uxor duci.
units.tr: Give me an example of a fault in the number of parts. Gellius, book 5, chapter 12, has an argument of Bias, by which he concluded that a wife should not be taken, because he who has a beautiful wife has [κόσμῳ], and he who has an ugly one [illegible]. But Favorinus rightly taught that the fault lies in the part that has been left out, for a wife of middling and ordinary appearance may be taken.

units.la: De Partium enumeratione.
units.tr: On the Enumeration of the Parts.

units.la: CAP. XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: EQVITVR, opinor, ut de multiplici disiunctione quæ Partium enumeratio appellatur, differamus. Quid est Partium enumeratio? Est formula tractandi loci vel ex speciebus vel ex partibus: cùm aut de genere totóve aut de vna specie, partéve concluditur. id est, vel affirmatur, vel negatur. In quo vitium maximū est, speciem vllam partémve principalem prætermittere.
units.tr: Next, I think, we should discuss the multiple disjunction called the enumeration of parts. What is the enumeration of parts? It is a method of treating a topic either from species or from parts, when something is concluded about the genus or the whole, or about one species or part. That is, it is either affirmed or denied. The greatest fault in it is to omit any principal species or part.

units.la: Quæ sunt Enumerationis regulæ? Eædem prorsus, quas superius in loco ex speciebus ad genus, aut ex partibus ad totum exposuimus, sed illa primaria, quam modò dixi, nequa vel species vel pars idonea prætermittatur. Itaq; illinc assumentur, quæ ad hunc locum pertinebūt. Tantùm illud adscribemus, caussarum coniunctionem & concursum videri ad hunc locum pertinere.
units.tr: What are the rules of enumeration? They are exactly the same as those we set out earlier in the topic from species to genus, or from parts to whole, but with the primary rule I have just mentioned: that no suitable species or part be omitted. So what pertains to this topic will be taken from there. We will add only this: the conjunction and concurrence of causes seems to belong to this topic.

units.la: Quotuplex huius loci vis est? Triplex.nam aut vniuersum cōfirmat, aut vniuersum refellit, aut vnā de omnibus partem remotis ceteris affirmat. Vniuersum auté affirmatur, cùm ex cōiunctis vel formis genus, vel partibus totum concluditur. Quinetiam ex caussis eodem modo concludi eventus potest. Idem refellitur cùm ex iisdem disiunctis & remotis totum remouetur. Pars autem affirmatur, cùm singulis disiunctis & reliquis remotis, una quæ superest, concluditur.
units.tr: How many kinds of force does this topic have? Three. For it either confirms the universal, or refutes the universal, or affirms one part from all of them, with the rest removed. The universal is affirmed when the genus is concluded from the conjoined forms, or the whole from the parts. Indeed, an outcome can be concluded from causes in the same way. The universal is refuted when the whole is removed by the same disjoined and removed items. A part is affirmed when, with each of the disjoined items and the rest removed, the one that remains is concluded.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de affirmatione generis. Sumatur illud ex lib. de divinat.1. Si sunt dii, neque ante declarant hominibus quæ futura sunt, aut non diligunt homines: aut quid euenturum fit, ignorant: aut existimant nihil intereffe hominum scire, quid futurum fit aut non censent esse suæ maiestatis, præsignificare hominibus quę sunt futura:aut ea ne ipsi quidem dij significare possunt. At neque non diligunt nos: sunt enim benefici, generíque hominum amici:neque ignorant ea quæ ab ipsis constituta, & designata sunt: neque nostra nihil interest, scire ea quæ eventura sunt. erimus enim cautiores, si sciemus: neque hoc alienum ducunt maiestate sua: nihil est enim beneficentia præstantius. neque non possunt futura prænoscere. non igitur sunt dij: nec significant futura. Sunt autem dij, significant ergo.
units.tr: Give an example of affirming the genus. Take it from Cicero's book On Divination, book 1: "If there are gods, then either they do not declare beforehand to men what is going to happen, or they do not love men; or they are ignorant of what will come about; or they think it makes no difference to men to know what is going to happen; or they do not think it befitting their majesty to signify beforehand to men what is to come; or the gods themselves cannot signify these things. But they do love us: for they are beneficent and friends to the human race. Nor are they ignorant of those things which have been set and determined by them. Nor is it of no concern to us to know what is going to happen: for we would be more cautious if we knew. Nor do they think it beneath their majesty: for nothing is more excellent than beneficence. Nor can they not foreknow the future. Therefore they are not gods, nor do they signify the future. But they are gods; therefore they signify."

units.la: Cedo exemplum de refutatione generis vniversi. Sumatur illud ex lib. de nat. deorum 3.Omne corpus, aut aër, aut aqua, aut ignis, aut terra est:aut id quod est concretum ex his, aut ex aliqua parte eorum. horum autem nihil est quod non intereat. Nihil igitur sempiternum est.
units.tr: Give an example of refuting the universal. Take it from Cicero's book On the Nature of the Gods, book 3: "Every body is either air, or water, or fire, or earth, or what is composed of these, or of some part of them. But none of these is not perishable. Therefore nothing is everlasting."

units.la: Cedo exemplum de affirmatione Totius. Dixi superius in loco ex partibus regulamhuius affectionis hanc esse:Positis partibus compositis, totum concedi. quare videndum, ut forma & compositio simul adsit: veluti. Si fundamentum est,& parietes, & contignatio, & tectum,& omnia composita:certè est domus. Si & radix est & truncus, & rami,& folia, & omnia forma constent: id est non avulsa, aut excisa sint: certè est arbor.
units.tr: Give an example of affirming the whole. I said above that the rule for this affection in the topic from parts is this: once the composite parts are given, the whole is granted. So we must see that form and composition are both present, for example: If there is a foundation, and walls, and beams, and a roof, and all the composite parts, then certainly there is a house. If there is both root and trunk, and branches, and leaves, and all things hold together in their form, that is, are not torn away or cut out, then certainly there is a tree.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de affirmatione ex caussarum concursu. Superiùs dictum est,ex causfarum omnium concursu & enumeratione ef-sectum concludi. veluti : Si est aqua cum hordeo & lupulo ad potum coćta[?], est ceruisia. Si & acuto ingenio est, & disputandi arte institutus, & in eadem exercitatus, est Dialeċticus[?]. Atque hoc loco sæpe Oratores in conieċturalibus constitutionibus vtuntur: Iurisconsulti in præsumptionibus, veluti in illo Herennij: Aiax in sylua postquàm resciuit, quæ fecisset per insaniam, gladio incubuit. Vlysses interuenit.occisum conspicatur. E corpore cruentum telum educit. Teucer interuenit.cùm fratrem occisum, & inimicum fratris cum gladio cruento videt, capitis arcessit.
units.tr: Give an example of affirmation from the concurrence of causes. It was said above that an effect is concluded from the concurrence and enumeration of all its causes. For example: If there is water mixed with barley and hops for drinking, then it is beer. If someone has a sharp wit and is trained in the art of disputing and practised in it, then he is a dialectician. In this place orators often use this topic in conjectural arguments, and jurists in presumptions, as in that passage of Herennius: After Ajax learned in the woods what he had done through madness, he fell upon his sword. Ulysses comes upon him and sees him dead; he draws the bloody weapon out of the body. Teucer comes in, and when he sees his brother dead and the brother's enemy with a bloody sword, he summons him on a capital charge.

units.la: Cedo exemplum de partis vnius affirmatione. Locus hic aut duarum partium est, aut plurium. de duabus fumatur exemplû illud ex Cluentiana: Sed cùm effet hæc illi proposita conditio, vt aut iustè piéque accusaret, aut acerbè indigneque moreretur: accusare quoquomodo posset, quam illo modo emori maluit. Item: Si constat corruptum illud esse iudiciū,aut ab Habito, aut ab Oppianico corruptū est. si doceo non ab Habito, vinco non ab Oppianico: si ostendo ab Oppianico, purgo Habitum.
units.tr: Give an example of affirming one part. This topic has either two parts or several. From two, take that example from the Pro Cluentio: "But since the condition put to him was that he must either accuse justly and piously, or die bitterly and unworthily, he preferred to accuse in whatever way he could rather than die in that manner." Likewise: "If it is established that the trial was corrupted, it was corrupted either by Habitus or by Oppianicus. If I prove it was not by Habitus, I win by showing it was not by Oppianicus; if I show it was by Oppianicus, I clear Habitus."

units.la: Cedo exemplum de pluribus. Sumatur illud ex Rabiriana: Atqui videmus hæc in rerū naturatria fuisse: vt aut cum Saturnino effet, aut cum bonis,aut lateret. Latere mortis erat instar turpissimæ: cum Saturnino esse furoris & & sceleris: virtus & honestas & pudor eũ cum Consulibus esse cogebat. Item illud ex lib.de Orat.2.Aut Senatui parendum de salute Reip. fuit,aut aliud consilium constituendũ,aut sua sponte faciédum. Aliud consilium superbum, suum arrogans: utendum igitur fuit consilio Senatus.
units.tr: Give an example from several parts. Take that from the Pro Rabirio: "But we see that in the nature of things there were three options for him: to be with Saturninus, or with the good citizens, or to lie hidden. To lie hidden was like a most shameful death; to be with Saturninus was the mark of madness and crime; virtue, honour and shame compelled him to be with the consuls." Likewise that from the book On the Orator, book 2: "Either the Senate had to be obeyed concerning the safety of the Republic, or some other plan had to be adopted, or it had to be done of one's own accord. Another plan is proud, one's own is arrogant; therefore the Senate's plan had to be followed."

units.la: De Enthymemate. CAP. XIII.
units.tr: On the Enthymeme. CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: [?]VONIAM[?] de Syllogismo satis videtur dictum, deinceps ad Enthymema veniamus, in quo locum esse medio superius dixisti. Quid est Enthymema? Argumentatio quæ ex sola propositione, vel assumptione constat. Itaque συλλογισμὸς ἀτελής, id est truncā, mutila, imminuta ratiocinatio ab Aristotele appellatur. Nam in eo medium quidé vi ipsa inest, sed tamen diserte nō apponitur. Dicitur autem ἀπὸ τὸ ἐνθυμεῖσθαι[?] id est cogitare & commentari: unde Commentum à Quintiliano & Commentatio Latinè nominatur.
units.tr: Since enough seems to have been said about the syllogism, let us now come to the enthymeme, in which you said earlier that the middle term has its place. What is an enthymeme? It is an argument consisting of the major premise alone, or of the minor premise alone. Hence Aristotle calls it an incomplete syllogism [συλλογισμὸς ἀτελής], that is, a truncated, maimed, curtailed reasoning. For in it the middle term is indeed present in its force, but it is not expressly stated. It is called from enthymeisthai [ἀπὸ τὸ ἐνθυμεῖσθαι], that is, to think over or to consider; whence in Latin it is called a commentum by Quintilian, and a commentatio.

units.la: Quotuplex est Enthymema? Ego triplex facio. Vulgare, Aristotelicum,& Cicerònianū. Vulgare autem dico ex vulgi opinione, qua Enthymemata nominantur omnes syllogismi trunci:id est, in quibus vel propositio, vel assumptio deest:quæ nos superius argumenta nominari diximus.veluti, Virtus sola res est, qua uti nemo malè potest. Ergo sola virtus est bonum. Addatur propositio:fiet Syllogismus. Id demum bonum est,quo nemo vti malè poteft. Item,Pecunia quisque vti malè potest. Ergo non est bonum. Addita propositione, fiet Syllogismus. Nihil bonū est,quo quisque male vti potest. Item:Sapiens est:ergo est beatus: id est ex loco generis Medium. Omnes sapiētes sunt beati. quo adhibito plenus & perse&tus existet syllogismus.
units.tr: How many kinds of enthymeme are there? I make three: the vulgar, the Aristotelian, and the Ciceronian. I call it vulgar according to common opinion, by which every truncated syllogism is called an enthymeme, that is, one in which either the major or the minor premise is lacking; these we said above are called arguments. For example: Virtue alone is a thing that no one can use badly. Therefore virtue alone is good. Add the major premise and there will be a syllogism: That which no one can use badly is good. Likewise: Anyone can use money badly. Therefore money is not good. Add the major premise and there will be a syllogism: Nothing is good that anyone can use badly. Likewise: He is wise, therefore he is blessed; this is from the topic of the genus. Add the premise: All wise men are blessed, and the syllogism will be complete and perfect.

units.la: Quod est Enthymema Ariftotelicū? Quod conítat ἐκ τῶν ἐνδόξων ἢ συμεῖων[?] : id est, cósentaneis & signis. Consentaneum est, quod adiun&tum probabile, aut verisimile, in locorū tra&tione appellari diximus. Itaque ex loco adiunctorum tota hæc sumitur argumentatio. veluti:Cui quis inuidet,eum odit. Quoniam hic miles est,gloriosus est. Quoniam auarus est, etiam contemptor est iurisiurandi. Quoniam studiosus est,à bello alienus est. Caufla tum dubia(inquit in Ligariana Cicero) quòd erat aliquid in vtraque parte quæ probari pofet:nunc melior ea certè iudicanda est, quam etiam dij adiuuerunt. Et in Lelio : Quam charus ciuitati Scipio fuerit, mœrore funeris indicatum est.
units.tr: What is the Aristotelian enthymeme? It is one that is constructed from [ἐκ τῶν ἐνδόξων ἢ σημείων] probabilities and signs, that is, from what is consistent and from signs. That is consistent which we said, in treating the topics, is attached and probable or likely. Accordingly, this whole kind of argument is taken from the topic of attendant circumstances, for example: Whoever envies someone hates him. Since this man is a soldier, he is glorious. Since he is greedy, he also despises the oath. Since he is studious, he is averse to war. Cicero says in the Pro Ligario: "The case was then doubtful, because there was something on each side that could be proved; now that case is certainly to be judged the better one, which even the gods have helped." And in the Laelius: "How dear Scipio was to the state was shown by the grief at his funeral."

units.la: Quid est,constare ἐκ τῶν σημείων[?] ? Signū est, quod ex eo quod est,aliud quid efle arguit. Est autem aut non necessarium, aut necessarium. quod Græci τεκμήριον vocant. Non neceffariū est,veluti,Si cui celeriter arteria mouetur, febricitat. Si pallet,ægrotat. Si corpus est luridum, dum, veneno interiit. Si puluerulentis est pedibus,redit ex itinere. Si Aegyftus est defidio sus , est adulter. Necessarium autem,fiue τεκ-μηριον est:veluti: Si cicatrix est, fuit vulnus. Si lac habet,peperit . Si vmbra est, corpus est in sole.
units.tr: What does it mean to consist of signs [ἐκ τῶν σημείων]? A sign is that which, from what it is, argues that something else is. It is either not necessary or necessary, which the Greeks call tekmērion [τεκμήριον]. A non-necessary sign is, for example: If someone's pulse beats quickly, he has a fever. If he is pale, he is ill. If his body is livid, he died of poison. If his feet are dusty, he has come back from a journey. If the Egyptian is idle, he is an adulterer. A necessary sign, or tekmērion, is for example: If there is a scar, there was a wound. If she has milk, she has given birth. If there is a shadow, the body is in the sun.

units.la: Quid appellas Enthymema Ciceronianû? Quod cöftat ex sola propositione argumēti ex repugnātibus, quæ detracta negatione cū interrogatione pnunciatur.At quoniā acutissimæ & grauissimę huiusmodi sententiæ sunt, pter commune Enthymematū nomen suū effecerunt.Sed in Topicis Ciceronis,vbi exemplaproponuntur , nota interrogationis omissa est.Hunc metuere, alterum in metu nō ponere?Sic enim Dialecticus protulisset:Non & hunc imbecillum metuere debebas , & illum valentem in metu non ponere. Item:Eam quā nihil accusas,damnas:bene quam meritam esse autumas,dicis malè mereri?Quod ex repugnantium loco ita concluderetur:Non & quæ non accusata est, damnanda est: & quæ bene merita est, malè merita dicenda est. Item : Id quod scis,prodest: nihil id quod nescis,obest? pro,Non & quod scis,prodest:& quod nescis, non obest. Contrariorum enim cōtraria sunt consequentia. Omnes autem illi sunt versus ex vetere Poeta , vt ipse in Oratore ostendit. Vbi postremum hunc oratorio more sic inuertit:Quod scis,nihil prodest: quod nescis,multum obest.Et à Græcis ἐνθυμήματα hæc omnia no minari dicit, cùm contrariis contraria opponuntur : quam Latino vocabulo Relationem contrariorum appellat.
units.tr: What do you call the Ciceronian enthymeme? It is one that consists of a single premise, an argument from opposites, which is pronounced with the negation removed and in the form of a question. But because sentences of this kind are very sharp and weighty, they have made their own name apart from the common name of enthymeme. In Cicero's Topics, where examples are set out, the sign of interrogation has been omitted. "Do you fear this man, and not put that other man in fear?" For the dialectician would have put it thus: "You ought to fear not only this man, who is weak, but also to put that man, who is strong, in fear." Likewise: "You condemn her whom you do not accuse; do you say that she who has deserved well has deserved ill?" This would be concluded from the topic of opposites thus: "She who is not accused ought not to be condemned, and she who has deserved well must not be said to have deserved ill." Likewise: "What you know is useful; what you do not know is not harmful?" For: "What you know is useful, and what you do not know is not harmful." For the consequences of contraries are contrary. All these verses are from an old poet, as he himself shows in the Orator, where he turns the last one in the manner of an orator: "What you know is of no use; what you do not know does great harm." And he says that the Greeks call all these enthymēmata when contraries are set against contraries; this he calls in Latin the relation of contraries.

units.la: Quibus ex locis eruitur Enthymema?Ex iisdem omnibus,ex quibus & perfectus syllogismus. Sed tum demum grauissimum & vehementissimum est, cùm ex contrariis & repugnantibus & minoris comparatione componitur.veluti:Alienum &valentem alis : Parentem senio confectum negligis. Item in Catone maiore : Quod adolescentes, & ij quidem non solùm indocti, sed etiam rustici contemnùt,id doćti senes extimescét?Et Philippica2. Quid indignius, quàm viuere eum qui imposuit diadema: cùm omnes fateantur eum iure interfectum,qui imposuerit.Item inMiloniana:Eius mortis sedetis auctores ,cuius vitam si putetis per vos restitui posse nolitis.Item in eadem:Quem igitur cum omnium gratia noluit,hunc voluit cum aliquorū querela? quem iure,quê loco, quê tépore, quê impunè nô accusas: hûc iniuria,iniquo loco, alieno tépore, cum periculo capitis nô dubitauit occidere? In eodé genere illa sunt : Filiu obsequenté exheredas : alienum heredem instituis. Alienos iuvas:cognatos deseris.Hostibus opitularis,amicos lædis. Peregrinos iuvas:ɔiues[?] negligis. Item illa ex Rhetorum antithetis:Inimicis te placabilem :amicis te inexorabilem præbes. In otio tumultuaris, in tumultu solus es otiosus . Tacito cùm opus est, clamas : cùm loqui conuenit,obmutescis. in pace bellum quæris: in bello pacem desyderas.
units.tr: From what topics is an enthymeme drawn? From all the same topics from which a perfect syllogism is drawn. But it is then most weighty and most forceful when it is composed from contraries, from opposites, and from comparison of the lesser. For example: You neglect a stranger who is strong in arms, and a parent worn out with age. Likewise in the Cato Maior: "Shall learned old men fear what young men, and not only the unlearned but even the rustic, despise?" And in the Second Philippic: "What is more outrageous than that he should live who has put on the diadem, when all admit that he who has put it on has been rightly killed?" Likewise in the Pro Milone: "You are the authors of that death whose life, if you think it could be restored through you, you would not wish restored." Likewise in the same speech: "He whom he wished dead with the good will of all, did he wish dead with the complaint of some? Whom you do not accuse rightly, in the right place, at the right time, with impunity, did he not hesitate to kill unjustly, in an unfit place, at an untimely moment, at the risk of his own life?" In the same kind are these: You disinherit an obedient son and institute a stranger as heir. You help strangers and desert your kinsmen. You aid enemies and injure friends. You help foreigners and neglect your fellow citizens. Likewise these from the antitheses of the rhetoricians: You show yourself gentle to enemies and unyielding to friends. In peace you stir up tumult; in tumult you are idle alone. When silence is needed you shout; when speaking is fitting you fall dumb. In peace you seek war; in war you long for peace.

units.la: De Sorite Dialectico. CAP. XIIII.
units.tr: On the Dialectical Sorites. CHAP. XIIII.

units.la: ACTENVS de Argumentationibus quæ medium habent disseruimus. Deinceps de iis quæ non habent, videamus. Quæ sunt Argumentationes quæ Medium non habent? Sorites, Inductio, & Exemplum.
units.tr: We have now discussed the arguments that have a middle term. Next let us consider those that do not. What are the arguments that have no middle term? The sorites, induction, and the example.

units.la: Quid est Sorites? Argumẽtatio quæ pluribus attributis ordine superimpositis, vel ex primi conuenientia, etiam vltimū conuenire, vel ex postremi discrepantia, etiam primum dissidere cōcludit. Duplex enim gradatio est: vna in ascensu affirmans: altera in descensu, negans: ob eámque caussam à Cicerone Tela Penelopes appellatur: quippe quæ & texatur, & retexatur: hoc est, vicisim retróque commeet, & reciprocetur.
units.tr: What is a sorites? It is an argument which, by ordering several predicates in a series, concludes either that the last belongs to the subject because the first does, or that the first is excluded because the last is. For the sorites is a double gradation: one ascends by affirming, the other descends by denying. For this reason Cicero calls it Penelope's web, since it is both woven and unwoven, that is, it goes back and forth and is run in both directions.

units.la: Cedo aliquod exemplum. Lactantius hoc suppeditat: Si duo sunt sexus deorum, sequitur concubitus.si coeunt, habent domos & cubilia: si domos, etiam vrbes: si vrbes, etiam agros. Si agros non habent, ne vrbes quidē. Si vrbes non habent, ne domos quidem: si domibus carent, & concubitu carent: si concubitus ab his abest: & sexus igitur fœmineus. In diis autem videmus & fœminas esse. ergo dij non sunt. Quod est huius argumentationis firmamentum? Illud quod superiùs ex Aristotele propositum fuimus: Quoties alterum de altero ut de subiecto dicitur, quæcunque deinceps de attributo dicuntur, eadem omnia de subiecto quoque dicuntur. qua regula Soritis vim omnem Aristoteles complexus est: tametsi nusquam in ipsius Logicæ libris nominatim eius fiat mentio. Fuit enim hæc argumentationis forma Stoicorum propria: ut multis ex locis apud Ciceronem intelligitur, quo lubentius fortasse differendi artem Dialecticam interpretatur, quod in Soritis longa verborum series continuatur: sic, ut aliud ex alio nexum & omnia inter se apta colligatáque videantur.
units.tr: Let me give an example. Lactantius supplies this: If the gods are of two sexes, they couple. If they couple, they have homes and beds. If they have homes, they have cities too. If cities, then fields also. If they have no fields, they have no cities either. If they have no cities, they have no homes. If they lack homes, they lack intercourse. If intercourse is absent from them, then their sex is feminine. But we see that there are also goddesses among the gods. Therefore the gods do not exist. What is the foundation of this argument? It is the principle we set out earlier from Aristotle: whenever one thing is said of another as of a subject, whatever is said afterwards of the predicate is also said of the subject. Aristotle embraced the whole force of the sorites under this rule, although his books on Logic nowhere mention it by name. This form of argument was in fact peculiar to the Stoics, as many passages in Cicero make clear; perhaps for that reason he more willingly interprets the art of Dialectic as the art of arguing, since in the sorites a long chain of words runs on, so that one thing seems to follow from another and everything appears linked and fitted together.

units.la: Quotuplex est Sorites? Duplex: Dialecticus, qui & propositionum veritate & legitimo artificio constat: & sophisticus, qui aut à falsitate propositionis, aut ab artificij praetermissione vitiosus est.
units.tr: How many kinds of sorites are there? Two: the dialectical, which rests on both the truth of its premises and sound method; and the sophistical, which is faulty either because a premise is false or because the method has been neglected.

units.la: Unde dicitur Sorites? σωρὸς Graecis est acervus. Itaque ut ex multis granis superadditis fit acervus, sic ex multis subiectis & attributis inter se cofertis & connexis fit Sorites. Est enim argumentatio ex pluribus syllogismis constans: ut non absurdè Catenata dici posse videatur. quoniam ut catena annulis inter se connexis & confertis continetur, sic Sorites propositionibus syllogismorum inter se aptis & connexis conficitur.
units.tr: Why is it called a sorites? The Greeks call a heap [σωρὸς]. Just as a heap is made when many grains are added one upon another, so a sorites is made from many subjects and predicates gathered and connected with one another. For it is an argument made up of several syllogisms, so that it may not unfitly be thought of as a chain, since just as a chain is held together by rings linked and joined to each other, so a sorites is formed from propositions of syllogisms fitted and connected to one another.

units.la: Cedo aliquod exemplum in contexendo, Sumatur ille sextuplex ex Ciceronis libro de Finib.3. Illud perabsurdum est, bonum esse aliquid, quod non expetendum sit. aut expetendum, quod non placens. aut si id, non etiam diligendum. Ergo & probandum. Ita etiam laudabile. Id autem honestum. Ita fit ut quod bonum fit, id etiam honestum fit. Item illud ex lib. Tuscul.5. Anima ex se mouetur, quod ex se mouetur, princi-pium motus est, quod principium motus est, natum non est, quod natū nō est, est immortale. Igitur anima immortalis est. Ex eodem genere illud Themistoclis peruulgatum: qui filiolum suum Græciæ totius potentissimum esse hoc modo concludebat: Athenienses(inquibat)reliquis Græcis imperant. ego Atheniensibus. vxor mihi. ille vxori.
units.tr: Let me give an example of the building-up form. Take that six-membered sorites from Cicero's third book of On Ends: It is most absurd for something to be good which is not to be sought; or to be sought which is not pleasing; or, if it is pleasing, not also to be loved. Therefore it is also to be approved. So also it is praiseworthy. But what is praiseworthy is honourable. Thus it comes about that what is good is also honourable. Likewise that from the fifth book of the Tusculan Disputations: The soul moves itself; what moves itself is the source of motion; what is the source of motion has no beginning; what has no beginning is not generated; what is not generated is immortal. Therefore the soul is immortal. From the same kind is that well-known saying of Themistocles, who used to conclude in this way that his little son would be the most powerful man in all Greece: The Athenians, he said, rule the rest of the Greeks; I rule the Athenians; my wife rules me; my son rules my wife.

units.la: Cedo item aliud. Sumatur illud Ciceronis præclarum, & Christiana philosophia dignū, ex secundo de nat.deor.extremo: Nec verò vniuerso generi hominum solum, sed etiam singulis à diis immortalibus consuli & prouideri solet. licet enim contrahere vniuersitatem generis humani, eamque gradatim ad pauciores, postremo deducere ad singulos. nam si omnibus hominibus qui ubique sunt, Deos consulere censemus, his quoque consulunt, qui has nobiscum terras ab Oriente ad Occidentem colunt: sin autem his consulunt, qui quandam quasi magnam insulam colunt, quam nos orbem terræ vocamus, etiam iis consulunt, qui partes eius insulæ tenent: Europam, Asiam, Asricam[?].Ergo & earum partes diligunt, ut Romam,Athenas,Spartam,Rhodum:& earū urbium separatim ab universis singulos diligunt.
units.tr: Let me also give another. Take that splendid saying of Cicero, worthy of Christian philosophy, from the end of the second book of On the Nature of the Gods: "Nor indeed are the immortal gods accustomed to care for and provide for the human race as a whole only, but also for each single person. For we may contract the whole of mankind, and reduce it gradually to fewer, and finally bring it down to individuals. For if we think that the gods take care of all men who are anywhere, they also take care of those who inhabit these lands of ours from east to west. But if they care for those who inhabit a certain great island, which we call the globe of the earth, they also care for those who hold its parts: Europe, Asia, Africa. Therefore they also love its parts, such as Rome, Athens, Sparta, Rhodes; and they love single persons separately from those cities, apart from the whole."

units.la: Cedo aliud in retexendo exemplum . Summatur ex lib.de Diuinitat.2.Si Deus scit,quid casu & fortuito futurũ sit , certè illud eueniet. si certè eueniet,nulla fortuna est. Est autè fortuna.rerum igitur fortuitarum nulla est præsensio.Sic in lib. de Fato : Si omnia fato fiunt, appetitus in potestate nostra non est.si non appetitus,non assensio. si non assensio,nec actio: si non actio,nec laudatio , aut vituperatio iusta est.Ergo nec honores, nec supplicia. Hoc autem extremum vitiosum est. Ergo fato fieri omnia non possunt. Quod cùm ita fit, vides genus hoc argumenti non satis plenè vulgo appellari A primo ad vltimum : cùm vicissim addendum quoque sit, Ab vltimo ad primum.
units.tr: Let me give an example for the unwinding form. Take it from the second book of On Divination: If God knows what will happen by chance and by fortune, then certainly that will come to pass. If it certainly comes to pass, there is no fortune. But there is fortune. Therefore there is no foreknowledge of chance events. So also in the book On Fate: If all things happen by fate, appetite is not in our power. If not appetite, then not assent. If not assent, then not action. If not action, then neither praise nor blame is just. Therefore neither honours nor punishments are just. But this last conclusion is faulty. Therefore all things cannot happen by fate. Since this is so, you see that this kind of argument is not sufficiently fully named by common usage as "from the first to the last", since it must also be added in turn that it runs "from the last to the first".

units.la: Quid? Aristoteles nihilne prorsus de Sorite tradidit?Soritas quidem nusquā, quod meminerim,nominat : sed eos sanè diligèter tradat,li.1.posteriorum Analyt.cap.15.& aliquot insequentibus : ubi hoc primum statuit, Soritas in iis locum habere, quæ sine ullius medij opera atque interuētu[?], propter se attribuuntur. Deinde in iis subiectis quæ de nullo dicuntur, & in iis attributis summis, de quibus nihil dici atque enuntiari potest : quales funtomnes categoriæ. Tertio quoniam infinita non
units.tr: What then? Did Aristotle say nothing at all about the sorites? As far as I recall, he never names the sorites, but he certainly treats it carefully in the first book of the Posterior Analytics, chapter 15 and several of those that follow. There he first lays down that sorites take place in those things which are predicated of one another without the work or intervention of any middle term. Next, they concern those subjects which are predicated of nothing, and those highest predicates of which nothing can be said or asserted; such are all the categories. Third, since infinite things cannot be run through by the human mind and thought, the heaps of sorites are not infinite; but whether we proceed upward or go back down, still some end and limit is found, and the gradations are contained within a certain and finite number.

units.la: Vnder the page, in the same running text: no footnotes printed. possunt hominum mente & cogitatione percurri, propterea Soritarum aceruos infinitos non esse, sed siue sursum progrediamur, siue rursum descendamus: tamen exitum & finem aliquem reperiri, & gradationes certo & finito numero contineri.
units.tr: can be traversed by the mind and thought of men, so the heaps of the Sorites are not infinite. Whether we proceed upward or go back down again, some exit and end is still found, and the gradations are contained within a certain and finite number.

units.la: Quid est Sorites sophisticus? Loco tu quidem quæris. sed tamen quia certus nobis de sophisticis captionibus locus differendi conftitutus est, commodius videtur hanc quoque tractationem eum in locum differre.
units.tr: What is a sophistical sorites? You ask about a place that is still to come. But since a definite place has been set for us to discuss sophistical captions, it seems more fitting to defer this treatment to that place as well.

units.la: De Inductione & Exemplo. CAP. XV.
units.tr: On Induction and Example. CHAP. XV.

units.la: QVID[?] sequitur nunc? Ut de Inductione & Exemplo differamus: quæ vulgò separatis nominibus appellantur: cùm tamen Exemplum Inductionis speciem esse constet. Exemplum enim imperfecta inductio est.
units.tr: What follows now? Let us discuss Induction and Example, which are commonly called by separate names, although it is agreed that Example is a kind of Induction. For Example is an imperfect induction.

units.la: Quid est inductio? Aristoteles ita definit: Inductio est à rebus singulis ad universas progressio. Potest etiam hoc definiri modo: Argumentatio quæ vel ex omnibus singulis, universum: vel ex pluribus similibus, simile aliquod vel affirmando, vel negando concludit. Eáque argumentatio Socratica vulgò nominatur: quæ ex pluribus collationibus id de quo ambigitur, propter similitudinem concludit.
units.tr: What is induction? Aristotle defines it thus: induction is a progression from single things to universals. It can also be defined in this way: an argument which, either from all the single instances, concludes the universal, or, from several similar cases, concludes something similar, either by affirming or by denying. This argument is commonly called Socratic, because from several comparisons it concludes, on account of the similarity, the point under dispute.

units.la: Quamobrem Inductio medio adhibito nō tractatur? Quia vera inductio iis demum quæstionibus adhibetur, quæ sensibus diiudicantur,& medio carent.eáque re differt à ratiocinatione,quòd illa mentis & rationis conclusio est:hæc verò sensuum, qui rationis expertes sunt. Quanuis enim syllogismi instar tribus propositionibus componi possit, semper tamen inductio manebit: aut certè syllogismus epagogicus dicetur: quasi quis dicat,inductionalis.
units.tr: Why is induction not treated with a middle term? Because true induction is applied only to those questions which are judged by the senses and lack a middle term. For this reason it differs from reasoning: the one is a conclusion of the mind and reason, the other of the senses, which are without reason. Although it can be put together in three propositions like a syllogism, it will still remain induction, or at least it will be called an epagogic syllogism, as if one were to say "inductional."

units.la: Quamobrem Inductio argumentatio Socratica nominatur? Quoniam (vt Cicero & Quintilianus scribunt) ea plurimū est vsus in sermonibus Socrates, propterea quòd nihil ipse afferre ad persuadendū volebat: sed ex eo quod sibi ille dederat, quicum disputabat, aliquid cōficere malebat, quod ille ex eo quod iam concessisset, necessario approbare deberet. Itaque cùm plura interrogasset,quæ fateri aduersario necesse esset, nouissimè id de quo quærebatur inferebat, cui simile concessisset. hoc in ratiocinatione fieri nō potest:sed quod illic interrogatur,hîc fere sumitur.
units.tr: Why is induction called the Socratic argument? Because (as Cicero and Quintilian write) Socrates used it very much in his discourses, since he did not wish to bring anything forward himself to persuade, but preferred to build something out of what his opponent in the debate had granted him, which the other must necessarily approve from what he had already conceded. So when he had asked many questions, which the opponent had to admit, at last he drew the conclusion about the matter under inquiry, to which he had conceded something similar. This cannot be done in reasoning; what is asked there is here generally assumed.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Sunt (inquit Cicero) similitudines, quæ ex pluribus collationibus perveniunt, quò volunt. hoc modo: Si tutor fidem præstare debet, si socius, si cui mandaris, siquis fiduciam acceperit, debet etiam procurator. Ex codē genere illud est Vlpiani Iuriscōsulti: Si filiusfa. tenetur actionibus empti, venditi, locati, conducti, commodati, mandati: certè & depositi tenebitur. Hoc ex pluribus (inquit Cicero) perueniens quò vult, appellatur Inductio quæ Græcè ἐπαγωγὴ[?] nominatur, qua plurimum est vsus in sermonibus Socrates.
units.tr: Give an example. There are (says Cicero) likenesses which, through several comparisons, arrive wherever they wish. In this way: If a guardian ought to keep faith, if a partner, if one to whom something is entrusted, if one who has received a pledge of trust, a procurator ought to do so too. Of the same kind is that of the jurist Ulpian: If a son is liable to the actions of purchase, sale, letting, hiring, loan for use, and commission, he will certainly be liable also to deposit. This argument, arriving by several steps wherever it wishes (says Cicero), is called induction, which in Greek is named epagoge [ἐπαγωγή], and of which Socrates made very great use in his discourses.

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplum. Sumatur illud ex Quintiliano: Quod est pomū generosissimū? nónne quod optimum? concederetur. quid equus? qui generosissimus? nónne qui optimus? Et plura in eundem modum. deinde cuius rei gratia rogatum est. Quid homo? nónne is generosissimus, qui optimus? Eiusdem generis illa sunt, quæ superiùs exposuimus, quibus probatum est nullum imperium esse sempiternum: & religionem Christianam nullis hominum opibus extingui posse.
units.tr: Give another example. Let it be taken from Quintilian: What is the noblest fruit? Is it not the best? This would be conceded. What of a horse? Which is the noblest? Is it not the best? And many more in the same way. Then, for what purpose the question was asked. What of a man? Is he not the noblest who is the best? Of the same kind are those things which we set out above, by which it was proved that no empire is everlasting, and that the Christian religion cannot be extinguished by any resources of men.

units.la: Quotuplex inter Syllogismum & Inductionem differentia est? Aristoteles triplicem hanc statuit. Syllogismus in iis quæ medium habent, consumitur. Inductio verò in iis quæ non habét, & sensibus artis & rationis expertibus iudicantur. Itaque quoniam medium natura notius est eo de quo quæritur, notior quoque natura est ea ratiocinatio quæ per medium efficitur: at inductio apertior ac dilucidior est, sensuúmque iudicio familiarior: ac propterea in ore vulgi frequentior. Alterum discrimé est huiusmodi: Inductio à rebus singulis ad vniuersales progreditur. veluti: Adami vita fuit ærumnosa, fuit & Enochi, fuit & Nohæ: fuit item Abrahami, fuit Isaaci, lacobi, ceterorúmque piorum. Ergo piorum omnium vita infesta & ærumnosa est. Ratiocinatio verò ab vniuersalibus ad singulares perducit. veluti : Piorum omnium vita infesta & calamitosa est. Timotheus pietate colit. Quare Timothei vita erit ærumnosa. Tertium discrimē Aristoteles subtiliter hoc statuit, quòd syllogismus ex medio probat extremum in tertio : inductio verò ab extremo probat tertium in medio.
units.tr: How many kinds of difference are there between syllogism and induction? Aristotle lays down this threefold distinction. A syllogism is completed in those things which have a middle term. Induction, however, is in those things which do not have one, and are judged by the senses, which lack art and reason. Therefore, since the middle is by nature better known than that about which we inquire, the reasoning which is accomplished through the middle is also better known by nature; but induction is more evident and clearer, and more familiar to the judgement of the senses, and for that reason more frequent on the lips of the common people. The second difference is of this kind: induction proceeds from single things to universals, as: The life of Adam was full of hardship; so was that of Enoch, so was that of Noah; likewise that of Abraham, of Isaac, of Jacob, and of the other pious men. Therefore the life of all the pious is troubled and full of hardship. Reasoning, however, leads from universals to singulars, as: The life of all the pious is troubled and calamitous. Timothy cultivates piety. Therefore the life of Timothy will be full of hardship. The third difference Aristotle states subtly: a syllogism proves the extreme in the third through the middle, but induction proves the third in the middle from the extreme.

units.la: Cedo aliquod exemplum. Esto syllogismus huiusmodi: Quæ bile vacant, longæua & viuacia sunt. homo, equus, bos, elephas, asinus, bile vacant. ergo animalia hæc longæua & viuacia sunt. Hic ratiocinatio ex medio, quod est Bile vacant, probat maius extremū, quod est Longæuum, in minore : quod est subiectum. At si hoc concludamus modo : Homo, equus, bos, elephas, asinus, ceteráque bile vacant. hæc autem longæua sunt. quare quæ bile vacant, longæua sunt. tum verò conclusio hæc ex minore extremo, quod est subiectum, probat maius extremum conuenire medio. Atque hoc quidem syllogismi inductionalis exemplū est.
units.tr: Give some example. Let there be a syllogism of this kind: Those things which lack bile are long-lived and lively. Man, horse, ox, elephant, ass lack bile. Therefore these animals are long-lived and lively. Here the reasoning proceeds through the middle, which is "lacking bile," and proves the major extreme, which is "long-lived," of the minor, which is the subject. But if we conclude in this way: Man, horse, ox, elephant, ass, and the others lack bile; these are long-lived. Therefore those which lack bile are long-lived. Then indeed this conclusion, from the minor extreme, which is the subject, proves that the major extreme belongs to the middle. And this is indeed an example of an inductional syllogism.

units.la: Quid? quomodo ab eodem exemplo inductionem constituis? Hoc modo : Homo bilis expers est : & est longæuus. Equus item, elephas item, bos item, asinus item, ceteráque item quæ bile vacant. ergo quæ bile vacant, longæua sunt.
units.tr: Well, how do you constitute induction from the same example? In this way: Man lacks bile and is long-lived. Likewise the horse, likewise the elephant, likewise the ox, likewise the ass, and likewise the others which lack bile. Therefore those which lack bile are long-lived.

units.la: Quis est inductionis vsus? Aristoteles multis locis scribit, doctrinam omnem aut inductione, aut ratiocinatione parari. nam inductione principia & universa cognosci, quoniam a rerum singularum cognitione universarum cognitio ducitur. Itaque cognitionis principium recte appellatur: ratiocinatio vero principiis generalibus atque universis conficitur, ac progreditur: quae principia per inductionem probantur. Itaque inductionis maior est usus apud imperitos & multitudinem. syllogismi vero apud peritos & Dialecticos.
units.tr: What is the use of induction? Aristotle writes in many places that all doctrine is gained either by induction or by reasoning. For by induction principles and universals are known, since knowledge of the universal is derived from knowledge of single things. Thus induction is rightly called the beginning of knowledge; reasoning, however, is completed and proceeds from general and universal principles, which principles are proved by induction. Therefore induction is more used among the unskilled and the crowd, and the syllogism among the skilled and the dialecticians.

units.la: Quid est inductio Rhetorica quam exemplum appellari dicebas? Id Quintilianus ita definit: Exemplum est rei gestae, aut ut gestae, utilis ad persuadendum id quod intenderis, commemoratio. Aristoteles autem hoc modo, Exemplum est, cum extremum in medio inesse ostenditur per aliquid, quod simile fit tertio. παράδειγμα ὃ [?]ἔχει ὅταν τῷ μέσῳ τὸ ἄκρον ὑπάρχον [?]ἐξ ἑτέρου ὅμοιον τῷ τρίτῳ: id est, Exemplum est, cum in medio maius extremum inesse ostenditur ex aliquo quod sit simile tertio: sive subiecto. veluti: Ponatur quaestio, An bellum Atheniensium in Thebanos (quod Subiectum est) futurum sit calamitosum: (quod Attributum est) Sumatur medium: Bellum cum finitimis. tum ita ratio ineatur: Bellum cum finitimis suscipere perniciosum est. Bellum Atheniensium cum Thebanis est bellum cum finitimis. Ergo futurum est calamitosum. Propositio vero probetur ab eo quod est simile Subie&to.Nam Phocensibus cum Thebanis belligerari exitiosum fuit.
units.tr: What is rhetorical induction, which you said is called example? Quintilian defines it thus: an example is the recounting of a thing done, or as done, useful for persuading what you intend. Aristotle, however, defines it thus: an example is when the extreme is shown to be present in the middle through something which is like the third [παράδειγμα ἔχει ὅταν τῷ μέσῳ τὸ ἄκρον ὑπάρχῃ διὰ τοῦ ἐξ ἑτέρου ὁμοίου τῷ τρίτῳ]. That is, an example is when the greater extreme is shown to be present in the middle through something that is like the third, or the subject. For instance: Let the question be whether the war of the Athenians against the Thebans (which is the subject) will be calamitous (which is the attribute). Let the middle be: war with neighbours. Then the reasoning proceeds thus: To undertake war with neighbours is ruinous. The war of the Athenians with the Thebans is a war with neighbours. Therefore it will be calamitous. The proposition, however, is proved by something like the subject: for for the Phocians to wage war with the Thebans was disastrous.

units.la: Quid? nónne Syllogismus hic argumentatio est solida, & firma: sumpta ex genere ad speciem? Aristoteles ostendit Exemplum non habere eam rationem, quam habet Totum ad partem, aut pars ad Totum: sed quam pars una habet ad alteram: cùm ambæ quidem in eodem Toto continentur: sed altera notior est. Itaque Rhetores dicere solét, Exemplū ex unius singularis collatione alterum singulare confirmare. & Laertius in Platone scribit, Rhetoricā in particularib' versari. quia quod in parte quæritur, per id quod est in parte demonstratur. Dialeticam autem versari in universalibus, quia universalia per ea quæ in parte sunt, concludit.
units.tr: But is not this syllogism a solid and firm argument, taken from genus to species? Aristotle shows that the example does not have the relation which the whole has to the part, or the part to the whole, but that which one part has to another, when both are indeed contained in the same whole, but one is better known. So rhetoricians are accustomed to say that an example confirms one single case by comparison with another single case. And Laertius, in his account of Plato, writes that rhetoric deals with particulars, because what is sought in a part is demonstrated through what is in a part. But dialectic deals with universals, because it concludes universals through what is in the parts.

units.la: Sempérne argumentatio ab exemplo per syllogismum tractatur? Nihil minus.quin potius, ubi ratiocinatio conficitur, vocatur syllogismus: sed paradigmaticus: idest, (vt ita loquar) exemplaris. Formula igitur huius argumentationis propria est hæc: vt eius momentum sit in similitudine. veluti: Phocensibus calamitosum cum Thebanis bellum fuit: quia bella cum finitimis perniciosa sunt. Athenien-sibus igitur bellum cum Thebanis erit perniciosum. vt Exemplum & Quæstio ex medio, pari vtraque momento, pendeant. Denique vt momentum propositionis sit in exemplo, non in loco argumenti.alioqui Dialectica erit argumentatio, & solida, non fucata & Rhetorica.
units.tr: Is argument from example ever treated through a syllogism? Not at all. Rather, when the reasoning is completed, it is called a syllogism, but a paradigmatic one, that is, (so to speak) exemplary. The form of this argument is therefore proper to it, so that its force lies in the similarity. For instance: The war with the Thebans was disastrous for the Phocians, because wars with neighbours are ruinous. Therefore the war with the Thebans will be ruinous for the Athenians. So that the example and the question both hang from the middle, each of equal weight. Finally, the force of the proposition lies in the example, not in the place of the argument; otherwise dialectic would be the argument, and solid, not disguised and rhetorical.

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplum. Græcis gloriosum fuit Phalarim interficere, quia præclarum est tyrannide civitatem liberare.Romanis igitur laudi ducatur, quòd Cæsarem interfecerint. Ex eodem genere illud est ioculare Pasquilli: Tandem Maxime Pontifex galerum: Pasquillo tribuas tuo roganti. Si sensu sine sum, rude atque marmor, Complures quoque Episcopos creari,Ipso me mage saxeos videmus.
units.tr: Let me cite another example. For the Greeks it was glorious to kill Phalaris, because it is an excellent thing to free a state from tyranny. Therefore it should be counted to the praise of the Romans that they killed Caesar. Of the same kind is that witty verse of Pasquillus: "At last, Pontiff Maximus, you grant your hat to the Pasquil who begs you. If I were without sense, rude and marble, I would see many bishops created, more stony than I am."

units.la: Quid interest inter Argumentationem à simili: & Inductionem? Illa per Medium tractatur, & in iis demum quæ medium habent, versatur. hæc in iis quæ medium non habent. Præterea in forma hoc interest, quòd argumentum à simili ex una re simili de ceteris omnibus concludit. Inductio contrà ex ceteris omnibus ad unam. Firmamentum enim Similiū est huiusmodi: Quod in una re simili valet, valeat in ceteris. veluti: Ut tutori pupilli rem emere non licet, ita nec curatori, nec procura-tori, nec negotiorum gestori. At inductionis est illud: Quod in pluribus rebus similibus valet, etiam in hac valeat. veluti, Ut neque tutori, neque curatori, neque procuratori emere rem administratam licet, ita neque negotiorum gestori.
units.tr: What is the difference between argument from likeness and induction? The former is handled through a middle term, and it deals only with things that have a middle term; the latter deals with things that have none. Moreover, in form the difference is this: an argument from likeness concludes from one like thing about all the others, whereas induction concludes from all the others to one. For the strength of likeness-arguments is of this kind: what holds good in one similar thing holds good in the others. For example: just as it is not lawful for a guardian to buy his ward's property, so neither is it for a curator, nor a procurator, nor a manager of affairs. But the form of induction is this: what holds good in many similar things holds good also in this one. For example: just as it is not lawful for a guardian, a curator or a procurator to buy property under their administration, so neither is it lawful for a manager of affairs.

units.la: Quid interest inter argumentationem ab Exemplo & eam quæ est ex Paribus vel Similibus? Argumentum ex pari aut simili, ex uno concludit omnia. Exemplum vero ex uno unū tantùm concludit. Praeterea argumentum à simili proportione (ut superiùs dictum est) nititur. causam enim rei penitus intuetur. At exemplum, si modò Rhetoricum est, rem gestam extrinsecus nulla exquisita causa considerat. Nam Rhetores, quorum praecipuus huius generis usus est, quibúsque unus hic finis propositus est, ut iudicibus tenebras offundant, exemplo tractando argumentationes illas explicant.Quod enim exemplo fit, id etiam iure fieri vulgus putat: ut ait Cicero in Epistolis.
units.tr: What is the difference between argument from example and argument from equals or likes? An argument from equal or like things concludes all things from one. An example, on the other hand, concludes only one thing from one. Moreover, the argument from like proportion (as was said above) rests on the reason of the thing: it looks closely into the cause of the matter. But an example, if it is rhetorical, considers the deed done from outside, without any careful inquiry into its cause. For the rhetoricians, whose chief use this kind is, and for whom this one aim is set, namely to cast darkness over the judges, explain those arguments by handling examples. For the crowd thinks that what is done by precedent is also rightly done, as Cicero says in his Letters.

units.la: Cedo aliquod exemplum. Eliseus petiit à Deo, ut impios conviciatores fulgure perderet. Ergo idem Apostolis facere ius est. Haec Rhetorica inductio est, quae solam rei gestae si-militudinem extrinsecus considerat. At Christus causam esse dissimilem demonstrat. Ehudius Tyrannum Eglone interfecit. Moses seditiosum sua manu occidit. Ergo idem cuiuis Christiano facere ius est. dissimilis causa est. nam uterq; Magistratus sui iure id fecit. Quare ad vitandas harum argumentationum cap-tiones eò revocandus est adversarius, ut eadem ratio & causa subsit.
units.tr: Let me cite some example. Elisha asked God to destroy with lightning the impious revilers. Therefore it is right for the Apostles to do the same. This is a rhetorical induction, which considers only the outward likeness of the deed. But Christ shows that the cause is unlike. Ehud killed the tyrant Eglon; Moses killed a seditious man with his own hand. Therefore it is right for any Christian to do the same. The cause is unlike: for each of those acted by the right of his own magistracy. Hence, to avoid the snares of these arguments, the opponent must be brought back to the point that the same reason and cause underlie the matter.

units.la: Quid interest inter Inductionem & Exemplum? Aristoteles discrimen hoc statuit, quòd inductio ex singulis universis extremum in medio esse confirmat: nec syllogismum ad extrema connectit. Exemplum vero coiungit quidem : ex omnibus autem non probat. nāut[?] modò diximus, vnum ex vno tantummodo per exemplum confirmatur.
units.tr: What is the difference between induction and example? Aristotle lays down this distinction: induction confirms the extreme in the middle by means of the single cases taken together, and does not connect the syllogism to the extremes. An example, however, does connect, but does not prove from all cases; for, as we have just said, one thing is confirmed from one thing only through an example.

units.la: De Captionibus Sophisticis.
units.tr: On Sophistical Captions.

units.la: CAP. XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: Q[?]VONIAM de Argumētatione Dialectica satis dictum est, superest vt de sophistica differamus. Ac primum omnium quid est Sophistice? Falsa doctrinæ simulatio. nam Sophistæ dicebātur (inquit Aristoteles) qui ex ea quam præ se ferebant fucata & adulterina sapientia quæstū faciebant. quales nostris temporibus Rabulas forenses numerare possumus. Cicero autè lib.de Finib.2. ita definit: Sophistæ (inquit) dicebantur, qui ostentationis & quæstus causa philosophabantur. Itaque Sophistice definiri sic potest, Captario[?] verborum quę disputandi prudentiam fallaciter imitando adulterat. Nam eodem modo Sophisticæ argumētationes à Dialecticis differunt, quo adulterini numi à probis. Sophismata autem Seneca in Epistolis scribit, Cauillationes à Cicerone Latinè appellari.
units.tr: Since enough has been said about dialectical argument, it remains to discuss the sophistical. And first of all, what is sophistry? It is a false show of learning. For, says Aristotle, those were called sophists who made gain from the counterfeit and adulterated wisdom they professed. Among our own contemporaries we can count the legal wranglers as such. Cicero, in book 2 of De Finibus, defines them thus: "Sophists," he says, "were those who philosophised for show and for profit." Sophistry can therefore be defined as the catching at words, which corrupts the skill of disputing by falsely imitating it. For sophistical arguments differ from dialectical ones in the same way that counterfeit coins differ from genuine ones. Seneca, in his Letters, writes that what are called sophismata are called by Cicero, in Latin, cavillationes.

units.la: Quisnam huius doctrinæ est vsus? Idé planè, qui in mercatorum & argentariorum vita percipitur ex facultate probos numos ab adulterinis internoscendi: aut aurum aborichalco: vel argentum à Lytargyrina. Cauendum (inquit Cicero) diligenter ne fallant ea nos vitia, quae virtutem videntur imitari: ut fortitudinem audacia, iustitiam acerbitas, religionem superstitio, & illa disputandi prudentiam, concertatio captatioque verborum: & oratoriam vim inanis quaedam profluentia loquedi. Item in lib. Academ.2. Multi fallacibus & captiosis interrogationibus circumscripti atque decepti cum eas dissoluere non possunt, desciscunt a veritate. Oportet igitur & ea quae pro vero respoderi possunt, in promptu habere: & esse armatos, ut occurrere possimus interrogationibus eorum, captionesque discutere.
units.tr: What is the use of this doctrine? Plainly the same use that is found in the life of merchants and money-changers: the skill of distinguishing genuine coins from counterfeit ones, gold from brass, or silver from litharge. "We must take careful heed," says Cicero, "that we are not deceived by those vices which seem to imitate virtues: audacity for courage, harshness for justice, superstition for religion, and, for the skill of disputing, contentiousness and the catching at words, and, for the power of oratory, an empty flow of speech." Likewise in book 2 of the Academica: "Many people, circumvented and deceived by fallacious and captious questions, when they cannot resolve them, fall away from the truth. It is therefore necessary to have ready those answers which can be given in defence of the truth, and to be armed, so that we can meet their questions and shake off their traps."

units.la: Quis est finis Sophistarum? Finis quidem Sophistarum (ut ex Aristotele docuimus) est quaestus: sed opus in quo occupati sunt, est captio, sive vitiosa conclusio argumenti: qua eius quocum disputat assensionem captat: quae captio modo τὸ ἄπορον, modo συλλογισμὸς, modo ἔλεγχος appellatur: quo ipso nomine Captionem significari ex eo constat, quod ἐλέγχειν est capere, tenere, deprehensum convincere. & ἐληγχθεὶς, qui sic captus est, ut elabi non possit. Itaque librum Aristotelis περὶ σοφιστικῶν ἐλέγχων Latine sic interpretari possumus, De sophisticis captionibus. quanquam sunt qui de Reprehensionibus, interpretari malint, pro de vitiosis argumentationibus. Sed frequentius ἄπορος λόγος, genus hoc disputationis appellatur: quoniam ita perplexum inexplicabile est, vt exitum interrogato nullum praebeat. quanquam alij τὸ ἄπορον,genus: alij (vt Hermagoras) speciem fecerunt.
units.tr: What is the aim of the sophists? The aim of the sophists (as we have shown from Aristotle) is gain; but the work in which they are occupied is the captio, that is, a fallacious conclusion of an argument, by which they catch the assent of the person with whom they are disputing. This captio is called now to aporon [τὸ ἄπορον], now syllogismos [συλλογισμὸς], now elenchos [ἔλεγχος]. The name itself shows that captio is what is meant, since elenchein [ἐλέγχειν] is to catch, to hold, to convict someone who has been caught; and elenchthEis [ἐληλεγμένος] is one who has been so caught that he cannot escape. Thus Aristotle's book peri sophistikon elenchon [περὶ σοφιστικῶν ἐλέγχων] can be rendered into Latin as De sophisticis captionibus, "On Sophistical Captions." Some, however, prefer to translate it De reprehensionibus, "On Refutations", meaning fallacious arguments. But more often this kind of disputation is called aporos logos [ἄπορος λόγος], since it is so perplexing and inextricable that it offers the questioner no way out. Others have made to aporon a genus, and others (like Hermagoras) a species.

units.la: Quomodo tanta vis erat sophisticæ? Quoniam (vt Gellius scribit) lex est Dialecticæ disciplinæ, si de quapiam re quæratur, disputetúrque, atque ibi quid rogere, tum ne amplius quid dicas, quàm id solùm, quod es rogatus,aut aias, aut neges: eámque legem qui non seruant,& aut aliter quàm sunt rogati respondent,existimantur rudes indoctíque esse, neque disputandi morem & consuetudinem tenere.
units.tr: How could sophistry have such great force? Because (as Gellius writes) there is a rule of the dialectical discipline: if some matter is asked about and discussed, and a question is put to someone, then he should say nothing more than what he was asked, that is, either affirm or deny. Those who do not keep this rule, and answer otherwise than as they were asked, are thought to be rude and untaught, and not to observe the custom and practice of disputing.

units.la: Quotuplex istius ἀπόρᾳ[?] siue perplexitatis vitium est? Multiplex omnino. nä varia Stoici genera confinxerunt. Cicero quidem in veteri Rhetorico quadruplicem Reprehensionis modum exponit: sed qui ad hunc duplicem reuocari debeat. Verba illius hæc sunt:Omnis argumentatio reprehenditur, si aut ex iis quæ sumpta sunt non conceditur, (id est negatur) aliquod vnum pluráve:aut his cócesis,cóplexio confici ex his negatur: aut si genus ipsum argumentationis vitiosum ostenditur, aut si cótra firmam argumétationem alia æquè firma,aut firmior ponitur. Nā tertius modus in primo continetur perspicuè. Quartus autem ad deliberationes tantummodo pertinet. Sed tamen tota illa Ciceronis disputatio, quæ est in capite de Reprehensione lib. de Inuent.r. diligenter obseruanda est.
units.tr: How many kinds of this aporia, or perplexity, are there? Many indeed, for the Stoics devised various kinds. Cicero, in his old Rhetoric, sets out a fourfold manner of refutation, but it ought to be reduced to two. His words are these: "Every argument is refuted if either some one or more of the premises taken are not granted (that is, are denied), or, when these are granted, the conclusion drawn from them is denied; or if the kind of argument itself is shown to be faulty; or if, against a firm argument, another equally firm or firmer one is set up." For the third mode is clearly contained in the first, and the fourth pertains only to deliberations. Nevertheless, the whole of Cicero's discussion in the chapter on refutation in book 1 of De Inventione must be carefully observed.

units.la: Quomodo captiones vitantur? Suprema lex (inquit Gellius) in omnibus captionibus à Dialecticis hæc constituta est: Non esse captiosis interrogationibus respondendum. Sed tamen in hac captione si respondere placet, vitabitur sophisma per negationem, id est repudiationem falsæ propositionis, qua probationis impossibilis necessitas in Sophistam transfertur. velut in illo Zenonis: Quod ratione vtitur, melius est eo quod ratione non vtitur. nihil autem mundo melius. Ratione igitur mundus vtitur. Assumptio neganda est, quia hominis causa mundus creatus est. melior igitur homo est quàm mundus.
units.tr: How are captions avoided? The supreme rule laid down by the dialecticians in all captions, says Gellius, is this: one should not reply to captious questions. Yet if in this kind of caption one wishes to reply, the sophism will be avoided by denial, that is, by rejecting the false premise, by which the necessity of proving the impossible is transferred onto the sophist. As in that example of Zeno: "What uses reason is better than what does not use reason. Nothing, however, is better than the world. Therefore the world uses reason." The assumption is to be denied, because the world was created for the sake of man. Therefore man is better than the world.

units.la: Quoniam ita multa sunt captionum genera, neque pretium operæ est certum earum numerum definire, cedo mihi vsitatas aliquot earum species. Sumamus ψευδόμενον, ἀνυπόστατον [?] & σωρείτην [?]. id est, Mentientem, instabilem & acerualem.
units.tr: Since there are so many kinds of captions, and it is not worth the effort to fix their number exactly, let me instead give you a few of the usual species. Let us take the pseudomenon [ψευδόμενον], the anypostaton [ἀνυπόστατον] and the soreites [σωρείτην]; that is, the Liar, the Unstable and the Heap.

units.la: Quid est ψευδόμενος [?] Hunc Cicero in Lucullo mentientem appellat. eiúsque hoc exemplum profert: Si te mentiri dicis, idque verum dicis, mentiri verum dicis. Item, si dicis te mentiri verúmque dicis, mentiris. Dicis autem te mentiri, verúmque dicis, mentiris igitur.
units.tr: What is the Liar? Cicero, in the Lucullus, calls it the "lying one" and gives this example: "If you say that you are lying, and say that this is true, you say that lying is true. Likewise, if you say that you are lying and say that it is true, you are lying. But you say that you are lying and that it is true; therefore you are lying."

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplum. Iurisconsulti hoc proferunt: Lex Falcidia vetat testatorem amplius quarta bonorum parte in legatis consumere. nam eam integram heredi relinqui iubet. Qui quadringentos aureos habebat, trecentos legauit hac conditione, si legi Falcidiæ in suo testamento locus non effet. hîc si legi Falcidiæ locus est, Titio nihil debetur. at si ei nihil debetur, locus Falcidiæ nō erit. ac proinde legatum Titio debebitur. l. qui quadringenta, 88, D. ad leg. Falc.
units.tr: Here is another example. The jurists put forward this: the Falcidian law forbids a testator to spend more than a fourth of his goods on legacies, for it orders that this fourth be left whole to the heir. A man who had four hundred gold pieces bequeathed three hundred of them on this condition: that there should be no place for the Falcidian law in his will. Here, if there is a place for the Falcidian law, nothing is owed to Titius. But if nothing is owed to him, there will be no place for the Falcidian law; and therefore the legacy will be owed to Titius. Digest, law Qui quadringenta, 88, ad legem Falcidiam.

units.la: Cedo exemplum instabilis. Sumatur ex Lactant. lib.3. Somniauit quidam ne somniis crederet. Si credat, sequitur vt credendum non fit. Si non credat, sequitur vt credendum fit. Item: Si verum est quod dicunt Academici, nihil sciri posse, necesse est idipsum sciri quod nihil sciatur. Si autem scitur posse nihil sciri, falsum est quod dicitur nihil posse sciri. Ex eodem genere illud est: Epimenides dixit, omnes Cretenses esse mendaces. At ipse Cretensis fuit: Si verum dixit, illi non credendum. Si mentitus est, nihilo magis. Item illud apud Iurisconsul. si Titi' heres erit, Seius heres esto. Si Seius heres erit, Titi' heres esto. Iulianus inutile esse institutionem scribit, cùm conditio existere non posset. l. si Titius, 16, D. de cond. instit.
units.tr: Here is an example of the unstable. Take it from Lactantius, book 3: someone dreamed that he should not believe dreams. If he believes, it follows that he should not believe; if he does not believe, it follows that he should believe. Likewise: if it is true, as the Academics say, that nothing can be known, then it is necessary that this very thing be known, namely that nothing is known. But if it is known that nothing can be known, then what is said, that nothing can be known, is false. Of the same kind is this: Epimenides said that all Cretans are liars, but he himself was a Cretan. If he spoke the truth, he is not to be believed; if he lied, he is no more to be believed. Likewise that in the jurists: "If Titius shall be heir, let Seius be heir. If Seius shall be heir, let Titius be heir." Julian writes that the institution is useless, since the condition could not come about. Digest, law Si Titius, 16, de conditionibus institutionum.

units.la: Quomodo hæc verborum concertatio vitatur? Reuocando aduersario ad rectam & legitimam conclusionis componendæ formulã. δεῖ γὰρ ἐκ τῶν κειμένων συμβαίνειν τὸ συμπέρασμα, ὡς ἐξ ἀνάγκης: inquit Aristoteles. Id est: Oportet enim ex iis quæ posita sunt conclusionem existere, idque necessario. Nam (vt Cicero scribit in Academ.) concludi argumentum non potest, nisi his quæ ad concludendū sumpta erāt ita probatis,ut falsa eiusdem modi nulla possint esse. velut in illo quod ibidem subiicit: Si rebus comprehensis & præceptis nisa & progressa ratio efficit nihil posse comprehendi: quid potest reperiri, quod ipsum sibi repugnet magis? Nam alter disputabat sensibus certa quædam percipi.at cùm ad rationē perducta essent, incerta omnia effici. Sed huius quoque captionis in Sorite quàm maxima Sophistis facultas datur. Itaque jam tempus est, ut de Sorite sophistico disseramus.
units.tr: How is this contention of words avoided? By recalling the opponent to the right and lawful form of composing a conclusion. "For the conclusion must follow from the things laid down, of necessity" [δεῖ γὰρ ἐκ τῶν κειμένων συμβαίνειν τὸ συμπέρασμα, ὡς ἐξ ἀνάγκης], says Aristotle. That is: the conclusion must arise from the things that have been posited, and necessarily so. For (as Cicero writes in the Academica) an argument cannot be concluded unless the premises taken for concluding it have been so established that no falsehoods of the same kind can be among them. As in that which he adds: "If reasoning, built and advanced on things grasped and on precepts, produces the result that nothing can be grasped, what could be found that would contradict itself more?" For the one party argued that certain things are perceived by the senses, but when these were brought before reason, all things were made uncertain. But the sophists are given the greatest facility in this kind of caption also in the Sorites. Therefore it is now time to discuss the sophistical Sorites.

units.la: De Sorite Sophistico. CAP. XVII.
units.tr: On the Sophistical Sorites. CHAP. XVII.

units.la: QVID est Sorites Sophisticus? Multiplex syllogismus, qui minutis additionibus & detractionibus ab eo quod perspicuè [?] verum est, ad id quod perspicuè falsum est, vltrò citróque perducit. Nam (ut Julianus Jurisconsultus scribit) ea est natura cavillationis, quam Græci σωρείτης [?] appellant, ut ab evidenter veris per breuissimas mutationes disputatio ad ea quæ evidenter falsa sunt, perducatur.
