Itaque Cicero in Lucullo captiosissimum interrogationis genus hoc appellat, cum aliquid minutatim & gradatim additur, aut demitur.
units.tr: What is the sophistical sorites? It is a complex syllogism which, by small additions and subtractions, leads back and forth from what is plainly true to what is plainly false. For (as the jurist Julianus writes) this is the nature of the sophism that the Greeks call sōreitēs [σωρείτης]: a dispute is conducted from evidently true premises, through very brief changes, to conclusions that are evidently false. So Cicero, in the Lucullus, calls this the most deceptive kind of questioning, when something is added or taken away little by little and step by step.

units.la: Cur addidisti Vltro citróque? Quoniam hoc artificium tanquam Penelope telam retexens (quemadmodum superiùs ex Cicerone diximus) tollit ad extremum superiora.
units.tr: Why did you add "back and forth"? Because this device, like Penelope unweaving her web (as we said above from Cicero), finally undoes what it had built up.

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Ponatur quaestio:Decem vtrum pauca sunt, an ne multa? Si pauca respondeas: inferetur, quid si vnum addidero? quid si alterum,tertium,quartum?Et vicissim retro: Si multa,responderis. quid si vnum exemero?quid si alterū ,tertium,quartū? Quod in aceruo frumenti vsurpatur: vt nec decem, nec vndecim,nec singula singulatim ad quemuis numerum addita aceruum efficiant. Atque hoc illud est, quod Cicero in Lucullo scribit: Quod in numero conticuisti: si ad eum numerum vnum addidero, multáne erunt? progredere rursus, quoad videbitur. Cuius generis error ita manat, vt non videam quò non possit accedere. Atque hoc exemplum Cicero Verrina v.sed recte ac non sophistice imitatus est.Deinde (inquit) iudices, videtis, quàm infinitam sitis hominibus licentiam pecuniarum eripiendarum daturi. Si ternos denarios qui coegit, erit absolutus: quaternos denos denique,aut vicenos coget alius.quae erit reprehensio?In quo primùm iniuriae gradu resistere incipiet seueritas iudicis? quotus erit iste denarius qui nō fit ferendus? Et in quo primùm aestimationis iniquitas atque improbitas reprehendetur?
units.tr: Give me an example. Let the question be: Are ten a few, or are they many? If you answer that they are few, it will be asked: what if I add one? What if another, a third, a fourth? And conversely, going back: If they are many, you will answer. What if I take away one? What if another, a third, a fourth? This is what is used with a heap of grain: neither ten nor eleven, nor single grains added one at a time to any number, make a heap. This is what Cicero means in the Lucullus: "You fell silent at a certain number: if I add one to that number, will there be many? Go on again, as far as you like." The error of this kind spreads so widely that I cannot see where it cannot reach. Cicero imitated this example in the fifth Verrines, and did so rightly and not sophistically: "Then, judges, you see how much licence to steal money you would give to men. If the man who has extorted three denarii is acquitted, another will extort four, or ten, or finally twenty. What will be the blame? At what degree of wrong will the severity of the judge begin to resist? How large will that denarius be which must not be tolerated? And at what point will the unfairness and wickedness of the valuation first be condemned?"

units.la: Quomodo hæc vitabitur captio?Cicero his in Lucullo verbis demonstrat: At vitiosi sunt soritæ. Frangite igitur eos si potestis, ne molesti sint. placet enim Chrysippo, cùm gradatim interrogetur, verbi causa, Tria pauca sūt, ánne multa? aliquanto prius quàm ad multa peruenìat, quiescere, nec diutius captiosè interroganti respondere. Insistendum est igitur in singulis, ut qua cuiusque in parte vitium lateat, facilius demonstretur. Nam ut vitiato uno annulo cathena omnis dissoluitur, ita una interiecta propositione falsa tota coaceruatio concidit.
units.tr: How will this deception be avoided? Cicero shows this in the Lucullus with these words: "But the sorites are faulty. Break them, then, if you can, so that they cannot trouble you. For Chrysippus held that when one is questioned step by step, for example, 'Are three few, or are they many?', one should come to rest well before reaching 'many', and not answer the captious questioner for any longer. One must therefore insist on each single step, so that the flaw lying in each part may be more easily exposed. For just as, when one link is broken, the whole chain comes apart, so a single false premise inserted makes the whole heap collapse."

units.la: Cedo exemplum. Sumatur ex lib. de Nat. Deor.I. ubi cùm Velleius Epicureus sic disputasset, Si sunt dii, sunt beati. si beati, virtute præditi: si virtute præditi, etiam ratione utuntur. At ratio nìsi in hominis figura esse non potest. Ergo deorum forma humana est. Cùm igitur illò ventum esset, Ratio nìsi in hominis figura esse non potest. Tum Cotta: A beatis (inquit) ad virtutem, à virtute ad rationem video te peruenìsse gradibus: à ratione ad humanam figuram quomodo accedis? præcipitare istuc quidem est, non descendere. Præterea in progrediendo videndum est, ne nimium longè res producatur. Nam ut ex annulis ferreis qui magnete continentur, quo quisque magneti propior est, eò hæret tenaciùs, & quo quisque longinquior, eò laxior: ita sæpe in istiusmodi coacerua-tionibus quo quidque attributum primo subiecto remotius est, eò minus illi conuenit.
units.tr: Here is an example. Take it from the first book On the Nature of the Gods, where Velleius the Epicurean argued thus: "If there are gods, they are blessed. If they are blessed, they are endowed with virtue. If they are endowed with virtue, they also use reason. But reason cannot exist except in human form. Therefore the form of the gods is human." When they had come to the point, "reason cannot exist except in human form," Cotta replied: "I see that you have come from blessedness to virtue, from virtue to reason, by steps. But how do you get from reason to human form? That is falling headlong, not descending. Moreover, in advancing one must take care not to carry the matter too far. For just as iron rings held by a magnet hold more firmly the nearer each is to the magnet, and more loosely the farther away, so in such heaps of reasoning, the further a predicate is removed from the primary subject, the less it belongs to it."

units.la: CAP. XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: EINCEPS[?] de diuisione captionū videamus. Quotuplex est captatio sophistica? Duplex. vna in verbis, altera in rebus. Quæ autem captio ex verbis oritur, versatur in homonymia: id est multiplicitate vocabuli: ἀμφιβολία, ambiguitate: συνθέσει, coniunctione: διαιρέσει, diuisione: προσῳδία, accentu: & σχήματι[?] λέξεως, forma dictionis.
units.tr: Next, let us consider the division of fallacies. How many kinds of sophistical fallacy are there? Two: one in words, the other in things. A fallacy that arises from words turns on homonymy, that is, the multiple meaning of a term; on ambiguity [ἀμφιβολία]; on composition [συνθέσει], or conjunction; on division [διαιρέσει]; on accent [προσῳδία]; and on the form of expression [σχήματι λέξεως].

units.la: Quæ est captio per homonymiam? Cùm propter nominis similitudinem, quod vnius proprium est alteri tribuitur. veluti: Hercules est fortissimus. Ergo Hercules pictus est fortissimus. Ex hoc genere illud est Ciceronis ridiculum in Verrina vi: Nunquam tam male est Siculis, quin aliquid commodè & facetè dicat. velut in hac re. Aiebant in labores Herculis nō minus hunc immanissimum Verrē,q; illum aprum Erymanthium referri oportere. Nam Verres Herculis Agrigentini statuam magno labore demoliri & auferre conatus erat: neque tamen ille vlla labarat ex parte.
units.tr: What is the fallacy of homonymy? It occurs when, because of the similarity of a name, what belongs to one thing is attributed to another. For example: Hercules is the strongest. Therefore Hercules in a painting is the strongest. To this kind belongs Cicero's witty remark in the sixth Verrine: "Things are never so bad for the Sicilians that someone cannot say something clever and witty about them." For example, they used to say that this most monstrous Verres ought to be counted among the labours of Hercules no less than the Erymanthian boar. For Verres had tried, at great effort, to tear down and carry off the statue of Hercules at Agrigentum, yet that statue did not budge in any part.

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplum. Scriptor belli Gallici fuit doctissimus. Librarius sua manu scripsit bellum Gallicum. Ergo fuit doctissimus. Nam in propositione homonymia est inter Cæsarem & librarium. Item : Qui equuleos habet, potest equitare. Verres equuleos argēteos à Cn. Calidio abstulit. Ergo Verres (inquit Cicero) iactabit se, & in his equitabit equuleis. Sic Dionysius (inquit idem) cùm in fanum Iouis Olympij venisset, aureum ei detraxit amiculum, grandi pondere: atque in eo cauillatus est, æstate graue esse aureum amiculum, hyeme frigidum: cíque laneum pallium iniecit: cùm id esse aptum ad omne animi tempus diceret. Syllogismus erat huiusmodi: Humano corpori laneum pallium omni tempore aptum est. Istud est corpus humanum, aut quasi humanum. Ergo laneum pallium aptum est. Homonymia est propositionis & assumptionis.nam in illa corpus de animato dicitur, in hac de inanimato.
units.tr: Let me give another example. A writer of the Gallic War was most learned. A copyist wrote the Gallic War with his own hand. Therefore he was most learned. For in the premise there is homonymy between Caesar and the copyist. Likewise: whoever has little horses (equuleos) can ride. Verres took silver little horses from Gnaeus Calidius. Therefore, says Cicero, Verres will boast and ride on those little horses. Again, says the same author, when Dionysius came into the temple of Olympian Jove, he stripped off a golden cloak of great weight, and mocked it, saying that a golden cloak is heavy in summer and cold in winter; and he threw a woollen cloak around the god, saying that this was suitable for every season of the mind. The syllogism ran thus: A woollen cloak is suitable at all times for the human body. This is a human body, or something like one. Therefore a woollen cloak is suitable. The homonymy lies between the premise and the assumption: in the one, "body" is said of a living thing, in the other, of a lifeless thing.

units.la: Quomodo hæc vitabitur captio? Distinctione homonymiæ: cùm vocabulum in propositione indefinitè positum ex parte conceditur, ex parte negatur. veluti: Corpori humano cóuenit, duntaxat animato. Itē qui habet equuleos, dūtaxat animatos. Itē Scriptor belli Gallici, qui idē & autor, & scriptor est.
units.tr: How is this fallacy avoided? By distinguishing the homonym: when a term used indefinitely in the premise is granted in one sense and denied in another. For example: a human body suits only a living body. Likewise, one who has little horses has only living ones. Likewise, the writer of the Gallic War, who is also the author, is not merely a copyist.

units.la: Quæ est captio per amphiboliam? Cùm propter ancipitem aut dictionis aut sententiæ significationem, quod vni conueniebat, alteri tribuitur. Dictionis autem hæc exempla sunt: Gemmæ sunt lapilli pretiosi. Gemmæ sunt in vitibus.Ergo lapilli pretiosi sunt in vitibus. Omnis canis latrandi vim habet.Sydus quoddam est canis. Ergo Sydus quoddam latrandi vim habet.Eodémque illius pertinebat calumcalūnia, qui cùm triginta dierū essent cū hofte pactę induciæ, noctu populabatur agros, quòd dierum essent pactæ,non noctium induciæ. Quoniâ dies & nox contraria sunt : quod vnius proprium est, alteri non conuenit. Triginta dierū induciæ pacem dierum triginta faciunt. Noctibus igitur non pax, sed bellum conuenit. Sed Diei verbum interdum lucem significat. verùm more Romano dies (inquiunt Iurisconsulti) à media nocte ad mediam insequentem durat.l.more,8,D. de feriis. Ex eodem genere illud est apud Vlpianum de testamento militis: quod tamen factum à nondum milite fuerat. Nam captio erat in his verbis: Testamentum militis non rite factum,tamen propter militare priuilegium valet. Sed Vlp. respondet aliud esse testamentum militis, aliud testamentum à milite factum. l. Titius, 25,D.de testam.milit.
units.tr: What is the fallacy of amphiboly? It occurs when, because of the double meaning of a word or of a sentence, what belonged to one thing is attributed to another. Examples of a word are these: Gems are precious stones. Gems are on vines. Therefore precious stones are on vines. Every dog has the power of barking. A certain star is a dog. Therefore a certain star has the power of barking. To this belongs the trickery of that man who, when a truce of thirty days had been agreed with the enemy, ravaged the fields by night, arguing that the truce had been made for days, not for nights. For day and night are opposites, and what belongs to one does not belong to the other. A truce of thirty days makes peace for thirty days; therefore peace does not belong to the nights, but war does. But the word "day" sometimes means daylight; yet according to the Roman custom, as the jurists say, a day lasts from midnight to the following midnight (Dig. 2.12.8, "more"). Of the same kind is the passage in Ulpian concerning a soldier's will, which had nevertheless been made by one who was not yet a soldier. For the fallacy lay in these words: "A soldier's will, not validly made, is nevertheless valid because of the military privilege." But Ulpian replies that a soldier's will is one thing, and a will made by a soldier another (Dig. 29.1.25, "Titius").

units.la: Cedo itē aliud. Sumatur illud Stoicorū.Nihil mūdo melius est. quod ratione vtitur, melius est eo quod non vtitur.ratione igitur mūdus vtitur. Similiter(inquitCic.de Na.Deor. 3.)effici potest sapiente esse mundū, similiter beatū,similiter æternū.Similiter librū optimè legere.nā quod literatū est,melius est eo quod non est. Isto modo etiam disertus, & quidem Mathematicus, Musicus, denique doctrina eruditus, postremo philosophus erit mundus. Captio est igitur ex ambiguo.Nam melius intelligitur respectu sui cuiusque generis. Ergo in hac propositione, Mundus est omnium optimus: Negatio ita convertenda est: Bonitas intelligitur respectu naturarum & partium omnium, quibus constat mundus. At in assumptione Melius cum sui generis rebus ratione habet. tametsi longè maius huius syllogismi vitium esse superius docuimus. Nam si hominis causa mundus creatus est, melior homo est quàm mundus. In eodem genere illa captio est: Nemo est Aristide melior. hic sutor optimus est sutor. Ergo Aristides sutor est illo melior. Bonitas enim dicitur respectu sui cuiusque generis.
units.tr: Let me give another. Take that Stoic saying: Nothing is better than the world. What uses reason is better than what does not use reason. Therefore the world uses reason. In the same way, says Cicero (On the Nature of the Gods, 3), it can be shown that the world is wise, likewise blessed, likewise eternal, likewise that it reads books very well, for what is lettered is better than what is not. In this way too the world will be eloquent, and indeed a mathematician, a musician, in short learned in every branch of knowledge, and finally a philosopher. The fallacy therefore arises from ambiguity, for "better" is understood with respect to each thing's own kind. So in this proposition, "The world is the best of all things," the proposition must be understood thus: goodness is understood with respect to all the natures and parts of which the world consists. But in the assumption, "better" is taken with respect to things of their own kind. Yet we have shown earlier that the greater fault of this syllogism lies elsewhere: for if the world was created for the sake of man, then man is better than the world. Of the same kind is this fallacy: No one is better than Aristides; this cobbler is the best cobbler; therefore Aristides is a better cobbler than he is. For goodness is said with respect to each thing's own kind.

units.la: Quomodò hæc ambiguitatis captio vitatur? Per distinctionem ambiguitatis, cùm vocabulum ambiguè positum in propositione ex parte tantùm conceditur. veluti: Gemmæ sunt lapilli. nomine quidem verè proprieq; intelle&o[?]. Canis latrat: duntaxat qui est quadrupes.
units.tr: How is this fallacy of ambiguity avoided? By distinguishing the ambiguity, when a term used ambiguously in the premise is granted only in one sense. For example: Gems are stones, understood truly and properly in name. A dog barks: understood only of a four-footed animal.

units.la: Cedo exemplū de sententia. Veluti: Cùm Apollo cōsulente Pyrrho an bellū Romanis inferret, sic respondit: Aio te Aeacida Romanos vincere posse. Ité[?] illud: Iubeo poni statuā auream hastam tenetem. Item: Heres meus dato uxori meæ argenti quod elegerit, pondo centum. Eiusdemmodi est etiam illud apud Iurifconsultos: Lego pocula oleaginea paria duo. nam quatuor legatarius petebat: quasi scriptum fuisset bina paria, vel poculorum paria duo. l. qui quatuor, 30, D. de legat.
units.tr: Let me give an example from the sense of a sentence. For instance, when Apollo, consulted by Pyrrhus whether he should make war on the Romans, replied: "I say that you, descendant of Aeacus, can conquer the Romans." Likewise: "I order a golden statue to be set up of a man holding a spear." Likewise: "Let my heir give my wife a hundred pounds of whatever silver she chooses." Of the same kind is that passage of the jurists: "I bequeath two pairs of oil-flasks"; for the legatee claimed four, as if it had been written "two pairs" or "two pairs of flasks" (Dig. 30, "qui quatuor").

units.la: Cedo exemplum ambiguitatis in Syllogis-mo. mo. Quisquis arat littus, littus proscindit aratro: Ast operam perdens, littus perhibetur arare. Ergo operam perdens littus proscindit aratro. Item ex Aristotele: Quod quis videt, illud ipsum videt. Aliquis videt columnam. Columna igitur videt. Vitabitur autem captio hæc per distinctionem ambigui verbi, Arare littus: aut Videre, quòd in propositione est aliud quàm in assumptione significat.
units.tr: Let me give an example of ambiguity in a syllogism. Whoever ploughs the shore, ploughs the shore with the plough. But one who wastes his labour is said to plough the shore. Therefore one who wastes his labour ploughs the shore with the plough. Likewise, from Aristotle: What someone sees, that very thing he sees. Someone sees a column. Therefore the column sees. This fallacy is avoided by distinguishing the ambiguous word, "to plough the shore" or "to see," which in the premise means something other than in the assumption.

units.la: Cedo item aliud. Extat apud Ciceronem in libro de Finibus 4. eiusmodi: Vt in fidibus plurimis, si nulla earum incontenta numeris sit, vt concentum seruare possit, omnes æquè incontentæ sint. Sic peccata, quia discrepant, æquè discrepant. paria sunt igitur. Hic ambiguo ludimur. Æquè enim contingit omnibus fidibus, vt incontentæ sint: illud non continuò, vt æquè incontentæ. Collatio igitur ista te nihil iuuat. Nec enim omnes auaritias, si æquè auaritias esse dixerimus, sequitur etiam vt æquas esse dicamus. Aliud est igitur, Fides æquè omnes incontentæ sunt. aliud, Fides omnes æquè incontentæ sunt. In priore, aduerbium æquè pars est subiecti: in posteriore, pars attributi.
units.tr: Let me give yet another, which occurs in Cicero's Finibus, book 4: "As in many lyres, if none of them is out of tune with the musical scale, so that they can keep harmony, all are equally out of tune; so sins, since they are discordant, are equally discordant; therefore they are equal." Here we are misled by an ambiguity. For it is one thing that all the lyres are equally out of tune, and another that they are all out of tune equally. The adverb "equally" belongs to the subject in the first case, and to the predicate in the second. The comparison therefore does not help you. For if we say that all avarices are equally avarices, it does not follow that we should also say they are equal. So there is a difference between "the lyres are all equally out of tune" and "the lyres are all out of tune equally." In the former, "equally" is part of the subject; in the latter, part of the predicate.

units.la: Quæ est captio per Synthefin? Cùm verba quæ separanda erant alieno loco coniunguntur, veluti: Qui stat, potest currere: Dauus stat. Dauus igitur stans potest currere. Item: Qui non currit, potest currere. Dauus dormiens non currit. Ergo Dauus dormiens potest currere. Itē: Quod est in meis ædibus, est in oppido. Vnicus fons est in meis ædibus. Ergo vnicus fons est in oppido. Aristoteles lib.Rhetor. 11. ad hūc locum illud refert: Eum qui elementa nouit, verba etiam scire. quoniam eadem sunt.
units.tr: What is the fallacy of synthesis [σύνθεσις]? It occurs when words that ought to be separated are joined in the wrong place. For example: He who stands can run. Davus stands. Therefore Davus, standing, can run. Likewise: He who is not running can run. Davus, sleeping, is not running. Therefore Davus, sleeping, can run. Likewise: What is in my house is in the town. The only spring is in my house. Therefore the only spring is in the town. Aristotle, in book 11 of the Rhetoric on this passage, cites: One who knows the letters also knows the words, since they are the same things.

units.la: Quomodo vitabitur hæc captio? Per deiunctionem: cùm ea quæ in conclusione coniuncta sunt, separantur. Nam in conclusione participium Stans coniungit Dauum, qui stat, & quandiu stat: qui non currit, & quandiu non currit: quod est in ædibus separatim, & quod est in vrbe vniuersa. Potest etiam huc illud Aesopi ridiculum referri, qui cùm pedes quatuor porcinos in ollam coquendi caussa imposuisset: herus autem eius verberandi occasionem quærens vnum exemisset: ad haram [?] profectus vnum è saginato porco abscidit, atque in ollam imposuit. pòst cùm herus, neille [?] diffugeret veritus, pedem reposuisset, vbi autem ad cœnam ventum est, Aesopus quinque pedes in patinam effudisset, admiranti hero, ita respondit: Duo porci pedes habent octo. qui de octo quinque detrahit, tres habet reliquos. hic sunt quinque. Saginatus porcus qui in hara est, tres habet. Quadrat igitur numerus. Nam isto modo festinuè quæ separanda erant, coniunxit.
units.tr: How is this fallacy avoided? By division: when things that are joined in the conclusion are separated. For in the conclusion the participle "standing" joins Davus to "who stands," and to "for as long as he stands"; and "who is not running" joins to "for as long as he is not running"; and what is in the house is separated from what is in the whole city. Here one may also refer that ridiculous story of Aesop: when a man had put four pigs' feet into a pot to cook, and his master, looking for a chance to beat him, had taken one out, he went off to the sty and cut a foot from the fattened pig and put it in the pot. Afterwards, when the master, fearing that the pig would escape, had put the foot back, and when they came to dinner, Aesop, who had poured five feet into the dish, answered the astonished master thus: "Two pigs have eight feet. He who takes five from eight has three left. Here there are five. The fattened pig in the sty has three. So the number is right." For in this way he had hastily joined together what ought to have been separated.

units.la: Quæ est captio per Diærefin? Cùm verba quæ coiungenda erant separatur. veluti: Quinque sunt duo & tria. Duo & tria sunt par & impar. impar. Ergo quinque sunt numerus par & impar. Sic omnes Græciæ sapientes erant septem. Thales & Socrates erant sapientes Græciæ. Ergo Thales & Socrates erant septem. In eodem genere illud est Laertij, in Platonis vita: Pater meus aut alius est, quàm pater tuus, autidé. Si pater meus alius est ac pater tuus cùm fit alius quàm pater, non erit pater. si idé est, qui pater meus, idem cùm fit qui pater meus, meus erit pater. Atque in hunc numerum referri possunt, quæ in pronuntiatis separantur, cùm separanda non sunt: siue scripto siue sententia coniungantur. Scripto, veluti: Nocturnum furem ius est occidere. Nō enim separandum illud est, si se telo defendat. Sententia, veluti: Qui nihil agunt, ne alantur. Qui non laborat, ne manducet. Aegroti nihil agunt. Ergo ne alantur. Non enim separandum fuit, Cùm id possent. Ex eodem genere illud est quod Bulgarus Iurisconsultus falsò credidit esse Soritem: Quod in nullius bonis est, occupanti conceditur. Res diuinæ in nullius bonis sunt. Ergo res diuinæ occupanti conceduntur. Nam in propositione coniungendum fuit, Cùm eius conditionis esset, vt alicuius esse posset.
units.tr: What is the fallacy by division (per diairesin)? It occurs when words that should be joined are separated. For example: "Five are two and three. Two and three are even and odd. Therefore five is a number both even and odd." Likewise: "All the wise men of Greece were seven. Thales and Socrates were wise men of Greece. Therefore Thales and Socrates were seven." To the same kind belongs the example from Laertius in the life of Plato: "Either my father is other than your father, or he is the same." If my father is other than your father, then, since he is other than a father, he will not be a father. If he is the same, then, since he who is my father is the same as he who is my father, he will be my father. Those expressions can also be referred to this kind of fallacy which are divided in propositions when they should not be divided, whether they are joined in writing or in meaning. In writing, for example: "It is lawful to kill a nocturnal thief." For that should not be divided, if he defends himself with a weapon. In meaning, for example: "Those who do nothing, let them not be fed. Those who do not work, let them not eat. The sick do nothing. Therefore let them not be fed." For it should not have been divided, since they were able to do it. Of the same kind is what the jurist Bulgarus wrongly believed to be a sorites: "What is in no one's goods is granted to the one who occupies it. Sacred things are in no one's goods. Therefore sacred things are granted to the one who occupies them." For in the premise it ought to have been joined, since it was of such a kind that it could belong to someone.

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplum. Sumatur ex Gellij lib.16.cap.11.Siquis iis verbis interroget, Postulo vt respondeas, desierisne [?] facere adulterium, annon? Utcunque Dialectica lege refponderis, siue aias, siue neges, hærebis in captione:tam fi te dicas adulterum, quàm fi neges.Sit igitur alter ex Syllogismis huiusmodi: fi neget fe desiisse:Quod non desiisti facere,id pergis facere.Non desiisti facere adulterium. Ergo pergis facere adulterium.Respondendū est,captioné esse ex disiunctione connexorum. Quod non desij facere,cùm id facere coepisse.
units.tr: Let me give another example. Take it from Gellius, book 16, chapter 11. If someone asks in these words, "I demand that you answer whether you have stopped committing adultery or not," then whatever answer you give in the dialectical manner, whether you say yes or no, you will be caught in the trap, just as much if you say you are an adulterer as if you deny it. Let there then be another syllogism of this kind: if he denies that he has stopped: "What you have not stopped doing, you still keep doing. You have not stopped committing adultery. Therefore you still keep committing adultery." The answer is that the trap arises from a disjunction of connected things: "What I have not stopped doing, since I have begun to do it."

units.la: Profer etiam aliud. Sumatur ex eodem capite: Quicquid non perdidisti, habéne, an non habes? postulo vt aias, aut neges. Vtcunque responderit, capietur.Si non habere se negauerit quod non perdiderit, colligetur oculos eum non habere, quos non perdidit.Sin verò habere se dixerit, colligetur eum habere cornua, quæ non perdidit. Respondendum igitur captioné esse ex disiunctione connexorum. Quod non perdidi, cùm eius naturæ esset, vt perdi posset. In eodem genere videtur illud Æsopi ridiculum fuisse, qui, cùm herus ipsius in poculis dixisset, se posse mare totum ebibere, eiusque rei sponsionem secisset:postridie consilium ei dedit, vt in iudicio sponsionis diceret, se paratum esse mare interbibere, si modò flumina omnia quæ in illud influebant, arcerentur.
units.tr: Bring forward another example too. Take it from the same chapter: "Whatever you have not lost, do you have it or not? I demand that you say yes or no." Whatever he answers, he will be caught. If he denies that he has what he has not lost, it will be inferred that he does not have the eyes which he has not lost. But if he says that he has it, it will be inferred that he has horns, which he has not lost. The answer, therefore, is that the trap arises from a disjunction of connected things: "What I have not lost, since it was of such a nature that it could be lost." In the same kind seems to have been that ridiculous trick of Aesop, who, when his master had said over his cups that he could drink up the whole sea, and had made a wager on this, the next day advised him to say in the court of the wager that he was ready to drink up the sea, provided that all the rivers which flow into it were first blocked.

units.la: Quomodo vitatur hæc captio?Per coniunctionem. Nam duo & tria, Thales & Socrates, in assumptione & conclusione separata sunt: quæ in propositione coniuncta fuerant. Respondendum igitur, duo aut tria coniuncta, esse numerum impare: Thalem & Socratem, cum reliquis quinque esse septem.
units.tr: How is this trap avoided? By joining. For "two and three" and "Thales and Socrates" are separated in the minor premise and the conclusion, although they were joined in the major premise. The answer, therefore, is that two or three taken together make an odd number, and that Thales and Socrates, together with the remaining five, make seven.

units.la: Quæ est captio ex Accentu? Cùm ex prarium,error obiicitur. veluti, Omnia mala vitanda sunt. Poma sunt mala. Poma igitur vitanda sunt. Item populus est arbor. multitudo ciuium est populus. Ergo multitudo ci-uium est arbor. Huc etiam illa iocularia referuntur.
units.tr: What is the fallacy from accent? It is when an error is thrown against one through a wrongly placed accent. For example: "All evil things are to be avoided. Apples are evil things. Therefore apples are to be avoided." Likewise: "The poplar is a tree. A multitude of citizens is a poplar. Therefore a multitude of citizens is a tree." To this are also referred those jests.

units.la: Fília sub tilia mea net subtilia fila. Item:
units.tr: My daughter spins fine threads under the lime tree. Likewise:

units.la: Mala mali malo mala contulit omnia mundo, cùm prius Mala maxillam significet.
units.tr: The jaws of the evil one, with an apple, brought all evils to the world, although mala first signifies the jaw.

units.la: Quomodo captio hæc vitabitur? Diftinctione accentuum & pronûtiationis,quam tamen antiquis facilioré quàm nobis fuisse, fatis planè constat.
units.tr: How will this fallacy be avoided? By the distinction of accents and pronunciation, which, however, it is quite clear was easier for the ancients than for us.

units.la: Quæ est captio ex forma dictionis? Cùm id quod non eiusdem naturæ est, quasi eiusdé naturæ esset, accipitur. vt illud in epift.Sene-cæ:Mus est syllaba. mus autem cafeum rodit. Ergo syllaba cafeum rodit. Item: Mus est fyllaba.Syllaba non rodit cafeum. Mus ergo cafeum non rodit. Item illud : Homo est duarū syllabarum. Conftantinopolitanus est homo. Ergo Conftantinopolitanus est duarum fyl-labarum.Item illud Diogenià Sophista obiectum:Quod ego sum,tu non es. Ego sum homo.Non igitur homo es. Nam hîc quorū non eadem ratio & natura est, pro eo quasi eadem ratio effet,accipiuntur.
units.tr: What is the fallacy from the form of expression? It is when something that is not of the same nature is taken as if it were of the same nature. Such as that passage in a letter of Seneca: "'Mouse' is a syllable. But a mouse gnaws cheese. Therefore a syllable gnaws cheese." Likewise: "'Mouse' is a syllable. A syllable does not gnaw cheese. Therefore a mouse does not gnaw cheese." Likewise that: "Man has two syllables. The Constantinopolitan is a man. Therefore the Constantinopolitan has two syllables." Likewise that objection of the sophist Diogenes: "What I am, you are not. I am a man. Therefore you are not a man." For here things whose reason and nature are not the same are taken as if their reason were the same.

units.la: Quomodo hæc captio vitabitur? Difiunctione naturæ & rationis. Nam in propositione,Mus est animal.in assumptione,vox.Homo in propositionedictio est: in assumptione subsistantia. Sophista in propositione indiuiduū: in assumptione species.
units.tr: How will this fallacy be avoided? By the distinction of nature and reason. For in the major premise, "mouse" is an animal; in the minor, a word. "Man" in the major premise is a word; in the minor, a substance. "Sophist" in the major premise is an individual; in the minor, a species.

units.la: De Captionibus extra dictionem.
units.tr: On Fallacies Outside Language

units.la: CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: GENESIS deinceps de Captionibus quæ extra dictionem fiūt, videamus. Quot sunt captiones ex rebus? Sep-tem:ex vario accidente,ex parte ad infinitum, ex cōsequētibus,ex petitione principij, ex falsa causa, ex multiplici interrogatione,& ex non animaduersis insidiis.
units.tr: Next, let us consider the fallacies that arise outside the expression. What are the fallacies arising from things? There are seven: from accident, from the part to the infinite, from consequents, from begging the question, from a false cause, from multiple questioning, and from unnoticed traps.

units.la: Quæ est captio ex Accidente? Cùm in assumptione accidés ponitur dissentaneum ab eo,quod erat in propositione. veluti: Quam carnem emisti:eam comedisti.. crudam emisti. crudam igitur comedisti. Quod nix est, hoc grando non est. nix alba est. grando igitur alba non est.
units.tr: What is the fallacy from accident? It occurs when, in the minor premise, an accident is introduced that differs from the one in the major premise. For example: "The flesh you bought, you ate. You bought raw flesh. Therefore you ate raw flesh." And: "What is snow, hail is not. Snow is white. Therefore hail is not white."

units.la: Quomodo vitabitur hæc captio? Demonstratione dissentanei accidétis. nā de carne,in propositione,nullum erat carnis accidens positum,quod in assumptione adiunctum est. In altero:Nix quidem & grando, & glacies accidentia sunt,non subsistentiæ:nam aqua subsistentia est.materia quoque idem sunt.At verò dissimile in assumptione quàm in propositione accidens est positum.
units.tr: How is this fallacy avoided? By showing that the accident is different. In the first example, no accident of flesh was stated in the major premise that is added in the minor. In the second, snow, hail and ice are accidents, not substances, for water is a substance; they are also the same matter. But in the minor premise a different accident is posited from the one in the major premise.

units.la: Cedoaliud exemplum. Sumatur illud Anaxagoræ: Omnis aqua est atra. Nix est aqua. Ergo nix est atra. Hic quod in propositione de substantia dictum erat, in conclusione dicitur de accidenti. Atque ex eodé genere sunt, quæcunque dicuntur forma mutata non eadem permanere. veluti, cùm ex vuis, oliuis, spicis, vinum, oleum, frumentum factum est. ex auro, vel argento, vel ære, vas aliquod. ex lana, vestis: ex tabulis, nauis: ex arbore, trabes. vnde illæ apud Iurisconsultos quæstiones, species ex aliena materia facta cuius fit.
units.tr: Here is another example. Take that saying of Anaxagoras: "All water is black. Snow is water. Therefore snow is black." Here what was said in the major premise of the substance is, in the conclusion, said of an accident. To the same kind belong all those things said not to remain the same once their form has changed: for example, when wine, oil or grain is made from grapes, olives or ears of corn; a vessel from gold, silver or bronze; a garment from wool; a ship from planks; beams from a tree. Hence the questions among the jurists: whose is a thing made of another's material?

units.la: Cedo item aliud. Sumatur illud peruulgatum: Hic canis est pater. hic canis est tuus. Ergo hic canis est pater tuus. In assumptione accidens positum est, dissimile ab eo quod erat in propositione. Sic, Dauid est sanctus. Dauid est adulter. Ergo Dauid est sanctus adulter.
units.tr: Here is another example, a very common one: "This dog is your father. This dog is yours. Therefore this dog is your father." In the minor premise an accident is posited that differs from the one in the major premise. Likewise: "David is holy. David is an adulterer. Therefore David is a holy adulterer."

units.la: Quæ est captio ex parte ad infinitum? Hæc est quę vulgò dicitur A dicto secundum quid, ad dictum simpliciter: cùm id quod aliquatenus & quodammodo verè dictum est, quasi omnino & in totum pronunciatum accipitur. veluti, Aethiops est albus dentes: ergo Aethiops est albus. Vinum febricitanti noxium est. ergo vinum omnino est noxiũ. Dauid fuit adulter & homicida. ergo fuit improbus. Hoc vitioso argumento sæpe nationes malè audiùt. Quidam Cretenses sunt mendaces. ergo Cretenses omnes. Sic Pœni dicti sunt perfidi. Græ-[?] ci[?] teues. Ex eodem genere illud est festivum propter quod Plutarchus scribit argutatoré ab Antonij filio multo argento donatum fuiffe. Quodammodo febricitanti frigida præbenda est. Omnis qui febricitat, quodámodo febricitat. Omni ergo febriciti frigida præbenda est. Obseruatum est autem cum vitium hoc à parte ad infinitum admittitur, tum affirmatiuá esse conclusionem: contrá cum ab infinito ad partem, tum esse negatiuam.
units.tr: What is the fallacy from the part to the infinite? It is what is commonly called the argument from what is said in a certain respect to what is said absolutely: when what has been truly said in some respect and in some way is taken as if it were stated wholly and without qualification. For example: "The Ethiopian has white teeth; therefore the Ethiopian is white." "Wine is harmful to a feverish man; therefore wine is wholly harmful." "David was an adulterer and a murderer; therefore he was wicked." Nations are often ill spoken of through this faulty argument. "Some Cretans are liars; therefore all Cretans are." So the Carthaginians were called faithless, and the Greeks likewise. To the same kind belongs that witty remark for which Plutarch writes that a wrangling sophist was rewarded with a large sum of money by the son of Antony. "A feverish man should in some way be given cold things. Everyone who has a fever is in some way feverish. Therefore every feverish man should be given cold things." It is observed that when this fault from the part to the infinite is admitted, the conclusion is affirmative; conversely, when the argument goes from the infinite to the part, the conclusion is negative.

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplū. Sumatur illud quod Cicero lib.de Inuentione 2.existimauit esse ex ambiguo: Si pecunia indigetis, pecuniam non habetis. indigetis autem pecunia: mercaturæ enim, nisi ita effet, operam non daretis. Pauperes igitur estis. vel potius: Pecuniam igitur nullam habetis. Nam propositio finita erat: Si pecunia indigetis, ad rem amplificandam: pecuniam ad eam ipsam rem non habetis.
units.tr: Here is another example. Take the one which Cicero, in his book on Invention (2), judged to be based on ambiguity: "If you need money, you do not have money. But you need money, for you would not be engaged in trade unless you did. Therefore you are poor." Or rather: "Therefore you have no money at all." For the premise was limited: "If you need money" for the purpose of enlarging the business; "you do not have money" for that very purpose.

units.la: Quomodo vitatur hæc captio? Notatione partis, cùm illa regula profertur, quam superiùs tradidimus: Conclusione semper ad deteriorem fe partem applicare: neque vnquā aut ex particulari vniuersalé, aut ex definita inde finitam sequi: simúlque ostenditur, quantū intersit inter Esse quadantenus, & Esse omnino, infinitè, simpliciter.
units.tr: How is this fallacy avoided? By noting the part, when that rule is stated which we laid down earlier: always apply the conclusion to the weaker part, and never infer a universal from a particular, nor from a definite a definite conclusion. At the same time it is shown how much difference there is between being in some respect and being absolutely, without qualification, simply.

units.la: Quæ est captio ex consequentibus? Cùm ex consecutione reciprocatio infertur: id est ex eo quod quid consecutum est, idem ex contrario conuerti concluditur, qua de re in Lo-corum corum præceptione accurratè disseruimus· veluti:Si est piscis, natat. At non continuò si natat, piscis est.Si quis habet febrem, calet:at non continuò si quis calet,habet febrem.Si est ignis, calefacit. at non continuò si calefacit, est ignis.
units.tr: What is the fallacy from consequents? It occurs when a reciprocal conclusion is drawn from a consequence: that is, when from what follows from something it is concluded that the converse also follows. We have discussed this carefully in the teaching on places. For example: "If it is a fish, it swims. But it does not follow that if it swims, it is a fish." "If someone has a fever, he is warm; but it does not follow that if someone is warm, he has a fever." "If it is fire, it heats; but it does not follow that if it heats, it is fire."

units.la: Quæ est captio ex postulatu principij?Geometræ (inquit Cicero) non omnia docere solent,sed postulare , vt quædam sibi concedantur, quo facilius quæ volunt, explicent : hæc αἰτήματα Græci nominant. Videtúrque facetè Aristoteles hanc captionem sic appellasse, quasi Sophistæ Geometrarum more ac modo principium sibi concedi postularent, tàquam certum,quod tamé esset incertissimū. Itaque Græci hoc dicunt ἀμφισβητούμενον ἀνὶ ὁμολογού μένου τιθέναι[?]: sumere pro certo, quod dubium controuersúmque est:sumere pro argumento quod in disquisitione positum est: aliquid ad probandum assumere, quod ipsum est ambiguum : quoniam isto modo incertum per incertum concluditur.veluti : Utilis est philosophia:quia certam de rebus omnibus scientiâ affert. At cùm tam variæ sint philosophorum sectæ,illud ipsum ambiguū, an aliquid in Philosophia sit certi.Huius generis est illa quæ dicitur àCicerone Repetitio ab ultimo,Vtinam ne in nemore Pelio,&c.
units.tr: What is the fallacy of begging the question? "Geometers," says Cicero, "do not usually teach everything, but ask that certain things be granted to them, so that they may more easily explain what they want; the Greeks call these aitemata." And Aristotle seems wittily to have named this fallacy thus, as if the sophists, in the manner of geometers, demanded that a principle be granted to them as certain, when it was most uncertain. Hence the Greeks describe it as [to take as agreed what is disputed] (to amphisbētoumenon anti homologoumenou tithenai): to take as certain what is doubtful and disputed; to take as an argument what is itself under inquiry; to assume for proof something that is itself ambiguous, since in this way the uncertain is concluded through the uncertain. For example: "Philosophy is useful, because it brings certain knowledge of all things." But since the sects of philosophers are so various, it is itself ambiguous whether there is anything certain in philosophy. Of this kind is that which Cicero calls "repetition from the end": "Would that the Pelion grove had never...," and so on.

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplum. Extat præclarum apud Ciceronem lib.de Finib.4: Quarum(inquiūt)artiū summa crescere potest, earum etiam contrariarum summa poterit augeri. ad virtutis autem summam accedere nihil potestne vitia quidem igitur crescere poterunt, quæ sunt virtutum contraria. Vtrum igitur tandem, perspicuísne dubia aperiuntur, an dubiis perspicua tolluntur? Atqui hoc perspicuum est, vitia alia in aliis esse maiora: illud dubium, ad id quod summum bonum dicitis, ecquænam fieri possit accessio? Vos autem cùm perspicuis dubia debeatis illustrare, dubiis perspicua conanimi tollere.
units.tr: Here is another example, an excellent one, in Cicero's On Ends, book 4: "The sum of those arts, they say, can grow; the sum of their opposites can also increase. But can anything be added to the sum of virtue? Then can the vices, which are the opposites of the virtues, grow? Tell me, then, are doubtful things made clear by what is plain, or are plain things removed by what is doubtful? Yet it is plain that some vices are greater than others. That is doubtful: what addition can be made to what you call the highest good? But you, when you ought to clarify doubtful things by what is plain, try to remove what is plain by doubtful things."

units.la: Quomodo vitatur hæc captio? Cū id quod pro certo sumebatur dubium & controuersum esse ostenditur. Veluti: cùm apud Cicero-nem sic concluditur: Si diuinatio est, dii sunt. est autem diuinatio, ergo etiā dii sunt. Nā diuinationem esse, id vero incertum, atque ambiguum est. In eodem genere illud est: Piū [?] est orare pro mortuis. Nam ludas Machabæus magnam in illum vsum pecunià attribuit. Eodémque illud Pasquilli pertinet de Alexandro Pontifice.
units.tr: How is this fallacy avoided? When what was taken as certain is shown to be doubtful and disputed. For example, when in Cicero this argument is made: "If there is divination, there are gods. But there is divination; therefore there are gods too." For that divination exists is itself uncertain and ambiguous. Of the same kind is this: "It is a pious thing to pray for the dead. For Judas Maccabeus devoted a large sum of money to that purpose." To the same point belongs that lampoon about Pope Alexander:

units.la: Vendit Alexander cruces, altaria, Christum.
units.tr: Alexander sells crosses, altars, Christ.

units.la: Emerat ille prius, vendere iure potest.
units.tr: He had bought them before; by right he may sell them.

units.la: Nam si rectè non emerat, rectè non vendidit. Quod etiam ad magistratuum & dignitatum mercatores transferri potest,
units.tr: For if he did not buy them rightly, he did not sell them rightly. This can also be transferred to merchants of magistracies and dignities.

units.la: Quæ est captio ex falsa causa? Cùm id pro causa ponitur, quod causa non est. Veluti: Multi oratores abutuntur eloquentia ad perniciem reip.ergo eloquentia est perniciosa. Ebrietas est mala.ergo vinum malum. Multi religionis aut philosophiæ nomine abutuntur. Ergo aut religionis aut philosophiæ studio abstinendum est. Multi scripturæ sacræ lectione abutuntur. Ergo interdicenda est. Sic Cotta libro de Nat. deor.3. quia ratio pestifera fit multis, melius fuisse disputat, non dari hominibus rationem à diis, quàm tam magnificè & largè dari. Sic Anaxagoras, quia sciret aquam nigram esse, unde illa concreta esset: idcirco illam esse disputabat nigram.
units.tr: What is the fallacy from a false cause? It occurs when that is put forward as the cause which is not the cause. For example: "Many orators abuse eloquence to the ruin of the commonwealth; therefore eloquence is pernicious." "Drunkenness is bad; therefore wine is bad." "Many abuse the name of religion or of philosophy; therefore one must abstain from the study of either religion or philosophy." "Many abuse the reading of Holy Scripture; therefore it must be forbidden." So Cotta, in the third book of On the Nature of the Gods, argues that because reason has proved destructive to many, it would have been better for men not to be given reason by the gods than to be given it so magnificently and so generously. So Anaxagoras, because he knew that water was black, from which those things were formed, therefore maintained that it was black.

units.la: Quomodo vitatur hæc captio? Demonstratione verè causæ, qualis est in superioribus omnibus abusus rerum salutarium. Huic loco (inquit Cotta) sic soletis occurrere. non iccirco nō optimè nobis à diis esse prouisum, quòd multi eorum beneficio peruerse uterentur: etiam patrimoniis multos malè uti: nec ob eā causā beneficium à patribus nullum habere.
units.tr: How is this fallacy avoided? By demonstrating the true cause, as in all the above cases where the abuse of salutary things is at issue. To this argument, says Cotta, you are accustomed to reply thus: it does not follow that the gods have not provided for us most excellently because many misuse their benefits perversely; many also misuse their inheritances, yet we do not for that reason have no inheritance from our fathers.

units.la: Extat illud præclarum exemplum Tusc. 2.his verbis: Quod est (inquit auditor) maius argumentum nihil prodesse philosophiam, quàm quosdam perfectos philosophos turpitervivere? Nullum verò id quidem argumentum est: respondet Cicero. nam ut agri, nō omnes frugiferi sunt, qui coluntur: sic animi non omnes culti fructum ferunt. Causa igitur non in philosophia est, sed in animi vitio.
units.tr: There is that excellent example in the second book of the Tusculan Disputations, in these words: "What greater proof is there," says the listener, "that philosophy is of no benefit than that some who are complete philosophers live shamefully?" "But that is no proof at all," replies Cicero. "For just as not all cultivated fields are fruitful, so not all cultivated minds bear fruit. The cause therefore lies not in philosophy but in the vice of the mind."

units.la: Quæ est captio ex multiplici interrogatione? Cùm aut de uno plura, aut de pluribus unum, aut de pluribus plura interrogantur: ut quasi ad unam interrogationem respondeatur.De vno plura:veluti: Estne hic canis & pater & tuus?Nix éstne aqua, & alba? Item fi dimidium totius cuiusdam est album, alterum dimidium est nigrum : & quaeratur sitne illud album,an nigrum?De pluribus vnum : veluti, positis duobus, quorum alterum nigrum, alterum album fit, si quaeratur an ista sint alba, aut nigra? Plura de pluribus : veluti : Nónne sobrietas & ebrietas sunt bonum & malum?
units.tr: What is the fallacy arising from multiple questioning? It occurs when several things are asked about one, or one about several, or several about several, so that the answer seems to be given to one question. Of one, several: for example, "Is this dog both a father and yours?" "Is snow water, and white?" Likewise, if half of a certain whole is white and the other half black, and it is asked whether that whole is white or black? Of several, one: for example, given two things, one black and the other white, if it is asked whether these are white or black? Several about several: for example, "Are not sobriety and drunkenness good and bad?"

units.la: Cedo aliquod exemplum ad vsum vitæ accommodatum. Extant in lure ciuili huius generis immunera , vbi de stipulationibus agitur. nam aut plures ab vno, vel à pluribus,aut vnam rem , plurésve stipulari possunt: earúmque stipulationum variæ captiones sunt. singulas enim res singulis stipulationibus comprehendi oportet: qua de caufla ad vsum vitæ placuit, vt quoties plures res in stipulationem deducuntur,tot sint stipulationes quot res.veluti : Deditísne vos, populum Collatinum,vrbem, agros,aquam, terminos , delubra, vtensilia , diuina humanáque omnia in meam populíque R. ditionem?Dedimus.
units.tr: Let me give an example suited to the practice of life. Such cases of this kind are found in civil law, where stipulations are concerned. For several persons may stipulate from one, or one from several, or one or several things; and there are various fallacies in these stipulations. For each thing must be included in a separate stipulation. For this reason it has been established in practice that, whenever several things are brought into a stipulation, there shall be as many stipulations as there are things. For example: "Do you surrender to me and to the Roman people the Collatine people, the city, the fields, the water, the boundaries, the shrines, the utensils, and all things divine and human, under my power and that of the Roman people?" "We do."

units.la: Quomodo vitabitur hæc captio? Rerum coniunctarum separatione : vnde à Iurifconsultis constitutum est, vt qui plures res stipulanti certás se daturum spondet , de iis tantum obligetur. veluti, Spondes te Dauum & Stichum daturum? Stichum spondeo. Sic in illis superioribus : Canis hic pater est suorû catulorum,meus dominio. Nix est aqua respectu materiæ, alba respectu formæ. Hoc separatim album est. Illud separatim nigrum. Sobrietas separatim bonum est. Ebrietas separatim malum.
units.tr: How will this fallacy be avoided? By separating the things that are joined together. Hence the jurists have ruled that one who promises to give several specified things to a stipulator is bound only for those separately. For example: "Do you promise to give Davus and Stichus?" "I promise Stichus." So in the earlier examples: this dog is the father of its own puppies, and mine by ownership. Snow is water with respect to its matter, and white with respect to its form. This is white taken separately; that is black taken separately. Sobriety taken separately is good; drunkenness taken separately is bad.

units.la: Quæ est captio ex non animaduersis infidiis? Cùm id quod diuerso respectu est multiplex, pro simplici positum contradictionem efficit. Nã quod Ariftoteles τῷ τῇ ἐλέγχῳ ἀγ-ροίᾳ[?] appellat, ego captionem non animaduerfam interpretor: non, vt eruditi multi, reprehenfionis ignorantiam. Captió verò, fiue infidiæ, sunt huiusmodi: duo respectu vnius sunt duplum, respectu quatuor, sunt dimidiatum. Ergo duo est numerus duplus, & non duplus. Contradictio enim est cùm idem de eodem & dicitur & negatur. Item: Aethiops à dentibus est albus: à cute niger. Ergo idem & albus est, & non albus. Dauid à pietate est probus: ab adulterio improbus. Ergo idem est & probus, & non probus.
units.tr: What is the fallacy arising from unnoticed traps? It occurs when something that is manifold in different respects is taken as simple, and thereby produces a contradiction. For what Aristotle calls [ἀγνοία τοῦ ἐλέγχου], I interpret as an unnoticed fallacy, not, as many learned men do, ignorance of refutation. The traps, or snares, are of this sort: two is double one and half of four. Therefore two is a double number and not double. For a contradiction arises when the same thing is both affirmed and denied of the same thing. Likewise: the Ethiopian is white in his teeth and black in his skin. Therefore the same man is both white and not white. David is upright in piety and wicked in adultery. Therefore the same man is both upright and not upright.

units.la: Quænam huius appellationis caussa est? Quia ἐλέγχειν[?] (vt superiùs diximus) est capere, coarguere, & prehensum tenere. Itaque qui positas in interrogationibus insidias non animaduerterit, facilè fe in laqueum induit, veluti: qui ad illa rogata: Duo nónne sunt duplum vnius? Duo nónne sunt dimidium quatuor? simpliciter & incautè responderit: prius fe deprehensum sentiet, quàm sibi tendi laqueum animaduerterit. Protinus enim Sophista sic inferet: Duo sunt duplum. Duo sunt dimidium. Ergo duo est numerus duplus, & non duplus.
units.tr: What is the reason for this name? Because ἐλέγχειν (as we said above) means to seize, to convict, and to hold fast what has been caught. So whoever does not notice the traps laid in questions will easily entangle himself in the snare. For example, if someone, answering these questions, "Are not two the double of one? Are not two half of four?", responds simply and carelessly, he will perceive that he has been caught before he notices that a snare has been set for him. For at once the sophist will infer: "Two is double. Two is half. Therefore two is a double number and not double."

units.la: Quomodo vitabitur hæc captio? Tota hæc argutia, (inquit Aristoteles) τὸ μὴ διαφέρειν, τί ἐστι συλλογισμὸς, ἢ τί ἔλεγχος, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τῷ ἐλέγχειν τῷ λόγῳ γίνεται [?] quod sic interpretor: Nascitur ex eo, quod non discernitur ratiocinatio à captione: non prius constituitur quid sit syllogismus, & quid elenchus: sed ratio, id est distinctio multiplicis respectus, omittitur. Debuit enim ita respondéri: Duo cùm habent rationem ad unum, sunt duplum, at cùm habent rationem ad quatuor, sunt dimidiatum. Vitabitur ergo hæc argutia distinctione respectus.
units.tr: How will this fallacy be avoided? "This whole subtlety," says Aristotle, arises because one fails to distinguish what a syllogism is, or what a refutation is, but the argument comes about in the refuting [τὸ μὴ διαφέρειν, τί ἐστι συλλογισμὸς, ἢ τί ἔλεγχος, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τῷ ἐλέγχειν τῷ λόγῳ γίνεται]. This I interpret as follows: it arises from the fact that reasoning is not distinguished from the trap; the nature of a syllogism and of a refutation is not first settled; and the distinction of the manifold respect is omitted. For the answer ought to have been: "Two, since it has a relation to one, is double; but since it has a relation to four, it is half." This fallacy will therefore be avoided by distinguishing the respect.

units.la: Cedo aliud exemplum. Nónne qui oculos habet, videt? Nónne qui dormit, oculos habet, & tamen non videt? Ergo qui oculos habet, idem videt, simul non videt. Distinguenda fuit ratio respectuum. Qui oculos habet, si utatur, videt: si non utatur, non videt.
units.tr: Let me give another example. Does not he who has eyes see? Does not he who sleeps have eyes, and yet not see? Therefore he who has eyes both sees and at the same time does not see. The relations of respect ought to have been distinguished. He who has eyes sees if he uses them; if he does not use them, he does not see.

units.la: Quid? Nónne imprudentia hæc non animadverti laquei commune omnium captionum nomen est? Sané verò. Itaque multis verbis Aristoteles demonstrat ad hoc unum principium fallaces & captiosas conclusiones omnes revocari posse: qua de causa definitione Elenchi prodidit longam & copiosam: & (ut opinor) in libris nostris vitiatam: cuius hæc sententia est: Elenchus est contradictio quæ ambiguitate & nominum & rerum [?] concicitur, cùm quæ aut modo, aut tempore, diuersam rationem habent, quasi vnum & idem perpetuò essent, sumuntur. huius autem captionis vsus est in Soritis vel maximus:cùm is qui interrogatur,imprudens ab eo quod concesit, ad id quod non vult concedere, deducitur.
units.tr: What then? Is not this heedlessness, the failure to notice the snare, the common name of all fallacies? Certainly. Hence Aristotle, in many words, shows that all deceptive and captious conclusions can be traced back to this one principle; for which reason he gave a long and copious definition of elenchus, and (as I think) one corrupted in our books. Its sense is this: an elenchus is a contradiction produced by ambiguity of names and of things, when things that have a different relation in respect of manner or time are taken as if they were always one and the same. The use of this fallacy is greatest in the sorites, when the one questioned, unawares, is led from what he has conceded to what he does not wish to concede.

units.la: FINIS.
units.tr: END.
